q_other_signs.q: Along with the ABS light, which of these is true?
q_other_signs.help: The red BRAKE light usually says BRAKE or shows an exclamation mark inside a circle. It is different from the amber ABS light.

opts.a: The red BRAKE light is on too
The brake pedal feels soft or sinks, or the car takes longer to stop
Only the ABS light (maybe the traction control light too), and the brakes feel normal
I'm not sure

q_pedal.q: With the car parked and the engine running, press the brake pedal firmly. How does it feel?
q_pedal.help: A healthy pedal feels firm and stops well above the floor. Hold steady pressure for about 10 seconds and notice whether it slowly sinks.

opts.a: Firm and high, the same as always
Soft, spongy, or it slowly sinks
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When did the ABS light come on, or what happened just before?

opts.a: Right after the battery died, was jumped, or was replaced
After brake, tire, wheel bearing or suspension work, or after hitting a pothole or curb
It comes and goes, often over bumps or in wet, snowy or salty weather
It came on by itself and stays on
I'm not sure

result.title: ABS and red brake light together can mean a real brake problem
result.now: Don't drive it. Check the brake fluid level if you can, then have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the brake fluid is below the MIN line, there may be a leak. Don't just top it up and go.
If the parking brake was partly on and both lights go out when you fully release it, have the brakes and ABS checked soon. Driving with the parking brake on can overheat the rear brakes.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, keep clear of it and let it cool. Tell the tow driver or mechanic.
result.why: The red brake light warns about the main braking system, not just the anti-lock part. When both are on, the system that balances braking between front and rear wheels may also be off, or fluid may be low. The rear wheels can lock and the car can spin in a hard stop.

causes.name: Low brake fluid from a leak or very worn pads
causes.clues: Fluid below the MIN mark, wet spots near a wheel, or a pedal that feels lower than usual.
causes.against: A full reservoir makes this less likely.

causes.name: ABS module or wheel speed sensor fault that can also switch off front-to-rear brake balance
causes.clues: Fluid level is normal and the pedal feels normal.

causes.name: Parking brake not fully released
causes.clues: Both lights went out when you released the parking brake fully.
causes.against: If it's released and the red light stays on, it's not this.

you: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.
With the engine off and cool, check the brake fluid level against the MIN and MAX marks.
shop: ABS and brake system code scan
Brake pad and hydraulic system check

result.title: A soft or sinking pedal means the brakes themselves need attention
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic check the brakes where it is.
if: If you're on the road now, slow down gently, use a lower gear, and pull over somewhere safe.
If you see fluid near a wheel or under the car by the pedal area, mention it when you call for help.
result.why: With an ABS fault alone, normal braking is designed to keep working. A pedal that feels soft or sinks is different: it can point to air in the lines, a fluid leak or a master cylinder problem, and the brakes can get worse quickly.

causes.name: Brake fluid leak
causes.clues: Low fluid in the reservoir, or wet, oily spots near a wheel or on the inside of a tire.

causes.name: Master cylinder problem
causes.clues: The pedal slowly sinks under steady pressure, but no leak is visible.

causes.name: Air in the brake lines
causes.clues: Recent brake work, and the pedal feels spongy from the first press.

you: Check the brake fluid level with the engine off.
Look for wet spots under the car and on the inside of each wheel.
shop: Master cylinder test (a shop will usually rule out leaks and air before replacing it)
Brake bleed and ABS code scan

result.title: Low battery voltage can set the ABS light. It may clear on its own
result.now: Make sure the battery clamps are tight, then turn the car off for a minute and restart it. Many cars turn the light off after a short, gentle drive once they see the wheels moving normally. Until it goes out, anti-lock braking is off, so leave extra stopping distance.
if: If the red BRAKE light comes on, or the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, stop driving and get the brakes checked before going further.
If the light stays on after a few drives, get the ABS codes read. A stored fault may need clearing, or a sensor or its wiring may need testing.
If the battery keeps going low, have the battery and alternator tested. The ABS light can keep coming back until that's fixed.
result.why: The ABS system checks itself every time you start the car. If the voltage dips during a weak start or a jump, it can log a fault and switch off as a precaution. Once the power is steady, it often passes its self-check again.

causes.name: Fault logged during a low-voltage start
causes.clues: The light came on the same day the battery died or was jumped.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery connection
causes.clues: Other odd warning lights flicker, or the problem changes when you wiggle a battery cable.

causes.name: Weak battery or charging problem
causes.clues: Slow cranking or a battery light while driving.

you: Check that the battery clamps are tight and clean.
Restart the car and drive a short distance to see if the light goes out.

result.title: A wheel speed sensor or its wire may have been disturbed or damaged
result.now: Get the ABS codes read within the next few days. If the light came on right after a repair, go back to the shop that did the work.
if: If the brake pedal starts to feel different (soft, sinking or pulling to one side) or the red BRAKE light comes on, stop driving it and have it checked where it is.
Until it's fixed, leave extra stopping distance and brake earlier, especially in rain or snow.
If you smell burning or feel heat from one wheel after recent brake work, a brake may be dragging. Pull over safely, let it cool, and call the shop before driving further.
result.why: Each wheel has a sensor that tells the ABS how fast it is turning. Brake, hub or suspension work can leave a sensor unplugged or a wire stretched, and a hard pothole can crack the sensor or the toothed ring it reads.

causes.name: Wheel speed sensor unplugged or damaged
causes.clues: The light came on right after work on one wheel, or after a hard hit.

causes.name: Damaged sensor wiring
causes.clues: A wire near a wheel is hanging, rubbing or cut.

causes.name: Damaged or dirty tone ring
causes.clues: Recent axle or hub replacement, or heavy rust on the hub.

you: Look behind each wheel for an unplugged connector or a dangling wire. Don't touch hot brake parts.
shop: ABS code scan to find which wheel
Live wheel speed sensor data on a test drive
Sensor wiring and tone ring inspection

result.title: An on-and-off ABS light often points to a wheel speed sensor or its wiring
result.now: Book an ABS check when convenient, and ask the shop to read the stored codes even if the light is off that day.
if: If the red BRAKE light comes on, or the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, stop driving it and get the brakes checked before going further.
If the light starts staying on, or it's winter and the roads are slick, get it checked within a few days.
If the brake pedal pulses or grinds during gentle stops on dry roads, the ABS may be acting when it shouldn't. Get it checked soon.
result.why: When the light comes and goes, the ABS is usually getting a weak or broken signal from one wheel. Rust, road salt and flexing wires are common causes. While the light is on, anti-lock braking is off.

causes.name: Wheel speed sensor with a weak signal
causes.clues: The light comes on at low speed or over bumps, then goes away after a restart.

causes.name: Wiring chafed or corroded near a wheel
causes.clues: Worse in wet or salty weather.

causes.name: Rust buildup under the sensor
causes.clues: Older car in a snowy, salted area.

you: Note when the light comes on: speed, weather and road surface.
Check whether it goes out after you restart the car.
shop: ABS code scan, including stored codes
Wheel speed sensor data on a test drive
Wiring and connector inspection at each wheel

result.title: The anti-lock system has switched off and needs a code scan
result.now: Get the ABS codes read within the next few days. Until then, leave extra following distance and brake earlier.
if: If the red BRAKE light comes on, or the pedal feels soft or sinks, stop driving it.
If the brake fluid is below the MIN line, don't drive it until the brakes are inspected, even if you can't see a leak. Low fluid can mean a leak or badly worn pads.
If you're facing rain, snow or ice, get it checked before you drive in those conditions.
result.why: A steady ABS light means the system found a fault and turned anti-lock braking off. Normal braking is designed to keep working without it, but the wheels can lock and skid in a hard stop. An ABS code scan tells the shop which wheel or circuit to test first.

causes.name: Wheel speed sensor or its wiring
causes.clues: The most common cause. The traction or stability light is often on too.

causes.name: Low brake fluid
causes.clues: Fluid near or below the MIN line. Some cars turn on the ABS light for this.
causes.against: A full reservoir makes this less likely.

causes.name: ABS module, pump or fuse problem
causes.clues: The light came on with no other warning, and sensors test fine.
causes.against: Less common than a sensor.

you: Check the brake fluid level with the engine off.
Note whether the traction or stability light is on too.
shop: ABS code scan (a basic engine code reader may not see ABS codes)
ABS fuse, pump and module check

q_warning_signs.q: Are you noticing any of these along with the warm air?

opts.a: The engine temperature gauge is climbing or in the red
A burning smell, squeal or grinding noise when the A/C is on
None of these
I'm not sure

q_pattern.q: Which best describes what the A/C is doing?
q_pattern.help: First make sure the A/C button is on (its light is lit), the temperature is set to the coldest setting, and the fan is on.

opts.a: Air blows normally but never gets cold
Cold while driving, but warm when stopped or in traffic
Starts cold, then turns warm after a while
Cold on one side of the car, warm on the other
Very little air comes out, even on high
I'm not sure

q_compressor.q: With the engine running, turn the A/C on and off a few times while someone watches the front of the A/C compressor. What happens?
q_compressor.help: The compressor is driven by the engine belt. On most cars, the center of its pulley (the clutch) clicks and starts spinning when the A/C turns on. Some newer cars have a compressor with no clutch, so you won't see this.

opts.a: It clicks on and the center spins, but the air is still warm
No click, and the center of the pulley doesn't spin
It clicks on and off every few seconds
I can't see it / I'm not sure

result.title: The engine is overheating. Cooling the engine comes before the A/C
result.now: Turn off the A/C, pull over safely and switch off the engine. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see steam or coolant on the ground, don't open the radiator cap. Hot coolant can burn you.
If the gauge was only slightly above normal and dropped when you turned off the A/C, it's still a cooling problem. Don't use the car until it's checked.
If you see smoke (not just steam) or smell burning from under the hood, move everyone away from the car and call for help.
result.why: The A/C condenser and the engine radiator sit together and share the same cooling fans. When the fans or cooling system fail, the A/C turns warm and the engine overheats. Driving an overheating engine can cause serious engine damage.

causes.name: Cooling fan not working
causes.clues: It's worst at idle or in traffic, and you don't hear the fan running.

causes.name: Low coolant from a leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, or green, orange or pink fluid under the car.

causes.name: Broken or slipping belt
causes.clues: A squeal, or the battery light came on too.

you: Once the engine is fully cool, check the coolant level in the overflow tank.
shop: Cooling fan and fan relay test

result.title: The A/C compressor or its clutch may be failing
result.now: Turn the A/C off and leave it off. If the burning smell, squeal or grinding doesn't stop within a minute or so, pull over safely and switch off the engine. If it stops with the A/C off, have the system checked within a few days.
if: If the noise or burning smell continues with the A/C off, you see smoke, or the battery or temperature warning comes on, don't drive it. The belt may be close to failing, and on many cars it also drives the water pump and alternator. Have it towed.

If the noise stops completely with the A/C off, the compressor or its clutch is a likely source. A shop will usually check the clutch, bearing and belt before deciding whether the compressor itself needs replacing.
result.why: A compressor that's seizing drags on the belt, which can make it squeal, smell hot, or even break. On many cars that same belt runs the alternator, power steering and water pump, so a seized compressor can become a bigger problem.

causes.name: Compressor wearing or starting to seize
causes.clues: Grinding or rumbling that starts the moment the A/C turns on.

causes.name: Worn compressor clutch or bearing
causes.clues: Noise from the compressor pulley even with the A/C off.

causes.name: Worn or slipping belt
causes.clues: A squeal when the A/C kicks on, and a glazed or cracked belt.

you: Note whether the noise stops when you switch the A/C off.

result.title: Not enough air may be flowing over the condenser when you're stopped
result.now: If the temperature gauge climbs above normal, turn off the A/C, pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Otherwise watch the gauge and book an A/C and cooling fan check when convenient.
if: If the temperature gauge climbs above normal, turn off the A/C, pull over safely and switch off the engine. Don't drive on until the cooling system is checked, as an overheating engine can be badly damaged.
If you don't hear or see the cooling fan running at idle with the A/C on, get it checked within a day or two and avoid long idling until then.
If the condenser in front of the radiator is packed with leaves or bugs, gently rinsing it with a garden hose may help.
result.why: At speed, air rushes through the condenser and removes heat from the refrigerant. When you stop, the electric cooling fan has to do that job. If the fan is weak or the condenser is blocked, the A/C warms up at idle and cools again once you're moving.

causes.name: Cooling fan not running or weak
causes.clues: You don't hear the fan running at idle with the A/C on.

causes.name: Blocked or damaged condenser
causes.clues: Debris, bent fins or damage on the grille area at the front of the car.

causes.name: Refrigerant level slightly off
causes.clues: The A/C has been getting weaker over time.

you: With the engine idling and the A/C on, check whether the fan behind the grille is spinning.
Look through the grille for leaves or debris on the condenser.

result.title: Ice forming inside the system or a compressor shutting off are common causes
result.now: Turn the A/C off with the fan on high for a few minutes when it goes warm. If it then cools again, mention that to the shop. Book a check when convenient.
if: If you see water or ice dripping from under the dash, the evaporator drain may be blocked. Get it checked soon to avoid a wet carpet.

If the temperature gauge climbs above normal, turn off the A/C, pull over safely and switch off the engine. Don't drive on until the cooling system is checked, as an overheating engine can be badly damaged.
result.why: When the A/C starts cold and then fades, the part inside the dash that chills the air (the evaporator) may be icing over and blocking airflow, or the compressor may be shutting off as it gets hot. Both are common and fixable.

causes.name: Evaporator icing up
causes.clues: Airflow from the vents gets weaker as the air gets warmer.

causes.name: Compressor clutch gap too wide or overheating
causes.clues: It works fine on short trips but fades on long, hot drives.

causes.name: Low or incorrect refrigerant charge
causes.clues: Cooling has been getting weaker over months.

you: Note how long it takes to turn warm, and whether airflow drops too.

result.title: A blend door inside the dash may be stuck
result.now: Try changing the temperature from full hot to full cold on each side and listen for clicking behind the dash. Book a check when convenient.
if: If the temperature resets itself or the climate controls act strangely, the control module may need to be checked.
If both sides are slightly cool but neither is cold, low refrigerant is more likely.
result.why: Cars with separate driver and passenger temperatures use small doors in the dash to mix hot and cold air. If one door's motor fails, that side stays stuck on warm while the other side cools normally.

causes.name: Blend door motor (actuator) not working
causes.clues: Repeated clicking or tapping behind the dash.

causes.name: Climate control needs recalibrating
causes.clues: It started after a battery was disconnected or replaced.

causes.name: Low refrigerant
causes.clues: On some cars, low refrigerant makes one side warm first.
causes.against: If one side is very cold, refrigerant is probably fine.

you: Listen for clicking behind the dash when you change the temperature.
Check your owner's manual for a climate control reset procedure.

result.title: A clogged cabin air filter or a blower problem is a common cause
result.now: Check the cabin air filter, usually behind the glove box, and replace it if it's dirty.
if: If you smell burning or hot plastic from the vents or see smoke, turn the fan off and pull over safely. Don't use the fan again until the wiring is checked.
If the fan only works on high, the blower resistor or its control is a common cause. Book a check.
If no air comes out at all on any speed, check the fuse for the blower, then book a check.
result.why: The A/C may be cooling fine, but if little air comes out, the car still feels warm. A dirty cabin filter is the most common cause and is easy to change on most cars.

causes.name: Clogged cabin air filter
causes.clues: Airflow has slowly gotten weaker, or there's a musty smell.

causes.name: Failing blower motor or resistor
causes.clues: Some fan speeds don't work, or the fan makes noise.

causes.name: Iced evaporator
causes.clues: Airflow gets weaker after the A/C has been on a while.

you: Inspect the cabin air filter.
Try every fan speed.

result.title: The compressor runs, but the system isn't cooling. Low refrigerant or a stuck blend door are common causes
result.now: Set the temperature to full cold and recirculate, then book an A/C check that includes a pressure test and leak check.
if: If the air is actually hot, like the heater, a blend door stuck on heat is more likely than a refrigerant problem.
If you hear grinding when it runs, turn off the A/C and get it checked within a few days.

If the temperature gauge climbs above normal, turn off the A/C, pull over safely and switch off the engine. Don't drive on until the cooling system is checked, as an overheating engine can be badly damaged.
result.why: A running compressor means the electrical side is working. Warm air then usually means there isn't enough refrigerant to carry heat away, or something inside the dash is mixing in hot air.

causes.name: Low refrigerant from a slow leak
causes.clues: The A/C has been getting weaker for weeks or months.

causes.name: Blend door stuck on heat
causes.clues: The air feels hot, not just cool-ish, and the temperature knob changes nothing.

causes.name: Worn compressor or expansion valve problem
causes.clues: Refrigerant level checks out but it still doesn't cool.

you: Turn the temperature from cold to hot and feel whether the air changes.
shop: Leak detection with dye or an electronic detector

result.title: The compressor isn't turning on. Low refrigerant, a fuse or the clutch are common causes
result.now: Check the A/C fuse and relay in the fuse box (your owner's manual shows which), then book an A/C check.
if: If the fuse is blown, replace it once with the same rating. If it blows again, stop and have the wiring checked.

If the engine temperature gauge is also high, the car may be switching the A/C off to protect the engine. Pull over safely, switch off the engine, and don't drive on until the cooling system is checked.
result.why: The A/C has a safety switch that won't let the compressor run if refrigerant pressure is too low. A blown fuse, failed relay or worn compressor clutch can also stop it. Without the compressor running, there's no cooling at all.

causes.name: Refrigerant too low for the compressor to run
causes.clues: The A/C got weaker over time before it stopped completely.

causes.name: Blown A/C fuse or failed relay
causes.clues: It stopped suddenly with no warning.

causes.name: Compressor clutch or pressure switch problem
causes.clues: Tapping the compressor or cycling the A/C sometimes makes it work.

you: Check the A/C fuse and relay in the fuse box.
shop: Compressor clutch power and gap check

result.title: Low refrigerant from a leak is a common cause
result.now: Book an A/C check that includes finding the leak, not just a refill.
if: If you add refrigerant from a can yourself, it may cool for a while, but overfilling can make cooling worse and damage the compressor. Fixing the leak is the real repair.
If you hear grinding when the compressor runs, turn the A/C off and get it checked within a few days.
result.why: When the compressor clicks on and off every few seconds, the system is often sensing pressure that's too low. Refrigerant doesn't get used up, so if it's low, it has usually leaked out somewhere. A pressure test confirms it before anything is added.

causes.name: Slow leak at a hose, seal or fitting
causes.clues: Cooling has faded over weeks or months, or oily residue on A/C lines.

causes.name: Leaking condenser
causes.clues: Damage from road debris on the front of the car.

causes.name: Faulty pressure switch
causes.clues: Pressures test normal but the compressor still cycles quickly.

you: Look for oily residue on the A/C lines and at the front of the condenser.
shop: Leak detection with dye or an electronic detector
Evacuate and recharge to the correct amount after repair

result.title: An A/C check is the best next step
result.now: Make sure the A/C button is on and the temperature is set to full cold, then book an A/C check when convenient.
if: If the temperature gauge climbs above normal, turn off the A/C, pull over safely and switch off the engine. Don't drive on until the cooling system is checked, as an overheating engine can be badly damaged.
If you hear grinding or smell burning with the A/C on, turn it off. If it doesn't stop with the A/C off, or you see smoke, pull over and switch off the engine.
result.why: Most warm-A/C cases come down to low refrigerant, a compressor that isn't running, a fan problem or a stuck door in the dash, and a technician can test for each of them. Because the A/C shares fans and a belt with the engine, keep an eye on the temperature gauge and any burning smell until it's checked.

causes.name: Low refrigerant
causes.clues: Cooling faded over time.

causes.name: Compressor not running
causes.clues: It stopped suddenly.

causes.name: Cooling fan or blend door problem
causes.clues: It's warm only at idle, or only on one side.

you: Note whether it's warm all the time or only at idle.
Check the cabin air filter.

q_what.help: SRS stands for Supplemental Restraint System, which means the airbags and seat belt tensioners. The separate PASSENGER AIRBAG OFF light, usually near the center of the dash or by the mirror, is a different indicator.

opts.a: The airbag or SRS light stays on or flashes after the car starts
A PASSENGER AIRBAG OFF (or ON/OFF) indicator is lit
An airbag went off in a crash
It came on after a minor bump or collision, and no airbags went off
I'm not sure

q_trigger.q: Did anything happen around the time the light came on?

opts.a: The horn, steering wheel buttons or cruise control stopped working too
A front seat was moved, removed or cleaned, or something got pushed under a seat
The battery died, was jumped, or was replaced
A seat belt buckle feels loose, or the seat belt reminder acts oddly
Nothing obvious, or I'm not sure

result.title: The passenger airbag indicator is often normal. Check who's in the seat
result.now: Check whether the light matches who's sitting there. It should show OFF when the seat is empty or holds a small child or child seat, and ON (or go out) when an adult sits normally.
if: If an adult is sitting upright and it still says OFF, have the passenger seat sensor checked within a few days. The passenger airbag may not deploy for them until it's sorted out.
If the main airbag or SRS light is also on, have the airbag system checked soon.
result.why: Many cars have a weight or occupant sensor in the passenger seat that turns that airbag off for an empty seat or a small passenger. The OFF light is usually telling you what it decided, which isn't necessarily a fault.

causes.name: Normal operation
causes.clues: The seat is empty, holds a bag, or has a child or child seat.
causes.against: If an adult sits there and it shows OFF, it's not normal.

causes.name: Passenger sitting out of position
causes.clues: The passenger is leaning, slouching, or has feet on the dash.

causes.name: Faulty passenger seat sensor
causes.clues: It says OFF for an adult sitting normally, or it changes over bumps.

you: Remove any items from the passenger seat and seat back pocket, then have an adult sit upright and watch the indicator.
Check the owner's manual for how the indicator should behave in your car.

result.title: After an airbag deploys, the system must be repaired before driving
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed to a collision repair shop or dealer.
if: If anyone was hurt, get medical care first. Airbag injuries and crash injuries aren't always obvious right away.
If you smell fuel, see smoke, or see fluid leaking after the crash, move everyone away from the car and call for help.
result.why: A deployed airbag can't protect you again, and the crash sensors and control module usually need replacing too. The crash itself may also have damaged steering, suspension, or lights.

causes.name: Deployed airbags and seat belt tensioners
causes.clues: Visible airbags, or seat belts that locked and won't retract.

causes.name: Crash data stored in the airbag module
causes.clues: The light stays on even after the airbags are replaced.

you: Photograph the damage and the dashboard for your insurer.
shop: Replacement of deployed airbags, tensioners and crash sensors

result.title: A crash sensor or its wiring may have been damaged in the bump
result.now: Have the airbag system scanned within the next few days, ideally by the shop repairing the collision damage.
if: If the steering, lights or brakes don't work right after the bump, a red warning light is on, or you smell fuel or see fluid leaking, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If you're filing an insurance claim, ask for the airbag scan to be part of the repair estimate.
result.why: Crash sensors sit near the front bumper and in the doors or pillars. Even a minor impact can damage a sensor or its wiring, and the system then switches itself off and turns the light on.

causes.name: Damaged front or side crash sensor
causes.clues: The bump was near the front corner or a door.

causes.name: Damaged or disconnected wiring
causes.clues: Bodywork or bumper parts were pushed in or removed.

causes.name: Stored crash event in the airbag module
causes.clues: The impact was hard enough to register, even without deployment.

you: Note exactly where the car was hit.

result.title: The steering wheel clockspring is a likely place to start
result.now: Have the airbag system checked within the next few days. Until then, your driver's airbag may not work, and the horn may not either.
if: If the horn doesn't work, get it fixed sooner. You can't warn other drivers.
If cruise control or other wheel buttons stop working, avoid relying on them until it's repaired.
result.why: The clockspring is a coiled ribbon cable behind the steering wheel. It keeps the driver's airbag, horn and wheel buttons connected while you turn the wheel. When it wears or breaks, all of these can stop working at once.

causes.name: Worn or broken clockspring
causes.clues: The horn or wheel buttons stopped working at the same time, or work only in some steering positions.

causes.name: Clockspring damaged during steering work
causes.clues: The steering wheel, column or an alignment was worked on recently.

causes.name: Driver airbag connector fault
causes.clues: Only the airbag light is on, and the horn and buttons work.

you: Test the horn and steering wheel buttons with the wheel straight and turned each way.

result.title: A connector under a front seat may have been disturbed
result.now: Remove any loose items from under the front seats, then have the airbag codes read and the connector checked within a few days. Don't unplug or reseat the connector yourself.
if: If the light came on right after someone removed or reinstalled the seats, go back to them. The connector may not be fully plugged in.
If the light comes and goes when you slide the seat, mention that to the shop. It can point to a worn wire.
result.why: Side airbags and seat belt tensioners are wired through connectors under the front seats. Sliding the seat, items jammed underneath, or seat removal can loosen a connector or strain a wire, and the system turns the light on.

causes.name: Loose seat airbag or tensioner connector
causes.clues: The light came on after seat movement, cleaning or removal.

causes.name: Worn wiring under the seat
causes.clues: The light flickers when the seat moves.

causes.name: Faulty seat sensor
causes.clues: Only the passenger side is affected.

you: Look under the front seats for objects pressing on wires. Don't touch the connectors.
Check for open airbag recalls with your VIN.

result.title: Low battery voltage can leave a stored airbag fault
result.now: Turn the car off for a minute, then restart it and watch whether the light goes out after a few seconds.
if: If the light stays on after a few restarts, have the airbag codes read and cleared. Many cars keep the fault stored until a scan tool clears it.
If the battery keeps going low, have the battery and charging system tested.
result.why: The airbag system checks itself at every start. A weak battery or a jump start can make that check fail and log a fault. On some cars it clears itself, on others it stays until a technician clears it.

causes.name: Fault logged during a low-voltage start
causes.clues: The light came on the same day the battery died or was jumped.

causes.name: Loose battery connection
causes.clues: Other warning lights flicker too.

causes.name: A separate airbag fault that showed up at the same time
causes.clues: The light stays on after the code is cleared.

you: Check that the battery clamps are tight.
Restart the car a few times and watch the light.
shop: Airbag system code scan and clear

result.title: A seat belt buckle or tensioner fault may be the cause
result.now: Have the airbag and seat belt system checked within a few days. Keep wearing the belt and make sure it latches firmly every time.
if: If a belt won't latch or won't hold when you tug it, don't use that seat until it's repaired.
If a coin, crumb or other object is stuck in the buckle, mention it to the shop rather than prying it out with metal tools.
result.why: Seat belt buckles have switches that tell the airbag system whether you're belted, and the belts have tensioners that tighten in a crash. A faulty buckle switch or tensioner circuit turns the airbag light on.

causes.name: Buckle switch problem
causes.clues: The seat belt reminder chimes even when buckled, or doesn't chime when unbuckled.

causes.name: Tensioner circuit fault
causes.clues: The light came on after the seat or trim was removed.

causes.name: Debris in the buckle
causes.clues: The buckle feels gritty or sticks.

you: Buckle and unbuckle each front belt and watch the seat belt reminder light.

result.title: The airbag system has a fault and may not deploy in a crash
result.now: Have the airbag system scanned within the next few days. Also check for open airbag recalls using your VIN.
if: If there's an open airbag recall on your car, contact a dealer right away and follow the recall instructions.
If the horn or steering wheel buttons stop working too, mention it. It points to the clockspring.
result.why: When the airbag light stays on, the system may have disabled some or all airbags because it can't confirm they'll work properly. The car may drive the same, but you may not have full crash protection. An airbag scan tool reads the stored codes, which tell the shop which circuit to test first.

causes.name: Steering wheel clockspring
causes.clues: Horn or wheel buttons acting up.

causes.name: Seat connector, buckle or occupant sensor
causes.clues: Seats were moved recently, or the seat belt reminder acts oddly.

causes.name: Crash sensor or airbag module fault
causes.clues: A past collision, or water got into the car.

you: Ask a dealer for your brand whether an airbag recall is open on your VIN.
Note whether the horn and steering wheel buttons work.
shop: Airbag (SRS) code scan (a basic engine code reader can't read these)

q_when.q: When does the battery go dead?
q_when.help: The battery warning light is usually red and shaped like a small battery.

opts.a: While driving or soon after, or the battery light came on while driving
After sitting overnight or for a day or two
Only after sitting for a week or more
Mostly on cold mornings
I'm not sure

q_age.help: Look for a date sticker or stamped code on top or on the side of the battery. Most car batteries last about 3 to 5 years, less in hot climates.

opts.a: Older than about 4 years
Newer than that
I'm not sure
A light stays on after I lock the car (trunk, glove box, dome or under the hood)
Something was added recently: a dash cam, remote starter, stereo, alarm or tracker
I mostly drive short trips, under about 15 minutes
There's crusty buildup on the battery terminals, or a cable is loose
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: The alternator may not be recharging the battery
result.now: Get the charging system tested within the next day or two. Most auto parts stores can test it in the parking lot. Avoid long trips and night driving until then.
if: If the battery light is on and the headlights, wipers or gauges start acting up, don't keep driving. The car is running on what's left in the battery and may shut off. Pull over somewhere safe and call for a tow.
If the temperature gauge rises or the steering suddenly gets heavy, the drive belt may have come off. Pull over, switch off the engine and have it towed.
If you smell burning or hear a loud squeal from the engine, the drive belt may have slipped or broken. Stop and have it towed.
result.why: While the engine runs, the alternator powers the car and recharges the battery. If it stops charging, the car slowly drains the battery until it dies, often while you're driving. A new battery alone won't fix that and will go flat too, which is why a charging test comes first.

causes.name: Alternator not charging
causes.clues: The battery light flickers or stays on, the headlights dim at idle, or there's a whining noise.

causes.name: Worn or broken drive belt
causes.clues: Squealing, a burning rubber smell, or the steering suddenly feels heavy.
causes.against: If the belt is visibly in place and quiet, it's less likely.

causes.name: Loose or corroded charging cable
causes.clues: The problem comes and goes, or buildup on the battery terminals.

you: Watch whether the battery light comes on while driving.
Look for the drive belt at the front of the engine with the engine off.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the charging cables

result.title: Batteries slowly drain when a car sits for weeks
result.now: First look at the battery: if it's swollen, cracked, leaking, very hot or smells like rotten eggs, don't jump-start or charge it. Keep sparks away and have it checked. If it looks normal, jump or charge the battery, then drive at least 30 minutes. If the car often sits for a week or more, use a battery maintainer (a small plug-in charger) while it's parked.
if: If it dies after only a few days, something may be draining it. Have a parasitic draw test done.
If the battery is more than 4 years old, have it tested. An older battery can't sit as long.
result.why: Modern cars use a small amount of power even when off, to keep memory, alarms and keyless entry ready. Over a few weeks, that can flatten a healthy battery, especially an older one or in cold weather.

causes.name: Normal standby drain
causes.clues: It only happens after long periods parked.
causes.against: If it dies after a night or two, the drain is too high to be normal.

causes.name: Aging battery
causes.clues: The battery is more than 4 years old, or the car has been cranking slowly.

causes.name: Short trips not recharging it
causes.clues: The car is only driven a few minutes at a time when it is used.

you: Check the age of the battery.
Use a battery maintainer during long stretches parked.

result.title: The battery may be worn out and unable to hold a charge
result.now: Have the battery and charging system tested. Most auto parts stores do this free. If the battery fails, replace it with one that matches your car's specs.
if: If the battery tests good, ask for a charging test and a parasitic draw test so you're not left guessing.
If a new battery also goes flat within weeks, that points to the charging system or a drain rather than the battery.
result.why: As batteries age, they lose the ability to store power. One that's several years old may start the car fine in warm weather, then die after a cold night or a day of sitting.

causes.name: Worn-out battery
causes.clues: It's more than 4 years old, it's worse on cold mornings, and the crank has been slow.

causes.name: Alternator not fully charging
causes.clues: The battery light flickers, or the lights dim at idle.

causes.name: Something draining it while parked
causes.clues: It goes flat after a single night.

you: Check the date on the battery.
Notice whether it cranks slowly before it dies completely.

result.title: Start with a battery and charging test
result.now: Have the battery and charging system tested. Most auto parts stores do this free, and it tells you whether the battery, the alternator or something else is to blame.
if: If the battery fails the test, replace it.
If both test good but it keeps dying, ask a shop for a parasitic draw test.
result.why: The three usual suspects are an old battery, an alternator that isn't charging and a drain while parked. A quick test rules the first two in or out, so you don't replace parts on a guess.

causes.name: Worn-out battery
causes.clues: It's more than 4 years old, or the car cranks slowly.

causes.name: Alternator not charging
causes.clues: The battery light has come on while driving.

causes.name: Something draining it while parked
causes.clues: It dies after a night or two of sitting.

you: Look for a date on the battery.
Note how long the car sat before it went dead.

result.title: A light that stays on may be draining the battery
result.now: Find the light that stays on and make sure its door, lid or switch is closing it off. Then charge the battery or drive for at least 30 minutes.
if: If the light won't turn off even when the door or lid is closed, its switch or wiring may be at fault. Removing that bulb stops the drain until a shop can check the switch.
If you can't find anything left on, have a shop do a parasitic draw test.
result.why: A small bulb left on can flatten a battery overnight. Trunk, glove box and under-hood lights are easy to miss because you can't see them with everything closed.

causes.name: Trunk, glove box or hood light staying on
causes.clues: A faint glow at night, or the light stays on when you press its switch by hand.

causes.name: Door switch not reading closed
causes.clues: A door-open warning, or the dome light doesn't turn off.

causes.name: Interior light switch left on
causes.clues: Someone used the map or dome light recently.

you: Check the car in the dark for any glow from the trunk, glove box or cabin.
Press each light's switch by hand and see if the light goes out.
shop: Door, trunk and hood switch check

result.title: An added accessory may be draining the battery
result.now: Unplug or switch off the new accessory for a few nights. If the battery stops dying, have it rewired properly.
if: If it still dies with the accessory unplugged, have a parasitic draw test done.
If you notice a hot wire, a burning smell or smoke near the accessory, don't use the car. If it's safe to do so, disconnect the accessory, and have the wiring checked before driving.
result.why: Dash cams with parking mode, remote starters, alarms and stereos are common causes of drain when they're wired to stay on all the time. The timing of the problem is a strong clue.

causes.name: Accessory wired to constant power
causes.clues: The problem started soon after it was installed.

causes.name: Faulty installation
causes.clues: Spliced wires, loose connections, or the accessory acts up.

causes.name: Unrelated drain or an aging battery
causes.clues: Unplugging the accessory changes nothing.

you: Unplug the accessory and see if the battery still dies.
Check its settings for a parking or standby mode.

result.title: Short trips may not give the battery time to recharge
result.now: Take a 30-minute drive at least once a week, or use a battery maintainer when the car is parked at home.
if: If it still dies with longer drives, have the battery and alternator tested.
If the battery is more than 4 years old, test it now. Short trips are hard on older batteries.
result.why: Starting the engine uses a big burst of power, and the alternator needs time to put it back. A string of short trips, especially with lights, heat and wipers on, can slowly leave the battery too low to start the car.

causes.name: Not enough driving to recharge
causes.clues: Mostly short trips, cold weather, and lots of electrical use.

causes.name: Aging battery
causes.clues: It's several years old.

causes.name: Weak alternator
causes.clues: The lights dim at idle.

you: Track whether longer drives stop the problem.
Check the age of the battery.

result.title: A poor battery connection may be stopping it from charging
result.now: With the engine off, clean the battery terminals with a battery terminal brush and a baking soda and water mix, then tighten the clamps so they don't move by hand.
if: If the buildup keeps coming back quickly, have the battery checked for a leak.
If it still dies after cleaning, have the battery and alternator tested.
result.why: Corrosion and loose clamps add resistance. The battery may not charge fully while driving and may not deliver full power when you start the car, so it looks like a dead battery.

causes.name: Corroded terminals
causes.clues: White, green or blue crusty buildup on the posts or clamps.

causes.name: Loose clamp
causes.clues: A clamp you can twist by hand.

causes.name: Damaged cable
causes.clues: Swelling or corrosion under the cable's insulation near the clamp.

you: Wear gloves and eye protection when cleaning terminals.
Check that each clamp is tight.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the battery cables

result.title: Something may be draining the battery while the car is off
result.now: Have the battery tested first. If it's healthy, book a parasitic draw test so a shop can find what's staying on.
if: If the battery fails the test, replace it, then watch whether the problem comes back.
If you smell burning, a wire feels hot, or you see smoke, step away from the car and call for help if it gets worse. Don't use the car until the wiring is checked.
result.why: When a fairly new battery dies after a night or two, something is often staying powered after the car shuts down. A shop measures the drain with the car off and checks circuits one at a time to find it.

causes.name: A module or relay that may not be shutting off
causes.clues: Odd behavior like a fan, radio or light running after the car is off.

causes.name: Hidden light staying on
causes.clues: Trunk, glove box or hood light.

causes.name: Weak battery or charging system
causes.clues: Slow cranking, or the battery light on while driving.

you: Listen for anything still running a few minutes after you lock the car.
Check for lights that stay on.

q_symptoms.q: Besides the battery light, is anything else happening?

opts.a: The temperature gauge is rising, the steering got heavy, or I heard a squeal or slap from the engine
Lights are dimming, the gauges or radio act up, or the engine stumbles
I smell burning or see smoke
Nothing else. The car runs normally
I'm not sure

q_behavior.q: How does the battery light behave?

opts.a: It stays on the whole time I'm driving
It flickers, or comes on at idle and goes out when I press the gas
It came on after a jump start, a new battery or other battery work
My car is a hybrid or electric car
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine's drive belt may have broken or slipped off
result.now: Pull over where it's safe and turn off the engine. Once it's off, look at the front of the engine for a missing or shredded belt, and have the car towed.
if: If the temperature gauge is high, don't open the radiator cap until the engine has fully cooled.
If the belt is in place but the gauge is still rising, the cooling system may also have a problem. Still have it towed.
result.why: On many engines, one belt (the serpentine belt) spins the alternator, the water pump and the power steering pump. If it breaks, the battery stops charging, the steering can get heavy, and the engine can overheat within minutes.

causes.name: Broken or worn-out drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal or loud slap followed by the light, or a belt that looked cracked.

causes.name: Failed belt tensioner or pulley
causes.clues: Squealing or chirping in the weeks before, or the belt is in place but loose.

causes.name: Seized alternator or water pump
causes.clues: A grinding noise before the belt came off.

you: With the engine off, look for a missing, loose or shredded belt at the front of the engine.
Note what the temperature gauge showed.
shop: Cooling system check if it overheated

result.title: The battery is running out. The car may stall soon
result.now: Get off the road at the first safe spot, turn off the engine, and have the car towed or call roadside assistance.
if: If you're on a highway, turn off the A/C, heater fan, radio and heated seats to save power while you get to the shoulder.
If the engine stalls, turn on your hazard lights and steer firmly to the side. Steering and braking will feel heavier.
result.why: Dimming lights and electrical glitches mean the alternator isn't charging and the battery is nearly empty. Once the voltage drops too far, the engine can stall without warning and the power steering may stop working.

causes.name: Failed alternator
causes.clues: The light has been on for a while, or there was a whining or grinding noise.

causes.name: Broken drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal or slap before the light came on.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery or alternator cable
causes.clues: Recent battery work, or crusty buildup on the terminals.

you: Once the engine is off, check that the belt is in place.
Check that the battery clamps are tight.

result.title: An electrical part or belt may be overheating
result.now: Pull over, turn off the engine, get out, and step away from the car. Call for help if you see smoke or flames.
if: If the smell fades and there's no smoke, still don't restart it. Have it towed.
If you see smoke or flames, stay well back and call 911.
result.why: A burning smell with the battery light can mean the alternator is failing internally and overheating, a slipping belt is rubbing on a seized pulley, or a wire is shorting. These can cause a fire.

causes.name: Alternator overheating
causes.clues: A hot electrical smell from the front of the engine.

causes.name: Belt slipping on a seized pulley
causes.clues: A burning rubber smell and a squeal.

causes.name: Shorted battery or charging wire
causes.clues: A melted-plastic smell, or a cable that's hot to the touch.

result.title: The alternator may have stopped charging
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe and turn the engine off. The car is running on battery power alone and can stall without warning, and the steering and brakes can get heavier. Arrange a tow or a mobile mechanic rather than finishing your trip. If you must move to a safer spot first, turn off the A/C, fan, radio and heated seats and go only as far as you need.
if: If the lights dim, the gauges act up or the engine stumbles, get off the road right away, wherever is safe.
If the temperature gauge rises or the steering suddenly gets heavy, the drive belt may have come off. Pull over, switch off the engine and have it towed.
If the car is at home, a battery and alternator test before your next trip can save you from being stranded.
result.why: With the light on steadily, the car is running on stored battery power only. How long that lasts depends on the battery and how much you have switched on. The car may also not restart once you turn it off.

causes.name: Alternator wearing out
causes.clues: A whining noise that rises with engine speed, or headlights that dim at idle.

causes.name: Loose or slipping drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal on startup or in wet weather.

causes.name: Loose or corroded charging cable or fuse
causes.clues: Recent battery work, or corrosion on the terminals.

you: Check that the belt is in place and not cracked or shiny.
Check that the battery clamps are tight and clean.

result.title: The charging system may be weak or have a loose connection
result.now: Have the battery and charging system tested within a few days. Keep electrical loads light until then.
if: If the light starts staying on, or the lights dim while driving, treat it as urgent and keep trips as short as possible.
If the temperature gauge rises or the steering suddenly gets heavy, the drive belt may have come off. Pull over, switch off the engine and have it towed.
If you hear a squeal when the light flickers, the belt may be slipping.
result.why: A light that flickers or comes on only at idle often means the charging output is borderline. The alternator may be wearing out, the belt may be slipping, or a connection may be loose. These usually get worse over time.

causes.name: Alternator starting to fail
causes.clues: Lights dim at idle and brighten when you rev.

causes.name: Slipping or worn belt
causes.clues: A squeal, especially on cold or wet mornings.

causes.name: Loose battery clamp or ground strap
causes.clues: The light flickers over bumps.

you: Check that the battery clamps are tight.
Listen for a belt squeal when the light flickers.
shop: Alternator output test at idle and higher speed
Voltage-drop test on cables and ground straps

result.title: A loose connection or a deeply drained battery are common causes
result.now: With the engine off, check that both battery clamps are tight and clean, and that no cable was knocked loose during the jump or battery swap.
if: If the clamps were loose and the light goes out after tightening, that was probably the cause. Have the charging system tested if the light comes back.
If the light stays on with tight clamps, have the battery and alternator tested soon. A dead battery can hide an alternator that's failing.
If the temperature gauge rises or the steering suddenly gets heavy, the drive belt may have come off. Pull over, switch off the engine and have it towed.
result.why: Battery work often leaves a clamp slightly loose. A badly drained battery can also strain the charging system after a jump. Sometimes the battery went dead in the first place because the alternator was already failing.

causes.name: Loose battery clamp
causes.clues: A clamp you can twist by hand.

causes.name: Alternator already failing
causes.clues: The battery died for no obvious reason, like lights being left on.

causes.name: Blown charging fuse or damaged cable
causes.clues: Jumper cables were connected backward, even briefly.

you: Tighten and clean the battery clamps.
Check whether the light goes out after a restart.

result.title: The system that charges the small 12-volt battery may have a fault
result.now: Have the car checked within a few days, ideally by a shop that works on hybrids or EVs. Keep trips short and electrical loads light until then.
if: If other warning lights or a "check hybrid system" message appear, or the car loses power, pull over and call for help.
If the car won't power on at all, it may need a jump of the 12-volt battery. Check the owner's manual for the jump points.
result.why: Hybrids and electric cars don't use a regular alternator. A converter charges the small 12-volt battery from the big drive battery. If it fails, the 12-volt battery runs down, and the car can shut off or refuse to start.

causes.name: Weak or failing 12-volt battery
causes.clues: The car has been slow to power on, or the 12-volt battery is several years old.

causes.name: DC-to-DC converter not charging
causes.clues: A new 12-volt battery doesn't make the light go away.

causes.name: Loose 12-volt connection
causes.clues: Recent work near the 12-volt battery.

you: Note any other warning lights or messages.
Check the owner's manual for where the 12-volt battery is.

result.title: The charging system may not be keeping the battery charged
result.now: Keep driving to a minimum and have the battery and alternator tested within a day or two. Many auto parts stores test them free.
if: If the lights dim, the car stumbles, the steering gets heavy or the temperature gauge rises, get off the road and turn the engine off.
If the car won't restart after you turn it off, have it towed rather than relying on repeated jump starts.
result.why: The battery light means the car isn't getting the charge it needs. The most common causes are a failing alternator, a belt problem, or a loose cable, and all three can leave you stranded once the battery runs down.

causes.name: Failing alternator
causes.clues: The light stays on, or lights dim at idle.

causes.name: Belt problem
causes.clues: Squealing, or the belt looks cracked or loose.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery cable
causes.clues: Buildup on the terminals, or recent battery work.

you: Check that the battery clamps are tight.
With the engine off, look at the belt.

q_signs.help: A flashing check engine light is different from one that stays on steady. Flashing means a misfire that's bad enough to damage parts.

opts.a: The check engine light is flashing, or the engine shakes or stumbles badly
I smell raw fuel strongly, or see fuel dripping
It's a diesel, and there's just a puff when I accelerate hard
Steady black smoke, often with worse fuel mileage
I'm not sure
The check engine light is on and stays on (not flashing)
The engine runs rough, sputters or hesitates
It's a diesel, and it's down on power
The engine air filter hasn't been changed in a long time
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: A serious misfire may be sending unburned fuel into the exhaust
result.now: Slow down, pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive it further. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you smell something very hot or see a glow under the car, step away from the car. An overheated catalytic converter can start a fire on dry grass.
If the light stops flashing after a restart, the problem is still there. Have it checked before driving.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means one or more cylinders isn't firing properly. The fuel sent to that cylinder goes straight into the exhaust, which makes black smoke and can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter.

causes.name: Ignition coil or spark plug problem
causes.clues: The shaking is steady, and it got worse in rain or under load.

causes.name: Fuel injector stuck open
causes.clues: A strong fuel smell, and hard starting when warm.

causes.name: Internal engine problem
causes.clues: Ticking or knocking along with the misfire.
causes.against: Less common than an ignition fault.

shop: Ignition coil and spark plug test
Compression test on the misfiring cylinder

result.title: Fuel may be leaking, which is a fire risk
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn off the engine and step away from the car. Don't drive or restart it. Have it towed.
if: If you see smoke or flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
If there's no visible leak but the fuel smell is strong, it still needs to be checked before you drive it.
result.why: A strong raw fuel smell with black smoke can mean an injector or fuel line is leaking, either into the engine or onto hot parts. Fuel near a hot engine or exhaust can catch fire.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector or fuel line
causes.clues: Wet spots on the engine or under the car, or a smell strongest near the engine.

causes.name: Fuel pressure regulator leaking
causes.clues: Fuel smell from the engine, black smoke, and poor mileage.

causes.name: Injector stuck open
causes.clues: Rough running and hard starts after the car sits.

you: From a safe distance, look for dripping fuel under the car.

result.title: A brief puff on a diesel under hard throttle can be normal
result.now: Check that the engine air filter is clean. If the puffs are small, the engine runs normally and no warning lights are on, keep an eye on it and mention it at your next service.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive on until it's checked.
If you smell raw fuel or see fuel dripping, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine, step away and don't drive it until it's checked.
If the smoke is heavy, lasts more than a moment, or comes with less power, have it checked.
If the engine has been modified or tuned, extra smoke may come from the tune itself. It can still wear parts faster.
result.why: Diesels can briefly add more fuel than the air can match when you accelerate hard, which makes a short puff of dark smoke. Modern diesels with particulate filters usually show little or none, so heavy or lasting smoke deserves a look.

causes.name: Normal short burst under hard acceleration
causes.clues: Only a quick puff, with normal power and fuel economy.
causes.against: If it's heavy or lasting, look for a fault.

causes.name: Dirty air filter
causes.clues: Long time since the last filter change, or dusty driving conditions.

causes.name: Boost or injector problem starting
causes.clues: Power is a little lower, or fuel economy has dropped.

you: Check the engine air filter.
Notice whether the puff is bigger than it used to be.

result.title: A sensor or fuel control problem may be making it run rich
result.now: Have the codes read within a few days. Many auto parts stores will scan them for free, which gives the shop a head start.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive on until it's checked.
If you smell raw fuel or see fuel dripping, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine, step away and don't drive it until it's checked.
If the smoke gets heavier or the engine starts running rough, get it checked sooner.
result.why: The engine computer decides how much fuel to add based on its sensors. If one reports the wrong airflow, temperature or oxygen level, the computer can add too much fuel. That shows up as black smoke, a fuel smell and poor mileage, and can damage the catalytic converter over time.

causes.name: Mass airflow (MAF) sensor reading wrong
causes.clues: Hesitation, rough idle, or a dirty or recently disturbed air filter box.

causes.name: Oxygen sensor reading wrong
causes.clues: Poor mileage and a sulfur or fuel smell.

causes.name: Coolant temperature sensor reading wrong
causes.clues: Black smoke mostly when warm, or the temperature gauge acts oddly.

causes.name: High fuel pressure or leaking injector
causes.clues: Fuel smell and hard starts after the car sits.

you: Have the codes read and write them down.
Check the engine air filter.
shop: Code scan with live sensor data
A shop will usually compare live sensor readings and check for air or vacuum leaks before replacing a sensor

result.title: Weak spark or leaky injectors are common reasons fuel goes unburned
result.now: Have it checked within a few days. Drive gently and avoid long trips until then.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive on until it's checked.
If you smell raw fuel or see fuel dripping, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine, step away and don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: When a cylinder doesn't burn its fuel completely, the leftover fuel comes out as black smoke. Worn spark plugs, weak coils or injectors that drip instead of spraying are common reasons. Left alone, it can damage the catalytic converter.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs or an ignition coil problem
causes.clues: Rough idle, stumbling under load, and plugs that are overdue.

causes.name: Leaking or dirty fuel injectors
causes.clues: Fuel smell, hard starts after sitting, or a rough idle.

causes.name: Low compression in a cylinder
causes.clues: A steady misfire in one cylinder that doesn't clear with new plugs.
causes.against: Less common.

you: Check your maintenance records for when the spark plugs were last replaced.
Have the codes read.

result.title: A diesel with heavy black smoke and low power may have an air, boost or injector problem
result.now: Check the engine air filter and have the engine checked within a few days. Avoid towing or heavy loads until then.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive on until it's checked.
If a warning light about the particulate filter or reduced power comes on, have it checked promptly.
If power drops suddenly with a loud whine, pull over and turn off the engine. The turbocharger may be failing.
If you smell raw fuel or see smoke from under the hood rather than the tailpipe, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn off the engine and don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: A diesel needs plenty of air to burn its fuel cleanly. If the turbo isn't building boost, the air filter is clogged, or an injector is spraying too much, there's extra fuel with nothing to burn it, which makes black smoke and cuts power.

causes.name: Clogged air filter or intake restriction
causes.clues: Overdue air filter, or dusty or off-road driving.

causes.name: Boost leak or turbocharger problem
causes.clues: Hissing or whistling, low power, especially going uphill.

causes.name: Worn or leaking fuel injectors
causes.clues: Rough idle, knocking, or smoke at idle.

causes.name: EGR valve stuck open
causes.clues: Smoke and low power, often with a check engine light.

you: Check the engine air filter.
Look for loose or oily intake hoses between the turbo and the engine.

result.title: A clogged air filter may be choking the engine
result.now: Check the engine air filter. If it's dark and clogged with dirt or debris, replace it.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive on until it's checked.
If you smell raw fuel or see fuel dripping, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine, step away and don't drive it until it's checked.
If a new filter doesn't clear up the smoke, have the codes read and the engine checked.
If a steady check engine light comes on or the engine runs rough, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: An engine needs the right mix of air and fuel. A badly clogged air filter can restrict airflow, which is most noticeable on older engines and diesels. It's an easy, inexpensive thing to rule out first.

causes.name: Clogged engine air filter
causes.clues: Overdue filter, dusty roads, or debris like leaves or a nest in the air box.
causes.against: On most modern gas engines, a dirty filter alone rarely causes heavy black smoke.

causes.name: Faulty sensor making it run rich
causes.clues: A check engine light, or poor mileage that doesn't improve with a new filter.

you: Open the air filter box and look at the filter against a light.
Check the air box and intake for leaves or debris.
shop: Fuel trim and MAF sensor check

result.title: The engine may be running rich. A code scan and fuel trim test are the place to start
result.now: Check the engine air filter, then book a check and ask for a code scan and fuel trim test.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive on until it's checked.
If a steady check engine light comes on, get it checked sooner.
If you smell raw fuel or see fuel dripping, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine, step away and don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: Black smoke usually means too much fuel for the amount of air. Even without warning lights, it hurts fuel economy and can foul spark plugs and damage the catalytic converter over time.

causes.name: Sensor reading wrong (MAF, oxygen or coolant temperature)
causes.clues: Poor mileage and a fuel smell.

causes.name: Leaking or dirty injectors
causes.clues: Rough idle or hard starts after sitting.

causes.name: Restricted air intake
causes.clues: Dirty air filter or debris in the air box.

you: Check the engine air filter.
Track your fuel mileage over a couple of tanks.

blue-smoke-from-exhaust.title: Blue or gray smoke from exhaust

q_when.q: When do you see the blue or gray smoke?
q_when.help: Have someone watch the tailpipe while you start the car and then press the gas, or check in a mirror. Blue smoke is easiest to see in sunlight.

opts.a: Heavy smoke along with an oil warning light, knocking, or the engine running badly
Just a puff on startup that clears in a few seconds, mostly after the car has sat
Mostly when I press the gas hard
Right after an oil change or after I added oil
All the time, at idle and while driving
I'm not sure

q_turbo.q: Does your engine have a turbocharger?
q_turbo.help: Many newer small engines are turbocharged. Look for "turbo", "T", "TSI", "EcoBoost" or similar on the car's badges, or check the owner's manual.

opts.a: Yes, it's turbocharged
No
I'm not sure

q_oil_level.q: With the engine off on level ground, pull the oil dipstick. Where is the oil level?
q_oil_level.help: Wipe the dipstick, push it all the way back in, then pull it out again to read it. Some newer cars show oil level on the dash instead.

opts.a: Very low or not on the dipstick at all
A bit low, and I've been adding oil between changes
Above the full mark
Between the marks, where it should be
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine is burning a lot of oil and may be damaged
result.now: Pull over and turn off the engine. Don't drive it any further. Have it towed to a shop.
if: If there's smoke from under the hood, step away from the car and don't open the hood until it has cooled.
If the oil was very low, adding oil may not undo damage already done. Have it checked before you start it again.
result.why: Heavy blue smoke with an oil light, knocking or rough running means the engine is losing oil fast or has internal damage. Running an engine low on oil can destroy it within minutes.

causes.name: Engine very low on oil
causes.clues: The oil light is on, or the dipstick shows little or no oil.

causes.name: Major internal engine damage
causes.clues: Knocking or rattling, rough running, or a flashing check engine light.

causes.name: Failed turbocharger (turbo engines)
causes.clues: A sudden loss of power with a whine or siren-like noise, then heavy smoke.

result.title: Worn valve stem seals are a common cause
result.now: Check the oil level every couple of weeks and top it up as needed. Book a check when convenient.
if: If the puff gets bigger, or you start adding oil often, have it checked sooner.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and turn off the engine right away. Have it towed.
If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive on until it's checked.
If a steady check engine light comes on, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: Valve stem seals keep oil from running down into the cylinders. When they harden with age, oil can seep past while the car sits, then burn off in a puff of smoke on startup. It's common on higher-mileage engines and usually gets worse slowly. A compression or leak-down test helps the shop tell seals from rings.

causes.name: Worn valve stem seals or valve guides
causes.clues: A puff on startup after sitting, and sometimes when you let off the gas going downhill.

causes.name: Faulty PCV valve
causes.clues: Oil residue in the air intake, or a rough idle.

causes.name: Worn piston rings
causes.clues: Smoke also shows up when accelerating, not just on startup.
causes.against: Less likely if the smoke only appears on startup.

you: Check the oil level regularly and keep track of how much you add.
Note whether smoke only appears on startup or also while driving.

result.title: Oil may be getting past worn piston rings
result.now: Check the oil level weekly and top it up so it never runs low. Book an engine check when convenient.
if: If you're adding more than a quart every 1,000 miles or so, get it checked soon.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and turn off the engine right away. Have it towed.
If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive on until it's checked.
result.why: Piston rings seal the gap between the pistons and the cylinder walls. When they wear or stick, oil gets into the combustion chamber and burns, especially under load when you press the gas. Some engines are known for this.

causes.name: Worn or stuck piston rings
causes.clues: Smoke when accelerating, steady oil use, and sometimes lower power.

causes.name: Faulty PCV valve
causes.clues: Oil in the air intake, or a whistling noise.
causes.against: An easier fix, so a shop will usually rule it out first.

causes.name: Leaking turbocharger seals
causes.clues: Only if the engine is turbocharged.

you: Write down how much oil you add and how many miles between top-ups.
Check if your vehicle has a known oil consumption issue or extended warranty.

result.title: The turbocharger may be leaking oil
result.now: Check the oil level and top it up if needed. Have the turbo inspected within a few days, and avoid hard acceleration until then.
if: If you hear a loud whine or siren-like noise, or lose power suddenly, pull over and turn off the engine. Have it towed.
If the oil level drops quickly, don't keep driving it until it's checked.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and turn off the engine right away. Have it towed.
result.why: A turbocharger spins very fast and is lubricated by engine oil. When its seals or bearings wear, oil leaks into the intake or exhaust and burns, mostly when the turbo is working hard. A failing turbo can get worse suddenly.

causes.name: Worn turbocharger seals or bearings
causes.clues: Smoke under hard acceleration, oil in the intake pipes, and a new whine.

causes.name: Blocked turbo oil drain or PCV problem
causes.clues: Oil being pushed out past the turbo seals even though the turbo spins freely.

causes.name: Worn piston rings
causes.clues: Smoke at other times too, and high oil use.

you: Check the oil level.
Listen for a new whistling or whining sound when accelerating.
shop: Intake and intercooler check for oil
A shop will usually check the PCV system and turbo oil drain before replacing the turbo

result.title: There may be too much oil, or some was spilled during the oil change
result.now: Check the oil level on level ground with the engine off. If it's well over the full mark, have the extra drained before you drive it.
if: If smoke comes from under the hood or under the car rather than the tailpipe, oil may be dripping onto the hot exhaust. Pull over, turn off the engine and don't drive it until it's checked.
If the level is correct and the smoke fades within a day or two of driving, spilled oil burning off is the likely reason.
If the smoke continues and the level is correct, have it checked.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and turn off the engine right away. Have it towed.
result.why: Too much oil can get whipped up by the spinning crankshaft and pushed into the intake, where it burns. Oil spilled on the engine or exhaust during a change can also smoke for a short while. Both are usually simple to sort out once the cause is confirmed.

causes.name: Oil overfilled
causes.clues: The dipstick reads above the full mark right after a change or top-up.

causes.name: Oil spilled during the change
causes.clues: Smoke seems to come from under the hood, and it fades over a few drives.

causes.name: Oil filter or drain plug leaking onto the exhaust
causes.clues: Fresh drips under the car after the oil change.

you: Check the dipstick on level ground with the engine off for a few minutes.
Look under the car for fresh drips near the oil filter and drain plug.
shop: Filter and drain plug leak check

result.title: The engine is dangerously low on oil
result.now: Don't drive it, and don't start the engine with the oil this low. If the oil light was on or the engine knocked, have it towed instead of starting it.
if: If you top it up to the full mark and the engine starts quietly with no oil light, call a shop before you drive it. They can tell you whether to bring it in or have it towed, and find out where the oil is going.
If it takes several quarts to reach the full mark, look for a major leak and don't start it until it's checked.
result.why: An engine that's burning oil can use it faster than you'd expect. Once the level is very low, the engine's moving parts can lose lubrication and wear out or seize quickly.

causes.name: Heavy oil burning
causes.clues: Blue smoke and no oil spots under the car.

causes.name: Oil leak
causes.clues: Oil spots where you park, or an oily underside.

causes.name: Missed oil changes
causes.clues: It's been a long time since the last oil change.

you: Add the oil type listed in your owner's manual until it reaches the full mark.
Look under the car for leaks.
shop: Engine noise and oil pressure check

result.title: The engine is burning oil and needs to be checked
result.now: Top up the oil to the full mark and have the engine checked within a few days. Check the oil before every longer drive until then.
if: If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and turn off the engine right away. Have it towed.
If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive on until it's checked.
If a steady check engine light comes on, mention it to the shop. Burning oil can foul spark plugs and damage the catalytic converter.
If the oil level drops below the add mark between checks, don't drive it until it's been checked.
result.why: Smoke all the time plus a dropping oil level means oil is reaching the cylinders steadily. The engine can run low on oil without warning, and burning oil also wears out spark plugs and the catalytic converter over time.

causes.name: Worn piston rings
causes.clues: Smoke when accelerating, high mileage, or a known oil-use issue on your engine.

causes.name: Worn valve stem seals or guides
causes.clues: Worst on startup and when letting off the gas downhill.

causes.name: PCV valve or turbocharger problem
causes.clues: Oil in the intake, or a turbo engine with smoke under boost.

you: Track how much oil you add and how often.
Look at the spark plugs if you're comfortable doing so. Oily deposits support oil burning.

result.title: A small amount of oil burning or a PCV problem are possible causes
result.now: Keep checking the oil level every week or two, and book a check when convenient.
if: If the oil level starts dropping, have it checked sooner.
If smoke comes from under the hood or under the car rather than the tailpipe, oil may be dripping onto the hot exhaust. Pull over, turn off the engine and don't drive it until it's checked.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and turn off the engine right away. Have it towed.
result.why: If the oil level stays steady, the engine isn't burning much yet. A sticking PCV valve can pull a little oil into the intake, and early seal wear can cause light smoke before oil use becomes noticeable.

causes.name: PCV valve sticking
causes.clues: Oil residue in the air intake hose, or a rough idle.

causes.name: Early valve seal or ring wear
causes.clues: Light smoke that appears mainly on startup or under hard acceleration.

causes.name: Oil leak onto the exhaust
causes.clues: Smoke comes from under the car rather than the tailpipe, and there are oily spots underneath.

causes.name: Transmission fluid being burned (some older automatics)
causes.clues: The transmission fluid level drops, or shifting has changed.
causes.against: Rare on modern cars.

you: Mark the oil level and check it again in a week.
Look under the car for oily spots or a wet exhaust pipe.

opts.a: One corner sits lower than the others, or I heard a bang or loud clunk
It keeps bouncing after bumps, like a boat
The nose dives when I brake, or the back squats when I accelerate
It leans or sways a lot in turns
It has air suspension, and it's sagging or a suspension warning is on
The ride is suddenly harsh and every bump hits hard
I'm not sure

q_bounce_test.q: With the car parked, push down hard on one corner and let go. Try each corner. What happens?
q_bounce_test.help: Press on the body above each wheel with your weight, then release. A healthy shock lets the car rise and settle with about one rebound.

opts.a: One or more corners bounce two or more times
Every corner settles after about one bounce
I'm not sure / I can't check

q_leak.q: With a flashlight, look at the shocks or struts behind each wheel. Do any look wet or oily?
q_leak.help: Shocks and struts are the tube-shaped parts near each wheel, often inside the coil spring. A light film of dust is normal. Look for wet, oily residue running down the body of the shock.

opts.a: Yes, one or more is wet and oily
No, they look dry
I'm not sure

result.title: A broken coil spring or failed suspension part may be the cause
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic to inspect it where it is.
