if: If a broken spring end is touching the tire, don't move the car at all. It can cut the tire.
If the car has air suspension, a failed air spring can also make a corner drop. Mention it to the shop.
result.why: A corner that suddenly sits low, often after a bang over a bump, often means a coil spring has snapped or a mount has failed. A broken spring can damage the tire and changes how the car steers and brakes.

causes.name: Broken coil spring
causes.clues: A bang over a bump, a corner sitting low, and sometimes a rattle or scraping from that wheel.

causes.name: Failed strut mount
causes.clues: A clunk from the top of the front suspension, and the body sits off level.

causes.name: Failed air spring (air suspension only)
causes.clues: The corner drops after sitting, with a suspension warning on the dash.

you: From a safe distance, compare the gap between each tire and the fender above it.
shop: Spring and strut mount inspection on a lift
Tire and wheel check for damage

result.title: A leaking shock or strut may no longer be controlling bouncing
result.now: Have the shocks or struts inspected within the next few days. A shop will confirm the oil is coming from the shock and not from somewhere above it before recommending replacement. Until then, drive gently, slow down for bumps and leave extra stopping distance.
if: If the car is hard to control on bumpy roads or bounces off line in curves, don't drive it until it's fixed.
If one corner suddenly sits lower, you hear a bang or a new loud clunk, a tire rubs, or the steering suddenly feels loose or pulls hard, stop driving and have it inspected where it is.
If the front shocks or struts are replaced, an alignment is usually needed afterward.
result.why: Shocks and struts use fluid to soak up bouncing. Once fluid leaks out, that corner keeps bouncing, the tire loses contact with the road over bumps, and braking and steering get worse.

causes.name: Worn shock or strut seal
causes.clues: Wet, oily residue on the shock body, and a bouncy corner.

causes.name: Damaged shock
causes.clues: A recent hard impact, or a dented shock body.

you: Note which corner is wet and which bounces the most.

result.title: Worn shocks or struts are a common cause
result.now: Book a suspension inspection and ask them to check the shocks or struts.
if: If the car nose dives hard when braking or is hard to control on bumpy curves, get it checked within a few days.
If you see oily residue on any shock or strut, have it inspected soon.
If one corner suddenly sits lower, you hear a bang or a new loud clunk, a tire rubs, or the steering suddenly feels loose or pulls hard, stop driving and have it inspected where it is.
result.why: Shocks and struts wear out gradually, so the change is easy to miss. Worn ones let the car keep bouncing after bumps, dive when braking and sway in turns. That reduces grip and can make stopping distances longer.

causes.name: Worn shocks or struts
causes.clues: Bouncing after bumps, nose dive when braking, and high mileage on the original parts.

causes.name: Sagging springs
causes.clues: The car sits lower than it used to, especially at the rear.

causes.name: Worn strut mounts or bushings
causes.clues: Clunks or creaks over bumps.

you: Do the bounce test on each corner.
Look for cupped, scalloped wear on the tires.

result.title: Worn sway bar parts or shocks may be letting the car lean
result.now: Book a suspension inspection and ask them to check the sway bar links, sway bar bushings and shocks.
if: If you hear clunking or knocking over bumps, mention it. Sway bar links often make that sound when they wear.
If the car feels unstable in turns, slow down for curves and get it checked within a few days.
If one corner suddenly sits lower, you hear a bang or a new loud clunk, a tire rubs, or the steering suddenly feels loose or pulls hard, stop driving and have it inspected where it is.
result.why: The sway bar links the left and right sides of the suspension to keep the car level in turns. When its links or bushings wear, or the shocks are tired, the body leans more and the car feels less stable.

causes.name: Worn or broken sway bar links
causes.clues: A knock or rattle over small bumps.

causes.name: Worn sway bar bushings
causes.clues: A clunk or squeak when going over bumps or turning.

causes.name: Worn shocks or struts
causes.clues: Bouncing after bumps as well as leaning.

you: Listen for knocking over small bumps with the windows down.
shop: Sway bar link and bushing inspection

result.title: The air suspension may have a leak or a compressor problem
result.now: Have the air suspension checked within the next few days. Drive gently and keep speeds down until then.
if: If a corner drops low enough that the tire rubs or the car scrapes, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If the dash message says not to drive, or the car drops suddenly while moving, pull over safely and have it inspected before driving further.
If the car only sags after sitting overnight and then rises, a slow leak is likely. Get it checked before the compressor wears out from overwork.
result.why: Air suspension holds the car up with air springs filled by a small compressor. A leak in a spring or line, or a tired compressor, lets the car sag and changes how it rides and handles.

causes.name: Leaking air spring or air line
causes.clues: One corner sags after sitting, and the compressor runs often.

causes.name: Compressor or relay not working
causes.clues: The whole car sits low and you don't hear the compressor run.

causes.name: Ride height sensor fault
causes.clues: The car sits at an odd height with a warning light, but no obvious leak.

you: Note which corner sags and how long it takes after parking.
Listen for the compressor running after you start the car.
shop: Leak test of air springs and lines

result.title: A harsh, jittery ride often points to tire pressure or a damaged suspension part
result.now: Check the tire pressures against the sticker in the driver's door jamb. If they're right, book a suspension inspection.
if: If one corner suddenly sits lower, you hear a bang or a new loud clunk, a tire rubs, or the steering suddenly feels loose or pulls hard, stop driving and have it inspected where it is.
If you hear new clunks or rattles, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: Overinflated tires make every bump sharper. If the pressures are right, a seized shock, a broken spring or worn bushings can stop the suspension from absorbing bumps the way it should.

causes.name: Tires overinflated
causes.clues: The tires were recently filled, or pressures are above the door jamb number.

causes.name: Damaged or seized shock or strut
causes.clues: One corner feels much stiffer than the others in the bounce test.

causes.name: Broken spring or worn bushings
causes.clues: Clunks or rattles over bumps, or the car sits unevenly.

you: Check the tire pressures when cold.
Do the bounce test on each corner and compare.

result.title: The shocks may be fine. Check tires, springs and bushings next
result.now: Check the tire pressures, then book a suspension inspection and describe when the car bounces.
if: If the bouncing only happens with a heavy load, check that you're within the weight limit on the door jamb sticker.
If the car dives hard when braking, ask the shop to test the shocks while driving. A simple bounce test doesn't catch every worn shock.
If one corner suddenly sits lower, you hear a bang or a new loud clunk, a tire rubs, or the steering suddenly feels loose or pulls hard, stop driving and have it inspected where it is.
result.why: A shock can pass a quick bounce test and still be weak at speed. Low tire pressure, sagging springs and worn bushings can also make a car feel floaty or unsettled.

causes.name: Shocks worn but not obvious when parked
causes.clues: High mileage on the original shocks, or bouncing mostly at highway speeds.

causes.name: Low or uneven tire pressure
causes.clues: A soft, wallowing feel.

causes.name: Sagging springs or worn bushings
causes.clues: The car sits lower than it used to, or clunks over bumps.

you: Check the tire pressures.
Measure from the center of each wheel to the fender edge and compare side to side.

q_pedal.q: How does the brake pedal feel?
q_pedal.help: Press it firmly with the engine running and the car in Park. A healthy pedal stops high and feels firm.

opts.a: Soft or spongy, or it slowly sinks toward the floor
The red BRAKE warning light is on
Firm and normal, and no brake warning light
I'm not sure

q_light.q: With the engine running and the parking brake fully released, is the red BRAKE light on?
q_light.help: It may say BRAKE or show a circle with an exclamation mark. It also comes on when the parking brake is set, so release that first.

opts.a: Yes, it's on
No, it's off
I'm not sure

q_where.q: Where did you find the fluid?

opts.a: On the inside of a wheel or tire
Along a metal line or rubber hose under the car
Under the hood, around the brake fluid reservoir near the windshield
On the floor inside the car, under the pedals
I haven't seen a leak, but the fluid level looks low
I'm not sure

q_level.q: Look at the brake fluid reservoir under the hood. Where is the level?
q_level.help: It's a see-through plastic tank, usually on the driver's side near the windshield, marked MIN and MAX. You can read it without opening the cap. Brake fluid damages paint, so wipe up any drips right away.

opts.a: At or near MAX, and I see no wet spots anywhere
Between the lines but closer to MIN, and I see no wet spots
At or below MIN, or empty
I'm not sure

result.title: The brakes may be losing pressure. Don't drive the car
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the pedal sinks while you're driving, pump it, apply the parking brake gradually and steer to a safe stop.
If you can't find any outside leak, a master cylinder leaking internally can cause the same sinking pedal. It still needs a tow.
result.why: A soft or sinking pedal means the brake system can't hold pressure, because fluid is escaping or air has gotten in. Together with a leak, this means braking could fail. The car isn't safe to use until it's repaired.

causes.name: Leak at a caliper, wheel cylinder, line or hose
causes.clues: Wet fluid near a wheel or along the underside of the car.

causes.name: Master cylinder problem
causes.clues: The pedal slowly sinks while you hold steady pressure, with or without a visible leak.

causes.name: Air in the brake lines
causes.clues: Recent brake work, or the reservoir ran very low.

shop: Brake line, hose and caliper inspection
Brake bleed and pedal test after repair

result.title: The red brake light with a leak can point to low brake fluid
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the parking brake was partly on, release it fully and look again. Even if the light goes out, have the suspected leak checked before using the car.
If the ABS light is also on, mention it. Some brake faults turn on both.
result.why: The red brake light comes on when the parking brake is set or when the fluid in the reservoir drops too low. With a leak, low fluid is the likely reason, and the next stage can be a pedal that sinks to the floor.

causes.name: Low fluid from a leak
causes.clues: Wet spots near a wheel or under the car, or a reservoir at or below MIN.

causes.name: Very worn brake pads
causes.clues: Squealing or grinding, and a long time since the last brake job.
causes.against: Pad wear alone rarely drops the level fast enough to explain fresh drips.

causes.name: Faulty fluid level sensor or parking brake switch
causes.clues: The reservoir is full and there's no sign of a leak.

you: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.
Look at the brake fluid reservoir level without opening it.
shop: Brake fluid level and leak inspection

result.title: A brake caliper or wheel cylinder may be leaking
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If fluid has soaked the brake pads or shoes, a shop will usually replace them as well. Contaminated pads don't grip properly.
If it turns out to be thick black grease instead of slick fluid, it may be a torn axle boot. Still have it checked before using the car.
result.why: Each wheel has a caliper, or a wheel cylinder on drum brakes, that uses brake fluid to press the pads or shoes. A leak there drains fluid and can coat the pads, so that wheel brakes poorly. The pedal can go soft with little warning.

causes.name: Caliper piston seal leaking
causes.clues: Wet, slick fluid on the inside of a front wheel.

causes.name: Leaking wheel cylinder (drum brakes)
causes.clues: Wetness on the inside of a rear tire, on a car with rear drum brakes.

causes.name: Loose bleeder screw or brake hose fitting
causes.clues: The leak started after recent brake work.

you: Without driving the car, look at the inside of each tire for a wet, oily film.

result.title: A brake line or hose may be leaking
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the lines look heavily rusted, ask the shop to inspect all of them, not just the leaking section.
result.why: Brake lines carry fluid under high pressure to each wheel. Steel lines rust from road salt, and rubber hoses crack with age. A leaking line can burst when you brake hard, causing a sudden loss of braking.

causes.name: Rusted steel brake line
causes.clues: An older car driven in snowy, salted areas, with flaky rust along the lines.

causes.name: Cracked or worn rubber brake hose
causes.clues: Wetness at the flexible hose near a wheel, or visible cracks.

causes.name: Loose fitting
causes.clues: Fluid at a connection, especially after recent brake work.

shop: Full brake line and hose inspection on a lift

result.title: The master cylinder or its reservoir may be leaking
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If it's only old, dried residue from a past top-up and the level holds steady, a technician can confirm that and clear the car to use.
If your car is a manual, the clutch often shares this fluid. Mention it if the clutch pedal also feels different.
result.why: The master cylinder turns your foot pressure into brake fluid pressure. If it leaks outside or its seals fail inside, the pedal can sink and braking power drops. Brake fluid also eats paint, so bubbled or peeling paint below it is a clue.

causes.name: Leaking master cylinder seal or line fitting
causes.clues: Fresh wetness below the master cylinder, or peeling paint underneath.

causes.name: Cracked reservoir or loose cap
causes.clues: Wetness around the reservoir itself.

causes.name: Spill from an earlier top-up
causes.clues: Dry residue, and the level stays the same over several days.
causes.against: Fresh wetness that returns after the area is cleaned points to a real leak.

you: Note whether the area looks freshly wet or just has old residue.
Look at the reservoir level without opening it.

result.title: Fluid under the pedals could be from the brake or clutch system
result.now: Don't drive it until it's checked. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If it's plain water or smells sweet, it may be an A/C drain or heater core leak instead. Still have the brake fluid level and pedal checked before driving, and mention any sweet smell or foggy windows to the shop.

If the car is a manual and the clutch pedal feels soft or sticks, the clutch system may be the source. Many cars share the brake fluid reservoir with the clutch, so it still needs checking before you drive.
result.why: The brake master cylinder, and on manual cars the clutch master cylinder, sit just in front of the pedals. A leak there can run back toward the pedal area. Both use brake fluid, and many cars share one reservoir, so either leak can lead to low brake fluid.

causes.name: Leaking clutch master cylinder (manual cars)
causes.clues: A soft, sticking or sinking clutch pedal.
causes.against: Not possible on an automatic.

causes.name: Leaking brake master cylinder or pushrod seal
causes.clues: A soft or sinking brake pedal, and the brake fluid level dropping.

causes.name: Water or coolant
causes.clues: Plain water, or a sweet smell and foggy windows.
causes.against: Brake fluid is slick and has little smell.

you: Touch a drop: slick and nearly odorless suggests brake or clutch fluid, watery or sweet suggests water or coolant.
Look at the brake fluid reservoir level without opening it.
shop: Brake and clutch master cylinder inspection

result.title: Low brake fluid with no obvious cause should be treated as a leak
result.now: Don't drive it until a technician has checked the brakes. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the brakes were worked on recently, ask that shop to check for a loose fitting or bleeder screw first.
If the brake pads turn out to be worn almost through, that can explain part of the drop, but the pads need replacing right away.
result.why: The brake system is sealed, and the fluid level only drops slightly as pads wear. At or below MIN means very worn pads or fluid escaping somewhere you can't see, and braking can fail if it keeps dropping.

causes.name: Hidden leak at a caliper, line or hose
causes.clues: Damp areas on the inside of a wheel or along the underside.

causes.name: Very worn brake pads
causes.clues: Squealing or grinding, and a long time since the last brake job.

causes.name: Master cylinder leaking into the brake booster
causes.clues: No outside leak, but the level keeps dropping and the pedal feels different.

you: Without driving the car, look at the inside of each tire for a wet film.

result.title: The fluid you found may not be brake fluid, but have the brakes checked
result.now: Have the brakes inspected within the next few days so a shop can identify the fluid and confirm the brakes aren't leaking. Check the reservoir again before each drive until then.
if: If the brake fluid level drops when you check again, treat it as a leak and don't drive the car until it's checked.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the red BRAKE light comes on, the car pulls to one side when braking, or you smell burning from a wheel, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
result.why: A full reservoir and a firm pedal are good signs, but they don't prove there's no leak. A slow leak can take time to lower the level. Other fluids near the wheels, like shock absorber oil or axle grease, can also look similar.

causes.name: Leaking shock absorber or strut
causes.clues: An oily film on the shock body behind the wheel, and a bouncier ride.

causes.name: Torn CV axle boot
causes.clues: Thick black grease sprayed around the inside of a front wheel.

causes.name: Power steering or other fluid
causes.clues: Reddish or amber fluid toward the front of the car.

you: Recheck the brake fluid level in a few days.
Look at the shocks behind each wheel for an oily film.
shop: Shock, strut and axle boot inspection
Brake inspection to rule out a leak

result.title: The level may be dropping as the brake pads wear, but a leak needs to be ruled out
result.now: Have the brakes inspected within the next few days. A shop will usually check pad thickness and look for leaks before deciding whether it's just pad wear. Don't top it up to MAX yourself before the inspection, as the level helps them judge.
if: If the level keeps dropping between checks, or you spot any wet areas near the wheels, treat it as a leak and don't drive the car until it's checked.
If the level reaches MIN or the red brake light comes on, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the red BRAKE light comes on, the car pulls to one side when braking, or you smell burning from a wheel, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
If you hear grinding when you brake, the pads may be worn down to metal. Don't drive it until they're checked.
result.why: As brake pads wear thinner, the brake pistons sit further out and hold more fluid, so the reservoir level drops slowly over many months. That can be normal. A sudden drop, or any dampness near the wheels, is not, and from here it isn't possible to tell the two apart.

causes.name: Brake pad wear
causes.clues: A slow drop over months, and the pads are getting old.

causes.name: Slow leak not yet visible
causes.clues: The level drops noticeably within weeks.

you: Note the level and check it again in a couple of weeks.
Listen for squealing from the brakes, a common pad wear warning.

result.title: Treat it as a brake leak until someone checks
result.now: Don't drive it until a technician has checked the brakes. A mobile mechanic can come to you, or have it towed.
if: If the technician finds the reservoir full, the pedal firm and no leak, the fluid was probably something else.
result.why: Without knowing whether the brake fluid is low or the warning light is on, it isn't possible to rule out a brake leak. Because brakes can fail suddenly when fluid runs low, it's safer to have them checked before using the car.

causes.name: Brake fluid leak
causes.clues: Slick, clear to brown fluid near a wheel or under the car.

causes.name: Another fluid near the wheels
causes.clues: Shock oil, axle grease or power steering fluid.

you: Take a photo of the fluid and where you found it to show the technician.
shop: Brake fluid level and leak inspection

q_pedal.q: How do the brakes feel and how is the car stopping?
q_pedal.help: A healthy pedal feels firm and stops well above the floor. If the car is parked, start the engine and press the pedal firmly for about 10 seconds.

opts.a: Soft, spongy, or sinking toward the floor, or the car takes longer to stop
Normal, the same as always
I'm not sure, or I haven't driven it since the light came on

q_parking.q: Is the parking brake fully released?
q_parking.help: The parking brake may be a hand lever, a small pedal by your left foot, or a button marked P or with a brake symbol. Push it all the way down or release it fully, then watch the light.

opts.a: It was partly on. I released it and the light went out
It's fully released and the light stays on
It's an electric parking brake button, and there's a fault message or the light is flashing
I'm not sure

q_fluid.q: With the engine off, where is the brake fluid level in the reservoir?
q_fluid.help: The reservoir is a small see-through plastic tank, usually high on the driver's side near the back of the engine bay. The cap often says brake fluid or DOT 3/DOT 4, and the side has MIN and MAX marks.

opts.a: At or below the MIN mark
Between MIN and MAX
I can't find it or I'm not sure

q_leak.q: Do you see any sign of a leak?
q_leak.help: Brake fluid is clear to light brown and feels slick, a bit like light oil. Check the ground under each wheel, the inside of each tire, and under the car near the brake pedal.

opts.a: Yes, wet or oily spots near a wheel, on a tire, or under the car
No leak that I can see
I'm not sure

q_abs_too.q: Is the amber ABS light on as well?

opts.a: Yes, the ABS light is on too
No, only the red brake light
I'm not sure

result.title: The brakes may be losing pressure. This is a safety problem
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic inspect the brakes where it is.
if: If you're on the road now, slow down gently, shift to a lower gear, and use the parking brake gradually if the pedal won't stop you. Pull over somewhere safe.
If you see fluid dripping, tell the tow or repair service so they bring the right parts.
result.why: A red brake light with a soft or sinking pedal usually means the hydraulic system can't build normal pressure. That often comes from a fluid leak or a master cylinder problem, and braking can get worse without warning.

causes.name: Brake fluid leak
causes.clues: Low fluid in the reservoir, or wet spots near a wheel or on the inside of a tire.

causes.name: Master cylinder problem
causes.clues: The pedal slowly sinks under steady pressure with no visible leak.

causes.name: Air in the brake lines
causes.clues: Recent brake work, and the pedal has felt spongy since.

result.title: Often this is a parking brake that isn't fully released
result.now: Release the parking brake all the way. Push a lever fully down, press a foot pedal to release it, or press the electric button with your foot on the brake. Then check that the light goes out.
if: If the light stays on with the parking brake fully off, check the brake fluid level next.
If you drove a long way with the parking brake on and smell burning or see smoke from a rear wheel, pull over, let the brakes cool, and have them checked before driving further.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the car is slow to stop or pulls to one side, or you smell burning from a wheel, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
result.why: The same red light shows when the parking brake is on, and a lever pulled up just one click can be enough to turn it on. It's the most common reason for this light and the simplest to fix.

causes.name: Parking brake partly applied
causes.clues: The light goes out when you fully release it.
causes.against: If it stays on with the brake fully released, look elsewhere.

causes.name: Parking brake switch sticking
causes.clues: The light flickers when you jiggle the lever or pedal.

causes.name: Low brake fluid
causes.clues: The light stays on with the parking brake off.

you: Release the parking brake fully and watch the light.
Jiggle the lever or pedal to see if the light flickers.

result.title: The electric parking brake may have a fault
result.now: Get the electric parking brake checked within a few days. When you park, use Park (or leave it in gear on a manual) and turn the wheels toward the curb on a slope.
if: If the parking brake won't release, the car feels like it's dragging, or you smell burning from a rear wheel, don't drive it. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
If the light came on right after a battery was replaced or jumped, restart the car once. Some systems need a moment to reset.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the car is slow to stop or pulls to one side, or you smell burning from a wheel, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
result.why: Cars with a parking brake button often flash the red brake light or show a message when the electric parking brake has a fault. The regular brakes work separately, but the parking brake may not hold the car or may not release properly, so have the whole brake system checked.

causes.name: Parking brake motor or caliper fault
causes.clues: A grinding or whirring sound at a rear wheel when you press the button.

causes.name: Low voltage after a battery problem
causes.clues: It started after a dead battery or jump start.

causes.name: Switch or wiring fault
causes.clues: The button doesn't respond at all.

you: Read the message on the dash and look it up in the owner's manual.
Note whether the parking brake applies and releases when you press the button.
shop: Parking brake motor and wiring test

result.title: Brake fluid may be leaking. The brakes could fail
result.now: Don't drive it, even after topping up the fluid. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you must move the car a few feet out of danger, do it very slowly and test the brakes first.
result.why: Low fluid plus a visible leak usually means the brake system is losing the fluid it needs to stop the car. Topping it up only hides the problem, and the leak can get worse suddenly.

causes.name: Leaking brake hose or line
causes.clues: Wet spots near a wheel or along the underside, often on older cars in salty areas.

causes.name: Leaking caliper or wheel cylinder
causes.clues: Fluid on the inside of one tire or wheel.

causes.name: Leaking master cylinder
causes.clues: Fluid under the car near the pedal area, or on the back of the engine bay.

result.title: Brake fluid is low with no visible leak. Get the brakes inspected before driving
result.now: Don't drive it until the brakes are inspected, even if the pedal feels normal. A mobile mechanic can come to you, or have it towed. Topping it up isn't a fix: low fluid can come from a leak you can't see or from badly worn pads.
if: If you have to move the car a few feet out of danger, do it very slowly and test the brakes first.
If the inspection finds worn pads and no leak, the shop will usually replace the pads and then set the fluid to the right level.
If you top it up, use only the fluid type printed on the cap, and still have the brakes inspected before driving.
result.why: Brake fluid doesn't get used up. The level falls slowly as brake pads wear, so a low level can mean the pads are thin. It can also mean fluid is escaping somewhere that's hard to see, such as inside a wheel or at the back of the engine bay. A website can't tell those apart, so it's safest to have it checked before the car is used.

causes.name: Worn brake pads
causes.clues: Squealing or grinding when braking, or no brake work in a long time.
causes.against: If the pads were replaced recently, a leak is more likely.

causes.name: Slow leak
causes.clues: The level keeps dropping after a top-up, or damp spots near a wheel.

causes.name: Master cylinder seals leaking
causes.clues: Dampness around the reservoir or behind the engine bay.

you: Look at the inside of each tire and under the car near the pedal area for wet, oily spots.
Look through the wheel spokes at the brake pad thickness if you can see it.

result.title: Brake and ABS lights together mean brake balance may be off
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic to read the brake codes.
if: If both lights went out after a restart, still get the codes read soon. The fault is stored and may come back.
result.why: With fluid at a normal level, both lights on usually means the ABS system has a fault that also switches off electronic brake balance. That system keeps the rear wheels from locking in a hard stop. Without it, the car can skid or spin.

causes.name: Wheel speed sensor fault
causes.clues: Recent brake or wheel work, or a hard pothole hit.

causes.name: ABS module or pump fault
causes.clues: Both lights came on with no clear trigger.

causes.name: Low voltage after a battery problem
causes.clues: It started right after a dead battery or jump start.

you: Check whether both lights stay on after you turn the car off and restart it.
shop: ABS and brake system code scan

result.title: A fluid level sensor or parking brake switch may be giving a false signal
result.now: Don't drive it until the brakes are checked. A red BRAKE light that stays on with the parking brake fully released can mean low brake fluid or a brake fault, even when the pedal feels normal. With the engine off, look at the brake fluid level, then have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic check it.
if: If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the car is slow to stop or pulls to one side, or you smell burning from a wheel, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
If jiggling the parking brake makes the light flicker, the switch may be the cause. Mention that to the shop.
If the amber ABS light comes on as well, or the fluid level drops toward MIN, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
result.why: With the parking brake off, fluid between the marks and a normal pedal, the light may be getting a false signal from a stuck fluid level float or a worn parking brake switch. A red brake light can also report other brake faults, so a shop should confirm the cause rather than assuming it's the switch.

causes.name: Parking brake switch sticking
causes.clues: The light flickers when you move the lever or pedal.

causes.name: Brake fluid level sensor sticking
causes.clues: Fluid is near the MIN mark, or the light flickers on turns or bumps.

causes.name: Brake system fault that needs a scan
causes.clues: On some cars, this light also reports other brake faults.

you: Jiggle the parking brake lever or pedal and watch the light.
Note whether the light flickers on turns or over bumps.

result.title: Treat a red brake light as serious until it's checked
result.now: Don't drive it until the brake fluid and brakes are checked. If you can't check them yourself, have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to come to you.
if: If someone can show you the fluid level and it's between MIN and MAX with a firm pedal, the cause may be less urgent. Have it checked within a few days, and don't drive it if the pedal changes.
result.why: With the parking brake off, the red light usually means low brake fluid or a brake system fault. Without knowing the fluid level, there's no safe way to rule out a problem that affects stopping.

causes.name: Low brake fluid
causes.clues: Worn pads, or wet spots near a wheel.

causes.name: Brake system or ABS fault
causes.clues: The ABS light is on too.

causes.name: Faulty switch or sensor
causes.clues: The brakes feel completely normal.

you: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.
Look under the car and inside each wheel for wet spots.
shop: Brake fluid level and leak check

q_what_happens.help: A caliper is the clamp at each wheel that squeezes the brake pads against the disc (rotor).

opts.a: Smoke from a wheel, or a strong burning smell
The brake pedal feels hard or high, and all the wheels seem to drag
The parking brake won't fully release, or its warning light stays on
The car pulls to one side while driving
It started right after brake work
The car feels held back, doesn't coast well, or one wheel seems hot
I'm not sure

q_where.q: After a short drive with little braking, hold your hand near each wheel without touching it. Which fits?
q_where.help: A 10-minute drive on quiet roads with gentle braking works best. A dragging brake gives off noticeably more heat than the others.

opts.a: One front wheel is much hotter than the other
One or both rear wheels are much hotter
They all feel about the same
I'm not sure

q_parking.help: Most cars have either a hand lever, a foot pedal, or an electronic button (often marked with a P in a circle).

opts.a: The red brake light stays on even though the parking brake is fully released
I have a hand lever or foot pedal, and the rear still drags after releasing it
I have an electronic parking brake, and it won't release or shows a warning
I'm not sure

result.title: A brake may be overheating, possibly from sticking on
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, turn off the engine and let the brakes cool for at least 30 minutes. Then have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If there are flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.

If it happened only after a long, steep downhill with heavy braking and all the wheels were hot, the brakes may have overheated from use rather than sticking. Overheating can still damage pads, rotors and fluid, so have them checked before driving further. On long hills, use a lower gear.
If the brake pedal felt soft, sank, or the car took longer to stop, the brakes may not work normally even after cooling. Don't drive it.
If you see fluid around the inside of a wheel, tell the shop. A brake fluid leak can lead to brake failure.
result.why: Smoke or a burning smell usually means a brake is getting far hotter than normal. That often happens when it doesn't release, so it rubs constantly. Overheated brakes can fade and stop working well, and in bad cases can set grease or the tire alight.

causes.name: Sticking caliper
causes.clues: The smell and heat come from one wheel, and the car pulls toward that side.

causes.name: Parking brake left on or not releasing
causes.clues: The heat is at the rear, and the parking brake light may be on.

causes.name: Heavy braking on a long descent
causes.clues: It happened at the bottom of a steep hill, and all wheels are hot.
causes.against: If only one wheel is hot, a sticking brake is more likely.

you: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.
Once cool, look for fluid around the inside of each wheel.
shop: Pad and rotor heat damage check

result.title: A problem in the brake hydraulics or booster may be holding all the brakes on
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the brakes release after the car sits and cools, then drag again after driving, tell the shop. It can point to the master cylinder or the brake fluid.
If anyone recently added fluid, tell the shop what was used. The wrong fluid can make seals swell.
If you smell burning or see smoke from any wheel, keep everyone clear of the hot wheels and let them cool before anyone goes near them.
result.why: When every wheel drags at once, the cause is often in the parts shared by all four brakes: the master cylinder, the brake booster, or the fluid itself. Brakes that won't release can overheat quickly and then fade when you need them.

causes.name: Master cylinder not releasing pressure
causes.clues: The drag builds up as you drive and eases when the car sits.

causes.name: Brake booster or pedal not returning
causes.clues: The pedal sits higher than normal or doesn't spring back fully.

causes.name: Contaminated or wrong brake fluid
causes.clues: Recent fluid top-up from an unknown bottle, or very dark fluid.

shop: Brake booster and pedal return check

result.title: A sticking brake caliper is a likely cause
result.now: A dragging brake can overheat and stop working well, so don't drive it until it's checked. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you smell burning or see smoke, stop and let it cool, then have it towed.
If the pull gets stronger, the pedal feels soft or different, or the car takes longer to stop, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the red brake warning light comes on, stop driving and have the brakes checked before going further.
result.why: Calipers slide on pins and use a piston that can corrode or stick. When one doesn't release, its pads keep rubbing. That wheel gets hot, the car pulls toward it, and the pads and rotor wear out fast. A shop will usually check the slide pins, piston and hose before deciding which part needs replacing.

causes.name: Seized or sticking caliper slide pins
causes.clues: Pads on that wheel are worn unevenly, inner versus outer.

causes.name: Sticking caliper piston
causes.clues: An older car, or a torn rubber boot around the piston.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose acting like a one-way valve
causes.clues: The drag gets worse after each stop.

you: After a short drive, compare how much heat each wheel gives off, without touching them.
Look for brown or black brake dust heavier on one wheel.
shop: Raise the car and spin each wheel by hand
Caliper, slide pin and piston inspection

result.title: The parking brake may not be fully releasing
result.now: Make sure the lever or pedal is fully released. If the drag and any hot or burning wheel go away completely, have the rear brakes and cables checked within a few days. If it still drags, don't drive it. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If it's stuck after a cold, wet night, it may free up once the car warms. Have the cables checked anyway, since it will likely happen again.
If you smell burning or see smoke from the rear, stop and have it towed.
If the red brake light stays on after the parking brake is fully released, or the pedal feels soft, don't drive it until the brakes are checked. That can mean low brake fluid.
result.why: Parking brake cables can rust or freeze, and the springs or parts inside rear brakes can stick. When they don't fully release, the rear brakes keep rubbing, overheat and wear quickly.

causes.name: Rusted or frozen parking brake cable
causes.clues: It happens in cold or wet weather, or the lever feels stiff.

causes.name: Rear brake parts sticking or out of adjustment
causes.clues: One rear wheel is hotter, or there's a scraping noise.

causes.name: Parking brake switch out of adjustment
causes.clues: The light stays on but the wheels turn freely.

you: Check the lever or pedal goes all the way to its released position.
Compare heat from the rear wheels after a short drive, without touching them.

result.title: The electronic parking brake may not be releasing
result.now: Check the owner's manual for the release steps, which usually involve the brake pedal, the button and the engine running. If it won't release, have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic rather than forcing it.
if: If the battery is weak or was recently disconnected, the system may need a reset or a scan tool.
If a rear brake is hot, smells burning or is smoking, don't drive it until it's been checked.
If the pedal feels soft or the red brake light stays on once the parking brake is released, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
result.why: An electronic parking brake uses small motors at the rear calipers. A weak battery, a failed motor or a system fault can stop it from releasing, and driving against it can damage the brakes quickly.

causes.name: Parking brake motor or caliper fault
causes.clues: A parking brake warning message and a grinding or whirring sound from one rear wheel.

causes.name: Low battery voltage
causes.clues: Slow cranking or other electrical warnings.

causes.name: System needs a reset after brake work
causes.clues: It started after the rear brakes were serviced.

you: Follow the manual's release steps exactly.
Note any message on the dash.

result.title: The red brake light with the parking brake off can mean low brake fluid
result.now: Don't drive until the brakes are checked. With the engine off, look at the brake fluid level in the reservoir, then have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the fluid is low, look for wet spots near the wheels or under the car. A leak can lead to brake failure.
If the fluid is full and the pedal feels normal, a parking brake switch fault is possible, but let a technician confirm it before driving.
Topping up the fluid isn't a fix. Low brake fluid with no leak you can see still needs an inspection before driving, since leaks can hide inside the wheels or under covers.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, don't move the car.
result.why: The red brake light covers the parking brake and the brake fluid level. If it stays on with the parking brake released, fluid may be low from a leak or very worn pads, which can affect stopping.

causes.name: Low brake fluid from a leak
causes.clues: Wet spots near a wheel, or a soft pedal.

causes.name: Very worn brake pads
causes.clues: Grinding when braking, and fluid only slightly low.

causes.name: Parking brake switch stuck on
causes.clues: Fluid is full and the brakes feel normal.

you: Check the brake fluid level against the MIN and MAX marks.
Look for wet spots inside the wheels or under the car.

result.title: Something from the recent brake work may be binding
result.now: Stop driving it for now. A brake left binding after recent work can overheat and stop working well. Call the shop that did the work, tell them which wheel is hot or noisy, and ask them to come to you or arrange a tow.
if: If you smell burning or see smoke, stop and have it towed.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, stop driving and have it towed.
If the red brake warning light comes on or the car takes longer to stop, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: New pads that fit too tightly, slide pins that weren't cleaned and lubricated, or a parking brake that needs adjusting can all keep a brake from releasing fully. The shop that did the work will want to know, and it's often a straightforward recheck, but it shouldn't wait.

causes.name: Pads binding in the caliper bracket
causes.clues: One wheel hot, starting right after new pads.

causes.name: Slide pins dry or caliper not seated
causes.clues: Noise or pulling to one side after the job.

causes.name: Rear brakes or parking brake over-adjusted
causes.clues: The rear wheels drag after rear brake work.

you: Note which wheel is warmest after a short drive, without touching it.
shop: Recheck pad fit and slide pins
Spin each wheel by hand on a lift

result.title: No wheel stands out, so something besides a single brake may be holding the car back
result.now: Check the tire pressures, then book a check for the wheel bearings and drivetrain when convenient.
if: If you hear a hum or growl that changes when you steer, a wheel bearing is a possibility. Get it checked sooner.
If the engine revs but the car is slow to pick up speed, the transmission may be slipping.
If you notice a burning smell, smoke, or one wheel much hotter than the others, treat it as a dragging brake: pull over, let it cool, and don't drive further until it's checked.
If the brake pedal feels high, hard, soft or different, have the brakes checked before driving further.
result.why: If no wheel is hotter than the others, a single sticking brake is less likely, but the hand test is rough and can't rule it out. Low tires, a worn wheel bearing, or an engine or transmission problem can also make a car feel sluggish or coast poorly. A shop can spin each wheel on a lift to check.

causes.name: Low tire pressure
causes.clues: One or more tires look low, or the tire pressure light is on.

causes.name: Worn wheel bearing
causes.clues: A hum or growl that rises with speed.

causes.name: Engine or transmission not delivering full power
causes.clues: A check engine light, or high revs without much speed.

you: Check all tire pressures.
Note any noises and when they happen.
shop: Spin each wheel by hand on a lift

result.title: Have the brakes checked to find which wheel is dragging
result.now: Make sure the parking brake is fully released. If the car still feels held back, don't drive it until the brakes are checked: a dragging brake can overheat and stop working well. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you notice smoke, a strong burning smell, or the pedal feels different, stop driving and have it towed.
If the car pulls to one side, get it checked within a few days.
If the red brake warning light comes on, have the brakes checked before driving further.
result.why: A shop can lift the car and spin each wheel by hand to find one that doesn't turn freely. That quickly shows whether a caliper, the parking brake or something else is causing the drag.

causes.name: Sticking caliper
causes.clues: One wheel hotter or dustier, or pulling to one side.

causes.name: Parking brake not releasing
causes.clues: Drag from the rear, especially in cold or wet weather.

causes.name: Something other than the brakes
causes.clues: Low tires or a humming wheel bearing.

you: Check the parking brake is fully released.
Look for one wheel with much more brake dust than the others.
shop: Spin each wheel by hand on a lift

q_level.q: Is the oil pressure light on, or how low is the oil on the dipstick?
q_level.help: The oil pressure light is red and usually looks like an old-fashioned oil can. Check the dipstick with the car on level ground, a few minutes after shutting off the engine. Some cars show the oil level on the dash instead of a dipstick.

opts.a: The oil pressure light is on or flickers, or there's little or no oil on the dipstick
It's low, or I keep having to add oil between changes
I haven't checked / I'm not sure

q_where.q: Do you see any signs of where the oil is going?

opts.a: Oil spots under the car, or oily, wet areas on the engine
A burning oil smell from under the hood, or light smoke from the engine area
Blue-gray smoke from the tailpipe
Oily film in the coolant reservoir, or the coolant level is dropping too
No drips, no smoke, no smell: the oil just disappears
I'm not sure

q_smoke_when.q: When do you see the blue-gray smoke?
q_smoke_when.help: Burning oil smoke is bluish-gray and has a sharp, acrid smell. Thin white vapor on a cold morning that disappears after a few minutes is normal condensation.

opts.a: A puff at startup, especially after the car sat overnight, then it clears
Steadily while driving, and more when accelerating
The engine has a turbo, and there's smoke under acceleration or a whistling or whining sound
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be dangerously low on oil
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Shut the engine off and don't run it until you've added the correct oil to the full mark. If the oil pressure light stays on after that, have it towed.
if: If the engine was knocking or ticking loudly before you stopped, have it towed even after adding oil. There may already be damage.

If the oil pressure light came on while the engine was running, have the engine checked before driving it again, even if the light goes off after topping up. Low oil pressure can damage the engine before any noise shows up.

If the oil light never came on and the dipstick now reads full, topping up is the first step, but it isn't proof the engine is unharmed. Call a shop to find where the oil went, and check the level before every start until then.
If you see smoke from under the hood, or the temperature gauge is high, don't restart the engine.
result.why: Oil protects every moving part of the engine. When there's too little, oil pressure drops and metal parts start grinding against each other. Running the engine like this for even a short time can ruin it.

causes.name: Oil consumed or leaked over time without being topped up
causes.clues: It's been a long time since the last oil change or check.

causes.name: Sudden large leak
causes.clues: A fresh puddle under the car, or oil sprayed under the hood.

causes.name: Oil pump or pressure problem
causes.clues: The oil pressure light is on even though the dipstick shows full. A shop will usually test oil pressure with a gauge before replacing a sensor or pump.

you: With the engine off, check the dipstick on level ground.
Look under the car for a fresh puddle.
shop: Oil pressure test with a gauge
Check for engine damage, such as bearing noise

result.title: Check the oil level the right way first
result.now: Park on level ground, turn the engine off, wait a few minutes, then pull the dipstick, wipe it, push it fully back in and pull it out again to read the level.
if: If the oil is below the low mark, add the oil type listed in your owner's manual a little at a time until it reaches the full mark.
If you find yourself adding oil more than once between oil changes, have it checked to find out where it's going.
If the oil pressure light comes on at any point, stop driving and shut the engine off.
If the engine knocks or ticks loudly, don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: Readings taken on a slope or right after shutdown can look lower than the real level. A correct reading tells you whether there's really a problem, and how fast the oil is going down.

causes.name: Normal oil use between changes
causes.clues: A small drop over thousands of miles, with no smoke or leaks.

causes.name: Slow leak
causes.clues: Spots under the car where it's usually parked.

causes.name: Engine burning oil
causes.clues: Blue-gray smoke from the tailpipe.

you: Check the oil level on level ground with the engine off.
Write down the mileage each time you add oil, and how much you added.

result.title: The engine may be leaking oil
result.now: Keep the oil topped up to the full mark, check it every time you fill up with fuel, and book a leak inspection when convenient.
if: If the drips are bigger than a coin each day or form a puddle, get it checked within a few days.
If you smell burning oil or see smoke from under the hood, don't keep driving. Oil on a hot exhaust can catch fire. Pull over, turn off the engine and have it checked before driving further.
If the oil level drops below the low mark between checks, stop driving and add oil before going further.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and shut the engine off right away.
result.why: Oil spots under the car or wet, grimy areas on the engine usually mean oil is escaping from a gasket or seal. Small leaks are common on older engines, but they tend to get worse and can leave the engine low on oil. A shop will usually clean the area or use dye to find the exact source before replacing a gasket.

causes.name: Leaking valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Oil on the top or sides of the engine, sometimes with a burning smell.

causes.name: Leaking oil pan gasket or drain plug
causes.clues: Drips from the very bottom of the engine, or a leak that started after an oil change.

causes.name: Oil filter loose or its seal damaged
causes.clues: A leak that started right after an oil change.

causes.name: Leaking front or rear main seal
causes.clues: Oil at the front of the engine near the belts, or where the engine meets the transmission.

you: Put cardboard under the engine overnight and note where the drips land.
Check that the oil filler cap is on tight.
shop: Leak inspection, often with a UV dye
Engine cleaning and recheck to pinpoint the source

result.title: Oil may be leaking onto hot engine or exhaust parts
result.now: Don't drive it until the source is found. Let the engine cool fully, check the oil level, then have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to look at it.
if: If you see more than light wisps of smoke, or any flames, pull over, shut the engine off and get everyone out.
If the smell is strong inside the cabin, open the windows and keep the engine off until it's checked.
If the smell started right after an oil change and you see no smoke, spilled oil burning off is possible. Call the shop that did the change and have them check it before you rely on the car.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the oil is below the low mark, don't start the engine.
result.why: A burning oil smell or light smoke from under the hood often means oil is dripping onto the hot exhaust manifold or engine. A valve cover gasket is a common source. Besides losing oil, it's a fire risk, and there's no way to tell from the driver's seat how much is reaching the exhaust.

causes.name: Leaking valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Oil seeping from the top edge of the engine, with smoke near the exhaust manifold.

causes.name: Oil spilled during an oil change
causes.clues: The smell started right after an oil change and fades within a few drives.
causes.against: If the smell keeps coming back, a real leak is more likely.

causes.name: Leaking oil filter housing or oil cooler seal
causes.clues: Oil collecting near the filter area, sometimes running down onto the exhaust.

you: With the engine cold, look for wet oil on top of the engine and around the exhaust manifold.
Check that the oil filler cap is tight.
shop: Oil filter housing and cooler seal check

result.title: Oil may be mixing with coolant, possibly from a head gasket or oil cooler
result.now: Stop driving it. Check the oil and coolant levels with the engine cold, and have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the temperature gauge has been climbing, don't start the engine again until it's been checked.
If the oil on the dipstick looks milky or like light-brown chocolate milk, coolant is getting into the oil too.
If you see steam or white smoke from under the hood or the tailpipe, keep the engine off.
result.why: Oil and coolant run in separate passages and should never mix. An oily film in the coolant often points to a failed head gasket or oil cooler. Mixed fluids lose their ability to lubricate and cool, and driving on can cause overheating and serious engine damage. A shop will usually pressure test the cooling system before deciding what needs repair.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: Overheating, white exhaust smoke with a sweet smell, or bubbles in the coolant reservoir.

causes.name: Failed oil cooler
causes.clues: Oil in the coolant without overheating, on engines that have an oil cooler.

causes.name: Cracked cylinder head or engine block
causes.clues: Severe overheating in the past.
causes.against: Less common than a head gasket or oil cooler.

you: With the engine cold, look in the coolant reservoir for an oily or brown film.
Check the dipstick for milky oil.

result.title: The engine may be burning oil slowly inside
result.now: Keep the oil at the full mark, write down the mileage each time you add oil, and book a check when convenient.
if: If you're adding about a quart every 1,000 miles or more, that's at the high end of what most engines should use. Get it checked sooner.
If the check engine light comes on or the engine starts to misfire, oil may be fouling the spark plugs. Have it checked soon.
If your engine has a known oil-consumption problem, ask the dealer about recalls or service bulletins.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and shut it off right away.
result.why: Many engines use some oil between changes, and burning a small amount may produce no smoke you can see. Worn piston rings, worn valve seals or a clogged crankcase ventilation (PCV) valve can raise oil use gradually. Keeping a log tells the shop whether it's normal or getting worse.

causes.name: Clogged or stuck PCV valve
causes.clues: Oil residue in the air intake, oil leaks starting in several places, or a whistling noise.

causes.name: Worn or stuck piston rings
causes.clues: High mileage, fewer oil changes than recommended, or a known engine design issue.

causes.name: Worn valve stem seals
causes.clues: A puff of smoke at startup now and then.

causes.name: Slow leak you can't see yet
causes.clues: Oil drips that only show up on the highway and are blown away.

you: Log the mileage and amount each time you add oil.
Look at the tailpipe for black, oily soot.
Make sure you're using the oil type and viscosity in the owner's manual.
shop: Spark plug inspection for oil fouling

result.title: Worn valve stem seals are a likely cause
result.now: Keep the oil topped up, note how often you add it, and book a check when convenient.
if: If the smoke starts showing up while driving too, the piston rings may also be worn. Get it checked sooner.
If the engine misfires or the check engine light comes on, have it checked within a few days.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and shut the engine off right away.
result.why: Valve stem seals keep oil from running down into the cylinders. When they harden with age, oil seeps in while the car sits, and burns off as a puff of blue smoke at startup. It usually develops slowly, but the oil level still needs watching, because running low on oil is what damages engines. A shop will usually do a consumption test before recommending seal work.

causes.name: Worn or hardened valve stem seals
causes.clues: A puff of blue smoke at startup after sitting, then clear.
causes.against: If the smoke continues while driving, rings are more likely.

causes.name: Worn valve guides
causes.clues: Higher mileage, or ticking from the top of the engine.

causes.name: Turbo seal seepage (turbo engines)
causes.clues: The engine has a turbocharger.

you: Watch the tailpipe during a cold start.
Log how much oil you add and when.

result.title: Worn piston rings or a ventilation problem are possible
result.now: Check the oil level every time you fill up with fuel, keep it at the full mark, and have the engine checked within the next few days.
if: If the smoke is heavy or the oil drops fast enough to need oil every few days, don't drive it until it's checked.
If the check engine light flashes or the engine shakes, stop driving it. Oil may be fouling the spark plugs and damaging the catalytic converter.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and shut it off right away.
result.why: Steady blue smoke while driving usually means oil is getting into the cylinders and burning. Worn piston rings are one cause. A clogged ventilation (PCV) valve can push oil into the intake and cause the same symptom, and it's a much simpler fix, so a shop will usually check it before any engine work.

causes.name: Clogged PCV valve or crankcase ventilation problem
causes.clues: Oil in the air intake tube, or oil leaks appearing in several places.

causes.name: Worn or stuck piston rings
causes.clues: High mileage, low power, or smoke that gets worse under load.

causes.name: Worn valve guides or seals
causes.clues: Smoke is also worse at startup or when slowing down.

you: Watch the tailpipe while someone accelerates firmly.
Log the mileage and amount each time you add oil.

result.title: The turbocharger seals may be leaking oil
result.now: Check and top up the oil, then have the turbo checked within the next few days. Drive gently and avoid hard acceleration until then.
if: If the smoke is heavy, the whining turns into a grinding or siren-like noise, or power drops suddenly, stop driving and have it towed.
If the engine revs up on its own and won't shut off, get away from the vehicle and call for help.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and shut the engine off right away.
result.why: A turbo spins very fast on a thin film of engine oil. When its seals or bearings wear, oil can be pushed into the intake or exhaust and burned, which shows up as blue smoke under boost. A failing turbo can come apart and damage the engine. A shop will usually check the oil return line and ventilation system before replacing the turbo.

causes.name: Worn turbocharger seals or bearings
causes.clues: Blue smoke under acceleration, a whistle or whine, and oil in the intake piping.

causes.name: Restricted turbo oil return line
causes.clues: Oil leaking from the turbo area.

causes.name: Clogged crankcase ventilation (PCV) system
causes.clues: Oil in the intake piping even though the turbo has no play.

you: Note whether the smoke is worst under acceleration.
Listen for a new whine or whistle from the engine.

result.title: Keep the oil topped up and have the source tracked down
result.now: Top up the oil to the full mark, check it every time you fill up with fuel, and book an inspection when convenient.
if: If the oil drops below the low mark between checks, get it checked within a few days.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and shut the engine off right away.
If you see smoke from under the hood or the engine starts knocking, pull over and shut it off.
result.why: Oil only goes two places: out through a leak or into the engine where it burns. A shop can quickly look for leaks and test whether the engine is burning oil. Your record of how often you add oil helps them a lot.

causes.name: Slow oil leak
causes.clues: Spots where the car is parked, or oily areas on the engine.

causes.name: Engine burning oil
causes.clues: Blue-gray exhaust smoke, or oily soot in the tailpipe.

causes.name: Clogged PCV valve
causes.clues: Oil use that crept up over time.

you: Log how much oil you add and at what mileage.
Put cardboard under the engine overnight.

q_danger.q: Is there smoke from under the hood, or is the oil pressure light on?
q_danger.help: The oil pressure light usually looks like a red oil can with a drip. A faint whiff of smoke after parking is different from smoke you can see while driving.

opts.a: Yes, visible smoke from under the hood
The oil pressure or low oil light is on
No, but there's blue-gray smoke from the tailpipe
No smoke and no warning lights
I'm not sure

q_recent.q: Has the car had an oil change or engine work in the last few days?

opts.a: Yes
No
I'm not sure

q_level.q: With the engine off and the car on level ground, what does the oil dipstick show?
q_level.help: Pull the dipstick (usually a yellow or orange handle), wipe it, push it all the way back in, then pull it out and read where the oil reaches between the two marks. Some newer cars show oil level on the dashboard instead.

opts.a: The level is fine and I don't see drips under the car
The level is low and there are oily spots under the car
The level is low, but I don't see any drips
It's below the lowest mark, or there's no oil on the stick at all
I'm not sure, or I can't check it

result.title: Oil may be burning on hot engine parts. Treat it as a fire risk
result.now: If you see smoke and think your car may be on fire, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine. Get everyone out. Leave the hood closed. Move at least 100 feet from the car and stay away from traffic. Call 911 from a safe spot, even if you can't see flames. Once it has cooled and there's no fire, have it towed.
if: If the smoke stops once the engine cools and you find a cap or dipstick that wasn't secured, the oil level and any spilled oil still need checking before you drive.
If the oil pressure light came on or the temperature gauge is high, don't restart the engine.
result.why: Visible smoke usually means a fair amount of oil is hitting very hot parts. Engine oil can ignite on a hot exhaust, and a leak big enough to smoke can also run the engine low on oil.

causes.name: Major valve cover or gasket leak
causes.clues: Oil running down the side of the engine onto the exhaust.

causes.name: Oil filler cap left off or loose
causes.clues: Oil sprayed around the top of the engine, often after an oil change.

causes.name: Oil filter or line leak
causes.clues: Oil sprayed under the engine, and the oil level dropping fast.

causes.name: A different fluid, like power steering or transmission fluid
causes.clues: The oil level is fine, but another fluid is low.

shop: Exhaust and heat shield inspection for oil residue

result.title: The engine may be running low on oil or losing oil pressure
result.now: Pull over and turn off the engine. Don't restart it until you've checked the oil level. If it's empty or the light stays on, have it towed.
if: If the oil level was very low and topping it up makes the light go off, don't assume the engine is undamaged. Have it checked before relying on the car, and ask the shop whether it should be towed in.
If the engine was knocking or ticking loudly, don't restart it.
If you see smoke from under the hood, step away from the car.
result.why: A burning oil smell plus an oil pressure light often means a leak has drained enough oil that the engine isn't being protected. Running an engine without oil pressure can destroy it within minutes.

causes.name: Major oil leak
causes.clues: Oil on the ground, on the engine, or smoke.

causes.name: Engine burning a lot of oil
causes.clues: Blue-gray exhaust smoke and no visible leak.

causes.name: Failed oil pump or pressure sensor
causes.clues: The oil level is full but the light is still on. A shop will usually test oil pressure with a gauge before replacing the sensor or pump.

you: Wait a few minutes after shutting off, then check the dipstick.

result.title: The engine may be burning oil internally
result.now: Check the oil level, top it up to the full mark if needed, and get it checked within a few days. Check the level every time you fill up until then.
if: If the oil drops below the lowest mark between checks, don't drive it until it's topped up.
If the check engine light is flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. If the engine runs rough, get it checked right away.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and shut it off right away.
result.why: When oil gets past worn seals or rings, it burns with the fuel and leaves as blue-gray exhaust smoke with a burning oil smell. The level often drops with no drips under the car. A shop will usually check the crankcase ventilation (PCV) system first, since it's a simpler fix than internal engine work.

causes.name: Stuck or clogged PCV valve
causes.clues: Oil use started suddenly, or there's oil in the air intake.

causes.name: Worn valve stem seals
causes.clues: A puff of blue smoke on startup or after idling, then it clears.

causes.name: Worn piston rings
causes.clues: Steady blue smoke when accelerating, often on a high-mileage engine.

causes.name: Leaking turbocharger seals (turbo engines)
causes.clues: Blue smoke and oil in the intake piping.

you: Track how much oil you add and over how many miles.
Notice whether the smoke shows at startup or while accelerating.
shop: Spark plug inspection for oil fouling

result.title: Oil spilled during the service may be burning off
result.now: Check the oil level, make sure the filler cap is tight and the dipstick is fully seated, and look under the car for fresh drips. If everything looks right, watch whether the smell fades over the next few drives.
if: If you see fresh drips, or the smell gets stronger instead of fading, have the shop recheck the oil filter and drain plug right away.
If you see smoke from under the hood, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the oil level is low or the oil pressure light comes on, don't drive it. Call the shop that did the work.
result.why: It's easy to spill a little oil on the engine or exhaust during an oil change. It can smell for a few drives, then fade. A loose filter, drain plug or cap is the thing to rule out, and the shop that did the work can recheck it quickly.

causes.name: Spilled oil burning off
causes.clues: The smell is fading day by day, and there are no drips.

causes.name: Loose or double-gasketed oil filter
causes.clues: Fresh oil drips under the front of the engine.

causes.name: Loose drain plug or filler cap
causes.clues: Oil on the bottom of the engine, or sprayed around the cap.

you: Check the oil level and filler cap.
Put cardboard under the engine overnight.
shop: Recheck the oil filter and drain plug
Clean spilled oil off the engine and exhaust

result.title: A slow oil seep onto the exhaust, often from the valve cover gasket
result.now: Look for oily residue on top and down the sides of the engine, check the oil level weekly, and book a check.
if: If the oil level starts dropping or you see drips, get it checked within a few days.
If you see smoke from under the hood, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and shut it off right away.
result.why: A very small leak can drip onto the exhaust and cook, giving a strong smell long before the oil level drops. The valve cover gasket on top of the engine is a common source. A shop will usually clean the area or use dye to confirm the source before replacing a gasket.

causes.name: Valve cover gasket seep
causes.clues: Oily residue along the top edge of the engine.

causes.name: Oil filter housing or cooler gasket
causes.clues: Residue near the oil filter.

causes.name: Oil from a past spill or overfill
causes.clues: An oil change in the last few weeks.

you: Look for wet, oily areas on the engine with a flashlight.
Check the oil level weekly.
shop: Dye test if the source isn't clear

result.title: An active oil leak may be reaching hot parts
result.now: Don't keep using the car until the leak is checked. Top up the oil to the full mark with the type in your owner's manual, then have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to look at it.
if: If the oil level drops noticeably after the engine runs for a short time, don't run it again.
If you see smoke from under the hood or the oil light comes on, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn off the engine and step away from the car.
If the engine knocks or ticks loudly, don't start it again until it's checked.
result.why: A low oil level plus spots under the car means oil is escaping fast enough to matter. It can run the engine low and, if it lands on the exhaust, create smoke and a fire risk.

causes.name: Valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Oil running down the sides of the engine.

causes.name: Oil pan gasket or drain plug
causes.clues: Drips under the bottom of the engine.

causes.name: Front or rear main seal
causes.clues: Oil at the front of the engine behind the pulley, or where the engine meets the transmission.

you: Put cardboard under the engine overnight to see where it drips.
Track how much oil you add.

result.title: The oil may be dangerously low
result.now: Don't run the engine. Add oil of the type in your owner's manual until it reaches the full mark, a little at a time, rechecking as you go.
if: If it holds a full level, the oil light stays off and the engine sounds normal, that's encouraging but not proof the engine is unharmed. Have the leak or oil use found before relying on the car, and check the level before every start until then.
If it takes a lot of oil, you see oil pouring out, or the engine knocks or ticks loudly, don't run it. Have it towed.
result.why: With little or no oil on the dipstick, the engine's bearings and moving parts aren't being protected. Running it like that can ruin the engine quickly. The smell suggests some of the missing oil is ending up on hot parts.

causes.name: Significant oil leak
causes.clues: Oil spots under the car and oil on the engine.

causes.name: Engine burning oil
causes.clues: Blue-gray exhaust smoke and no visible leak.

causes.name: Missed oil changes
causes.clues: It's been a long time since the last oil change.

you: Add oil and recheck the level.
Look under the car for fresh oil.
shop: Engine noise and oil pressure check

result.title: Get the oil level and leaks checked soon
result.now: Have the oil level checked at a shop or parts store within a few days, and look under the car for fresh oil spots in the meantime.
if: If you see smoke from under the hood or the oil light comes on, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the engine starts knocking or ticking, stop driving it.
result.why: A burning oil smell usually means oil is somewhere it shouldn't be. Knowing the oil level tells you whether it's a small seep or something that could leave the engine short of oil.

causes.name: Oil seeping onto the exhaust
causes.clues: The smell is strongest after a drive, from the hood.

causes.name: Engine burning oil
causes.clues: Blue-gray smoke from the tailpipe.

causes.name: Spill from a recent oil change
causes.clues: Recent service, and the smell is fading.

you: Look for fresh oil spots under the car.
Note when the smell is strongest.

q_smoke.q: Do you see smoke, or does anything else feel wrong along with the smell?
q_smoke.help: Look at each wheel and at the hood. Smoke near one wheel almost always means a brake problem.

opts.a: Smoke from one wheel, or one wheel is much hotter than the others
Smoke from under the hood

No smoke, just the smell

q_when.q: When do you notice the smell?

opts.a: After a long downhill, heavy braking, or pulling a trailer
After driving with the parking brake partly on
From under the hood, often with a squeal on startup or when the A/C kicks on
When pulling away or going uphill in a manual car
During normal driving, with no obvious reason

q_drive_feel.q: Does the car feel or sound different while you drive?
q_drive_feel.help: A brake that won't fully let go makes the car feel like it's being held back, as if you're driving with the brakes lightly on.

opts.a: It feels held back, pulls to one side, or coasts poorly
A rubbing or scraping sound, especially when turning or over bumps
It drives normally, the smell just comes and goes
It smells more like burning plastic than rubber
I'm not sure

result.title: A brake may be stuck on and overheating, or the brake system may have a problem
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, turn off the engine and let the brakes cool. Don't drive it further. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If there are flames or the smoke gets heavier, get everyone away from the car and call 911.

If the parking brake was on, release it fully and let everything cool for at least 30 minutes. Even if the smell clears, overheated brakes can be weakened, so have them checked before driving further.
If the brake pedal feels soft, sinks, or the red brake warning light is on, the brakes may not stop the car normally. Don't drive it, even after it cools.
result.why: When a brake doesn't release, it rubs constantly and builds up a lot of heat. That heat can boil the brake fluid and burn the pads, which can leave you with weak or failing brakes. A soft pedal or red brake light can also mean the hydraulic system is losing pressure. In rare cases an overheated brake can start a fire.

causes.name: Stuck brake caliper
causes.clues: Smoke or smell from one wheel, the car pulls to one side, or that wheel is far hotter than the others.
causes.against: If all four wheels feel about the same, a single stuck caliper is less likely.

causes.name: Parking brake not fully released or sticking
causes.clues: It's coming from a rear wheel, or the parking brake light stayed on.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose holding pressure on one wheel
causes.clues: The problem started or got worse after heavy braking.
causes.against: Less common than a stuck caliper.

causes.name: Low brake fluid or a hydraulic problem
causes.clues: The pedal feels soft or sinks, or the red brake light stays on with the parking brake released.

you: Without touching anything, look for smoke near each wheel.
Check that the parking brake is fully released.
Once everything is cool, check the brake fluid level in the reservoir.
shop: Brake inspection with the wheels off
Brake hose and fluid condition check
Wheel temperature comparison after a short test

result.title: Something under the hood is burning or slipping badly
result.now: If you see smoke and think your car may be on fire, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine. Get everyone out. Leave the hood closed. Move at least 100 feet from the car and stay away from traffic. Call 911 from a safe spot, even if you can't see flames. Once it has cooled and there's no fire, have it towed.
if: If the smoke stops once the engine is off and you can see a shredded or missing belt, it still needs a tow. The belt often drives the water pump and the charging system.
If the temperature gauge was climbing or a red warning light came on, don't restart the engine.
result.why: Smoke from under the hood with a rubber smell usually means a belt is slipping or shredding, a hose is melting against something hot, or fluid is burning on the engine. Any of these can lead to overheating, a dead battery or a fire if you keep driving.

causes.name: Slipping or failing drive belt
causes.clues: A loud squeal, a battery or temperature warning, or heavy steering.

causes.name: Seized pulley, A/C compressor or other belt-driven part
causes.clues: A grinding or squealing noise that started recently.

causes.name: Hose or wiring touching a hot part
causes.clues: A smell that's more like melting plastic, or a hose that's been recently worked on.

causes.name: Oil or fluid leaking onto the hot exhaust
causes.clues: A recent oil change or a known leak, and blue-gray smoke.

shop: Drive belt, tensioner and pulley inspection
Check of belt-driven parts for a seized bearing

result.title: The brakes may have gotten very hot from heavy use
result.now: If you can, pull over safely and let the brakes cool for 20–30 minutes. On long downhills, use a lower gear so the engine helps slow the car and you don't ride the brakes.
if: If the pedal felt soft, sank, or the car took longer to stop, don't drive on after it cools. Have the brakes and brake fluid checked first. Overheated fluid can leave the brakes weak.
If the smell keeps coming back during normal driving, a brake may be dragging. Get it checked within a few days.
If you see smoke from a wheel, one wheel stays much hotter than the others, or the car pulls to one side, don't drive further until the brakes are checked.
result.why: Long downhill stretches and heavy loads make the brakes work hard. The pads can get hot enough to give off a sharp, burnt smell. A one-time smell after that kind of driving is common, but very hot brakes don't stop as well until they cool.

causes.name: Brakes overheated from heavy use
causes.clues: It happened on a steep descent, in mountain driving, or while hauling.
causes.against: If the smell shows up on flat roads with light braking, look for a dragging brake instead.
