causes.name: New brake pads bedding in
causes.clues: The pads were replaced recently.

causes.name: Dragging brake made worse by heavy use
causes.clues: One wheel stays much hotter, or the smell lingers after it cools.

you: After it cools, see if the car rolls freely and doesn't pull to one side.
Notice whether the smell returns during normal, gentle driving.
shop: Brake fluid condition and moisture test

result.title: The parking brake may have been rubbing while you drove
result.now: Release the parking brake fully, check that its warning light goes out, and let the wheels cool before driving on.
if: If the smell continues once it's fully released, the parking brake may be sticking. Have it checked within a few days.
If you drove a long way with it on, have the rear brakes inspected. The pads or shoes may be glazed or worn.
If the pedal feels soft or different, the car takes longer to stop, or the red brake light stays on after release, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
If you see smoke from a wheel, keep clear and let it cool.
result.why: Driving with the parking brake partly on makes the rear brakes rub the whole time. That creates heat and a strong burnt smell. Once it's released and cooled, the smell usually fades. If it doesn't, something may still be dragging.

causes.name: Parking brake not fully released
causes.clues: The parking brake light was on, or you forgot to release it.

causes.name: Sticking parking brake cable or mechanism
causes.clues: It was released, but a rear wheel still drags. This is more common in winter or on older cars.

you: Make sure the parking brake lever, pedal or button is fully off.
After cooling, push the car gently on a flat surface to see if it rolls freely.
shop: Parking brake cable and adjustment check
Electronic parking brake scan if equipped

result.title: A drive belt may be slipping
result.now: Have the belt, tensioner and pulleys checked within the next few days. Keep trips short until then.
if: If the battery light or temperature warning comes on, or steering gets heavy, pull over and stop. The belt may have broken. Have it towed.
If you see smoke from under the hood, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn off the engine and don't drive it.
result.why: The drive belt runs the alternator, and on many cars the water pump and power steering. When it slips over a pulley, the friction makes a burnt rubber smell and often a squeal. A slipping belt can wear through and snap. A shop will usually check the tensioner and pulleys before replacing the belt, since a bad pulley will ruin a new belt.

causes.name: Worn or glazed drive belt
causes.clues: Cracks or a shiny surface on the belt, and a squeal on cold starts.

causes.name: Weak belt tensioner
causes.clues: The tensioner arm bounces or the belt flaps at idle.

causes.name: Pulley or belt-driven part starting to seize
causes.clues: The smell is worse with the A/C on, or there's a grinding or whirring noise.

causes.name: Fluid on the belt
causes.clues: A leak of oil, coolant or power steering fluid near the front of the engine.

you: With the engine off, look at the belt for cracks, fraying or a shiny glazed surface.
Notice whether the smell or squeal gets worse with the A/C on.
shop: Check of belt-driven parts for bearing noise

result.title: The clutch is likely slipping or being overworked
result.now: Have the clutch checked within a few days. Until then, pull away gently and avoid resting your foot on the clutch pedal.
if: If the engine revs rise but the car doesn't speed up to match, the clutch is slipping. Get it checked as soon as you can.
If you see smoke from under the car or it won't move in gear, stop and have it towed.
result.why: A clutch that slips turns engine power into heat instead of motion, which gives off a sharp burnt smell. A single smell after a tricky hill start is common. A smell that keeps coming back often means the clutch is worn.

causes.name: Worn clutch
causes.clues: The engine revs climb in high gears without the car speeding up, especially uphill.

causes.name: Driving habit (riding the clutch or slow hill starts)
causes.clues: It only happens after hill starts, heavy loads or stop-and-go traffic.

causes.name: Oil contaminating the clutch
causes.clues: A known engine or transmission oil leak, and grabbing or slipping.

you: On a quiet, safe road, in a high gear at a low speed, press the gas firmly once. If the revs jump without the car speeding up, the clutch is slipping. Don't repeat it, since each try adds heat.
Notice whether the clutch now engages higher in the pedal travel than it used to.
shop: Inspection for oil leaks at the bellhousing

result.title: A brake may be dragging
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, turn off the engine and let the brakes cool. Don't drive further until the brakes are checked. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see smoke from a wheel, keep everyone clear and let it cool. Call 911 if you see flames.
If the brake pedal feels soft, sinks, or the red brake light comes on, the brakes may not stop the car normally. Don't move it.
If the parking brake was partly on, release it fully and let everything cool. Overheated brakes can still be weakened, so have them checked before relying on the car.
result.why: When a brake doesn't fully let go, it rubs constantly. That makes the car feel held back, can pull it to one side, and creates a hot, burnt smell. A brake hot enough to smell can fade and stop the car less well, and it can overheat further if you keep driving.

causes.name: Sticking caliper or caliper slides
causes.clues: The car pulls to one side, and one wheel is hotter or has more brake dust.

causes.name: Sticking parking brake
causes.clues: The drag seems to come from the rear.

causes.name: Worn brake hose or brake fluid problem
causes.clues: More than one wheel drags, or the pedal feels different.

you: After it has cooled, carefully hold your hand near (not on) each wheel to compare heat. Don't drive just to test it.
Look for one wheel with much more brake dust than the others.
shop: Brake inspection with the wheels off

result.title: Something may be rubbing on a tire or touching the hot exhaust
result.now: When the car has cooled, look under it and around the tires for a plastic bag, loose shield, sagging hose or rubbed tire. Book a check if you can't find the source.
if: If a tire shows a bald strip, bulge or rubbed sidewall, have it looked at before your next drive.
If the smell gets stronger or you see smoke, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the car starts pulling to one side or feels held back, a brake may be dragging. Pull over, let it cool, and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: A smell that comes and goes, without any change in how the car drives, often comes from something brushing a tire when you turn, or a bit of plastic or rubber stuck on the hot exhaust. These are usually easy to fix once found.

causes.name: Debris stuck on the exhaust
causes.clues: You recently drove over trash or a plastic bag, and the smell is strongest after you stop.

causes.name: Tire rubbing on the fender liner or a part
causes.clues: A rubbing sound when turning or over bumps, new or larger tires, or a loose plastic liner.

causes.name: Hose or wire resting on a hot part
causes.clues: The smell comes from under the hood, and a hose or clip looks out of place.

causes.name: Small oil leak dripping onto the exhaust
causes.clues: Oily spots under the engine, or a smell more like hot oil.

you: Once everything is cool, look under the car and along the exhaust for anything stuck to it.
Turn the steering fully each way and look for rub marks on the tires and liners.

result.title: A burning plastic smell can be wiring, or plastic touching something hot
result.now: Don't drive it until you know where the smell is coming from. Park, turn off the engine, and once it's cool, look under the car for plastic stuck to the exhaust. If you can't find an outside source, or the smell comes from the dash, vents or under the hood, have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see smoke from the dash, vents or under the hood, pull over, turn off the engine and get out.
If a fuse keeps blowing or something electrical stops working along with the smell, don't drive it until it's checked.
If you find only a melted bag or bit of plastic on the exhaust, have it removed once everything is cool. If the smell keeps coming back after that, have the car checked.
result.why: A burning plastic smell can come from something minor, like a bag melting on the exhaust. It can also come from overheated wiring, a failing blower motor or a short circuit, which can lead to a fire. From the driver's seat there's no reliable way to tell which, so it's worth finding the source before driving on.

causes.name: Plastic stuck to the exhaust
causes.clues: The smell is strongest outside the car, near the back or underneath.

causes.name: Overheating electrical part or wiring
causes.clues: The smell comes through the vents or dash, or something electrical acts up.

causes.name: Failing heater blower motor or resistor
causes.clues: The smell starts when the fan is on, or some fan speeds don't work.

you: Notice whether the smell changes when you turn the fan, heater or A/C on and off.
Once cool, look under the car for melted plastic on the exhaust.
shop: Electrical system inspection for heat damage

result.title: Have the brakes and belts checked to find the source
result.now: Note when the smell shows up and where it seems strongest, then have the brakes and under-hood area inspected within a few days.
if: If you see smoke, the brake pedal changes, or a warning light comes on, pull over and stop.
If the smell gets stronger with each drive, get it checked within a day or two.
If one wheel is much hotter than the others or the car pulls to one side, a brake may be dragging. Don't drive further until it's checked.
result.why: Most burning rubber smells come from the brakes, a belt, the clutch or something touching the exhaust. A technician can usually narrow down the source with a careful look and a short test drive.

causes.name: Dragging brake
causes.clues: The smell is near a wheel, or the car feels held back.

causes.name: Slipping drive belt
causes.clues: The smell is under the hood, with a squeal.

causes.name: Something touching the exhaust
causes.clues: The smell is strongest after you park.

you: Write down when you notice the smell and whether it's stronger near one wheel or the hood.

q_danger.q: Is there any smoke, or is a warning light or the temperature gauge telling you something's wrong?

opts.a: Yes, there's smoke from under the hood or around a wheel
The temperature gauge is high, or a red warning light is on
No smoke and no warning lights
I'm not sure

q_type.help: Smells are easiest to tell apart right after you stop. Step out and sniff near the hood and each wheel.

opts.a: Burning oil: sharp and acrid, like a hot frying pan
Burning rubber, or hot brakes (often described as burning carpet)
Burning plastic or hot wiring
Sweet, like syrup or maple
A burnt, acrid smell while the clutch slips on a manual car
I'm not sure

q_rubber.q: When and where do you notice it?

opts.a: Near one wheel, and that wheel is much hotter than the others or the car pulls to one side
After going down a long hill, towing, or a lot of hard braking
From the engine, along with a squeal when starting or turning
Under the car, like something got caught on the exhaust
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When is the smell strongest?

opts.a: From the vents, the first few times I use the heat this season
Near one wheel after driving
From the hood after I park
After an oil change or other engine work in the last few days
I'm not sure

result.title: Something is hot enough to smoke. Treat it as a fire risk
result.now: If you see smoke and think your car may be on fire, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine. Get everyone out. Leave the hood closed. Move at least 100 feet from the car and stay away from traffic. Call 911 from a safe spot, even if you can't see flames.
if: If the smoke stops once the engine is off and you can see it was oil or coolant on a hot part, it still needs repair before the car is used again.
If the smoke is at a wheel, the brake may be stuck on. Don't touch the wheel. It can be extremely hot.
If the brake pedal felt soft or the car was harder to stop, tell the tow driver and the shop.
result.why: Smoke usually means oil, coolant, plastic or a brake part is burning or boiling. Any of those can turn into a fire, and it's impossible to tell how bad it is while driving.

causes.name: Oil or fluid leaking onto the exhaust
causes.clues: Blue-gray smoke from under the hood with a burning oil smell.

causes.name: Coolant boiling over
causes.clues: White, sweet-smelling steam, often with a high temperature gauge.

causes.name: Brake stuck on
causes.clues: Smoke at one wheel, and that wheel is very hot.

causes.name: Electrical short
causes.clues: Burning plastic smell, sometimes with a blown fuse or dead accessories.

shop: Engine bay inspection for leaks and burn marks

result.title: The engine may be overheating or losing oil
result.now: Pull over safely and turn off the engine. Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If the oil pressure light was on, don't restart the engine. It can be destroyed within minutes without oil pressure.
Never open the radiator or coolant cap while the engine is hot.
If you see steam or smoke from under the hood, step away from the car and don't open the hood until it has cooled.
result.why: A burning smell with a high temperature reading or a red warning light can mean the engine is in trouble right now. Overheating and low oil pressure both cause serious damage quickly.

causes.name: Coolant leak and overheating
causes.clues: A sweet smell, steam, or the temperature gauge in the red.

causes.name: Very low engine oil
causes.clues: The oil pressure light is on and you smell burning oil.

causes.name: Charging system fault
causes.clues: The battery light is on, with a burning rubber or electrical smell.

you: Once the engine is fully cold, check the oil and coolant levels.
shop: Code scan and charging system check

result.title: Oil may be dripping onto the hot exhaust
result.now: With the engine off and on level ground, check the oil level and top it up if needed. Get the leak checked within a few days.
if: If you see smoke from under the hood, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the oil is below the lowest mark on the dipstick, don't drive it until it's topped up.
If the car just had an oil change, a little spilled oil may be burning off. That often fades within a few drives. If it doesn't, have the shop that did the work recheck it.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the temperature gauge rises, pull over and turn off the engine.
result.why: A burning oil smell often comes from a small leak above the exhaust. The oil cooks on hot metal and the smell comes into the cabin through the vents. A gasket is a common source, and leaks tend to get worse. A shop will usually confirm the source before replacing anything.

causes.name: Leaking valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Oily residue on top of the engine, with the smell strongest after a drive.

causes.name: Spilled oil from a recent oil change
causes.clues: The smell started right after an oil change and is fading.

causes.name: Loose oil filter, drain plug or filler cap
causes.clues: Fresh drips under the car or oil sprayed around the filler cap.

you: Check the oil level.
Look for oily residue on top of the engine and drips under the car.
shop: Dye test if the source isn't clear

result.title: A burning plastic smell may be an electrical short
result.now: Pull over, turn off the engine and don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic check it.
if: If you see smoke or flames, get everyone out and away from the car and call 911.

If you find a plastic bag stuck on the exhaust and the smell is completely gone once it's removed (with everything cool), an electrical fault is less likely. If the smell returns, have the car checked before driving it.
result.why: Burning plastic or hot wiring can mean a wire, connector or electrical part is overheating. That can melt insulation and start a fire, so it's not something to drive on.

causes.name: Shorted or overheating wiring
causes.clues: A sharp electrical smell, blown fuses, or things that stop working.

causes.name: Failing blower motor or resistor
causes.clues: The smell comes from the vents and the fan acts strangely or only works on some speeds.

causes.name: Plastic stuck on the exhaust
causes.clues: The smell is strongest outside, under the car.

causes.name: Aftermarket accessory wiring
causes.clues: A recently added stereo, lights, charger or dash cam.

you: Once the car is off and cool, look under the car for plastic stuck to the exhaust.
shop: Electrical inspection for melted wiring or connectors

result.title: A sweet smell often points to a coolant leak
result.now: Check the coolant overflow tank level when the engine is cold, top it up if needed, and get it checked within a few days. Watch your temperature gauge.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the smell is strong inside the car or the windshield fogs with a greasy film, the heater core may be leaking. Keep the windows cracked, and don't drive if the windshield fogs and won't clear.
If you see steam from under the hood, or the coolant level drops again quickly after topping up, don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: Coolant has a sweet, syrupy smell when it hits hot engine parts. Even a small leak can drain the system over time and lead to overheating.

causes.name: Leaking radiator hose or clamp
causes.clues: Crusty residue on a hose, or drips under the front of the car.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: The smell is strongest inside, with a damp passenger carpet or foggy windshield.

causes.name: Water pump or radiator leak
causes.clues: Drips at the front of the engine or under the radiator.

you: Check the coolant level when cold.
Look for drips or crusty residue around hoses.

result.title: The clutch may be overheating, often from slipping or riding it
result.now: Take your foot fully off the clutch pedal while driving and avoid slipping it on hills. Book a check if the smell comes back without heavy use.
if: If the engine revs rise but the car doesn't speed up, the clutch is slipping. Get it checked within a few days.
If the smell came from one hard hill start or getting unstuck, let it cool. It may be a one-off.
If you see smoke from under the car or it won't move in gear, stop and have it towed.
result.why: A clutch works by friction. Slipping it, riding the pedal or a worn clutch makes heat, and the friction material gives off a sharp burnt smell.

causes.name: Driving habits (riding or slipping the clutch)
causes.clues: It happens on hill starts, in heavy traffic or when towing.

causes.name: Worn clutch
causes.clues: The engine revs up without the car speeding up, especially in higher gears.

causes.name: Oil on the clutch from a leak
causes.clues: Oil drips where the engine meets the transmission.

you: On a quiet, safe road, in a high gear at low speed, press the gas firmly once. If the revs jump but the car doesn't speed up, the clutch is slipping. Don't repeat it, since each try adds heat.
shop: Leak check at the rear main seal

result.title: A brake may be stuck on and dragging
result.now: Pull over and let it cool. Don't touch the wheel. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If the parking brake was left on, release it and let the brakes cool. Even if the smell and pull go away, overheated brakes can be weakened, so have them checked before relying on the car.
If you see smoke at the wheel, stand well back.
If the brake pedal feels soft, sinks, or the red brake light is on, don't move the car.
result.why: When a brake doesn't release, it keeps rubbing and gets extremely hot. That can make the brakes fade, damage the parts, and in bad cases start a fire.

causes.name: Sticking brake caliper
causes.clues: One wheel much hotter than the others and the car pulls to that side.

causes.name: Parking brake not fully released
causes.clues: The smell comes from the rear wheels, or the parking brake light is on.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose
causes.clues: The drag comes and goes, and the caliper looks fine.

you: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.

result.title: Your brakes may have overheated from heavy use
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe and let the brakes cool for 15–30 minutes. On long downhills, shift to a lower gear so the engine helps slow the car.
if: If the pedal felt soft, sank, or the brakes faded, don't drive on after they cool. Have them checked before driving further.
If the smell comes back during normal driving, a brake may be dragging. Get it checked soon.
If you see smoke from a wheel, one wheel stays much hotter than the others, or the car pulls to one side, a brake may be dragging. Don't drive further until it's checked.
result.why: Long downhill braking or towing can heat brake pads past their comfort zone, and they give off a sharp smell. It often goes away once they cool, but very hot brakes don't stop as well, and repeated overheating can damage the pads, rotors and fluid.

causes.name: Brakes overheated on a long descent or while towing
causes.clues: The smell appeared after a long hill or a heavy load.

causes.name: New pads still bedding in
causes.clues: The brakes were just replaced.

causes.name: Dragging brake
causes.clues: One wheel hotter than the others, even after normal driving.

you: Once cool, press the pedal. If it feels soft or sinks, don't drive it. A firm pedal is a good sign, but it isn't proof the brakes weren't damaged.
After a normal drive, carefully hold your hand near each wheel (without touching) to see if one is much hotter.

result.title: A slipping drive belt may be causing the burning rubber smell
result.now: With the engine off, look at the belt for cracks, glazing or fraying, and get it checked within a few days.
if: If the battery light comes on, the steering gets heavy or the temperature rises, pull over and turn off the engine. The belt may have broken. Have it towed.
If the belt is visibly frayed or missing pieces, don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: The drive belt runs the alternator, power steering and often the water pump. When it slips on a pulley it heats up and smells like burning rubber. A stuck pulley or a weak tensioner is often behind it, so a shop will usually check those before replacing the belt.

causes.name: Worn or loose drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal at startup or when turning the wheel, and a shiny, cracked belt.

causes.name: Seized or dragging pulley
causes.clues: A pulley that grinds or won't spin freely.

causes.name: Weak belt tensioner
causes.clues: The belt flutters or jumps while the engine runs.

you: With the engine off, look at the belt for cracks and shiny, glazed sides.

result.title: Something may be stuck on the hot exhaust
result.now: Once the car has cooled for at least 30 minutes, look under the car along the exhaust for a plastic bag, leaves or other debris and carefully remove it.
if: If you can't reach it or it's melted on, have a shop remove it.
If the smell continues with nothing stuck there, get it checked within a few days.
If you see smoke and think the car may be on fire, get everyone out, leave the hood closed, move at least 100 feet away and call 911, even if you can't see flames.
result.why: Plastic bags, road debris and leaves can wrap around the exhaust and melt or smolder. It smells alarming, but once it's removed the smell usually goes away.

causes.name: Plastic bag or debris on the exhaust
causes.clues: The smell is strongest outside the car, under the middle.

causes.name: Leaves under the heat shield
causes.clues: You recently parked on or drove through leaves.

causes.name: Fluid leak onto the exhaust
causes.clues: Oily residue or drips near the exhaust.

you: With the exhaust cool, look along it for debris.

result.title: It may be dust burning off the heater
result.now: Run the heat on high for a few minutes with a window cracked. If it's dust, the smell usually fades within minutes.
if: If the smell lasts more than a day or two of use, or smells like plastic, have the blower motor and wiring checked.
If the smell is sweet or the windshield fogs, it may be a heater core leak. Check your coolant level.
If you see smoke from the vents or dash, pull over, turn off the engine and get out.
result.why: Dust settles on the heating parts over the summer. The first few times you use the heat, it can burn off with a brief, dusty smell. That's common and normally fades quickly.

causes.name: Dust on the heater parts
causes.clues: First use of the season, and the smell fades in minutes.

causes.name: Dirty cabin air filter
causes.clues: Weak airflow and a musty or dusty smell.

causes.name: Failing blower motor or resistor
causes.clues: A plastic or electrical smell, or the fan only works on some speeds.

you: Check whether the smell fades after a few minutes.
Look at the cabin air filter (your owner's manual shows where).

result.title: Hard to pin down without a look. Get it checked within a few days
result.now: Check your oil and coolant levels when the engine is cool, look under the car for drips or debris, and get it checked within a few days.
if: If you see smoke or the smell becomes plastic-like or electrical, pull over and turn off the engine.
If a warning light comes on or the temperature gauge rises, stop driving it.
result.why: Burning smells come from oil, coolant, brakes, belts, the clutch or wiring. A technician can usually find the source quickly by looking for leaks, hot spots and burn marks.

causes.name: Oil leaking onto the exhaust
causes.clues: The smell is strongest at the hood after a drive.

causes.name: Dragging brake
causes.clues: The smell is near one wheel.

causes.name: Slipping belt
causes.clues: A squeal from the engine.

you: Note when the smell happens and where it's strongest.
Check the oil and coolant levels.

q_what_happens.q: What happens when you try to start it?
q_what_happens.help: Cranking is the rrr-rrr-rrr sound of the engine turning over before it fires. A slow crank sounds drawn out and labored, like rrrr... rrrr... rrrr.

opts.a: It cranks slowly but does start
It cranks slowly, then gives up or turns into clicking
I smell burning or see smoke near the engine or battery
The engine turns a little, then stops hard with a thunk, or this started after driving through deep water
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When is the slow crank worst?

opts.a: On cold mornings
When the engine is hot, right after a drive
After the car has sat for a few days
Every time, and it's slowly getting worse
I'm not sure

q_jump.q: Does a jump start or battery booster make it crank at normal speed?

opts.a: Yes, it cranks quickly and starts
No, it's still slow even with a good jump
I haven't tried one
I'm not sure

result.title: A cable, connection or the starter may be overheating
result.now: Stop trying to start it and step away from the car. Once nothing is smoking, have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If smoke keeps coming or you see flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
If the smell was only faint and faded right away, still don't keep cranking. A shorted cable can start a fire.
result.why: A burning smell while cranking usually means a lot of current is going somewhere it shouldn't, or the starter is straining against something. Heavy battery and starter cables carry enough power to melt insulation.

causes.name: Starter motor overheating or shorted
causes.clues: Smell or smoke from low on the engine, after long or repeated cranking.

causes.name: Damaged or shorted battery cable
causes.clues: Melted or chafed insulation, or a cable that's hot to the touch.

causes.name: Engine not turning freely
causes.clues: The crank was labored or stopped abruptly.

shop: Battery cable and starter wiring inspection
Check that the engine turns freely by hand

result.title: Something may be stopping the engine from turning
result.now: Don't keep trying to start it. Have it towed to a shop.
if: If this happened after driving through deep water, water may be in the engine. Cranking it again can bend internal parts.
result.why: A healthy engine spins evenly when cranking, even if slowly. If it stops hard with a thunk, something inside may be blocking it, such as water or coolant in a cylinder, or a seized part. Forcing it with the starter can turn a fixable problem into a major one.

causes.name: Water or coolant in a cylinder
causes.clues: Recent deep water, white smoke before, or coolant level dropping.

causes.name: Seized or damaged engine part
causes.clues: Knocking, an oil light or low oil before this started.

causes.name: Starter gear jamming
causes.clues: A grinding sound, and the engine seemed fine before.

you: Check the oil level on the dipstick without starting the engine.
shop: Turn the engine over by hand
Check cylinders for water or coolant

result.title: The battery may be getting weak, and cold makes it show
result.now: Have the battery tested soon. Many auto parts stores do this free. A load test shows whether it needs replacing, which is more likely if it's more than 4 years old.
if: If the battery tests good, ask for a charging test and check the battery cables for corrosion.
If the slow crank turns into clicking, it's close to leaving you stranded. Have the battery charged and tested right away.
If you smell burning or see smoke near the battery, cables or starter, stop trying to start it.
result.why: Cold weather lowers how much power a battery can deliver and makes engine oil thicker, so the starter has to work harder. A battery that's starting to fail often shows it first on cold mornings.

causes.name: Aging battery
causes.clues: It's more than 4 years old, and it's fine once the day warms up.

causes.name: Corroded or loose battery cables
causes.clues: Buildup on the terminals.

causes.name: Oil that's too thick for the season
causes.clues: A recent oil change with a different oil than your owner's manual lists.

you: Check the date on the battery.
Look at the terminals for buildup.
Check your owner's manual for the right oil.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the battery cables

result.title: The starter may be wearing out, especially when hot
result.now: Have the battery and starter tested at your next opportunity. A shop can measure how much power the starter draws.
if: If it sometimes won't crank at all when hot, but starts after it cools, the starter or its wiring may be close to failing. Get it checked soon.
If it's also slow when cold, start with the battery and cables.
If you smell burning while cranking, stop trying to start it.
result.why: Heat from the engine raises the electrical resistance in a worn starter and its cables. A starter that's on its way out often cranks slowly or not at all when hot, then works again once things cool down. A shop will usually test the cables and ground connections before replacing the starter.

causes.name: Worn starter motor
causes.clues: Slow or no crank only when the engine is hot.

causes.name: Poor cable connection at the starter or ground
causes.clues: It comes and goes, and the battery tests fine.

causes.name: Weak battery
causes.clues: It's also slow on cold mornings.
causes.against: If it's only slow when hot, the battery is less likely.

you: Note whether it only happens after a drive.
Check the battery terminals.
shop: Voltage-drop test on starter cables and ground

result.title: The battery may be draining while the car sits
result.now: Have the battery tested. If it's healthy, watch whether the slow crank only happens after the car sits.
if: If it only happens after a week or more of sitting, a battery maintainer may be all you need.
If it happens after just a night or two, ask a shop for a parasitic draw test.
If the battery is swollen, cracked or leaking, don't jump or charge it. Have it replaced by a shop.
result.why: Cars use a little power even when off. If something stays on, or the battery is aging, a few days of sitting leaves too little charge to spin the starter at full speed.

causes.name: Something staying on while parked
causes.clues: A trunk, glove box or dome light that stays on, or an added accessory.

causes.name: Aging battery
causes.clues: It's more than 4 years old.

causes.name: Short trips not recharging the battery
causes.clues: Mostly drives of a few minutes.

you: Check for lights that stay on after you lock the car.
Check the date on the battery.

result.title: Often a weak battery or a poor battery connection
result.now: Check that the battery clamps are clean and tight, then have the battery and charging system tested. Many auto parts stores do this free.
if: If the battery and cables test fine, the starter is the next thing to test. A shop will usually do a voltage-drop test on the cables before replacing the starter.
If the battery light has come on while driving, have the alternator tested too.
If you smell burning or see smoke while cranking, stop trying to start it.
If the engine was knocking, or the oil light was on before this started, don't keep cranking. Have it checked.
result.why: The starter needs a big burst of power. A weak battery or a corroded connection can't deliver it, so the engine turns slowly. These are common causes and the easiest to check.

causes.name: Weak or aging battery
causes.clues: It's more than 4 years old, or it's worse on cold mornings.

causes.name: Corroded or loose battery cable or ground
causes.clues: Buildup on the terminals, or a clamp that moves by hand.

causes.name: Worn starter
causes.clues: The battery tests good but the crank is still slow.

you: Check the battery terminals.
Check the date on the battery.
Try a jump start and see if it cranks faster.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the battery cables

result.title: The battery may be low. Find out why before it leaves you stranded
result.now: If it started on a jump, a longer drive helps put some charge back, but it won't fully recharge a flat battery. Get the battery and charging system tested within the next few days.
if: If the battery light comes on while driving, the alternator may not be charging and the car could stall once the battery runs down. Get it to a shop as soon as possible, and avoid long trips and night driving.
If the battery is more than 4 years old, a load test will show whether it needs replacing.
result.why: A jump fixing the slow crank suggests the battery didn't have enough charge. The question is whether the battery is worn out, isn't being recharged, or is being drained while parked.

causes.name: Aging battery
causes.clues: More than 4 years old, or slow cranks on cold mornings.

causes.name: Alternator not charging
causes.clues: The battery light flickers or stays on, or the lights dim at idle.

causes.name: Drain while parked
causes.clues: It's worst after the car sits.

you: Watch for the battery warning light.
Check the date on the battery.

result.title: Possibly a failing starter or a bad cable connection
result.now: Check that the battery clamps are clean and tight. If it still cranks slowly with a good jump, book a starter and cable test.
if: If it stops cranking altogether, have it towed or call a mobile mechanic rather than cranking over and over.
If you smell burning while cranking, stop right away.
If the engine was knocking, or the oil light was on before this started, don't keep cranking. The engine itself may be hard to turn.
result.why: When a good jump doesn't speed up the crank, the battery is less likely to be the main problem. Power may be getting lost in a cable or ground connection, or the starter itself may be worn and drawing too much current. A shop will usually test the cables before replacing the starter.

causes.name: Worn starter motor
causes.clues: It's worse when hot, or it has been getting slower over months.

causes.name: Corroded cable or engine ground strap
causes.clues: A cable that's warm after cranking, or corrosion at either end.

causes.name: Engine harder to turn than normal
causes.clues: Wrong oil, or a recent engine problem.

you: Clean and tighten the battery clamps.
Look for a loose or broken ground strap between the engine and body.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the positive cable and ground

q_how.q: What happens as the engine dies?
q_how.help: If your car has a tachometer (RPM gauge), watch it as you slow down. A normal warm idle usually sits somewhere under 1,000 RPM and stays steady.

opts.a: It jolts or shudders to a stop, like stalling a stick-shift car without the clutch
The RPMs dip low or the idle gets rough, then it fades out
It cuts out instantly with no dip, like it was switched off
It's a manual and it dies as I stop
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When is it most likely to die?

opts.a: When I press the brake, and the pedal feels hard or I hear a hiss
When the engine is cold, then it's better once warm
When the A/C, headlights or rear defroster are on, or as I turn the wheel
Mostly once the engine is fully warm
No clear pattern / I'm not sure

q_manual.q: Are you pressing the clutch in before the engine speed drops too low?

opts.a: Yes, the clutch is in and it still dies
Not always. It happens when I brake without the clutch
I'm not sure

result.title: The transmission may not be disengaging from the engine as you stop
result.now: Don't drive it until it's checked. It may stall again at the next stop. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic to scan the transmission.
if: If a check engine or transmission light is on, the stored codes can help point the shop in the right direction.
If it only happened once and you can't repeat it, still have it scanned before relying on the car in traffic.
result.why: An automatic has a lock-up clutch inside the torque converter that links the engine directly to the transmission at cruising speed. It's supposed to release as you slow down. If it stays locked, the car drags the engine down like stalling a manual car.

causes.name: Torque converter clutch solenoid stuck
causes.clues: A jolt right as you stop, often with a transmission code.
causes.against: If the RPMs fade slowly instead of a jolt, an idle problem is more likely.

causes.name: Low or worn transmission fluid
causes.clues: Harsh shifts, slipping, or a reddish leak.

causes.name: Faulty torque converter
causes.clues: Shudder at steady speeds as well.

you: Note any transmission or check engine light.
Look for red or brown fluid under the car.
shop: Transmission fluid level and condition check

result.title: A sensor or electrical fault may be cutting the engine
result.now: Don't drive it until it's diagnosed. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic scan for codes.
if: If it also shuts off while driving at speed, see our guide on stalling while driving. It's the same family of problems.
If the dash lights flicker or go out as it dies, mention it. That can point to wiring or the ignition switch.
result.why: A smooth idle that suddenly stops, with no dip or roughness, often means the engine lost spark or fuel all at once. That's more typical of a sensor or a loose electrical connection than an idle problem. A shop will usually check codes and wiring before replacing a sensor.

causes.name: Failing crankshaft position sensor
causes.clues: It happens when warm and restarts after cooling.

causes.name: Loose wiring, ground or relay
causes.clues: It happens over bumps or comes and goes.

causes.name: Worn ignition switch
causes.clues: The dash lights blink off as it dies.

you: Note whether the dash lights go out as it dies.
Check your VIN for open recalls.

result.title: A leak in the brake booster may be stalling the engine
result.now: Don't drive it. Brake assist may be reduced. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic inspect the booster and vacuum hose.
if: If the pedal also sinks toward the floor, there may be a brake fluid problem too. Don't drive it under any circumstances.
result.why: The brake booster uses engine vacuum to make braking easier. If the booster or its hose leaks, pressing the brake lets a big rush of air into the engine. The idle drops or stalls, and the pedal gets harder to push.

causes.name: Leaking brake booster
causes.clues: A hiss when you press the brake, and the idle dips each time.

causes.name: Cracked or loose booster vacuum hose
causes.clues: A hiss from the engine bay near the brake pedal side.

causes.name: Faulty booster check valve
causes.clues: The pedal is hard on the first press after starting.

you: With the engine idling and the car in Park, press the brake and listen for a hiss.
shop: Vacuum hose and check valve inspection

result.title: The idle control or a temperature sensor may be off when the engine is cold
result.now: Get it checked within the next few days. Until then, let the engine warm up for a minute before you drive, and leave extra room at stops.
if: If it starts dying when warm too, stalls more than once in a trip, or ever stalls while turning or crossing traffic, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the check engine light comes on, a code scan will help the shop.
If the brake pedal feels hard or the car is harder to stop, don't drive it.
If it does stall while moving, braking and steering will take much more effort. Press the brake firmly and hold it.
result.why: A cold engine needs extra fuel and a slightly higher idle. If a temperature sensor reads wrong or the idle system is dirty, the engine can stumble and die at stops until it warms up.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control valve
causes.clues: A low or uneven idle.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: The temperature gauge acts oddly, or fuel economy has dropped.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: A hissing sound or a rough idle that smooths out when warm.

you: Note the outside temperature and how long the car had run.
Listen for hissing under the hood.
shop: Code scan and live sensor data

result.title: The idle may be too low to handle extra load
result.now: Get it checked within the next few days. Until then, turn off the A/C and extra electrical loads in stop-and-go driving.
if: If it stalls more than once in a trip, or ever stalls while turning or crossing traffic, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the headlights dim noticeably at idle or the battery light comes on, have the alternator tested too.
If the brake pedal feels hard or the car is harder to stop, don't drive it.
If it does stall while moving, braking and steering will take much more effort. Press the brake firmly and hold it.
result.why: The A/C compressor, power steering and a weak charging system all add load to the engine at idle. If the idle control can't raise engine speed to match, the engine sags and dies.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control fault
causes.clues: The idle drops sharply when the A/C kicks on.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: Hissing, or a rough idle.

causes.name: Weak alternator or battery
causes.clues: Dimming lights at idle, or the battery light.

you: Watch the RPM gauge as you switch the A/C on at idle.

result.title: Possibly a vacuum leak, a sticking valve or a dirty airflow sensor
result.now: Get it checked within the next few days, and have the codes read even if the check engine light is off.
if: If it stalls more than once in a trip, or ever stalls while turning or crossing traffic, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the temperature gauge is reading high, see our overheating guide and don't drive it.
If the brake pedal feels hard or the car is harder to stop, don't drive it.
If it does stall while moving, braking and steering will take much more effort. Press the brake firmly and hold it.
result.why: Once warm, the engine runs on a lean, tightly controlled idle. Extra air from a leak, exhaust gas from a stuck-open EGR valve, or a dirty sensor that misreads the airflow can tip it over into stalling.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: Hissing, a rough idle, or a check engine light for a lean condition.

causes.name: EGR valve stuck open
causes.clues: Rough idle when warm that's fine at speed.

causes.name: Dirty mass airflow sensor or throttle body
causes.clues: Hesitation when pulling away, or poor fuel economy.

you: Listen for hissing under the hood with the engine idling.
Note any check engine light.
shop: Airflow sensor and throttle body inspection

result.title: The engine may not be holding a steady idle
result.now: Get it checked within the next few days. Have the codes read and the idle system inspected.
if: If it stalls more than once in a trip, or ever stalls while turning or crossing traffic, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the brake pedal feels hard when it stalls, don't drive it.
If you smell raw fuel or the check engine light flashes, stop driving it and have it towed.
If it does stall while moving, braking and steering will take much more effort. Press the brake firmly and hold it.
result.why: At idle, the engine has very little power in reserve. Anything that upsets the air, fuel or spark balance, like a dirty throttle body, a vacuum leak or a weak fuel supply, can make it fade out as you stop.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control fault
causes.clues: A low, uneven idle.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: Hissing, or a check engine light for a lean condition.

causes.name: Weak fuel pump or clogged filter
causes.clues: Hesitation when accelerating as well.

you: Watch the RPM gauge as you slow down.
Note whether A/C, temperature or braking makes it worse.

result.title: On a manual, the engine dies if the clutch isn't in before you stop
result.now: Press the clutch in as the engine speed drops close to idle, before the car comes to a stop, and see if the stalling stops.
if: If it still dies with the clutch fully in, the idle system is the more likely problem. Get it checked soon.
If the clutch pedal feels different, like higher, softer or sticking, have the clutch system checked.
If it does stall while moving, braking and steering will take much more effort. Press the brake firmly and hold it.
result.why: With a manual, the engine is connected to the wheels until you press the clutch. If you slow down in gear without pressing it, the wheels drag the engine below idle and it stalls. That's normal behavior, not a fault.

causes.name: Clutch pressed too late
causes.clues: It only happens when braking in gear.
causes.against: If it dies with the clutch fully in, this isn't the cause.

causes.name: Low or unstable idle
causes.clues: The RPMs wander or dip at stops.

causes.name: Clutch not fully releasing
causes.clues: Grinding when shifting, or the car creeps with the clutch in.

you: Try pressing the clutch earlier as you slow down.
Watch whether the idle is steady with the clutch in.

q_light.q: Is the check engine light on right now?
q_light.help: The check engine light is the engine-shaped symbol, usually yellow or orange. A flashing light is more serious than a steady one.

opts.a: Yes, and it's flashing
Yes, it's on and steady
No, no warning lights
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When does the jerk happen?

opts.a: As the automatic transmission changes gears: a hard bump or slam
Cruising gently around 30 to 50 mph, like driving over rumble strips
When I press the gas harder, pull away or climb a hill: the engine stumbles or bucks
Only when I first press the gas or lift off: a single clunk or jolt
It's a manual, and it bucks or shudders as I let the clutch out
I'm not sure

q_engine.help: These clues separate an ignition problem from a fuel or air problem.

opts.a: It's worse on damp or rainy days, or the engine also shakes when idling
It sputters and loses power like it's starving, especially uphill or at higher speeds
It hesitates and then surges, or the idle is uneven and I hear a hiss
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be misfiring badly enough to cause damage
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic instead of continuing on.
if: If the light stops flashing after a restart, don't trust it. The fault is still there, so get it checked before using the car.
If you smell fuel or see smoke, step away from the car and call for help.
If the temperature gauge is high or the oil pressure light is on, don't restart the engine.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means the engine computer has detected misfires severe enough to damage the catalytic converter. Unburned fuel goes into the exhaust and can overheat it. The jerking you feel is likely cylinders cutting in and out.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: The jerk is strongest under load, and the engine also shakes at idle.

causes.name: Fuel injector stuck or not working
causes.clues: The misfire stays on the same cylinder even after the coil is swapped.

causes.name: Internal engine problem, such as low compression
causes.clues: Ticking or knocking, oil or coolant loss, or a misfire that doesn't move when the coil and plug are swapped between cylinders.
causes.against: Much less common than coil or spark plug problems.

you: Note what you were doing when the light started flashing.
Note any other warning lights on the dash.
shop: Code scan and misfire counts by cylinder
Ignition coil and spark plug inspection

result.title: An engine fault is stored. The code will narrow it down
result.now: Have the trouble codes read within the next few days. Many auto parts stores do it free. Drive gently until then and avoid hard acceleration.
if: If the light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
If the code points to the transmission, keep trips short and get it checked as soon as you can.
If the car loses power, starts shaking harder, or you smell fuel, stop driving it and have it towed.
result.why: A steady check engine light means the computer has found a fault, but not one it treats as immediately damaging. Jerking with a steady light is often an early misfire, a fuel delivery problem or a sensor giving bad readings. The stored code tells the shop where to start.

causes.name: Early misfire from a worn spark plug or ignition coil
causes.clues: The jerk is worse under load or uphill, and the engine may shake at idle.

causes.name: Faulty sensor, such as the airflow or throttle sensor
causes.clues: Hesitation followed by a surge, or worse fuel economy.

causes.name: Fuel delivery problem
causes.clues: Sputtering at higher speeds or on hills.

you: Get the codes read and write down the full letters and numbers.
Note when the jerk happens: speed, how hard you press the gas, and whether the engine is cold or warm.

result.title: Possibly a misfire from a worn spark plug or ignition coil
result.now: Book a check within the next few days, and avoid hard acceleration until then.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
If the spark plugs are past the replacement interval in your owner's manual, tell the shop.
If the car loses power in traffic or you smell fuel, stop driving it and have it towed.
result.why: When a spark plug or coil is weak, a cylinder can fail to fire just when the engine is working hardest. You feel that as a jerk or buck. Moisture makes weak ignition parts worse, which is why it can be worse on damp days. A shop will usually find which cylinder is misfiring and swap parts between cylinders to test before replacing anything.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs
causes.clues: High mileage, or plugs past their replacement interval.
causes.against: Less likely if the plugs were replaced recently.

causes.name: Failing ignition coil or plug wire
causes.clues: Worse in damp weather, or a check engine light that comes and goes.

causes.name: Clogged or failing fuel injector
causes.clues: A misfire on one cylinder that doesn't move when the coil is swapped.

you: Check your service records for the last spark plug change.
Have the codes read if the check engine light has come on, even briefly.

result.title: The engine may not be getting enough fuel under load
result.now: Book a check within the next few days. Until then, keep the tank above a quarter full and avoid hard acceleration and long climbs.
if: If it starts stalling or losing power in traffic, stop driving it and have it towed.
If it began right after a fill-up, tell the shop. Bad or watery fuel can cause this.
If you smell raw fuel, stop driving it and have it towed. A fuel leak is a fire risk.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
result.why: When you accelerate hard, the engine needs much more fuel. A weak fuel pump, a clogged filter or dirty injectors may keep up at idle but fall short when you ask for power, so the engine sputters and jerks. A shop will usually test fuel pressure and volume before replacing a pump.

causes.name: Weak fuel pump
causes.clues: Worse uphill, at higher speeds or when the tank is low.

causes.name: Clogged fuel filter
causes.clues: A slow loss of power over months, on cars that have a replaceable filter.

causes.name: Dirty or failing fuel injectors
causes.clues: A rough idle and worse fuel economy.

causes.name: Contaminated fuel
causes.clues: It started suddenly right after a fill-up.

you: Notice whether it's worse when the tank is low.
Think back to whether it started right after a fill-up.
shop: Fuel pressure and volume test under load

result.title: An air leak or a dirty airflow sensor may be throwing off the fuel mix
result.now: Book a check when convenient. A shop can find most air leaks quickly with a smoke test.
if: If the check engine light comes on or the hesitation gets worse, get it checked within a few days.
If the engine starts stalling at stops, have it looked at before relying on the car.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
result.why: The engine computer measures the air coming in to decide how much fuel to add. A cracked vacuum hose lets in air it didn't measure, and a dirty airflow sensor misreads it. Either way the mix comes out wrong, so the car hesitates and then surges.

causes.name: Vacuum leak from a cracked hose or intake gasket
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or a high or uneven idle.

causes.name: Dirty or faulty mass airflow sensor
causes.clues: Hesitation then surge, and worse fuel economy.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body
causes.clues: A rough idle, or the car feels sticky right off the pedal.

you: With the engine idling and the car in Park, listen from the front of the car for a hiss.
With the engine off, look for cracked or loose rubber hoses on top of the engine.
Check that the air filter isn't badly clogged.
shop: Code scan and live airflow data

result.title: The automatic transmission may be shifting harshly
result.now: Book a transmission check within the next few days. Until then, accelerate gently and avoid towing or heavy loads.
if: If the engine revs but the car doesn't speed up, or a transmission warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If you see red or pink fluid where you park, tell the shop. Low fluid causes harsh shifts.
If you smell burning from under the car, stop driving and have it checked.
result.why: A jolt right as the gears change usually means the transmission isn't controlling the shift smoothly. Low or worn-out fluid, a shift control problem or worn internal parts can all cause it. Catching it early often keeps the repair smaller, and a shop will usually check fluid, codes and software before suggesting major work.

causes.name: Low or worn-out transmission fluid
causes.clues: Red or pink drips, or fluid that's dark and smells burnt.

causes.name: Shift solenoid or transmission control fault
causes.clues: A transmission warning light, or shifts that are smooth sometimes and harsh other times.

causes.name: Worn internal clutches
causes.clues: High mileage, slipping, or harsh shifts that keep getting worse.

you: If your car has a transmission dipstick, check the level and color the way your owner's manual describes. Many are checked with the engine warm and running.
Look for red or pink spots where you park.
shop: Road test with live transmission data

result.title: This may be torque converter shudder
result.now: Book a transmission check when convenient. Tell the shop it feels like rumble strips at steady, light cruising.
if: If it gets worse quickly, or you notice slipping or a transmission warning light, get it checked within a few days.
If you see red or pink fluid under the car, get it checked sooner.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving. That points to an engine misfire.
result.why: The torque converter connects the engine to an automatic transmission. At steady, light cruising it locks up to save fuel, and if that lockup clutch grabs unevenly, the car shudders as if crossing rumble strips. Worn fluid is a common cause, and it tends to get worse over time. A shop will usually check the fluid and any updates or service bulletins before replacing the converter.

causes.name: Worn or contaminated transmission fluid
causes.clues: The fluid hasn't been changed in a long time, or it looks dark.

causes.name: Worn torque converter lockup clutch
causes.clues: The shudder stops when you press harder or lift off the gas.

causes.name: Engine misfire under light load
causes.clues: A check engine light, or a shake at idle.
causes.against: A misfire usually feels worse when you press harder, not lighter.

you: Note the speed range where it happens.
Notice whether a little more or a little less gas makes it stop.
shop: Road test watching torque converter lockup data

result.title: Possibly worn engine mounts or play in the drive axles
result.now: Book a check when convenient, and ask the shop to inspect the engine and transmission mounts and the drive axles.
if: If you hear a loud bang, or the clunk is getting worse quickly, get it checked within a few days.
If you also hear clicking when turning sharply, a worn axle joint is a possibility. Get it checked soon.
result.why: Mounts are rubber blocks that hold the engine and transmission in place. When they wear out, the engine rocks when you get on or off the gas, and you feel it as a clunk or jolt. Worn axle joints can feel very similar.

causes.name: Worn or broken engine or transmission mount
causes.clues: A clunk when shifting into Drive or Reverse, or more vibration at idle.

causes.name: Worn CV joint or U-joint
causes.clues: Clicking when turning, or a clunk that seems to come from under the car rather than the engine bay.

causes.name: Loose exhaust hanger or heat shield
causes.clues: A thump or rattle along with the clunk.

you: Notice whether the clunk also happens when shifting into Drive or Reverse.
Listen for clicking while making slow, tight turns in an empty parking lot.
shop: Drive axle, CV joint and U-joint check

result.title: The clutch may be grabbing unevenly (clutch chatter)
result.now: Book a check when convenient. Until then, let the clutch out slowly and smoothly.
if: If the engine revs but the car doesn't speed up in higher gears, the clutch is slipping. Get it checked within a few days.
If you smell burning after pulling away, avoid slipping the clutch and get it checked soon.
If you see smoke from under the car, stop and have it towed.
result.why: When the clutch grabs unevenly as you let it out, the car shudders or bucks. Oil on the clutch, worn clutch parts or weak engine mounts are the usual reasons.

causes.name: Contaminated or worn clutch disc
causes.clues: Chatter that's worse when hot, or a burning smell.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mounts
causes.clues: A clunk along with the chatter.

causes.name: Worn or uneven flywheel
causes.clues: Chatter plus vibration you can feel through the pedal.

you: Notice whether it's worse when the car is fully warmed up.
Look for oil drips between the engine and the transmission.
shop: Check for an oil leak onto the clutch

result.title: Jerking needs a code scan and a short road test to pin down
result.now: Have the codes read and book a check. Tell the shop when the jerk happens: speed, how hard you press the gas, and whether the engine is cold or warm.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
If the jerking gets worse or the car starts losing power, stop driving it and have it towed.
If you smell fuel or see smoke, pull over, turn off the engine and get away from the car.
result.why: Jerking can come from the engine, the transmission or worn mounts, and they can feel alike from the driver's seat. A code scan plus a short road test usually separates them quickly.

causes.name: Ignition misfire
causes.clues: Worse under load or uphill.

causes.name: Fuel delivery problem
causes.clues: Sputtering at higher speeds.

causes.name: Transmission shift problem
causes.clues: It happens exactly as the gears change.

you: Keep notes on when it happens.
Have the codes read even with no light on. Some faults are stored before the light comes on.

q_when.q: When does the car pull?

opts.a: It started suddenly and pulls hard
Only when I brake
Only when I accelerate
All the time, even on a flat road
Only on some roads, usually drifting toward the curb or road edge
I'm not sure

q_sudden.q: Did you notice any of these when it started?

opts.a: A tire looks flat or very low
A bang or clunk, or one corner now sits lower than the others
A burning smell, or one wheel is much hotter than the others
It started after hitting a pothole or curb
None of these / I'm not sure

q_pressure.q: Check all four tire pressures when the tires are cold and compare them with the sticker in the driver's door jamb. What did you find?
q_pressure.help: Use the number on the door jamb sticker, not the maximum printed on the tire. "Cold" means the car has been parked for a few hours or driven less than a mile.

opts.a: One tire is noticeably lower than the others
They're all close to correct
I can't check right now / I'm not sure
It started after new tires or a tire rotation
It started after hitting a pothole or curb, or after an accident
The steering also feels loose, or there's clunking over bumps
One wheel feels much hotter than the others after a drive
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: A flat or very low tire is likely pulling the car
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe and stop. Put on the spare or call roadside assistance.
if: If the tire is only somewhat low, has no visible damage, and you have a portable pump with you, inflating it where you are may be an option. Have it checked for a leak right away. Don't drive on a tire that's flat, has a bulge or keeps losing air.
If the spare is a small temporary one, follow the speed and distance limits printed on it.
If you hear a bang or clunk, or a corner still sits low after the tire is fixed, have the suspension checked before driving.
result.why: A tire that's lost a lot of air drags on that side and pulls the car toward it. Driving on it can destroy the tire, damage the wheel and make the car harder to control.

causes.name: Puncture from a nail or screw
causes.clues: The tire lost air over hours or days.

causes.name: Damage from a pothole or curb
causes.clues: Sudden air loss right after an impact, or a bulge on the sidewall.

causes.name: Leaking valve stem or wheel rim
causes.clues: Slow, repeated air loss with no visible puncture.

you: Look for a nail, screw or cut in the tread.
Check the spare's pressure before you rely on it.
shop: Tire leak inspection and repair or replacement

result.title: A suspension or steering part may have broken
result.now: Pull over safely and stop. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic to look at it where it is.
if: If a tire is touching the body or a broken spring is pressing against it, don't move the car at all.
If the steering wheel is now badly off-center, that's another sign something is bent or broken.
result.why: A sudden hard pull with a bang, or a corner that sits low, can point to a broken coil spring, a broken or bent control arm, or a failed ball joint. These parts hold the wheel in place, so a failure can affect steering and braking.

causes.name: Broken coil spring
causes.clues: One corner sits lower, and there was a bang or clunk over a bump.

causes.name: Bent or broken control arm or tie rod
causes.clues: A hard impact, and the wheel looks tilted or the steering is off-center.

causes.name: Failed ball joint
causes.clues: Clunking that got worse before this happened.

you: From a safe spot, look at whether one corner sits lower or a wheel looks tilted.
shop: Suspension and steering inspection on a lift
Spring, control arm and ball joint check

result.title: A brake may be sticking on that side
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe and let the brakes cool. Don't touch the wheel. Don't drive further until the brakes are checked. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see smoke from a wheel, keep everyone clear and let it cool. Call 911 if you see flames.
If the brake pedal feels soft or goes lower than usual, or the red brake light comes on, don't move the car.
If the parking brake was partly on, release it fully and let everything cool. Overheated brakes can still be weakened, so have them checked before relying on the car.
result.why: When a brake caliper or hose doesn't release fully, that wheel keeps braking lightly. The car pulls toward that side, the wheel gets very hot, and the brakes can overheat and stop working as well as they should. A shop will usually check the slide pins, piston and hose before deciding what to replace.

causes.name: Sticking brake caliper
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter than the others, with a burning smell or extra brake dust on that wheel.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose
causes.clues: The pull comes and goes, and the brake on that side seems to stay on after you release the pedal.

causes.name: Parking brake not fully releasing
causes.clues: It's the rear wheel that's hot, and the parking brake has been sticky.

you: After it has cooled, carefully hold your hand near (not on) each wheel to compare heat. Don't drive just to test it.
Make sure the parking brake is fully released.
shop: Brake caliper and slide pin inspection
Check each wheel spins freely on a lift

result.title: A hit to a wheel may have knocked the alignment out or bent a part
result.now: Have the alignment and front suspension inspected within the next few days. Drive gently until then. If you have to fight the steering wheel to stay in your lane, don't drive it; have it towed.
if: If the pull gets stronger, the steering wheel is badly off-center, or you hear clunking, stop driving and have it towed.
If a tire has a bulge or a wheel is dented, don't drive on it. Put on the spare.
If you notice a burning smell or one wheel much hotter than the others, pull over and let it cool. Don't drive further until the brakes are checked.
result.why: A pothole, curb or accident can shift the alignment or bend a tie rod, control arm or wheel. Even a small bend can make the car pull and wear the tires quickly. If a part is bent, an alignment alone won't fix it, so a good shop will check for bent parts as part of the alignment.

causes.name: Alignment knocked out
causes.clues: The steering wheel is now off-center when driving straight.

causes.name: Bent tie rod or control arm
causes.clues: The alignment can't be set back to normal, or one wheel looks tilted.

causes.name: Damaged tire or bent wheel
causes.clues: A bulge, a dent in the rim, or a new vibration.

you: Check the tire and wheel on the side that was hit.
Note whether the steering wheel is centered when driving straight.
shop: Steering and suspension parts inspection for bends

result.title: A pull when braking usually means one brake is working harder than the other
result.now: Have the brakes inspected within the next few days. Until then, brake early and gently, and leave extra following distance.
if: If the pedal feels soft or sinks, or you see fluid near a wheel, stop driving and have it towed.
If the pull is strong enough to move you out of your lane, don't drive it until it's fixed.
If you smell burning, hear grinding, or the red brake light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: When the brakes on one side grip harder or the other side grips less, the car turns toward the stronger side every time you stop. It can come from a sticking caliper, contaminated pads or a worn suspension part that shifts under braking.

causes.name: Sticking or seized brake caliper
causes.clues: One wheel is hotter, or that wheel has more brake dust.

causes.name: Brake pads contaminated with oil or brake fluid
causes.clues: A wet or oily look on the inside of one wheel.

causes.name: Worn control arm bushings
causes.clues: A clunk when you first brake, and the pull comes on suddenly.

you: Look for wet spots on the inside of each wheel.
Compare how hot each wheel feels (without touching) after driving.

result.title: Pulling only under acceleration points to the drivetrain or its mounts
result.now: Book an inspection of the engine mounts, axles and front suspension bushings.
if: If you hear clunking or clicking when accelerating, get it checked within a few days.
If the car is a powerful front-wheel-drive model and the pull is mild under hard acceleration only, some of this can be normal.
result.why: On front-wheel-drive cars, power going to the front wheels can tug the steering to one side, especially under hard acceleration. Worn mounts or bushings let parts shift under load and make this much stronger.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mounts
causes.clues: A jolt or clunk when you start accelerating.

causes.name: Worn control arm bushings
causes.clues: Clunks over bumps and a pull that changes between accelerating and braking.

causes.name: Mismatched tires on the front
causes.clues: Different brands, sizes or wear on the two front tires.

you: Check that both front tires are the same brand and size, with similar wear.

result.title: This may be the slope of the road, not the car
result.now: Test on a flat, empty parking lot. Drive straight slowly and loosen your grip on the wheel for a moment. If the car stays straight there, the road slope is a possible cause.
if: If the car drifts on a flat lot too, check the tire pressures and book an alignment check.
If the steering wheel is off-center when driving straight, have the alignment checked.
result.why: Most roads are built slightly higher in the middle so rain drains off. That slope gently pushes cars toward the edge. A mild drift that only happens on some roads is often just that.

causes.name: Road crown (slope)
causes.clues: The drift goes away on flat roads and changes when you change lanes.

causes.name: Slightly low tire
causes.clues: One tire is a few PSI lower than the others.

causes.name: Alignment slightly off
causes.clues: The drift is there on flat roads too, or the tires wear on one edge.

you: Test on a flat parking lot.
Check all four tire pressures.

result.title: A low tire may be why it's pulling
result.now: Inflate all four tires to the pressure on the driver's door jamb sticker, then see if the pull goes away.
if: If the same tire is low again within a few days, have it checked for a leak.
If the pressures are right and it still pulls, book an alignment check.
If the tire has a bulge, cut or nail in it, don't drive on it. Put on the spare or call roadside assistance.
result.why: A tire with less air has more drag and a slightly smaller rolling size, so the car pulls toward that side. It's the simplest cause to rule out and the cheapest to fix.

causes.name: Low tire pressure on one side
causes.clues: One tire reads lower than the others, or the TPMS light is on.

causes.name: Slow leak
causes.clues: The same tire keeps losing air.

causes.name: Alignment off as well
causes.clues: The pull stays after the pressures are correct.

you: Inflate the tires and test drive on a flat road.
Recheck the low tire after a day or two.

result.title: A new or rotated tire may be causing the pull
result.now: Go back to the tire shop and ask them to swap the two front tires side to side and check the alignment.
if: If the pull switches to the other side after the swap, one tire is likely the cause. The tire shop can advise on replacing it.
If the pull stays the same after the swap, the alignment is the more likely problem.
result.why: Some tires are built slightly unevenly inside, which makes them roll toward one side. This is called tire pull or radial pull. It shows up right after tires are installed or moved, and swapping the front tires is a simple way to check for it.

causes.name: Tire with built-in pull (radial pull)
causes.clues: The pull started right after new tires or a rotation.

causes.name: Mismatched front tires
causes.clues: Different brands, models or wear levels on the front.

causes.name: Alignment off
causes.clues: The pull stays the same no matter which tires are on the front.

you: Check that the front tires match and the pressures are correct.
shop: Swap front tires side to side and road test

result.title: Worn steering or suspension parts may be letting a wheel shift
result.now: Have the steering and front suspension inspected within the next few days. Drive gently until then.
if: If the steering suddenly feels much looser or the car is hard to keep in its lane, stop driving and have it towed.
If parts are replaced, have an alignment done afterward.
If you hear a loud clunk followed by a change in steering, or a corner sits lower, pull over and have it towed.
result.why: When tie rods, ball joints or bushings wear, the wheel can move out of position as you drive. That causes a pull that may come and go, along with clunks and uneven tire wear. A shop will usually check each joint for play on a lift before deciding which part needs replacing.

causes.name: Worn control arm bushings
causes.clues: A pull that changes between accelerating and braking, and clunks over bumps.

causes.name: Worn tie rod ends
causes.clues: Extra play in the steering wheel and wear on one edge of a front tire.

causes.name: Worn ball joints
causes.clues: Clunking or creaking when turning or going over bumps.

you: Look for uneven wear on the inner or outer edges of the front tires.
Listen for clunks over speed bumps.
shop: Steering and suspension inspection on a lift
Tie rod and ball joint play check

result.title: Wheel alignment is a common cause of a steady pull
result.now: Check all four tire pressures first. If they're correct, book an alignment check.
if: If the tires are wearing on one edge, get the alignment done soon to avoid ruining them.
If the pull suddenly gets stronger or you hear clunking, get it checked within a day or two.
If you notice a burning smell or one wheel much hotter than the others, a brake may be dragging. Pull over, let it cool, and don't drive further until it's checked.
result.why: Alignment is the angle of the wheels. It slowly drifts out with normal wear, bumps and potholes, and when the angles differ side to side the car pulls. Uneven tire wear and an off-center steering wheel often come along with it.

causes.name: Alignment out of spec
causes.clues: The steering wheel is off-center, or the tires wear on one edge.

causes.name: Low or uneven tire pressure
causes.clues: One tire is lower than the others.

causes.name: Worn suspension parts
causes.clues: Clunks over bumps, or the pull comes and goes.

you: Check the tire pressures.
Look for wear on the inner or outer edges of the tires.
shop: Alignment check with printed before-and-after readings

q_warning_signs.q: Along with the pull, do you notice any of these?
q_warning_signs.help: These signs tell us whether the brakes themselves are failing, which changes how urgent this is.

opts.a: The brake pedal feels soft, sinks, or the red brake warning light is on
A grinding or metal-on-metal scraping noise when I brake
A burning smell, or one wheel is much hotter than the others after a drive
The steering wheel shakes or the pedal pulses when I brake
None of these, it just pulls
I'm not sure

q_when.q: Does the car also drift to one side when you're NOT braking?
q_when.help: On a straight, flat road, loosen your grip slightly for a second or two. A small drift toward the edge of the road is normal on crowned roads. A steady tug to one side is not.

opts.a: Yes, it drifts a little even when cruising
No, it only pulls when I brake
I'm not sure

q_tires.q: Check the tire pressures with a gauge when the tires are cold. What did you find?
q_tires.help: The correct pressures are on a sticker inside the driver's door jamb, not the number on the tire sidewall.

opts.a: One tire is noticeably lower than the rest
All pressures are correct
I haven't checked / I'm not sure
It started right after brake work or new tires
It always pulls the same way, and harder the harder I brake
I feel a clunk or shift when I first press the brake, then the pull
There's a wet, oily spot on the inside of one wheel or tire
I'm not sure

result.title: The brake system may be losing pressure. Don't drive it
result.now: Park the car and have it towed, or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If the brake fluid reservoir is low or you see fluid near a wheel, mention that to the shop. It points to a leak.
If the pedal still goes to the floor after pumping it, the brakes may not stop the car at all. Don't move it.
Topping up the brake fluid isn't a fix. Even if the level comes back up and you see no leak, have the brakes inspected before driving.
result.why: A soft or sinking pedal, or the red brake light, can mean the hydraulic system that pushes the brake pads isn't holding pressure. When one side loses pressure, the car pulls toward the side that's still braking, and full brake failure can follow.

causes.name: Brake fluid leak
causes.clues: Low fluid in the reservoir, or a wet spot near a wheel or under the car.
causes.against: A full reservoir and dry wheels make a leak less likely.

causes.name: Damaged brake hose or line
causes.clues: Rust on the metal lines, or a cracked or bulging rubber hose near one wheel.

causes.name: Failing master cylinder
causes.clues: The pedal slowly sinks while you hold it down at a stop, with no visible leak.

you: Look at the brake fluid level in the reservoir under the hood.
Look behind each wheel for wet, oily spots.

result.title: The brake pads on one side may be worn down to metal
result.now: Stop using the car and have it towed or call a mobile mechanic. If the pads are down to metal, each stop makes the damage worse.
if: If the grinding only happens for the first few stops after rain or a car wash, it may be light surface rust. Have the brakes inspected anyway, since you also have a pull.
If the pedal also feels soft or sinks, treat it as a brake failure risk and don't move the car.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, keep clear and let it cool.
result.why: Grinding plus a pull usually means one side's pads are gone and metal is scraping on the rotor. That side brakes poorly and unevenly, so the car tugs and stopping distances get longer.

causes.name: Brake pads worn to the backing plate
causes.clues: A squeal for weeks that turned into grinding, or it's been a long time since the last brake job.

causes.name: Sticking caliper that wore one side's pads early
causes.clues: One wheel is dirtier with brake dust or hotter than the others.
