causes.name: A stone or debris caught in the brake
causes.clues: The noise started suddenly, often after a gravel road.
causes.against: Debris usually makes a constant scraping, not just when braking.

you: Look through the wheel spokes at the pads. Very thin pads or shiny grooves in the rotor are bad signs.

result.title: A brake caliper may be sticking and dragging on one wheel
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe and let the brakes cool. Don't drive further until the brakes are checked. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see smoke from a wheel, keep everyone clear and let it cool. Call 911 if you see flames.
If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, or the red brake light comes on, don't move the car.
If the parking brake was partly on, release it fully and let everything cool. Overheated brakes can still be weakened, so have them checked before relying on the car.
result.why: A caliper squeezes the pads against the rotor. If its piston or slide pins stick, that brake drags or grabs unevenly, so the car pulls and the wheel gets very hot. Overheated brakes can fade and stop working well. A shop will usually check the slide pins, piston and hose before deciding which part to replace.

causes.name: Sticking caliper piston
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter than the others, and that side has more brake dust.

causes.name: Seized caliper slide pins
causes.clues: Uneven wear between the inner and outer pad on the same wheel.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose holding pressure
causes.clues: The drag gets worse after several stops and eases after the car sits.

you: Without touching, check whether one wheel is still giving off much more heat than the others. Don't drive just to test it.
Compare brake dust on the front wheels.
shop: Caliper piston and slide pin inspection
Wheel spin test with the car raised
Pad wear comparison side to side

result.title: Uneven brake rotors may be causing both the shake and the pull
result.now: Book a brake inspection in the next week or two. Leave extra following distance until then.
if: If the shaking is getting worse quickly or you also hear grinding, get it checked within a day or two.
If one wheel is also hotter than the others, a sticking caliper may have damaged the rotor. Get it checked sooner.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, you smell burning, or the red brake light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: When a rotor's surface wears unevenly, the pads grab harder in some spots than others. You feel that as a pulsing pedal or shaking wheel, and if one side is worse the car can tug toward it. A shop will usually measure the rotors and check the calipers before deciding whether to resurface or replace them.

causes.name: Uneven rotor thickness or deposits
causes.clues: The shake is strongest when braking from highway speed.

causes.name: Sticking caliper overheating one rotor
causes.clues: One wheel runs hotter, or has more brake dust.

causes.name: Worn suspension or steering parts
causes.clues: Clunks over bumps, or the steering feels loose.

you: Notice whether the shake is in the steering wheel (usually front brakes) or the seat and pedal (often rear brakes).

result.title: Uneven tire pressure is a common, easy-to-fix cause of a pull
result.now: Check all four tires with a gauge when cold and set them to the pressures on the driver's door jamb sticker.
if: If the same tire is low again within a few days, it probably has a slow leak. Get it repaired soon.
If the pull is still there with correct pressures, have the alignment and brakes checked.
If the pedal feels soft, you hear grinding, or you smell burning from a wheel, don't keep driving. Have the brakes checked first.
result.why: A low tire has more drag and a different grip than the others, so the car drifts toward it, and braking makes that pull stronger. It's the quickest thing to rule out.

causes.name: Low pressure in one tire
causes.clues: One tire looks lower, or the tire pressure light has been on.

causes.name: Mismatched or unevenly worn tires
causes.clues: Different tire brands or tread depths on the same axle.

causes.name: Wheel alignment out of spec
causes.clues: The steering wheel sits off-center when driving straight.
causes.against: If correcting the pressure fixes it, alignment is less likely.

you: Check and set all tire pressures.
Compare tread depth and tire type left to right.

result.title: Possibly alignment or a tire issue, or a dragging brake
result.now: Book an alignment and brake inspection when convenient, ideally within a couple of weeks.
if: If one wheel feels much hotter than the others after a drive, a brake may be dragging. Get it checked within a day or two.
If the steering also feels loose or clunks over bumps, get it checked sooner.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, pull over, let it cool and don't drive further until it's checked.
If the pedal feels soft or the red brake light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: A car that drifts while cruising and pulls harder when braking usually has a steady cause, like alignment or a tire problem, that braking makes more noticeable. A brake that's slightly dragging can do the same thing.

causes.name: Wheel alignment out of spec
causes.clues: A recent pothole or curb hit, or the steering wheel sits off-center.

causes.name: Tire problem (uneven wear or internal damage)
causes.clues: The pull changes if the front tires are swapped side to side.

causes.name: Dragging brake
causes.clues: One wheel is hotter or dustier than the other.

you: After a drive, compare how warm each wheel feels by holding your hand near it.
Look at the front tires for wear on just one edge.

result.title: Something from the recent work may need adjusting
result.now: Take it back to the shop that did the work within the next few days and tell them exactly when it pulls.
if: If the pedal feels soft or the pull is strong or sudden, don't drive it. Have the shop come to you or have it towed.
If new pads were installed, a slight pull for the first few dozen stops can happen while they bed in. If it doesn't fade, have it checked.
If you smell burning or one wheel is much hotter than the others, pull over, let it cool, and have it towed back rather than driven.
result.why: A pull that shows up right after brake or tire work is often linked to that work. Mismatched pads, a caliper not moving freely, air in the brake lines, or tires that differ side to side can all cause one side to brake differently. The shop that did the work will want to know and can usually recheck it quickly.

causes.name: Caliper or pads not installed or lubricated correctly
causes.clues: The pull started right after a brake job.

causes.name: Mismatched or new tires on one side
causes.clues: Only one or two tires were replaced, or tires were rotated.

causes.name: Air in the brake lines
causes.clues: The pedal feels softer than before the work.

you: Note which way it pulls and how hard you're braking when it happens.
Check the tire pressures.
shop: Brake bleed if the pedal is soft

result.title: One side may be braking harder than the other
result.now: Get the brakes inspected within the next few days. Until then, brake early and gently, and leave extra following distance.
if: If the pull suddenly gets stronger, the pedal changes, or you hear grinding, stop driving it and have it towed.
If one wheel is much hotter than the others after driving, a caliper may be sticking. Get it checked within a day or two, and don't drive it if there's a burning smell.
If the red brake light comes on or you see fluid near a wheel, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: A consistent pull that grows with harder braking usually means the brakes on the left and right aren't gripping equally. The car pulls toward the side that's working better, so the other side may barely be braking.

causes.name: Sticking caliper or seized slide pins
causes.clues: Uneven brake dust or uneven pad wear between sides.

causes.name: Contaminated brake pads
causes.clues: A leak near one wheel, or recent work that may have left grease on the pads.

causes.name: Collapsed or blocked brake hose
causes.clues: The pull is worse after several stops in a row.

causes.name: Uneven tire pressure
causes.clues: One tire looks lower than the others.
causes.against: If the car doesn't drift at all when not braking, this is less likely.

you: Check tire pressures.
Compare the brake dust and wheel warmth on each side after a short drive.
shop: Brake inspection with pad and rotor measurement

result.title: Worn suspension or steering parts may be shifting when you brake
result.now: Have the suspension and steering inspected within the next few days. Avoid hard braking until then.
if: If the steering suddenly feels very loose, wanders a lot, or you hear a loud clunk followed by a change in steering, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the brake pedal feels soft or the red brake light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: Braking shifts a lot of weight forward. If a control arm bushing, ball joint or tie rod is worn, the wheel can move out of position under that load. The clunk is the part shifting, and the pull follows.

causes.name: Worn control arm bushings
causes.clues: A clunk when you start braking, and the pull eases once the car settles.

causes.name: Worn ball joint or tie rod end
causes.clues: Clunks over bumps, loose-feeling steering, or uneven tire wear.

causes.name: Loose brake caliper mounting
causes.clues: A clunk at the moment you press or release the brake, at one wheel.

you: Note whether you hear clunks over bumps too.
Look at the front tires for wear on just one edge.
shop: Suspension and steering inspection with the wheels off the ground
Ball joint and tie rod play check

result.title: Fluid may be leaking onto the brakes at one wheel
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic check that wheel.
if: If the brake fluid reservoir is low, the leak is probably brake fluid. Brake failure is a real risk.
If the reservoir is full, the fluid may be gear oil or grease from an axle seal, which can still soak the pads and reduce braking on that side.
Don't try to clean the pads and drive on. Fluid-soaked pads usually can't be trusted, and a shop will find and fix the leak first.
result.why: Pads soaked with fluid lose much of their grip, so that wheel barely brakes and the car pulls toward the other side. If the fluid is brake fluid, the whole system can also lose pressure.

causes.name: Leaking brake caliper or wheel cylinder
causes.clues: Low brake fluid, a wet caliper or wet inside surface of the tire.

causes.name: Leaking brake hose or line
causes.clues: Fluid along a hose or line near the wheel.

causes.name: Axle seal or grease leak
causes.clues: Thick, dark, smelly oil on a rear wheel, with full brake fluid.

you: Check the brake fluid level under the hood.
Note which wheel is wet.
shop: Pad and shoe check for contamination

result.title: A brake pull needs a proper inspection to find the cause
result.now: Check your tire pressures, then get the brakes and steering inspected within the next few days.
if: If the pedal goes soft, the red brake light comes on, or you hear grinding, stop driving and have it towed.
If the pull is getting stronger, get it checked within a day or two.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, pull over, let it cool and don't drive further until it's checked.
result.why: A car that pulls when braking has an imbalance between the left and right side, in the brakes, tires or suspension. Most causes are straightforward to fix, but some get worse quickly, so it shouldn't wait long.

causes.name: Sticking caliper or uneven brakes
causes.clues: One wheel hotter or dustier than the others.

causes.name: Tire pressure or tire problem
causes.clues: One tire low or worn differently.

causes.name: Worn suspension or alignment
causes.clues: Clunks over bumps or an off-center steering wheel.

you: Check tire pressures.
Note which way it pulls and whether it happens on every stop.

q_warning.help: A "misfire" is when one cylinder of the engine doesn't fire properly. It feels like a stumble, jerk or uneven shake, often with a loss of power.

opts.a: The check engine light is flashing
The check engine light is on (not flashing), and the engine feels rough or weak
The shaking started suddenly and is violent, or there's a new thumping sound
No warning lights. The engine pulls fine but the car vibrates
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When is the shaking worst?
q_when.help: Pay attention on a smooth road. Notice whether the shake follows how hard you press the gas, or how fast you're going.

opts.a: A light shudder at about 20 to 45 mph with gentle gas, like driving over rumble strips (automatic)
A jolt or clunk when I first press the gas or let off, and the engine seems to rock
It gets worse the harder I accelerate and fades when I coast
It shows up at a certain speed whether I'm on the gas or coasting
I'm not sure

q_drive_clues.help: A CV axle is the shaft that turns the front wheels on most cars. A driveshaft is the long tube under rear-wheel-drive cars, trucks and many 4WD vehicles.

opts.a: Clicking when turning, or dark grease splattered inside a front wheel
It's a truck, rear-wheel-drive or 4WD vehicle, and I hear a clunk when shifting into gear
It's a front-wheel-drive car and I haven't noticed anything else
I'm not sure

result.title: A flashing check engine light usually means a severe misfire
result.now: Ease off the gas, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you smell fuel, see smoke or the engine is losing a lot of power, step away from the car once it's off.
If the light stops flashing after a restart, the misfire may come back. Still have it checked before driving any distance.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward hot or a red warning light comes on, turn the engine off as soon as you are stopped safely.
result.why: A flashing light usually means the misfire is bad enough to cause damage now. Unburned fuel goes into the exhaust and can overheat the catalytic converter, which can be costly to replace and is a fire risk in extreme cases.

causes.name: Faulty ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: The shake is worst under load, like going uphill or merging, and the engine feels like it's missing a beat.

causes.name: Fuel injector problem
causes.clues: A misfire that stays on one cylinder even after the coil and plug are checked.

causes.name: Internal engine problem
causes.clues: Low compression from a valve or head gasket issue, sometimes with white exhaust smoke or coolant loss.
causes.against: Much less common than a coil or plug fault.

you: Note whether the light flashes only when accelerating or all the time.
If you have a code reader, write down any codes for the shop.
shop: Code scan and misfire counter data
Ignition coil and spark plug inspection

result.title: The engine may be misfiring under load
result.now: Get the code read and the engine checked within the next few days. Until then, keep trips short, drive gently and avoid hard acceleration and towing a trailer.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving. Have it towed.
If the shaking gets worse or the car loses power on the highway, pull over when it is safe and have it towed.
If you smell fuel or a strong rotten-egg smell, or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward hot, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: A steady check engine light with a rough, weak feeling under acceleration often means one cylinder isn't firing properly when the engine is working hardest. Worn spark plugs and failing ignition coils are common reasons, but the code and a few tests are needed to know which part is at fault.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs or a failing ignition coil
causes.clues: The plugs are due by your service schedule, or the shake is worse in damp weather or going uphill.

causes.name: Vacuum or intake air leak
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or a rough idle as well.

causes.name: Dirty or failing fuel injector or low fuel pressure
causes.clues: Hesitation and stumbling when you press the gas harder.

you: Have the code read. Many auto parts stores will do this free.
Check your service records for when the spark plugs were last changed.

result.title: Sudden, violent shaking can mean a tire or wheel is failing
result.now: Slow down, pull over somewhere safe and stop. Walk around the car and look at each tire. Call roadside assistance if anything looks wrong.
if: If a tire has a bulge, a flat spot, exposed cords or looks out of shape, don't drive on it. Put on the spare if you can do it safely off the road, or have the car towed.
If the lug nuts on a wheel are loose or missing, don't move the car. Call for help.
If the tires look fine, have the car towed to a shop. A broken axle joint, driveshaft joint or mount can also cause a sudden shake.
If you smell burning or fuel, or see smoke, stay away from the car and call for help.
result.why: A shake that appears suddenly and hard is different from one that grew over weeks. It often means a tire's internal belts have separated, a wheel is loose, or a drive part has broken. Any of these can lead to losing control.

causes.name: Tire tread separation or damaged tire
causes.clues: A rhythmic thump that speeds up with the car, or a visible bulge or lump.

causes.name: Loose wheel
causes.clues: A wheel was removed recently, or you hear clicking or clunking from one corner.

causes.name: Broken CV joint, driveshaft joint or engine mount
causes.clues: A loud clunk when accelerating, or the shake only happens on the gas.

you: Look at each tire for bulges, lumps or exposed cords.
Check that the lug nuts are all present.
shop: Tire and wheel inspection on a lift
Lug nut and wheel stud check

result.title: A light shudder at moderate speeds is often linked to the transmission's torque converter
result.now: Book a transmission check and ask the shop to look for a torque converter shudder and the condition of the transmission fluid.
if: If the transmission starts slipping, shifting harshly or a transmission warning light comes on, get it checked within a few days.
If the check engine light comes on, have the code read. A mild misfire can feel just like this.
If the check engine light flashes, or the shake becomes violent, pull over when it is safe and have it towed.
If you smell something burning or see fluid dripping under the car, stop driving it and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: In an automatic, the torque converter has a clutch that locks up at cruising speeds to save fuel. When that clutch or the fluid is worn, it can grab unevenly, which feels like rolling over rumble strips under light gas. A misfire can feel very similar, so a shop will usually check for engine codes as well.

causes.name: Torque converter clutch shudder
causes.clues: It happens with light gas at 20 to 45 mph and goes away if you press harder or ease off.
causes.against: Doesn't apply to manual transmissions.

causes.name: Old or degraded transmission fluid
causes.clues: The fluid hasn't been changed in a long time, or it looks dark or smells burnt.

causes.name: Mild engine misfire
causes.clues: A check engine light, or a rough feeling at idle too.

you: Note the speed and how hard you're pressing the gas when it happens.
Check your records for the last transmission fluid service.
shop: Road test watching torque converter lockup data

result.title: Worn engine or transmission mounts are a possible cause
result.now: Book an inspection of the engine and transmission mounts.
if: If the clunk becomes loud or the engine visibly lifts when you rev it, get it checked within a few days. A broken mount can let other parts get damaged.
If there's also a misfire or check engine light, the engine may be shaking harder than the mounts can absorb. Have the code read too.
If the check engine light flashes, or you get a sudden violent shake or a loud bang, pull over when it is safe and have it towed.
result.why: Mounts are rubber blocks that hold the engine and transmission in place and soak up vibration. When they crack or collapse, the engine rocks when you put power on or let off, and you feel it as a jolt or shake through the car. A shop will usually inspect the mounts and the drive axles together, because a worn axle joint can feel similar.

causes.name: Worn or broken engine mount
causes.clues: A clunk when you start moving, shift between Drive and Reverse, or let off the gas.

causes.name: Worn transmission mount
causes.clues: A thump when shifting into gear, and a vibration felt through the floor.

causes.name: Worn inner CV joint
causes.clues: The shake builds with harder acceleration rather than being a single jolt.

you: With the hood open and someone in the driver's seat holding the brake pedal down hard, watch the engine as they shift between Drive and Reverse without pressing the gas. Stand well to the side, never in front of the car. A big lurch suggests a mount worth having checked.
shop: Visual mount inspection for cracks and separation
Engine torque test watching mount movement

result.title: A worn CV axle is a likely cause
result.now: Have the front axles inspected within the next few days. Drive gently and avoid hard acceleration until then.
if: If you hear loud clicking or clunking, or the shaking gets suddenly worse, pull over when it is safe and have it towed. A broken axle leaves the car unable to move.
If the rubber boot is torn but the joint isn't noisy yet, mention it to the shop. Catching a torn boot early can sometimes save the joint.
If the check engine light flashes, pull over and stop driving.
result.why: On front-wheel-drive cars, the CV axles carry power to the wheels through flexible joints. When the inner joint wears, it can wobble under load, so the shake grows as you accelerate and fades when you coast. A torn rubber boot lets grease out and dirt in, which speeds this up. A shop will usually check the axles for play and the mounts before deciding which part is at fault.

causes.name: Worn inner CV joint
causes.clues: The shake builds with harder acceleration and eases when you lift off.

causes.name: Torn CV boot
causes.clues: Dark grease splattered on the inside of the wheel or nearby parts.

causes.name: Worn engine mount
causes.clues: A jolt or clunk when you start or stop accelerating.

you: With a flashlight, look behind each front wheel for torn rubber boots or thrown grease.
In an empty parking lot, turn sharply and accelerate slowly. Listen for clicking.
shop: CV axle and boot inspection on a lift
Check for play in the inner and outer joints

result.title: A worn driveshaft joint is a possible cause
result.now: Have the driveshaft and its joints inspected within the next few days. Drive gently until then.
if: If you hear a loud clunk, a squeak that matches road speed, or a new scraping noise from under the car, pull over when it is safe and have it towed. A driveshaft that comes loose can cause serious damage and loss of control.
If the vehicle was recently lifted or lowered, the driveshaft angles may have changed.
If the vibration suddenly becomes much stronger, pull over and stop driving.
result.why: The driveshaft carries power from the transmission to the rear axle through small universal joints. When a joint wears or the shaft goes out of balance, it shakes more when it's under load and often clunks when you shift into gear.

causes.name: Worn universal joint (U-joint)
causes.clues: A clunk shifting into Drive or Reverse, or a squeak at low speed.

causes.name: Worn driveshaft center support bearing
causes.clues: Common on longer trucks and vans. A shudder when pulling away from a stop.

causes.name: Driveshaft out of balance or bent
causes.clues: Vibration that rises with speed, after hitting something under the car.

you: Note whether the clunk happens every time you shift between Drive and Reverse.
shop: U-joint and center bearing inspection for play

result.title: This points to a tire or wheel issue more than an acceleration problem
result.now: Have the tires balanced and inspected at a tire shop.
if: If a tire has a bulge, a lump or exposed cords, don't drive on it. Put on the spare or have the car towed.
If the shaking suddenly becomes violent or you hear a new thumping, slow down and pull over safely.
If balancing doesn't fix it, ask the shop to check for a bent wheel, a tire that's out of round, or worn suspension parts.
result.why: If the shake depends on speed and not on the gas pedal, it's most likely coming from something that spins with the wheels. An out-of-balance tire, a bent wheel or a damaged tire is the usual reason, though worn wheel bearings or suspension parts can feel similar.

causes.name: Tire out of balance
causes.clues: It showed up after new tires or after a wheel weight fell off, and it's strongest in one speed range.

causes.name: Bent wheel
causes.clues: It started after hitting a pothole or curb.

causes.name: Damaged or out-of-round tire
causes.clues: A bulge, lump or patchy wear on the tread.

you: Look for bulges and uneven wear on each tire.
Check that the tire pressures match the sticker in the driver's door jamb.

result.title: Have a shop road-test it to find where the shake comes from
result.now: Book a check and tell the shop when the shake happens: the speed, how hard you're pressing the gas, and whether it fades when you coast.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
If the shake suddenly becomes violent or you hear a new clunk, pull over and have it towed.
If you smell fuel or burning, or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: Shaking under acceleration can come from the engine, the axles, the mounts or the tires. A short road test with a technician usually narrows it down quickly.

causes.name: Worn CV axle or driveshaft joint
causes.clues: Shake that grows with harder acceleration.

causes.name: Engine misfire
causes.clues: A rough, stumbling feel or a check engine light.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mounts
causes.clues: A jolt when starting or stopping acceleration.

causes.name: Tire or wheel balance
causes.clues: Shake that follows speed rather than the gas pedal.

you: Note the speed when it starts and whether it changes when you coast.
Look for a check engine light.

q_warning.q: Besides the shaking, do any of these happen?
q_warning.help: These are signs the brakes themselves aren't working properly, which matters more than the shake.

opts.a: The pedal feels soft or sinks, or the car pulls hard to one side when braking
Loud grinding or scraping, like metal on metal
A burning smell, smoke, or one wheel is much hotter than the others
None of these, the brakes stop the car normally
I'm not sure

q_where.q: Where do you feel the shaking most when you brake?
q_where.help: Front brake problems usually show up in the steering wheel and brake pedal. Rear brake problems are felt more in the seat or the whole car.

opts.a: In the steering wheel
In the brake pedal, which pulses up and down
In the seat or through the whole car
The car shakes when I'm not braking too, it just gets worse when I brake
I'm not sure

q_when.q: Which of these fits the steering wheel shake best?

opts.a: It's worst when braking from highway speed, and fine otherwise
It started right after new brakes, new tires or a tire rotation
The car also clunks over bumps, wanders, or the steering feels loose
I'm not sure

result.title: The braking system may be failing. Don't drive it
result.now: Park the car and have it towed to a shop, or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If the red brake warning light is on or the brake fluid is low, that adds to the evidence of a leak or worn brakes. Don't top it off and drive.
Not finding a leak doesn't mean the brakes are safe. Fluid can leak inside the system or somewhere you can't see.
If the car pulls hard to one side, a caliper or brake hose on one side may be stuck or failing.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, keep away from it until it cools.
result.why: A soft or sinking pedal can mean the brakes don't have enough hydraulic pressure to stop the car, and a hard pull can mean one side is braking much more than the other. Either can get worse without warning, so the car shouldn't be driven until it's inspected.

causes.name: Brake fluid leak
causes.clues: A low fluid level, a wet spot near a wheel, or a soft pedal that keeps getting worse.

causes.name: Stuck or seized caliper on one side
causes.clues: The car pulls hard to one side, and that wheel gets very hot.

causes.name: Air in the brake lines or failing master cylinder
causes.clues: A spongy pedal, or a pedal that slowly sinks while you hold it down at a stop.

you: With the engine off, check the brake fluid level in the reservoir under the hood.
Look behind each wheel and under the car for wet, oily spots.
shop: Brake system inspection on a lift

result.title: The brake pads may be worn down to metal
result.now: Avoid driving the car. Have it towed, or have a mobile mechanic inspect the brakes where it's parked.
if: If the grinding only happened once after the car sat in the rain, it may have been surface rust. If it happens again, or you're unsure, have the brakes inspected before driving further.
If the brake pedal also feels soft or sinks, the red brake light is on, or the car pulls hard, don't drive it at all.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, keep away from it until it cools.
result.why: Grinding when braking often means the pad material is gone and metal is scraping the rotor. That can reduce braking power and quickly gouges the rotor, which causes shaking. The longer it goes, the worse and more costly the damage. A shop will measure the pads and rotors to confirm what is worn.

causes.name: Brake pads worn down
causes.clues: A squeal for weeks before the grinding started, or a long time since the last brake job.

causes.name: Rock or debris caught in the brake
causes.clues: The grinding started suddenly after driving on gravel.

causes.name: Rusted or damaged rotor
causes.clues: The car sat for a long time, or the rotor surface looks rough and grooved.

you: Look through the wheel spokes at the brake pad and rotor for deep grooves or very thin pads.

result.title: A brake may be sticking and overheating
result.now: Pull over safely and let the brakes cool. Then have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic check it.
if: If you see flames or heavy smoke, get away from the car and call for help.
If the pedal feels soft, sinks, or braking takes much more force, don't drive it. Overheated brakes can fade.
Even if the smell happened once after a long downhill stretch and goes away after cooling, have the brakes inspected before driving far. A brake that overheats once can do it again.
result.why: A burning smell or one very hot wheel can mean a brake isn't releasing fully. The constant rubbing overheats the pad and rotor, which causes shaking and can fade the brakes or, in rare cases, start a fire.

causes.name: Sticking or seized caliper
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter than the others, and the car may pull to that side.

causes.name: Stuck caliper slide pins
causes.clues: Uneven pad wear, with one pad much thinner than the other on the same wheel.

causes.name: Parking brake not fully releasing
causes.clues: The heat and smell come from a rear wheel.

you: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.
After the car cools, carefully hold your hand near (not on) each wheel to compare heat.

result.title: The front brake rotors may be uneven, often called warped
result.now: If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, the red brake warning light comes on, or you hear grinding, stop driving and have it towed. Otherwise: Have the brakes inspected within the next few days. Until then, allow extra stopping distance and avoid hard braking from high speed.
if: If the shaking gets suddenly worse, or the pedal starts feeling soft or sinking, stop driving and have it towed.
If you hear grinding, smell burning, or the red brake warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If the pads are also low, the shop will usually measure the rotors to decide whether they can be resurfaced or need replacing.
result.why: When the brake rotor's surface becomes uneven, the pads grab harder on some spots than others as it spins. You feel that as a pulse in the pedal or a shake in the steering wheel, usually worst when slowing from higher speeds. It's common and fixable, but it tends to get worse, can lengthen stopping distances and wears the pads unevenly. A shop will usually measure the rotors and check the calipers before deciding on a repair.

causes.name: Uneven rotor thickness or pad deposits
causes.clues: A steady pulse in the pedal that gets worse when braking from highway speed.

causes.name: Overheated rotors
causes.clues: The car does a lot of towing, mountain driving or hard braking.

causes.name: Sticking caliper
causes.clues: One wheel runs hotter than the others, or the pads are wearing unevenly.

you: Note whether the shake is in the pedal, the steering wheel, or both.
Note the speed at which it's most noticeable.
shop: Pad thickness and wear pattern check

result.title: The rear rotors or brake drums may be uneven
result.now: If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, the red brake warning light comes on, or you hear grinding, stop driving and have it towed. Otherwise: Have the brakes inspected within the next few days. Mention that you feel it in the seat rather than the steering wheel. Allow extra stopping distance until then.
if: If the pedal starts to feel soft or sinks, or you hear grinding, stop driving and have it towed.
If you smell burning, see smoke from a rear wheel, or the red brake warning light comes on, stop driving and have it checked before driving further.
If the parking brake also feels weak or grabby, ask the shop to check it at the same time.
result.why: Rear brake problems don't usually reach the steering wheel, so you feel them in the seat or the whole car instead. Rear rotors can become uneven like the fronts, and drum brakes can go slightly out of round.

causes.name: Uneven rear rotors
causes.clues: A shudder through the seat when braking, especially from higher speeds.

causes.name: Out-of-round rear brake drums
causes.clues: The car has drum brakes at the rear, and the shudder is worse at lower speeds.

causes.name: Sticking rear caliper or parking brake
causes.clues: One rear wheel runs hotter, or there's a burning smell after driving.

you: Check whether the shake changes if you brake gently versus firmly.

result.title: Worn suspension parts or a tire problem may be making it shake
result.now: Get the front suspension, tires and brakes inspected within the next few days. Drive gently and avoid highways until then.
if: If you see a bulge on a tire, or the steering suddenly feels much looser, don't drive it. Use the spare or have it towed.
If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, or the red brake light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If the shake only happens when braking, the rotors are the more likely cause.
result.why: Braking shifts the car's weight forward and puts extra load on the front suspension. Worn joints, bushings or a damaged tire that cause a mild shake normally can feel much worse when you brake, and loose steering parts are a safety risk. A shop will usually inspect the suspension, tires and brakes together to find which is responsible.

causes.name: Worn control arm bushings or ball joints
causes.clues: Clunks over bumps, or the steering wheel jerks when braking.

causes.name: Worn tie rod ends
causes.clues: Loose or wandering steering.

causes.name: Out-of-balance or damaged tire
causes.clues: A shake at highway speed that's there even without braking, or a visible bulge.

you: Look over each tire for bulges, cuts or uneven wear.

result.title: It may be related to the recent work
result.now: If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, the red brake warning light comes on, or you hear grinding, stop driving and have it towed. Otherwise: Go back to the shop that did the work within a day or two. Let them know what you feel and ask them to check the wheel lug nuts, rotors and balance. Shops want to hear about this and it's usually a quick check.
if: If you hear clicking or clunking from a wheel, or feel a wobble, stop driving. A wheel may be loose. Have it towed.
If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, or you smell burning, stop driving and have it checked before going further.
If it was a brake job, new pads sometimes need a proper break-in. Ask the shop if that was done.
result.why: Lug nuts that aren't tightened evenly can distort a rotor and cause a shake under braking. New rotors can also have a slight runout, or a tire may have lost a balance weight. These are common and a shop can check them quickly.

causes.name: Uneven or loose lug nuts
causes.clues: The shake started right after a tire change or rotation.

causes.name: Rotor runout or rust between the rotor and hub
causes.clues: New rotors were installed, and the shake started right away.

causes.name: Missing wheel balance weight
causes.clues: The steering wheel also shakes at highway speed without braking.

you: Check that none of the lug nuts look loose or missing.

q_type.q: Is your car an automatic or a manual (stick shift)?
q_type.help: If there are only two pedals, gas and brake, it's an automatic. A manual has a third pedal, the clutch.

opts.a: Automatic (two pedals)
Manual (three pedals, with a clutch)
I'm not sure

q_auto.q: What happens when you try to put it in Drive or Reverse?
q_auto.help: Keep your foot firmly on the brake while you shift.

opts.a: The shifter won't move out of Park at all
The shifter moves, but the car doesn't move and the engine just revs when I press the gas
It goes into gear, but only after a pause of a few seconds, often with a thump
It moves in Reverse but not Drive, or the other way round
It goes into gear, but the car feels held back, like the brakes are on
I'm not sure

q_auto_display.q: When you move the shifter, does the gear letter on the dash (P, R, N, D) change to match?
q_auto_display.help: Most cars show the selected gear on the instrument panel or next to the shifter.

opts.a: No, it stays on the same letter or doesn't match the shifter
The shifter feels loose or floppy
Yes, it matches, but the car still won't move
I'm not sure
There's a reddish puddle under the car, or it was leaking fluid recently
I heard a bang or loud clunk, then it stopped moving
It had been slipping or revving oddly between gears before it quit
None of these / I'm not sure

q_manual.q: What happens when you try to drive off?
q_manual.help: The clutch is the pedal on the far left. Pressing it to the floor lets you change gears.

opts.a: The clutch pedal feels soft, sinks to the floor, or stays down
The clutch pedal feels normal, but gears grind or won't go in, especially from a stop
The gear goes in, but when I let the clutch out the engine revs and the car barely moves
I heard a bang or loud clunk, and now it won't move in any gear
The shifter feels loose or floppy and doesn't select gears
I'm not sure

result.title: The shift lock may be holding the shifter in Park
result.now: With the key in ON or the engine running, press the brake pedal firmly and try again. If it still won't move, use the shift lock release, a small slot or button near the shifter (your owner's manual shows where).
if: If the brake lights don't come on when you press the pedal, a brake light switch or fuse is the likely cause. Get that fixed before driving in traffic, because drivers behind you can't see you stop.
If the car is parked on a slope, set the parking brake, hold the brake pedal down and shift with a firm, steady pull. The car's weight can bind the Park lock.
If the brake pedal feels soft, sinks or is much harder to press than usual, don't drive the car. Have the brakes checked first.
If the release lets you shift but the problem keeps coming back, have it checked soon rather than relying on the release.
result.why: Automatic cars won't let you leave Park unless they sense your foot on the brake. If that signal doesn't arrive, a small lock keeps the shifter in place. The cause is often simple and electrical rather than a transmission failure, but a shop can confirm it with a quick test.

causes.name: Faulty brake light switch or blown fuse
causes.clues: The brake lights don't come on when you press the pedal.
causes.against: If the brake lights work normally, look at the other causes first.

causes.name: Weak or dead battery
causes.clues: Dim dash lights, slow cranking, or a push-button or dial shifter.

causes.name: Car's weight resting on the Park lock
causes.clues: Parked on a slope without the parking brake set first, and the shifter feels jammed rather than locked.

causes.name: Failed shift lock part or shift cable
causes.clues: The brake lights work, and the manual release lets you shift.

you: Have someone check whether the brake lights come on.
Check the brake light fuse.
Try the shift lock release.

result.title: A delay before it engages often points to low fluid or internal transmission wear
result.now: Have the transmission checked within the next few days. If your car has a transmission dipstick, check the fluid level the way your owner's manual describes first.
if: If the delay gets longer, or the engine revs before the car moves, stop driving and have it towed.
If you see reddish fluid under the car, don't drive it until the leak is found.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke from under the car, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away.
If it slips or loses drive while you're moving, pull over when it is safe and have it towed.
result.why: An automatic transmission uses fluid pressure to engage each gear. When the fluid is low or worn, or internal seals are tired, it can take longer to build that pressure. A shop will usually check the fluid and codes before deciding on any repair, and catching it early often means a smaller one.

causes.name: Low transmission fluid
causes.clues: Reddish spots where you park, or the delay is worse when the engine is cold.

causes.name: Old or burnt fluid
causes.clues: Dark fluid with a burnt smell, or no transmission service in many years.

causes.name: Worn internal seals or valve body problem
causes.clues: Harsh or late shifts as well as the delay.

causes.name: Transmission control fault
causes.clues: A check engine or transmission warning light is on.

you: Look for reddish spots where you park.
Note whether it's worse when cold or after a long drive.
Check the fluid if your car has a dipstick.
shop: Transmission fluid level and condition check

result.title: The transmission may have lost one or more of its gears
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed to a transmission shop or a general repair shop.
if: If it's blocking traffic, put it in Neutral and push it out of the way with help, or call roadside assistance.
If you find the fluid very low, tell the shop. A leak may be a much easier fix than internal damage.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: Drive and Reverse use different clutches or bands inside the transmission. When one direction works and the other doesn't, one of those may have failed or isn't getting enough fluid pressure. A car that can't be relied on to go forward isn't safe in traffic, and forcing it can cause more damage.

causes.name: Low transmission fluid
causes.clues: A leak, or delayed engagement in the weeks before.

causes.name: Worn or failed clutch pack or band inside the transmission
causes.clues: That gear slipped or flared before it quit.

causes.name: Shift solenoid or valve body fault
causes.clues: A transmission or check engine light, or the car seems stuck in one gear.

you: Look for reddish fluid under the car.
Note any warning lights on the dash.

result.title: The parking brake or a stuck brake may be holding the car back
result.now: Make sure the parking brake is fully released (pedal, lever or electronic switch), then try moving off gently. If the car still feels held back, don't keep driving it. Have the brakes checked first.
if: If a wheel smokes, smells burning or is too hot to go near, stop. Let it cool and have the car towed.
If it still feels held back with the parking brake off, have the brakes checked before driving any further.
If the brake pedal feels hard, soft or different than usual, or the red brake warning light stays on, have it checked before driving.
result.why: If you can feel the transmission go into gear but the car struggles to roll, something is resisting the wheels. A parking brake that's on, partly on or frozen, or a brake caliper that won't release, are common causes. A brake that stays on can overheat, so it shouldn't be driven on.

causes.name: Parking brake still on or partly on
causes.clues: The brake warning light is on, or the electronic parking brake didn't release.

causes.name: Parking brake frozen or rusted
causes.clues: Cold, wet weather, or the car sat unused for a while.

causes.name: Stuck brake caliper
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter than the others, there's a burning smell, or the car pulls to one side.

you: Check the parking brake warning light.
After a short, slow move, hold your hand near (not on) each wheel to feel for one that's much hotter.
shop: Parking brake cable and mechanism check

result.title: The shifter may have come disconnected from the transmission
result.now: Set the parking brake firmly and don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you can't be sure the car is in Park (or in gear, on a manual), block the wheels as well as setting the parking brake.
If the shifter suddenly goes loose while you're driving, pull over safely and stop as soon as you can.
result.why: A cable or rod connects the shifter to the transmission. If it breaks, or the small bushing that holds it falls apart, moving the shifter no longer changes gears, so the transmission can be left in any gear, including one that lets the car roll. It's often a small part, but the car isn't safe to use until it's checked and fixed.

causes.name: Worn-out shift cable bushing
causes.clues: The shifter feels loose or floppy. This is a common wear part.

causes.name: Broken, stretched or disconnected shift cable or linkage
causes.clues: The dash gear display doesn't match the shifter position.

causes.name: Linkage not reconnected after a repair
causes.clues: Recent work near the transmission or under the center console.

you: Note whether the dash gear display changes when you move the shifter.
Note whether the shifter feels loose or moves with almost no resistance.

result.title: The transmission may have lost its fluid
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed so the leak can be found and fixed before more damage is done.
if: If you can see where it's leaking, take a photo for the shop.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: An automatic transmission needs fluid pressure to engage any gear. A large leak, like a split cooler line or a damaged pan, can drain it quickly, and the car stops moving. Running it with too little fluid, even briefly, can ruin the transmission. A shop will find the leak and check for damage before refilling and road-testing.

causes.name: Leaking transmission cooler line
causes.clues: A puddle toward the front of the car and a sudden loss of drive.

causes.name: Leaking pan, gasket, seal or drain plug
causes.clues: Drips under the middle of the car, or a recent fluid service.

causes.name: Leaking axle seal
causes.clues: Fluid on the inside of a front wheel or tire.

you: Note the color of the fluid and where the puddle is.
Check the dipstick if your car has one.
shop: Check for damage from running low

result.title: An axle or drive shaft may be broken
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed, ideally on a flatbed truck.
if: If the engine sounds normal and you can feel it go into gear, but the wheels don't turn, that points more to a broken axle or drive shaft than to the transmission.
If fluid is pouring out under the car, tell the tow driver and the shop.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: A loud bang or clunk followed by no movement often means something between the transmission and the wheels has snapped. The engine and transmission may be fine, but the power isn't reaching the wheels. Clicking when turning in the days before often points to a worn CV joint. A shop will inspect the axles, drive shaft and differential to confirm.

causes.name: Broken CV axle
causes.clues: Clicking when turning beforehand, a front-wheel-drive car, or grease spattered inside a front wheel.

causes.name: Broken drive shaft or U-joint
causes.clues: A rear-wheel or all-wheel-drive vehicle, with clunking or vibration beforehand.

causes.name: Broken parts inside the differential or transmission
causes.clues: Grinding noises, or a fluid leak after the bang.

you: Look behind each front wheel for a torn rubber boot or sprayed grease.
From beside the car, without getting under it, look for a drive shaft hanging down.

result.title: The transmission doesn't seem to be sending power to the wheels
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed to a shop and ask for a transmission diagnosis.
if: If the fluid turns out to be very low, a leak may be the real cause, which is often a smaller repair.
If a transmission or check engine light is on, the stored codes will help the shop.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: When the gear display shows Drive and the engine revs but the car doesn't move, the transmission isn't engaging. Possible reasons include very low fluid, worn internal clutches, a failed torque converter or pump, or an electronic fault. A shop will usually check the fluid, codes and pressure before deciding what has failed. Revving it harder won't help and can cause more damage.

causes.name: Very low transmission fluid
causes.clues: Reddish spots where you park, or delayed engagement in the weeks before.

causes.name: Worn internal clutches
causes.clues: Slipping, or the revs flaring between gears before it quit.

causes.name: Failed torque converter or transmission pump
causes.clues: A whine that rises and falls with engine speed.

causes.name: Electronic control fault
causes.clues: A transmission warning light, or it was stuck in one gear before it quit.

you: Check the fluid if your car has a dipstick.
Note any warning lights on the dash.

result.title: The clutch hydraulics may have failed
result.now: Don't drive it. Check the clutch fluid reservoir and look for leaks, then have it towed or call a mobile mechanic to the car.
if: If the reservoir is low and there's fluid near the clutch pedal or under the car, a leaking clutch master or slave cylinder is a possible cause.
If the brake pedal also feels soft, don't move the car at all. On many cars the brakes and clutch share one fluid reservoir.
If the reservoir is low, don't just top it up and drive. Not seeing a leak doesn't rule one out, and on a shared reservoir the brakes can be affected too.
result.why: Most manual cars use fluid pressure to release the clutch. If the pedal sinks or stays down, that pressure may be gone, so the clutch can't release and gears grind or won't go in. Forcing it into gear risks damaging the transmission and leaves you without control of when the car moves.

causes.name: Leaking clutch slave cylinder
causes.clues: Fluid dripping near where the engine meets the transmission.

causes.name: Failed clutch master cylinder
causes.clues: Fluid on the carpet or under the dash near the pedal, or the pedal sinks slowly.

causes.name: Air in the clutch line
causes.clues: Recent clutch work, or the reservoir ran low.

causes.name: Broken clutch cable
causes.clues: An older or cable-operated car, and the pedal went limp with no resistance.

you: Check the clutch fluid reservoir level (your owner's manual shows where).
Look for wet fluid near the pedal and under the car.
shop: Clutch master and slave cylinder test

result.title: The clutch may not be fully releasing
result.now: Press the clutch all the way to the floor and wait two or three seconds before selecting first or Reverse, and book a clutch check in the next few days.
if: If the gears go in easily with the engine off but grind with it running, that points to the clutch not releasing. Tell the shop.
If the clutch pedal starts to feel soft or sinks, or the brake pedal feels soft, stop driving and have it towed.
If you smell burning from the clutch, stop and let it cool before trying again.
If it only grinds going into Reverse, make sure the car is fully stopped and pause a moment first. Many manuals grind in Reverse if you shift too quickly.
result.why: Gears go in smoothly only when the clutch fully disconnects the engine from the transmission. If it doesn't fully release, parts inside are still spinning and the gears clash. Low fluid, air in the line or a worn clutch are common reasons, and a shop will usually check the hydraulics before looking at the clutch itself.

causes.name: Low clutch fluid or air in the line
causes.clues: The pedal feels slightly soft, or the clutch only releases right at the floor.

causes.name: Worn or warped clutch parts
causes.clues: The clutch grabs very high or very low, or shudders when you pull away.

causes.name: Worn synchros in the transmission
causes.clues: It grinds mainly in one gear, especially when shifting quickly while moving.
causes.against: If it grinds going into every gear from a stop, the clutch is more likely.

you: Check the clutch fluid reservoir.
With the engine off, try selecting gears. If they go in easily, the clutch is the more likely problem.

result.title: The clutch may be slipping badly
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed to a shop.
if: If you smell burning, let the car sit and cool before anyone works on it.
If the car doesn't creep at all when you let the clutch out, a broken axle or drive shaft is also possible. Tell the shop.
result.why: When the gear goes in but the engine revs without moving the car, the clutch may no longer be gripping. That usually builds gradually as the clutch wears, then suddenly gets much worse. Oil on the clutch, or a hydraulic problem keeping it partly released, can do the same, so a shop will check those before replacing the clutch.

causes.name: Worn-out clutch disc
causes.clues: Revs flaring in higher gears for a while before, or a burning smell.

causes.name: Clutch hydraulics not letting it fully engage
causes.clues: The pedal is slow to come back up, or feels different than usual.

causes.name: Oil leaking onto the clutch
causes.clues: Oil dripping from where the engine meets the transmission.

causes.name: Broken axle or drive shaft
causes.clues: A bang beforehand, and no movement at all in any gear.
causes.against: If the car creeps slightly as you let the clutch out, the clutch is more likely.

you: Note whether you smell burning after trying to move.
Look for oil dripping between the engine and transmission.

result.title: A shop needs to see what's stopping it from moving
result.now: Set the parking brake, note what you see and hear when you try to shift, and have it towed or call roadside assistance.
if: If you see a puddle under the car or smell burning, don't try again. Tell the tow driver.
If the shifter won't leave Park, check whether the brake lights work. That's a common, simple cause.
If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, don't try to move the car. Tell the tow driver and the shop.
result.why: Without knowing whether the shifter moves, whether the engine revs, or whether there's a leak, it's hard to narrow it down safely. A technician can quickly tell a shifter problem from a fluid, clutch or axle problem.

causes.name: Shifter or shift lock problem
causes.clues: The shifter won't move, or feels loose.

causes.name: Low fluid or a transmission fault
causes.clues: A reddish puddle, or the engine revs but the car doesn't move.

causes.name: Clutch or axle problem
causes.clues: A manual car, or a bang or clunk before it stopped moving.

you: Record a short video with sound of what happens when you try to shift. It helps the shop a lot.

q_what_happens.q: What happens when you turn the key or press Start?
q_what_happens.help: "Cranking" is the whirring sound of the engine turning over (rrr-rrr-rrr) before it fires up.

opts.a: Nothing at all: no sound, and the dash stays dark
Rapid clicking or chattering (click-click-click)
One loud click, then nothing, but the dash lights come on
The engine cranks normally but never fires up
It starts, then stalls within a few seconds
I'm not sure

q_lights.q: When you turn the key to ON (or press Start without your foot on the brake), do the dash lights come on brightly?
q_lights.help: Turn the headlights on too. If they're dim or flicker when you try to start, the battery is the likely culprit.

opts.a: No, or they're very dim
Yes, bright, but the engine doesn't turn over
Yes, and the engine turns over but won't run
I'm not sure

q_jump.q: Have you tried a jump start or a battery booster?

opts.a: Yes, and it started
Yes, and it still just clicks
Not yet
I'm not sure

q_cranks_clues.help: These clues separate a fuel problem from an ignition or security problem.

opts.a: The fuel gauge is low or near empty
A key, lock or security light is flashing on the dash
I smell fuel strongly after cranking
It ran fine before, then died while driving and now won't restart
None of these / I'm not sure
Right after starting, every time
Mostly on cold mornings, then it's fine once warm
When I put it in gear or turn on the A/C
I'm not sure

result.title: The battery may be completely drained or disconnected
result.now: First look at the battery: if it's swollen, cracked, leaking, very hot or smells like rotten eggs, don't jump-start or charge it. Keep sparks away and have it checked. If it looks normal, check that the battery cables are tight and free of crusty white or green buildup, then try a jump start or a battery booster.
if: If a jump start works, drive for at least 30 minutes or have the battery and charging system tested soon, because it may die again.
If nothing at all happens even with a good jump, a main fuse, the ignition switch or a cable may have failed. Have it towed to a shop.
result.why: With no sound and no dash lights, there's essentially no electrical power reaching the car. That most often comes from a dead battery or a loose or corroded battery cable, and occasionally a blown main fuse. A battery test will confirm whether the battery itself is worn out or just drained.

causes.name: Dead or drained battery
causes.clues: Lights left on, a car that sat for weeks, a battery older than 4–5 years, or very cold weather.
causes.against: If the dash lights come on brightly, the battery is less likely to be the main problem.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery cable
causes.clues: Crusty buildup on the terminals, or a cable you can wiggle by hand.

causes.name: Blown main fuse or failed ignition switch
causes.clues: A jump start changes nothing at all.
causes.against: Much less common than a battery problem.

you: Check whether the dome light and headlights work.
Look at the battery terminals for corrosion or loose clamps.
Try a jump start or a battery booster pack.
shop: Parasitic draw test if the battery keeps dying
Main fuse and ignition circuit check

result.title: Rapid clicking often means the battery is too weak to turn the starter
result.now: First look at the battery: if it's swollen, cracked, leaking, very hot or smells like rotten eggs, don't jump-start or charge it. Keep sparks away and have it checked. If it looks normal, check that the battery clamps are tight and clean, then try a jump start or a battery booster.
if: If it starts with a jump, have the battery and alternator tested soon. Most auto parts stores do this free.
If it still only clicks with a good jump, the battery cables or the starter are the more likely problem.
result.why: The starter needs a big burst of power. A weak battery has enough to light the dash and make the starter's switch click, but not enough to spin the engine, so you hear rapid clicking as it tries over and over.

causes.name: Weak or discharged battery
causes.clues: Dim lights, a slow crank in recent days, cold weather, or a battery older than 4–5 years.

causes.name: Corroded or loose battery terminal
causes.clues: Visible buildup, or the clicking changes when you wiggle a cable.

causes.name: Alternator not charging
causes.clues: The battery light came on while driving, or the battery keeps going flat.
causes.against: If the car started fine yesterday after a long drive, a charging fault is less likely.

you: Check the battery terminals.
Try a jump start or a booster pack.
Note whether the battery warning light came on recently while driving.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the battery cables

result.title: The battery was low. Find out why before it happens again
result.now: Keep the engine running for a while or drive it at least 30 minutes, then get the battery and charging system tested within the next few days.
if: If the battery warning light comes on while driving, pull over when it's safe and turn off everything you don't need. The alternator may not be charging, and the car could die on the road, so have it towed or checked where it is.
If the battery light comes on and the temperature gauge starts climbing, pull over and turn the engine off. On many cars one belt drives both the alternator and the water pump.
If it was a one-time mistake, like lights left on, a test will tell you if the battery recovered.
result.why: A jump start fixing it suggests the battery didn't have enough charge. The question is why: an aging battery, an alternator that isn't recharging it, or something draining it while the car is parked. A battery and charging test will usually show which before anything is replaced.

causes.name: Aging battery
causes.clues: The battery is more than 4–5 years old, or the car cranks slowly on cold mornings.

causes.name: Alternator not charging
causes.clues: The battery light flickers or stays on, the headlights dim at idle, or there's a whining noise.

causes.name: Something draining the battery while parked
causes.clues: It keeps happening after the car sits overnight or for a few days.

you: Watch for the battery warning light while driving.
Note how old the battery is (often stamped on a label on top).

result.title: Possibly a bad battery connection or a failing starter
result.now: Check that the battery clamps are tight and clean. If they are and a jump doesn't help, have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If cleaning or tightening the cables fixes it, have the cables checked for hidden corrosion soon.
If you're stuck somewhere unsafe, call roadside assistance rather than repeatedly cranking.
If a battery cable is hot to the touch, or you smell burning or see smoke, stop trying to start it and step away.
result.why: When even a good jump only produces clicking, enough power isn't reaching the starter motor. That can point to a poor connection somewhere in the heavy cables, or to a starter that's worn out. A voltage-drop test usually tells the two apart before any part is replaced.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery cable or ground strap
causes.clues: Buildup on the terminals, or a cable that's warm or loose.

causes.name: Failing starter motor or solenoid
causes.clues: The starter has been slow or noisy recently, or tapping it has made it work before.

causes.name: Battery with an internal fault
causes.clues: The battery is old and won't hold a charge even after charging.

you: Tighten and clean the battery clamps.
Check the ground strap from the engine to the body for a loose or broken connection.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the positive and ground cables

result.title: Possibly the starter, or a poor connection to it
result.now: Make sure the car is fully in Park (or press the clutch on a manual) and try again. If it still only clicks once, the car will need a tow or a mobile mechanic.
if: If it starts in Neutral but not Park, the gear-position (neutral safety) switch may be the problem.
If it starts after a few tries, get the starter checked soon. It may get worse.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the hood, stop trying and step away from the car.
result.why: Bright dash lights mean the battery has some power. One loud click often means the starter's switch (solenoid) is getting the signal but the motor isn't turning, which points to a worn starter or a bad connection to it. A shop will usually test the cables and connections before replacing the starter.

causes.name: Worn starter motor or solenoid
causes.clues: Starting has been hit-or-miss lately, or the starter sounded slow or grinding.

causes.name: Gear-position (neutral safety) or clutch switch
causes.clues: It starts in Neutral but not Park, or it depends on how you press the clutch.

causes.name: Bad cable connection at the starter
causes.clues: The problem comes and goes, especially after rain or rough roads.

you: Try starting in Neutral.
On a manual, press the clutch fully to the floor.

result.title: It may simply be out of fuel, or the gauge may be wrong
result.now: Add a few gallons of fuel and try again. On a slope, the engine may not be able to pick up the last bit of fuel in the tank.
if: If it starts after adding fuel, but the gauge showed fuel left, have the fuel gauge checked so it doesn't leave you stranded.
If it still cranks without starting after adding fuel, the fuel pump may have failed. Have it towed.
If you smell raw fuel after adding fuel or cranking, stop and look for a leak. Don't keep trying to start it.
result.why: An engine that cranks normally but never fires usually isn't getting fuel or spark. A low tank is the simplest explanation, and fuel gauges can read wrong.

causes.name: Out of fuel
causes.clues: The gauge is near empty, or the car is parked on a hill.

causes.name: Faulty fuel gauge sender
causes.clues: The gauge has acted strangely before.

causes.name: Failing fuel pump
causes.clues: Adding fuel doesn't help, and you can't hear a brief hum from the rear when you turn the key to ON.

you: Add fuel.
With the car quiet, turn the key to ON and listen for a 2-second hum from the back of the car.
shop: Fuel pump power and ground check

result.title: The anti-theft system may not be recognizing your key
result.now: Try your spare key. For push-button start, hold the key fob right against the Start button, or put it where your owner's manual says, while you press Start.
if: If the spare works, replace the battery in your main key fob or have the key checked.
If neither key works, the car may need a dealer or locksmith with the right equipment to reprogram the key.
result.why: A flashing key or security light usually means the car's immobilizer is blocking fuel or ignition because it can't read a valid key. The engine will crank but won't run until it recognizes one.

causes.name: Dead key fob battery
causes.clues: The remote's range has been getting shorter.

causes.name: Damaged or unprogrammed key
causes.clues: A new copy that wasn't programmed, or a key that's been dropped or got wet.

causes.name: Immobilizer system fault
causes.clues: Neither key works.

you: Try the spare key.
Replace the key fob battery (often a coin battery).

result.title: The engine may be flooded, or fuel may be leaking
result.now: Stop cranking. Look under the car and around the engine for wet spots or dripping fuel. If you see any, don't try to start it again and have it towed.
if: If there's no visible leak, open the hood and wait 15–20 minutes. Only if the smell has faded, try once: press the gas pedal fully to the floor and hold it while you crank for up to 10 seconds. On most fuel-injected cars this cuts fuel to help clear a flooded engine.
Not seeing a leak doesn't prove there isn't one. If the smell stays strong, comes back or gets stronger, don't crank again. Have it towed.
If it still won't start after that one try, have it towed.
result.why: A strong fuel smell after cranking can mean fuel is reaching the engine but not burning, which can flood it. It can also mean a leak, which is a fire risk.

causes.name: Flooded engine
causes.clues: Several long cranking attempts, especially on a cold engine.

causes.name: Fuel leak
causes.clues: A wet spot under the car, or a smell that's strongest near one area.

causes.name: No spark (ignition fault)
causes.clues: Fuel is getting there but nothing ignites it.

you: Look for dripping fuel or wet spots.
Don't smoke or use flames nearby.

result.title: The fuel pump or a crankshaft sensor may have failed
result.now: Don't keep cranking it. Have the car towed to a shop.
if: If it restarts after cooling down for 30 minutes or more, don't count on it. These parts can fail completely soon after, so get it checked before driving any distance.
If you heard a loud bang, rattling or knocking, or the temperature gauge was in the red before it died, don't try to restart it. Tell the shop.
If the engine sounds different when cranking, such as faster or more even than usual, stop cranking. A broken timing belt can do this.
result.why: An engine that shuts off while driving and won't restart has usually lost fuel or spark. Common causes include a fuel pump that's stopped working or a crankshaft position sensor, the part that tells the engine computer when to fire. A shop will test fuel pressure and check for codes before replacing either.

causes.name: Failed fuel pump
causes.clues: No hum from the rear when you turn the key to ON, or sputtering before it died.

causes.name: Failed crankshaft position sensor
causes.clues: It died suddenly with no sputter, and may restart once cool.

causes.name: Fuel pump relay or fuse
causes.clues: It died suddenly. These are cheap to check first.

causes.name: Broken timing belt or chain
causes.clues: The engine cranks faster or sounds different than usual, and it died suddenly.
causes.against: Less common than a fuel or sensor fault.

you: Listen for the fuel pump hum.
Note whether a check engine light came on before it died.
shop: Scan for crank and cam sensor codes
Fuel pump relay and fuse check
Timing belt or chain check if the cranking sounds unusual

result.title: The engine may not be getting fuel or spark. A shop can test it
result.now: Try once or twice more, each time for no more than 10 seconds. If it doesn't fire, have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you smell fuel or see a leak, stop trying and keep flames away.
If a check engine light is on, a code reader can give the shop a head start.
If the cranking sounds faster, uneven or different than usual, stop trying. A broken timing belt can do this and more cranking won't help.
result.why: A normal crank suggests the battery and starter are working. The engine needs fuel, spark and air at the right time to run, so one of those is likely missing. Telling which one takes a few quick tests.

causes.name: Fuel delivery problem (pump, relay, filter)
causes.clues: No hum from the rear when you turn the key to ON.

causes.name: Ignition problem (sensor, coil, wiring)
causes.clues: A check engine light, or rough running in the days before.

causes.name: Security system blocking the start
causes.clues: A key or lock light on the dash.

you: Listen for the fuel pump hum.
Look for a flashing key or security light.

result.title: Starts then stalls: check the key system first, then idle and fuel delivery
result.now: Look for a flashing key or security light right after it stalls, and try the spare key. If that doesn't help, have the car checked before relying on it.
if: If it stalls while you're driving, not just at startup, don't drive it. When the engine stalls, steering and braking can take much more force, which is dangerous in traffic.
If you smell fuel, stop trying to start it and look for a leak.
result.why: When a car fires up and dies within seconds, the security system is often letting it start and then cutting fuel because it doesn't recognize the key. If the key is fine, the idle control or fuel delivery may not be keeping it running.

causes.name: Immobilizer not recognizing the key
causes.clues: A key or security light, or it happens with one key but not the other.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control fault
causes.clues: The idle has been low or uneven.

causes.name: Weak fuel pump or clogged filter
causes.clues: Sputtering or hesitation when you press the gas.

you: Watch for a security light.
Try the spare key.

result.title: Cold-start stalling often points to idle control or a sensor reading wrong
result.now: Let it idle for 30 seconds before driving off on cold mornings, and book a check.
if: If the check engine light comes on or it starts stalling when warm too, get it checked sooner.
If it stalls while you're moving, pull over when it is safe and don't drive it until it's checked. Steering and braking can take much more force when the engine stalls.
result.why: A cold engine needs extra fuel and a higher idle. If a temperature sensor gives the computer the wrong reading, or the idle system is dirty, the engine can die until it warms up. Live sensor data at a shop usually shows which.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control valve
causes.clues: A low, uneven idle.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: The temperature gauge acts oddly, or fuel economy has dropped.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or a rough idle that smooths out when warm.

you: Note the outside temperature when it happens.
Listen for hissing from the engine bay.
shop: Code scan and live sensor data

result.title: The idle may be too low to handle extra load
result.now: Get it checked within the next few days. Don't hold the gas to keep it running while you shift into gear, because the car can lurch.
if: If it stalls while driving or as you come to a stop, don't drive it until it's checked. Steering and braking can take much more force when the engine stalls.
If the check engine light is steady, have the code read before driving further. If the check engine light is flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: Shifting into gear or turning on the A/C adds load to the engine. If the idle control can't raise the engine speed to match, the engine stumbles and dies.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control fault
causes.clues: The idle drops noticeably when the A/C kicks on.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: Hissing, or a rough idle.

causes.name: Torque converter clutch not releasing (automatic)
causes.clues: It stalls when coming to a stop, like stalling a manual car.

you: Notice whether the A/C makes the stall more likely.

result.title: Let a shop or roadside service take a look
result.now: Note anything you see or hear when you try to start it, then call roadside assistance or have it towed to a shop.
if: If you smell fuel or burning, stop trying to start it.
result.why: Without knowing whether there's power and whether the engine turns over, it's hard to narrow it down safely. A technician can check the battery, starter and fuel in a few minutes.

causes.name: Battery or connection problem
causes.clues: The most common cause of a no-start.

causes.name: Starter problem
causes.clues: A click with no crank.

causes.name: Fuel or ignition problem
causes.clues: It cranks but won't run.

you: Record a short video with sound of what happens when you try to start it. It helps the shop a lot.

q_what_happens.q: What happens when you turn the key off or press the Start/Stop button?
q_what_happens.help: "Dieseling" (also called run-on) is when an engine keeps coughing and chugging unevenly for a few seconds after you switch it off.

opts.a: The engine keeps running smoothly, even with the key off or removed
The engine coughs, chugs or shakes for a few seconds, then stops
Push-button start: pressing the button doesn't turn it off
The engine stops, but I hear a fan or whirring under the hood
The engine revs higher and higher by itself (diesel engine)
I'm not sure

q_after_off.q: Right after you switch off, which fits best?
q_after_off.help: The tachometer is the gauge that shows engine speed (RPM). If it still shows a reading, the engine is still running.

opts.a: The tachometer still shows RPM and exhaust keeps coming out
The dash goes dark, but a fan or pump keeps running under the hood
The engine shakes or coughs briefly, then stops
I'm not sure

q_park.q: What does the dashboard show when you press the button to turn it off?

opts.a: A message like "Shift to Park", or the gear display doesn't show P
It shows P with no message, but the button doesn't respond
I'm not sure

q_vehicle_type.q: Does the engine have a carburetor or fuel injection?
q_vehicle_type.help: Most cars built since the early 1990s have fuel injection. A carburetor is found mainly on older vehicles, classic cars and some small engines.

opts.a: Carburetor (older or classic vehicle)
Fuel injection (most modern cars)
I'm not sure

q_hot.q: Has the engine been running hotter than usual?

opts.a: Yes, the temperature gauge is high or in the red
No, the temperature gauge is normal
I'm not sure

result.title: An electrical fault may be keeping the engine powered
result.now: Don't drive it. Put it in Park with the parking brake on, turn the key to ON and back to OFF firmly, and if it keeps running, call roadside assistance or a mobile mechanic.
if: If you're comfortable with the fuse box, pulling the fuel pump fuse or relay (shown in the owner's manual) will usually make the engine stall within a few seconds.
If it's a manual, you can stall it: with the parking brake on and your foot hard on the brake, put it in a high gear and release the clutch.
If it's in a closed space, open the doors or garage door right away and get everyone out.
If you smell burning plastic or see smoke from the dash, steering column or fuse box, get out, step away and call for help.
result.why: On a modern car, turning the key off cuts power to the fuel and ignition systems. If the engine keeps running normally, something is still feeding that power, often a worn ignition switch or a relay stuck closed. A shop will test the switch, relays and wiring to find which. Until it's fixed, you can't count on being able to shut the engine off.

causes.name: Worn or faulty ignition switch
causes.clues: The key feels loose or different, or the dash and radio act oddly when you jiggle the key.

causes.name: Stuck main or ignition relay
causes.clues: It happens on push-button cars too, sometimes with a click from the fuse box.

causes.name: Wiring fault after a repair or accessory install
causes.clues: It started after a remote starter, alarm or stereo was installed.

you: Note whether the dash lights and radio stay on with the key removed.
Think back to any recent electrical work or accessories added.

result.title: Classic engine run-on (dieseling)
result.now: Make sure the idle isn't set too high, and book a tune-up check when convenient.
