if: If it happens mainly after hard driving on hot days, let it idle for 30 seconds before switching off.
If the engine also pings or knocks under load, get it checked sooner, because the same hot spots can damage the engine.
If the temperature gauge is high or in the red, or you smell fuel, don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: On carbureted engines, fuel can keep getting pulled in after the ignition is off. Hot carbon deposits or a high idle can then ignite it, so the engine chugs on unevenly for a few seconds. It's common on older vehicles and is often fixed with adjustments and cleaning once a shop checks the idle and timing.

causes.name: Idle speed set too high
causes.clues: The idle sounds fast, or the engine was recently adjusted.

causes.name: Carbon buildup in the engine
causes.clues: Lots of short trips, pinging under load, or high mileage.

causes.name: Failed anti-dieseling (idle stop) solenoid
causes.clues: Run-on started suddenly on a carburetor that has one.
causes.against: Not every carburetor has one.

causes.name: Fuel octane too low or ignition timing off
causes.clues: Pinging or knocking when accelerating.

you: Check the owner's manual or engine label for the correct fuel grade.
Note whether it happens mainly when the engine is very hot.

result.title: Overheating may be making the engine run on
result.now: Switch the engine off, let it cool completely, and don't drive it until the overheating is fixed. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see steam or coolant leaking, stay away from the radiator cap. It can spray scalding coolant.
If the coolant is low, don't just top it up and drive. The reason it went low and overheated needs to be found first.
If you hear knocking, or see smoke or a red oil pressure light, don't restart the engine.
result.why: An overheating engine has hot spots that can ignite fuel even after the ignition is off. The run-on is a symptom; the overheating is the bigger danger, and it can warp or crack engine parts.

causes.name: Low coolant or a cooling system leak
causes.clues: Puddles under the car, a sweet smell, or steam.

causes.name: Failed cooling fan, thermostat or water pump
causes.clues: It overheats mostly at idle, or the gauge climbs quickly.

causes.name: Ignition timing or mixture problem
causes.clues: Pinging, poor power, or recent engine adjustments.

you: Once fully cold, check the coolant level.
Look for leaks under the car.
shop: Thermostat, fan and water pump check

result.title: A shake at shutdown on a modern car often points to engine mounts
result.now: Book a check when convenient and mention exactly when the shake happens.
if: If you also feel a clunk when shifting into gear or accelerating, worn engine mounts are more likely. Get them checked sooner.
If the engine truly keeps running after the key is off, or you smell fuel, don't drive it and have it checked right away.
If the check engine light is flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. If the temperature gauge runs high, have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Fuel-injected engines cut fuel the moment you switch off, so true run-on is rare. What feels like run-on is often the engine rocking as it stops, which worn mounts let you feel more. Less often, a leaking injector lets fuel in after shutdown. A shop will usually inspect the mounts and check for codes before deciding.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mounts
causes.clues: A clunk when shifting into gear, or extra vibration at idle.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector
causes.clues: A fuel smell, hard starting when warm, or a rough start.

causes.name: Heavy carbon buildup
causes.clues: Pinging under load, or a check engine light.

you: Have someone watch the engine while you switch off and see if it rocks a lot.
Notice any clunk when shifting from Park into Drive or Reverse.

result.title: The car doesn't think it's in Park
result.now: With your foot on the brake, move the shifter out of Park and firmly back into Park, then press the button again.
if: If it keeps happening, have the shifter's Park switch checked soon. Leaving the car in accessory mode can drain the battery.
If the car won't stay in Park or rolls, don't leave it. Set the parking brake and have it checked before driving again.
result.why: Most push-button cars won't fully shut down unless they detect the shifter in Park. A worn switch in the shifter, or something like a coin or spilled drink in the shifter, can stop it from registering Park.

causes.name: Worn or faulty Park position switch in the shifter
causes.clues: Wiggling the shifter makes the message go away.

causes.name: Debris or a spill in the shifter
causes.clues: Something was dropped or spilled near the shifter recently.

causes.name: Shift cable out of adjustment
causes.clues: The gear display doesn't match where the shifter sits.

you: Push the shifter firmly into Park and check the gear display.
Look around the shifter for debris or signs of a spill.
shop: Check for open recalls or service bulletins

result.title: The Start/Stop button or keyless system isn't responding
result.now: Press and hold the Start/Stop button for a few seconds. That shuts off most cars even when a quick press doesn't. Book a check when convenient.
if: If holding the button doesn't shut it off, don't leave it running and don't drive it. Call roadside assistance or a mobile mechanic.
If the key fob battery is weak, replace it. Some cars act oddly when they can't read the fob.
result.why: Push-button systems use a switch and a computer to decide when to shut down. A sticky button, a weak fob battery or a module fault can stop a short press from working, while a long press often overrides it.

causes.name: Worn or sticky Start/Stop button
causes.clues: You have to press harder or more than once.

causes.name: Weak key fob battery
causes.clues: A "key not detected" message, or the remote range has dropped.

causes.name: Keyless ignition module fault
causes.clues: Other odd behavior, like the car not locking or warning lights.

you: Try holding the button down for a few seconds.
Replace the key fob battery.
Check the owner's manual for the shutdown procedure.
shop: Code scan of the keyless system
Check for software updates or service bulletins

result.title: This sounds like the cooling fan or a pump finishing its job
result.now: Wait up to several minutes. On many cars the radiator fan or an electric coolant pump runs after shutdown to cool the engine, then turns off by itself.
if: If the fan keeps running for a long time or the battery goes flat overnight, have the fan relay checked.
If you see steam or smell coolant, or the temperature gauge was high before you switched off, the engine may be overheating. Have it checked before driving again.
If you smell burning or see smoke, step away from the car.
result.why: Fans and some pumps are controlled separately from the engine and can keep running after a hot drive, especially in warm weather or after towing. This is normal on many cars. A tachometer reading of zero and no exhaust from the tailpipe confirm the engine itself is off.

causes.name: Normal after-run cooling
causes.clues: It happens after hot days or long drives and stops within several minutes.

causes.name: Stuck fan relay or temperature sensor fault
causes.clues: The fan runs for a long time even on a cold engine, or the battery keeps going flat.

causes.name: Engine running hot
causes.clues: The temperature gauge has been higher than usual.

you: Time how long the noise lasts after you switch off.
Check that the tachometer reads zero and no exhaust comes out.

result.title: This may be a diesel engine runaway, which is an emergency
result.now: Get everyone away from the vehicle. If it's a manual and you can do it safely, hold the brakes hard, put it in the highest gear and release the clutch to stall the engine.
if: If there's fire or heavy smoke, move well away and call 911.
If the engine stops, don't restart it. Have it towed to a shop.
Don't reach into the engine bay or try to block the air intake by hand. The engine can pull in loose items and the parts are very hot.
result.why: A diesel engine can keep running and speeding up on fuel it isn't supposed to get, most often engine oil. The key can't shut off that fuel supply, and the engine can overspeed until it fails badly.

causes.name: Oil leaking into the intake from a failed turbocharger seal
causes.clues: Heavy blue or white smoke and a high-pitched whine before it happened.

causes.name: Engine oil overfilled or crankcase vapors pulled into the intake
causes.clues: Oil was recently added or changed.

causes.name: Fuel system or governor fault
causes.clues: The engine revved up without heavy smoke.

shop: Oil level and crankcase ventilation check

result.title: Find out whether the engine is truly still running
result.now: After switching off, watch the tachometer and check for exhaust at the tailpipe. Then book a check and tell the shop what you saw.
if: If the engine clearly keeps running with the key off, don't drive it. Call roadside assistance or a mobile mechanic.
If it's just a fan or whirring noise that stops within several minutes, that's often normal. Mention it to the shop if the temperature gauge has been running high.
result.why: A fan running after shutdown, an engine that coughs briefly and an engine that won't stop at all have very different causes and urgency. A quick look at the gauges and the tailpipe tells them apart.

causes.name: Normal cooling fan after-run
causes.clues: The dash is dark and the noise stops on its own.

causes.name: Engine run-on or shutdown shake
causes.clues: A brief cough or shudder, then silence.

causes.name: Electrical fault keeping the engine powered
causes.clues: The engine keeps running normally with the key out.

you: Record a short video with sound right after you switch off. It helps the shop a lot.

q_now.q: Is the light flashing right now with the engine running?
q_now.help: Flashing means blinking on and off about once a second. A light that stays lit without blinking is a steady check engine light, which is usually less urgent.

opts.a: Yes, and the engine is shaking, stumbling or losing power
Yes, but the engine feels fairly normal
It flashed earlier, but now it's steady or off
I'm not sure

q_shaking.q: Does the engine feel like it's shaking, stumbling or jerking, especially when you press the gas?

opts.a: Yes
No, it feels smooth
I'm not sure
I smell raw fuel or burning, or see smoke
The temperature gauge is high, or I've been losing coolant
It started right after filling up with fuel, or after running very low
None of these
I'm not sure
Only when accelerating hard, climbing a hill or carrying a heavy load
Only right after a cold start, then it settled down
Just once, and it hasn't happened since
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be misfiring badly. Stop driving it now
result.now: Pull over where it's safe, turn off the engine, and have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you're on a highway, get to the shoulder or the next safe exit with gentle throttle and your hazard lights on, then turn the engine off.
If you smell fuel or burning, or see smoke, step away from the car and call for help.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward red or a red warning light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: A flashing light with shaking usually means one or more cylinders aren't firing. Unburned fuel goes into the exhaust and burns in the catalytic converter, which can overheat it within minutes. Every mile you drive raises the repair bill and the fire risk. A shop will check misfire data by cylinder and test the coil, plug and injector before replacing anything.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil
causes.clues: A sudden, steady miss that's worse when accelerating.

causes.name: Worn or fouled spark plug
causes.clues: High miles since the last spark plug change, or the miss has been building over time.

causes.name: Fuel injector stuck or not firing
causes.clues: A fuel smell, or the miss is just as bad at idle.

causes.name: Mechanical engine problem
causes.clues: Ticking or knocking, or a timing belt or chain that's due.

you: Note when the shaking is worst: at idle, when accelerating, or all the time.
Don't restart the engine just to test it.
shop: Code scan and misfire counts by cylinder
Ignition coil and spark plug test

result.title: A misfire may be happening even if you can't feel it. Don't keep driving
result.now: Pull over where it's safe and turn off the engine. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you're in heavy traffic, ease off the gas, avoid hard acceleration, and get off the road at the first safe spot.
If the light goes steady after a restart, the fault is still stored. Have the code read before driving any distance.
If you smell raw fuel or burning, or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and get everyone away from the car.
result.why: The computer flashes the light when it counts enough misfires to risk overheating the catalytic converter. A misfire on one cylinder isn't always easy to feel, especially at steady speed, but the damage to the converter still happens.

causes.name: Failing ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: A slight stumble under load or at idle.

causes.name: Fuel injector problem
causes.clues: A faint fuel smell, or worse fuel mileage lately.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: A hissing sound from the engine bay.

you: Note whether there's a hesitation when you accelerate.
Listen for hissing from the engine bay with the engine off and cool.
shop: Code scan and misfire counts by cylinder
Ignition coil and spark plug test

result.title: Fuel or exhaust heat may be creating a fire risk
result.now: Pull over, turn off the engine, get everyone out and away from the car, and call for help.
if: If you see smoke or flames, stay well back and call 911.
If the smell fades and there's no smoke, still don't restart it. Have it towed.
result.why: A severe misfire sends raw fuel into a very hot exhaust. That can make the catalytic converter glow red-hot and ignite anything nearby, like dry grass under the car. A fuel smell can also mean a leak near hot engine parts.

causes.name: Overheated catalytic converter from misfire
causes.clues: A burning or sulfur smell from under the car.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector or fuel line
causes.clues: A strong raw fuel smell under the hood.

causes.name: Oil or fluid on hot exhaust
causes.clues: Bluish smoke, or a burning oil smell.

result.title: Coolant may be getting into the engine
result.now: Pull over, turn off the engine, and have the car towed. Don't open the radiator cap while the engine is hot.
if: If you see white, sweet-smelling smoke from the exhaust, mention it to the shop. It can point to coolant burning in the engine.
If the coolant level is low once it's fully cool, don't top it up and restart to test it.
result.why: A misfire together with overheating or coolant loss can mean coolant is leaking into a cylinder, for example through a failed head gasket. Coolant doesn't burn, so that cylinder misfires. Driving on it can warp the engine and cause major damage. A shop will pressure-test the cooling system and test for combustion gases before deciding what has failed.

causes.name: Failed head gasket
causes.clues: White exhaust smoke, a sweet smell, or bubbles in the coolant reservoir.

causes.name: Cracked cylinder head or intake gasket leak
causes.clues: Coolant loss with no visible leak.

causes.name: Overheating causing misfires
causes.clues: The temperature gauge climbed before the light started flashing.

you: Once the engine is fully cool, check the coolant level in the reservoir.
Note any white smoke or sweet smell.

result.title: Bad or wrong fuel, or fuel starvation, may be causing the misfire
result.now: Pull over where it's safe, turn off the engine, and have the car towed. Tell the shop where and when you filled up.
if: If you think the wrong fuel went in (like diesel in a gas car), don't restart it. The tank may need draining.
If it happened when the tank was nearly empty, add fuel, but still have it checked before driving.
If you smell raw fuel or burning, or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and get everyone away from the car.
result.why: Water in the fuel, the wrong fuel, or a fuel pump struggling on an almost-empty tank can all leave the engine without the right mixture. That causes misfires across several cylinders at once, which flashes the light.

causes.name: Contaminated or wrong fuel
causes.clues: It began within a few miles of filling up.

causes.name: Fuel starvation from a very low tank or weak pump
causes.clues: The gauge was near empty, or it's worse going uphill or around corners.

causes.name: Clogged fuel filter or injectors
causes.clues: Gradual loss of power over time before this.

you: Keep your fuel receipt and note the station and pump.
Note how much fuel was in the tank before it started.

result.title: Possibly a weak ignition coil or worn spark plugs
result.now: If the light flashes again or the engine shakes hard, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Otherwise: Get it checked within a few days. Until then, drive gently, avoid hard acceleration and steep hills, and don't tow or haul anything.
if: If the light flashes again or the car shakes, pull over and turn the engine off.
If it's happening more often, stop driving it and have it checked right away.
If you smell raw fuel or burning, or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and get everyone away from the car.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward red or a red warning light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Spark plugs and coils need more energy to fire when the engine is working hard. A weak coil or worn plug can cope at light throttle but misfire under load. A shop will usually swap or test the coil and inspect the plugs to confirm which one is at fault, and the repair is often fairly simple if it's done before the catalytic converter is damaged.

causes.name: Weak ignition coil
causes.clues: A stumble or jerk when accelerating or going uphill.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs
causes.clues: High miles since they were last changed.

causes.name: Fuel delivery weakness
causes.clues: A general loss of power at higher speeds too.

you: Check your service records for the last spark plug change.
Have the stored code read.
shop: Code scan and misfire counts by cylinder
Ignition coil test or swap test

result.title: A cold-start misfire may be a coil, plug or injector starting to fail
result.now: If the light flashes again or the engine shakes hard, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Otherwise: Get it checked within a few days. Don't drive off while the engine is shaking. If it shakes on a cold start, wait until it runs smoothly, and if it doesn't settle within a minute or two, turn it off and get it checked.
if: If the light flashes while you're driving, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you notice coolant loss or white exhaust smoke at startup, have it checked right away.
If you smell raw fuel or burning, or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and get everyone away from the car.
result.why: A cold engine is harder to fire, so a weak coil, worn plug or leaky injector often shows up there first. A misfire that only happens cold and then clears up is an early warning that often gets worse. The stored code and a few tests will show which part is involved.

causes.name: Weak ignition coil or worn spark plug
causes.clues: Worse in cold or damp weather.

causes.name: Leaking or sticking fuel injector
causes.clues: A fuel smell at startup.

causes.name: Small coolant leak into a cylinder
causes.clues: White smoke at startup, or coolant slowly going down.

you: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold.
Note the outside temperature when it happens.
shop: Cooling system pressure test if coolant is dropping

result.title: The misfire may come back. Get the code read soon
result.now: If the light flashes again or the engine shakes hard, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Otherwise: Have the stored code read within a few days. Drive gently and keep trips short until then.
if: If the light flashes again, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the light is now steady, follow the same plan: get the code read soon.
If you smell raw fuel or burning, or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and get everyone away from the car.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward red or a red warning light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: The computer stores a misfire code even after the light stops flashing. A one-time flash often comes from a part that's starting to fail, and it's usually much cheaper to fix now than after it damages the catalytic converter.

causes.name: Ignition coil or spark plug starting to fail
causes.clues: A brief stumble when it flashed.

causes.name: One-off fuel or moisture problem
causes.clues: It happened in heavy rain or right after a fill-up.

causes.name: Loose connector on a coil or injector
causes.clues: Recent engine work.

you: Have the stored code read.
Note the conditions when it flashed.
shop: Code scan including stored misfire data
Ignition coil and spark plug inspection

result.title: Check the light now: if it's blinking, stop driving
result.now: If the light is blinking, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. If it's steady and the car drives normally, have the code read within a few days.
if: If the light blinks at any point, treat it as urgent: pull over, turn the engine off and have it towed.
If it's steady and the car drives normally, it's usually less urgent, but still get the code read.
If you smell raw fuel or burning, or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and get everyone away from the car.
result.why: A flashing light and a steady light mean very different things. Flashing means a misfire that can damage the catalytic converter right now. Steady means a fault worth checking, which is usually not an emergency unless the car runs poorly or other warning lights come on.

causes.name: Misfire
causes.clues: The light blinks, often with shaking.
causes.against: A smooth-running engine with a steady light makes a severe misfire less likely.

causes.name: Emissions or sensor fault
causes.clues: The light is steady and the car drives normally.

you: Watch whether the light is blinking or steady.
Have the code read.

q_driving.q: How is the car driving right now?

opts.a: It shakes, stumbles or jerks, or the light sometimes flashes
The temperature gauge is high, or a red oil or battery light is on too
It's down on power, shows a "reduced power" message, or shifts strangely
I smell raw fuel
It drives normally
I'm not sure

q_fuel_up.q: Did the light come on within a day or two of filling up with fuel?

opts.a: Yes
No
I'm not sure

q_clues.q: Have you noticed any of these?
q_clues.help: Idle is the engine speed when you're stopped with your foot off the gas. A rough idle feels like a shudder or uneven pulsing.

opts.a: Worse fuel mileage, or a rotten egg smell from the exhaust
A rough or uneven idle, but it drives fine
The light comes and goes on its own, or showed up after a cold or damp spell
None of these. The car seems completely normal
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be misfiring. Stop driving it until it's checked
result.now: Pull over where it's safe, turn off the engine, and have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the shaking was brief and has stopped, don't assume the problem is gone. Have the code read before you drive it again.
If you smell fuel or see smoke, step away from the car and call for help.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward red or a red warning light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Shaking or stumbling with the check engine light on usually means one or more cylinders aren't firing. Unburned fuel then goes into the exhaust, where it can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter, and in bad cases start a fire. Driving on it can turn a small repair into a big one. The code and misfire data tell the shop which cylinder and parts to test.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or worn spark plug
causes.clues: The shaking is worse when you accelerate or climb a hill.

causes.name: Fuel injector problem
causes.clues: A fuel smell, or the misfire stays even at idle.

causes.name: Vacuum leak or mechanical engine problem
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or a ticking or knocking noise from the engine.

you: Note whether the light was steady or flashing.
Note when the shaking happens: at idle, when accelerating, or all the time.
shop: Spark plug and ignition coil check

result.title: A red warning light comes first. Stop and deal with that
result.now: Pull over safely, turn off the engine, and don't restart it. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the temperature gauge is high, don't open the radiator cap until the engine has fully cooled. Hot coolant can burn you.
If the red oil light came on, check the oil level once the engine is off. Even if adding oil turns the light off, have it checked before driving again.
If the coolant is low, don't just top it up and drive. The reason it went low needs to be found first.
If the red battery light is on together with a rising temperature gauge, a drive belt may have failed. Don't restart the engine.
result.why: Red warning lights mean something that can damage the engine or leave you stranded within minutes: overheating, low oil pressure or a charging failure. The check engine light is often just reporting the same problem. The red light sets the urgency.

causes.name: Engine overheating
causes.clues: Temperature gauge high, steam, or a sweet smell.

causes.name: Low oil pressure
causes.clues: Red oil can light, ticking or knocking noise.

causes.name: Charging system failure
causes.clues: Red battery light, dimming lights or gauges acting up.

you: Note which red light is on and what the temperature gauge shows.
Once the engine is off and cool, check the oil and coolant levels.

result.title: The car may have gone into a protective low-power mode
result.now: Get off highways and busy roads when it's safe and have it towed. Limp mode means the car has found a fault serious enough to protect itself, and it may not keep up with traffic.
if: If you can't keep up with traffic or the car hesitates badly when you press the gas, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If the light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward red or a red warning light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the engine stalls, or steering or braking suddenly takes more effort, pull over safely and don't drive it further.
result.why: When the computer sees a fault that could damage the engine or transmission, it often limits power or holds a single gear to protect them. The car can still move, but it can be dangerously slow merging or on hills. A code scan points to the cause.

causes.name: Throttle or accelerator pedal sensor fault
causes.clues: A "reduced power" message, or the gas pedal feels unresponsive.

causes.name: Transmission fault
causes.clues: Harsh or delayed shifts, or it stays in one gear.

causes.name: Turbocharger or boost problem
causes.clues: A turbocharged engine that suddenly feels flat, sometimes with a whooshing sound.
causes.against: Doesn't apply if your engine has no turbo.

you: Note any message on the dash.
Note whether the shifting feels different.

result.title: A fuel leak is possible. Don't drive until it's found
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off, look under the car for wet spots or dripping fuel, and have the car towed to a shop.
if: If you see fuel dripping or pooling, keep everyone away, don't start the car, and call for help.
Not seeing a drip doesn't rule out a leak. Fuel can leak onto hot parts and evaporate before it reaches the ground.
If the only smell is near the filler door and it fades, check that the gas cap is on and tight. If the smell returns or is ever noticeable inside the car, have it checked before driving.
result.why: The check engine light often comes on for fuel vapor leaks. A faint smell from a loose cap is minor, but a strong raw fuel smell can mean liquid fuel is leaking near hot engine or exhaust parts, which is a fire risk.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line, injector or fuel rail
causes.clues: A strong smell under the hood, or wet spots on the engine.

causes.name: Leaking fuel tank, filler neck or vapor hose
causes.clues: The smell is strongest near the back of the car.

causes.name: Loose or damaged gas cap
causes.clues: A faint smell near the filler door, just after filling up.
causes.against: A loose cap rarely causes a strong smell inside the car.

you: Look under the car for wet spots.
Don't smoke or use flames nearby.

result.title: A loose or worn gas cap is a common cause
result.now: Take the gas cap off, check the rubber seal for cracks, and put it back on until it clicks. Then drive normally for a few days.
if: If the light hasn't gone off after a week of normal driving, have the code read. It may be another leak in the fuel vapor system.
If the car starts running poorly or the light flashes, stop and have it checked.
If you smell fuel strongly, especially inside the car or under the hood, don't drive it. Have it checked.
result.why: The fuel system is sealed to keep gasoline vapor in. If the cap isn't tight after a fill-up, the computer can detect a small leak and turn on the light. The light doesn't go out right away after you fix it. It usually needs several days of driving to recheck. If it stays on, the code will show whether the cap or another part of the system is the cause.

causes.name: Gas cap not tightened
causes.clues: The light came on a day or two after filling up.

causes.name: Worn or cracked gas cap seal
causes.clues: The cap doesn't click, or the rubber ring is cracked or flattened.

causes.name: Other fuel vapor system leak
causes.clues: A new, tight cap doesn't make the light go away.

you: Tighten the gas cap until it clicks.
Look for cracks in the cap's rubber seal.
Have the code read. Many auto parts stores do it free.

result.title: Possibly an oxygen sensor or catalytic converter problem
result.now: Have the code read and book a check within the next couple of weeks.
if: If the rotten egg smell is strong or you notice a rattle under the car, get it checked sooner.
If the car loses power or the exhaust seems blocked, have it checked before driving further. A blocked converter can get very hot.
If you smell raw fuel or burning, or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Oxygen sensors measure the exhaust so the computer can adjust the fuel mix. When one fails, mileage often drops. A worn catalytic converter can't clean the exhaust properly, which can cause a sulfur smell. A shop will usually test the sensors and check for misfires or fuel mixture problems before replacing a converter, since those can damage a new one too.

causes.name: Failing oxygen sensor
causes.clues: Fuel mileage has dropped, and the car has high miles.

causes.name: Worn catalytic converter
causes.clues: A rotten egg smell, a rattle from under the car, or sluggish acceleration.

causes.name: Engine running too rich or lean
causes.clues: A rough idle or hesitation as well.

you: Track your fuel mileage over a couple of fill-ups.
Have the code read.
shop: Code scan and live sensor data
Catalytic converter efficiency and back-pressure test

result.title: A small misfire or vacuum leak may be the cause
result.now: Have the code read and get it checked within a few days. Keep trips short and gentle until then.
if: If the shaking gets worse while driving or the light starts flashing, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you hear a hiss from the engine bay, mention it to the shop.
If you smell raw fuel or burning, or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: A rough idle with the check engine light on often means a cylinder is misfiring now and then, or extra air is getting in through a cracked hose. Caught early, these are often simple repairs once a shop confirms the cause. Left alone, a misfire can damage the catalytic converter.

causes.name: Worn spark plug or weak ignition coil
causes.clues: The roughness is a steady miss, or the car is due for spark plugs.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or the idle is high or hunts up and down.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or fuel injector
causes.clues: The idle has slowly gotten worse over months.

you: Listen for hissing from the engine bay.
Have the code read.

result.title: Possibly a sensor or wiring fault that comes and goes
result.now: Have the code read while the light is on, or ask a shop to read stored codes, and book a check when convenient.
if: If the light starts flashing or the car runs badly, get it checked right away.
If you have an emissions test coming up, get it fixed first. Cars with recent faults often fail.
If you smell raw fuel or burning, or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward red or a red warning light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: A light that turns itself off often means the fault cleared for now, but the code stays stored. Damp or cold weather can bring out marginal sensors, connectors and small vapor leaks. The stored code shows the shop where to start testing.

causes.name: Marginal sensor
causes.clues: The light returns in the same weather or driving conditions.

causes.name: Corroded connector or chafed wire
causes.clues: It shows up after rain or car washes.

causes.name: Small fuel vapor leak
causes.clues: The gas cap seal is old, or the light first came on after a fill-up.

you: Write down when the light comes on (weather, speed, after fuel).
Have the codes read, including stored ones.
shop: Code scan including stored and pending codes

result.title: Get the code read. That's the fastest way to know what it is
result.now: Have the trouble code read within the next week or so. Many auto parts stores do it free, or a shop can do it.
if: If the light starts flashing or the car shakes, pull over and turn the engine off.
If any red warning light comes on or the temperature gauge rises, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you smell raw fuel or burning, or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: A steady light with a car that drives normally is usually not an emergency, but it's not something to ignore either. The code tells the shop which system to test. Waiting months can let a small fault damage something more expensive, and a second problem may hide behind the light that's already on.

causes.name: Fuel vapor (evaporative) system leak
causes.clues: No change in how the car runs.

causes.name: Oxygen or airflow sensor fault
causes.clues: Slightly worse fuel mileage.

causes.name: Early misfire or ignition problem
causes.clues: An occasional stumble or rough idle.

you: Check that the gas cap is tight.
Have the code read and write it down.
shop: Code scan and freeze frame data
Tests for the system the code points to

q_behavior.help: "READY" is the light or word on the dash that tells you a hybrid is switched on and able to drive, even when the gas engine is off.

opts.a: There's smoke, a burning smell, or it's been in a crash or flood
It shut down or lost drive power while I was driving
It won't start or won't show READY
It drives, but feels weaker or the gas engine runs much more than usual
It drives normally. Only the warning is on
I'm not sure

q_no_ready.q: When you press the power button with your foot on the brake, what happens?

opts.a: The dash is dim, flickers, or nothing lights up
The dash lights up normally, but READY never comes on
I'm not sure

q_clues.help: The hybrid battery has its own cooling fan. Its air intake is usually a small vent near the rear seat or in the trunk area.

opts.a: The battery charge display swings quickly between full and low
A fan is loud near the rear seat, or something is covering the vent there
The engine temperature is high, or it came on after a long drive in the heat
The 12-volt battery is old, or the car has been slow to wake up lately
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: A high-voltage problem is possible. Get away from the car
result.now: Get everyone out and move away from the car. If there's smoke or fire, call 911 and tell them it's a hybrid.
if: If there's no smoke, still don't try to start it. Have it towed and tell the tow company it's a hybrid.
If it was in a flood, keep it parked outside and away from buildings until it's inspected.
result.why: A damaged or water-soaked high-voltage battery can short out, overheat or catch fire, sometimes hours later. This isn't something to test yourself.

causes.name: Damaged high-voltage battery or cables
causes.clues: A recent crash, or damage under the car.

causes.name: Water inside the battery or electronics
causes.clues: Flooding, deep water, or a leak into the cabin or trunk.

causes.name: Overheating inverter or battery
causes.clues: A burning smell from the rear seat area or under the hood.

result.title: The hybrid system may have shut itself down to protect itself
result.now: Get to a safe spot, put it in Park and turn it off. Have the car towed to a shop that works on hybrids.
if: If it restarts and seems fine, don't count on it. The fault that shut it down is stored and can happen again.
If the engine temperature warning is on too, don't restart it.
If you see smoke, smell burning plastic, or hear popping or hissing from the battery area, get everyone out, move away and call 911.
result.why: When the hybrid computer sees a serious fault in the battery, inverter or motors, it can cut drive power entirely. Losing power on the road is dangerous, so it needs to be diagnosed before you drive again. A hybrid scan will show which system set the fault.

causes.name: Inverter fault or overheating
causes.clues: It shut down after a long drive or in hot weather, or the engine temperature was high.

causes.name: Failing hybrid battery
causes.clues: The battery display had been swinging quickly, or fuel economy had dropped.

causes.name: Electrical fault, including a weak 12-volt battery
causes.clues: Several warning lights came on together.

you: Take a photo of the dash with all the warnings showing.

result.title: The hybrid system appears to be blocking the car from starting
result.now: Try once more with your foot firmly on the brake. If READY still doesn't come on, have the car towed to a shop that works on hybrids.
if: If a jump to the 12-volt battery brings READY back, still get the hybrid codes read before relying on the car.
If you see smoke, smell burning plastic, or hear popping or hissing from the battery area, get everyone out, move away and call 911.
result.why: If the dash powers up normally but READY never appears, the hybrid computer has likely found a fault it won't let you drive with. That can be a battery, inverter or insulation problem, or sometimes a weak 12-volt battery, and it needs a proper scan.

causes.name: Hybrid battery or inverter fault
causes.clues: Warnings had appeared before, or fuel economy had dropped.

causes.name: High-voltage insulation fault
causes.clues: Water exposure or a recent leak into the car.

causes.name: Weak 12-volt battery
causes.clues: The battery is old, or the car sat unused for weeks.
causes.against: If the dash lights are bright and steady, the 12-volt battery is less likely.

you: Check the owner's manual for where the 12-volt battery or jump points are.

result.title: The small 12-volt battery may be weak
result.now: Jump-start the 12-volt battery using the points shown in your owner's manual, or use a booster pack. Then get the 12-volt battery tested.
if: If READY comes on after a jump, have the 12-volt battery tested within a few days. Hybrid 12-volt batteries often fail with little warning.
If the dash lights up normally but READY still won't come on, the hybrid system has a fault. Have it towed to a shop.
If the 12-volt battery is swollen, cracked, leaking or smells like rotten eggs, don't jump it. Have it checked.
If you see smoke, smell burning plastic, or hear popping or hissing from the battery area, get everyone out, move away and call 911.
result.why: A hybrid still uses a regular 12-volt battery to wake up its computers. When it's weak, the dash can go dim and the hybrid system may throw warnings or refuse to start. This can happen even when the large hybrid battery has no problem, so a shop will usually test the 12-volt battery first.

causes.name: Aging or drained 12-volt battery
causes.clues: The car sat for a while, the battery is over 4–5 years old, or the dash is dim.

causes.name: Loose or corroded 12-volt battery connection
causes.clues: Buildup on the terminals or a loose clamp.

causes.name: Charging problem from the hybrid system
causes.clues: The 12-volt battery keeps going flat even after replacement.

you: Find the 12-volt battery or jump points in your owner's manual.
Check the battery clamps for corrosion.

result.title: The hybrid battery may be getting weak
result.now: Have the hybrid system scanned within the next few days, ideally at a shop that works on hybrids. Drive gently until then.
if: If the car loses power sharply or a red warning appears, pull over and have it towed.
If the battery cooling vent is blocked, clear it first. Heat makes a weak battery worse.
If the engine temperature climbs toward red, pull over and turn it off.
If you see smoke, smell burning plastic, or hear popping or hissing from the battery area, get everyone out, move away and call 911.
result.why: A hybrid battery is made of many sections. As some wear out, the battery can't hold a steady charge, so the gauge jumps around and the gas engine has to work more. The computer often flags it before it fails completely. A shop will usually compare section voltages and check the cooling fan and sensors before recommending battery work, since those can cause similar warnings.

causes.name: Worn hybrid battery sections
causes.clues: Higher mileage or an older car, worse fuel economy, and a fast-swinging charge display.

causes.name: Battery overheating from poor cooling
causes.clues: A blocked or dusty vent near the rear seat, or hot weather.

causes.name: Battery sensor or wiring fault
causes.clues: The car drives normally with no change in fuel economy.

you: Check that the battery cooling vent isn't blocked.
Compare your recent fuel economy with what you usually get.
shop: Battery cooling fan and filter check

result.title: The hybrid battery may be running hot because its cooling vent is blocked
result.now: Find the battery cooling vent (usually near the rear seat). Move anything covering it and vacuum dust or pet hair from the grille.
if: If the warning stays on after a few drives, have the battery cooling fan and filter checked.
If the car feels weaker or the gas engine runs much more than usual, get the hybrid system scanned soon.
If you see smoke, smell burning plastic, or hear popping or hissing from the battery area, get everyone out, move away and call 911.
result.why: The hybrid battery is cooled by cabin air pulled through a small vent. A bag, jacket or layer of dust can block it, and a hot battery triggers warnings and wears out faster.

causes.name: Blocked cooling vent
causes.clues: Something was sitting on or against the rear seat, or the vent looks dusty.

causes.name: Clogged cooling fan or filter
causes.clues: The fan is loud or runs a lot, especially with pets in the car.

causes.name: Failing cooling fan
causes.clues: No fan sound at all, or a rattle from the rear.

you: Clear and vacuum the vent.
Listen for the battery fan running after a drive.
shop: Cooling fan and filter cleaning or replacement

result.title: The inverter or engine cooling may not be working properly
result.now: Pull over when it's safe, put it in Park and turn it off. Once everything has cooled, check both coolant reservoirs. Many hybrids have a separate one for the inverter. Have it checked before it's driven again, and have it towed if a reservoir is low or the engine temperature was high.
if: If the engine temperature is in the red or there's steam, pull over when it's safe and turn it off. Stay away from the radiator and reservoir caps, and have it towed.
If either reservoir is low or empty, don't top it up and drive. The reason it went low needs to be found first.
If you see smoke, smell burning plastic, or hear popping or hissing from the battery area, get everyone out, move away and call 911.
result.why: The inverter turns battery power into motor power and gets very hot. Most hybrids cool it with its own coolant and electric pump. If that pump fails or the coolant is low, the inverter can overheat and the system flags a fault. Overheating can damage the inverter or the engine, so a shop will test the pump and pressure-test the cooling system before it's driven.

causes.name: Failed inverter coolant pump
causes.clues: The warning comes on after a few minutes of driving, especially in warm weather.

causes.name: Low inverter or engine coolant
causes.clues: A low reservoir, or pink or green drips under the front.

causes.name: Cooling fan problem
causes.clues: It's worst in slow traffic.

you: With everything cool, check the coolant level in each reservoir.
Look for coolant drips under the front of the car.

result.title: The hybrid system has a stored fault that needs a scan
result.now: Have the hybrid system scanned within the next few days, ideally at a shop that works on hybrids. Don't clear the code first. The shop needs it.
if: If the car loses power, shows a red warning or the temperature climbs, pull over and have it towed.
If the check engine or ABS light is on too, mention it. Faults elsewhere can set off the hybrid warning.
If you see smoke, smell burning plastic, or hear popping or hissing from the battery area, get everyone out, move away and call 911.
result.why: The hybrid warning covers many systems, and some faults outside the hybrid parts can trigger it too. Without other clues, the stored code is the fastest way to the real cause.

causes.name: Hybrid battery or inverter fault
causes.clues: Worse fuel economy or a weaker feel.

causes.name: Fault in another system triggering the warning
causes.clues: The check engine or ABS light is on too.

causes.name: Weak 12-volt battery
causes.clues: Slow or odd start-ups lately.

you: Check that the battery cooling vent isn't blocked.
Take a photo of all the warnings on the dash.

q_other_signs.q: Along with the clicking, is any of this happening?
q_other_signs.help: Pick the most serious one that fits.

opts.a: A loud clunking or banging that's getting worse fast, or the car hesitates to move when I press the gas
The steering feels loose, the car wanders, or there's a clunk over bumps too
A vibration or shudder when I accelerate, even going straight
No, it's just the clicking
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When exactly do you hear it?

opts.a: While driving through a tight turn: a steady click-click-click that speeds up as the car speeds up
A pop or clunk when I turn the steering wheel while stopped or barely moving
A fast ticking from the dashboard that matches the turn signal
A single click when I first brake or start moving after changing direction
I'm not sure

q_boot.q: Can you check the rubber boots on the front axles?
q_boot.help: Park on level ground. Turn the steering wheel all the way to one side, then shut the engine off, set the parking brake and look behind the front tire. The CV boot is the accordion-shaped rubber cover where the axle meets the wheel. Check both sides.

opts.a: A boot is torn or split, or there's dark grease sprayed around the inside of the wheel
The boots look intact and dry
My car is rear-wheel drive
I'm not sure, or I can't see them

result.title: A CV joint or axle may be close to breaking
result.now: Park it and don't drive any further. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If the engine revs but the car won't move, the axle may have broken. Don't keep trying to drive.
If the steering suddenly feels loose, the car pulls hard, or a wheel looks tilted, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: A CV joint that has gone from clicking to clunking or banging may be badly worn. When it fails, the wheel stops getting power and the car can stop moving, sometimes in traffic. In rare cases it can damage nearby parts. A shop will check the axles for play and look at the mounts, which can also clunk.

causes.name: Badly worn outer CV joint
causes.clues: Clicking for weeks or months, now turning into clunking.

causes.name: Worn inner CV joint
causes.clues: Clunks when you press or let off the gas.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mount
causes.clues: A clunk when you shift into Drive or Reverse, and the engine visibly rocks.

you: With the engine off, look for a torn CV boot or grease sprayed inside the wheel.
shop: CV axle and joint inspection for play

result.title: A steering or suspension joint may be worn
result.now: Have the steering and suspension inspected before the car is driven further. A tow or a mobile mechanic is the safest way to get it checked.
if: If the steering suddenly feels very loose, the car pulls hard, or a wheel looks tilted, don't move the car. Have it towed.
If the clunk over bumps is the main noise and the steering feels normal, see our clunk-over-bumps guide too.
result.why: Clicking or popping plus loose steering or clunks over bumps can point to worn parts that hold the wheel in place, like ball joints, tie rod ends or sway bar links. These usually wear gradually, but a ball joint or tie rod that separates can make you lose control, and the site can't tell how worn yours are. A shop will check each joint for play to find which one.

causes.name: Worn ball joint
causes.clues: A clunk or pop over bumps and when turning, and uneven tire wear.

causes.name: Worn tie rod end
causes.clues: Loose or vague steering, and the car wanders on the highway.

causes.name: Worn sway bar link or bushing
causes.clues: A rattle or clunk over small bumps, but steering feels normal.
causes.against: Less likely to cause loose steering.

you: Notice whether the steering wheel has more free play than it used to.
Look at the front tires for uneven wear on the inner or outer edge.
shop: Ball joint and tie rod play check
Sway bar link and bushing inspection

result.title: A worn inner CV joint or axle may be the cause
result.now: Have the axles checked within a few days. Accelerate gently until then.
if: If the vibration gets worse quickly or turns into a clunking, stop driving and have it towed.
If the vibration happens only at highway speed and not when accelerating, a tire balance problem is more likely.
If the check engine light is on, have the code read. A misfire can feel similar. If the light flashes, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: The inner CV joint lets the axle change length as the suspension moves. When it wears, it often causes a shudder when accelerating, sometimes with clicking in turns. It tends to get worse over time. A shop will usually check the axles and mounts together, because a worn mount can feel similar.

causes.name: Worn inner CV joint
causes.clues: Shudder under acceleration that goes away when you coast.

causes.name: Bent or damaged axle
causes.clues: Started after hitting a curb or pothole.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mount
causes.clues: A clunk when shifting into gear, and the shake is felt more in the seat.

you: Notice whether the shudder happens only when accelerating, not when coasting.
With the engine off, look at the inner axle boots near the transmission for tears or grease.
shop: CV axle inspection and test drive

result.title: A torn CV boot may have let grease out and dirt in
result.now: Book an inspection within the next week or so. Avoid sharp turns at speed until it's checked.
if: If the clicking turns into a clunking or banging, stop driving and have it towed.
If it hasn't started clicking yet, ask the shop whether replacing just the boot is still an option. The longer it waits, the more likely the joint itself is damaged.
If the steering suddenly feels loose, the car pulls hard, or a wheel looks tilted, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: The CV boot keeps grease in and dirt and water out of the joint. Once it tears, the joint can run dry and wear quickly. Clicking in turns suggests wear has already started, and it tends to get louder until the joint fails. A shop will check the joint for play to see whether the boot or the axle needs attention.

causes.name: Torn outer CV boot
causes.clues: Grease sprayed on the inside of the wheel or nearby parts, and clicking in tight turns.

causes.name: Torn inner CV boot
causes.clues: Grease near the transmission end of the axle, and a shudder when accelerating.

you: With the engine off, look closely at both boots on each front axle.
Turn slowly in a circle in an empty parking lot, both directions, and note which way the click is louder.

result.title: A worn outer CV joint on a front axle is a likely cause
result.now: Book an axle inspection in the next couple of weeks. Avoid hard acceleration in tight turns until then.
if: If the clicking gets louder, happens when driving straight, or turns into a clunk, get it checked soon.
If you hear a bang and the car won't move, don't keep trying to drive. Have it towed.
If the steering suddenly feels loose, the car pulls hard, or a wheel looks tilted, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: Front-wheel-drive and many all-wheel-drive cars have CV joints that let the front wheels steer and get power at the same time. When the outer joint wears, it often clicks in a steady rhythm during tight turns. It usually gets worse gradually, but once it starts clunking it can fail without much more warning.

causes.name: Worn outer CV joint
causes.clues: Clicking in tight turns that gets faster as the car speeds up, louder turning one way.
causes.against: Less likely if your car is rear-wheel drive.

causes.name: Torn CV boot you can't see
causes.clues: The tear is on the back side of the boot, or grease has been washed off.

causes.name: Worn strut mount or suspension part
causes.clues: The noise is a pop when turning the wheel, not a steady click.

you: In an empty parking lot, drive slowly in a tight circle each way. A steady click points to the CV joint on the outside of the turn.
Ask a shop or a friend to look at the CV boots from underneath.
shop: CV joint and boot inspection on a lift

result.title: On a rear-wheel-drive car, a front steering or suspension part is more likely
result.now: Book a front suspension and steering check in the next couple of weeks.
if: If the steering feels loose or the car wanders, have it checked before driving further.
If it's a four-wheel drive truck or SUV with the front axle engaged, the front CV or U-joints are possible too.
If the click comes with braking and the car pulls or the brake pedal feels different, have the brakes checked before driving further.
result.why: Rear-wheel-drive cars don't send power through the front wheels, so the classic CV-joint click doesn't apply up front. Clicking or popping when turning is more often a strut or shock mount, a ball joint, or loose brake hardware. A shop will usually check each for play.

causes.name: Worn strut mount or upper bearing
causes.clues: A pop or click when turning the wheel at low speed.

causes.name: Worn ball joint or tie rod end
causes.clues: Clunks over bumps, or loose steering.

causes.name: Loose brake caliper or pads shifting
causes.clues: A single click at the first stop after changing direction.

you: Notice whether it's a steady rhythm or a single pop.
Check whether it happens only when you turn the wheel while stopped.

result.title: A worn strut mount or its bearing is a likely cause
result.now: Book a front suspension check. Mention that it pops when you turn the wheel at low speed.
if: If the steering feels loose or you also hear clunks over bumps, have it checked before driving further.
If the steering wheel feels like it sticks and then jumps, have it checked before driving further. Steering that binds can make the car harder to control.
result.why: On many cars the top of each front strut sits on a mount with a bearing that lets it turn with the steering. When that bearing or rubber mount wears, it can bind and then pop as you turn the wheel, especially when the car is barely moving. A ball joint can make a similar pop, so a shop will usually check both.

causes.name: Worn strut mount or bearing plate
causes.clues: A pop or creak when turning the wheel while stopped or parking.

causes.name: Worn ball joint
causes.clues: A pop over bumps as well as when turning.

causes.name: Worn sway bar link or bushing
causes.clues: A clunk over small bumps.

you: With the car parked in Park and the parking brake on, have someone turn the steering wheel back and forth while you stand beside each front wheel and listen.
Note which side the pop comes from.

result.title: That's the turn signal. If it's clicking fast, a bulb may be out
result.now: Walk around the car with the turn signal on and check each front and rear signal bulb, including the side markers.
if: If a bulb is out, replace it. The ticking should go back to normal speed.
If all bulbs work but the ticking is fast, check the bulb sockets for corrosion or have the wiring looked at.
result.why: The normal turn signal tick comes from a relay or the car's computer. Many cars flash faster on purpose when a bulb is out, to warn you that other drivers can't see your signal.

causes.name: Burned-out turn signal bulb
causes.clues: Fast ticking only when signaling one direction.

causes.name: Corroded bulb socket or bad connection
causes.clues: The bulb looks fine but flickers or works on and off.

causes.name: Wrong bulb type
causes.clues: Started after a bulb was replaced recently.

you: Check every turn signal bulb, front and rear.
Check the owner's manual for the correct bulb type.

result.title: Brake pads or a caliper may be shifting slightly when the car changes direction
result.now: Mention it at your next brake service, or book a quick brake check if it's new or getting louder.
if: If the click becomes a clunk, or the car pulls or vibrates when braking, have the brakes checked before driving further. A loose caliper is a safety problem.
If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, you hear grinding, or the red brake warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If the noise started after recent brake work, let the shop that did it know. They'll want to check it, and it's usually a quick fix.
result.why: Brake pads sit in clips with a tiny bit of room to move. When you switch from Reverse to Drive and brake, the pads can shift and click once. Missing or worn clips, or a loose caliper bolt, can make it louder, so a shop will check the clips and bolts.

causes.name: Worn or missing pad clips
causes.clues: A single click on the first stop after changing direction.

causes.name: Loose caliper or bracket bolt
causes.clues: A louder clunk when braking, possibly after brake work.

causes.name: Worn suspension bushing
causes.clues: A clunk when braking hard, not only after changing direction.

you: Notice whether it only happens on the first stop after changing direction.
shop: Brake pad clip and caliper bolt check

result.title: Often a CV joint or front suspension part. Have it inspected
result.now: Book a front axle and suspension check in the next couple of weeks. Note when you hear the click so you can tell the shop.
if: If the clicking turns into clunking, the steering feels loose, or the car hesitates to move, stop driving and have it towed.
If the brake pedal feels different or the red brake warning light comes on, have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Clicking when turning usually comes from a worn CV joint or a front suspension part. Where and when it happens tells the shop which one, and a quick inspection on a lift usually confirms it.

causes.name: Worn outer CV joint
causes.clues: A steady click in tight turns that speeds up with the car.

causes.name: Worn strut mount
causes.clues: A pop when turning the wheel at low speed.

causes.name: Worn ball joint or tie rod end
causes.clues: Clunks over bumps, or loose steering.

you: Record a short video with sound while turning slowly in an empty parking lot. It helps the shop.

q_danger.q: Along with the clunk, do you notice any of these?

opts.a: The steering feels loose, the car wanders, or it pulls suddenly
A wheel looks tilted, or one corner of the car sits lower than the rest
It started right after a tire change or brake job, or a wheel feels wobbly
None of these, just the clunk
I'm not sure

q_where.q: Where does the clunk seem to come from?
q_where.help: It can be hard to tell from inside the car. Having a passenger sit in the back, or driving slowly over a speed bump with the windows down, can help.

opts.a: The front of the car
The back of the car
I'm not sure

q_front.q: Which description fits the clunk best?

opts.a: A light knock or rattle on small bumps and rough roads at low speed
A heavier thud on big bumps or dips, and the car bounces more than it used to
Worst when turning, like pulling into a driveway or over a curb
It also clunks when I brake hard or start moving
I'm not sure

q_rear.q: Which description fits the clunk best?

opts.a: It might be something loose in the trunk, cargo area or spare tire well
A heavy thud on big bumps, and the rear bounces or bottoms out
It also clunks when I shift into gear or take off from a stop
A light knock on small bumps and rough roads
I'm not sure

result.title: A worn ball joint or tie rod may be affecting your steering
result.now: Slow down and pull over as soon as it's safe. Have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic inspect it where it is.
if: If a wheel is visibly tilted in or out at the top, don't move the car at all.
If you're stuck somewhere unsafe, turn on your hazard lights and call roadside assistance.
result.why: A clunk together with loose or wandering steering can mean a joint that connects the wheel to the steering or suspension is badly worn. If one of these parts separates, you can lose control of that wheel. A shop will check each joint for play with the car lifted.

causes.name: Worn ball joint
causes.clues: A clunk over bumps and when turning, with the car wandering or tires wearing on one edge.

causes.name: Worn inner or outer tie rod end
causes.clues: Play in the steering wheel, and the car needs constant small corrections to go straight.

causes.name: Loose or damaged steering rack mounting
causes.clues: A clunk you can feel through the steering wheel when turning.

shop: Ball joint and tie rod play check with the car lifted

result.title: A suspension part may have broken
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed, and keep it on flat ground until then.
if: If a tire is rubbing on the body or a part is touching the tire, the tire can be damaged quickly. Don't move the car.
If you're on the side of a road, turn on your hazard lights and wait for help away from traffic.
result.why: A corner that suddenly sits low, or a wheel that's tilted, can mean something that holds the wheel in place has broken or come apart. A clunk is often the moment it happened, or the broken part moving over each bump.

causes.name: Broken coil spring
causes.clues: One corner sits lower, and you may hear a clunk or scrape over bumps. Common on cars driven in road salt.

causes.name: Separated ball joint or broken control arm
causes.clues: A wheel is tilted, or the car steers very oddly.

causes.name: Failed strut mount
causes.clues: A loud clunk from the top of the suspension, and the corner sits wrong.

you: From a safe spot, compare the height of each corner of the car.
Look for a broken spring coil behind the wheel, without getting under the car.
shop: Full suspension inspection on a lift
Spring, control arm and strut mount check

result.title: A loose wheel is possible. Check the lug nuts before going any further
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe and don't drive further until the lug nuts are checked. If you have a lug wrench, tighten each nut firmly in a star pattern. Otherwise call roadside assistance or the shop that did the work.
if: If any nuts were loose, have a shop tighten them to the correct torque and check for damaged studs before regular driving.
If the nuts are tight and the clunk continues, a brake part may have come loose. Have it checked before driving further. The shop that did the work will want to know and can check it quickly.
If the brake pedal feels soft or different, or you hear grinding, don't drive it. Have it towed.
result.why: A clunk or wobble that starts right after a wheel was off can mean the lug nuts have loosened, or a brake caliper or bracket bolt is loose. Lug nuts can settle over the first few dozen miles, which is why many shops recommend a re-check, and a loose wheel can come off.

causes.name: Loose lug nuts
causes.clues: A clunk or rhythmic knock that started soon after tire work, sometimes with a wobble.

causes.name: Loose brake caliper or bracket
causes.clues: The clunk happens when braking or changes direction, and started after brake work.

causes.name: Damaged wheel studs
causes.clues: A nut won't tighten fully, or a stud is missing or broken.

you: Check each lug nut with a lug wrench.
Look for missing nuts or broken studs.

result.title: Possibly a worn sway bar link or bushing
result.now: Book a suspension check. Mention that the knock is on small bumps and rough roads at low speed.
if: If the steering starts to feel loose or the clunk gets much louder, have it checked before driving further.
If the car starts to lean more in turns, the sway bar may have disconnected. Take turns gently and get it checked soon.
If a wheel looks tilted or one corner sits lower, don't drive it. Have it towed.
result.why: Sway bar links connect the anti-roll bar to the suspension. Their small joints and rubber bushings wear out and let the bar knock on uneven pavement. It's one of the most common causes of a light clunk, but more serious parts like ball joints can sound similar, so an inspection is the way to rule them out.

causes.name: Worn sway bar end link
causes.clues: A light knock or rattle on rough roads, especially when one wheel hits a bump at a time.

causes.name: Worn sway bar bushings
causes.clues: A thud or squeak over bumps, sometimes worse in cold weather.

causes.name: Loose exhaust or heat shield
causes.clues: A tinny rattle that also happens when you rev the engine in Park.
causes.against: A heavier knock is less likely to be the exhaust.

you: Drive slowly over a bump with one side of the car and listen for the side the knock comes from.
shop: Sway bar link and bushing inspection

result.title: Worn shocks, struts or their mounts may be the cause
result.now: Book a suspension check within the next week or two, and slow down for big bumps and potholes until then.
if: If the car bottoms out hard, nosedives when braking, or a corner sits lower, get it checked within a few days.
If you see oil running down a shock or strut, mention it. That often means it's leaking and worth a closer look.
If the steering feels loose, the car wanders or pulls suddenly, or a wheel looks tilted, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
result.why: Shocks and struts control how the car moves after a bump. When they wear, the suspension can hit its stops and thud, and the car bounces more. Worn strut mounts or bump stops can also clunk. Worn shocks can make stopping distances longer and the car less stable. A shop will usually inspect the shocks, mounts and bump stops before recommending which to replace.

causes.name: Worn shocks or struts
causes.clues: The car keeps bouncing after bumps, or the tires show cupped wear.

causes.name: Worn strut mount or bearing
causes.clues: A clunk from the top of the suspension, sometimes when turning the steering wheel too.

causes.name: Missing or broken bump stop
causes.clues: A hard thud only on big dips or with a heavy load.

you: Push down hard on each corner of the car and let go. It should settle after about one bounce.
Look for oily wetness on the shocks or struts.
shop: Strut mount and bump stop check

result.title: A worn ball joint or tie rod end may be the cause
result.now: Have the front suspension and steering inspected before the car is driven further. A mobile mechanic or a tow is the safest way to get it checked.
if: If the steering feels loose, the car wanders or a wheel looks tilted, don't move the car. Have it towed.
If the clunk gets louder quickly, don't wait. Get it checked right away.
result.why: Ball joints and tie rod ends are the pivots that let the front wheels steer and move up and down. When they wear, they can clunk over bumps and especially when turning. Unlike a sway bar link, a badly worn ball joint can separate and cause a loss of control, and how worn it is can only be judged with the car lifted. A strut mount can make a similar noise, so the shop will usually check both.

causes.name: Worn lower or upper ball joint
causes.clues: Clunking when turning into driveways or over curbs, and uneven tire wear.

causes.name: Worn tie rod end
causes.clues: Some play or looseness in the steering wheel.

causes.name: Worn strut mount
causes.clues: A clunk or pop when turning the steering wheel while parked.

you: Look at the front tires for wear on the inside or outside edge.
Note whether there's any play in the steering wheel.
shop: Ball joint play check with the car lifted

result.title: Worn control arm bushings may be the cause
result.now: Book a suspension check within the next week or two.
if: If the car pulls when braking or the steering feels vague, have it checked before driving further.
If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, stop driving and have it towed.
If you also feel a clunk when shifting into gear, mention it. Worn engine or transmission mounts can feel similar.
result.why: Control arms hold each wheel in position, and they mount to the car through rubber bushings. When the rubber cracks or tears, the arm can shift back and forth as you brake, accelerate and hit bumps, causing a clunk. A shop will usually check the bushings, mounts and ball joints to see which is moving.

causes.name: Worn control arm bushings
causes.clues: Clunks when braking, starting off and over bumps, sometimes with a pull when braking.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mount
causes.clues: A clunk when shifting into Drive or Reverse, or when you press the gas hard.

causes.name: Worn ball joint
causes.clues: The clunk is worse when turning.

you: Note whether the clunk happens when braking, accelerating, or both.
shop: Control arm bushing inspection with a pry bar

result.title: It may just be something loose in the back
result.now: Empty the trunk or cargo area, check that the spare tire and jack are clamped down tightly, then drive the same route again.
if: If the clunk is gone, it was probably the cargo or spare. Secure it.
If the clunk is still there, book a suspension check.
result.why: A loose spare tire, jack, toolkit or items rolling around in the back can make a surprisingly suspension-like clunk over bumps. It takes a few minutes to rule out before paying for an inspection.

causes.name: Loose spare tire or jack
causes.clues: The clunk is in the very back and sounds hollow.

causes.name: Items in the trunk or a loose seat latch
causes.clues: It changes with what you carry.

causes.name: Worn rear shock or link
causes.clues: The clunk stays after emptying the back.

you: Empty the trunk and tighten the spare tire hold-down.
Check that the rear seats latch firmly.
shop: Rear suspension inspection if the noise continues

result.title: A worn driveline part or mount may be clunking
result.now: Book a check within the next week or two and mention that it also clunks when shifting into gear or taking off.
if: If you feel a vibration that gets worse with speed, have it checked before driving further. A worn U-joint can fail and let the driveshaft drop.
If there's a loud bang and the car stops moving under power, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If you hear a new scraping sound from under the car, pull over and have it towed.
result.why: A clunk that happens both over bumps and when the drivetrain takes up power often points to something with play in it, like a universal joint on the driveshaft, a mount, or the rear axle bushings.

causes.name: Worn universal (U) joint
causes.clues: A clunk when shifting into gear on rear-wheel or 4WD vehicles, sometimes with a squeak or vibration.

causes.name: Worn engine, transmission or differential mount
causes.clues: The clunk is loudest when starting off or letting off the gas suddenly.

causes.name: Worn rear axle or trailing arm bushings
causes.clues: Clunks over bumps and when braking from the rear.

you: Note whether the clunk happens when shifting between Drive and Reverse while stopped.

result.title: Something in the suspension may be worn. A lift inspection can usually find it
result.now: Book a suspension and steering inspection within the next week or two, and slow down for bumps until then.
if: If the steering feels loose, the car wanders, or the clunk gets suddenly louder, pull over when it's safe and have it checked before driving further.
If a wheel looks tilted or one corner sits lower, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If it only happens in the back and could be cargo, empty the trunk first and see if it stops.
result.why: Many suspension parts can clunk, and they're much easier to tell apart with the car lifted and the parts pried on. Most causes are wear items, but some, like ball joints, affect steering control, so it's worth not putting it off for long.

causes.name: Worn sway bar link
causes.clues: A light knock on rough roads.

causes.name: Worn shock, strut or mount
causes.clues: A heavier thud and more bouncing.

causes.name: Worn ball joint or tie rod
causes.clues: Clunking that's worse when turning.

you: Record a short video with sound while driving over a speed bump.
Note when it happens: small bumps, big bumps, turning or braking.
shop: Suspension and steering inspection on a lift

q_how_bad.q: How bad is the slipping right now?
q_how_bad.help: "Slipping" means the engine revs (RPM) jump up when you press the gas, but the car speeds up much less than it should.

opts.a: The engine revs, but the car barely moves or won't move at all
It slips when accelerating hard, going uphill, or in higher gears
It slipped with a strong burning smell after heavy use (towing, hill starts, hard launches)
I'm not sure it's slipping

q_test.q: On a safe, open road in 4th or 5th gear, press the gas firmly. What happens?
q_test.help: Only do this where it's safe and legal. Watch the tachometer (the RPM gauge) and the speedometer together.

opts.a: The RPM jumps quickly, but the speed barely changes
RPM and speed rise together, but the car just feels weak
I'm not sure

q_pedal.q: How does the clutch pedal feel?
q_pedal.help: The engagement point is where the clutch starts to grab as you let the pedal up.

opts.a: It feels normal, but the clutch grabs very near the top of the pedal
It feels soft or spongy, sticks down, or comes back up slowly
It has no slack at the top, or the clutch cable feels tight
It feels normal
I'm not sure
The clutch is original or has a lot of miles on it
There's oil dripping from where the engine and transmission meet
The clutch was replaced recently
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: The clutch may have failed or lost its grip and can't move the car
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed to a shop or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the clutch pedal also feels soft or goes to the floor, a hydraulic leak can cause the same symptom. On cars where the clutch shares the brake fluid reservoir, treat a low level as a possible brake problem too.
If you're in traffic, turn on your hazard lights and get to the shoulder if you can roll there safely.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the car, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and let everything cool. Don't keep trying to get it moving.
result.why: When the car barely moves even though the engine revs, the clutch usually isn't gripping. Trying to drive like this overheats what's left of the clutch and can damage the flywheel, and the car may not be able to keep up with traffic.

causes.name: Clutch disc worn down to the end of its life
causes.clues: Slipping got gradually worse over weeks or months.

causes.name: Clutch hydraulic fault keeping the clutch partly released
causes.clues: A soft or sinking pedal, or low fluid in the clutch reservoir.

causes.name: Broken pressure plate or clutch disc
causes.clues: It happened suddenly, sometimes with a bang or rattling.

you: From the parked car, check the clutch fluid reservoir level (on many cars it shares the brake fluid reservoir).
shop: Clutch, pressure plate and flywheel inspection

result.title: The clutch disc may be worn
result.now: Get the clutch checked within the next few days. Until then, drive gently, avoid hard acceleration and hills, and keep your foot off the clutch pedal except when shifting.
if: If the car starts to struggle to move or you smell burning often, stop driving it and have it towed.
If you tow a trailer, don't until the clutch is fixed.
If you see smoke from under the car or the burning smell is strong, stop as soon as it's safe and let it cool before going anywhere.
If the clutch pedal goes soft, sinks or stays on the floor, don't drive it. You may not be able to shift or stop smoothly.
result.why: The clutch disc has friction material that wears down with use, just like brake pads. As it thins, the clutch grips with less force, so it slips first under heavy load and later all the time. A worn disc doesn't recover, and ongoing slipping heats and can damage the flywheel. A shop will usually do a slip test and check the pedal free play and hydraulics before recommending a new clutch, since those can cause the same symptom.

causes.name: Normal wear of the clutch disc
causes.clues: High mileage, lots of city or hill driving, and a gradual onset.
causes.against: If the clutch is fairly new, look at adjustment or oil contamination instead.

causes.name: Weak pressure plate springs
causes.clues: Slipping despite a disc that isn't very old, sometimes after overheating.

causes.name: Riding the clutch
causes.clues: Resting a foot on the pedal or slipping the clutch to hold the car on hills.

you: Note which gears slip and whether hills or hard acceleration make it worse.
Notice whether the clutch grabs higher in the pedal travel than it used to.
shop: Clutch pedal free-play and hydraulic check
Clutch disc, pressure plate and flywheel inspection when removed

result.title: The clutch may have overheated from heavy use
result.now: Let the clutch cool for at least 30 minutes, then drive gently and see whether the slipping has stopped. Book a check when convenient.
if: If it keeps slipping after it has cooled down, the clutch is likely damaged. Get it checked within a few days.
