If you see smoke from under the car, or the burning smell is very strong, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and let it cool before going any further.
If the car struggles to get moving after the clutch has cooled, don't drive it. Have it checked where it is or towed.
If the clutch pedal feels soft, sinks or stays down, don't drive it.
result.why: Towing, repeated hill starts and hard launches make the clutch slip on purpose, which creates a lot of heat. A hot clutch grips less and gives off a sharp burning smell. A single episode doesn't always leave lasting damage, but you can't tell that from the driver's seat, and repeated overheating wears a clutch out fast.

causes.name: Clutch overheated from heavy use
causes.clues: It happened right after towing, traffic on a hill or a hard launch.

causes.name: Already-worn clutch made worse by heat
causes.clues: It had been slipping a little before.

causes.name: Glazed clutch disc or flywheel
causes.clues: A slight slip or shudder that remains after cooling.

you: After it cools, check whether it still slips in a high gear.
Use the parking brake on hill starts instead of slipping the clutch.
shop: Clutch and flywheel inspection if slipping continues

result.title: A clutch hydraulic problem may be keeping the clutch from fully engaging
result.now: Check the clutch fluid reservoir and look for leaks near the pedal and transmission. Have the system checked within the next few days, or before driving at all if the reservoir is shared with the brakes and it's low.
if: If the pedal goes to the floor and stays there, don't drive it. You may not be able to shift. Have it towed.
If the clutch shares the brake fluid reservoir and the level is low, don't just top it up and carry on. Have the brakes and clutch inspected before driving further, even if you can't see a leak.
If the brake pedal also feels soft, sinks, or the brake warning light is on, stop driving and have it towed. A shared reservoir means a leak can affect both.
result.why: Most clutches are worked by fluid pressure, like brakes. If the master or slave cylinder is sticking, or the fluid is low or contaminated, the clutch can stay partly released, so it slips even though the disc itself may be fine. A shop will usually check the hydraulics before replacing the clutch.

causes.name: Sticking or leaking slave cylinder
causes.clues: Fluid near the bell housing (where the engine meets the transmission), or a pedal that returns slowly.

causes.name: Faulty clutch master cylinder
causes.clues: Fluid under the dash near the pedal, or a pedal that sinks.

causes.name: Low, old or contaminated fluid
causes.clues: The reservoir is low or the fluid looks dark.

you: Check the clutch fluid reservoir level and color.
Look for wet spots under the dash near the pedal and under the car near the bell housing.
shop: Clutch master and slave cylinder inspection

result.title: The clutch may be out of adjustment
result.now: Have the clutch adjustment checked when convenient. Until then, avoid hard acceleration and keep your foot off the pedal while driving.
if: If the slipping gets worse or you smell burning, get it checked within a few days, and don't drive it if the car struggles to move.
If your car has a hydraulic clutch with no adjuster, a sticking hydraulic part is more likely.
If you see smoke from under the car or the clutch pedal stays on the floor, stop driving it.
result.why: The clutch needs a little slack at the top of the pedal so it can clamp fully when released. If a clutch cable is too tight, or the pedal doesn't come all the way up, the clutch stays partly released and slips under load.

causes.name: Clutch cable too tight or self-adjuster stuck
causes.clues: No slack at the top of the pedal on a cable-operated clutch.

causes.name: Pedal not returning fully
causes.clues: A floor mat or worn pedal stop keeps the pedal from coming all the way up.

causes.name: Worn clutch disc
causes.clues: On some designs, a worn disc also removes pedal slack.

you: Make sure the floor mat isn't catching the clutch pedal.
Gently press the pedal by hand to feel for slack before it gets firm.
shop: Clutch pedal free-play check and adjustment

result.title: Oil may be leaking onto the clutch and making it slip
result.now: Check the engine oil level and top it up if needed, then have the leak and clutch checked within the next few days.
if: If the oil level is well below the low mark or the oil pressure light comes on, don't drive it.
If the leak is heavy, with oil dripping steadily or puddling, don't drive it until it's checked. Oil on hot parts can catch fire and the engine can run low.
If you see smoke from under the car or smell burning oil, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off. Oil dripping onto hot exhaust parts can be a fire risk.
result.why: The clutch sits right next to the rear engine seal and the transmission input seal. If either leaks, oil can soak the clutch disc, which then slips and often chatters. A shop will usually confirm where the oil is coming from before quoting. If the disc is soaked, cleaning rarely fixes it, so the leak and the clutch are often repaired together.

causes.name: Leaking rear main engine seal
causes.clues: Engine oil dripping from where the engine and transmission meet.

causes.name: Leaking transmission input shaft seal
causes.clues: Gear oil, which smells strong and sulfur-like, in the same area.

causes.name: Clutch fluid leaking from the slave cylinder
causes.clues: Low clutch fluid and a soft pedal.

you: Check the engine oil level on the dipstick.
Place cardboard under the car overnight and note where the drips land.
shop: Leak inspection with the bell housing cover removed
Rear main seal and input shaft seal check

result.title: A recently replaced clutch may need adjusting or have an installation problem
result.now: Contact the shop that did the work and have them check it within the next few days. Drive gently until then.
if: If the slipping is slight and the clutch is only a few hundred miles old, the shop may advise a short break-in period of easy driving.
If the slipping is getting worse, stop driving it hard and get it checked right away to avoid ruining the new parts.
If you smell burning, see smoke or the pedal goes to the floor, stop driving and call the shop that did the work.
result.why: New clutches need correct adjustment and clean, oil-free parts. A pedal or hydraulic system that isn't set up right, oil on the new disc, or a flywheel that wasn't resurfaced or replaced can all cause slipping soon after a repair.

causes.name: Incorrect adjustment or air in the hydraulics
causes.clues: The pedal feels different from before, or the clutch grabs very high.

causes.name: Oil or grease on the new disc
causes.clues: Slipping with chatter, or an oil leak that wasn't fixed during the repair.

causes.name: Wrong or faulty part
causes.clues: Slipping from day one, even when driven gently.

you: Keep the repair paperwork handy and note when the slipping started.
Look for oil drips where the engine meets the transmission.

result.title: If RPM and speed rise together, the clutch probably isn't slipping
result.now: Book a check for low engine power when convenient, and mention any warning lights or other symptoms.
if: If the check engine light is flashing or the engine shakes, don't drive it. Have it checked right away.
If a wheel smokes, smells of burning or is much hotter than the others after a drive, a brake may be dragging. Don't keep driving; let it cool and have it checked before driving further.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward red or a red warning light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: A slipping clutch shows up as revs rising faster than speed. If they rise together and the car still feels sluggish, the engine isn't making full power or something is holding the car back.

causes.name: Engine power problem (air, fuel or ignition)
causes.clues: A check engine light, rough running or hesitation.

causes.name: Dragging brake
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter than the others, or there's a burning smell near a wheel.

causes.name: Clogged air filter or exhaust restriction
causes.clues: Gradual loss of power over time.

you: Check for warning lights.
After a drive, carefully hold your hand near each wheel (without touching) to compare heat.

result.title: Have a technician confirm whether the clutch is slipping
result.now: Book a clutch check when convenient and describe when the problem happens: which gear, uphill or flat, and how the pedal feels.
if: If the car struggles to get moving or you smell burning, stop driving and get it checked right away.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, check the clutch fluid reservoir. If it's low and shared with the brakes, have it inspected before driving further.
If the clutch pedal goes to the floor and stays there, don't drive it.
result.why: Clutch slip, low engine power and dragging brakes can all feel like the car isn't pulling. A technician can do a quick slip test and road test to tell them apart.

causes.name: Worn clutch
causes.clues: Revs jump in high gears or on hills.

causes.name: Clutch hydraulic or adjustment problem
causes.clues: The pedal feel has changed.

causes.name: Engine power problem
causes.clues: A check engine light or rough running.

you: Note which gears and situations feel wrong.
Check the clutch fluid reservoir level.

q_feel.q: Besides the noise, how does the steering feel?
q_feel.help: "Loose" means the wheel moves a bit before the car responds, or you're constantly correcting to stay straight.

opts.a: Loose or vague, the car wanders, the wheel is crooked, or there's a heavy clunk
Heavier than usual, or there's a whine as well as the groan
It feels normal. It's just the noise
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When do you hear the creak most?

opts.a: Turning the wheel at low speed or while parking
Turning while going over bumps, dips or driveways
Mostly in cold or wet weather, and it fades as the car warms up
Only in very tight turns, with a scrubbing or hopping feeling
I'm not sure

q_source.q: Where does the sound seem to come from?
q_source.help: Try turning the wheel back and forth with the car stopped and the engine running, with a window down.

opts.a: Up near the top of a front wheel, sometimes with a pop or a small jolt in the steering wheel
Low down near a front wheel, a dry creak like an old door hinge
Inside the car: the steering column, the dash or the wheel itself
I'm not sure

result.title: A worn steering or suspension joint may be close to failing
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic inspect the front end.
if: If you're on the road when it starts, slow down gently, avoid hard braking and sharp turns, and pull over as soon as it's safe.
If a front wheel leans in or out at the top, a ball joint may have separated. Don't move the car at all.
result.why: Creaking plus loose steering or a heavy clunk suggests a ball joint or tie rod end is badly worn. These parts connect the wheels to the car and the steering. If one separates, you can lose control of that wheel.

causes.name: Badly worn ball joint
causes.clues: Creaking and clunking over bumps, uneven tire wear, a wheel that looks tilted.

causes.name: Worn tie rod end
causes.clues: Play in the steering wheel and wandering at highway speed.

causes.name: Broken coil spring or control arm mount
causes.clues: One corner sits lower than the others, or a loud clunk when turning.

you: Without moving the car, look at the front wheels from the front. Note if one leans in or out at the top, and tell the shop or tow driver.
shop: Ball joint and tie rod inspection with the wheels off the ground
Front suspension inspection on a lift

result.title: The power steering may not be giving full assist
result.now: If your car has a power steering fluid reservoir, check the level with the engine off. Get the steering checked within the next few days, and avoid highway driving and long trips until then.
if: If the steering becomes very hard to turn, or a steering warning light comes on, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If the fluid is low, top it up with the type in your owner's manual and have the leak found. If it's dripping steadily, don't drive it until it's checked.
If the steering gets heavier while you're driving, or the fluid level keeps dropping, stop driving it and have it checked before going further.
If you smell hot fluid or see smoke from under the hood, pull over, turn the engine off and step away. Power steering fluid on hot parts can burn.
result.why: A groan with heavier steering often means the power steering isn't giving full assist. On cars with hydraulic steering, low fluid or a worn pump are common causes, and a shop will usually find the leak or pressure-test the pump before replacing anything. On electric steering, it can be a motor or sensor fault.

causes.name: Low power steering fluid from a leak
causes.clues: A low reservoir, or reddish or amber drips under the front.
causes.against: Doesn't apply if your car has electric power steering with no reservoir.

causes.name: Worn power steering pump
causes.clues: The fluid level is fine but the groan or whine is getting louder.

causes.name: Electric power steering fault
causes.clues: A steering warning light, or the heaviness comes and goes.

you: Check the power steering fluid level, if your car has a reservoir.
Look under the front of the car for fresh drips.
shop: Power steering fluid and leak inspection
Code scan for electric steering faults

result.title: Possibly a dry or worn ball joint
result.now: Have the front suspension inspected within the next few days. Until then, avoid potholes, curbs and sharp turns at speed.
if: If the steering starts feeling loose, the car wanders, or you hear clunking, stop driving it and have it towed.
If a shop finds the joint is only dry and not loose, it may just need grease, if it's the type that can be greased.
If a front wheel looks tilted in or out at the top, don't move the car. Have it towed.
If you hear a loud bang or clunk and the steering changes, stop as soon as it's safe and call for a tow.
result.why: Ball joints are pivots that let the front wheels steer and move up and down. When the grease inside dries out or the joint wears, it creaks as it moves, especially when you turn and hit a bump at the same time. A worn ball joint gets worse over time and can eventually separate, so a shop will usually check it for play with the wheels off the ground to tell a dry joint from a worn one.

causes.name: Worn or dry lower ball joint
causes.clues: A creak like a squeaky door when turning over bumps, coming from low near the wheel.

causes.name: Torn ball joint boot
causes.clues: A split rubber boot lets grease out and dirt in.

causes.name: Worn control arm bushing
causes.clues: Creaking over bumps even when driving straight.

you: Bounce the front of the car by pushing down on it while parked and listen for the creak.
Look behind the front wheels for torn rubber boots.
shop: Ball joint play check with the wheels off the ground
Front suspension inspection on a lift

result.title: Possibly dry rubber bushings, often in the sway bar or control arms
result.now: Book a front suspension check when convenient, and mention that it's worse in cold or wet weather.
if: If the creak becomes a clunk, or it starts happening in warm weather too, get it checked within a few days.
If the steering feels loose or the car wanders, stop driving it and have it checked right away.
If you hear a loud bang or clunk and the steering changes, stop as soon as it's safe and call for a tow.
result.why: The suspension uses rubber bushings to cushion metal parts. As they age, they harden and creak when they twist, and cold or wet weather makes it worse. Dry bushings are often more noise than danger, but only an inspection can rule out a worn joint, and worn bushings can affect handling and tire wear over time.

causes.name: Dry or worn sway bar bushings
causes.clues: Creaking over bumps and in turns, worse in the cold.

causes.name: Worn control arm bushings
causes.clues: Creaking plus a slight clunk when braking or accelerating.

causes.name: Dry strut mount
causes.clues: The creak is near the top of the wheel when turning.

you: Note whether the noise happens only when the weather is cold or damp.
Bounce the front of the car while parked and listen.
shop: Sway bar link and bushing check

result.title: Possibly the tires scrubbing in tight turns, which can be normal
result.now: Check your tire pressures and set them to the numbers on the sticker inside the driver's door. If you have 4WD or AWD with a selectable mode, make sure it's in 2WD or Auto on dry pavement.
if: If you have a part-time 4WD system that's engaged on dry pavement, switch it off. Driving that way can damage the drivetrain.
If the noise or hopping happens in normal turns too, or the 4WD warning light is on, book a check.
If the steering feels loose, the car wanders, or you hear clunking, stop driving it and have it checked right away.
result.why: At full lock, the front tires turn at slightly different angles and can scrub on the pavement, which makes a groan, especially on smooth parking garage floors. A 4WD system locked in on dry pavement causes a similar binding or hopping feel. If the noise happens outside those tight turns, it's worth an inspection rather than assuming it's normal.

causes.name: Normal tire scrub at full lock
causes.clues: Only in very tight turns on smooth floors, and nothing else is wrong.

causes.name: 4WD engaged on dry pavement
causes.clues: A part-time 4WD truck or SUV with 4WD switched on.
causes.against: Doesn't apply to two-wheel-drive cars.

causes.name: AWD or differential problem
causes.clues: Binding or shuddering in turns even in normal mode, or mismatched tires.

you: Check that all four tires are inflated correctly.
Check the 4WD selector or dash indicator.
Make sure all four tires are the same size and similarly worn.

result.title: Possibly a worn strut mount or strut bearing
result.now: Book a front suspension check when convenient. Mention that the creak or pop happens when turning at low speed.
if: If you feel a jolt or clunk through the wheel over bumps, or the steering feels notchy, get it checked within a few days.
If the steering starts feeling loose or the car wanders, stop driving it and have it checked right away.
If one front corner suddenly sits lower or you heard a loud bang, a coil spring may have broken. Don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: On many cars, the top of each front strut sits in a mount with a bearing that rotates when you steer. When the bearing wears or the rubber dries out, it creaks, groans or pops as you turn, especially at low speed. It's often not urgent, but it tends to get worse, and a technician should confirm the noise isn't from a ball joint or spring.

causes.name: Worn strut bearing
causes.clues: A creak or pop when turning while parked, sometimes felt in the steering wheel.

causes.name: Worn strut mount rubber
causes.clues: A clunk over bumps along with the creak.

causes.name: Worn strut or broken coil spring
causes.clues: One corner sits lower or the car bounces more than usual.

you: With a window down, turn the wheel back and forth while parked and note which side the sound comes from.
Check whether one front corner sits lower than the other.
shop: Front suspension inspection on a lift

result.title: The noise may be in the steering column or trim, not the suspension
result.now: With the car parked, turn the wheel slowly and see whether the steering wheel cover or the plastic trim around the column is rubbing.
if: If the airbag warning light is on, have the car checked soon. A worn clock spring inside the steering wheel can affect the airbag and horn.
If the steering feels notchy, sticks, catches, or has play before the wheels respond, don't drive it until it's checked. A worn steering shaft joint affects your control of the car.
result.why: If the creak comes from inside the car, the cause is usually something rubbing in the steering column or the trim around it. Trim rubbing is a comfort issue, but a worn steering shaft joint or clock spring can sound similar, so it's worth having a technician confirm which it is.

causes.name: Steering wheel or column trim rubbing
causes.clues: The creak changes when you press on the plastic around the column.

causes.name: Dry or worn steering shaft joint
causes.clues: A creak or slight clunk felt through the wheel, often heard by the driver's feet.

causes.name: Worn clock spring
causes.clues: A rubbing sound inside the wheel, sometimes with the airbag light or horn not working.

you: Press gently on the column trim while turning the wheel and listen for changes.
Check whether the airbag light is off after the car starts.
shop: Airbag system code scan if the light is on

result.title: Have the steering and front suspension inspected
result.now: Book a front-end inspection when convenient. Record a short video with sound of the creak while turning the wheel to show the technician.
if: If the steering feels loose, the car wanders, or you hear clunking, stop driving it and have it checked right away.
If the steering gets heavier or you hear a whine, check the power steering fluid, if your car has a reservoir.
If a front wheel looks tilted, or the steering suddenly gets very hard to turn, pull over and don't drive it.
result.why: Creaks when turning come from a handful of joints in the steering and suspension. A technician can check them all for wear in a few minutes with the car on a lift.

causes.name: Worn strut mount or bearing
causes.clues: Creaking or popping at low speed when turning.

causes.name: Dry or worn ball joint
causes.clues: Creaking when turning over bumps.

causes.name: Dry suspension bushings
causes.clues: Worse in cold or wet weather.

you: Note whether it happens parked, at low speed, over bumps, or only in cold weather.
Bounce the front of the car while parked and listen.
shop: Front suspension inspection on a lift
Ball joint and tie rod check

dashboard-lights-all-on.title: Many dashboard lights on at once

opts.a: Lots of lights come on for a few seconds when I start the car, then go out
The lights flicker, or the gauges, dash or radio cut in and out
Several lights came on together and stay on
It started right after a jump start, a battery change, or the battery died
The steering got heavy, the engine stumbled, or the car is losing power
I'm not sure

q_flicker.q: Is the battery light one of them, or are the headlights dimming too?
q_flicker.help: The battery light usually looks like a small car battery with + and – marks.

opts.a: Yes, the battery light is on, or the headlights dim and brighten
No, but it happens over bumps or when I touch the key
Only the gauge cluster glitches. Everything else works normally
I'm not sure

q_which.help: Red lights are the most serious. Yellow or amber ones mean something needs checking.

opts.a: A red light like oil pressure, engine temperature, or the red brake light
ABS and traction or stability control (maybe the yellow brake light too)
Check engine, plus traction control or other driving aids
A mix of unrelated lights, like airbag, ABS, steering and transmission
I'm not sure

result.title: This sounds like the normal startup self-check
result.now: If every light goes out within a few seconds of the engine starting, there's usually nothing to fix. Keep an eye on it for the next few starts.
if: If any light stays on after the engine is running, look it up in your owner's manual and follow that light's advice.
If a light that normally comes on at startup doesn't come on at all, have the bulb or system checked. It may not warn you when it should.
If a red light such as oil pressure, temperature or brake stays on after starting, don't drive. Turn the engine off and get it checked.
result.why: When you switch the car on, it lights up most of its warning lights for a moment to show that the bulbs and systems work. They should all go out once the engine is running.

causes.name: Normal bulb and system check
causes.clues: All lights go out within a few seconds of starting.
causes.against: If any light stays on after starting, it's a real warning.

causes.name: Slow-to-clear warning after a weak start
causes.clues: Some lights take longer to go out on cold mornings or after slow cranking.

you: Watch the dash for 10 seconds after the engine starts.
shop: Code scan if any light stays on

result.title: Lights after battery trouble are often leftover low-voltage warnings
result.now: Check that the battery clamps are tight and clean, then drive a short distance. Many of these lights clear on their own once the systems see steady voltage.
if: If the battery light stays on with the engine running, the battery may not be charging. Have the alternator and battery tested before relying on the car for longer trips.
If the lights are still on after a few drives, have the codes read. Some systems, like steering or windows, need a reset after battery work.
If a red oil pressure, temperature or brake light stays on, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and get it checked before driving.
If the lights flicker, the steering gets heavy or the engine stumbles, get off the road somewhere safe. The battery may not be charging.
result.why: When voltage drops low, many computers in the car store faults at once and turn on their lights. After a jump or a new battery, some lights clear by themselves, and others need a short drive or a reset to go out.

causes.name: Faults stored during low voltage
causes.clues: The battery went flat or was disconnected just before.

causes.name: Loose battery clamp after the work
causes.clues: A clamp that moves when you twist it.

causes.name: Battery still low or failing
causes.clues: Slow cranking, or the battery is more than 4–5 years old.

you: Check the battery clamps.
Note which lights clear after a short drive and which stay on.

result.title: The charging system may be failing, and the car could be running low on power
result.now: Get off the road somewhere safe while the car still runs, then turn it off. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the engine temperature is rising too, the drive belt may have broken. Don't restart the engine.
If you're stuck somewhere unsafe, turn on your hazard lights and call roadside assistance.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the hood or the dash, turn the car off and get everyone out.
result.why: When the alternator stops charging, the car runs on battery alone. As voltage drops, the computers turn on warnings, lights flicker, steering assist can cut out, and eventually the engine stops. That often happens in traffic.

causes.name: Alternator failure
causes.clues: The battery light is on, the headlights dim, and there may be a whine or burning smell.

causes.name: Broken or slipping drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal before it happened, or the temperature gauge rising.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery cable or ground
causes.clues: Crusty terminals, or the problem changes over bumps.

you: With the engine off, look for a missing or loose drive belt.
Check the battery clamps.
shop: Voltage-drop test on battery and ground cables

result.title: Possibly a voltage problem from the battery, a cable or the alternator
result.now: Check that the battery clamps are tight and clean, then get the battery and charging system tested within the next few days.
if: If the battery light comes on or the headlights dim, get off the road and have it towed.
If a red warning light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the steering gets heavy or the engine stumbles, get off the road while the car still runs.
If you smell burning plastic or see smoke, pull over, turn the car off and get out.
result.why: Every computer in the car needs steady voltage. A weak battery, a loose cable or a tired alternator can make many warnings appear at once or flicker. It's a common reason for a dash full of lights, and a shop will usually test the battery and charging system before replacing any modules.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery terminal or ground strap
causes.clues: The lights change over bumps, or there's buildup on the terminals.

causes.name: Weak battery
causes.clues: Slow cranking, or a battery older than 4–5 years.

causes.name: Alternator starting to fail
causes.clues: Lights dim at idle and brighten with revs.

you: Check the battery clamps and the ground strap from the engine to the body.
Watch whether the lights change when you rev the engine slightly in Park.
shop: Voltage-drop test on battery and ground cables

result.title: The gauge cluster itself may be failing
result.now: Book a check when convenient. Make sure the battery clamps are tight first, since low voltage can look the same.
if: If the speedometer or fuel gauge becomes unreliable, get it fixed sooner. You need to know your speed and fuel.
If the battery light comes on or other systems act up, treat it as a voltage problem and get it checked within a few days.
If you can't trust the temperature gauge or warning lights, you may not be warned about overheating or low oil pressure. Watch for steam, hot smells or new noises, and pull over if you notice any.
result.why: If only the gauges glitch while the engine, lights and radio work normally, the problem is usually inside the cluster or its connector, not the rest of the car.

causes.name: Failing instrument cluster
causes.clues: Gauges drop to zero or reset, but everything else runs fine.

causes.name: Loose cluster connector or ground
causes.clues: It happens over bumps or after dash work.

causes.name: Low voltage
causes.clues: Dim lights or slow cranking too.
causes.against: If the battery tests fine and nothing else flickers, low voltage is less likely.

you: Check the battery clamps.
Record a short video of the glitch for the shop.

result.title: A red warning means stop, whatever else is on
result.now: Pull over where it's safe and turn the engine off. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the red brake light is on and the pedal feels soft or sinks, don't drive it at all.
If the red light was oil pressure, check the oil level once the engine is off, but don't restart it even if it looks full.
If you smell burning or see smoke, get everyone out and away from the car.
If the check engine light is flashing as well, the engine may be misfiring badly: pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: Red warnings for oil pressure, engine temperature and brakes mean a risk of engine damage or a safety failure. Even if other lights came on at the same time, the red one decides what you do.

causes.name: Low oil pressure
causes.clues: A red oil can symbol, ticking or knocking.

causes.name: Engine overheating
causes.clues: The temperature gauge is high, or there's steam.

causes.name: Brake fluid low or brake system fault
causes.clues: The red brake light with a soft or low pedal.

causes.name: Charging failure setting off several warnings
causes.clues: The battery light is on too, and lights flicker.

you: With the engine off, check the oil level and the coolant reservoir once cool.
Check the brake fluid reservoir level.

result.title: One ABS problem can turn on all of these lights together
result.now: Check the brake fluid reservoir first. If it's at or below MIN, don't just top it up; have the brakes inspected before driving further. If the level is fine and the pedal feels normal, drive gently, leave extra stopping distance, and have the ABS codes read within the next few days.
if: If the red brake light comes on or the pedal feels soft, low or sinks, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the speedometer also acts up, a wheel speed sensor is even more likely.
If braking takes more force than usual, the pedal travels further, the car pulls when braking, or you hear grinding, stop driving it and have the brakes checked.
result.why: Traction and stability control rely on the ABS system's wheel speed sensors. When ABS has a fault, the others switch off too, so several lights appear at once. Most cars are designed to keep basic braking when ABS has a fault, but you lose the anti-skid help in an emergency or on slippery roads. This guide can't check your brakes, so treat any change in the brake pedal as a brake problem.

causes.name: Faulty wheel speed sensor or its wiring
causes.clues: The lights came on after rain, a pothole or recent brake or suspension work.

causes.name: Low brake fluid
causes.clues: The brake fluid reservoir is near or below MIN. Low fluid can mean worn pads or a leak, even if you can't see one.

causes.name: ABS module fault
causes.clues: Lights that come and go with no other pattern.

you: Check the brake fluid reservoir level.
Note whether the lights came on after rain or a bump.

result.title: An engine fault often switches off traction control and other aids too
result.now: Have the codes read within the next few days. Many auto parts stores can read the check engine code for you.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over and stop driving it.
If power drops or a reduced power message appears, the car may not accelerate normally in traffic. Avoid highways and busy roads and get it checked before relying on it.
If the temperature gauge climbs or a red warning light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: On many cars, a check engine fault makes the computer turn off traction control, stability control or cruise control as a precaution. Fix the engine fault and the other lights usually go out with it.

causes.name: Engine sensor or misfire fault
causes.clues: A steady check engine light, rough idle or less power.

causes.name: Loose gas cap or small emissions leak
causes.clues: The light came on soon after refueling and the car runs normally.

causes.name: Throttle or pedal sensor fault
causes.clues: Sluggish acceleration or a reduced power message.

you: Make sure the gas cap is tight.
Get the code read at a parts store or with your own code reader.
shop: Misfire and ignition tests if needed

result.title: The car's computers may not be talking to each other properly
result.now: Check that the battery clamps are tight, then have a shop scan all the computers within the next few days.
if: If the steering gets heavy, the brakes feel different or the car loses power, stop driving it.
If it started after a leak, a car wash or heavy rain, mention it. Water in a connector is a common cause.
If you smell burning or see smoke, turn the car off and get out.
If a red oil pressure, temperature or brake light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Modern cars connect their computers on a shared network. A low-voltage problem, a bad ground or one failing module can disrupt it, so systems that have nothing in common all report faults at once.

causes.name: Low voltage or a bad ground connection
causes.clues: A weak battery, slow cranking, or lights that change with engine speed.

causes.name: Water in a wiring connector or module
causes.clues: Wet carpets, a leak, or it started after heavy rain.

causes.name: Failing module or damaged wiring
causes.clues: Recent accident or electrical work, or chewed wires.

you: Check the battery clamps.
Feel for damp carpets in the footwells and trunk.

q_what.q: What happens after you shift into Drive or Reverse?

opts.a: It doesn't engage at all, or only moves if I rev the engine
There's also a burning smell, or red or pink fluid under the car
A pause only on the first drive of the day, then it's fine
A pause of a second or more every time, then it catches (maybe with a thud)
I'm not sure

q_which.q: Is it slow to engage in Drive, Reverse, or both?

opts.a: Reverse only
Drive only
Both
I'm not sure

q_fluid.q: Have you been able to check the transmission fluid?
q_fluid.help: Many cars have a transmission dipstick, often with a yellow or red handle; others have none and must be checked by a shop. Your owner's manual explains how. Healthy fluid is usually red or pink and doesn't smell burnt.

opts.a: Yes, it's low
The level is OK, but it's dark brown or smells burnt
The level and color look normal
My car has no dipstick / I'm not sure
When the engine is hot, after driving a while
About the same whether hot or cold
It started right after a fluid change or battery work
I'm not sure

result.title: The transmission may not be building enough pressure to drive the car
result.now: Put it in Park, turn the engine off and have the car towed. Don't rev the engine to force it into gear.
if: If there's red or pink fluid under the car, a major leak is the likely cause. Mention it when you call.
If the shifter moves but the gear display doesn't change, the shift cable or linkage may be broken. That's often a simpler repair.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the car, step away. Transmission fluid on hot exhaust parts can catch fire.
result.why: When an automatic won't engage, or only catches after revving, it usually isn't getting enough fluid pressure to apply the clutches. Revving it can make the car lurch without warning and adds heat and wear to parts that are already slipping.

causes.name: Very low fluid from a leak
causes.clues: Red or pink fluid under the car, or a recent bump underneath.

causes.name: Failing transmission pump or badly worn internal parts
causes.clues: A whine that changes with engine speed, and a delay that got worse over weeks.

causes.name: Broken shift cable or linkage
causes.clues: The shifter feels loose, or the gear shown on the dash doesn't match the shifter.

you: From outside the car, look for red or pink fluid underneath.
Check whether the gear indicator on the dash matches the shifter position.

result.title: A transmission leak or overheating may be behind the delay
result.now: Don't use the car for now. Turn the engine off and have it towed.
if: If you see smoke, step away from the car. Fluid dripping on the exhaust can catch fire.
If it's only a few drops and there's no burning smell, check the fluid level once the car is cool, but still have it inspected before driving it.
If a transmission temperature warning came on, tell the shop when you call.
result.why: The transmission needs a full supply of fluid to build pressure quickly when you select a gear. A leak lets the level drop, which causes the delay, and a burning smell means fluid or parts are overheating.

causes.name: Leaking pan gasket, cooler line or seal
causes.clues: Red or pink fluid under the middle or front of the car.

causes.name: Overheating from internal slipping
causes.clues: A sharp burnt smell after driving.

causes.name: Fluid dripping onto the exhaust
causes.clues: Smoke from under the car along with the leak.

you: Note the color of any fluid under the car.

result.title: A first-start delay can mean fluid is draining back overnight
result.now: After starting, wait a few seconds with your foot on the brake before shifting, and book a transmission check when convenient.
if: If the delay gets longer or starts happening after short stops too, get it checked within a few days.
If you find the fluid low, top it up with the correct type and have the leak found within a few days. Low fluid usually means it's escaping somewhere.
If you smell burning, the car lurches into gear, or it slips while driving, stop driving it and have it checked.
result.why: When a car sits overnight, some fluid can drain out of the torque converter and passages, especially past worn seals. The transmission then needs a moment to refill and build pressure before the gear catches. It's an early warning sign worth catching before it gets worse.

causes.name: Fluid draining out of the torque converter or passages
causes.clues: Only after sitting for hours, and fine for the rest of the day.

causes.name: Hardened or worn internal seals
causes.clues: Older or high-mileage car, and worse in cold weather.

causes.name: Slightly low fluid
causes.clues: A small leak, or a level at the low mark.

you: Time the delay on a few mornings so you can tell if it's getting worse.
Look for red or pink drips where you park.

result.title: A delay only in Reverse can point to a worn reverse clutch, band or seals
result.now: Have the transmission checked within the next few days. Until then, hold the brake firmly until Reverse fully engages before backing up.
if: If Reverse stops engaging at all, don't keep trying. Have it checked before using the car.
If the fluid is low, top it up with the correct type and have the leak found. Low fluid often shows up in Reverse first.
If you smell burning or the car lurches backward when Reverse catches, stop using it and have it checked.
result.why: Reverse uses its own clutch or band inside the transmission, and it often needs more pressure than Drive. When that part or its seals start to wear, or the fluid is a little low, Reverse is often the first gear to show a delay. A shop will usually check the fluid, codes and pressure before recommending internal repairs.

causes.name: Worn reverse clutch, band or seals
causes.clues: High mileage, and the delay in Reverse is slowly getting longer.

causes.name: Low fluid
causes.clues: Red or pink drips, or a level below the mark.

causes.name: Sticking valve or solenoid
causes.clues: The delay comes and goes, sometimes with a check engine light.

you: Check the fluid level if your car has a dipstick.
Time the delay so you can tell if it's getting worse.

result.title: Low transmission fluid may be causing the delay, and it's likely leaking somewhere
result.now: Top up with the exact fluid type listed in your owner's manual, then have the leak found within the next few days.
if: If the delay continues after topping up, keep trips short and get it checked sooner.
If the level drops again quickly or you see fluid dripping, stop using the car until the leak is fixed.
If you see smoke or smell burning fluid, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away. Fluid on the exhaust can catch fire.
result.why: With low fluid, the transmission pump has to work harder to build pressure, so there's a pause before the gear catches. Fluid doesn't get used up in normal driving, so a low level usually means a leak, even if you can't see drips.

causes.name: Leaking pan gasket or seal
causes.clues: Red or pink drips under the middle of the car.

causes.name: Leaking cooler line
causes.clues: Drips near the front of the car, under the radiator.

causes.name: Level set too low at a recent service
causes.clues: The delay started soon after a fluid change.

you: Recheck the level after a few days.
Put cardboard under the car overnight to spot drips.
shop: Correct fluid level check to factory procedure

result.title: Worn or overheated fluid, possibly with internal wear
result.now: Have the transmission inspected within the next few days and ask whether a fluid service is right for its condition.
if: If the shop finds metal debris in the pan, a deeper repair may be needed rather than just new fluid. Ask them to show you what they found.
If the delay gets much longer or it starts slipping, stop driving it and have it towed.
If a transmission temperature warning comes on or you smell burning, stop driving it and have it towed.
result.why: Dark, burnt-smelling fluid has been overheated and no longer protects or seals as well. That can slow how quickly gears engage, and it often means parts inside have been working harder than they should.

causes.name: Overdue fluid service
causes.clues: No record of a fluid change, especially with towing or heavy use.

causes.name: Worn internal seals or clutches
causes.clues: High mileage, and the delay is slowly getting longer.

causes.name: Past overheating
causes.clues: A history of towing, mountain driving or a transmission temperature warning.

you: Find your records of the last transmission fluid service.

result.title: A delay that's worse when hot can point to internal wear leaking pressure
result.now: Have the transmission checked within the next few days, and avoid towing or long hot drives until then.
if: If a transmission temperature warning comes on or you smell burning, stop driving it and have it towed.
If it starts slipping while driving, get it checked right away.
result.why: Hot fluid is thinner, so it escapes more easily past worn seals and a worn pump. That lowers pressure when you select a gear, causing a pause. The problem usually grows as the wear continues. A shop will usually do a pressure test hot and cold before deciding on a repair.

causes.name: Worn transmission pump
causes.clues: A whine that rises with engine speed.

causes.name: Worn internal seals
causes.clues: High mileage, and fine when cold.

causes.name: Worn or overheated fluid
causes.clues: Dark fluid or a burnt smell.

you: Note how long you'd been driving when the delay was worst.
shop: Line pressure test hot and cold

result.title: A steady delay with normal fluid may point to a pressure control or internal problem
result.now: Have the codes read and the transmission checked within the next few days.
if: If the delay gets longer or it starts slipping, stop driving it and have it towed.
If a code points to a solenoid or sensor, the repair may be smaller than a rebuild.
If you smell burning or a transmission temperature warning comes on, stop driving it and have it towed.
result.why: If the fluid is full and clean but the delay happens every time, the problem may be in how pressure is controlled or held. A shop will usually scan for codes and test pressure and solenoids before recommending a rebuild. That can be an electronic solenoid, a sticking valve, or wear to seals and clutches.

causes.name: Faulty pressure control solenoid
causes.clues: A check engine light, or harsh shifts as well.

causes.name: Sticking valve in the valve body
causes.clues: The delay varies from one day to the next.

causes.name: Worn seals or clutches
causes.clues: High mileage and a delay that's slowly getting longer.

you: Time the delay in Drive and Reverse.

result.title: A delay that started after service may be a fluid level, fluid type or relearn issue
result.now: Check the service invoice for the fluid type used, and ask the shop that did the work to recheck the level.
if: If the wrong fluid was used, have it corrected soon. The wrong type can cause delays and harsh shifts.
If it started after battery work and is improving day by day, the transmission may be relearning. Book a check if it hasn't settled after about a week.
If the delay is getting worse, it slips, or you smell burning, stop driving it and have it checked.
result.why: Transmission fluid levels must be set using a specific procedure, often with the engine warm. An incorrect level, the wrong fluid, or learned settings wiped by a battery disconnect can all cause a delay into gear.

causes.name: Fluid level set wrong
causes.clues: The delay started right after a fluid change.

causes.name: Wrong fluid type
causes.clues: The invoice lists a fluid not named in your owner's manual.

causes.name: Shift adaptations reset after battery work
causes.clues: It started after battery work and is slowly improving.

you: Compare the fluid on the invoice with your owner's manual.
shop: Fluid level check to factory procedure
Transmission adaptation relearn with a scan tool

result.title: Have the transmission checked before the delay gets longer
result.now: Book a transmission check within the next week or two. Time the delay in Drive and Reverse so you can tell the shop.
if: If the delay grows quickly, it starts slipping, or you smell burning, stop driving it and have it towed.
If you can check the fluid and it's low, top it up with the correct type and look for a leak.
result.why: Delayed engagement means the transmission is slow to build pressure. It's often an early sign of low fluid or wear that's cheaper to deal with now than later.

causes.name: Low or worn fluid
causes.clues: Drips under the car or no record of a fluid service.

causes.name: Worn internal seals
causes.clues: Worse on cold mornings or when hot.

causes.name: Pressure control fault
causes.clues: A warning light or harsh shifts too.

you: Time the delay in Drive and Reverse.
Look for red or pink drips where you park.

electrical-accessories-not-working.title: Windows, locks or radio stopped working

q_warning_signs.q: Did it happen along with any of these?

opts.a: A burning smell, smoke, or a switch or panel that feels hot
The battery light came on, or the lights and gauges are dimming or flickering
Right after rain, a car wash, an open window or water getting inside
None of these
I'm not sure
One or more power windows
Door locks or the key fob
The radio or center screen
Several different things at once (for example radio, power outlets and windows)
Things cut in and out, especially over bumps or when a door moves
I'm not sure

q_window.q: When you press the switch for the problem window, what happens?

opts.a: I hear a motor whir or grinding, but the glass doesn't move, or it dropped or tilted
None of the passenger windows work from their own switches, but they work from the driver's door
Nothing happens, and it's just one window
It moves very slowly or stops partway
I'm not sure
One door won't lock or unlock, and may buzz or click
The key fob doesn't work, but the lock switch inside the car does
No door responds to the inside switch or the fob
I'm not sure

q_radio.q: What is the radio or screen doing?

opts.a: It's asking for a code, or shows 'CODE' or 'LOCKED', after battery work or a jump
It's completely dead and dark
It turns on but freezes, restarts by itself or has no sound
I'm not sure

result.title: An electrical part or wire may be overheating. Treat it as a fire risk
result.now: Turn the car off, take the key out and get everyone out. Don't use it again until it's inspected. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see flames or heavy smoke, move well away and call 911.
If the smell came from one window switch or door, mention that to the shop. Some switches have been recalled for overheating, so check for recalls with your VIN.
result.why: A burning smell or a hot switch along with failed accessories means current is going where it shouldn't, and wiring is heating up. That can turn into a fire, so the car shouldn't be used until the cause is found.

causes.name: Shorted or water-damaged switch
causes.clues: The smell or heat is at one switch, often a window switch.

causes.name: Damaged or pinched wiring
causes.clues: Recent work behind a panel, or an aftermarket accessory was added.

causes.name: Overheated motor or connector
causes.clues: A window or seat motor that strained or stuck just before the smell.

you: Ask a dealer for your brand whether a recall affecting the electrical system is open on your VIN.
shop: Wiring and connector inspection for heat damage

result.title: The charging system may be failing, and accessories may be shutting down to save power
result.now: Get off the road somewhere safe and turn off electrical extras. Don't set out again until the battery and alternator have been tested. A mobile mechanic or a tow is the safest way to get it checked, because the car may shut off without much warning.
if: If the lights keep dimming, the steering gets heavy or the engine starts to stumble, get off the road right away. The car may shut off.
If the problem cleared after a jump start or new battery, still have the alternator tested.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the hood, turn the car off and get everyone out.
result.why: When voltage drops, many cars shut off non-essential accessories first, so windows and the radio can stop working before the engine does. A battery light suggests the car isn't charging properly, and a shop will usually test the battery, alternator and cables before replacing anything.

causes.name: Failing alternator
causes.clues: A battery light, a whining noise, or lights that dim at idle.

causes.name: Weak or failing battery
causes.clues: Slow cranking, or the battery is more than 4–5 years old.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery or ground cable
causes.clues: Crusty terminals, or things flicker over bumps.

you: Check that the battery clamps are tight and clean.

result.title: Water may have gotten into a switch, connector or module
result.now: Dry the interior as much as you can, leave the affected switches alone for now, and have the electrical system checked within a few days.
if: If anything smells hot or burnt, turn the car off and don't use it until it's inspected.
If the carpet is wet, find where the water is getting in. Modules under the seats and carpet are easily damaged.
If the airbag light comes on, or the car won't start or acts on its own, have it checked before relying on it. Modules under the seats and carpet include safety systems on many cars.
result.why: Switches, connectors and control modules don't tolerate water. Moisture can make them stop working, act on their own, or short out. Some recover once dry; others are damaged. A shop will usually dry and test the connector or module before deciding whether anything needs replacing.

causes.name: Water in a door switch or connector
causes.clues: A window left open in rain, or problems on one door only.

causes.name: Wet control module
causes.clues: Damp carpet, or several unrelated things acting up.

causes.name: Blocked drains or leaking seals letting water in
causes.clues: Repeated wet carpet or a musty smell.

you: Check the carpet and under the floor mats for dampness.
Note which door or area got wet.
shop: Connector and module inspection for corrosion

result.title: A blown fuse is a common and easy thing to check first
result.now: Use your owner's manual to find the fuse for the item that stopped working, and replace it with one of the same rating if it's blown.
if: If the new fuse blows right away or soon after, stop replacing it. There's a short circuit, so book a repair.
If the fuses are fine and several things are still dead, have the wiring and control modules checked.
If you smell burning or see smoke, turn the car off and get out. Don't keep swapping fuses.
If what stopped working is something you need to drive safely, like headlights, wipers, brake lights or turn signals, get it fixed before driving in conditions where you need it.
result.why: Fuses protect circuits by burning out when something draws too much current. When several things on one circuit stop together, or something dies with no warning, a fuse is a quick first thing to check. A fuse that blows is a symptom, so if it keeps happening the shop will look for the short behind it.

causes.name: Blown fuse
causes.clues: Several things on the same circuit died at once, often after plugging something into a power outlet.

causes.name: Failed relay
causes.clues: The fuse is fine but nothing on that circuit works.

causes.name: Wiring or control module fault
causes.clues: Fuses are fine and other unrelated things act strangely.

you: Check the fuses in the interior and under-hood fuse boxes. A blown fuse has a broken metal strip inside.
Unplug any chargers or accessories from the power outlets.
shop: Short-circuit diagnosis if the fuse keeps blowing

result.title: The window regulator, the track that moves the glass, may have broken
result.now: Stop pressing the switch so the motor doesn't burn out, and book a repair. If the window is down, cover the opening to keep rain out.
if: If the glass has fallen into the door and the car must be left parked, secure the opening with plastic and tape and park somewhere protected.
If you smell burning from the door, stop using the switch and get it checked soon.
result.why: The motor is working if you hear it, but the regulator that carries the glass has broken a cable or a plastic clip. The glass then slips, tilts or drops into the door.

causes.name: Broken window regulator cable or clip
causes.clues: A snap or crunch, then the glass dropped or tilted.

causes.name: Stripped motor gear
causes.clues: The motor whirs freely but nothing moves at all.

causes.name: Glass came loose from its mount
causes.clues: The glass rattles or sits crooked in the frame.

you: Listen at the door while someone presses the switch.
shop: Door panel removal and regulator inspection

result.title: The window lock button on the driver's door may be turned on
result.now: Find the window lock button on the driver's door switch panel (often marked with a window and a lock or an X) and press it to turn it off.
if: If the passenger switches still don't work with the lock off, the master switch or wiring may be faulty. Book a check.
If just one passenger switch doesn't work, that switch is the likely problem.
result.why: The window lock disables the passenger window switches, usually so children can't open them. It's easy to bump by accident, and it makes the windows seem broken.

causes.name: Window lock button turned on
causes.clues: All passenger switches stopped together, but the driver can still move every window.

causes.name: Faulty driver's master switch
causes.clues: The lock button doesn't change anything.

causes.name: Wiring fault in the driver's door
causes.clues: Other driver's door functions act up too.

you: Press the window lock button and try the passenger switches again.

result.title: Possibly a worn window motor, switch or door wiring
result.now: Try the window from the driver's master switch as well as its own switch, then book a repair when convenient.
if: If it works from the driver's switch but not its own, that door's switch is a likely suspect.
If the window is stuck open, cover it and get it fixed soon to keep rain and thieves out.
If it moves slowly or stops partway, a dry or dirty window track or a tired motor are possibilities.
result.why: When a single window does nothing or struggles, the fault is usually in that door: its switch, its motor, or the wires that pass through the door hinge area, which flex every time the door opens.

causes.name: Worn window motor
causes.clues: It has been slow for a while, or it works if you tap the door panel.

causes.name: Faulty window switch
causes.clues: It works from the driver's master switch but not its own.

causes.name: Broken wire between the door and the body
causes.clues: Other things in that door (lock, mirror, speaker) also stopped.

you: Try both switches.
Check whether the lock and speaker in that door still work.

result.title: The lock motor (actuator) in that door may be failing
result.now: Use the key or the manual lock on that door for now, and book a repair when convenient.
if: If the door won't open from inside or outside, get it fixed soon. It can be a problem in an emergency.
If other things in that door have also stopped, a broken wire in the door hinge area is more likely.
result.why: Each door has a small motor that moves the lock. They wear out over time, and a weak one often buzzes or clicks without moving the lock, especially in cold weather.

causes.name: Worn door lock actuator
causes.clues: A buzz or weak click from that door, or it works sometimes.

causes.name: Broken wire in the door hinge area
causes.clues: The window or mirror on that door also acts up.

causes.name: Frozen or sticky lock mechanism
causes.clues: It only happens in cold weather.

you: Listen at the door while someone presses the lock button.
Check whether other features in that door work.

result.title: A weak key fob battery is a common cause
result.now: Replace the key fob battery, which is usually a coin-type battery listed in your owner's manual.
if: If your spare fob works, the main fob's battery or the fob itself is the problem.
If neither fob works with new batteries, the car's receiver or the fobs may need checking or reprogramming by a dealer or locksmith.
result.why: If the switch inside the car locks and unlocks all the doors, the lock motors and wiring are working. That leaves the fob or the car's receiver, and a weak fob battery is a common cause and the easiest to try first.

causes.name: Dead fob battery
causes.clues: The range has been getting shorter.

causes.name: Damaged fob
causes.clues: It was dropped or got wet.

causes.name: Fob lost its programming or receiver fault
causes.clues: Neither fob works, even with new batteries.

you: Try the spare fob.
Replace the fob battery.

result.title: The radio's anti-theft code needs to be entered
result.now: Look for the radio code card in your owner's manual or glove box and enter the code as the manual describes.
if: If you can't find the code, a dealer for your car's brand can usually look it up with your VIN and proof of ownership.
If you enter the wrong code several times, it may lock you out for a while. Leave the radio on and wait as the manual describes.
result.why: Many radios lock themselves when the battery is disconnected, as a theft deterrent. They need the original code before they'll work again. Usually nothing is broken.

causes.name: Anti-theft lock after the battery was disconnected or went flat
causes.clues: It started right after battery work or a dead battery.

causes.name: Radio needs to be re-paired with the car
causes.clues: A code doesn't work, or a message asks for a dealer.

you: Find the radio code card.
Check the owner's manual for the code entry steps.

result.title: The radio or screen may need a software reset or update
result.now: Try a reset: turn the car off, open and close the driver's door, wait a few minutes, then restart. Check your owner's manual for a specific reset procedure.
if: If the screen also controls things like climate, defrost or the backup camera and those stop working, get it checked within a few days, and don't rely on the camera when reversing.
If it started after a phone was connected, try deleting the phone from the system and re-pairing it.
result.why: Modern radios are small computers. Freezing, rebooting or losing sound is often a software glitch that a reset or update fixes. If it keeps happening, the unit, its amplifier or its wiring may need repair.

causes.name: Software glitch
causes.clues: It comes and goes, and a restart temporarily fixes it.

causes.name: Failed amplifier or speaker wiring
causes.clues: The screen works but there's no sound from any speaker.

causes.name: Low battery voltage
causes.clues: It reboots when you start the car or use other accessories.

you: Try a reset.
Note the software version shown in the infotainment settings, if available, and ask the shop whether an update applies.

result.title: A broken or loose wire is possible, often where the wires pass into a door
result.now: Note exactly what cuts out and when, then book an electrical diagnosis when convenient.
if: If you smell burning or anything feels hot, turn off the car and don't use it until it's inspected.
If the problems happen when the door opens or closes, the wires in the door hinge area are a likely place to check first.
If headlights, wipers or other lights cut out, don't drive at night or in bad weather until it's fixed.
result.why: Things that cut in and out with bumps or door movement usually come from a wire that's cracked inside its insulation, or a connector that's loose or corroded. The wires that run through the door hinge area flex constantly and are a common failure point.

causes.name: Broken wires in the door hinge boot
causes.clues: Problems with one door's windows, locks, mirror or speaker together.

causes.name: Loose or corroded ground connection
causes.clues: Several unrelated things flicker or reset over bumps.

causes.name: Loose connector behind a panel
causes.clues: It started after a stereo, alarm or other accessory was installed.

you: Open and close the door slowly while someone watches whether the feature cuts in and out.

q_warnings.q: Is any of this happening along with the knock?
q_warnings.help: Warning lights on the dash change the answer a lot. Pick the most serious one that fits.

opts.a: The red oil pressure light (oil can) is on or flickering
The check engine light is flashing, or the engine is shaking or running rough
The temperature gauge is high or in the red, or there's steam
No warning lights, and the engine runs normally
I'm not sure

q_oil_level.q: What does the oil dipstick show?
q_oil_level.help: Park on level ground, turn the engine off and wait a few minutes. Pull the dipstick, wipe it, push it back in fully, then pull it out again and look where the oil reaches. Some newer cars show the oil level on the dash instead.

opts.a: Between the two marks
Below the low mark, or barely on the stick
I'm not sure, or I can't check it

q_sound.q: What does the knock sound like, and when do you hear it?

opts.a: A light rattling or pinging, like marbles in a can, when accelerating or climbing hills
A deep, heavy knock that gets faster as the engine revs, and it's there even at idle
A knock that's loudest right after a cold start and fades as the engine warms up
A light tapping or ticking, quieter than a knock
It seems to come from under the car, or changes over bumps rather than with engine speed
I'm not sure

q_fuel.help: Your owner's manual and the inside of the fuel door say which fuel your engine needs: regular, premium recommended, or premium required.

opts.a: My car needs premium and I've been using regular, or it started right after a fill-up
I use the right fuel, and the pinging has been building over months
The check engine light is on (steady) along with the pinging
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may not be getting enough oil
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off and don't restart it. Have it towed, or have a mobile mechanic check it where it's parked.
if: If the oil is low, adding the right oil is a good first step, but don't run the engine until a mechanic has listened to it. Damage may have already started.
If the oil light was on while driving, tell the shop roughly how long the engine ran that way.
If you see smoke or smell burning oil, step away from the car.
result.why: Oil keeps the engine's moving metal parts from touching. A knock with low oil or an oil pressure light means parts may already be hitting each other. Running it this way, even for a few minutes, can destroy the engine.

causes.name: Low oil level
causes.clues: The dipstick reads low, the car is overdue for an oil change, or it burns or leaks oil.

causes.name: Oil pump or pickup problem
causes.clues: The oil level is fine but the pressure light still comes on.

causes.name: Worn engine bearings
causes.clues: A deep knock that follows engine speed.

you: Check the oil level with the engine off on level ground.
Look under the car for fresh oil drips.
shop: Oil pressure test with a gauge
Engine noise diagnosis with a stethoscope
Oil filter and drain inspection for metal particles

result.title: The engine may be misfiring badly
result.now: Pull over safely and turn the engine off. Have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you smell something like rotten eggs or burning, keep away from the exhaust. The catalytic converter may be overheating.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the temperature gauge is in the red, don't restart the engine.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means the engine is misfiring badly enough to cause damage. Unburned fuel can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter, and a rough-running engine can knock and shake. Driving on makes the damage worse.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: Shaking at idle and when accelerating, and the engine lost power.

causes.name: Fuel injector problem
causes.clues: A misfire on one cylinder that won't go away.

causes.name: Internal engine damage
causes.clues: A heavy knock along with the shaking.

you: Note whether the light flashes all the time or only under load.
shop: Ignition coil and spark plug check

result.title: The engine may be overheating, which can cause knocking and damage
result.now: Pull over safely and turn the engine off. Let it cool and have it towed or checked by a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see steam, don't open the hood until it stops, and never open the radiator cap while hot.
If the coolant is low once cool, a leak is likely. Topping it up doesn't fix the reason it overheated, so have it checked before driving.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the knock gets heavier, don't restart the engine.
result.why: An overheating engine is far more likely to knock because the fuel ignites too early in the hot cylinders. Running it hot can warp the cylinder head or blow the head gasket.

causes.name: Low coolant or a coolant leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, drips under the car, or a low reservoir.

causes.name: Failed fan, thermostat or water pump
causes.clues: It overheats in traffic or the gauge climbs quickly.

causes.name: Head gasket problem
causes.clues: White exhaust smoke or coolant that keeps disappearing.

you: Once fully cool, check the coolant reservoir level.
Look for drips under the front of the car.

result.title: This may be serious internal wear, such as a rod bearing
result.now: Stop driving and turn the engine off. Have it towed to a shop for diagnosis.
if: If the oil is low, adding oil won't undo the wear. Still don't drive it.

If the knock turns out to be a loose part outside the engine, like a torque converter bolt or flywheel, it can be a smaller repair. A shop will usually listen with a stethoscope and check oil pressure before deciding.
result.why: A deep knock that speeds up with the engine and is there at idle usually comes from inside the engine, often a worn connecting rod bearing. Each turn of the engine hammers the worn part, and it can fail suddenly and badly damage the engine.

causes.name: Worn connecting rod bearing
causes.clues: A deep, rhythmic knock that gets louder when you rev or let off the gas.

causes.name: Low oil or oil pressure
causes.clues: The oil was low, overdue for a change, or the oil light has flickered.

causes.name: Cracked flexplate or loose torque converter bolts (automatic)
causes.clues: The knock is at the back of the engine and changes when you shift into gear.

you: With the engine off, check the oil level.
Record a short video with sound at idle. It helps the shop.
shop: Oil analysis or filter inspection for metal

result.title: A knock only when cold can be piston slap or a lifter that quiets as oil pressure builds
result.now: Make sure the oil level is correct and the oil change is up to date, then book a check when convenient.
if: If the knock lasts after the engine is warm, or gets louder over time, get it checked soon.
If the oil pressure light flickers on startup, don't drive it. Have it checked first.
If the knock becomes deep and heavy, follows engine speed and is there when warm, stop driving and have it checked.
result.why: Pistons are slightly loose in their cylinders until they warm up and expand, which can cause a light knock for a minute or two. A lifter that loses oil overnight can also tap until oil pressure builds. Some engines make a mild cold-start noise for a long time, but only a technician listening to yours can tell whether it's that or early wear.

causes.name: Piston slap
causes.clues: A hollow knock for the first minute or two after a cold start, then quiet.

causes.name: Lifter bleeding down overnight
causes.clues: A tapping or clicking that fades within seconds of starting.

causes.name: Wrong oil thickness or overdue oil change
causes.clues: The noise started after an oil change, or it's past due.

you: Check the oil level and when the oil was last changed.
Note how long the knock lasts after starting.
shop: Check for known issues on your engine

result.title: A light tap or tick can come from the valve train, injectors or an exhaust leak
result.now: Check the oil level, and book a check when convenient.
if: If the oil is low, top it up with the right oil and have the car checked for leaks or oil burning.
If the ticking turns into a heavier knock, stop driving it and get it checked.
See our engine-ticking guide for more detail.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Many engines tick lightly, but a new or louder tick is worth having checked. Fuel injectors click as they open, and valves and lifters tap if oil is low or parts are worn. A small exhaust leak near the engine can also tick, especially when cold.

causes.name: Lifter or valve noise
causes.clues: A tap that matches engine speed, worse with low oil.

causes.name: Exhaust manifold leak
causes.clues: Louder when cold, and quieter as the engine warms.

causes.name: Normal fuel injector noise
causes.clues: A light, even ticking that's always been there, especially on direct-injection engines.

you: Check the oil level.
Note whether it's louder when cold.

result.title: The noise may not be from the engine at all
result.now: Book an inspection when convenient. Tell the shop the noise follows bumps or road speed, not engine speed.
if: If you hear clunks over bumps and the steering feels loose, stop driving it and have it checked before going further.
If something is dragging under the car, pull over safely and look, or have it checked before driving further.
If a pipe or heat shield is hanging down, or you smell exhaust inside the car, don't drive it until it's fixed.
result.why: A loose heat shield, exhaust hanger or suspension part can rattle or knock and sound like it's coming from the engine. If the noise changes with bumps or road speed rather than revving, the engine is less likely to be the source, but a technician should confirm it.

causes.name: Loose exhaust heat shield
causes.clues: A tinny rattle at certain engine speeds or over bumps.

causes.name: Broken exhaust hanger or loose exhaust part
causes.clues: A knock when going over bumps or when starting and stopping the engine.

causes.name: Worn suspension part
causes.clues: A clunk over bumps or when turning.

you: With the engine off and the exhaust cool, look under the car for a loose or hanging heat shield or pipe.
Rev the engine gently while parked. If the noise doesn't appear, the engine is less likely.
shop: Exhaust system and heat shield inspection

result.title: Have the knock diagnosed soon, before it gets worse
result.now: Check the oil level, limit driving to short, gentle trips, and have it checked within a few days.
if: If the oil pressure light comes on, the check engine light flashes, or the knock gets louder, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the knock only happens when accelerating, try a tank of the fuel your owner's manual recommends.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward the red or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Knocking ranges from mild fuel pinging to serious internal wear. Without knowing what it sounds like, it's safest to check the oil and have a technician listen soon.

causes.name: Fuel-related pinging
causes.clues: Only when accelerating or climbing hills.

causes.name: Low oil or valve train noise
causes.clues: The oil level is low, or the noise is a lighter tap.

causes.name: Internal wear (bearings)
causes.clues: A deep knock at idle that follows engine speed.

you: Check the oil level.
Record a short video with sound at idle and while revving gently. It helps the shop a lot.
shop: Code scan including knock sensor data

result.title: The fuel's octane may be too low for your engine
result.now: Check your owner's manual for the right fuel, and fill up with that grade at your next stop. Accelerate gently until then.
if: If the pinging is still there after a full tank of the right fuel, book a check.
If the check engine light comes on or the engine loses power, get it checked soon.
If the knock is deep and heavy, is there at idle, or the check engine light flashes, stop driving and have it checked. That isn't fuel pinging.
result.why: Pinging happens when fuel ignites too early in the cylinder. Engines built for higher-octane fuel are more prone to it on regular. Modern engines can adjust to reduce it, but heavy, sustained pinging can still damage pistons over time.

causes.name: Fuel octane lower than the engine needs
causes.clues: Your car needs or recommends premium, and you've been using regular.
causes.against: Less likely if your car is designed for regular and you've always used it.

causes.name: A tank of poor-quality fuel
causes.clues: It started right after a fill-up at an unfamiliar station.

causes.name: Heavy load or heat
causes.clues: Worse when towing, carrying a heavy load or in hot weather.

you: Check the fuel recommendation in your owner's manual or on the fuel door.
Run a full tank of the correct fuel and see if the pinging stops.
shop: Code scan and knock sensor data

result.title: Carbon buildup or a lean-running engine are possible causes
result.now: Book a check in the next couple of weeks. Until then, use the fuel your manual recommends and avoid flooring it up hills.
if: If the check engine light comes on or the pinging gets louder, get it checked soon.
If the engine also runs hot, have the cooling system checked too.
If the check engine light flashes or the engine shakes, pull over and stop.
result.why: Over time carbon builds up in the cylinders, raising compression and creating hot spots that make fuel ignite early. A vacuum leak, a clogged fuel injector or a faulty EGR valve can also make the engine run lean and hot, which leads to pinging.

causes.name: Carbon deposits in the cylinders
causes.clues: A high-mileage engine, lots of short trips, and pinging that built up slowly.

causes.name: Engine running lean (vacuum leak, fuel delivery)
causes.clues: A hissing sound, rough idle, or hesitation.

causes.name: EGR system problem
causes.clues: Pinging mostly at steady cruising or light acceleration.

you: Try a tank of the fuel grade your manual recommends.
Listen for hissing from the engine bay with the engine running.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim data

result.title: The engine computer may have detected knock, or the knock sensor may be faulty
result.now: Have the codes read within a few days. Use the fuel your manual recommends and accelerate gently until then.
if: If the light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over and stop.
If the engine also feels weak or slow, the computer may be protecting it. Get it checked sooner.
If the temperature gauge rises or the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: The knock sensor listens for pinging so the engine computer can adjust the timing and protect the engine. A steady check engine light with pinging can mean real knock it can't control, or a sensor that isn't doing its job. A shop will usually check the wiring and the data before replacing the sensor.

causes.name: Faulty knock sensor or wiring
causes.clues: A knock sensor code, and power feels down.

causes.name: Engine running lean
causes.clues: Lean or fuel trim codes, rough idle or hesitation.

causes.name: Carbon buildup
causes.clues: High mileage and pinging that built up over time.

you: Have the codes read. Many parts stores do this free.
shop: Fuel trim and vacuum leak check

q_how_hot.q: How hot is it running right now (or the last time it happened)?
q_how_hot.help: On most cars the needle sits near the middle once the engine is warm. Some cars have only a light: red usually means hot, blue means still cold.

opts.a: The gauge is in the red, a red temperature light or message is on, or there's steam from under the hood
Higher than normal, but not in the red
It ran hot earlier but is back to normal now
I'm not sure

q_signs.q: Do you notice any of these?
