opts.a: Steam, or a sweet, syrupy smell from under the hood
A temperature warning light or message on the dash
None of these. The gauge just looks higher than usual
I'm not sure

q_coolant_level.q: Once the engine has cooled for at least 30 minutes, where is the coolant level in the see-through overflow tank?
q_coolant_level.help: The overflow tank is a plastic bottle near the radiator with MIN and MAX (or COLD and FULL) marks. Only check it when the engine is cold, and don't open the radiator cap itself.

opts.a: Below the MIN mark, or the tank is empty
Between MIN and MAX
I haven't checked / I'm not sure

q_leak_signs.q: Do you see any clues about where the coolant is going?
q_leak_signs.help: Coolant is usually green, orange, pink, blue or yellow, feels slightly slimy, and smells sweet.

opts.a: Drips or a puddle under the front of the car, or wet, crusty spots on hoses or the radiator
Thick white exhaust smoke that smells sweet, milky oil on the dipstick, or bubbles in the coolant tank
No leak I can see anywhere
I'm not sure

q_when.q: The coolant is full. When does it run hot?

opts.a: Only when idling or in slow traffic. It cools down once I'm moving
Mostly at highway speed, climbing hills or towing
It climbs within a few minutes of starting, or the heater blows cold while the gauge is high
The needle jumps around, but the heater stays hot and there's no steam or smell
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be overheating. Stop as soon as it's safe
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, turn the engine off and let it cool for at least 30 minutes. Then call for a tow or a mobile mechanic rather than restarting it.
if: If you're stuck in traffic and can't pull over yet, turn the A/C off and the heater on full hot with the fan on high. This pulls some heat away from the engine until you can stop.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, pull over as soon as it's safe and shut it off right away.
If coolant is pouring out or you see flames or heavy smoke, get everyone away from the car.
If the check engine light starts flashing, the engine may be misfiring from the heat. Pull over when it's safe and turn it off.
result.why: A gauge in the red or steam from the engine usually means it can no longer get rid of heat fast enough. Every extra minute of running can warp the cylinder head or blow the head gasket, turning a simple hose or fan repair into a major engine repair.

causes.name: Low coolant from a leak
causes.clues: Steam, a sweet smell, a puddle under the front of the car, or an empty overflow tank once cool.

causes.name: Cooling fan not working
causes.clues: It got hot while idling or in traffic, not at highway speed.
causes.against: If it overheated at steady highway speed, the fan matters much less.

causes.name: Water pump, thermostat or burst hose
causes.clues: It got hot quickly, the heater blew cold, or there was a sudden cloud of steam.

causes.name: Head gasket failure
causes.clues: White, sweet-smelling exhaust smoke, or bubbles in the coolant tank.

you: Once fully cool, look at the overflow tank level and under the car for drips.
Note what you saw: steam, smells, smoke and how fast the gauge rose. It helps the shop.
shop: Cooling fan and fan relay test
Combustion gas (block) test for a head gasket leak

result.title: Check the coolant level before driving again
result.now: Don't drive it again until you've checked the coolant. With the engine fully cold, look at the overflow tank. If it's below MIN, top it up to the MAX line with the coolant type listed in your owner's manual, and have the cooling system checked before relying on the car.
if: If the tank was empty or very low, coolant is escaping somewhere. Have the leak found before driving, because it will usually overheat again.
If the level is between MIN and MAX, come back and answer the questions again with that. The cause is more likely a fan, thermostat or pump.
If you see a puddle, milky oil or sweet-smelling white exhaust smoke, don't drive it. Have it towed or checked where it is.
If the gauge ever reaches the red, a red temperature light comes on or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Low coolant is one of the most common reasons an engine runs hot, and it's easy to check safely once the engine is cold. The level tells you whether you're dealing with a leak or a problem with the fan, thermostat or pump.

causes.name: Low coolant
causes.clues: The tank is below MIN, or you've had to top it up before.
causes.against: A full tank makes this less likely, though air in the system can still cause trouble.

causes.name: Cooling fan problem
causes.clues: It runs hot in traffic and cools down when moving.

causes.name: Thermostat or water pump
causes.clues: The coolant is full but it still heats up quickly.

you: Check the overflow tank level with the engine cold.
Look under the front of the car for drips after it's been parked.
Watch whether the radiator fan runs once the engine is warm and idling.
shop: Code scan for temperature sensor and fan codes

result.title: Coolant may be leaking out, so the engine can't stay cool
result.now: Don't drive it until the leak has been checked. Once the engine is cold you can top up the overflow tank to MAX with the right coolant, but since it has already run hot, have a mobile mechanic look at it or have it towed.
if: If the gauge reaches the red, a red temperature light comes on or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off right away.
If coolant is pouring out or the tank empties quickly, don't start the engine again.
If the oil looks milky or there's sweet-smelling white exhaust smoke, mention it. It may point to an internal leak.
Once a shop has found the leak, they can tell you whether it's OK to drive the car to have it repaired.
result.why: The cooling system is sealed, so coolant usually only goes down when it's escaping somewhere. Once enough is lost, the engine can't move heat to the radiator and the temperature climbs. Fixing the leak early often means a hose, clamp or radiator repair rather than engine damage. A pressure test usually shows where it's coming from.

causes.name: Leaking radiator hose or clamp
causes.clues: Wet or crusty spots at hose ends, or a hose that feels soft and swollen.

causes.name: Leaking radiator
causes.clues: Drips from the very front of the car, or crusty colored deposits on the radiator.

causes.name: Leaking water pump
causes.clues: Drips or a crusty trail near the engine-belt end of the engine.

causes.name: Worn radiator or tank cap
causes.clues: Coolant residue around the cap, or the tank overflows when hot.

you: Put a piece of cardboard under the engine overnight to see where it drips.
Look for wet or crusty colored deposits on hoses, the radiator and around the engine.

result.title: Possible head gasket leak: coolant may be getting into the engine
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic test it.
if: If a test rules out a head gasket, a leaking intake gasket or EGR or oil cooler (on some engines) can cause similar signs, and those are usually less serious.
If the oil looks milky, don't start the engine at all. Coolant mixed into oil can quickly damage the bearings.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, don't restart it.
result.why: Sweet-smelling white exhaust smoke, milky oil, or bubbles in the coolant tank all suggest coolant and combustion gases are mixing inside the engine. Driving on it can spread the damage, but catching it early often keeps the repair smaller. A shop will usually run a combustion gas test and a pressure test before recommending head work.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: Bubbles in the coolant tank while running, white sweet-smelling exhaust, or coolant loss with no leak.

causes.name: Warped or cracked cylinder head
causes.clues: The engine was badly overheated recently.

causes.name: Leaking oil cooler or intake gasket
causes.clues: Milky oil without white exhaust smoke, on engines that have these parts.

you: With the engine off and cool, check the dipstick and under the oil filler cap for a milky, light-brown sludge.
shop: Combustion gas (block) test on the coolant

result.title: Coolant may be escaping somewhere you can't see
result.now: Don't drive it until the cooling system has been pressure-tested. Not seeing a leak doesn't mean the coolant is safe to top up and forget. Once the engine is cold you can top up the tank, but have a mobile mechanic test it or have it towed.
if: If the gauge reaches the red, a red temperature light comes on or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you notice white sweet-smelling exhaust smoke or milky oil, don't start the engine. That can point to an internal leak.
If the windows fog up or the passenger floor is damp, the heater core is a possible source. Mention it to the shop.
Once a shop has found where the coolant is going, they can tell you whether it's OK to drive the car to have it repaired.
result.why: Some leaks only happen when the system is hot and under pressure, and the coolant evaporates before it can drip. Others leak inside the car or inside the engine. A pressure test usually shows where it's going.

causes.name: Small leak that evaporates when hot
causes.clues: A sweet smell after driving, or crusty colored deposits on hoses or the water pump.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: A sweet smell inside, foggy windows, or a damp passenger floor.

causes.name: Internal leak (head gasket)
causes.clues: White exhaust smoke, milky oil, or bubbles in the coolant tank.
causes.against: If the oil and exhaust look normal, this is less likely.

you: Mark the coolant level and check how fast it drops.
Feel the passenger-side carpet for dampness.
Check the oil for a milky look.

result.title: The radiator fan may not be doing its job
result.now: Until the cooling fan has been checked, only drive if you can avoid idling and stop-and-go traffic, and watch the temperature gauge the whole time. Get it checked within the next few days.
if: If the gauge rises in traffic, turn the A/C off and the heater on full hot, and pull over and switch off before it reaches the red.
If the fan never spins at all with the engine hot, don't drive it in any traffic until it's fixed.
If you see steam or smell hot coolant, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: At speed, air rushes through the radiator by itself. When you're stopped, the fan has to pull that air through. Running hot only in traffic and cooling off once moving is a classic sign that the fan isn't working properly. A shop will usually check the fuse, relay and wiring before replacing the fan motor.

causes.name: Failed electric fan motor
causes.clues: The fan doesn't spin even with the engine hot or the A/C on.

causes.name: Fan relay, fuse or wiring fault
causes.clues: The fan works sometimes, or a check engine light is on.

causes.name: Worn fan clutch (belt-driven fans)
causes.clues: Common on trucks and older rear-wheel-drive cars. The fan spins freely by hand with the engine off and cold.

you: With the engine warm and idling and the A/C on, see whether the radiator fan is spinning. Keep hands and clothing clear, because electric fans can start on their own.
shop: Cooling fan motor and relay test
Code scan for fan circuit codes

result.title: The radiator or coolant flow may not be keeping up under load
result.now: Avoid towing, long climbs and high speeds, and get the cooling system checked within the next few days.
if: If the gauge climbs above its normal spot, ease off, and pull over and turn the engine off before it reaches the red.
If the front of the radiator is packed with leaves, bugs or dirt, gently rinsing it with a garden hose at low pressure (not a pressure washer) may help.
If you see steam, smell hot coolant or a red temperature light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Under heavy load the engine makes the most heat, so a cooling system that's only partly working shows up first on hills, on the highway, or when towing. Common culprits restrict how much coolant flows or how much heat the radiator can release.

causes.name: Partly clogged radiator
causes.clues: An older radiator, coolant that hasn't been changed in years, or debris blocking the front.

causes.name: Thermostat not opening fully
causes.clues: The gauge rises slowly under load but drops when you ease off.

causes.name: Weak water pump
causes.clues: A whine or grinding noise near the belt, or a coolant trail from the pump.

you: Look at the front of the radiator through the grille for debris.
Note when the gauge rises: hills, speed or towing.

result.title: Coolant may not be circulating: thermostat, water pump or trapped air
result.now: Don't drive it until it's checked. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If coolant was recently changed or added, trapped air may be the cause. A shop can bleed the air out.
If you hear grinding or see coolant dripping near the engine belt, the water pump may have failed. Mention it to the shop.
result.why: If the engine heats up within minutes, or the heater blows cold while the gauge is high, hot coolant isn't moving through the engine and heater the way it should. That will overheat the engine again on almost any drive.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck closed
causes.clues: The gauge rises quickly and the upper radiator hose stays cool while the engine is hot.

causes.name: Failed water pump
causes.clues: A grinding or whining noise, or coolant leaking from near the belt.

causes.name: Air trapped in the cooling system
causes.clues: It started after coolant work, or you hear gurgling behind the dash.

you: Note whether the problem started right after any coolant service or repair.
shop: Hose temperature comparison with an infrared thermometer

result.title: It may be a faulty temperature sensor or gauge, not real overheating
result.now: Get the temperature sensor and gauge checked within the next few days. Until a shop confirms the engine isn't really overheating, treat any high reading as real: watch for steam, smells or a heater that turns cold, and pull over if the needle reaches the red.
if: If a temperature warning light comes on, you see steam, or the heater suddenly blows cold, treat it as real overheating. Pull over and turn the engine off.
If the check engine light is on, a code scan can quickly point to the sensor.
result.why: A real overheating engine usually shows other signs, like steam, a sweet smell or a heater that turns cold. A needle that jumps around while everything else seems normal often means the sensor or its wiring is sending a bad signal. A shop can compare it with the real temperature.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: The needle jumps suddenly, or a check engine light is on.

causes.name: Loose or corroded sensor wiring
causes.clues: It changes over bumps or in wet weather.

causes.name: Low coolant around the sensor
causes.clues: The overflow tank is low, which can leave the sensor in an air pocket.
causes.against: If the coolant is full, this is less likely.

you: Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
Note whether the heater stays hot when the needle reads high.
shop: Code scan and live temperature data
Infrared temperature check of the engine

result.title: Treat it as possible overheating until it's checked
result.now: Before driving again, check the coolant level with the engine cold. Then have the cooling system checked within the next few days.
if: If the gauge reaches the red, a temperature light comes on, or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the coolant tank is low, have the cooling system checked before driving. Low coolant usually means a leak, even if you can't see one.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, pull over and turn it off right away.
result.why: Without clear signs it's hard to say whether the engine is truly overheating. Checking the coolant and getting a quick cooling system test is the safest way to avoid serious engine damage.

causes.name: Low coolant
causes.clues: One of the most common causes of running hot.

causes.name: Cooling fan problem
causes.clues: It runs hotter in traffic.

causes.name: Thermostat or sensor fault
causes.clues: The gauge moves oddly or rises quickly.

you: Check the coolant level when cold.
Take a photo of the gauge when it reads high, so the shop knows what you saw.
shop: Code scan and live temperature data

q_what_happens.q: Which best describes what the engine is doing?
q_what_happens.help: Idle speed is shown on the tachometer (the RPM gauge). A warm engine usually idles somewhere under 1,000 RPM, but it varies by car.

opts.a: The car keeps speeding up when I lift off the gas, or the gas pedal sticks or comes up slowly
It idles high only for the first minute or two after a cold start, then settles down
It stays high even after the engine is fully warmed up
The RPM needle rises and falls by itself while stopped (hunting or surging)
I'm not sure

q_warm_clues.help: These clues separate a leak, a sensor problem and a car that simply needs to relearn its idle.

opts.a: It started right after the battery was disconnected or replaced, or the throttle was cleaned
I hear a hiss or whistle from under the hood, or the check engine light is on
The temperature gauge stays low or the heater is weak
The idle also goes up and down by itself
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: The throttle or gas pedal may be sticking open
result.now: Don't drive it. With the engine off, check that the floor mat isn't pushing on or catching the gas pedal. If the mat isn't the cause, have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the car speeds up on its own while you're driving, shift to Neutral, brake firmly and steer to a safe place, then turn the engine off.
If a loose or extra floor mat was trapping the pedal, remove it, secure the correct mat with its clips, and check that the pedal now springs back fully before using the car.
result.why: An engine that keeps revving when you lift your foot means the throttle isn't closing. That can make the car hard to slow down or stop, so it's a safety problem, not just an annoyance.

causes.name: Floor mat pushing on or trapping the gas pedal
causes.clues: An extra mat stacked on top of another, a mat that slides forward, or a pedal that frees up when you move the mat.
causes.against: If the pedal sticks with the mat removed, look elsewhere.

causes.name: Sticking gas pedal or throttle body
causes.clues: The pedal feels gritty or slow to return, or the problem is worse in cold or damp weather.

causes.name: Electronic throttle or pedal sensor fault
causes.clues: A check engine light or a reduced power message along with the revving.

you: With the engine off, press the gas pedal and let go. It should snap back smoothly.
Make sure there's only one floor mat on the driver's side and it's held by its clips.
Check for open recalls on your vehicle using your VIN.
shop: Code scan and live pedal and throttle position data

result.title: This sounds like the normal fast idle of a cold engine
result.now: If the idle drops back to normal within a few minutes, there's usually nothing to repair. Keep an eye on it.
if: If the idle stays high after the temperature gauge reaches its normal spot, have it checked.
If the idle is only a little higher with the A/C or defroster on, that's normal too. The engine raises it to carry the extra load.
If the car pushes forward when you lift off the gas, or the gas pedal sticks or comes up slowly, don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: A cold engine runs a higher idle on purpose. It helps the engine run smoothly and warms up the parts that clean the exhaust faster. Once warm, the computer brings the idle back down.

causes.name: Normal cold-start fast idle
causes.clues: Higher RPM for a minute or two after starting, especially on cold mornings, then it settles.
causes.against: If it never settles, something else is going on.

causes.name: Normal idle boost from A/C or electrical load
causes.clues: The idle rises slightly when you turn on the A/C, defroster or headlights.

you: Watch the tachometer as the engine warms up and note how long the high idle lasts.
Compare idle with the A/C on and off.
shop: Code scan and idle speed check if it doesn't settle

result.title: The engine computer may need to relearn its idle
result.now: Let the engine idle in Park until it's fully warm with everything switched off, then drive normally for a few days. Many cars relearn the idle on their own.
if: If the idle is still high after a few days of normal driving, a shop can run the idle relearn procedure for your vehicle.
If the high idle comes with a check engine light, get the code read.
If the car pushes forward when you lift off the gas or is hard to slow down, stop driving it and have it checked.
result.why: Disconnecting the battery or cleaning the throttle can erase what the engine computer learned about holding a steady idle. Until it relearns, the idle can sit high or wander.

causes.name: Lost idle settings after a battery disconnect
causes.clues: The problem started right after a battery change, jump start or disconnect.

causes.name: Throttle cleaned without a relearn
causes.clues: It started right after the throttle body was cleaned.

you: Check your owner's manual for an idle relearn step after battery disconnection.
Note whether the idle improves over a few drives.
shop: Idle relearn procedure with a scan tool

result.title: A vacuum leak is a possible cause
result.now: Have the check engine code read, then book a vacuum leak test when convenient.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine runs very rough, stop driving and have it checked.
If you find a hose that has popped off, a shop can usually fix it quickly.
If the brake pedal feels hard or needs more force than usual, a brake booster hose may be leaking. Have it checked before driving further.
If the car pushes forward when you lift off the gas, stop driving it and have it towed.
result.why: The engine sets idle by controlling how much air gets in. A cracked hose or leaking gasket lets in extra air the computer can't control, so the idle rises. A hiss is often the leak itself. A shop will usually smoke-test the intake to find the leak before replacing parts.

causes.name: Cracked, split or disconnected vacuum hose
causes.clues: A hiss or whistle at idle, or an older car with brittle rubber hoses.

causes.name: Leaking intake gasket or air intake boot
causes.clues: A lean-mixture check engine code, or a rough idle along with the high idle.

causes.name: Leaking brake booster hose or PCV valve
causes.clues: The idle changes when you press the brake pedal.

you: With the engine idling, listen around the top of the engine for a hiss. Keep hands away from belts and the fan.
Have the check engine code read. Many auto parts stores do this free.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim data

result.title: The engine may think it's still cold
result.now: Book a check when convenient. Mention that the temperature gauge stays low or the heater is weak.
if: If the temperature gauge ever climbs into the red, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the check engine light is on, get the code read. It can point toward the sensor or thermostat circuit, and a shop will usually confirm with live data before replacing parts.
If the coolant is low, have the cooling system checked for a leak soon. Low coolant can lead to overheating.
result.why: The computer keeps a fast idle until it sees the engine is warm. A thermostat stuck open keeps the engine from warming up, and a faulty temperature sensor can report cold when it isn't. Either way the idle stays high.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck open
causes.clues: The temperature gauge stays low on the highway, and the heater is lukewarm.
causes.against: If the gauge reads normal and the heater is hot, the thermostat is probably fine.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: A check engine light, worse fuel economy, or a gauge that reads oddly.

causes.name: Low coolant
causes.clues: The coolant reservoir is below the MIN line.

you: With the engine cold, check the coolant reservoir level.
Note where the temperature gauge sits after 15 minutes of driving.
shop: Code scan and live coolant temperature data

result.title: The idle control system may be dirty or faulty
result.now: Book a check when convenient. Note whether the surging happens warm or cold, and with the A/C on or off.
if: If the engine stalls when you slow down or come to a stop, avoid driving it until it's checked. When the engine dies, steering and braking take much more effort.
If you also hear a hiss, a vacuum leak is the more likely cause.
If the car pushes forward when you lift off the gas, stop driving it and have it towed.
result.why: The engine uses a throttle valve or a small idle air valve to hold a steady idle. When carbon builds up or a part starts failing, the computer keeps overcorrecting and the RPM hunts up and down.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body
causes.clues: Black buildup around the throttle plate, and an idle that has slowly gotten worse.

causes.name: Faulty idle air control valve (older cars)
causes.clues: The surging comes and goes, and may be worse when cold.
causes.against: Many newer cars have no separate idle valve.

causes.name: Small vacuum leak
causes.clues: A faint hiss, or a check engine code for a lean mixture.

you: Watch the tachometer at idle and note how far it swings.
Have the check engine code read if the light is on.

result.title: A high idle that won't settle needs a quick check
result.now: Have the check engine code read if the light is on, and book an inspection when convenient.
if: If the car pushes forward when you lift off the gas, or the pedal sticks, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the temperature gauge stays low, mention it. It can point to a thermostat or sensor.
If the check engine light flashes or the engine shakes, pull over safely and turn it off.
result.why: A high idle usually comes from extra air getting in, a sensor telling the computer the engine is cold, or an idle control part that isn't working. A technician can tell which with a scan tool and a smoke test.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: A hiss under the hood.

causes.name: Temperature sensor or thermostat
causes.clues: A low temperature gauge or weak heat.

causes.name: Dirty or faulty throttle body
causes.clues: The idle goes up and down.

you: Note the RPM at idle once warm, with the A/C off.
Record a short video of the tachometer at idle for the shop.

q_signs.q: Do you notice any of these along with the sputtering?
q_signs.help: The check engine light is the orange engine-shaped light on the dash. Flashing means a misfire is happening right now and is serious.

opts.a: The check engine light is flashing, or the engine shakes violently
A strong smell of raw fuel
The temperature gauge is high, or there's white smoke with a sweet smell
The check engine light is on, but steady (not flashing)
None of these
I'm not sure

q_pattern.q: When does it sputter or misfire?

opts.a: All the time, even at idle: a steady shake or putt-putt rhythm
Mainly when accelerating, climbing a hill or carrying a load
Mostly in rain or damp weather, or on cold starts
It comes and goes, and sometimes it nearly stalls
Mostly when the fuel tank is low
I'm not sure

q_load.help: These clues separate an ignition problem from a fuel problem.

opts.a: The spark plugs are old or I don't know when they were last changed
It started right after I filled up with fuel
It feels weak and starved, worse at highway speed or uphill
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: A severe misfire may be happening. Stop driving to avoid damage
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you can't stop right away, ease off the gas, avoid hard acceleration and get off the road as soon as it's safe.
If you see smoke, smell burning, or notice a glow under the car, get everyone out and away from the vehicle.
If the temperature gauge is high or the oil pressure light is on, don't restart the engine.
result.why: A flashing check engine light means misfires are severe enough to send unburned fuel into the exhaust. That fuel burns inside the catalytic converter and can overheat it, destroying it and creating a fire risk. Violent shaking usually means at least one cylinder has stopped working.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: Sudden onset, and the engine feels like it's running on fewer cylinders.

causes.name: Fuel injector stuck open or not firing
causes.clues: A fuel smell from the exhaust, or a misfire on one cylinder that doesn't move when coils are swapped.

causes.name: Mechanical damage, like a burnt valve or low compression
causes.clues: A ticking or tapping noise, or the misfire started after overheating.
causes.against: Less common than ignition problems.

shop: Code scan and misfire counts by cylinder

result.title: A fuel leak or a stuck injector is possible. Don't drive it
result.now: Pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car. Have it towed.
if: If you see fuel dripping or pooling, move well away and call for help. Don't let anyone smoke nearby.
If the smell was brief and only right after refueling, a loose fuel cap is possible. But with the engine sputtering too, still have it checked before driving.
result.why: Sputtering together with a strong fuel smell can mean fuel is leaking onto the engine, or an injector is dumping too much fuel into a cylinder. Either way, raw fuel near hot engine and exhaust parts is a fire risk.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line, rail or injector seal
causes.clues: Wet spots on top of the engine or under the car.

causes.name: Fuel injector stuck open
causes.clues: The smell comes from the exhaust, and the engine runs very rough.

causes.name: Misfire sending unburned fuel into the exhaust
causes.clues: A flashing or steady check engine light.

you: From a safe distance, look for wet spots under the car.

result.title: Coolant may be getting into the engine, often from a head gasket problem
result.now: Pull over and turn the engine off. Don't open the radiator cap while it's hot. Have the car towed.
if: If the coolant level is low once the engine is fully cold, that supports a coolant leak. Still don't drive it until it's checked.
If you see steam or smoke from under the hood, step away from the car.
result.why: A misfire with overheating or sweet-smelling white smoke points to coolant leaking into a cylinder. Coolant doesn't burn, so that cylinder misfires. Driving an overheating engine can warp or crack major parts quickly.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: White smoke that smells sweet, coolant level dropping, overheating.

causes.name: Cracked cylinder head
causes.clues: The engine overheated badly before the misfire started.
causes.against: Less common than a head gasket.

causes.name: Overheating from a cooling system failure, causing misfires
causes.clues: A coolant leak, a broken belt, or a fan that isn't running.

you: Once the engine is fully cold, check the coolant level in the overflow tank.

result.title: One cylinder may not be firing, often from a coil or plug problem
result.now: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Otherwise: Have it checked within the next few days. Keep trips short and gentle until then.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the shaking gets much worse, pull over and stop driving.
If there's a ticking or tapping noise with the misfire, mention it. It may point to a valve or mechanical problem.
If you smell raw fuel or burning, see smoke, or the temperature gauge rises, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the engine nearly stalls or cuts out, stop driving it and have it checked.
result.why: A steady miss you can feel even at idle usually means one cylinder isn't firing at all. Common reasons are a failed ignition coil or spark plug, and a shop will usually read the code and swap the coil between cylinders to confirm before replacing parts. Driving on it for long wastes fuel and can damage the catalytic converter.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil
causes.clues: Sudden onset, a steady check engine light, and a code that names one cylinder.

causes.name: Worn or fouled spark plug
causes.clues: Plugs that are overdue, or oil found in the spark plug well.

causes.name: Clogged or failed fuel injector
causes.clues: The misfire stays on the same cylinder after the coil is swapped.

causes.name: Low compression in one cylinder
causes.clues: A ticking noise, or the misfire continues after coils and plugs are replaced.
causes.against: Less common than coil or plug problems.

you: Have the check engine code read. Many parts stores do this free.
shop: Code scan and misfire counts by cylinder
Injector and compression tests if needed

result.title: Possibly worn spark plugs or a weakening ignition coil
result.now: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Otherwise: Have the ignition system checked within the next few days, and avoid hard acceleration until then.
if: If the plugs are overdue, new plugs are a common fix, but have the codes read and the coils checked too so the right part gets replaced.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
If you smell raw fuel or the engine nearly stalls, stop driving it and have it checked.
result.why: Under load, the engine needs a stronger spark to light the fuel. Worn plugs or a tired coil can get by at idle but miss when you accelerate, which feels like sputtering or jerking. Misfires that are left alone tend to get worse.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs
causes.clues: The plugs haven't been changed in a long time.

causes.name: Weak ignition coil or cracked coil boot
causes.clues: The misfire is worse under load, and the code names one cylinder.

causes.name: Worn spark plug wires (older cars)
causes.clues: Visible cracks on the wires, or sparking you can see in the dark.
causes.against: Many newer cars have no plug wires.

you: Check your maintenance records for the last spark plug change.
Have the check engine code read if the light is on.

result.title: Damp or cold-start misfires often point to worn ignition parts
result.now: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Otherwise: Book an ignition system check when convenient. Try to bring it in on a damp day or for a cold start so the shop can see it happen.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over and stop driving.
If it only happens on the first cold start and clears in a minute, mention whether the car is driven mostly on short trips.
result.why: Moisture lets spark escape through cracked coil boots, plug wires or dirty plugs before it reaches the cylinder. Cold engines are also harder to fire, so weak ignition parts show up first in damp or cold conditions.

causes.name: Cracked coil boots or spark plug wires
causes.clues: Worse on rainy or foggy days, or after washing the engine.

causes.name: Worn or fouled spark plugs
causes.clues: Plugs that are overdue, or a car used mostly for short trips.

causes.name: Water collecting around the spark plugs
causes.clues: A clogged drain at the base of the windshield, or water pooling on top of the engine.

you: Note the weather and engine temperature each time it happens.
shop: Coil boot and plug wire inspection

result.title: The engine may not be getting enough fuel
result.now: Have it checked within the next few days. Avoid long trips and highways until then.
if: If it stalls while driving, stop driving it and have it towed. Losing power in traffic is dangerous.
If the check engine light comes on, have the code read. A lean code points toward fuel or air problems.
If you smell raw fuel, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: Sputtering that comes and goes, or that's worse when you need more power, can mean fuel supply is falling short. A weak pump or clogged filter may keep up at light throttle and then run short when demand rises. Left alone, it can leave you stranded. A shop will usually test fuel pressure and volume before replacing the pump.

causes.name: Weak or failing fuel pump
causes.clues: Worse at highway speed, uphill, or with a low tank. A whine from the rear of the car.

causes.name: Clogged fuel filter
causes.clues: Higher mileage and no record of a filter change.

causes.name: Dirty mass airflow sensor or vacuum leak
causes.clues: A rough idle, hissing under the hood, or a lean code.

you: Note whether it's worse with a low tank.
Listen for a whine from the back of the car.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim data

result.title: The engine may be running short of fuel when the tank is low
result.now: Keep the tank at least a quarter full and see if the sputtering stops.
if: If it still sputters with a fuller tank, the fuel pump or filter may need checking. Book a check within a few days.
If it stalls while driving, stop driving it and have it checked before using it again.
If you smell raw fuel, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and have it checked before driving.
result.why: On turns, hills or hard braking, fuel sloshes away from the pump's pickup when the tank is low, and the engine briefly runs short. A pump that's getting weak shows this sooner. Keeping more fuel in the tank also helps the pump stay cool.

causes.name: Fuel sloshing away from the pickup
causes.clues: Only happens below a quarter tank, especially on curves or hills.

causes.name: Weakening fuel pump
causes.clues: A whine from the rear, or sputtering at highway speed too.

causes.name: Fuel gauge reading higher than the actual level
causes.clues: You've run out before when the gauge showed fuel left.

you: Keep the tank above a quarter for a week and note if the problem goes away.

result.title: You may have a tank of poor-quality fuel or the wrong grade
result.now: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Otherwise: Check your receipt for the right fuel grade, drive gently, and refill with fresh fuel from a busy station once the tank is low.
if: If you put diesel in a gas car (or gas in a diesel), stop driving it right away and have it towed. The tank will need to be drained.
If the sputtering doesn't improve after fresh fuel, have it checked. If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
If you smell raw fuel or the engine shakes hard, pull over and stop driving.
result.why: Water or dirt in the fuel, makes the engine run rough and sputter. When the problem starts right after filling up, the fuel is a likely link.

causes.name: Water or contamination in the fuel
causes.clues: It started right after filling up.

causes.name: Lower octane than your engine requires
causes.clues: Your manual says premium is required and you used regular. You may hear pinging.

you: Check the fuel grade on your receipt against your owner's manual.

result.title: Get the codes read, then have the misfire diagnosed
result.now: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Otherwise: Have the check engine codes read (many parts stores do this free), then book a check soon and describe when the sputtering happens.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over and stop driving.
If it sputters at idle all the time or nearly stalls, get it checked within a few days.
If you smell raw fuel, see smoke or the temperature gauge rises, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Misfires come from spark, fuel or compression problems. Stored codes often name the cylinder involved, which narrows it down quickly. A note of when it happens helps the shop find the cause without guessing.

causes.name: Ignition problem (plugs, coils, wires)
causes.clues: A common cause of misfires.

causes.name: Fuel delivery problem
causes.clues: Sputtering under load or with a low tank.

causes.name: Vacuum leak or sensor problem
causes.clues: A rough idle or hissing sound.

you: Keep a note of when it happens: cold or warm, idle or accelerating, weather, fuel level.

q_fuel_type.q: Could the wrong type of fuel have gone in?
q_fuel_type.help: Check your receipt or the pump you used.

opts.a: Yes: diesel in a gas car, or gas in a diesel
No, the right type, but maybe poor quality or the wrong grade
I'm not sure

result.title: The wrong type of fuel went in
result.now: Don’t start the engine. If it’s running, pull over when it’s safe and turn it off. Don’t restart it. Have it towed: the tank will need to be drained.
if: If you smell raw fuel, keep sparks and flames away and move away from the car.
If you realize at the pump before starting the engine, leave it off and ask the station for help moving the car.
result.why: Diesel in a gas engine, or gas in a diesel, doesn't burn the way the engine is built for. Running it can damage the fuel system and engine, so the tank and fuel lines need to be drained before it's started again.

causes.name: Diesel in a gas car
causes.clues: Heavy smoke, very rough running or the engine dying soon after filling up.

causes.name: Gas in a diesel
causes.clues: Knocking, loss of power or the engine stopping soon after filling up.

you: Check your receipt and the pump you used to confirm which fuel went in.
shop: Drain and flush the tank and fuel lines

q_warning.q: Right before or as it died, did you notice any of these?

opts.a: Temperature gauge in the red, steam, or a hot smell
Oil pressure light, or loud knocking from the engine
Battery light on, or lights and gauges dimmed or flickered
Sputtering, shaking, loss of power, or a flashing check engine light
Nothing like that. It just shut off
I'm not sure
Suddenly, like flipping a switch, with no sputter
It sputtered, surged or lost power first
When I hit a bump or my knee bumped the key or key ring
I'm not sure

q_fuel.q: What was the fuel gauge showing?

opts.a: Near empty, or the low fuel light was on
A quarter tank or more
I'm not sure
Yes, it restarts and runs normally, sometimes only after cooling down
No, it cranks but won't start
No, it won't crank and the dash went dark
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may have overheated and shut down
result.now: Don't restart it. Let it cool for at least 30 minutes with the hood closed, then have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see coolant leaking or the reservoir is empty once cool, a leak or failed hose is likely. Mention it when you call.
Never open the radiator cap on a hot engine. Hot coolant can spray out.
If the oil pressure light came on or the engine knocked, tell the shop. Don't restart it.
result.why: An engine that gets hot enough to stall can warp or crack parts. Restarting it, or driving even a short distance, can turn a hose or thermostat repair into a major engine repair.

causes.name: Coolant leak or low coolant
causes.clues: A sweet smell, steam, or a puddle under the front of the car.

causes.name: Failed cooling fan or water pump
causes.clues: It overheated in traffic or with the A/C on.

causes.name: Head gasket damage
causes.clues: White exhaust smoke or coolant loss with no visible leak.

you: Once fully cool, check the coolant reservoir level.
Look for leaks under the car.
shop: Cooling fan and water pump check

result.title: The engine may have lost oil pressure
result.now: Don't restart it. Check the oil level on the dipstick, then have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the oil is very low, adding oil won't undo any damage. Have it checked before running it.
If the engine was knocking loudly before it stopped, it may be seriously damaged.
result.why: Oil keeps metal parts from grinding against each other. When pressure drops, damage happens fast, and an engine that stalls with knocking may have seized. Restarting it can make the damage much worse.

causes.name: Very low oil level
causes.clues: An overdue oil change, oil leaks, or burning oil smell.

causes.name: Failed oil pump or blocked oil pickup
causes.clues: The oil level is fine but the light came on.

causes.name: Internal engine damage
causes.clues: Loud knocking before it died.

you: Check the oil level on the dipstick with the engine off.
shop: Oil pressure test with a gauge
Check whether the engine turns freely by hand

result.title: The charging system may have failed and let the battery run down
result.now: Don't count on it restarting and running. Have it towed to a shop or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If a jump gets it running, it will likely die again within minutes. Don't drive it in traffic.
If you smelled burning rubber or heard a squeal first, the drive belt may have broken.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the hood, get everyone out and away from the car.
result.why: If the alternator stops charging, the car runs on the battery alone. Lights dim, gauges act up, and then the engine shuts off once the battery is too low to keep it running. A shop will usually test the alternator, belt and cables before replacing anything.

causes.name: Failed alternator
causes.clues: The battery light came on before it died.

causes.name: Broken or slipping drive belt
causes.clues: Squealing, a burning rubber smell, or heavy steering.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery or charging cable
causes.clues: Flickering lights, or it happened after a bump.

you: Look at the drive belt with the engine off.
Check the battery clamps for looseness or buildup.

result.title: A worn ignition switch may be cutting power
result.now: Don't drive it until the ignition switch is checked. Have it towed, and check your VIN for open safety recalls.
if: If there's an open recall, the dealer will fix it at no charge.
Until it's fixed, keep only the car key on the ring. A heavy key ring makes this worse.
result.why: A worn ignition switch can slip from Run to Accessory or Off when it's jostled. The engine shuts off, and on some cars the airbags may be disabled too. Some vehicles have had recalls for exactly this.

causes.name: Worn ignition switch
causes.clues: It happens over bumps or when the key is touched.

causes.name: Heavy key ring pulling on the key
causes.clues: Lots of keys or accessories hanging from the car key.

causes.name: Loose wiring connection at the switch
causes.clues: Dash lights flicker over bumps.

you: Ask a dealer for your brand to confirm which recalls are still open for your VIN.
Remove extra keys from the ring.

result.title: It may have run out of fuel
result.now: Get somewhere safe, add a few gallons of fuel, and try to restart. It may need several tries of a few seconds each to refill the fuel lines.
if: If the check engine light was flashing before it died, don't restart it; have it towed.
If it still won't start after adding fuel, the fuel pump may have been damaged. Have it towed.
If the gauge showed fuel left when it died, have the gauge checked so it doesn't happen again.
If it stalls again with fuel in the tank, don't rely on it in traffic. Have it checked before driving again.
If you smell raw fuel, don't try to restart it.
result.why: Sputtering and surging before a stall is a common sign of fuel starvation. When the tank is low, hard turns, hills or braking can slosh fuel away from the pickup and the engine starves.

causes.name: Out of fuel
causes.clues: The gauge was near empty or the low fuel light was on.

causes.name: Inaccurate fuel gauge
causes.clues: The gauge has read oddly before.

causes.name: Fuel pump struggling on a low tank
causes.clues: It sputters at low fuel levels even when there's some left.

you: Add fuel and try again.
Note how many miles you drove since the last fill-up.

result.title: Possibly a fuel delivery problem or a severe misfire
result.now: Don't drive it until it's checked. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic who can scan for trouble codes.
if: If the check engine light was flashing, the catalytic converter can be damaged by running it. Don't keep trying to drive it.
If you smell raw fuel, keep sparks and flames away and don't restart it.
result.why: Sputtering, surging or losing power before a stall usually means the engine wasn't getting enough fuel or wasn't burning it properly. A weak fuel pump, a clogged filter or a bad sensor are common causes, and they tend to get worse. A shop will usually check codes and fuel pressure before replacing the pump.

causes.name: Weak fuel pump or clogged fuel filter
causes.clues: Worse going uphill or under hard acceleration, with no flashing light.

causes.name: Faulty airflow or throttle sensor
causes.clues: A steady check engine light, surging, or a rough idle.

causes.name: Severe misfire from an ignition coil or plugs
causes.clues: A flashing check engine light and shaking.

you: Note whether the check engine light was on or flashing.
Listen for the brief fuel pump hum from the rear when you turn the key to On.
shop: Code scan and live sensor data
Ignition coil and spark plug check

result.title: A failing sensor or electrical connection may be cutting the engine
result.now: Don't rely on it until it's diagnosed. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic scan for trouble codes, even if no warning light is on.
if: If you're stuck somewhere unsafe and it restarts, move it only as far as a safe spot, then call for a tow.
If it only restarts after cooling down, tell the shop. That pattern often points to a heat-sensitive sensor.
result.why: An engine that cuts out instantly with no sputter has usually lost spark or the signal that controls it. A crankshaft position sensor that fails when hot is a common cause, and a shop will usually check codes and the sensor signal before replacing it. These problems come and go, so it may run fine for days before cutting out again.

causes.name: Failing crankshaft or camshaft position sensor
causes.clues: It dies suddenly when warm and restarts after cooling.

causes.name: Loose wiring, ground or fuel pump relay
causes.clues: It happens over bumps, or it restarts right away.

causes.name: Worn ignition switch
causes.clues: The dash lights blink off as it dies.

you: Write down when it happens: warm or cold, speed, bumps.
Ask a dealer for your brand to confirm which recalls are still open for your VIN.
shop: Code scan, including stored and pending codes
Crank and cam sensor signal test

result.title: A failed fuel pump or crankshaft sensor is possible
result.now: Stop cranking it. Have the car towed to a shop.
if: If a key or security light is flashing, try your spare key. The anti-theft system can block the engine from running.
If it restarts after sitting, don't count on it. These parts often fail completely soon after.
If you smell raw fuel, stop cranking and keep away from the car.
result.why: If the engine cranks normally but won't fire after dying on the road, it has usually lost fuel or spark. A fuel pump that stopped running and a crankshaft sensor that stopped reporting are common causes, and a shop will usually check fuses, relays and codes first.

causes.name: Failed fuel pump
causes.clues: No hum from the rear when you turn the key to On.

causes.name: Failed crankshaft position sensor
causes.clues: It died suddenly with no sputter.

causes.name: Fuel pump relay or fuse
causes.clues: Sudden failure. These are quick to check first.

you: Listen for the fuel pump hum.
Look for a flashing key or security light.
shop: Code scan for crank and cam sensor codes
Fuel pump relay and fuse check

result.title: The car lost electrical power, possibly at the battery connection
result.now: Get to safety, then check whether a battery cable is loose or has come off. If you can't fix it on the spot, have it towed.
if: If tightening a loose clamp brings everything back, have the cables and fuses checked before you rely on the car again.
If you smell burning, don't touch the wiring. Step away and call for help.
result.why: When the engine and dash both go dead at once, the car has lost its main power. A loose or corroded battery cable is a common cause. A blown main fuse or a failed ignition switch can do the same.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery cable
causes.clues: A clamp that moves by hand, or it happened over a bump.

causes.name: Blown main fuse or fusible link
causes.clues: Cables are tight but there's still no power.

causes.name: Failed ignition switch
causes.clues: Power comes and goes when you move the key.

you: With the engine off, check that both battery clamps are tight.

result.title: Have it diagnosed before you drive it again
result.now: Have the car towed to a shop or call a mobile mechanic to scan it where it sits.
if: If a warning light came on, tell the shop which one. It narrows things down quickly.
If you smell fuel or burning, don't try to restart it.
result.why: An engine that shuts off while moving can stall again at a worse moment, like in an intersection or on a highway. The cause can be fuel, spark, electrical or overheating, and a scan plus a few tests will usually show which.

causes.name: Fuel delivery problem
causes.clues: Sputtering or loss of power first.

causes.name: Sensor or ignition failure
causes.clues: It cut out suddenly with no warning.

causes.name: Charging system failure
causes.clues: The battery light came on or the lights dimmed.

you: Write down what happened just before it died.
Check your VIN for open recalls.

q_warning.q: Do you notice any of these along with the ticking?
q_warning.help: The oil pressure light usually looks like a red oil can with a drip. A "knock" is a deeper, heavier thud than a tick, more like a hammer than a pen tapping.

opts.a: The red oil pressure light is on or flickering
It's become a deep, heavy knock that gets louder when I press the gas
The check engine light is flashing, or the engine is shaking
None of these, just the ticking
I'm not sure

q_oil_level.q: What does the oil dipstick show?
q_oil_level.help: Park on level ground, turn the engine off and wait a few minutes. Pull the dipstick (usually a yellow or orange handle), wipe it, push it back in fully, then pull it out and read where the oil line sits between the two marks. Some newer cars show the oil level on the dash instead.

opts.a: It's below the lower mark, or barely touching it
It's between the marks
I haven't checked yet
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When is the ticking most noticeable?

opts.a: Mostly right after a cold start, and it fades within a few minutes
A light, fast tick at idle, like a sewing machine, that has always been there
It's louder when I accelerate or climb a hill
Only while the car is moving, and it speeds up with road speed, not engine speed
All the time, warm or cold, and it speeds up when I rev the engine
I'm not sure

q_other_signs.q: Does anything else come with the ticking?

opts.a: The engine runs rough, or the check engine light is on (steady)
I smell exhaust under the hood, or hear a puffing sound
No, just a steady tick from the top of the engine
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may not be getting enough oil. Shut it off
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe, shut the engine off and check the oil level. Don't restart it until you know the oil is full. If the light stays on with full oil, have it towed.
if: If the oil was very low and adding oil turns the light off, have it checked before relying on the car again. Running low on oil can damage the engine, and the oil went somewhere.
If the ticking turns into a knock, don't restart the engine at all.
If the light stays on or flickers after the oil reads full, don't restart the engine.
If you see smoke or smell burning oil from under the hood, keep away from the engine and let it cool.
result.why: The oil pressure light means oil isn't being pushed through the engine with enough force. Ticking along with it can mean the top of the engine is running short of oil. Running the engine like this can damage it within minutes.

causes.name: Very low oil level
causes.clues: An oil change is overdue, you've seen oil spots under the car, or the engine burns oil.
causes.against: If the dipstick reads full, low oil isn't the cause.

causes.name: Oil pump or oil pickup problem
causes.clues: The oil is full but the light stays on, especially at idle when warm.

causes.name: Oil pressure sensor or wiring fault
causes.clues: The light flickers but the engine sounds normal apart from the tick.
causes.against: A shop will usually confirm the real oil pressure with a gauge before blaming the sensor.

you: With the engine off and cooled for a few minutes, check the oil level on the dipstick.
Look under the car for fresh oil drips.
shop: Mechanical oil pressure test with a gauge
Oil pickup and pump inspection if measured pressure is low

result.title: A deep knock can mean serious internal engine wear
result.now: Stop driving and shut the engine off. Check the oil level, then have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic listen to it.
if: If the oil is very low, add oil, but don't run the engine to "test" it. A shop should listen first.
If the knock is only a light pinging when you accelerate hard, it may be fuel knock instead. See the engine knocking guide.
If the oil pressure light came on before or with the knock, mention it to the shop.
result.why: A tick is usually a small part at the top of the engine. A heavy knock that grows with engine speed can come from worn bearings deep in the engine. Running it can turn a repairable problem into a destroyed engine.

causes.name: Worn connecting rod bearing (rod knock)
causes.clues: A deep, rhythmic knock that gets louder under load and higher engine speed, often after running low on oil.

causes.name: Loose or worn timing chain
causes.clues: A rattle or slap from the front of the engine, often worst at startup.

causes.name: Severe valvetrain wear from oil starvation
causes.clues: The oil was low or very old, and the noise came on quickly.

you: Check the oil level without starting the engine.
Note whether the oil pressure light came on before the noise.
shop: Check the oil and filter for metal particles

result.title: A severe misfire is possible. A flashing light is a serious warning
result.now: Slow down and pull over when it's safe. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic rather than driving on.
if: If the light stops flashing and stays steady, the misfire may have eased, but have it checked before driving any distance. If it starts flashing again, stop.
If you smell fuel or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward red, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means the engine is misfiring badly enough to send unburned fuel into the exhaust. That can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter. A loose spark plug or ignition problem can also make a ticking or puffing sound.

causes.name: Loose or cracked spark plug
causes.clues: A sharp tick or puff from one spot on top of the engine, often after recent plug work.

causes.name: Failing ignition coil
causes.clues: Shaking that's worst under acceleration, sometimes in damp weather.

causes.name: Fuel injector problem
causes.clues: Rough idle, fuel smell, or poor fuel economy.

you: Note whether the light flashes all the time or only when accelerating.
If you have a code reader, read and save the codes.
shop: Code scan and misfire counter data

result.title: Low oil is a likely reason for the ticking
result.now: Add the oil type listed in your owner's manual until the dipstick reads full, then listen again with the engine warm. Get the car checked within a few days to find out where the oil is going.
if: If the oil pressure light comes on at any point, pull over as soon as it's safe, shut the engine off and don't drive it.
If the ticking turns into a deeper knock, stop driving and shut the engine off.
If the ticking doesn't fade after topping up, limit driving and get it checked soon. Running low may have worn something.
If you need to add more than a quart between oil changes, the engine is leaking or burning oil.
If the level drops noticeably within a day, or you see smoke or smell burning oil, don't keep driving it. Have it checked first.
result.why: The top of the engine is the last place oil reaches. When the level is low, parts like lifters and rocker arms don't get enough oil and start to tick. Topping up often quiets it, but low oil usually means it's leaking or burning somewhere.

causes.name: Oil leak
causes.clues: Oil spots where you park, or oily residue on the engine.

causes.name: Engine burning oil
causes.clues: Blue smoke from the exhaust, especially at startup, and no visible leak.

causes.name: Overdue oil change
causes.clues: It's well past the oil change reminder or mileage.

you: Top up the oil and recheck the level after a day of driving.
Look under the car and around the engine for oil.
Check when the last oil change was.
shop: Oil pressure test if the ticking continues

result.title: Check the oil level first. It's the most important clue
result.now: Park on level ground, turn the engine off, wait a few minutes and check the dipstick. If it's low, add the oil type listed in your owner's manual until it reads full.
if: If the oil was low and the ticking goes away after topping up, find out where the oil is going within a few days.
If the oil is full and the ticking continues, book a check so a technician can pinpoint the source.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over as soon as it's safe, shut the engine off and don't drive it.
If the ticking turns into a deep knock, or the check engine light flashes, stop driving and shut the engine off.
result.why: Low oil is one of the most common causes of engine ticking, and also the one that can do the most damage if ignored. It takes two minutes to check and tells you whether this is urgent.

causes.name: Low oil level
causes.clues: An oil change is overdue, or you've seen drips under the car.

causes.name: Noisy lifters or valve adjustment
causes.clues: A steady tick from the top of the engine with full oil.

causes.name: Exhaust leak
causes.clues: Louder when cold or when accelerating.

you: Check the oil level on the dipstick.
Record a short video with sound of the ticking at idle and when revving.

result.title: A tick that fades as the engine warms is often lifters or a small exhaust leak
result.now: Let the engine idle for 30 seconds or so after a cold start before driving off, and book a check when convenient.
if: If the ticking starts lasting longer or happens when warm too, get it checked sooner.
If you smell exhaust inside the car, get it checked right away. Exhaust fumes in the cabin are dangerous.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the tick turns into a knock, pull over as soon as it's safe, shut the engine off and don't drive it.
result.why: Hydraulic lifters can lose some oil overnight and tick until oil pressure fills them back up. A cracked exhaust manifold or leaking gasket can also tick when cold, then go quiet as the metal heats up and expands to seal the gap.

causes.name: Lifters bleeding down overnight
causes.clues: The tick comes from the top of the engine and is gone within a minute or two.

causes.name: Exhaust manifold leak
causes.clues: A puffing tick from one side of the engine, louder when you accelerate from cold, sometimes with an exhaust smell.

causes.name: Wrong oil thickness or old oil
causes.clues: The tick started after an oil change, or the oil is overdue.

you: Note how long the tick lasts after a cold start.
Check that the oil level is full and the oil type matches your owner's manual.
shop: Cold-start listen with an engine stethoscope

result.title: This may be normal fuel injector or fuel pump ticking
result.now: Check that the oil is full, then listen with the hood open. A steady, light, fast tick that hasn't changed over time is often the normal sound of the fuel injectors. A technician can confirm this by listening at your next service.
if: If the tick gets louder, changes in sound, or comes with a check engine light or rough running, book a check.
If you're not sure what's normal for your car, ask a shop to listen to it at your next service.
If the oil pressure light comes on, or the tick turns into a knock, pull over as soon as it's safe, shut the engine off and don't drive it.
result.why: Fuel injectors open and close many times a second, and many engines, especially direct-injection ones, make a light ticking sound that's part of normal operation. Some emissions valves click softly too. A noise that's always been there and hasn't changed is less likely to be a new fault, but only someone listening to the car can confirm it.

causes.name: Normal fuel injector noise
causes.clues: A light, even tick at idle that's been there since you've owned the car.
causes.against: If the sound is new or getting louder, something else is more likely.

causes.name: Normal high-pressure fuel pump noise (direct injection)
causes.clues: A ticking from the top of the engine that's more noticeable on a cold engine with the hood open.

causes.name: Evaporative (purge) valve clicking
causes.clues: A soft clicking that comes and goes at idle.

you: Check the oil level.
If you already recorded the sound, share it with your mechanic and mention when it occurred.
shop: Code scan if a warning light is on

result.title: An exhaust leak near the engine is possible
result.now: Get it checked within a few days. Until then, keep trips short. If you notice any exhaust smell inside the car, don't keep driving it.
if: If you smell exhaust inside the car, stop driving and get to fresh air. If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning: get everyone into fresh air and call 911 from outside the car.
If the check engine light comes on, mention it to the shop. A leak can affect the oxygen sensor readings.
If the tick turns into a knock or the oil pressure light comes on, pull over as soon as it's safe and shut the engine off.
result.why: A crack in the exhaust manifold or a leaking gasket lets exhaust puff out each time a cylinder fires, which can sound like a ticking that speeds up with the engine. It often gets louder under load. Exhaust leaks near the engine can let fumes into the cabin.

causes.name: Leaking exhaust manifold gasket
causes.clues: A puffing tick from one side of the engine, louder when accelerating.

causes.name: Cracked exhaust manifold
causes.clues: Louder when cold, quieter when warm, sometimes with a black sooty mark on the manifold.

causes.name: Broken or loose manifold bolt or stud
causes.clues: The noise started suddenly, sometimes after a cold snap.

you: With the engine cold, look for black soot around where the exhaust meets the engine.
Note whether the tick is louder on a cold engine.

result.title: A spark plug or ignition problem may be causing the tick
result.now: Get the codes read and the engine checked within a few days. Avoid hard acceleration and long trips until then.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing, slow down and stop driving as soon as it's safe.
If you smell fuel, stop driving and have it towed.
If the engine shakes hard or loses power, pull over when it's safe and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: A spark plug that's loose or has a cracked insulator can let combustion gas escape, making a sharp ticking or puffing sound along with a misfire. A steady check engine light with rough running points to the ignition system.

causes.name: Loose or damaged spark plug
causes.clues: A sharp tick from one spot on top of the engine, especially after recent tune-up work.

causes.name: Failing ignition coil
causes.clues: Rough running under acceleration, often with a misfire code.

causes.name: Noisy or sticking fuel injector
causes.clues: Rough idle and a fuel smell.

you: If you have a code reader, read and note the codes.
Note whether the roughness is worse at idle or under acceleration.
shop: Spark plug inspection and torque check

result.title: Possibly a noisy lifter or valves that need adjusting
result.now: Keep the oil topped up and on schedule, and book a check when convenient so a technician can pinpoint the source.
if: If the ticking gets louder quickly or turns into a knock, stop driving and have it checked right away.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over as soon as it's safe, shut the engine off and don't drive it.
If the check engine light is flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: A steady tick from the top of the engine that follows engine speed often comes from the valvetrain, the parts that open and close the valves. A worn or sticky lifter, or valves that are out of adjustment, tap with every turn of the engine.

causes.name: Sticky or worn hydraulic lifter
causes.clues: A tick from the top of the engine that may get better or worse with oil changes.

causes.name: Valves out of adjustment
causes.clues: Common on engines with screw or shim-type adjusters, and on high-mileage engines that haven't had a valve adjustment.

causes.name: Worn rocker arm or camshaft
causes.clues: The noise has been slowly getting louder over months.

you: Make sure the oil is full and the right type for your engine.
Record a video with sound at idle and when revving.

result.title: A tick that follows road speed is more likely a tire, wheel or brake than the engine
result.now: Park and look closely at each tire for a nail, screw or stone stuck in the tread, and check the tire pressures.
if: If you find a nail or screw, have the tire repaired or replaced soon, and don't pull it out yourself unless you're ready to fit the spare.
If the clicking is loudest when turning, it may be a worn CV joint. See the clicking when turning guide.
If a tire is losing air or a wheel feels wobbly, don't drive on it. Fit the spare or call roadside assistance.
If the noise changes when you brake, or braking feels different, have the brakes checked before driving further.
result.why: If the ticking follows road speed rather than engine speed (it doesn't change when you rev the engine while parked, but gets faster as the car goes faster), it isn't coming from the engine. Something turning with the wheels is making it, and the most common culprit is something stuck in a tire.

causes.name: Nail, screw or stone in a tire
causes.clues: A steady tick-tick that gets faster as you speed up, sometimes with slow air loss.

causes.name: Worn CV joint
causes.clues: Clicking that's loudest during tight turns.

causes.name: Brake wear indicator or loose brake part
causes.clues: The noise changes when you press the brake.

you: Inspect each tire's tread and sidewall.
Check the tire pressures.
Notice whether the tick gets faster with road speed during ordinary driving, and whether it's there when you rev the engine while parked in Park.

q_symptoms.q: Does anyone in the car have a headache, dizziness, nausea, unusual sleepiness or confusion?
q_symptoms.help: These are early signs of carbon monoxide exposure. Carbon monoxide has no smell, so you can be affected even when the exhaust smell seems mild.

opts.a: Yes
No
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When do you notice the fumes most?

opts.a: In heavy traffic or behind other vehicles, and it clears on an open road
When the rear hatch, tailgate, trunk or back windows are open
When parked with the engine running, especially in snow or a garage
Most of the time, whatever the traffic
I'm not sure

q_noise.q: Have you noticed any new sound from the exhaust or engine?

opts.a: The exhaust is louder, rumbling, roaring or rattling underneath
A ticking or puffing sound from the engine, loudest when cold
No new sounds
I'm not sure

result.title: Treat this as possible carbon monoxide exposure
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn off the engine, get everyone out into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car.
if: Even if symptoms improve in fresh air, follow the 911 dispatcher's advice and get checked. Carbon monoxide effects can linger, especially for children, pregnant people and anyone with heart or lung problems.
Don't use the car again until a shop has found and fixed the source. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
result.why: Exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which you can't see or smell. It replaces oxygen in your blood and can cause headaches, dizziness and confusion before you realize anything is wrong. Symptoms in the car mean enough is getting in to be dangerous.

causes.name: Exhaust leak under the car or at the engine
causes.clues: A louder exhaust, a rattle, or a smell that's there whatever the traffic.

causes.name: Blocked tailpipe or running in an enclosed space
causes.clues: The car was idling in snow, a garage or another tight space.

causes.name: Fumes drawn in through an open hatch or bad seal
causes.clues: The rear hatch or windows were open, or the rear seals are damaged.

shop: Exhaust system leak inspection on a lift
Body seal and rear hatch seal inspection

result.title: You may be smelling other vehicles' exhaust
result.now: Switch the climate control to recirculate in heavy traffic and when following trucks or older vehicles, then switch back to fresh air on open roads.
if: If the smell continues on open roads with no traffic around, your own car may be leaking. Pull over when it's safe, get into fresh air and don't use the car again until the exhaust has been checked. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.

If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Get medical advice even if they start to feel better.
If your exhaust sounds louder than usual, or you hear a new rattle underneath, your own exhaust may be leaking. Don't keep driving it until it's checked.
result.why: In fresh-air mode the car pulls in air from just in front of the windshield, so fumes from the vehicle ahead come straight in. Recirculate mode keeps reusing the cabin air. If the smell comes and goes with traffic and clears on open roads, the source is probably outside your car, but a leak of your own can't be ruled out without a check.

causes.name: Fumes from nearby vehicles
causes.clues: Worse in stop-and-go traffic, tunnels or behind diesel trucks.
causes.against: If you smell it on empty roads, this is less likely.

causes.name: Small leak in your own exhaust
causes.clues: The smell is there even with no other cars around.

you: Notice whether the smell disappears on open roads.
Try recirculate mode in traffic and see if the smell stops.

result.title: Exhaust may be getting pulled in through the back of the car
result.now: Keep the rear hatch, trunk and back windows closed while driving, and have the rear seals and exhaust checked within a few days.
if: Avoid driving with the hatch open. If you can't avoid it for a short trip, open the front windows and set the fan to fresh air on high.
If the smell is there even with everything closed, don't drive it until the exhaust and seals are checked.

If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Get medical advice even if they start to feel better.
result.why: As a car moves, low air pressure forms behind it and can pull exhaust toward the back. With a hatch or window open, or a worn seal, those fumes get sucked into the cabin. Wagons, SUVs and hatchbacks are especially prone to this.

causes.name: Driving with the rear hatch or windows open
causes.clues: The smell only appears when something at the back is open.

causes.name: Worn or damaged hatch or trunk seal
causes.clues: Torn or flattened rubber, or water also getting into the trunk.

causes.name: Exhaust leak near the rear or a damaged tailpipe
causes.clues: A louder exhaust, or the tailpipe is bent or points up toward the bumper.

you: Check the rubber seals around the hatch or trunk for tears.
Look at the tailpipe for damage or holes.
shop: Smoke test of the rear body openings

result.title: Exhaust may be building up around the car because it can't escape
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn off the engine and get into fresh air. Before running the engine again, clear snow from the tailpipe and around the car, or move it out of any enclosed space with the engine off.
if: If the smell continues outdoors with a clear tailpipe, don't use the car. There may be an exhaust leak, so have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.

If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Get medical advice even if they start to feel better.
result.why: When the tailpipe is buried in snow or the car is in a garage or tight space, exhaust gathers around the car and seeps in through vents and seals. Carbon monoxide can reach dangerous levels quickly, even when the smell seems faint.

causes.name: Tailpipe blocked by snow
causes.clues: The car was parked in or near a snowbank, or snow built up while idling.

causes.name: Idling in an enclosed space
causes.clues: The car was running in a garage, parking structure or other tight space.

causes.name: Exhaust leak made worse while idling
causes.clues: The smell is there outdoors with a clear tailpipe.

you: With the engine off, clear snow from the tailpipe and the area around the car.
Never warm the car up inside a garage, even with the door open.

result.title: The exhaust system may be leaking under the car
result.now: Don't use the car until it's repaired. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic to inspect the exhaust.
if: If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Get medical advice even if they start to feel better.
If part of the exhaust is hanging or dragging, don't move the car at all until it's secured or towed.
result.why: A louder exhaust plus fumes inside usually means exhaust is escaping before it reaches the tailpipe, often under the cabin floor. It can seep in through gaps in the floor and seals, carrying carbon monoxide you can't smell.

causes.name: Rusted or cracked exhaust pipe or muffler
causes.clues: A deep rumble or roar, worse when accelerating, especially on an older car or in salted-road areas.

causes.name: Failed exhaust joint, gasket or flex pipe
causes.clues: A puffing or rasping sound under the middle of the car.

causes.name: Broken hanger or damage from road debris
causes.clues: A rattle or clunk underneath, or the exhaust hangs lower than before.

you: With the engine off and cool, look under the car for hanging pipes or obvious holes.
shop: Exhaust system leak inspection on a lift

result.title: The exhaust manifold or a gasket near the engine may be leaking
result.now: Don't use the car until the leak is fixed, because the fumes can be pulled in through the vents. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
