if: If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Get medical advice even if they start to feel better.
If you also smell burning oil or see smoke under the hood, keep away from the engine and call for help.
result.why: The exhaust manifold collects exhaust right at the engine, close to where the ventilation system draws in outside air. A crack or a failed gasket there makes a ticking or puffing sound and can send fumes straight through the vents, especially with the heat or fan on.

causes.name: Failed exhaust manifold gasket
causes.clues: Ticking that's loudest on a cold start and quiets as the engine warms up.

causes.name: Cracked exhaust manifold
causes.clues: A ticking that gets louder over time, sometimes with black soot marks near the engine.

causes.name: Broken or loose manifold bolts or studs
causes.clues: Common on older engines, often with soot around one corner of the manifold.

result.title: Exhaust may be leaking somewhere and needs to be found before you use the car
result.now: Avoid using the car until the source is found. Have a mobile mechanic inspect it, or have it towed to a shop, so nobody has to breathe the fumes on the way.
if: If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Get medical advice even if they start to feel better.
If the exhaust gets louder or you hear a new rattle underneath, mention it to the shop. It helps them find the leak.
If the smell only shows up in heavy traffic and clears completely on open roads, it may be outside air, but have the exhaust checked to be sure. If it doesn't clear, don't keep driving it.
result.why: Fumes inside with no obvious noise can come from a small leak, a damaged seal, or a hole where exhaust can seep into the body. Even small leaks can let in carbon monoxide, and carbon monoxide has no smell, so a faint exhaust smell doesn't mean a small dose.

causes.name: Small exhaust leak
causes.clues: Black soot marks around an exhaust joint, or a faint puff you can hear at idle.

causes.name: Damaged body seal, floor plug or rust hole
causes.clues: Missing rubber plugs in the floor, rust holes, or water also getting in.

causes.name: Engine running poorly
causes.clues: A check engine light, rough running or a strong fuel smell in the exhaust.

you: Note whether the smell is worse when stopped, when accelerating or with the heat on.
Check for warning lights.
If you have a battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm, it can warn you if fumes are getting in.
shop: Exhaust system leak inspection on a lift
Code scan if a warning light is on

q_urgent.q: First, are any of these happening?

opts.a: The brake pedal feels soft or sinks, or the red BRAKE light is on
I smell gasoline, or the fluid smells like gas
The temperature gauge is high, there's steam, or a temperature warning is on
The oil pressure light (an oil can symbol) is on
None of these
I'm not sure

q_color.help: Dab some onto a white paper towel or slide white cardboard under the drip. Colors are much easier to see on white. Also rub a drop between your fingers to feel whether it's watery or slick.

opts.a: Clear and watery, with no smell
Light brown to black, and slippery
Red or pink, and oily
Green, orange, pink or yellow, watery, with a sweet smell
Clear to yellowish or light brown, slick, near a wheel
Blue, thin, smells like window cleaner
I'm not sure

q_location.q: Where is the spot under the car?
q_location.help: Imagine the car parked over it. Where the drip lands usually points to the part that's leaking.

opts.a: At the front, under the engine
Front passenger side, below where your feet would be
Under the middle of the car
Right next to one of the wheels
Toward the back of the car
I'm not sure

result.title: Possible brake fluid leak. Don't drive the car
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic to inspect the brakes.
if: If the brake pedal feels firm and the brake fluid reservoir is full, the fluid may be something else. Still have a technician confirm before you use the car.
If the car is already moving and the pedal sinks, pump the brakes, use the parking brake gently and steer to a safe stop.

If the brake fluid reservoir is low but you can't find a leak, still don't drive it. Fluid can leak where you can't see it, or the level can drop as pads wear. A shop should check before you top up and go.
result.why: Brake fluid is what makes the brakes work. A leak lets fluid out and air in, and the pedal can sink to the floor with little warning. Brake fluid is clear to yellowish or brown, feels slick, and often shows up near a wheel or under the driver's side of the engine bay.

causes.name: Leaking brake caliper or wheel cylinder
causes.clues: The inside of a wheel or tire looks wet or oily.

causes.name: Rusted or damaged brake line or hose
causes.clues: Drips along the underside of the car, often on older cars in salty-winter areas.

causes.name: Leaking master cylinder
causes.clues: Wetness under the hood on the driver's side near the windshield, or a pedal that slowly sinks.

you: With the engine off, look at the brake fluid reservoir under the hood and see whether it's below the MIN mark.
Without moving the car, check whether the inside of any wheel or tire looks wet.
shop: Brake fluid level and condition check
Brake line, hose and caliper inspection

result.title: A possible fuel leak is a fire risk
result.now: Don't start the car. Keep sparks, flames and cigarettes away, and have it towed to a shop.
if: If fuel is pouring or pooling, move everyone away from the car and call the fire department.
If the smell only happens right after filling up and fades quickly, the gas cap may not be sealing. Have a technician confirm there's no leak.
result.why: Gasoline is thin, evaporates quickly and has a strong smell. A leak near a hot exhaust or a spark can start a fire, so the car shouldn't run until the leak is found and fixed.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line or hose
causes.clues: Drips along the underside of the car, between the front and back.

causes.name: Leaking fuel tank or filler neck
causes.clues: Smell or drips near the back of the car, often worse after filling up.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector seal or fuel rail
causes.clues: The smell is strongest under the hood.

you: From a safe distance, note where the drip or smell is strongest.

result.title: Coolant may be leaking and the engine may be overheating
result.now: Turn the engine off as soon as it's safe. Don't open the radiator or coolant cap while it's hot. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you're stuck in traffic and can't pull over yet, turn the heater to full hot with the fan on high. It pulls some heat away from the engine.
If steam is pouring from under the hood, stay back and let it cool before opening anything.
If the oil pressure light comes on, or you hear knocking, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and don't restart it.
result.why: Running an overheating engine can warp or crack major parts within minutes. Coolant is the green, orange, pink or yellow sweet-smelling fluid, and losing it is one of the most common reasons engines overheat.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or coolant hose
causes.clues: Drips at the front of the car, or crusty residue at hose ends.

causes.name: Failing water pump
causes.clues: Drips below the front of the engine near the belts.

causes.name: Head gasket leak
causes.clues: White exhaust smoke with a sweet smell, or coolant disappearing faster than the drip explains.
causes.against: Less likely if you can see an obvious external leak.

you: Once the engine is fully cool, check the coolant overflow tank level.
shop: Radiator, hose and water pump inspection
Combustion gas test if no outside leak is found

result.title: The engine may be dangerously low on oil
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off and leave it off. After a few minutes, check the dipstick. If it's low, add the oil type listed in your owner's manual. If you can't, have it towed.
if: If the light stays on after the level is correct, or you hear ticking or knocking, don't run the engine. Have it towed.
If oil is pouring out, don't refill and restart. Have it towed.
Even if the light goes out after topping up, a leak big enough to leave a puddle can drain the oil again quickly. Have the leak checked before driving any distance.
result.why: The oil pressure light means oil isn't reaching the engine with enough pressure to protect it. Running even briefly like that can ruin the engine. A leak big enough to leave a puddle can drain the oil quickly.

causes.name: Large leak from the drain plug, oil filter or oil pan
causes.clues: A recent oil change, or a fresh puddle that keeps growing.

causes.name: Very low oil level from a slow leak or oil burning
causes.clues: Oil hasn't been checked in a while, or blue smoke from the exhaust.

causes.name: Failing oil pump or pressure sensor
causes.clues: The light stays on even though the oil level is full. A shop will usually measure the real oil pressure with a gauge before replacing the sensor or pump.

you: Check the oil level with the engine off and the car on level ground.
If the oil was just changed, look for a loose drain plug or oil filter.

result.title: Possibly just water from the air conditioning
result.now: Rub a drop between your fingers. If it's clear, odorless and not slippery, and you've been using the A/C or defroster, it's most likely normal A/C condensation, which doesn't need a repair.
if: If it feels slippery, smells sweet or has any color, it isn't plain water. Go back and pick the color instead.
If water is collecting on the passenger-side floor inside the car, the A/C drain may be blocked. Book a check.
result.why: The A/C pulls moisture out of the cabin air and drains it under the car, usually near the front passenger side. On hot, humid days it can leave a surprisingly large puddle. This is a normal part of how A/C works.

causes.name: Normal A/C condensation
causes.clues: Hot or humid weather, and the A/C or defroster was on.

causes.name: Water from the exhaust
causes.clues: Drips from the tailpipe, mostly on cold starts.

causes.name: Coolant leak
causes.clues: A faint sweet smell, a slick feel, or the coolant tank level dropping.
causes.against: Plain A/C water has no smell and isn't slick.

you: Check that the puddle is near the front passenger side.
Check the coolant overflow tank level when the engine is cold.
shop: A/C drain inspection if water gets inside the car

result.title: Likely an engine oil leak
result.now: Check the oil level on the dipstick and top up if needed. Book a check to find the source when convenient.
if: If the oil is below the low mark, or the spot is bigger than your hand after one night, get it checked within a few days.

If you see smoke or smell burning oil from under the hood, pull over, turn the engine off and let it cool. Oil may be dripping onto the hot exhaust, which can be a fire risk. Have it checked before driving further.
If the oil pressure light comes on, or you hear ticking or knocking, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off right away.
result.why: Engine oil is light brown when fresh, dark brown or black when used, and feels slippery. Many oil leaks are slow seeps from gaskets that harden with age and heat. The main risks are running low and oil dripping onto hot parts, so keep an eye on the level.

causes.name: Oil pan gasket or drain plug
causes.clues: Drips at the bottom of the engine, especially after a recent oil change.

causes.name: Valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Oil on the top or sides of the engine, or a burning-oil smell after driving.

causes.name: Crankshaft seal at the front or rear of the engine
causes.clues: Drips where the engine meets the transmission, or at the front behind the belts.

you: Check the oil level with the car on level ground and the engine off.
Slide cardboard under the engine overnight to see how much drips and from where.
With a flashlight and the engine off, look for wet, oily areas on the engine.
shop: Oil leak inspection, with dye if needed

result.title: Possibly transmission fluid or power steering fluid
result.now: Book a check within the next few days. If your car has a transmission dipstick or a see-through power steering reservoir, check those levels.
if: If the transmission slips, shifts hard or is slow to go into gear, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the steering suddenly gets heavy or hard to turn, pull over when it's safe and don't drive it until it's checked.
If it smells like gasoline, don't start the car. Keep sparks and flames away and have it towed.
If the fluid is thin, clear to yellowish and slick, or the brake pedal feels different, it may be brake fluid. Don't drive the car until it's checked.
result.why: Red or pink oily fluid is often automatic transmission fluid, and some power steering systems use it too. Transmission leaks tend to drip under the middle of the car, power steering leaks near the front. Running either system low can damage it.

causes.name: Transmission pan gasket, cooler line or seal
causes.clues: A spot under the middle or front of the car, or shifting that has changed.

causes.name: Power steering hose or pump
causes.clues: A spot near the front, or a whine when turning the wheel.
causes.against: Many newer cars have electric power steering with no fluid at all.

causes.name: Pink coolant
causes.clues: A sweet smell and a watery feel.
causes.against: Transmission and power steering fluid feel oily, not watery.

you: Note whether the spot is under the middle or the front of the car.
Rub a drop between your fingers: oily means transmission or power steering fluid, watery and sweet means coolant.
Check fluid levels where your owner's manual shows a dipstick or reservoir.
shop: Transmission and power steering leak inspection

result.title: Possibly a coolant (antifreeze) leak
result.now: With the engine cold, check the coolant overflow tank and top it up with the type in your owner's manual. Get the leak checked within a few days and watch the temperature gauge.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
If it's a steady drip, or the tank is low again within a day or two, have it towed rather than risk overheating.
If you see white smoke from the exhaust with a sweet smell, or the coolant keeps disappearing with no drip, mention it to the shop and avoid driving until it's checked.
result.why: Coolant is usually green, orange, pink or yellow, feels watery and smells sweet. Small leaks tend to grow, and running low on coolant leads to overheating, which can badly damage the engine.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or coolant hose
causes.clues: Drips at the front of the car, or crusty, colored residue at hose ends.

causes.name: Leaking water pump
causes.clues: Drips below the front of the engine near the belts.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: A sweet smell inside the car, a damp passenger floor, or windows that fog up.
causes.against: Usually leaks inside the car rather than underneath it.

you: Check the coolant overflow tank level when the engine is cold.
Look for crusty residue around the radiator and hose ends.
Wipe up the puddle so pets can't drink it.
shop: Radiator, hose and water pump inspection

result.title: Possibly windshield washer fluid
result.now: Fill the washer fluid reservoir and watch for drips. A cracked tank or a loose hose is a common cause.
if: If it smells sweet or the coolant tank is also dropping, it may be coolant. Get it checked within a few days.
If the washers don't spray, the pump or a hose is probably where it's leaking.
result.why: Washer fluid is usually blue, thin like water, and smells like window cleaner. A washer leak won't harm the car, but you need working washers to see clearly in bad weather.

causes.name: Cracked washer fluid reservoir
causes.clues: The tank empties within days without using the washers.

causes.name: Loose or split washer hose
causes.clues: Drips mostly after using the washers.

causes.name: Coolant
causes.clues: A sweet smell, or the coolant tank is dropping too.
causes.against: Washer fluid smells like window cleaner, not sweet.

you: Fill the reservoir and look under it for drips.
Smell the fluid: window cleaner means washer fluid, sweet means coolant.
shop: Washer reservoir, pump and hose inspection

result.title: Fluid under the engine is often oil or coolant
result.now: With the engine cold and off, check the oil dipstick, the coolant overflow tank and the brake fluid reservoir. Whichever is low may be the leak. Book a check to confirm.
if: If either level is below the low mark, top it up and get it checked within a few days.
If the temperature gauge rises or the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the brake fluid reservoir is below the MIN mark, don't drive the car until it's inspected, even if you can't see where it's leaking.
If you see smoke or smell burning from under the hood, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and let it cool before doing anything else.
result.why: The engine sits at the front of most cars, and the two fluids it holds the most of are oil and coolant. Checking both levels is the fastest way to tell which one you're losing.

causes.name: Engine oil leak
causes.clues: Brown or black, slippery, and the oil level is dropping.

causes.name: Coolant leak
causes.clues: Watery, sweet-smelling, and the coolant tank is dropping.

causes.name: Power steering fluid leak
causes.clues: Red or amber and oily, with a whine when turning.
causes.against: Many newer cars use electric steering with no fluid.

you: Check the oil level, the coolant overflow tank and the brake fluid reservoir.
Slide white cardboard under the engine overnight to see the color.

result.title: A drip toward the back is often exhaust water, axle oil or fuel
result.now: If it's clear water dripping from the tailpipe, that's usually normal condensation. Otherwise, note its color and smell and book a check when convenient.
if: If it smells like gasoline, don't start the car. Have it towed.
If it's slick and right next to a rear wheel, it may be brake fluid. Don't drive the car until it's checked.
If it's thick oil with a strong, sulfur-like smell near the middle of the rear axle, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: Exhaust makes water as it runs, and it often drips from the tailpipe on cold starts. Rear-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive cars also have gear oil in the rear axle. The fuel tank sits at the back too, so smell is an important clue.

causes.name: Exhaust condensation
causes.clues: Clear water from the tailpipe, mostly on cold mornings or short trips.

causes.name: Rear axle (differential) oil leak
causes.clues: Thick, dark oil with a strong smell, on a rear-wheel or all-wheel-drive car.

causes.name: Fuel tank or fuel line leak
causes.clues: A gasoline smell.

causes.name: Rear brake leak
causes.clues: Slick fluid on the inside of a rear wheel.

you: Note whether the drip comes from the tailpipe or from under the car.
Smell the fluid from a safe distance.
shop: Rear axle seal and cover check

result.title: Collect a sample so you or a shop can identify the leak
result.now: Slide a large piece of white cardboard under the car overnight. In the morning, note the color, where it dripped and how big the spot is, then book a check.
if: If the brake pedal feels soft or the brake light is on, don't drive the car.
If you smell gasoline, don't start the car and keep flames away.
If a warning light comes on, follow what that light means first.
If the temperature gauge is high or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Color, feel and location together identify nearly every leak. A clean white surface makes the color obvious, and where the spot lands points to the part that's leaking.

causes.name: Engine oil
causes.clues: Brown or black and slippery, under the engine.

causes.name: Coolant
causes.clues: Green, orange, pink or yellow, watery and sweet.

causes.name: A/C water
causes.clues: Clear and odorless, near the front passenger side.

you: Take a photo of the spot on the cardboard to show the shop.
Check the oil, coolant and brake fluid levels with the engine off. If the brake fluid is below MIN, don't drive the car until it's inspected.

q_what_happens.help: "4WD" sends power to all four wheels. On part-time 4WD you select it with a switch or lever. AWD works on its own with no switch.

opts.a: Loud grinding, banging or clunking under the vehicle, or a burning smell
It feels tight, hops or scrubs the tires when turning in 4WD on pavement
I select 4WD but the indicator flashes or never comes on
The 4WD light is on, but it still acts like only two wheels are driving
A Service 4WD, Service AWD or 4x4 warning light or message is on
I'm not sure

q_noise.q: When do you hear the noise?

opts.a: Only for a moment when shifting into 4WD, then it engages
Only when turning on dry pavement in 4WD, along with a tight or hopping feeling
Constantly while driving, or with a burning smell or fluid leak
I'm not sure

q_engage_how.q: How were you trying to engage it?
q_engage_how.help: Most part-time systems shift into 4 High while rolling slowly in a straight line. 4 Low usually needs the vehicle stopped or barely rolling, in Neutral. Some trucks also have hubs you turn by hand on the front wheels.

opts.a: While parked, going fast, or turning, or I tried 4 Low without stopping in Neutral
My truck has dials on the front wheel centers (manual locking hubs)
I followed the owner's manual steps and it still won't engage
I'm not sure

q_message.q: Along with the warning, do you notice anything else?

opts.a: Grinding, banging, or the vehicle shudders or jerks
The ABS or traction control light is on too
One tire was recently replaced, or the tires don't match in size or wear
Nothing else, it drives normally
I'm not sure

result.title: This is likely driveline binding from using part-time 4WD on pavement
result.now: Shift back to 2WD (or 2 High) as soon as you're on dry pavement. Driving straight for a short distance usually releases the tension.
if: If it won't come out of 4WD, try reversing straight for a few feet, then shift again.
If you have full-time 4WD or AWD and feel this, it isn't normal. Have the vehicle checked soon.
If you hear banging or grinding, or the binding continues in 2WD, stop driving and have it checked before going further.
result.why: Part-time 4WD locks the front and rear axles together. In a turn the wheels need to travel different distances, and on grippy pavement they can't slip to make up the difference, so the driveline winds up. That's why part-time 4WD is meant for loose or slippery surfaces only.

causes.name: Part-time 4WD used on dry or grippy pavement
causes.clues: It happens in tight turns like parking lots, and goes away in 2WD.
causes.against: If it happens in 2WD too, look for another cause.

causes.name: Mismatched tire sizes front to rear
causes.clues: Different brands, sizes or very different tread depths.

you: Check which 4WD modes your owner's manual allows on dry pavement.
Check that all four tires are the same size and similar in wear.
shop: Transfer case and axle inspection if the binding happens in 2WD
Tire size and tread depth check

result.title: It may need to be engaged a specific way
result.now: Check your owner's manual for the exact steps. For 4 High, most trucks want slow, straight rolling. For 4 Low, stop or barely roll, shift to Neutral, then select 4 Low.
if: If the light keeps flashing after you follow the steps exactly, roll forward or backward a few feet in a straight line. That often lets the gears line up.
If it still won't engage, the actuator or switch may be at fault. Book a check.
If you hear grinding or banging while it tries to engage, stop trying and have it checked.
result.why: Many 4WD systems won't shift unless speed, gear position and steering are right. A flashing light usually means the system is waiting for the gears to line up or for the right conditions.

causes.name: Engagement steps not met
causes.clues: It was tried while parked, at speed, in a turn, or in gear for 4 Low.

causes.name: Gears not lined up yet
causes.clues: The light flashes, then turns solid after rolling a short distance.

you: Follow the owner's manual steps exactly.
Roll a few feet in a straight line and watch whether the light turns solid.
shop: Code scan of the 4WD module if it still won't engage

result.title: The front hubs may not be locked
result.now: Stop the vehicle, then turn both front hub dials fully to LOCK before selecting 4WD.
if: If one hub won't turn or won't stay locked, have the hub checked.
If both hubs are locked and the front wheels still don't drive, have the transfer case and front axle checked.
result.why: With manual hubs, the front wheels aren't connected to the front axle until you lock them. The transfer case can be in 4WD, but no power reaches the front wheels if the hubs are free.

causes.name: Hubs left in FREE
causes.clues: One or both dials point to FREE.

causes.name: Worn or damaged locking hub
causes.clues: The dial feels loose, or it pops back out.

you: Check both hub dials are fully turned to LOCK.
With 4WD selected, see whether both front wheels pull on a loose surface.
shop: Front axle and transfer case check

result.title: A shift motor, actuator or 4WD switch may be at fault
result.now: Book a check, and don't count on 4WD until it's fixed. Have the 4WD module codes read.
if: If you need 4WD for snow, mud or towing soon, get it checked before then.
If you hear grinding or the vehicle jerks, stop using 4WD and have it inspected right away.
result.why: On most modern trucks, a switch tells a module to run an electric motor that shifts the transfer case. Some also use an actuator to connect the front axle. If any of these fail, the system can't complete the shift.

causes.name: Transfer case shift motor fault
causes.clues: No whir or click from under the vehicle when you select 4WD.

causes.name: Front axle actuator or automatic hub fault
causes.clues: The transfer case shifts, but the front wheels don't drive.

causes.name: Faulty 4WD switch, fuse or wiring
causes.clues: The indicator doesn't respond at all.

you: Check the 4WD fuses listed in the owner's manual.
Listen for a brief motor sound from under the vehicle when selecting 4WD.
shop: Shift motor and actuator test before any parts are replaced

result.title: Power may not be reaching the front wheels
result.now: Have it checked within a few days. Don't rely on 4WD in snow, mud or on steep ground until it's fixed.
if: If you hear clunking or grinding from the front, stop using 4WD and have it inspected before driving further.
If your truck has manual hubs, check that both are locked first.
If a driveshaft looks loose or hanging, or you hear metal scraping, don't move the vehicle. Have it towed.
result.why: The 4WD light only shows what the switch or transfer case thinks is happening. If the front axle isn't connected, or a part between the transfer case and front wheels has failed, the front wheels won't pull.

causes.name: Front axle actuator or automatic hubs not engaging
causes.clues: The light comes on but only the rear wheels spin when stuck.

causes.name: Broken front driveshaft, axle shaft or CV joint
causes.clues: Clicking or clunking in turns, or grease spattered inside a front wheel.

causes.name: Worn transfer case chain or shift fork
causes.clues: Grinding or a loose clunk from the middle of the vehicle.

you: On a loose surface, see if the front wheels turn when the rear wheels spin.
Look for torn rubber boots or grease around the front axles.

result.title: The 4WD or AWD system has stored a fault
result.now: Book a code scan and inspection. Until then, drive gently in 2WD (or as your AWD vehicle allows), and don't count on 4WD or AWD.
if: If you hear grinding or banging or the vehicle jerks, stop and have it towed.
If the ABS or traction light comes on too, mention it. A wheel speed sensor is a common cause.
If you smell burning or see fluid leaking from the middle or ends of the vehicle, stop and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: A Service 4WD or AWD message means the system saw a problem and may have turned itself off to protect the parts. Many vehicles still drive in this state, but the extra traction may not be there when you need it.

causes.name: Shift motor, actuator or switch fault
causes.clues: 4WD won't engage, or engages slowly.

causes.name: Wheel speed sensor problem
causes.clues: ABS or traction control lights come on too.

causes.name: Low or worn fluid in the transfer case or rear drive unit
causes.clues: A shudder in turns, or fluid service is overdue.

you: Note when the message appears and whether it goes away after restarting.
Check that all four tires match in size and wear.
shop: Transfer case and differential fluid check

result.title: A wheel speed sensor problem is a possible cause
result.now: Have the codes read and the brakes checked within a few days. Until then, drive gently and allow extra stopping distance, especially on slippery roads.
if: If the red brake warning light comes on too, or the brake pedal feels soft, sinks or takes more effort, don't drive it. Have the brakes checked first.
If a wheel bearing is humming or growling, or a wheel feels loose, get it checked before driving further.
result.why: The 4WD, AWD, ABS and traction systems all share wheel speed information. When one sensor fails, all of them may switch off at once. With the ABS light on, the anti-lock function and the extra traction may not work, so the wheels can lock in a hard stop on a slippery road.

causes.name: Failed or dirty wheel speed sensor
causes.clues: The lights came on after driving through snow, mud or water.

causes.name: Damaged sensor wiring
causes.clues: Recent suspension, brake or wheel work.

causes.name: Worn wheel bearing
causes.clues: A hum or growl that changes when you steer.

you: Note which warning lights are on.
Look for torn or loose wires near each wheel.
shop: Wheel speed sensor live data check

result.title: Mismatched tires may be upsetting the system
result.now: Within a few days, have all four tires measured for size and tread depth, then match them as your owner's manual requires.
if: If you notice shuddering or binding in turns, have the transfer case or rear drive unit checked.
If only one tire was replaced on an AWD vehicle, ask the tire shop whether it needs to be shaved to match the others.
If you hear grinding or banging, or the vehicle jerks, stop and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: AWD and 4WD systems expect all four wheels to turn at almost the same speed. A new tire next to worn ones, or a different size, makes them turn at different speeds all the time. That can set a warning and wear out the parts that split power between the axles.

causes.name: One new tire with three worn ones
causes.clues: The warning came on soon after replacing a single tire.

causes.name: Different tire sizes or a low tire
causes.clues: Mixed tire brands or sizes, or one tire low on air.

you: Check all four tire pressures.
Check that all four tires have the same size printed on the sidewall.
shop: Tread depth and tire circumference check

result.title: A brief grind when engaging often means the shift is happening too fast or a part is wearing
result.now: Engage 4WD only at the speed and conditions in your owner's manual, and have it checked within a few days if the grind continues.
if: If the grinding continues after it engages, or there's a burning smell, stop and have it towed.
If it only happens when shifting at higher speeds, try slowing down first. If it still grinds, have it checked.
result.why: Gears and the front axle connection need to spin at matching speeds to engage smoothly. Shifting too fast, or a worn actuator or hub, can make them clash briefly before they lock in.

causes.name: Shifting at too high a speed or while turning
causes.clues: It only grinds when you shift on the move.

causes.name: Worn front axle actuator or locking hub
causes.clues: A grind or ratchet sound from a front wheel.

causes.name: Worn transfer case parts or low fluid
causes.clues: Grinding from the middle of the vehicle, or a leak.

you: Try engaging at a slow, steady speed in a straight line.
Look under the middle of the vehicle for fluid leaks.
shop: Front axle actuator and hub inspection

result.title: There may be damage in the transfer case, axles or driveshaft
result.now: Pull over safely, turn the engine off, and have the vehicle towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see a driveshaft hanging or hear metal scraping, don't move the vehicle at all.
If you smell burning, keep away from the underside until it cools.
result.why: Constant grinding, banging or jerking can mean parts in the driveline are slipping or broken. Driving on them can lock a wheel or drop a driveshaft, and the damage spreads fast.

causes.name: Transfer case failure (chain, gears or low fluid)
causes.clues: Grinding or banging from the middle of the vehicle, or a leak there.

causes.name: Broken driveshaft joint (U-joint)
causes.clues: A clunk when shifting into gear, or vibration that got worse quickly.

causes.name: Front or rear differential failure
causes.clues: Howling or grinding from one end, or a leak at an axle.

shop: Transfer case and differential fluid inspection

result.title: Have the 4WD system scanned and inspected
result.now: Book a check, and don't rely on 4WD or AWD until it's confirmed working. Note any lights or messages on the dash.
if: If you hear grinding or banging, or the vehicle shudders, stop and have it towed.
If it only acts up on dry pavement in part-time 4WD, switch back to 2WD. That may be normal binding.
result.why: 4WD trouble can come from how it's being engaged, a failed actuator or sensor, or worn driveline parts. A scan and a quick inspection usually narrow it down fast.

causes.name: Engagement steps not met
causes.clues: The indicator flashes and never turns solid.

causes.name: Actuator, shift motor or sensor fault
causes.clues: A Service 4WD or AWD message.

causes.name: Worn driveline parts
causes.clues: Grinding, clunking or a leak under the vehicle.

you: Read the 4WD section of your owner's manual.
Photograph any dash messages for the shop.

q_where.q: Which of these best describes the gas smell?

opts.a: Fuel is dripping, or there's a wet spot under the car that smells like gas
It's strong inside the car while driving or idling
Mostly right after filling up
A faint smell outside the car, when parked or after starting
I'm not sure

q_look.q: With the engine off, look under the car and around the engine. Do you see anything wet?
q_look.help: Use a flashlight. Gasoline looks like thin, clear-to-amber liquid, evaporates fast and smells strongly of gas. Don't use a lighter or match to look.

opts.a: Yes, there's a wet spot or drip that smells of gas
No, everything looks dry but I still smell gas
I'm not sure
The gas cap wasn't tight, or a check engine or gas cap light came on
Fuel splashed on the car, my shoes or my clothes
The pump nozzle keeps clicking off, or fuel overflows while filling
The smell lasts for hours, or there's a wet spot near the gas tank or filler
I'm not sure

q_outside.q: Is the check engine light on, and where is the smell strongest?
q_outside.help: A steady check engine light often means the car has detected a fuel vapor leak. Any auto parts store or shop can read the code.

opts.a: The check engine light is on
No light. The smell is only at the tailpipe for a few minutes after a cold start
No light. The smell is around the engine or under the car
I'm not sure

result.title: Fuel may be leaking from the car. This is a fire risk
result.now: Don't start the engine. Keep sparks, cigarettes and flames away, and have the car towed to a shop.
if: If the car is in a garage, open the garage door to air it out, but don't run the engine or flip electrical switches nearby.
If the leak is large or fuel is spreading, move everyone away and call 911.
If you see smoke or flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
result.why: Liquid gasoline gives off vapor that can ignite from a spark or a hot exhaust. A leak that drips while parked will usually get worse when the fuel system is under pressure with the engine running.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line
causes.clues: Drips along the underside of the car between the tank and the engine. Steel lines can rust through, especially in salted-road areas.

causes.name: Leaking fuel tank, filler neck or tank seal
causes.clues: The wet spot is under the gas tank or near the fuel filler.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector seal or fuel rail
causes.clues: Wetness or a strong smell on top of the engine.

shop: Fuel line and tank inspection on a lift

result.title: Fuel vapor is getting into the cabin, possibly from a leak
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe, turn off the engine, get out and open the doors. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you're carrying a gas can or gas-powered equipment, check it for leaks first. If that's the source, remove it and air the car out. If the smell doesn't fully clear, don't drive it until it's checked.
If anyone feels dizzy, sick or has a headache, get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car.
If you see smoke or flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
result.why: A strong gas smell inside means fuel vapor is building up where you're breathing and close to electrical parts. Common sources are a leak in the engine bay that gets pulled in through the vents, or a leak near the fuel pump access under the rear seat.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector seal or fuel line in the engine bay
causes.clues: The smell is worst with the fan on, or strong when you open the hood.

causes.name: Leaking fuel pump seal or tank fittings
causes.clues: The smell is strongest in the back seat area, often after a full fill-up.

causes.name: Spilled fuel or a leaking gas can in the car
causes.clues: You recently carried fuel or a lawn mower or generator.

you: Check for gas cans or fuel-powered equipment inside the car.
shop: Fuel pump seal and tank fitting check

result.title: A loose or worn gas cap is a common cause
result.now: Take the gas cap off and put it back on until it clicks. Check the rubber seal for cracks and replace the cap if it's damaged.
if: If the check engine light came on, it can take several days of driving to turn off after the cap is fixed.
If the smell or the light continues after a week with a good cap, have the fuel vapor (EVAP) system checked.
If the smell is strong inside the car, or you see drips or a wet spot under it, don't drive it. Have it checked first.
result.why: The gas cap seals in fuel vapor. If it isn't tight or its seal is worn, vapor escapes and you smell gas around the car, and the car's leak check may turn on the check engine light. Capless fillers can be blocked open by dirt in the same way.

causes.name: Gas cap not tightened
causes.clues: You recently filled up and may not have heard it click.

causes.name: Worn or cracked cap seal
causes.clues: The rubber ring is hard, cracked or missing.

causes.name: Dirty capless filler flap
causes.clues: On cars without a cap, the flap doesn't close fully.

you: Tighten the cap until it clicks.
Inspect the cap's rubber seal.
Check that the capless filler flap closes fully.
shop: EVAP smoke test if the light returns

result.title: Spilled fuel may be the source
result.now: Wipe off any fuel on the paint, wash it off shoes or clothes, and air the car out. If spilled fuel is the cause, the smell usually fades within a few hours.
if: If the smell is still strong the next day, look under the car for wet spots and have it checked if you find any.
If fuel soaked into the carpet, clean it right away and keep the windows open. Don't smoke in the car.
If anyone feels dizzy, sick or gets a headache, get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car. Air the car out before driving it.
result.why: Even a small splash of gasoline smells strong until it evaporates. Fuel on shoes, clothes or the car's paint near the filler can make it seem like the car is leaking.

causes.name: Fuel splashed while filling
causes.clues: The pump overflowed or dripped when you pulled the nozzle out.

causes.name: Fuel on shoes, clothes or floor mats
causes.clues: The smell is strongest near your feet and fades over time.

causes.name: A fuel leak instead
causes.clues: The smell doesn't fade, or there are wet spots under the car.
causes.against: If it fades within a few hours, a leak is less likely.

you: Wipe and wash any fuel residue.
Check floor mats and shoes.
Look under the car the next morning for wet spots.
shop: Fuel system leak inspection if the smell doesn't go away

result.title: The fuel vapor system may not be venting properly while you fill up
result.now: Fill slowly with the nozzle on its lowest setting, stop at the first click, and book a check of the fuel vapor (EVAP) system when convenient.
if: If fuel spits back out of the filler, stop filling and wipe up the spill. If fuel drips under the car when you're not filling up, don't start it. Have it towed.
If the gas smell is strong inside the car while driving, pull over, turn off the engine and air it out. Don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: As fuel goes in, the air and vapor in the tank must escape through the vapor system. If a vent valve or the charcoal canister is clogged, the vapor can't get out, so the pump keeps shutting off and fuel can spit back out of the filler.

causes.name: Clogged charcoal canister or vent valve
causes.clues: The pump clicks off over and over, and a check engine light may come on.

causes.name: Topping off past the first click
causes.clues: You often add fuel after the pump shuts off. This can flood the canister with liquid fuel.

causes.name: Kinked or blocked filler vent hose
causes.clues: The problem started after work near the gas tank or after hitting road debris.

you: Stop filling at the first click.
Try a different pump to rule out a sensitive nozzle.

result.title: The fuel filler neck or tank may be leaking. This can be a fire risk
result.now: Avoid driving the car until the leak is found. Park it outdoors away from buildings, keep sparks and flames away, and have a mobile mechanic inspect it or have it towed to a shop.
if: If fuel is dripping or pooling, move everyone away and call the fire department.
Don't fill the tank again until it's been checked. A fuller tank can push more fuel out of a damaged filler or fitting.
If you see smoke or flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
result.why: A smell that lingers long after filling can mean fuel or vapor is escaping near the top of the tank or from the filler pipe. These leaks often show up only when the tank is full, because that's when fuel reaches the damaged spot.

causes.name: Rusted or cracked filler neck
causes.clues: Wetness or a strong smell behind the rear wheel on the filler side, worst after filling.

causes.name: Leaking fuel pump seal or tank fitting
causes.clues: The smell is strongest in the back seat or under the middle of the car, mostly when the tank is full.

causes.name: Loose or cracked vapor hose
causes.clues: A smell without any visible wetness.

you: Check behind the rear wheel on the filler side for wetness after a fill-up.
Note whether the smell fades as the tank level drops.
shop: Fuel tank, filler neck and fitting inspection on a lift

result.title: The fuel vapor (EVAP) system may have a leak
result.now: Check that the gas cap clicks tight, then have the check engine code read and the car checked within a few days.
if: If you see liquid fuel dripping, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If the light is flashing or the engine runs rough, pull over and turn it off.
If the smell gets strong, especially inside the car, pull over, turn off the engine and air it out. Don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: Cars trap gas vapor from the tank in a charcoal canister and burn it in the engine later. If a hose, valve or seal in that system leaks, vapor escapes and the car's self-test turns on the check engine light. A code scan narrows down which part.

causes.name: Loose or worn gas cap
causes.clues: It started after a fill-up.

causes.name: Cracked EVAP hose or faulty purge or vent valve
causes.clues: An EVAP leak or valve code, and a smell near the tank or engine.

causes.name: Liquid fuel leak
causes.clues: Wet spots under the car or a strong smell that doesn't go away.

you: Tighten the gas cap until it clicks.
Have the trouble code read for free at many auto parts stores.

result.title: A brief fuel smell from the tailpipe on cold starts is often normal
result.now: Note how long the smell lasts after starting and mention it at your next service, or book a check when convenient if it's getting stronger.
if: If the smell lasts after the engine warms up, or you see black smoke, have it checked within a few days.
If the check engine light comes on or the engine runs rough, get it checked soon.
If you smell raw fuel under the hood or under the car, not just at the tailpipe, don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: A cold engine needs extra fuel, and the catalytic converter doesn't clean the exhaust until it heats up. That can leave a faint gas smell at the tailpipe for a minute or two. If the engine keeps running rich once warm, something is off with the fuel mixture.

causes.name: Normal cold-start enrichment
causes.clues: It fades within a few minutes and the car runs smoothly.

causes.name: Engine running rich
causes.clues: Worse gas mileage, black smoke, or a smell that lasts once warm.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector
causes.clues: Rough idle at startup, or a strong smell at the engine too.

you: Note whether the smell fades once the engine is warm.
Track your gas mileage.
shop: Code scan with fuel trim data
Oxygen sensor and coolant temperature sensor check

result.title: There may be a small fuel or vapor leak. Have it found before driving
result.now: Avoid driving the car until the source is found. Park it outdoors away from buildings, keep sparks and flames away, and have a mobile mechanic inspect it or have it towed to a shop.
if: If you find drips or wet spots, keep everyone away from the car and keep flames and sparks away.
If the smell is strong inside the car, open the doors and air it out without starting the engine.
If you see smoke or flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
result.why: A gas smell with no visible puddle can come from a small seep that evaporates before it drips, or from a vapor hose. Small fuel leaks rarely fix themselves and can grow, and not seeing a drip doesn't rule out fuel reaching hot engine parts.

causes.name: Fuel injector seal or fuel rail seep
causes.clues: The smell is strongest at the engine, especially right after starting.

causes.name: EVAP hose or canister leak
causes.clues: A smell near the gas tank, often stronger in hot weather.

causes.name: Seeping fuel line connection
causes.clues: Damp or stained areas along fuel lines underneath.

you: With the engine off, use a flashlight to look for damp or stained spots on top of the engine and underneath.
Note whether the smell is worse after starting or in hot weather.

q_stopping.q: How does the car stop when you brake?
q_stopping.help: This is the most important question. A change in how the car stops matters more than the noise itself.

opts.a: Normally. Only the noise is new
It takes longer to stop, the pedal feels soft or goes lower, or the red brake light is on
It pulls hard to one side, or a wheel smells hot or burning
The pedal or steering wheel shakes or pulses along with the grinding
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When do you hear the grinding?

opts.a: Only on the first few stops after the car sat, or after rain or a wash, then it's gone
Every time I brake: a harsh metal-on-metal grind
A light scraping that comes and goes, often after driving on gravel
Even when I'm not braking, and it changes with speed or when turning
Only during a hard stop or on a slippery road, with a buzzing pulse in the pedal
It started right after new brakes were put on
I'm not sure

result.title: The brakes may not be working properly. Treat this as a safety problem
result.now: Don't drive it. Park it somewhere safe and have it towed, or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you're on the road now, slow down gently, use a lower gear if you can, and pull over somewhere safe.
If you see fluid near a wheel or the brake fluid reservoir is low, tell the shop. Low fluid with no visible leak still needs checking before the car is driven.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, keep away from it and let it cool.
result.why: Grinding plus longer stops or a soft pedal can mean the brakes have lost some of their ability to stop the car. Pads worn to metal, a fluid leak or a damaged caliper can all do this, and it can get worse suddenly.

causes.name: Pads worn through to metal
causes.clues: There was a squeal for weeks or months before the grinding started.

causes.name: Brake fluid leak
causes.clues: A soft or sinking pedal, the red brake light, or a wet spot near a wheel.

causes.name: Damaged caliper or piston
causes.clues: Badly worn pads let the piston push out too far, and the pedal changed suddenly.

you: With the engine off and cool, check the brake fluid reservoir level.
Look for wet spots on the inside of the wheels.

result.title: A brake may be stuck on and overheating
result.now: Pull over safely and let the wheel cool. Don't touch it. Have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic check it before using it again.
if: If you see smoke or flames, get everyone out and away from the car and call for help.
If the parking brake was left partly on, release it fully and let the brakes cool. Overheated brakes can lose grip, so have them checked before relying on the car.
If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, don't drive it.
result.why: A brake that won't release can keep grinding against the rotor. That builds a lot of heat, which causes the burning smell and the pull, and it can make the brakes fade or damage the wheel bearing.

causes.name: Sticking caliper or slide pins
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter or dustier, and the car pulls to that side.

causes.name: Parking brake not releasing
causes.clues: The heat is at a rear wheel.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose
causes.clues: The pull comes and goes.

you: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.
Notice which wheel smells hotter from a distance. Don't touch it.

result.title: The rotors may be worn or damaged, often along with the pads
result.now: Avoid driving it until the brakes are inspected. Have a mobile mechanic check it where it's parked, or have it towed to a shop.
if: If the pedal feels soft, sinks or the car takes longer to stop, don't drive it at all.
If the pulsing only happens during a hard stop on a slippery road, with no grinding on normal stops, it may be the ABS working. Mention it to the shop.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, keep away from it and let it cool.
result.why: A pulsing pedal means the rotor surface is uneven. Combined with grinding, that can mean the pads have worn into the rotor or the rotor is badly rusted or scored. Metal-on-metal contact can reduce braking and gets worse with every stop.

causes.name: Pads worn into the rotor
causes.clues: Grinding on most stops, and a squeal before it started.

causes.name: Uneven or rusted rotors
causes.clues: The car sat for a long time, or the rotor has a rough ring or lip on its surface.

causes.name: Sticking caliper
causes.clues: One wheel gets hotter than the others.

you: Look through the wheel spokes at the rotor surface. Deep grooves or a rough surface point to damage.
Notice whether the shake is in the pedal or the steering wheel.

result.title: Probably surface rust on the rotors scraping off
result.now: Brake gently a few times. If it's surface rust, the noise usually clears within the first few stops.
if: If the grinding lasts beyond the first few miles, have the brakes inspected soon.
If the car sat for weeks or months, have the rotors checked. Heavy rust can pit them.
If the pedal feels soft, the car takes longer to stop, or the grind is harsh, stop driving and have it checked.
result.why: Brake rotors are bare iron and rust quickly when wet. After rain, a car wash or sitting overnight, the first stops scrape that rust off, which can sound like a brief grind. A brief grind that clears within a few stops is usually this.

causes.name: Light surface rust
causes.clues: Only on the first stops after the car sat or got wet, and gone soon after.
causes.against: If it happens on every stop all day, look for another cause.

causes.name: Heavier rust from long storage
causes.clues: The car sat for weeks, and the rotor edges look crusty.

you: Notice whether the noise is gone after the first few stops.
Look at the rotors through the wheel spokes for a shiny surface after driving.
shop: Rotor inspection if the noise doesn't clear

result.title: The brake pads may be worn down to bare metal
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed to a shop, or have a mobile mechanic inspect the brakes where it's parked.
if: If you're on the road now, slow down gently, leave plenty of room, and pull over somewhere safe. Then call for help.
If the pads were replaced recently and the grind started suddenly, a pad may have come apart. It still needs checking before you drive.
result.why: A harsh grind on every stop often means the pad lining is gone and the metal backing is rubbing the rotor. That can cut braking ability and damage the rotor quickly. Waiting can also damage the caliper.

causes.name: Pads worn through
causes.clues: There was a squeal for a while before, and the pads haven't been replaced in a long time.
causes.against: Less likely if the pads are new.

causes.name: Pad lining separated from its backing
causes.clues: The grind started suddenly on fairly new pads.

causes.name: Seized caliper wearing one pad unevenly
causes.clues: The noise is from one wheel, and that wheel runs hotter.

you: Look through the wheel spokes. If you can't see any pad material between the metal plate and the rotor, the pads are likely worn out. Tell the shop what you saw.

result.title: A small stone or bit of debris may be caught in the brake
result.now: Drive slowly in a safe place and back up a short distance. That often frees a trapped stone. If the scraping continues, book a brake check.
if: If the scraping becomes constant or turns into a harsh grind, have it checked right away.
If the pedal feels soft, the car takes longer to stop, or the brakes feel different in any way, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: Small stones can get caught between the rotor and the thin metal dust shield behind it, causing a scraping sound that comes and goes. It often stops once the stone falls out, but it can score the rotor if it stays, so have it checked if the sound continues.

causes.name: Stone caught between the rotor and the dust shield
causes.clues: Started after gravel or a dirt road, and the noise is light and on and off.

causes.name: Bent dust shield touching the rotor
causes.clues: Started after a tire change or hitting something.

causes.name: Early pad wear
causes.clues: The pads are getting old, and a squeal came first.

you: Notice which wheel the sound comes from.
Look behind the wheel for a stone or a bent metal shield.
shop: Remove the wheel and check the rotor and dust shield

result.title: Possibly a wheel bearing, a dragging brake or a shield rubbing
result.now: Have it checked within a few days. Drive gently and avoid highways until then.
if: If the wheel feels loose, the steering suddenly feels different, or the noise gets louder fast, stop driving and have it towed.
If one wheel is hot or smells burnt, a brake is sticking. Don't drive it.
result.why: A grind that happens without braking and changes with speed or turning is less likely to be normal pad contact. It's often a worn wheel bearing, a brake that isn't fully releasing, or the dust shield rubbing the rotor.

causes.name: Worn wheel bearing
causes.clues: A grinding or growling that gets louder with speed and changes when you turn one way.

causes.name: Brake dragging
causes.clues: One wheel is hotter or dustier than the others.

causes.name: Dust shield rubbing the rotor
causes.clues: A light scraping that started after a tire change or hitting something.

you: Notice whether the noise changes when you gently turn left vs. right at speed.
Notice if one wheel smells hot after a drive. Don't touch it.
shop: Wheel bearing play and noise check

result.title: That may be the anti-lock brakes (ABS) doing their job
result.now: If it only happens during hard stops or on slippery roads, it's usually the ABS working as designed. Keep firm pressure on the pedal when you feel it.
if: If the buzzing happens during normal, gentle stops on dry roads, or the ABS light comes on, have the brakes checked.
If the car doesn't slow down as it should, or the pedal feels soft, stop driving and have it towed.
If the red brake warning light comes on, don't drive until the brakes are checked.
result.why: During a hard stop or on ice, rain or gravel, the ABS pulses the brakes rapidly so the wheels don't lock up. You can feel a buzz in the pedal and hear a grinding or chattering sound. That's how ABS is designed to work.

causes.name: Normal ABS operation
causes.clues: Only during hard or slippery stops, with a pulsing pedal.
causes.against: Not normal if it happens on dry roads during gentle stops.

causes.name: Faulty wheel speed sensor
causes.clues: The ABS kicks in at low speed on dry roads, or the ABS light is on.

you: Notice whether it only happens on slippery surfaces or in hard stops.
Watch for the ABS warning light.
shop: ABS code scan if it happens during normal stops

result.title: New brakes shouldn't grind. Something may need adjusting
result.now: Call the shop that did the work and arrange for them to recheck it within the next day or two. Drive gently and leave extra stopping room until then.
if: If the pedal feels different or the car takes longer to stop, don't drive it. Call the shop and ask them to come to you or arrange a tow.
If you smell burning or a wheel is much hotter than the others, stop and let it cool. Ask the shop to come to you or arrange a tow.
result.why: A little noise while new pads bed in can happen, but a true grind usually points to a fitting problem: a pad not seated right, a shield bent during the job, or old rotors with a worn lip that new pads are hitting.

causes.name: Pad or clip not seated correctly
causes.clues: The grind started right after the job and is constant.

causes.name: Old rotors not replaced or resurfaced
causes.clues: Only the pads were changed.

causes.name: Dust shield bent during the repair
causes.clues: A light scrape, even when not braking.

you: Check the invoice to see whether rotors were replaced.
Note which wheel it comes from.

result.title: Treat grinding as a brake problem until it's checked
result.now: Don't drive it until the brakes are inspected. Grinding can mean the pads are worn down to metal, and stopping can get worse quickly. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If the pedal feels soft, the car takes longer to stop, or the grind is harsh on every stop, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If it was only on the first stop or two after rain, it may just be rust. Still mention it at the inspection.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, pull over and let it cool. Don't keep driving.
result.why: Grinding has harmless causes, like surface rust, but it's also the classic sign of pads worn to metal. Without knowing when it happens, it's safest to have the pads and rotors looked at quickly.

causes.name: Pads worn to metal
causes.clues: There was a squeal before, and the pads are old.

causes.name: Surface rust
causes.clues: Only after the car sits or gets wet.

causes.name: Debris or a bent shield
causes.clues: A light scrape after gravel or a tire change.

you: Record a short video with sound when it happens. It helps the shop.
Look at the pads through the wheel spokes.

q_pedal.q: How does the clutch pedal feel, and can you get into gear?
q_pedal.help: The clutch pedal should feel firm and spring back up on its own every time.

opts.a: The pedal is soft, sinks to the floor, or stays down
It's hard to get into any gear, and it grinds into most gears, even from a stop
The pedal feels normal and it shifts, but it grinds sometimes
I'm not sure
Only reverse
Mainly one or two forward gears (often 2nd or 3rd)
Most gears, including first from a stop
I'm not sure

q_how.q: When does it grind into that gear?
q_how.help: Synchronizers (synchros) are small rings inside the gearbox that match gear speeds so they slide together quietly. Each forward gear has one.

opts.a: Only when I shift quickly or at high revs. A slow, deliberate shift is fine
Even when I shift slowly and press the clutch all the way down
Mostly when the car is cold, and it gets better as it warms up
It also pops out of gear on its own
I'm not sure

result.title: The clutch hydraulic system may have lost pressure
result.now: Pull over safely and turn the engine off. Don't drive it, because you may not be able to shift or stop the car from creeping. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the brake pedal also feels soft, the shared fluid reservoir may be low. Don't move the car at all.
If pumping the clutch pedal a few times brings it back, that points to a leak or air in the system. It still needs fixing before you drive.
If the shared fluid reservoir is low but you can't see a leak, don't top it up and drive. Have it inspected first, because the brakes may be affected too.
result.why: Most manual cars use fluid to push the clutch apart when you press the pedal. If fluid leaks out or a seal fails, the pedal can sink and the clutch stays partly engaged, so the gears grind and the car may not stop pulling in gear.

causes.name: Failing clutch master cylinder
causes.clues: The pedal sinks slowly, and there may be fluid on the carpet under the pedal.

causes.name: Leaking clutch slave cylinder
causes.clues: Fluid dripping near the bell housing, where the engine and gearbox meet.

causes.name: Broken clutch cable or linkage
causes.clues: On cable-operated clutches, the pedal suddenly goes limp with no resistance.
causes.against: Doesn't apply to hydraulic clutches.

you: With the engine off, check the clutch fluid reservoir (on many cars it's shared with the brake fluid reservoir).
Look for wet spots under the dash near the pedal.

result.title: The clutch may not be fully releasing
result.now: Check that the floor mat isn't stopping the clutch pedal from reaching the floor, then get the clutch checked within the next few days.
if: If the pedal starts feeling soft or sinking, or you can't get into gear at all, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If it only happened after a recent clutch repair, the adjustment or bleeding may need to be redone.
If the brake pedal also feels soft or sinks, or the shared brake and clutch fluid reservoir is low, don't drive it. Have it inspected first.
result.why: When you press the pedal, the clutch should fully disconnect the engine from the gearbox. If it doesn't release all the way, the gears are still being turned while you try to shift, so they grind in every gear, even from a stop.

causes.name: Air or low fluid in the clutch hydraulics
causes.clues: The pedal feels slightly softer or lower than it used to.

causes.name: Clutch cable out of adjustment or stretched
causes.clues: An older car with a cable clutch, and the pedal engages near the floor.

causes.name: Warped clutch disc or worn pilot bearing
causes.clues: Grinding plus shuddering when pulling away, or noise that changes when you press the pedal.

you: Make sure the floor mat isn't under the pedal.
Check the clutch fluid reservoir level, if your car has one.
shop: Clutch release and pedal travel check
Clutch inspection if the hydraulics are fine

result.title: Grinding into reverse is often a timing issue, not a fault
result.now: Come to a complete stop, press the clutch fully, and wait two or three seconds before shifting into reverse.
if: If it still grinds after a full stop and a pause, the clutch may not be fully releasing. Book a check.
If the grinding is getting worse, or it's hard to get into other gears too, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: In many manual gearboxes, reverse doesn't have a synchronizer to match gear speeds. If the gears are still spinning when you shift, they clash. Waiting a moment after pressing the clutch lets them stop.

causes.name: Gears still spinning when shifting
causes.clues: It grinds only if you shift quickly, and waiting fixes it.

causes.name: Clutch not fully releasing
causes.clues: It grinds even after waiting, or other gears are getting notchy.

causes.name: Worn reverse gear teeth
causes.clues: A long history of reverse grinding.

you: Try stopping fully and waiting a few seconds with the clutch down before selecting reverse.
Try shifting briefly into a forward gear first, then into reverse.

result.title: A worn synchronizer for that gear is a common cause
result.now: Shift more slowly into that gear and pause briefly in neutral. Book a transmission check when convenient, and ask for the gear oil to be checked.
if: If it starts grinding even on slow shifts, or more gears start grinding, get it checked within a few days.
If the car pops out of gear, don't rely on it on hills or in traffic and get it checked soon.
result.why: Each forward gear has a synchronizer that matches speeds before the gear engages. When one wears, it may not keep up with quick shifts, so that gear grinds while the others are fine. It gets worse with time, but slowing your shifts reduces further wear.

causes.name: Worn synchronizer ring
causes.clues: One gear grinds on quick shifts, often 2nd or 3rd, and is fine when you go slowly.

causes.name: Low or incorrect gear oil
causes.clues: Several gears feel notchy, especially when cold.

causes.name: Clutch not fully releasing
causes.clues: Other gears grind a little too.
causes.against: If only one gear grinds, the clutch is less likely.

you: Try a slower shift with a short pause in neutral and see if the grind goes away.
Note which gear grinds and whether it's going up or down through the gears.
shop: Gear oil level and condition check

result.title: The synchronizer or gear may be badly worn
result.now: Avoid that gear where you can, and get the transmission checked within the next few days.
if: If more gears start grinding, or there's a whine or metallic noise while driving, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the gear oil is low or has metal flakes in it, there may be internal wear. A shop will usually check the oil and the clutch release before recommending gearbox repair.
If the car pops out of gear, don't rely on it on hills or in traffic.
result.why: Grinding even when you shift slowly with the clutch fully down can mean the gearbox can no longer match speeds for that gear. Continued grinding chips the gear teeth and can spread damage through the transmission.

causes.name: Badly worn synchronizer
causes.clues: One gear grinds every time, no matter how you shift.

causes.name: Damaged gear teeth or shift sleeve
causes.clues: A crunch plus a notchy, rough feel going into that gear.

causes.name: Clutch not fully releasing
causes.clues: Other gears also grind a little.

you: Note exactly which gear grinds and whether it's when shifting up or down.
shop: Gear oil level and condition check (look for metal particles)

result.title: The gear oil may be low, old or the wrong type
result.now: Book a check when convenient, and ask for the gear oil level and type to be checked against your owner's manual.
if: If you see a leak under the gearbox, get it checked within a few days. Low oil wears the gearbox quickly.
If it keeps grinding after it's fully warm, a worn synchronizer is more likely.
If more gears start grinding, or you hear a whine or metallic noise while driving, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: Synchronizers rely on the right gear oil to grip and match speeds. Oil that's low, old or too thick makes shifting stiff and grindy when cold, and it usually improves as the oil warms and thins.

causes.name: Low gear oil from a leak
causes.clues: Oily drips under the gearbox or around the axle seals.

causes.name: Old or wrong type of gear oil
causes.clues: It hasn't been changed in a long time, or a different fluid was used.

causes.name: Early synchronizer wear
causes.clues: One gear grinds more than the others.

you: Look under the gearbox for oily drips.
Check your service records for when the gear oil was last changed.
shop: Gear oil level and condition check
Gear oil change with the specified fluid

result.title: Worn parts inside the gearbox or a loose mount may be letting it slip out of gear
result.now: Get the transmission checked within the next few days. Until then, avoid using that gear on hills or in heavy traffic where you can.
if: If it pops out of gear often, or you can't keep it in gear, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If you also hear a clunk when accelerating or letting off, worn engine or transmission mounts may be part of the problem.
If it pops out of gear on a hill or in traffic, use the brakes and parking brake to hold the car before reselecting a gear.
result.why: A gear that grinds going in and then jumps out on its own often has worn engagement parts. Losing drive unexpectedly is a safety problem in traffic or on a slope, and the wear tends to get worse.

causes.name: Worn shift sleeve, gear teeth or synchronizer
causes.clues: It pops out of the same gear, often under load or when letting off the gas.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mounts
causes.clues: A clunk or rocking when accelerating, and the shifter moves when the engine rocks.

causes.name: Worn shift linkage or detent spring
causes.clues: The shifter feels loose or sloppy.

you: Note which gear it pops out of and whether it's when accelerating or slowing down.
shop: Gear oil check and transmission inspection

result.title: Have the clutch and gearbox checked
result.now: Book a check when convenient. Note which gears grind and when, and shift gently until it's looked at.
if: If the clutch pedal goes soft or sinks, or you can't get into gear, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If the car pops out of gear, get it checked within a few days.
If the brake pedal also feels soft or sinks, don't drive it. On many cars the clutch and brakes share a fluid reservoir.
result.why: Grinding when shifting comes from either the clutch not fully releasing or wear inside the gearbox. A technician can tell them apart quickly by checking the clutch release and the gear oil.

causes.name: Clutch not fully releasing
causes.clues: Grinding in most gears, especially from a stop.

causes.name: Worn synchronizer
causes.clues: Grinding in one gear, mainly on quick shifts.

causes.name: Low or wrong gear oil
causes.clues: Worse when cold.

you: Make sure the floor mat isn't blocking the clutch pedal.
Note which gears grind and whether it's worse when cold.
shop: Gear oil level and condition check

q_severity.help: The brake booster is the round canister behind the brake pedal, on the driver's side of the engine bay. It makes the pedal easier to press.

opts.a: Only when the engine is off, before I start it
It went hard after the engine stalled or shut off while driving
All the time with the engine running, and I can barely stop the car
It's stiffer than usual, but the car stops if I push harder
The pedal feels normal, but the car takes longer to stop
I'm not sure

q_clues.q: Do you notice either of these as well?

opts.a: A hissing sound when I press the pedal, or the idle stumbles when I brake
The steering has also become heavy (common on trucks and diesels)
Neither of these / I'm not sure
The brakes were just replaced (new pads or rotors)
The brakes got very hot, like on a long downhill or while towing, and I smell burning
The car also pulls to one side when braking
There's oil or fluid on the inside of a wheel
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: A hard pedal with the engine off is usually normal
result.now: Start the engine with your foot on the brake. The pedal should drop slightly and then feel normal.
if: If the pedal doesn't drop when the engine starts, the brake booster or its vacuum supply may have a problem. Have the brakes checked within a few days.
If the pedal is still hard once the engine is running, treat it as a brake fault and don't drive until it's checked.
If the pedal sinks toward the floor with the engine running, or the red brake light is on, don't drive it.
result.why: The brake booster stores enough vacuum for one or two assisted presses after the engine stops. Once that's used up, the pedal feels hard until the engine runs again. That's how most systems are designed to work.

causes.name: Normal booster behavior with the engine off
causes.clues: The pedal is hard only before starting, and feels normal once the engine runs.

causes.name: Weak booster or leaking check valve
causes.clues: The pedal doesn't drop at start-up, or the assist runs out right after you shut the engine off.

you: With the engine off, press the pedal several times until it's hard. Hold it down and start the engine. The pedal should sink slightly.
shop: Brake booster and check valve test

result.title: The engine shutting off may have taken away your brake assist
result.now: Once you're safely stopped, set the parking brake and don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic find out why the engine stalled.
if: If it restarts and the pedal feels normal again, an engine that stalls while driving still isn't safe. Have it checked before driving any distance.
If the pedal stays hard with the engine running, or sinks, or the red brake light is on, don't drive it.
If the temperature gauge was high or you saw steam before it stalled, don't restart it.
result.why: Most brake boosters rely on the running engine. When the engine dies, you may get one or two assisted presses, then the pedal turns hard and braking takes much more force. Steering assist may be lost too. The stall is the problem to find, and the brakes should be checked along with it.

causes.name: Fuel or ignition problem
causes.clues: Sputtering before it died, or a check engine light.

causes.name: Idle control problem
causes.clues: It stalls when slowing down or coming to a stop.

causes.name: Charging system failure
causes.clues: The battery light came on before the engine died.

you: Note any warning lights that came on before it stalled.
Note whether it stalled while slowing down or at speed.

result.title: Your brakes may have lost their power assist
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you hear a loud hiss when you press the pedal, tell the shop. It points to a torn booster or a disconnected vacuum hose.
If a brake system warning message is on (common on hybrids and electric cars), have it towed to a shop equipped for your model.
If the pedal sinks toward the floor or the red brake light is on, don't move the car at all.
result.why: With working assist, light pressure stops the car. Without it, you need far more force and the stopping distance grows, which is dangerous in an emergency stop. Common causes are a failed booster, a cracked or disconnected vacuum hose, or loss of whatever powers the booster.

causes.name: Cracked or disconnected vacuum hose
causes.clues: It happened suddenly, with hissing or a rough idle.

causes.name: Failed brake booster
causes.clues: Hissing from under the dash near the pedal, and the pedal doesn't drop when the engine starts.

causes.name: Failed vacuum pump or electric brake booster
causes.clues: A diesel, some turbocharged engines, a hybrid or an electric car, often with a warning message.

causes.name: Hydraulic booster or power steering problem
causes.clues: A truck or diesel, and the steering got heavy too.

you: With the car parked and in Park, listen for a hiss near the pedal or under the hood as you press the brake.
shop: Vacuum supply and check valve test
Code scan on cars with electric boosters

result.title: A vacuum leak at the brake booster or its hose is possible
result.now: Avoid driving it until the brakes are inspected. Have a mobile mechanic check it where it's parked, or have it towed to a shop.
if: If the pedal becomes very hard, sinks, or the red brake light comes on, don't move the car at all.
If the check engine light is on or the idle is rough, a leaking vacuum hose is more likely. Tell the shop.
result.why: The booster uses vacuum from the engine. A hiss when you press the pedal often means air is leaking in, either through a torn diaphragm inside the booster or a cracked hose or check valve. The leak reduces the assist and can also upset the engine's idle. A torn booster can get worse without warning.

causes.name: Torn booster diaphragm
causes.clues: The hiss comes from under the dash, near the pedal.

causes.name: Cracked vacuum hose or failed check valve
causes.clues: The hiss comes from under the hood, and the idle may be rough.

causes.name: Vacuum leak elsewhere on the engine
causes.clues: A rough idle or check engine light.
causes.against: If the hiss doesn't change when you press the brake, it's likely not the booster.

you: With a helper pressing the pedal, listen for where the hiss comes from.
Note whether the check engine light is on.

result.title: The power steering pump or drive belt may have stopped working, taking brake assist with it
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Have it towed.
if: If the battery light is on or the temperature gauge is climbing, a broken drive belt is likely. Pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and don't restart it.
If you see power steering fluid leaking or smell burning fluid, keep away from hot parts and tell the shop.
result.why: Some trucks, vans and diesel vehicles use a hydraulic brake booster powered by the power steering pump instead of engine vacuum. If the pump stops working, the steering and the brakes both get much heavier at once. On many engines, a broken belt also stops the alternator and water pump.

causes.name: Broken or slipping drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal beforehand, the battery light on, or the belt is missing.

causes.name: Low power steering fluid
causes.clues: A leak, or whining when you turn the wheel.

causes.name: Failed power steering pump or hydraulic booster
causes.clues: A whine, with the fluid level full.

you: With the engine off, look to see if the drive belt is still in place.
With the engine cold, check the power steering fluid level.

result.title: The brake booster may be losing some of its assist
result.now: Avoid driving it until the brakes are inspected. Have a mobile mechanic check it where it's parked, or have it towed to a shop.
if: If the pedal gets harder, sinks, or the red brake light comes on, don't move the car at all.
