If it's hard mainly on the first press after the car has been parked, the check valve may be leaking vacuum. Mention that to the shop.
result.why: When the pedal is stiffer than usual but the car still stops with extra effort, the booster may be giving only part of its normal help. Common reasons are a weak booster, a leaking check valve or hose, or low engine vacuum. It can get worse over time, sometimes suddenly.

causes.name: Weak brake booster
causes.clues: The pedal barely drops when you start the engine.

causes.name: Leaking check valve or vacuum hose
causes.clues: The first press after parking is hard, then it improves.

causes.name: Low engine vacuum
causes.clues: A rough idle or other engine performance problems.

you: With the engine off, press the pedal several times, hold it down, then start the engine. It should sink slightly.

result.title: New pads may not be bedded in yet, or the brakes need a recheck
result.now: Before driving further, call the shop that did the work, describe what you notice, and ask them to recheck it. Many shops can come to you or arrange to bring the car in.
if: If it's much harder to stop than before the work, don't drive it. Ask the shop to check it right away.
If the shop tells you it's normal bedding-in for the pads they fitted, follow their bedding-in steps and have it rechecked if it isn't clearly better within a few drives.
If the pedal sinks or feels soft, or the red brake light comes on, don't drive it.
result.why: New pads and rotors need a number of moderate stops to lay down a thin layer of pad material on the rotor, called bedding in. Until then they can grip less. A shop will usually check pad seating, the calipers and the brake fluid before deciding anything needs to change.

causes.name: Pads not bedded in yet
causes.clues: Just replaced, and getting better day by day.

causes.name: Contaminated pads or rotors
causes.clues: Grease or fluid got on them during the job, often with squealing.

causes.name: Pad type or a caliper that isn't working properly
causes.clues: The car pulls to one side, or it's no better after several days.

you: Note whether braking improves over the next few drives.

result.title: The brakes may have overheated and lost grip (brake fade)
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, set the parking brake and let the brakes cool for at least 30 minutes. Have the brakes checked before relying on them again.
if: If braking doesn't feel normal once the brakes are cool, or the pedal is soft, don't drive it. Have it towed.
Before moving the car again, call a shop or roadside assistance and describe what happened. If the brakes feel weak, soft or smell hot again at any point, stop and get help.
On long downhills, shift to a lower gear so the engine helps slow the car, instead of riding the brakes.
If you see smoke from a wheel, keep away from it until it cools.
result.why: Brake pads can only absorb so much heat. Constant or repeated braking, especially downhill or with a heavy load, overheats them so they grip less, and you often smell burning. They often recover once cool, but severe overheating can glaze the pads and damage the rotors, and very hot brakes can also boil the brake fluid.

causes.name: Overheated pads
causes.clues: A burning smell after long or hard braking.

causes.name: Glazed pads
causes.clues: Braking stays weak even after cooling, and the pads look shiny.

causes.name: Dragging brake adding heat
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter than the others.

you: Once cool, test the brakes gently at low speed in an empty, safe area.

result.title: A stuck caliper or a problem on one side of the brakes is possible
result.now: Avoid driving it until the brakes are inspected. Have a mobile mechanic check it where it's parked, or have it towed to a shop.
if: If a wheel smokes or smells burning, keep away from it and let it cool.
If you see fluid at one wheel, or the pedal feels soft or sinks, don't move the car at all.
result.why: When one side does less of the braking, the car stops less effectively and pulls toward the side that's working. A stuck caliper, a collapsed brake hose, or contaminated pads on one side are common causes.

causes.name: Seized caliper or slide pins
causes.clues: One wheel is hotter, or its pads are worn unevenly.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose
causes.clues: The pull comes and goes, or one wheel drags after braking.

causes.name: Contaminated pads on one side
causes.clues: Fluid or grease on that wheel.

you: Note which way the car pulls.
After a short drive, hold your hand near (not on) each wheel to compare heat.

result.title: Oil or brake fluid may have soaked the brakes on that wheel
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed so a shop can find the leak and check the brakes on that axle.
if: If it's brake fluid, the leak can also make the pedal soft or turn on the red brake light. Tell the shop what you've noticed.
If you see smoke or smell burning from that wheel, keep away from it and let it cool.
result.why: Brake pads lose much of their grip when oil, grease or brake fluid soaks into them, and it usually can't be reliably cleaned off, so a shop will often recommend new pads once the leak is confirmed. Fluid on a wheel also means something is leaking, and it may be the brake system itself.

causes.name: Leaking brake caliper or wheel cylinder
causes.clues: Wet fluid on the inside of the tire, and the brake fluid level is dropping.

causes.name: Leaking axle seal
causes.clues: Oily fluid at a rear wheel on a rear-wheel-drive vehicle, often with a gear-oil smell.

causes.name: Grease from a torn CV joint boot
causes.clues: Dark grease spattered inside a front wheel.
causes.against: This grease usually sprays around the wheel area rather than soaking the pads.

you: Check the brake fluid level.
Look inside the wheel for wet spots without touching hot parts.
shop: Pad and rotor condition check on the affected axle

result.title: Your brakes may be worn or not working fully. Have them inspected before driving
result.now: Avoid driving it until the brakes are inspected. Have a mobile mechanic check it where it's parked, or have it towed to a shop.
if: If the pedal gets hard to press, sinks, or the red brake light comes on, don't move the car at all.
If you hear grinding when braking, the pads may be worn down to metal. Tell the shop.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, keep away from it and let it cool.
result.why: When the pedal feels normal but the car takes longer to stop, the problem is often at the wheels: worn or glazed pads, worn rotors, or a caliper that isn't working well. Worn tires can also lengthen stops. These get worse with time and can lead to bigger repairs.

causes.name: Worn pads or rotors
causes.clues: Squealing or grinding, or the brakes haven't been checked in a while.

causes.name: Glazed pads
causes.clues: Heavy braking or riding the brakes recently.

causes.name: Caliper not applying fully
causes.clues: Pulling to one side, or uneven pad wear.

causes.name: Worn tires
causes.clues: Little tread left, and stops feel worse on wet roads.

you: Look through the wheel spokes at the brake pad thickness if you can see it.
Check the tire tread depth.

q_what_happens.q: What happens when you try to start it cold?
q_what_happens.help: "Cranking" is the whirring sound of the engine turning over (rrr-rrr-rrr) before it fires up.

opts.a: It cranks slowly and sluggishly, like it's struggling
Rapid clicking, or nothing at all
It cranks at normal speed but takes a long time to fire up
It starts, but shakes, runs rough or stalls until it warms up
It's a diesel and it cranks a long time, often with white smoke
I'm not sure

q_battery.q: Which of these fits your battery?
q_battery.help: The battery's date is often on a sticker or stamped on top. If you can't find it, choose "I'm not sure".

opts.a: It's older than about 4 years
It's newer, but the battery light has come on or the lights dim while driving
It's newer and tests fine, with no warning lights
I'm not sure
I smell raw fuel, or see a wet spot under the car
It starts much better if I turn the key to ON for a few seconds before cranking
The check engine light is on, or it runs rough after it starts
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: The battery may be too weak for cold starts
result.now: Check that the battery clamps are tight and free of crusty buildup, then have the battery tested. Many auto parts stores test batteries free.
if: If it fails a load test, replace it before it leaves you stranded. Age alone doesn't prove it's bad, but a battery older than about 4 to 5 years is worth testing before winter.

If it won't start at all, a jump start or booster pack may get you going. If you jump-start it, follow your owner's manual. Don't jump a battery that is cracked, leaking, swollen or smells like rotten eggs.
If the battery tests good, ask them to test the alternator and starter too.
If the battery light comes on or the lights dim while driving, the charging system may be the problem. Have it tested soon.
result.why: A battery loses a lot of its strength in the cold, while cold, thick oil makes the engine harder to turn. An aging battery that seems fine in summer often can't keep up on a cold morning.

causes.name: Aging or weak battery
causes.clues: The battery is more than 4 years old, and the crank has gotten slower over time.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery terminals
causes.clues: White or green buildup on the clamps.

causes.name: Battery not getting fully charged
causes.clues: Mostly short trips, or the car sits for days at a time.

you: Check and clean the battery terminals.
Find the battery's date code.
Have the battery tested.

result.title: The alternator may not be keeping the battery charged
result.now: Get the charging system tested within the next few days. Until then, avoid short trips with lots of lights and accessories on.
if: If the battery light comes on and stays on while driving, the car may run only until the battery is drained. Head for a safe place to stop rather than a long drive.
If the headlights get dim and the dash flickers, pull over safely. The battery is running out.
If the battery light comes on along with a rising temperature gauge or heavy steering, a broken drive belt is possible. Pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: A newer battery that keeps running low usually isn't getting recharged properly. Cold weather makes the problem show up first because starting takes more power.

causes.name: Failing alternator
causes.clues: The battery light flickers or stays on, or the lights dim at idle.

causes.name: Loose or worn drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal on startup, especially when cold or damp.

causes.name: Something draining the battery while parked
causes.clues: It's worst after the car sits overnight or for a few days.

you: Watch for the battery light while driving.
Listen for a belt squeal on startup.

result.title: A worn starter, poor cable connection or too-thick oil are possible causes
result.now: Check your owner's manual or the oil cap for the correct oil grade and compare it with your last oil change receipt. Then book a check of the starter and cables.
if: If the crank keeps getting slower or you hear grinding, get it checked soon. A starter that's failing usually gets worse.
If the battery cables feel warm after cranking, a poor connection is likely. Tell the shop.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the hood after cranking, stop trying to start it.
result.why: With a good battery, a slow cold crank points to something resisting the starter or limiting its power. A worn starter, a corroded cable or ground strap, or oil that's thicker than recommended can each do it.

causes.name: Worn starter motor
causes.clues: The crank is slow even when warm, or it has made grinding noises.

causes.name: Corroded cable or loose ground strap
causes.clues: Visible corrosion, or a cable that's warm after cranking.

causes.name: Engine oil that's too thick for the weather
causes.clues: A recent oil change with a different grade than the manual lists.

you: Check the oil grade used at the last oil change.
Look for corrosion on the battery cables and ground strap.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the battery cables

result.title: Fuel pressure may be draining away overnight
result.now: Turn the key to ON and wait a few seconds before cranking, or do it twice, to let the fuel pump build pressure. Book a check when convenient.
if: If it starts getting harder to start even with this trick, or it hesitates while driving, get it checked sooner.
If you smell fuel at any point, stop trying to start it and have it inspected before driving.
result.why: The fuel system is meant to hold pressure after you shut off the engine. If a valve in the pump or a leaky injector lets it bleed off overnight, the pump has to refill the lines before the engine can start, so it cranks longer.

causes.name: Leaking check valve in the fuel pump
causes.clues: Long crank after sitting for hours, but quick restarts after short stops.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector
causes.clues: A puff of black smoke on startup, or a fuel smell.

causes.name: Weak fuel pump
causes.clues: Hesitation under hard acceleration too.

you: Turn the key to ON and listen for the pump's 2-second hum from the back.
Note whether pre-priming makes it start quickly.

result.title: A sensor or ignition problem may be making cold starts harder
result.now: Have the trouble codes read, then book a check. Many parts stores read codes free.
if: If the check engine light is flashing, don't drive it. That usually signals a serious misfire that can damage the catalytic converter.
If it stalls while driving, don't drive it until it's fixed.
result.why: A cold engine needs extra fuel and a strong spark to start. For example, if the coolant temperature sensor tells the computer the engine is warm, it won't add that extra fuel. Worn spark plugs or weak coils also struggle most in the cold.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: The temperature gauge acts oddly, or the engine runs rich or lean when cold.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs or weak ignition coil
causes.clues: Rough running or a misfire code, especially on damp mornings.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or vacuum leak
causes.clues: A low or uneven idle after it starts.

you: Get the codes read and write them down.
Check when the spark plugs were last replaced.
shop: Code scan and live coolant temperature data

result.title: The engine may not be getting the right mix when cold
result.now: Let it idle for 30 seconds before driving off on cold mornings, and book a check when convenient.
if: If the check engine light flashes or the car shakes hard, don't drive it. A misfire can damage the catalytic converter.
If it stalls once you're moving, don't drive it until it's checked. Losing the engine can make steering and braking much harder.
If you smell fuel, stop the engine and keep sparks and flames away.
result.why: A cold engine needs a higher idle and extra fuel until it warms up. If a temperature sensor reads wrong, the idle system is dirty, or a cylinder misfires in the cold, the engine shakes or dies until it warms.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control fault
causes.clues: A low, uneven idle that improves when warm.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: The temperature gauge acts oddly, or fuel economy has dropped.

causes.name: Cold misfire from worn plugs or a weak coil
causes.clues: Shaking or a flashing check engine light right after starting.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or an idle that smooths out when warm.

you: Note the outside temperature when it happens.
Watch for a flashing check engine light.
shop: Code scan and live sensor data

result.title: Diesel cold starts often point to glow plugs or the battery
result.now: Turn the key to ON and wait for the coil-shaped glow plug light to go out before cranking. If it's still hard to start, book a check of the glow plugs and battery.
if: If the glow plug light flashes or stays on while driving, have the system scanned soon.
If it's very cold and the fuel looks cloudy or the engine starts then dies, the fuel may be gelling. Use a block heater if you have one and get it checked.
result.why: Diesel engines rely on glow plugs to warm the cylinders before a cold start. If some have failed, or the battery can't power them and the starter together, the engine cranks a long time and puffs white smoke until it catches.

causes.name: Failed glow plugs or glow plug controller
causes.clues: A long crank with white smoke that clears once it's running.
causes.against: If it starts fine with a long glow wait, a weak battery is more likely.

causes.name: Weak battery
causes.clues: A slow crank, or the battery is more than 4 years old.

causes.name: Fuel gelling in extreme cold
causes.clues: Very cold temperatures, and it starts then dies or loses power.

you: Wait for the glow plug light to go out before cranking.
Have the battery tested.
shop: Glow plug resistance and circuit test
Fuel filter and fuel condition check

result.title: Possible fuel leak. Stop trying to start it
result.now: Don't try to start it again. Keep sparks and flames away and have the car towed.
if: If fuel is dripping or pooling, move people away from the car and call the fire department.
If the smell fades and you can't see a wet spot, still have it checked before starting again. Fuel can leak where you can't see it.
result.why: A raw fuel smell or a wet spot can mean fuel is getting somewhere it shouldn't. A leak can also let fuel pressure drain away overnight, which causes long cranking, and fuel near hot parts is a fire risk.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line or fitting
causes.clues: A wet spot under the car along the fuel line route.

causes.name: Leaking injector seal or fuel rail
causes.clues: The smell is strongest at the engine.

causes.name: Flooded engine from repeated tries
causes.clues: Several long cranking attempts, and no visible leak.

you: From a distance, look for drips or wet spots under the car.
Don't smoke or use flames nearby.

result.title: Start with a battery test, then a shop check
result.now: Have the battery tested, since it's one of the most common causes of hard cold starts. If it passes, book a shop check and describe exactly what you hear.
if: If you smell fuel, stop trying to start it and keep sparks and flames away.
If it won't start at all, a jump start is a reasonable first try. If you jump-start it, follow your owner's manual. Don't jump a battery that is cracked, leaking, swollen or smells like rotten eggs.
If the check engine light flashes or the engine shakes hard after starting, don't drive it.
result.why: Hard cold starts come from three main areas: battery and starter, fuel delivery, and the sensors that set the cold-start fuel mix. The battery is the easiest and most common place to start.

causes.name: Weak battery
causes.clues: A slow crank, or the battery is more than 4 years old.

causes.name: Fuel pressure loss overnight
causes.clues: A normal crank that takes a long time to fire.

causes.name: Sensor or ignition problem
causes.clues: A check engine light, or rough running when cold.

you: Record a short video with sound of a cold start. It helps the shop a lot.
Have the battery tested.

q_temp.q: Before it was hard to start, was the temperature gauge higher than normal, or did you see steam?
q_temp.help: Most gauges sit near the middle once warm. Some cars only have a red thermometer warning light instead.

opts.a: Yes, it was high, in the red, or I saw steam
No, the gauge was in its normal spot
I'm not sure

q_what_happens.q: What happens when you try to start it hot?

opts.a: It cranks at normal speed but takes a long time to fire up
It cranks slowly, clicks or does nothing, then starts fine once it cools
It shuts off while driving when hot, and won't restart until it cools
I'm not sure
It mostly happens right after filling up with gas
It starts if I press the gas pedal partway, sometimes with a puff of black smoke
I smell raw fuel, or see a wet spot under the car
The check engine light is on
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be overheating. That needs to be fixed first
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn off the engine and let it cool for at least 30 minutes without opening the radiator cap. Then have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the coolant tank is low once the engine is cool, there's a leak or another fault behind it. Tell the shop.
If you see white smoke from the tailpipe or the coolant keeps disappearing, mention it. That can point to a head gasket problem.
Don't keep cranking or restarting the engine to test it. Each restart while it's overheated adds risk.
If you hear knocking, or the oil pressure light comes on, don't restart the engine at all.
result.why: An engine that runs too hot can be hard to restart, and starting it again risks serious damage like a warped cylinder head or blown head gasket. The overheating needs to be found and fixed first.

causes.name: Low coolant from a leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, drips under the front of the car, or a low overflow tank.

causes.name: Radiator fan not working
causes.clues: It runs hot in traffic or at idle, but is fine on the highway.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck closed
causes.clues: The gauge climbs quickly, with no visible leak.

you: Once fully cool, check the coolant level.
Look under the front of the car for coolant drips.

result.title: The starter or its wiring may be struggling when hot
result.now: Have the starter, battery and cables tested soon. Until then, plan stops so you aren't stranded if it won't restart.
if: If it gets worse or it fails to start several times, get it checked right away. A starter like this often fails completely.
If the battery is more than 4 to 5 years old, have it tested first.
If the temperature gauge was high, or you see steam, treat it as overheating first and don't keep trying to start it.
If you smell burning or see smoke after cranking, stop trying to start it.
result.why: Engine heat can raise the electrical resistance in a worn starter and its cables. A starter that's borderline when cold may only click or crank slowly when hot, then work again once it cools.

causes.name: Worn starter motor or solenoid
causes.clues: Slow cranking or a single click when hot, normal when cold.

causes.name: Corroded or loose battery cable or ground strap
causes.clues: Visible corrosion, or a cable that feels warm after cranking.

causes.name: Weak battery
causes.clues: The battery is older, or the crank is slow cold too.
causes.against: If it always cranks strongly when cold, the battery is less likely.

you: Check the battery terminals for corrosion.
Note whether it always works once cool.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the battery cables

result.title: A part may be failing when it heats up. Don't drive it until it's checked
result.now: Park it and have it towed to a shop, or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If it restarts after cooling down, don't count on it. These parts tend to fail more often and then completely.
If a check engine light came on, have the codes read. They can point a shop toward which part to test.
If the temperature gauge was high before it died, mention it. Overheating can cause the same symptom.
result.why: An engine that cuts out when hot and only restarts once cool often has a sensor, ignition part or fuel pump that stops working with heat. Losing the engine on the road can take away power steering and brake assist, so steering and braking need much more force.

causes.name: Crankshaft position sensor problem
causes.clues: It cuts out suddenly with no sputter, and restarts after cooling.

causes.name: Fuel pump problem
causes.clues: Sputtering or loss of power before it died.

causes.name: Ignition coil or ignition module problem
causes.clues: Misfiring or rough running when hot.

you: Note how long it runs before dying and how long it needs to cool.
Note any warning lights.

result.title: A stuck evaporative (EVAP) purge valve is a possible cause
result.now: After filling up, press the gas pedal slightly while cranking to help it start, and book a check when convenient.
if: If the check engine light comes on, have the codes read. EVAP faults usually set a code.
If it starts stalling at stops, get it checked sooner.
If you smell raw fuel around the car, stop trying to start it and have it inspected before driving.
result.why: Your car stores fuel vapor in a charcoal canister and burns it off while driving through a purge valve. If that valve sticks open, filling the tank pushes extra vapor into the engine, making it run too rich to start easily.

causes.name: Purge valve stuck open
causes.clues: Hard starts and a rough idle right after refueling only.

causes.name: Saturated charcoal canister
causes.clues: The tank is often filled past the first click of the pump.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector
causes.clues: Hard hot starts even when you haven't just refueled.

you: Note whether it only happens right after refueling.
Stop filling at the first click of the pump.

result.title: Extra fuel may be leaking into the engine after you shut it off
result.now: When it's hot, press the gas pedal partway while cranking to help clear the extra fuel. Book a check when convenient.
if: If you smell raw fuel around the car, stop trying to start it and have it inspected before driving.
If the check engine light starts flashing, don't drive it.
If it stalls while driving, don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: If an injector drips or fuel pressure is too high, fuel seeps into the hot engine while it sits. The engine then floods slightly on restart, so it needs a little extra air from the gas pedal, and may puff black smoke.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector
causes.clues: A puff of black smoke on hot restarts, or a misfire code.

causes.name: Faulty fuel pressure regulator
causes.clues: Fuel smell, or poor fuel economy.

causes.name: Coolant temperature sensor reading cold
causes.clues: The engine computer adds cold-start fuel to a hot engine. Often with a check engine light.

you: Note whether pressing the gas helps it start.
Notice any fuel smell after shutting it off.

result.title: Possible fuel leak. Stop trying to start it
result.now: Don't try to start it again. Keep sparks and flames away and have the car towed.
if: If fuel is dripping or pooling, move people away from the car and call the fire department.
If the smell fades and you can't see a wet spot, still have it checked before starting again. Fuel can leak where you can't see it.
result.why: A raw fuel smell or a wet spot can mean fuel is escaping. Leaked fuel on a hot engine or exhaust is a real fire risk, and the leak can also drop fuel pressure enough to cause hard starts.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line or fitting
causes.clues: A wet spot under the car along the fuel line route.

causes.name: Leaking injector seal or fuel rail
causes.clues: The smell is strongest at the engine.

causes.name: Flooded engine from repeated tries
causes.clues: Several long cranking attempts, and no visible leak.

you: From a distance, look for drips or wet spots under the car.
Don't smoke or use flames nearby.

result.title: A sensor fault may be confusing the engine computer when hot
result.now: Have the trouble codes read, then book a check. Many parts stores read codes free.
if: If the check engine light is flashing, don't drive it. That usually signals a serious misfire.
If it starts shutting off while driving, don't drive it until it's fixed.
If you smell raw fuel, stop trying to start it.
result.why: The computer sets fuel and spark timing based on sensor readings. A coolant temperature sensor reading wrong, or a crank sensor that weakens with heat, can make a hot restart slow or rough, and usually stores a code.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: The temperature gauge acts oddly, or there's a fuel smell on hot starts.

causes.name: Crankshaft or camshaft position sensor weakening
causes.clues: A long crank when hot, and sometimes stalling.

causes.name: EVAP purge valve fault
causes.clues: Worse right after refueling.

you: Get the codes read and write them down.
shop: Code scan and live sensor data
Crank and cam sensor signal test

result.title: Fuel pressure may be dropping while the engine sits hot
result.now: Try turning the key to ON for a few seconds before cranking to let the fuel pump build pressure. Book a check when convenient.
if: If it starts hesitating or losing power while driving, get it checked sooner.
If it ever dies while driving, don't drive it until it's fixed.
If you smell raw fuel, stop trying to start it and keep sparks and flames away.
result.why: The fuel system should hold pressure after shutdown. If it bleeds off while the engine sits hot, fuel in the lines can turn to vapor and the pump has to work longer to restart. A weak pump makes this worse in heat.

causes.name: Leaking check valve in the fuel pump
causes.clues: Long cranks after a short stop, better when you pre-prime with the key.

causes.name: Weak fuel pump
causes.clues: Hesitation under hard acceleration or on hot days.

causes.name: Leaking injector
causes.clues: A puff of black smoke on restart.

you: Note whether pre-priming with the key helps.
Listen for the pump's brief hum when you turn the key to ON.

result.title: A shop should check fuel pressure and sensors with the engine hot
result.now: Book a check, and ask the shop to test it after the engine is fully warm so the problem shows up.
if: If it shuts off while driving, don't drive it until it's fixed.
If you smell fuel, stop trying to start it and keep sparks and flames away.
If the temperature gauge is high or you see steam, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and let it cool. Don't open the radiator cap.
result.why: Hot-start problems usually come from fuel pressure bleeding off, a sensor that weakens with heat, or a starter struggling with engine heat. They often disappear once cool, so testing hot matters.

causes.name: Fuel pressure loss
causes.clues: A normal crank that takes a long time to fire.

causes.name: Heat-sensitive sensor
causes.clues: A check engine light, or stalling when hot.

causes.name: Starter heat soak
causes.clues: A slow crank or click when hot only.

you: Record a short video with sound of a hot restart.
Note how long the car sat before the hard start.

q_signs.q: Along with the hard shifts, do you notice any of these?

opts.a: It seems stuck in one gear, won't shift up, or feels very sluggish
A burning smell, or red or pink fluid under the car
A transmission temperature or transmission warning light
A loud clunk or bang, and the car jolts
None of these
I'm not sure
When I shift from Park into Drive or Reverse
When I press the gas or let off it suddenly
When the transmission changes gears while I'm driving
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When are the shifts harsh or late?
q_when.help: A "late" shift means the engine revs higher than usual before the transmission moves to the next gear.

opts.a: Only when the engine is cold, and it smooths out once warm
Shifts are late: it revs high before shifting up
One particular shift, every time (for example 1st to 2nd)
Hard downshifts when slowing down or coming to a stop
It started after the battery was disconnected or replaced, or after a fluid change
I'm not sure

q_fluid.q: Have you been able to check the transmission fluid?
q_fluid.help: Many cars have a transmission dipstick, often with a yellow or red handle; others have none and must be checked by a shop. Your owner's manual explains how. Healthy fluid is usually red or pink and doesn't smell burnt.

opts.a: Yes, it's low
The level is OK, but it's dark brown or smells burnt
The level and color look normal
My car has no dipstick / I'm not sure

result.title: The transmission may have gone into a protective "limp" mode
result.now: Keep any trips short and at low speed, and stay off highways where you can't keep up with traffic. Get the codes read and the transmission checked within a day or two.
if: If you also smell burning, see a temperature warning or the car loses drive, stop driving it and have it towed.
If turning the car off and restarting clears it for a while, don't count on that. The fault that caused it is still there.
If the check engine light is flashing or a red warning light comes on, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and have it towed.
result.why: When the transmission computer detects a problem, it often locks the transmission in one gear and shifts harshly to prevent further damage. That keeps the car movable at low speed, but it isn't meant for normal driving.

causes.name: Shift solenoid or pressure control fault
causes.clues: A check engine or transmission light, and harsh shifts before it got stuck.

causes.name: Faulty speed sensor or wiring
causes.clues: The speedometer jumps or drops out.

causes.name: Low fluid or internal slipping
causes.clues: Red or pink drips, or the revs flaring before it went into limp mode.

you: Note any warning lights or messages on the dash.
Look for red or pink fluid where you park.

result.title: The transmission may be leaking fluid or overheating
result.now: Pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and have the car towed.
if: If you see smoke, step away from the car. Fluid dripping on the exhaust can catch fire.
If it's only a few drops and there's no burning smell, check the level once the car is parked and cool, but still have it inspected before using the car.
If the car loses drive or won't go into gear, don't try to restart and move it. Wait for the tow.
result.why: Transmission fluid gives the transmission the pressure it needs to shift smoothly and keeps it cool. A leak lowers that pressure, which causes harsh shifts and slipping, and a burning smell means fluid or parts are overheating.

causes.name: Leaking pan gasket, cooler line or seal
causes.clues: Red or pink fluid under the middle or front of the car.

causes.name: Overheating from internal slipping
causes.clues: A sharp burnt smell after driving, with no visible leak.

causes.name: Fluid dripping onto the hot exhaust
causes.clues: Smoke from under the car along with the leak.

you: Note the color of any fluid under the car.

result.title: The transmission may be overheating, or it has flagged a fault
result.now: Pull over when it's safe, put it in Park and let it cool. Then have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the light goes off after cooling, it still needs checking before you rely on the car.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
If the car loses drive or the transmission slips, don't try to keep moving it. Wait for the tow.
result.why: Overheated transmission fluid breaks down and stops protecting the parts inside, which leads to harsh shifts, slipping and lasting damage. A warning light plus harsh shifting suggests the problem is already active, not just starting.

causes.name: Low fluid
causes.clues: A leak, or a level below the mark on the dipstick.

causes.name: Heavy load: towing, hills or hot weather
causes.clues: It happened while towing or climbing a long grade.

causes.name: Blocked or damaged transmission cooler
causes.clues: It keeps happening in traffic or warm weather.

you: Once it's cool, look for leaks under the car.

result.title: A clunk when shifting into gear can come from worn engine or transmission mounts
result.now: Book an inspection when convenient. Ask the shop to check the engine and transmission mounts and the driveline.
if: If the engine visibly lifts or rocks a lot when someone shifts into gear with the hood open (foot firmly on the brake), a broken mount is possible. Get it checked within a few days.
If the clunk gets louder or you feel new vibration while driving, have it checked sooner.
If you also smell burning, see red or pink fluid, or a transmission warning light comes on, stop driving it and have it checked before using the car.
result.why: Mounts are rubber blocks that hold the engine and transmission in place. When they wear out, the engine twists more as gear engages or power changes, and you feel it as a clunk or jolt even when the transmission itself is shifting normally.

causes.name: Worn or broken engine or transmission mount
causes.clues: A clunk shifting into Drive or Reverse, and more vibration at idle.

causes.name: Engine idling too high
causes.clues: The idle is higher than usual, so the car lurches when it goes into gear.

causes.name: Worn driveshaft joints or axle parts
causes.clues: A clunk when you press or let off the gas, especially on rear-wheel or all-wheel-drive vehicles.

you: With the hood open and someone holding the brake firmly, watch the engine as they shift into Drive and Reverse. Stand to the side, never in front of the car.

result.title: Hard shifts on one particular gear change can point to a solenoid or valve body problem
result.now: Have the codes read and book a transmission check within the next week or two. Note which shift is harsh.
if: If the shifts get noticeably worse, or the transmission starts slipping, get it checked within a few days.
If the car gets stuck in one gear, keep speeds low and have it checked right away.
If you smell burning, see a transmission temperature warning or the check engine light starts flashing, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
result.why: An automatic uses electric solenoids and a maze of passages called the valve body to control how firmly each gear engages. If a solenoid sticks or wears, that shift comes in too hard or at the wrong time. Stored codes and a road test with live data help a shop narrow it down before any parts are replaced.

causes.name: Sticking or worn shift or pressure control solenoid
causes.clues: A check engine light, or harsh shifts that come and go.

causes.name: Valve body wear
causes.clues: Harsh shifts that are worse when the transmission is warm.

causes.name: Worn clutch pack for that gear
causes.clues: A flare in revs right before the hard shift.

you: Write down which shift is harsh and at what speed.
Have the codes read if a warning light is on.
shop: Road test with live transmission data

result.title: Firm shifts only when cold can be normal warm-up behavior, or a sign of early wear
result.now: Let the car warm up for a minute or two and drive gently at first. Bring it up at your next service, or book a check if it gets worse.
if: If the shifts stay harsh after the car is warm, get it checked sooner.
If the fluid hasn't been changed in a long time, ask whether a fluid service is due for your car.
If you notice slipping, a burning smell or a transmission warning light at any time, stop driving it and have it checked before using the car.
result.why: Cold fluid is thicker, so shifts can feel firmer for the first few minutes, and many transmissions also change shift timing while warming up. If it's getting more noticeable, aging fluid or worn internal seals are the usual reasons.

causes.name: Thick cold fluid and normal warm-up shift strategy
causes.clues: Mildly firm shifts that disappear within a few minutes.
causes.against: If it's getting worse over time, there's likely more to it.

causes.name: Old or degraded fluid
causes.clues: No record of a fluid service, or dark fluid.

causes.name: Hardened internal seals
causes.clues: An older or high-mileage car, and the problem has grown over months.

you: Note the outside temperature and how long it lasts.

result.title: Late upshifts often come from a sensor, a solenoid or low fluid
result.now: Have the codes read and book a transmission check when convenient.
if: If the revs flare up without the car speeding up, that's slipping. Get it checked within a few days.
If it only shifts late in a sport or tow mode, check that mode isn't switched on. That's normal behavior for those modes.
If you smell burning or a transmission temperature warning comes on, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
result.why: The transmission decides when to shift using vehicle speed and how far you're pressing the gas. If a sensor sends the wrong reading, a solenoid is slow, or fluid is low, shifts come late and often land harder.

causes.name: Faulty throttle position or vehicle speed sensor
causes.clues: The speedometer acts strangely, or a check engine light is on.

causes.name: Sticking shift solenoid
causes.clues: Late shifts that come and go, sometimes with a code.

causes.name: Low or worn fluid
causes.clues: Red or pink drips, or dark fluid.

you: Check that sport, tow/haul or manual shift mode isn't switched on.
Look for red or pink drips where you park.
shop: Sensor data check on a road test

result.title: Hard downshifts when slowing can come from worn mounts or a control problem
result.now: Book a check when convenient and describe the speed where you feel the bump.
if: If the car feels like it's braking itself or nearly stalls when coming to a stop, get it checked within a few days. If it actually stalls, stop driving it: steering and braking take much more effort with the engine off.
If the check engine light is on, have the code read first.
If you smell burning or a transmission warning light comes on, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
result.why: As you slow down, the transmission steps down through the gears. A worn mount makes each of those shifts feel like a bump, while a sticking solenoid or a sensor problem can make the transmission downshift too firmly or at the wrong time.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mount
causes.clues: A clunk when shifting into Drive or Reverse too.

causes.name: Shift solenoid or valve body problem
causes.clues: Other shifts also feel harsh or erratic.

causes.name: Torque converter lockup not releasing smoothly
causes.clues: A shudder or near-stall as you come to a stop.

you: Note the speed where the bump happens.
shop: Road test with live transmission data

result.title: The transmission may just need to relearn your driving, or the wrong fluid was used
result.now: Drive normally for several days of mixed city and highway driving. Many transmissions relearn smooth shifts on their own.
if: If it started after a fluid change, confirm the exact fluid used matches your owner's manual. The wrong type can cause harsh shifts.
If it's no better after about a week, or it starts slipping, book a check. Some cars need a shop scan tool to reset or relearn shift settings.
If you smell burning, see fluid under the car or a transmission warning light comes on, stop driving it and have it checked before using the car.
result.why: Many automatics store learned settings that fine-tune each shift as parts wear. Disconnecting the battery can wipe those settings, so shifts feel firm until it relearns. After a fluid change, the wrong fluid or an incorrect level can also change how it shifts.

causes.name: Shift adaptations reset by a battery disconnect
causes.clues: Harsh shifts started right after battery work and are slowly improving.

causes.name: Wrong fluid type after a service
causes.clues: Harsh shifts started right after a fluid change.

causes.name: Fluid level set wrong after a service
causes.clues: Slipping or harsh shifts soon after a fluid change.

you: Check the service invoice for the fluid type used.
Note whether the shifts improve day by day.
shop: Transmission adaptation reset and relearn with a scan tool

result.title: Low transmission fluid may be the cause, and a leak is the usual reason it gets low
result.now: Top up with the exact fluid type listed in your owner's manual, then have the leak found within the next few days.
if: If harsh shifting or slipping continues after topping up, keep trips short and get it checked sooner.
If the level drops again quickly, stop using the car until the leak is fixed.
If you see smoke or smell burning, pull over, turn the engine off and step away. Fluid on the hot exhaust can catch fire.
result.why: Low fluid means low pressure inside the transmission, which can make gears engage late and then slam in. Fluid doesn't get used up in normal driving, so a low level usually means a leak somewhere.

causes.name: Leaking pan gasket or seal
causes.clues: Red or pink drips under the middle of the car.

causes.name: Leaking cooler line
causes.clues: Drips near the front of the car, under the radiator.

causes.name: Level set too low at a recent service
causes.clues: The problem started soon after a fluid change.

you: Recheck the level after a few days.
Put cardboard under the car overnight to spot drips.
shop: Correct fluid level check to factory procedure

result.title: Worn or overheated fluid may be playing a part in the harsh shifts
result.now: Have the transmission inspected within the next few days and ask whether a fluid service is right for its condition.
if: If the fluid smells strongly burnt or the shop finds metal debris, a shop will usually inspect further before deciding whether a fluid service alone is the right fix.
If slipping or a warning light appears, stop driving it and have it towed.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: Transmission fluid wears out with heat and miles. Old fluid loses the properties that let clutches engage smoothly, so shifts get harsh. Dark, burnt-smelling fluid also suggests the transmission has been running hot.

causes.name: Overdue fluid service
causes.clues: No record of a fluid change, especially with towing or heavy use.

causes.name: Overheating from towing, hills or heavy traffic
causes.clues: A burnt smell from the fluid.

causes.name: Internal wear
causes.clues: Debris in the fluid, or slipping as well as harsh shifts.

you: Find your records of the last transmission fluid service.

result.title: Get the codes read, then have the transmission checked
result.now: Have the transmission codes read and book a check within the next week or two. Note when the harsh shifts happen.
if: If it starts slipping, you smell burning or a warning light comes on, stop driving it and have it towed.
If you can check the fluid and it's low, top it up with the correct type and look for a leak.
If you see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: Harsh shifting can come from fluid, electronic controls, internal wear or worn mounts. Codes and a clear description of when it happens (cold or warm, which shift, up or down) let a shop narrow it down without guessing.

causes.name: Solenoid or sensor problem
causes.clues: A warning light or shifts that come and go.

causes.name: Low or worn fluid
causes.clues: Drips under the car or no record of a fluid service.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mounts
causes.clues: A clunk shifting into gear or when pressing the gas.

you: Keep a note of when it happens: cold or warm, which shift, up or down.
Look for red or pink drips where you park.

q_warning.q: Is the battery (charging) warning light on, or are other things acting strange, like gauges jumping or wipers slowing?
q_warning.help: The battery light usually looks like a small red battery with + and − signs. It warns that the car isn't charging, even though it's shaped like a battery.

opts.a: Yes, and the lights keep getting dimmer
Yes, the battery light is on, but the lights look about normal
No, it's just the lights
I'm not sure
Lights dim at idle, then brighten when I press the gas
Lights flicker or pulse while driving
Lights dip briefly when something turns on (A/C, windows, brakes)
Only one headlight is dim, flickers or is out
Both headlights are dim all the time, even at speed
Lights are dim mostly with the engine off or when starting
I'm not sure

q_flicker.q: What seems to set off the flicker?

opts.a: Bumps, or touching the headlight switch
It started after new LED or HID bulbs were put in
It's a steady pulse that changes with engine speed
I'm not sure

result.title: The alternator may have stopped charging, leaving the car running on the battery
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe and turn the engine off. Have it towed or call roadside assistance. It may not restart, and the lights could fail.
if: If you can't stop right away, turn off everything you don't need (radio, A/C, heated seats, rear defrost) to stretch the battery until you can pull over.
If you hear a squeal or the temperature gauge rises too, the belt may have broken. Turn off the engine as soon as you're safely stopped.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the hood or the dash, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: With the battery light on and lights fading, the battery is being drained instead of recharged. Once it runs low, the engine can shut off, and power steering, lights and wipers can all fail with it.

causes.name: Failed alternator
causes.clues: A whining or grinding noise from the engine, or the lights flickered in the days before.

causes.name: Broken or slipping belt
causes.clues: A squeal or slap, heavy steering, or the temperature gauge rising.

causes.name: Loose or corroded charging cable
causes.clues: The battery light flickered on and off over bumps before staying on.

you: Once safely stopped with the engine off, look to see if the belt is still on the pulleys.

result.title: The charging system may have a problem. Get it tested right away
result.now: Have the battery and alternator tested as soon as you can, ideally today. Many auto parts stores test them free. Before driving, look at whether the engine belt is still in place (engine off). Until it's tested, turn off electrical extras and avoid driving at night, on highways or far from help.
if: If the lights start dimming or the gauges act up, pull over and have it towed.
If the light only flickered once and went out, it can be a loose connection. Still have the system tested.
If the steering suddenly feels heavy, the temperature gauge rises or you hear a loud squeal, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. The belt may have failed.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: The battery light means the car's computer sees that the system isn't charging properly. The car can run for a while on the battery alone, but how long is hard to predict.

causes.name: Weak or failing alternator
causes.clues: A whining noise, or the lights dim at idle.

causes.name: Slipping or worn belt
causes.clues: A squeal on startup or when turning the steering wheel.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery or charging cable
causes.clues: Crusty buildup on the battery terminals, or the light flickers over bumps.

you: Check that the battery clamps are tight and clean.
Look at the belt for cracks or glazing (engine off).

result.title: The alternator may be getting weak, or the belt may be slipping
result.now: Have the battery and charging system tested when convenient. Most auto parts stores do this free.
if: If the battery light comes on or the car becomes slow to start, get it tested within a few days.
If it's slight and only happens with many accessories on, it can be normal on some cars. A test will tell you.
If you smell burning or the lights keep getting dimmer while driving, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
result.why: At idle, the alternator spins slowest and makes the least power. A healthy one still keeps up. If the lights dim noticeably at idle and brighten when you rev, the alternator or belt may not be keeping up with demand.

causes.name: Weakening alternator
causes.clues: The dimming has gotten worse over weeks, or there's a whine from the engine.

causes.name: Slipping belt
causes.clues: A brief squeal on cold starts or with the A/C on.

causes.name: Aging battery
causes.clues: The battery is more than 4–5 years old, or cranking is slower.

you: Note whether it's worse with the A/C, rear defrost or headlights on high.
shop: Alternator output test at idle and under load

result.title: A pulsing flicker can point to a failing alternator
result.now: Get the charging system tested within the next few days. Keep trips short and avoid night driving if you can.
if: If the battery light comes on or the lights start getting dimmer, pull over and have it towed.
If the flicker changes when you wiggle the battery cables (engine off), a loose connection is more likely.
If you smell burning or the alternator area feels very hot, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and have it checked before driving.
result.why: An alternator should give a steady voltage. When parts inside it wear out, the voltage pulses, and you see that as flickering lights that follow engine speed. If the alternator is the cause, it often gets worse until it stops charging, so it's worth testing rather than waiting.

causes.name: Failing alternator voltage regulator or diodes
causes.clues: A whine from the engine, or a battery that keeps going flat.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery or ground connection
causes.clues: Crusty buildup on terminals, or the flicker changes over bumps.

causes.name: Slipping belt
causes.clues: A squeal or chirp from the engine.

you: Check the battery terminals for tightness and corrosion.

result.title: A loose connection or worn headlight switch is a common cause
result.now: Check that the battery cables are tight and clean, then book an electrical check when convenient.
if: If the headlights go out completely, even briefly, get it fixed within a day or two and avoid driving at night.
If you smell burning or a connector feels hot, stop using the lights and get it checked right away.
result.why: When bumps or touching the switch make the lights flicker, power is being interrupted somewhere along the way. A worn switch, a loose plug or a corroded ground wire are the usual suspects.

causes.name: Worn headlight switch or stalk
causes.clues: Wiggling the switch makes the lights flicker.

causes.name: Loose or corroded ground wire or battery cable
causes.clues: Other things flicker too, like dash lights or the radio.

causes.name: Loose or melted headlight connector
causes.clues: Only one headlight flickers, or the plug looks browned.

you: Check the battery terminals.
Gently wiggle the headlight switch with the lights on and see if they flicker.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the lighting and ground circuits

result.title: The new bulbs may not be compatible with your car's electrical system
result.now: Put the original-type bulbs back in and see if the flicker stops.
if: If the flicker stops with the original bulbs, the new ones weren't a match for your car's lighting system.
If it still flickers with the original bulbs, have the wiring and switch checked.
If a bulb connector looks melted or browned, or you smell hot plastic, stop using those lights and have the wiring checked before driving at night.
result.why: Many cars check headlight bulbs by sending small pulses of power through them. Some LED and HID bulbs react to that with flicker, or set off a bulb-out warning. In that case the bulb, rather than the car, is often the issue.

causes.name: Bulb not compatible with the car's bulb-check system
causes.clues: It started right after the new bulbs went in.

causes.name: Loose fit or connector on the new bulb
causes.clues: Only one side flickers.

causes.name: Wiring or switch problem
causes.clues: Other lights flicker too.

you: Reinstall the original-type bulbs and compare.
Check that each bulb is seated and its plug is firmly connected.
shop: Body control module scan for bulb faults

result.title: A brief dip is often normal, but a big one points to the battery or connections
result.now: Check that the battery terminals are tight and clean, and have the battery and charging system tested when convenient.
if: If the dip is getting bigger or the battery light flickers with it, get it tested within a few days.
If the engine stumbles or nearly stalls when the dip happens, get it checked within a day or two.
If the engine actually stalls, stop driving it until it's checked. Steering and braking take much more effort with the engine off.
result.why: Big electrical loads, like the A/C fan or power windows, briefly pull extra power. A quick, small dip is normal on many cars. A deep or long dip means the battery, alternator or a connection is struggling to keep up.

causes.name: Aging battery
causes.clues: The battery is more than 4–5 years old.

causes.name: Weak alternator
causes.clues: The lights also dim at idle.

causes.name: Loose or corroded ground connection
causes.clues: Several things flicker at once, or it's worse over bumps.

you: Check the battery terminals.
Notice which accessory causes the biggest dip.

result.title: Often a bulb on its way out, or a loose bulb connector
result.now: Check that the bulb's plug is firmly connected, then try a new bulb. It's often best to replace both sides so they match.
if: If the new bulb also flickers or is dim, check the connector for melting or browning and have the wiring checked.
If the headlight is completely out, get it fixed promptly. Driving with one headlight is unsafe at night and can get you a ticket.
If the connector or housing smells burnt, stop using that light and have the wiring checked.
result.why: When only one light is affected, the problem is usually at that light: the bulb, its plug or its ground. Bulbs often dim or flicker before they burn out.

causes.name: Aging bulb
causes.clues: The bulb is several years old, or the other side was replaced recently.

causes.name: Loose or corroded bulb connector
causes.clues: The flicker changes if you tap the headlight housing.

causes.name: Moisture inside the headlight
causes.clues: Condensation or water droplets inside the lens.

you: Check the bulb connector.
Look for moisture inside the headlight.

result.title: Hazy lenses or aging bulbs are common reasons
result.now: Look at the headlight lenses. If they're yellow or cloudy, clean or restore them. If they're clear and the dash lights look normal, try new bulbs on both sides.
if: If the dash lights are dim too, or the battery is slow to start the car, have the charging system tested.
If it's hard to see the road at night, fix it before driving after dark.
If the lights get dimmer while you drive or the battery light comes on, pull over when it's safe and have the charging system checked before driving further.
result.why: Plastic headlight lenses yellow and cloud with age and sun, which blocks a lot of light. Bulbs also lose brightness over time. Both happen slowly, so you may not notice until it's quite bad.

causes.name: Yellowed or cloudy headlight lenses
causes.clues: The lenses look foggy or yellow from outside.

causes.name: Old bulbs
causes.clues: The bulbs are several years old.

causes.name: Low system voltage or poor ground
causes.clues: Dash lights are dim too, or the battery seems weak.
causes.against: If only the headlights are dim, this is less likely.

you: Inspect the lenses.
Compare your headlights with another car's on a wall at night.

result.title: The battery may be weak or not fully charged
result.now: Check that the battery terminals are tight and clean, then have the battery tested. Many auto parts stores do it free.
if: If the car cranks slowly or won't start, try a jump start and get the battery and alternator tested soon.
If the lights also dim while driving, the alternator may be the problem. Get it tested within a few days.
result.why: With the engine off, the lights run only on the battery. If they're dim then but bright once the engine is running, a low or worn battery is a common reason.

causes.name: Aging or weak battery
causes.clues: The battery is more than 4–5 years old, or cold mornings make starting slow.

causes.name: Corroded or loose battery terminals
causes.clues: Crusty white or green buildup on the terminals.

causes.name: Something draining the battery while parked
causes.clues: It's worse after the car sits for a few days.

you: Check the battery terminals.
Look for a date label on the battery.

result.title: Have the battery and charging system tested first
result.now: Check that the battery terminals are tight and clean, then have the battery and charging system tested when convenient.
if: If the battery light comes on or the lights keep getting dimmer, pull over and have it towed.
If only one light is affected, the bulb or its connector is a common cause.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: Most dim or flickering light problems come from the battery, alternator, a loose connection or the bulbs themselves. A charging system test is a quick way to check for the more serious causes first.

causes.name: Charging system problem
causes.clues: Lights change with engine speed, or the battery light flickers.

causes.name: Loose or corroded connection
causes.clues: Flickering over bumps.

causes.name: Aging bulbs or hazy lenses
causes.clues: Steady dimness that came on slowly.

you: Check the battery terminals.
Note whether it changes with engine speed or over bumps.

q_temp_gauge.q: Once the engine has run for 10-15 minutes, where is the temperature gauge?
q_temp_gauge.help: On most cars the needle sits near the middle once warm. Some cars have only a light: blue means still cold, red means too hot.

opts.a: Higher than normal or in the red, or a temperature warning is on
It stays low, near cold, and never reaches the middle
Normal, near the middle
My car has no gauge / I'm not sure

q_coolant.q: With the engine cold, where is the coolant level in the see-through overflow tank?
q_coolant.help: The overflow tank is a plastic bottle near the radiator with MIN and MAX (or COLD and FULL) marks. Only check it when the engine is cold.

opts.a: Below MIN, or empty
Between MIN and MAX
I haven't checked / I'm not sure

q_inside_signs.q: Do you notice any of these inside the car?

opts.a: A sweet, syrupy smell, a greasy fog on the inside of the windshield, or a damp passenger floor
None of these
I'm not sure

q_air_behavior.q: The coolant is full. Which of these fits best?

opts.a: It started right after the coolant was changed or the cooling system was repaired
It's warm while driving but goes cold at idle
One side (driver or passenger) is hot and the other is cold
I hear clicking or tapping behind the dash when I change the temperature
It's cold or barely warm all the time, with no other clues
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be running hot, with coolant not reaching the heater
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, turn the engine off and let it cool for at least 30 minutes. Then have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you can't pull over right away, turn the A/C off and keep the heater on full hot. Even a little heat it gives off helps the engine.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, pull over as soon as it's safe and shut it off right away.
If you see steam or smoke, step away from the car and don't open the hood until it has cooled.
Don't add coolant and carry on to see if it settles. An engine that has overheated needs checking before it's used again.
result.why: A cold heater combined with a high temperature gauge is a common sign that coolant is very low or isn't circulating. The heater core goes cold first because it sits at the end of the line. Without enough coolant, the engine can overheat badly in minutes.

causes.name: Very low coolant from a leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, steam, drips, or an empty overflow tank once cool.

causes.name: Failed water pump
causes.clues: A grinding or whining noise near the belt, or coolant dripping from that area.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck closed
causes.clues: The gauge climbs quickly after starting, even with full coolant.

causes.name: Head gasket leak
causes.clues: White sweet-smelling exhaust smoke or bubbles in the coolant tank.

you: Once fully cool, check the overflow tank and look under the car for drips.

result.title: The thermostat may be stuck open, so the engine never fully warms up
result.now: Book a check when convenient. A shop will usually confirm with live temperature data before replacing the thermostat. Until then, make sure your windshield can still be cleared before you drive.
if: If the windshield won't defrost, don't drive until it's clear. Get it fixed sooner in cold weather.
If the gauge reads low but the engine actually feels hot, the temperature sensor or gauge may be at fault instead.
If the gauge ever swings high or a temperature warning comes on, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: The thermostat keeps coolant in the engine until it reaches working temperature. If it's stuck open, coolant flows through the radiator all the time, so the engine stays cool and so does your heater, especially on the highway and in cold weather. It also hurts fuel economy.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck open
causes.clues: The gauge stays low, especially at highway speed, and heat is weak on cold days.

causes.name: Faulty temperature sensor
causes.clues: The gauge reads cold even after a long drive, but the engine feels hot.

causes.name: Cooling fan running constantly
causes.clues: The fan runs even when the engine is cold.

you: Note how long the gauge takes to move off cold on a cold day.
shop: Code scan and live temperature data

result.title: Check the coolant level first
result.now: With the engine fully cold, check the overflow tank. If it's below MIN, top it up to MAX with the coolant type in your owner's manual and see whether the heat returns.
if: If the level was low, the coolant went somewhere. Have the leak found within a few days.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the coolant is full and the heat is still cold, a blend door or clogged heater core is more likely.
If you see steam, smell coolant inside the car or the windshield fogs with a greasy film, don't keep driving. Have it checked first.
result.why: Low coolant is one of the most common reasons a heater goes cold, because the heater core is one of the first places to lose hot coolant when the level drops. It's quick and safe to check when the engine is cold.

causes.name: Low coolant
causes.clues: The tank is below MIN.

causes.name: Blend door problem
causes.clues: The coolant is full, and you hear clicking behind the dash.

causes.name: Clogged heater core
causes.clues: The coolant is full and the engine warms normally, but heat stays weak.

you: Check the overflow tank when cold.
Watch the temperature gauge on your next drive.

result.title: The heater core may be leaking inside the car
result.now: Top up the coolant when the engine is cold, and get the heater core checked within the next few days.
if: If the windshield fogs up so you can't see, don't drive it until it's fixed.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the coolant drops quickly, have it towed rather than keep refilling it.
result.why: The heater core sits behind the dash. When it leaks, hot coolant turns to vapor in the cabin, leaving a sweet smell and an oily fog on the glass, and it can soak the passenger carpet. Coolant vapor isn't something to breathe for long, and the fogging can block your view.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: A sweet smell inside, greasy fog on the windshield, or a wet passenger floor.

causes.name: Leaking heater hose connection behind the dash
causes.clues: The same signs, but the leak is near where the hoses pass through to the cabin.

causes.name: Water leak from the A/C drain or a seal
causes.clues: The wet floor is clear, with no smell, and it's worse after rain or A/C use.
causes.against: If the liquid is clear and odorless, coolant is unlikely.

you: Press a paper towel into the wet carpet and check for color and a sweet smell.
Wipe the inside of the windshield and see whether it leaves a greasy film.

result.title: Low coolant is a likely reason there's no heat
result.now: With the engine cold, top up the overflow tank to MAX with the right coolant, then have the leak found within the next few days. Until then, keep trips short and watch the temperature gauge.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the level drops again within a day or two, have it towed rather than keep driving.
If you see white sweet-smelling exhaust smoke or milky oil, don't drive it.
If the overflow tank was completely empty, the engine itself may be low too. Have it checked before driving rather than just refilling the tank.
result.why: When coolant is low, the heater core loses its supply of hot coolant first, so a cold heater is often the earliest warning. The engine can overheat next, so the leak needs finding.

causes.name: External leak (hose, radiator, water pump)
causes.clues: Drips under the front of the car, or crusty colored deposits.

causes.name: Worn radiator or tank cap
causes.clues: Residue around the cap.

causes.name: Internal leak (head gasket)
causes.clues: No visible leak, white exhaust smoke or milky oil.

you: Top up and mark the level, then check it each morning.
Put cardboard under the engine overnight to spot drips.
shop: Combustion gas (block) test if no leak is found

result.title: Air may be trapped in the cooling system
result.now: Have the shop that did the work bleed the air out of the cooling system within the next few days. Watch the temperature gauge closely until then.
if: If the gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you hear gurgling behind the dash, that's a sign of trapped air.
If you see steam or the coolant level keeps dropping, stop driving it and have it checked.
result.why: After coolant is drained or refilled, air can get trapped in the high points of the system, including the heater core. The air blocks hot coolant from reaching the heater, and a large air pocket can also cause overheating.

causes.name: Air trapped after coolant service
causes.clues: It started right after a coolant change or repair, and you may hear gurgling.

causes.name: Coolant level dropped as air worked out
causes.clues: The overflow tank level fell after the first few drives.

causes.name: New leak from the repair
causes.clues: Drips or wet spots near the parts that were worked on.

you: Check the overflow tank level when cold after each of the next few drives.
Listen for gurgling behind the dash at startup.

result.title: Coolant flow is weak at low engine speed
result.now: Check the coolant level when cold, and get the cooling system checked within the next few days.
if: If the temperature gauge rises at idle too, avoid traffic and pull over and turn the engine off if it nears the red.
If you hear grinding near the engine belt, the water pump may be failing. Don't drive it.
If you see steam or smell coolant, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: At idle, the water pump turns slowly and pushes less coolant. If the coolant is slightly low, there's an air pocket, or the pump or heater core is partly restricted, there isn't enough flow to keep the heater warm until the engine speeds up.

causes.name: Slightly low coolant or trapped air
causes.clues: The level is near MIN, or there's gurgling behind the dash.

causes.name: Partly clogged heater core
causes.clues: Coolant that hasn't been changed in years, or heat that's weak even when driving.

causes.name: Worn water pump
causes.clues: A whine near the belt, or a crusty trail below the pump.

you: Check the coolant level when cold.
Notice whether the heat comes back when you raise the engine speed in Park.

result.title: A blend door or its motor may be stuck
result.now: Try switching the climate control off and on, or turning the car off for a few minutes, then book a check when convenient.
if: If the windshield can't be cleared, don't drive until it's fixed.
If the clicking stops and the heat changes, the actuator may be slipping and could fail completely soon.
result.why: A small door behind the dash blends hot air from the heater core with cold air. A small electric motor moves it. When the motor's gears strip or it loses its position, the door stays on cold, often with a clicking or tapping sound. Cars with separate driver and passenger temperatures have a door for each side.

causes.name: Failed blend door actuator
causes.clues: Clicking or tapping behind the dash, or one side hot and the other cold.

causes.name: Actuator out of calibration
causes.clues: It started after a battery change or dead battery.

causes.name: Climate control panel fault
causes.clues: Buttons or displays also act strangely.

you: Change the temperature setting and listen behind the dash for a motor or clicking.
Compare the air from the driver and passenger vents.
shop: HVAC code scan and actuator test
Heater hose temperature check to rule out a coolant problem

result.title: The heater core may be clogged
result.now: Book a heating system check when convenient. Make sure your windshield can still be cleared in the meantime.
if: If the windshield won't defrost, don't drive until it's clear, and get it fixed sooner.
If the temperature gauge ever rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Over the years, old coolant can leave deposits that block the narrow passages in the heater core. The engine warms up normally and the coolant is full, but too little hot coolant gets through to warm the air.

causes.name: Clogged heater core
causes.clues: Coolant that hasn't been changed in a long time, and weak heat that slowly got worse.

causes.name: Stuck blend door
causes.clues: Clicking behind the dash, or a sudden change rather than a slow decline.

causes.name: Stuck heater control valve (some vehicles)
causes.clues: One heater hose is hot and the other stays cool.

you: Note whether the heat faded slowly over months or stopped suddenly.
shop: Blend door and HVAC actuator test
Heater core flush, if testing shows the core is restricted

result.title: Check the coolant, then have the heating system looked at
result.now: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold and book a check when convenient. Make sure you can clear the windshield before driving.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you notice a sweet smell inside or a damp passenger floor, get it checked within a few days.
If you see steam, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: If the engine warms up normally and the coolant is full, the cause is usually inside the heating system, like a stuck door or a clogged heater core. A shop can usually tell which by feeling the heater hoses and testing the controls.

causes.name: Blend door problem
causes.clues: Clicking behind the dash, or uneven heat side to side.

causes.name: Clogged heater core
causes.clues: Heat that faded slowly over time.

causes.name: Low coolant or trapped air
causes.clues: Gurgling behind the dash, or recent coolant work.

you: Check the coolant level when cold.
Listen for clicking behind the dash when changing the temperature.

q_signs.q: Do you notice any of these along with the hesitation?
q_signs.help: The check engine light is the orange engine-shaped light on the dash. Flashing is much more serious than steady.

opts.a: The check engine light is flashing, or the engine shakes hard
A strong smell of raw fuel
The engine revs climb, but the car doesn't pick up speed to match
The check engine light is on, but steady (not flashing)
None of these
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When does the hesitation happen most?

opts.a: Only when the engine is cold, and it goes away once warmed up
Right as I start pressing the pedal, like a dead spot, even with light gas
When I press the gas hard, like merging or climbing a hill
In rain or damp weather, or after a car wash
It started right after I filled up with fuel
I'm not sure

q_heavy_load.q: What does it feel like when you press the gas hard?
q_heavy_load.help: "Bogging" feels like the engine is starved and can't build power. A "stumble" or "jerk" feels like the engine cuts out for a split second.

opts.a: It bogs down and feels starved, and it gets worse uphill or at highway speed
It jerks or stumbles, like the engine is cutting out for a moment
It feels choked and won't rev freely, and there may be a rotten egg smell
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be misfiring badly enough to cause damage
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you're in traffic and can't stop right away, ease off the gas and avoid hard acceleration until you can get off the road.
If you smell fuel, see smoke, or notice a glow under the car, get everyone out and away from the vehicle.
result.why: A flashing check engine light means the engine computer has detected a misfire severe enough to harm the catalytic converter. Unburned fuel goes into the exhaust and makes it extremely hot, which can ruin the converter and, in rare cases, start a fire.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: The shaking feels like one cylinder has dropped out, often worse under load.

causes.name: Fuel injector stuck or not firing
causes.clues: A misfire on one cylinder that doesn't move when coils are swapped.

causes.name: Mechanical problem, like low compression in one cylinder
causes.clues: A ticking or tapping noise, or a misfire that started after overheating.
causes.against: Much less common than ignition problems.

shop: Code scan and misfire counts by cylinder
Ignition coil and spark plug inspection
Compression test if ignition and fuel check out

result.title: A fuel leak is possible. Don't drive it until it's checked
result.now: Pull over, turn the engine off and look for dripping fuel without getting close to hot parts. Have the car towed.
if: If you see fuel dripping or pooling, move well away from the car and call for help. Don't let anyone smoke nearby.
If the smell was brief and only right after refueling, check that the fuel cap is tight. If the smell comes back while driving, have it towed.
result.why: Hesitation plus a strong raw fuel smell can mean fuel is leaking from a line, injector or fuel rail, so less of it reaches the engine. Fuel near a hot engine or exhaust is a fire risk.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line or fuel rail connection
causes.clues: Wet spots under the car or on top of the engine, or a smell that's strongest outside the car.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector seal
causes.clues: The smell is strongest at the engine after it's been running.

causes.name: Engine running very rich from a fault
causes.clues: Black smoke from the exhaust and a check engine light.
causes.against: Usually no visible fuel drips.

you: Look under the car for wet spots from a safe distance.
Check that the fuel cap is closed and clicked tight.

result.title: This sounds more like the transmission slipping than an engine hesitation
result.now: Keep trips short and gentle, avoid highways and heavy traffic, and have the transmission checked within the next few days.
if: If the car stops moving, won't go into gear, or you smell burning, stop driving it and have it towed.
If you can check the transmission fluid and it's low, topping it up with the correct type may help until it's inspected.
If a transmission temperature or warning light comes on, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
