result.why: When the engine speeds up but the car doesn't, the power isn't getting through the transmission. That's different from an engine hesitation, where the revs themselves stumble. Slipping causes heat and wear, so it can get worse quickly.

causes.name: Low or worn transmission fluid
causes.clues: Red or pink spots under the car, or fluid that looks dark or smells burnt.

causes.name: Worn clutches inside the transmission
causes.clues: High mileage, and the slipping happens on certain shifts.

causes.name: Worn clutch (manual transmission)
causes.clues: On a stick shift, the revs jump when you accelerate hard in a higher gear.
causes.against: Doesn't apply to automatics.

you: Check the transmission fluid level if your car has a dipstick (see your owner's manual).
Look for red or pink spots where you park.
shop: Road test with live transmission data

result.title: Cold-only hesitation can point to a sensor or a small air leak
result.now: Give the engine 30 seconds or so after starting on cold mornings, and book a check when convenient.
if: If it starts hesitating when warm too, or the check engine light comes on, get it checked sooner.
If the temperature gauge acts oddly, mention it to the shop. It points toward the coolant temperature sensor.
If the check engine light starts flashing or you smell raw fuel, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: A cold engine needs a richer fuel mix. If a sensor tells the computer the engine is warmer than it is, or extra air is leaking in, the mix is too lean until the engine warms up and the stumble goes away.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: The temperature gauge reads oddly, or fuel economy has dropped.

causes.name: Vacuum leak from a cracked hose
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or a rough idle when cold that smooths out when warm.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body
causes.clues: A low or uneven idle, and higher mileage.

you: Listen for hissing around the engine when it's cold.
Note the outside temperature when it happens.
shop: Code scan and live sensor data

result.title: A dead spot off the line often comes from an air-measuring sensor or a dirty throttle
result.now: Book a check when convenient. If the check engine light is on, having the code read first gives the shop a head start.
if: If the dead spot makes it hard to pull out into traffic safely, get it checked within a few days and leave extra room until then.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
If you smell raw fuel, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: The engine computer decides how much fuel to add based on how much air is coming in and how far you've pressed the pedal. If the sensor that measures air is dirty, or the throttle is gummed up, the fuel mix is wrong for a moment and the engine stumbles before catching up.

causes.name: Dirty mass airflow sensor
causes.clues: Hesitation plus a slight drop in fuel economy. More likely if the air filter is dirty or was recently replaced with an oiled type.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or faulty throttle position sensor
causes.clues: The stumble happens at the same pedal position every time.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: Hissing under the hood, or a rough or high idle.

causes.name: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) valve stuck open
causes.clues: Rough idle and stumbling from a stop, often with a check engine light.

you: Check the engine air filter and replace it if it's dirty.
Have the check engine code read if the light is on. Many parts stores do this free.
shop: Code scan and live airflow and throttle data

result.title: Hesitation in damp weather often means spark is leaking from worn ignition parts
result.now: Book a check of the ignition system when convenient, ideally soon after it happens so the shop can see it.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over and stop driving.
If it only happened once after a pressure wash under the hood, it may clear up once things dry out. Get it checked if it comes back.
result.why: Moisture gives electricity an easy path to escape through cracked plug wires, coil boots or a dirty spark plug. The spark then doesn't reach the cylinder with full strength, so the engine stumbles when it needs the most power.

causes.name: Cracked spark plug wires or coil boots
causes.clues: Older car, and the problem is worse on foggy or rainy days.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs
causes.clues: The plugs haven't been changed in a long time, or you don't know when they were.

causes.name: Water getting into the area around the plugs
causes.clues: A clogged drain near the base of the windshield, or water pooling on top of the engine.

you: Note the weather each time it happens.
Check your maintenance records for the last spark plug change.
shop: Ignition coil, boot and wire inspection

result.title: You may have a tank of poor-quality fuel or the wrong grade
result.now: Check your receipt to make sure you got the right fuel grade, then drive gently and top up with fresh fuel from a busy station.
if: If you put diesel in a gas car (or gas in a diesel), stop driving it right away and have it towed. The tank will need to be drained.
If the hesitation doesn't improve after a fresh tank, or the check engine light comes on, book a check.
If the check engine light flashes, the engine shakes hard or it stalls, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
result.why: Fuel contaminated with water or dirt, or a lower octane than your engine needs, can cause stumbling and pinging under acceleration. When the problem starts right after a fill-up, the fuel is a likely link.

causes.name: Contaminated fuel
causes.clues: The problem started right after filling up, especially at a small or rarely busy station.

causes.name: Lower octane than your engine requires
causes.clues: Your owner's manual says premium is required, and you used regular. You may hear pinging.

you: Check the fuel grade on your receipt and compare it with your owner's manual.
Fill up with fresh fuel once the tank is low.
shop: Fuel sample check for water or contamination

result.title: The engine may be starved for fuel under load
result.now: Get it checked within the next few days. Until then, avoid hard acceleration and long highway trips.
if: If the engine cuts out or stalls while driving, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the check engine light comes on, have the code read. It can help point the shop toward the right system.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
If you smell raw fuel, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: Pressing the gas hard needs much more fuel than cruising. A weak fuel pump or clogged filter can keep up at light throttle, but runs short when you ask for power, so the car bogs down. This usually gets worse over time.

causes.name: Weak fuel pump
causes.clues: Worse uphill, at highway speed, or when the tank is low. A whine from the rear of the car.

causes.name: Clogged fuel filter
causes.clues: Higher mileage and no record of a filter change (some cars have it built into the pump).

causes.name: Clogged or dirty fuel injectors
causes.clues: A gradual loss of power and fuel economy over months.

you: Note whether it's worse when the fuel tank is low.
Listen for a whine from the back of the car when the engine is running.
shop: Fuel pressure and volume test under load
Code scan and fuel trim data

result.title: Possibly a misfire under load, from worn spark plugs or a weak ignition coil
result.now: Have the ignition system checked within the next few days, and avoid hard acceleration until then.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
If the plugs are overdue, mention it. A shop will usually check misfire data and inspect the plugs and coils before deciding what to replace.
If you smell raw fuel or burning, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: Under heavy throttle, the cylinders are packed with more air and fuel, and it takes a stronger spark to light them. Worn plugs or a weakening coil can manage at light throttle but miss under load, which feels like a jerk or stumble. Driving on a misfire can damage the catalytic converter.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs
causes.clues: The plugs haven't been changed in a long time, or you don't know when they were.

causes.name: Failing ignition coil
causes.clues: A steady check engine light, and the stumble feels like one cylinder cutting out.

causes.name: Clogged fuel injector on one cylinder
causes.clues: A misfire that stays on the same cylinder after the coil is swapped.

you: Check your maintenance records for the last spark plug change.
Have the check engine code read if the light is on.
shop: Code scan and misfire counts by cylinder

result.title: The exhaust may be partly blocked, sometimes by a clogged catalytic converter
result.now: Get it checked within the next few days, and keep trips short and gentle until then.
if: If you see a red glow under the car or smell burning, pull over, turn the engine off and step away.
If the power loss gets steadily worse, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: An engine has to breathe out as well as in. If the catalytic converter is clogged, exhaust can't escape fast enough and the engine feels choked when you ask for power. A rotten egg smell or a rattle from the converter are common clues. A shop will usually test exhaust back-pressure before replacing a converter, and look for what caused it to clog.

causes.name: Clogged catalytic converter
causes.clues: A rotten egg smell, a rattle under the car, or a history of misfires.

causes.name: Collapsed or damaged exhaust pipe or muffler
causes.clues: The car scraped something, or you can see a crushed pipe.

causes.name: Engine misfire that damaged the converter
causes.clues: A check engine light or rough running before the power loss started.

you: Look under the car for crushed or dented exhaust pipes, with the engine cold.
Note any rotten egg smell.

result.title: Get the codes read, then have the engine checked
result.now: Have the check engine codes read (many parts stores do this free), then book a check and describe exactly when the hesitation happens.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over and stop driving.
If the hesitation makes it hard to merge or pull out safely, get it checked within a few days.
If you smell raw fuel, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: Hesitation can come from ignition, fuel, air sensors or the exhaust. Stored codes and a note of when it happens (cold or warm, light or heavy throttle, after fueling) narrow it down much faster than parts swapping.

causes.name: Ignition problem (plugs, coils, wires)
causes.clues: A jerk or stumble, worse under load or in wet weather.

causes.name: Air or throttle sensor problem
causes.clues: A dead spot right as you press the pedal.

causes.name: Fuel delivery problem
causes.clues: Bogging down uphill or at highway speed.

you: Keep a short note of when it happens: cold or warm, light or hard throttle, weather, fuel level.
Check the engine air filter.

q_fuel_type.q: Could the wrong type of fuel have gone in?
q_fuel_type.help: Check your receipt or the pump you used.

opts.a: Yes: diesel in a gas car, or gas in a diesel
No, the right type, but maybe poor quality or the wrong grade
I'm not sure

result.title: The wrong type of fuel went in
result.now: Don’t start the engine. If it’s running, pull over when it’s safe and turn it off. Don’t restart it. Have it towed: the tank will need to be drained.
if: If you smell raw fuel, keep sparks and flames away and move away from the car.
If you realize at the pump before starting the engine, leave it off and ask the station for help moving the car.
result.why: Diesel in a gas engine, or gas in a diesel, doesn't burn the way the engine is built for. Running it can damage the fuel system and engine, so the tank and fuel lines need to be drained before it's started again.

causes.name: Diesel in a gas car
causes.clues: Heavy smoke, very rough running or the engine dying soon after filling up.

causes.name: Gas in a diesel
causes.clues: Knocking, loss of power or the engine stopping soon after filling up.

you: Check your receipt and the pump you used to confirm which fuel went in.
shop: Drain and flush the tank and fuel lines

q_danger.q: Along with the hissing, do you notice any of these?
q_danger.help: Steam looks like white vapor that disappears quickly in the air. Coolant often smells sweet, like syrup.

opts.a: Steam from under the hood, or the temperature gauge is high or in the red
A strong smell of raw fuel
Smoke or a burning smell
None of these
I'm not sure

q_check_gauge.q: With the car safely parked, look at the temperature gauge and under the hood. What do you see?
q_check_gauge.help: Look, but don't open the radiator or coolant cap while the engine is hot.

opts.a: The gauge is high or a temperature warning light is on
The gauge is normal and there's no steam, smoke or fuel smell
I'm not sure, or I can't tell

q_when.q: When do you hear the hiss?

opts.a: While the engine is running, most of the time
Only when I press or release the brake pedal
After I turn the engine off, for a minute or two
When the A/C is on, or right after I switch it off
I'm not sure

q_running.q: While it's hissing, does anything else seem off?
q_running.help: A "rough idle" means the engine shakes or the speed bounces up and down while you're stopped.

opts.a: Rough idle, stalling, or the check engine light is on
The coolant level keeps dropping, or there's a sweet smell
The engine runs normally. It's just the hiss
I'm not sure

q_after_off.q: After you turn the engine off, which fits best?

opts.a: A soft hiss that fades within a minute or two. The gauge was normal and there's no smell or drips
A sweet smell, drips under the front, or a low coolant reservoir
Bubbling or gurgling from the coolant reservoir after a hot drive
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be overheating, with coolant escaping as steam
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, turn the engine off and let it cool for at least 30 minutes. Don't open the coolant cap. Plan on a tow or a mobile mechanic.
if: If the gauge went into the red, don't restart it even after adding coolant. Running an overheated engine can warp or crack expensive parts.
If the gauge only rose a little and the engine is now cool, you can check the coolant level in the reservoir, but still have the leak found before relying on the car.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn it off and don't restart it.
result.why: Hissing with steam or a high temperature reading means coolant is boiling or spraying out under pressure. Without enough coolant the engine heats up fast, and driving further risks serious engine damage.

causes.name: Leaking or burst coolant hose
causes.clues: Steam or coolant spray from one spot, a wet or swollen hose, or a puddle under the front.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or radiator cap
causes.clues: Crusty green, orange or pink residue around the radiator or cap.

causes.name: Failed cooling fan, water pump or thermostat
causes.clues: It overheats mostly in traffic (fan), or there's a drip near the front of the engine (water pump).
causes.against: These cause overheating, but the hiss itself usually comes from coolant escaping somewhere.

you: Once the engine is fully cool, check the coolant reservoir level.
Look for wet spots or residue on hoses and the radiator.
shop: Head gasket check if it overheated badly

result.title: A fuel leak is possible. Treat it as a fire risk
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off, get everyone out, and keep sparks, flames and cigarettes away. Don't restart it. Have it towed.
if: If you see fuel dripping or pooling, move well away from the car and call for help.
If the smell fades quickly and there's no wet spot, it still needs to be checked before you drive it.
result.why: Fuel lines on modern engines carry fuel under pressure, so a small crack can hiss or spray. Fuel near a hot engine can catch fire, which is why this is a do-not-drive situation.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line or fitting
causes.clues: A wet spot or drip near the engine or under the car, with a strong gas smell.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector seal or fuel rail
causes.clues: The smell is strongest at the top of the engine.

causes.name: Evaporative (EVAP) system leak
causes.clues: A faint fuel smell with no drips, sometimes with a check engine light.
causes.against: An EVAP leak usually doesn't hiss loudly or drip.

result.title: Fluid may be leaking onto hot engine or exhaust parts
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off and step away until the smoke stops. Don't restart it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic look at it.
if: If you see smoke or flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
If the smoke stops quickly and you can see a small oil seep, it still needs to be checked before you drive it again.
result.why: A hiss with smoke or a burning smell usually means oil, coolant or another fluid is dripping onto the hot exhaust and boiling off. That can start a fire, and it means the engine is losing fluid it needs.

causes.name: Oil leak onto the exhaust
causes.clues: Blue-gray smoke and a burnt oil smell, often after an oil change or from a leaking valve cover gasket.

causes.name: Coolant leak onto hot parts
causes.clues: White, sweet-smelling vapor.

causes.name: Power steering or transmission fluid leak
causes.clues: A drip near the front, with low fluid in one of those reservoirs.

you: Once cool, check the oil and coolant levels.
Note the color of the smoke.
shop: Leak inspection with the engine running

result.title: Possibly a leak in the brake booster or its vacuum hose
result.now: Braking may take much more force than usual. If you're on the road, press the pedal firmly, leave plenty of room and pull over when it's safe. Have the brakes checked before using the car again, either by a mobile mechanic or with a tow.
if: If the pedal sinks toward the floor, feels soft, or the brake warning light comes on, don't drive it at all. That points to a hydraulic problem, not just the booster.
If the engine also idles rough or stalls when you press the brake, the leak may be large. Don't drive it.
If you smell burning or see brake fluid near the pedal or the master cylinder, don't drive it.
result.why: The brake booster uses engine vacuum to make the pedal easy to press. A hiss when you press or release the pedal often means air is leaking into the booster or its hose. If the booster loses its assist, the pedal gets hard and the car takes much longer to stop, and that can happen without warning.

causes.name: Leaking brake booster diaphragm
causes.clues: The hiss is under the dash near the pedal, and the pedal feels firmer than before.

causes.name: Cracked or loose booster vacuum hose or check valve
causes.clues: The hiss is under the hood, near the back of the engine on the driver's side.

causes.name: Worn seal at the master cylinder
causes.clues: Brake fluid residue where the master cylinder meets the booster.

you: With the engine off, pump the brake pedal a few times, hold it down, then start the engine. The pedal should sink slightly. If it doesn't, the booster may not be working.
Listen near the pedal and under the hood while someone presses the brake.
shop: Vacuum hose and check valve inspection

result.title: A vacuum leak is a likely cause
result.now: Get it checked within the next few days. A smoke test at a shop usually finds the leak quickly.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes badly, stop driving and have it towed.
If it stalls while you're driving, don't keep driving it. Losing power in traffic is dangerous.
If the brake pedal feels harder than usual, stop driving and have it checked. A vacuum leak can also weaken the brake booster.
result.why: The engine draws air through a network of rubber hoses and seals. When one cracks or comes loose, air rushes in with a hiss, and the extra air throws off the fuel mixture. That causes a rough idle, stalling and a check engine light.

causes.name: Cracked or disconnected vacuum hose
causes.clues: The hiss is louder at idle, and you can see an old, cracked or loose rubber hose.

causes.name: Leaking intake gasket or PCV valve and hose
causes.clues: A high or uneven idle, and lean-condition codes on a scan.

causes.name: Cracked air intake duct
causes.clues: A split in the large rubber duct between the air filter box and the engine.

you: With the engine idling, listen carefully around the top of the engine to find where the hiss is loudest. Keep hands and clothing away from belts and the fan.
Look for hoses that are cracked, brittle or popped off.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim readings

result.title: Possibly a small vacuum or air intake leak
result.now: Book a check when convenient, and mention that the hiss is there while the engine runs.
if: If a rough idle, stalling or a check engine light shows up, get it checked within a few days.
If the temperature gauge starts rising or you notice a sweet smell, treat it as a coolant leak and pull over.
If the brake pedal starts feeling harder than usual, stop driving and have it checked.
result.why: A steady hiss with the engine running well often means a small air leak that the engine is still compensating for. These tend to grow over time and can eventually cause rough running or poor fuel economy.

causes.name: Small vacuum hose leak
causes.clues: The hiss is loudest at idle and quieter when you rev the engine.

causes.name: PCV valve or hose
causes.clues: The hiss is near the valve cover on top of the engine.

causes.name: Small exhaust manifold leak
causes.clues: More of a ticking or puffing sound, loudest on a cold start.
causes.against: Exhaust leaks usually tick rather than hiss steadily.

you: Listen around the engine to find where the hiss is loudest, staying clear of moving parts.
Look for loose or cracked rubber hoses.

result.title: Possibly a coolant leak
result.now: When the engine is fully cool, check the coolant reservoir and top it up to the marked level if it's low. Get the leak found within the next few days, and watch the temperature gauge closely until then.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal or you see steam, pull over, turn the engine off and don't drive it further.
If you're adding coolant every few days, have it checked right away. A bigger failure may be close.
If you smell coolant inside the car or the windshield fogs with a greasy film, get it checked before driving further.
result.why: The cooling system runs under pressure, so a small crack or loose clamp can let coolant hiss out as it heats up. A slow leak can turn into overheating with little warning.

causes.name: Leaking hose or loose hose clamp
causes.clues: Wet spots or crusty residue on a hose or at its ends.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or radiator cap
causes.clues: Residue on the radiator, or the hiss seems to come from the cap.

causes.name: Leaking water pump
causes.clues: Drips or residue at the front of the engine, near the belts.

you: With the engine cold, check the coolant level in the reservoir.
Look under the front of the car for green, orange or pink drips.

result.title: Possibly the A/C system, which can hiss normally
result.now: Notice whether the A/C still blows cold. A brief hiss from the dash or under the hood right after you switch the A/C off is normal pressure settling.
if: If the A/C is blowing warm or the hiss is constant while it runs, book an A/C check. The refrigerant may be low from a leak.
If the hiss comes with a burning smell or a squeal from the belts, get it checked soon.
result.why: The A/C system holds refrigerant under high pressure. When the compressor cycles or shuts off, the pressure evens out, and you can hear a short hiss. That's normal. A hiss with poor cooling suggests a leak.

causes.name: Normal pressure equalizing
causes.clues: A short hiss after switching the A/C off, and it still cools well.

causes.name: Low refrigerant from a leak
causes.clues: The A/C is gradually getting weaker.
causes.against: If it still blows cold, a leak is less likely.

causes.name: Expansion valve or other A/C component fault
causes.clues: A constant hiss from behind the dash with poor cooling.

you: Feel whether the vents blow cold with the A/C on.
Note whether the hiss happens only briefly after switching the A/C off.

result.title: A short hiss after you park can be normal, but check the coolant
result.now: Next time the engine is fully cool, check that the coolant reservoir is between the marks and look under the front of the car for drips.
if: If the coolant is low or you see drips, have the cooling system checked within a few days.
If the hiss gets louder, lasts longer, or the temperature gauge reads higher than usual, get it checked soon.
If you see steam or smell burning, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: After you shut the engine off, hot coolant, the exhaust and the A/C system all settle, which can make soft hissing or ticking sounds for a minute or two. If the coolant level holds steady over the next week or so, with no smell or drips, normal settling is the likely explanation. Checking the level is how you tell.

causes.name: Cooling system or A/C settling after shutdown
causes.clues: A soft hiss that fades quickly, a normal gauge, and a steady coolant level.

causes.name: Small coolant leak hitting hot parts
causes.clues: A sweet smell after parking, or the coolant level slowly dropping.
causes.against: If the coolant level stays steady, a leak is unlikely.

causes.name: Weak radiator cap
causes.clues: Coolant in the reservoir overflows or the hiss comes from the cap area.

you: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold, and note it so you can compare in a week.
Look for drips under the front of the car after parking.

result.title: Treat it as a possible coolant leak until it's checked
result.now: Let the engine cool fully, then check the coolant level. Have the car checked within the next few days, and watch the temperature gauge whenever you drive.
if: If you see steam, smoke or the gauge rising, pull over, turn the engine off and don't drive it further.
If you smell fuel, don't start the engine. Have it towed.
result.why: The most common hissing that leads to real damage is coolant escaping, because it can lead to overheating. Checking the coolant level and the gauge helps rule that in or out.

causes.name: Coolant leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, drips, or a low reservoir.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: The hiss is there while the engine runs, with a rough idle.

causes.name: Normal settling after shutdown
causes.clues: A short hiss after you park, with nothing else wrong.

you: Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
Record a short video with sound of the hiss for the shop.

result.title: Have a shop pinpoint where the hiss is coming from
result.now: Book a check when convenient. Note when the hiss happens and record a short video with sound to show the technician.
if: If you see steam, the temperature gauge rises, or you smell fuel or burning, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the brake pedal starts feeling hard, stop driving and have the brakes checked. If the engine runs rough, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: Hissing can come from the cooling system, a vacuum leak, the brake booster or the A/C. If you can't tell when it happens, a technician can usually track it down with a pressure test and a smoke test.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: Hissing while the engine runs, louder at idle.

causes.name: Coolant leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell or a dropping coolant level.

causes.name: Brake booster leak
causes.clues: Hissing that changes when you press the brake.

you: Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
Notice whether the hiss changes with the brake pedal or the A/C.

q_danger.q: Along with the hum, do you notice any of these?

opts.a: Grinding or scraping, or a wheel feels loose or wobbly
A vibration in the steering wheel, seat or floor
None of these, just the hum
I'm not sure

q_weave.q: On an empty, straight road at the speed where it hums, gently steer a little left, then a little right. Does the hum change?
q_weave.help: When you steer, the car's weight shifts onto the outside wheels. A worn wheel bearing usually gets louder when it's carrying more weight, and quieter when it's carrying less. Keep the movements small and smooth.

opts.a: Yes: louder steering one way, quieter the other
No, it stays about the same
I'm not sure

q_surface.q: Which of these best describes the hum?

opts.a: It changes a lot when the road surface changes
It changes when I let off the gas or press it (rear-wheel, 4WD or AWD vehicle)
It follows engine speed, not road speed (it changes when the transmission shifts)
It stays the same no matter what I do
I'm not sure

q_tires.q: With the car parked, look at each tire and run your hand across the tread. What do you find?
q_tires.help: Check all four tires, including the inside edges if you can see them. Turning the steering wheel all the way makes the front tires easier to see.

opts.a: A bulge or bubble on the side, or cords or wire showing
The tread feels wavy, choppy or like saw teeth in one direction
The tires are new, or have chunky off-road or winter tread
They look and feel even
I'm not sure

result.title: A wheel bearing or wheel may be close to failing
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe. Check that the lug nuts are tight if you can, then have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If a lug nut is loose or missing, don't drive on it until all the nuts are tightened properly.
If you smell burning or a wheel is much hotter than the others, the brakes may be dragging or the bearing may be overheating. Don't touch it with bare hands.
result.why: A hum that turns into grinding, or comes with a loose or wobbly feel, can mean a wheel bearing is badly worn or something holding the wheel on is loose. In the worst case the wheel can separate from the car, so it isn't worth driving further.

causes.name: Badly worn wheel bearing
causes.clues: The hum has been getting louder for weeks and is now a grind or growl, sometimes with play in the wheel.

causes.name: Loose lug nuts
causes.clues: A wheel was recently removed, for tires or brakes, and a clunk or wobble started after that.

causes.name: Brake part dragging or worn to metal
causes.clues: Grinding that changes when you brake, or a hot, burning smell.

you: Check whether any lug nuts look loose or missing.
Don't drive further to test it.
shop: Wheel bearing play check with the car lifted

result.title: A worn wheel bearing is a likely cause
result.now: Have the wheel bearings checked within a few days. Until then, keep speeds moderate and avoid long highway trips.
if: If the hum turns into grinding, or the steering feels loose or wobbly, stop driving and have it towed.
If the ABS light comes on, mention it. Some wheel bearings carry the ABS sensor ring.
If you smell burning, a wheel is much hotter than the others, or a red brake warning light comes on, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
result.why: A hum that gets louder when you steer one way and quieter the other way often points to a wheel bearing. Steering shifts weight onto the outside wheels, so a bad bearing gets louder when it's loaded. A noise that's louder when steering left often points to a right-side bearing, and the other way around.

causes.name: Worn front wheel bearing
causes.clues: The hum changes clearly when you steer and seems to come from the front.

causes.name: Worn rear wheel bearing
causes.clues: The noise seems to come from behind you, and changes less when steering.

causes.name: Uneven tire wear
causes.clues: Wavy or choppy tread on one tire can also change with steering.
causes.against: Tire noise usually changes more with the road surface than with steering.

you: Note which way you steer when it gets louder.
Look at the tires for uneven wear.
shop: Wheel bearing play and roughness check with the car lifted
Chassis microphone test to pinpoint the corner

result.title: The differential or its fluid may be the source
result.now: Have the differential fluid level and condition checked within a few days, and keep speeds moderate until then.
if: If the noise turns into a clunk, grind or howl, or you see gear oil leaking near the axle, stop driving and have it towed.
If you tow a trailer or carry heavy loads, stop doing so until it's checked.
If you smell burning or hot gear oil, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: The differential lets the wheels on each side turn at different speeds. Its gears and bearings sit in thick gear oil. When the oil is low or the parts wear, they hum or whine, and the sound usually changes when you switch between pressing the gas and coasting.

causes.name: Low or worn-out differential fluid
causes.clues: Oily residue around the differential, or the fluid has never been changed on a high-mileage vehicle.

causes.name: Worn differential bearings
causes.clues: A hum or growl that rises with speed and is most noticeable when coasting.

causes.name: Worn or poorly adjusted ring and pinion gears
causes.clues: A whine that's loudest when accelerating, or that started after differential work.

you: Look for oily wet spots on or below the differential (the round housing between the drive wheels).
Note whether the noise is louder when pressing the gas or when coasting.
shop: Differential fluid level and condition check
Check the drained fluid for metal particles
Road test and chassis microphone test

result.title: A hum that follows engine speed may not be a wheel or tire
result.now: Book a check when convenient. Tell the shop the noise follows engine speed and changes when the transmission shifts.
if: If anyone gets a headache or feels dizzy or sleepy, pull over, get everyone out into fresh air and call 911. It may be carbon monoxide from an exhaust leak.
If the transmission slips, shifts harshly or a warning light comes on, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: Wheel bearings, tires and differentials follow road speed. If the hum changes when the transmission shifts, even at the same road speed, it's tied to the engine or transmission, such as exhaust drone, an accessory bearing or the transmission itself.

causes.name: Exhaust drone or a small exhaust leak
causes.clues: A deep drone at a certain engine speed, often on the highway, or a louder exhaust than usual.

causes.name: Worn accessory bearing (alternator, idler or tensioner pulley)
causes.clues: The hum is also there when you rev the engine in Park.

causes.name: Transmission noise
causes.clues: The hum changes with each gear, or there are shifting problems.

you: Rev the engine gently in Park and listen for the same hum.
Check the transmission fluid if your car has a dipstick for it.

result.title: Often a wheel bearing or tire noise. A shop can usually tell which
result.now: Check the tire pressures and look for uneven wear, then book a road test with a shop within the next week or two.
if: If the noise is getting louder week by week, get it checked sooner.
If it turns into grinding, or a wheel feels loose or wobbly, stop driving and have it towed.
If you smell burning or one wheel is much hotter than the others, pull over when it's safe and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Both worn bearings and noisy tires make a hum that rises with speed, and they can sound very similar from the driver's seat. A technician can lift the car, spin each wheel and check for play or roughness in a few minutes.

causes.name: Uneven tire wear
causes.clues: Overdue tire rotations, worn suspension, or the noise changes on different road surfaces.

causes.name: Worn wheel bearing
causes.clues: The noise has slowly grown louder and seems to come from one corner.

causes.name: Low tire pressure
causes.clues: The tire pressure light is on, or a tire looks low.

you: Check all tire pressures against the sticker on the driver's door frame.
Feel the tread for waves or uneven edges.
Note whether the noise changes on different road surfaces.
shop: Wheel bearing play and roughness check

result.title: The tire may be damaged, and it could fail suddenly
result.now: Don't drive on that tire. Put on the spare or call roadside assistance to have it changed or the car towed.
if: If you're not sure how to change a tire safely, wait for roadside help away from traffic.
If more than one tire looks damaged, have the suspension and alignment checked when the tires are replaced.
result.why: A bulge, bubble or exposed cords means the inside of the tire is damaged. That can cause a hum or thump and a vibration as the tire turns, and it can lead to a sudden blowout.

causes.name: Internal tire damage from a pothole or curb
causes.clues: A bubble on the sidewall, often after a hard impact.

causes.name: Tread separation
causes.clues: A lumpy or uneven tread area and a vibration that rises with speed.

causes.name: Tire worn through
causes.clues: Cords or wire showing, usually on the inside or outside edge.

you: Look at the damaged tire from a safe spot, without driving further.
shop: Tire inspection, and replacement if the damage is confirmed

result.title: Uneven (cupped) tire wear may be making the noise
result.now: Book a tire and suspension check. Ask the shop to look at the shocks or struts and the alignment, not just the tires.
if: If the wear has reached the cords, or there's a bulge, don't drive on that tire.
If you replace the tires without fixing the cause, the new ones will likely wear the same way.
result.why: Cupped or scalloped tread makes a rhythmic hum or "wub-wub" that rises with speed and often changes with the road surface. It's often caused by worn shocks or struts, poor alignment, or missed tire rotations.

causes.name: Worn shocks or struts
causes.clues: The car bounces after bumps, or feels floaty.

causes.name: Wheel alignment off
causes.clues: The car pulls to one side, or the steering wheel isn't straight.

causes.name: Tires not rotated or out of balance
causes.clues: Rotations have been skipped, or a vibration at certain speeds.

you: Feel the tread on all four tires, especially the rear ones.
Check the tire pressures.

result.title: The tires themselves may simply be noisy
result.now: Check that all four tires are at the pressure on the driver's door sticker, and listen for whether the noise changes on smooth versus rough pavement.
if: If the noise changes when you steer left or right, a wheel bearing is more likely. Have it checked.
If the noise gets steadily louder over weeks, book a check.
If a vibration, grinding or a wobbly feel comes with the noise, slow down and pull over when it's safe.
result.why: Chunky off-road, all-terrain and winter treads move a lot of air and hum noticeably at speed. New tires can sound different from your old ones too. A noise that changes mostly with the road surface and is the same on every tire is usually tread noise.

causes.name: Aggressive or winter tread pattern
causes.clues: The noise started when the tires were fitted and changes with the road surface.

causes.name: Incorrect tire pressure
causes.clues: One or more tires are well above or below the door sticker pressure.

causes.name: Worn wheel bearing
causes.clues: The noise changes when steering, or seems to come from one corner.
causes.against: Less likely if the noise began exactly when new tires went on.

you: Check all tire pressures.
Drive on different road surfaces and note whether the noise changes.
shop: Wheel bearing check if the noise changes when steering

key-wont-turn-in-ignition.title: Key won't turn in the ignition

q_wheel.help: Most cars lock the steering wheel when the key is out. If the wheel was turned when you parked, the lock pushes on the ignition and stops the key from turning.

opts.a: The steering wheel is locked and only moves a tiny bit either way
The steering wheel turns freely, but the key won't
The key won't go into the slot all the way
The key won't turn back to Off, or it won't come out
I'm not sure

q_wiggle.q: Gently rock the steering wheel left and right while you turn the key. What happens?
q_wiggle.help: Use light, steady pressure on the key, and push the wheel toward the side that has a little give. Don't force the key or use tools on it.

opts.a: The key turned and the wheel unlocked
It still won't turn, no matter which way I rock the wheel
I'm not sure

q_spare.q: Have you tried a spare key?
q_spare.help: A spare that has hardly been used is the fastest way to tell a worn key from a worn lock.

opts.a: Yes, and the spare turns normally
Yes, and the spare won't turn either
I don't have one, or haven't tried it
I'm not sure
The key has felt sticky or needed jiggling for weeks
My key is visibly worn, bent, or a new copy
It worked fine, then suddenly wouldn't turn at all
I'm not sure

result.title: It was likely the steering lock holding the key
result.now: If the key now turns smoothly every time, this was most likely the steering lock under pressure. Next time, straighten the wheels before you shut the car off and avoid leaning on the wheel as you get out.
if: If you need to rock the wheel almost every time, or it's getting harder, have the ignition lock checked before it jams for good.
If the car then won't crank or start, see our guide for when the car won't start.
result.why: The steering lock is a pin that drops into the steering column when the key is out. If the wheel is turned against it, the pin is pinched so tightly that the key can't turn. Rocking the wheel takes the pressure off and lets the key turn.

causes.name: Steering lock under tension
causes.clues: The wheel was turned when you parked, you parked against a curb, or the wheel got bumped after the key came out.

causes.name: Early wear in the ignition lock
causes.clues: It takes more force than it used to, even with the wheel straight.
causes.against: If it only happens after parking with the wheels turned, wear is less likely.

you: Park with the wheels straight and see if the problem goes away.
Notice whether the key turns easily when there's no pressure on the wheel.

result.title: Your key may be worn down or cut slightly wrong
result.now: Use the spare key if you have one, and have a new key made from the original factory code or the spare, not copied from the worn key.
if: If no key will turn, the lock itself is the more likely problem. Call a locksmith or the dealer.
If your car has a chip in the key, the new key will also need to be programmed to the car, or it may turn but not start.
result.why: The small cuts on a key wear down over years of use. Once they're rounded off, the pins inside the lock don't line up and the key won't turn. A copy made from a worn key copies the wear too.

causes.name: Worn key
causes.clues: The edges look smooth and rounded, the key is years old, or it works better when you wiggle it.
causes.against: If the spare won't turn either, the key isn't the main problem.

causes.name: Poorly cut copy
causes.clues: The problem started with a newly made key.

causes.name: Bent key
causes.clues: The key isn't straight when you sight down it, or a heavy key ring hangs from it.

you: Compare the main key and the spare side by side for rounded cuts.
Lighten a heavy key ring. The weight wears the lock and the key over time.
shop: Key programming if the key has a chip

result.title: The ignition lock may be wearing out
result.now: Book a locksmith or shop to look at the ignition lock soon, before it leaves you stuck somewhere. Until then, turn the key gently and don't force it.
if: If it gets to the point where only lots of jiggling works, treat it as urgent. It can jam completely at any time.
If the engine ever shuts off when the key is bumped while driving, don't drive it until it's repaired.
result.why: The ignition lock has small spring-loaded pins that wear along with the key. When it gradually gets harder to turn over weeks, lock wear is a common reason, and it rarely fixes itself.

causes.name: Worn ignition lock cylinder
causes.clues: It's gotten slowly worse, and the spare key is no better.

causes.name: Dirt or a dried-up lock
causes.clues: It's worse in cold or dusty conditions.

causes.name: Worn key
causes.clues: A spare key turns more easily.
causes.against: If the spare is just as stiff, the lock is the more likely culprit.

you: Try the spare key and compare how it feels.
Note whether a heavy key ring hangs from the key while driving.
shop: Lock cylinder repair or replacement, keyed to your existing key, if it is worn

result.title: The ignition lock may have jammed
result.now: Stop trying to force it. Call a locksmith who works on cars, or have the car towed to a shop or dealer.
if: If the lock looks scratched, pried or damaged, someone may have tried to steal the car. Take photos and consider reporting it.
If the key snaps off in the lock, leave the broken piece and call a locksmith.
result.why: When a key that worked fine suddenly won't turn, even with the wheel loose, something inside the lock may have broken or seized. Forcing it risks snapping the key or damaging the steering column.

causes.name: Failed ignition lock cylinder
causes.clues: A sudden change with no warning, and no key works.

causes.name: Damage from a theft attempt
causes.clues: Scratches or pry marks around the lock, or a loose trim cover.

causes.name: Steering lock stuck
causes.clues: The wheel is also locked solid and doesn't move at all.
causes.against: If the wheel turns freely, the steering lock isn't the problem.

you: Make sure you're using the right key for this car.
Look around the lock for scratches or pry marks.
shop: Ignition lock cylinder inspection, and repair or replacement if it has failed

result.title: Something is blocking the key, or the key is damaged
result.now: Check that you have the right key and that it's clean and straight, then look into the slot with a flashlight for dirt or a foreign object.
if: If the spare key goes in fine, have a new key cut from the spare or by code, not copied from the damaged one.
If no key will go in, or the lock looks damaged, call a locksmith rather than forcing it.
result.why: If the key won't slide in all the way, the pins in the lock can't line up, so it will never turn. That's often something on the key or in the slot, not a problem deeper in the car.

causes.name: Dirty, bent or damaged key
causes.clues: Gunk on the key, a visible bend, or a chipped edge.

causes.name: Debris or a foreign object in the lock
causes.clues: You can see something in the slot, or a child may have pushed something in.

causes.name: Damaged lock
causes.clues: Scratches, pry marks or a loose face on the lock.

you: Try the spare key.
Wipe the key clean and check that it's straight.
Shine a light into the slot.

result.title: The car may not register that it's in Park
result.now: With your foot on the brake, move the shifter firmly all the way into Park, then try turning the key back to Off.
if: If it still won't release and the dash lights are dim or dark, a weak battery may be the cause, since many cars need power to release the key.
If it happens often, have the shifter linkage and the key release checked.
If the car moved or rolled when you thought it was in Park, set the parking brake firmly before getting out and have the shifter checked before relying on Park again.
result.why: Automatic cars won't let the key turn to Lock or come out unless the transmission is fully in Park. If the shifter is a hair short of Park, or the part that senses Park is out of adjustment, the key stays trapped.

causes.name: Shifter not fully in Park
causes.clues: Moving the shifter or rocking the car slightly lets the key out.

causes.name: Weak or dead battery
causes.clues: Dim dash lights, or the car was slow to start.

causes.name: Faulty key release or shifter linkage
causes.clues: It keeps happening even when the shifter is firmly in Park.

you: Push the shifter firmly into Park with your foot on the brake.
Check whether the dash lights come on brightly.

result.title: Try the simple fixes first, then call a locksmith
result.now: Make sure the car is in Park, then turn the key gently while rocking the steering wheel left and right. Try the spare key if you have one.
if: If nothing works, call a locksmith who works on cars, or roadside assistance.
If you see damage around the lock, don't force it, and consider whether someone tried to steal the car.
result.why: Most stuck keys come down to the steering lock, a worn key or a worn lock. The two quick checks above help rule out the most common causes before you pay for help.

causes.name: Steering lock under tension
causes.clues: The wheel feels locked.

causes.name: Worn key
causes.clues: A spare key works better.

causes.name: Worn or jammed ignition lock
causes.clues: No key works, even with the wheel loose.

you: Rock the wheel while turning the key.
Try the spare key.

opts.a: It changed suddenly: the steering is very loose, clunks, or the car doesn't go where I steer
It's gotten looser gradually, and I keep making small corrections
It mostly wanders on the highway, in crosswinds or along grooves in the road
I'm not sure

q_play_test.q: With the engine running and the car parked with the wheels straight, gently rock the steering wheel left and right. What do you notice?
q_play_test.help: A little free movement is normal. You're feeling for the wheel moving an inch or more at the rim before you feel resistance or see the front tires start to move. A helper outside the car can watch the tires.

opts.a: The wheel moves a lot before the tires respond, or I feel or hear a clunk
It feels tight when parked, but loose over bumps or while driving
I'm not sure / I can't check

q_driving_clues.q: Which of these do you also notice?

opts.a: Clunking or knocking over bumps or when turning
The car keeps bouncing after bumps, or floats and sways
The tires are wearing on the inner or outer edges
None of these / I'm not sure
The tires are low, worn, or a mix of different brands or sizes
It's worst when the vehicle is heavily loaded or towing
The steering wheel is off-center, or the tires wear unevenly
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: A steering or suspension part may be failing
result.now: Slow down, pull over somewhere safe and stop. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If a front wheel looks tilted or turned differently from the other, don't move the car at all.
If the power steering warning light is on as well, mention it to the tow or repair shop.
Don't try to move the car under its own power, even slowly, until it has been checked.
result.why: Steering that goes loose suddenly, especially with a clunk, can mean a tie rod end, ball joint or steering linkage is close to separating. If one of these lets go, you can lose control of that front wheel.

causes.name: Failing tie rod end
causes.clues: A clunk when turning, and the steering wheel has a lot of free movement.

causes.name: Failing ball joint
causes.clues: Loud clunks over bumps, and a front wheel that may look tilted.

causes.name: Loose steering gear or rack mounting
causes.clues: A clunk from the front when you turn the wheel back and forth while parked.

you: From a safe spot, look at whether both front wheels sit at the same angle.
shop: Steering linkage inspection on a lift
Ball joint and tie rod play check
Steering rack or gearbox mounting check

result.title: Worn tie rods or a worn steering rack are possible causes
result.now: Avoid using the car until the steering has been inspected. If you're on the road now, slow down and pull over when it's safe. A mobile mechanic or a tow is the safest way to get it checked.
if: If you hear clunks, the play is getting worse, or the car doesn't go where you steer, don't move it at all.
If a front wheel looks tilted or turned differently from the other, don't move the car.
If a shop replaces steering parts, have an alignment done afterward.
result.why: Free movement in the steering wheel before the tires respond means something between the wheel and the tires has worn. Tie rod ends and the inner parts of the steering rack or gearbox are common places for this wear. A badly worn tie rod end can separate, which would leave that front wheel uncontrolled.

causes.name: Worn tie rod ends (inner or outer)
causes.clues: A clunk or knock when rocking the wheel, and wear on the edges of the front tires.

causes.name: Worn steering rack or steering gearbox
causes.clues: The tie rods check out but there's still play, or a fluid leak near the rack.

causes.name: Worn steering shaft joint
causes.clues: A clunk you feel in the steering column itself.

you: Have a helper watch a front tire while you rock the steering wheel slightly.

result.title: Worn ball joints or suspension bushings are possible causes
result.now: Avoid using the car until the front suspension has been inspected. If you're on the road now, slow down and pull over when it's safe. A mobile mechanic or a tow is the safest way to get it checked.
if: If the clunking gets louder, a front wheel looks tilted, or the car darts over bumps, don't move it at all.
If the shop finds only worn sway bar links or bushings, ask whether the car can be used until the repair, and follow their advice.
If the tires are wearing unevenly, have an alignment done after any repairs.
result.why: Ball joints and bushings hold the wheels in position while the suspension moves. When they wear, the wheel shifts over bumps and in turns, so the steering feels loose and the car wanders even if it feels tight when parked. A badly worn ball joint can separate, which can let a front wheel collapse or turn on its own. A shop can check each part for play on a lift to see which one is worn.

causes.name: Worn ball joints
causes.clues: Clunking or creaking over bumps and when turning.

causes.name: Worn control arm bushings
causes.clues: A clunk when braking or accelerating, and a pull that comes and goes.

causes.name: Worn sway bar links
causes.clues: A rattle or knock over small bumps.

you: Listen for clunks over speed bumps with the windows down.
shop: Ball joint play check on a lift

result.title: Worn shocks or struts may be letting the car float and wander
result.now: Book a suspension inspection and ask them to check the shocks or struts.
if: If a shock is leaking fluid or the car is hard to control on bumpy curves, get it checked within a few days.
If you also hear clunks, ask them to check the ball joints and bushings.
If the steering suddenly gets looser or you hear new clunks from the front, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
result.why: Shocks and struts keep the tires pressed firmly on the road. When they wear out, the car floats and sways, the tires lose grip over bumps, and the steering feels vague.

causes.name: Worn shocks or struts
causes.clues: Bouncing after bumps, nose diving when braking, swaying in turns.

causes.name: Worn strut mounts
causes.clues: A clunk or creak from the top of the front suspension when turning.

you: Push down hard on each corner and let go. More than one or two bounces suggests worn shocks.
Look for oily residue on the shocks or struts.

result.title: Alignment that's out of spec is a possible cause of wandering
result.now: Check the tire pressures, then book an alignment check and ask them to inspect the steering parts at the same time.
if: If the tires are wearing badly on one edge, get it done soon to save them.
If the shop finds worn steering or suspension parts, those will usually need repair before an alignment will hold.
If the steering suddenly gets looser, clunks, or the car doesn't go where you steer, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
result.why: The angles of the front wheels help the car track straight and the steering return to center. When those angles drift out, the car may wander, follow grooves in the road, and wear the tires unevenly.

causes.name: Alignment out of spec
causes.clues: Uneven tire wear, or an off-center steering wheel.

causes.name: Worn steering or suspension parts
causes.clues: Clunks, or the alignment won't stay set.

causes.name: Tire problem
causes.clues: Low pressure, worn tread or mismatched tires.

you: Check all four tire pressures.
Look for wear on the inner or outer edges of the tires.

result.title: The tires are a possible cause of the wandering
result.now: Set all four tires to the pressure on the driver's door jamb sticker and check the tread depth.
if: If the wandering continues with correct pressures, book an alignment and steering check.
If the tread is worn down or the tires are mismatched, replace them in matching pairs at least, ideally a full set.
If you see a bulge, bubble or cords showing on any tire, don't drive on it.
If you hear clunks or the steering suddenly gets looser, pull over when it's safe and have the steering checked before driving further.
result.why: Low pressure makes tires soft and slow to respond. Worn tread and mismatched tires grip differently side to side and tend to follow grooves in the road. These are the easiest causes to check.

causes.name: Low tire pressure
causes.clues: One or more tires below the door jamb number, or the TPMS light is on.

causes.name: Worn or unevenly worn tires
causes.clues: Shallow tread, or wear on one edge.

causes.name: Mismatched tires
causes.clues: Different brands, models or sizes on the same axle.

you: Check pressures when the tires are cold.
Check tread depth with a gauge or the wear bars molded into the tread.

result.title: Too much weight at the back may be lifting the front and lightening the steering
result.now: Check the load against the weight limits in your owner's manual and the door jamb sticker, and spread the weight more evenly.
if: If you're towing and the trailer sways, slow down gradually, don't brake hard, and pull over to rebalance the load.
If it wanders even when the vehicle is empty, have the steering and suspension inspected.
If the steering suddenly gets looser or you hear a clunk from the front, pull over when it's safe and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Heavy cargo behind the rear axle, or too much trailer tongue weight, presses the rear down and lifts the front. With less weight on the front tires, the steering feels light and the vehicle wanders. Worn rear shocks or springs make it worse.

causes.name: Overloaded or unevenly loaded vehicle
causes.clues: The rear sits noticeably low when loaded.

causes.name: Trailer hitch setup or tongue weight
causes.clues: Wandering or sway mainly when towing.

causes.name: Worn rear springs or shocks
causes.clues: The rear sags or bounces even with a normal load.

you: Compare the load with the weight limit on the door jamb sticker.
Check the tire pressures. Some vehicles list a higher pressure for heavy loads.
shop: Hitch setup and tongue weight check

result.title: Have the steering and front suspension inspected
result.now: Check the tire pressures, then book a steering and suspension inspection. Tell the shop when the car wanders and whether it's getting worse.
if: If the steering gets noticeably looser or you hear new clunks, stop driving it and have it towed or checked by a mobile mechanic.
If the car doesn't respond properly when you turn the wheel, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: Loose or wandering steering can come from the tires, the alignment, or wear in the steering and suspension parts. A technician can check for play in each part quickly with the car on a lift.

causes.name: Worn tie rods or steering rack
causes.clues: Free play in the steering wheel.

causes.name: Worn ball joints or bushings
causes.clues: Clunks over bumps.

causes.name: Tires or alignment
causes.clues: Uneven tire wear or low pressures.

you: Check the tire pressures.
Note when the wandering is worst.
shop: Steering and suspension play check on a lift

q_symptoms.q: Along with the low coolant, do you notice any of these?
q_symptoms.help: Coolant is usually green, orange, pink, blue or yellow, and smells sweet, like syrup.

opts.a: The engine runs hot, or a temperature warning has come on
White, sweet-smelling exhaust smoke that doesn't go away once the engine is warm
Foggy windows, a sweet smell inside the car, or a damp passenger floor
A sweet smell or wisps of steam from under the hood after driving, but no drips when parked
None of these. The level just keeps dropping
I'm not sure

q_how_fast.q: How fast does the level drop?
q_how_fast.help: Mark the level on the overflow tank with tape or take a photo when the engine is cold, then compare after a few days.

opts.a: Quickly. I'm topping it up every few days or every week
Slowly. A little every few weeks or months
It dropped once or twice after a coolant change or repair, then stayed put
I'm not sure

q_oil_cap.q: With the engine off and cool, pull out the oil dipstick and look under the oil filler cap. What do you see?
q_oil_cap.help: Normal oil is amber to dark brown or black. A little light-colored moisture under the cap can be normal after short trips in cold weather.

opts.a: Milky, light brown or foamy, like a chocolate milkshake
The oil looks normal
I'm not sure

result.title: Coolant loss may now be causing overheating. Stop driving it
result.now: If it's running hot, pull over somewhere safe and turn the engine off. Once it's cool, have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you're stuck in traffic and can't pull over yet, turn the A/C off and the heater on full hot to pull some heat away.
If you also see white exhaust smoke or milky oil, don't try to restart it.
If you see steam or smoke, step away from the car and don't open the hood or any cap until it has cooled.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn it off and don't restart it.
result.why: If the engine is running hot, there may no longer be enough coolant to protect it. Overheating can warp the cylinder head or blow the head gasket, which also causes coolant loss, so the problem can quickly feed itself.

causes.name: Head gasket leak
causes.clues: White sweet-smelling exhaust, milky oil, or bubbles in the coolant tank.

causes.name: Leak that only appears when hot
causes.clues: A sweet smell or steam after driving, but no drips when parked.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: Foggy windows or a damp passenger floor.

you: Once fully cool, check the overflow tank level and the oil for a milky look.

result.title: Coolant may be leaking inside the engine, often at the head gasket
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic test it.
if: If the oil looks milky, don't start the engine at all. Coolant in the oil can quickly ruin the bearings.
If a test rules out the head gasket, a leaking intake gasket, oil cooler or EGR cooler (on some engines) can cause similar signs.
result.why: Sweet-smelling white smoke that stays after warm-up, or milky oil, can mean coolant is getting into the cylinders or the oil. A shop will usually confirm this with a combustion gas test and a pressure test before any engine work. Driving on it can turn a gasket repair into a full engine replacement.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: White sweet-smelling exhaust, bubbles in the coolant tank, or past overheating.

causes.name: Cracked or warped cylinder head
causes.clues: The engine was badly overheated at some point.

causes.name: Leaking intake gasket, oil cooler or EGR cooler
causes.clues: Milky oil without heavy smoke, on engines that have these parts.

you: With the engine off and cool, check the dipstick and under the oil cap for milky sludge.

result.title: The heater core may be leaking inside the car
result.now: Top up the coolant when the engine is cold, and get the heater core checked within the next few days.
if: If the windshield fogs so you can't see, don't drive it until it's fixed.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: The heater core is a small radiator behind the dash. When it leaks, coolant escapes into the cabin as vapor or soaks into the carpet, so you never see a puddle under the car. The sweet smell and greasy fog on the glass are the usual clues.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: A sweet smell inside, a greasy film on the inside of the windshield, or a damp passenger floor.

causes.name: Leaking heater hose connection at the firewall
causes.clues: Wet or crusty spots where the hoses go through to the cabin.

causes.name: Water from a blocked A/C drain
causes.clues: Clear, odorless water on the floor, worse after A/C use.
causes.against: This explains a wet floor, but not dropping coolant.

you: Press a paper towel into the wet carpet and check for color and a sweet smell.
Wipe the inside of the windshield and look for an oily film.

result.title: A small leak may be boiling off when the engine is hot
result.now: Have a shop pressure-test the cooling system within the next few days. Keep the coolant topped up when cold until then.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you see heavy steam rather than faint wisps, stop driving it.
If you notice white sweet-smelling exhaust smoke or milky oil, stop driving it.
result.why: Under pressure, a hot cooling system can seep from a hose, the water pump or the radiator, and the coolant evaporates on hot engine parts before it can drip. That leaves a sweet smell and crusty residue instead of a puddle.

causes.name: Seeping hose or hose clamp
causes.clues: Crusty colored deposits at hose ends, or a soft, swollen hose.

causes.name: Water pump seal starting to leak
causes.clues: A crusty trail below the pump near the engine belt.

causes.name: Radiator or plastic tank seam leak
causes.clues: Residue along the edge of the radiator tanks.

causes.name: Worn radiator or tank cap
causes.clues: Coolant residue around the cap or the overflow tank.

you: With the engine cold, use a flashlight to look for crusty colored deposits on hoses, the radiator and the water pump.

result.title: A slow seep or a worn cap is a common cause
result.now: Keep the overflow tank between MIN and MAX when cold, and book a cooling system pressure test when convenient.
if: If the loss speeds up, or the temperature gauge rises above normal, get it checked within a few days.
If you notice white exhaust smoke or milky oil, stop driving it.
If you notice a sweet smell inside the car or greasy fog on the windshield, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: A very slow loss usually comes from a tiny seep that evaporates, or a radiator or tank cap that no longer holds pressure and lets coolant escape as vapor. A slow loss is usually less pressing than a fast one, but slow leaks tend to grow, and an internal leak can start small, so it's worth having tested.

causes.name: Worn radiator or tank cap
causes.clues: Residue around the cap, or the cap's rubber seal is cracked or flattened.

causes.name: Small seep from a hose or the water pump
causes.clues: Crusty colored deposits you can see with a flashlight.

causes.name: Early heater core leak
causes.clues: A faint sweet smell inside, especially with the heat on.

you: Mark the level when cold and track it over a few weeks.
Look for crusty deposits around hoses and the cap.

result.title: Trapped air may be working its way out after the service
result.now: With the engine cold, top up the overflow tank to the MAX line with the same coolant that was used, then check it again after the next few drives.
if: If the level keeps dropping after a week or so, there's a real leak. Have it pressure-tested.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal or the heater blows cold, get it checked within a few days. A large air pocket may need to be bled out.
If you see steam or smell coolant, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: After coolant is drained and refilled, air can stay trapped in the engine and heater. As it works its way out over the first few drives, coolant takes its place and the tank level drops. Once the air is gone, the level should hold steady.

causes.name: Air working out after coolant service
causes.clues: The drop happened right after a coolant change or repair, then stopped.

causes.name: Loose hose clamp from the repair
causes.clues: Wet or crusty spots near parts that were worked on.

you: Check the overflow tank level when cold after each of the next few drives.
Look around any parts that were recently replaced for wet spots.

result.title: Coolant is escaping fast. A pressure test can help find where
result.now: Get the cooling system pressure-tested within the next few days. Until then, check the level with the engine cold before every trip, top up as needed, keep trips short, avoid highways and towing, and watch the temperature gauge.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you need to add coolant after every drive, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If white sweet-smelling exhaust smoke appears, stop driving it.
If you see steam or the oil turns milky, stop driving it and have it towed.
result.why: Losing coolant every few days with normal-looking oil often means a leak that only opens up when the system is hot and under pressure, or one hiding behind the dash. It can also be an early head gasket leak that hasn't reached the oil yet. A pressure test and a combustion gas test can usually sort out which.

causes.name: Leak that only shows up hot and under pressure
causes.clues: A sweet smell after driving, or crusty deposits on hoses or the water pump.

causes.name: Heater core leak
causes.clues: Foggy windows, a sweet smell inside, or a damp passenger floor.

causes.name: Early head gasket leak
causes.clues: Bubbles in the coolant tank while running, or a little white smoke at startup.
causes.against: Normal oil makes a severe head gasket leak less likely, but doesn't rule out a small one.

you: With the engine cold, check hoses and the water pump for crusty deposits.
Feel the passenger-side carpet for dampness.

result.title: Track the level, then get a pressure test
result.now: Mark the coolant level when cold, top it up if needed, and book a cooling system pressure test when convenient.
if: If the level drops quickly, or the temperature gauge rises above normal, get it checked within a few days.
If you see white sweet-smelling exhaust smoke or milky oil, stop driving it.
If you notice a sweet smell inside the car or fog on the windshield, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: Knowing how fast the coolant is disappearing helps separate a minor seep from a serious internal leak. A pressure test is the standard way to find leaks you can't see.

causes.name: Small leak that evaporates
causes.clues: A sweet smell after driving.

causes.name: Worn radiator or tank cap
causes.clues: Residue around the cap.

causes.name: Heater core or internal leak
causes.clues: A damp passenger floor, foggy windows, or white exhaust smoke.

you: Mark the level when cold and recheck after a few days.

loss-of-power-when-accelerating.title: Car has no power when accelerating

q_signs.q: Which of these best describes what's happening?
q_signs.help: "Revs" is the engine speed shown on the tachometer (the RPM gauge). If you don't have one, listen for whether the engine gets louder without the car speeding up.

opts.a: The check engine light is flashing, and the engine shakes or stumbles
The temperature gauge is high or a temperature warning is on
It feels held back, with a burning smell or one very hot wheel
A "reduced engine power" or similar message, or it won't go above a low speed
The engine revs up but the car doesn't speed up to match
The engine just feels weak, especially uphill or when passing
I'm not sure
The check engine light is on and stays on (not flashing)
It sputters, jerks or hesitates when I press the gas
Power gets worse the faster I go, sometimes with a rotten egg smell
It's turbocharged, and I hear a whoosh, hiss or whistle
Nothing else. It has slowly gotten more sluggish
I'm not sure

result.title: A severe misfire may be robbing the engine of power
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive it further. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you smell something very hot or see smoke under the car, step away. An overheated catalytic converter can set dry grass on fire.
If the light stops flashing after a restart, the fault is still there. Have it checked before driving.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means one or more cylinders isn't firing properly. The engine loses power, and unburned fuel goes into the exhaust, where it can overheat and destroy the catalytic converter.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: Steady shaking that gets worse under load.

causes.name: Fuel injector problem
causes.clues: A fuel smell, or misfiring from a cold start.

causes.name: Internal engine problem
causes.clues: Ticking or knocking along with the misfire.
causes.against: Less common than an ignition fault.

shop: Ignition coil and spark plug test

result.title: The engine may be overheating and protecting itself
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive it further. Have it towed.
if: If you see steam or smoke from under the hood, step away and don't open the hood until it cools.
Never open the radiator or coolant cap on a hot engine.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn it off and don't restart it.
result.why: Many cars cut power when the engine gets too hot to protect it. An overheating engine can warp or crack major parts quickly, so it's not worth risking even a short drive.

causes.name: Low coolant from a leak
causes.clues: Coolant puddles, a sweet smell, or steam.

causes.name: Failed cooling fan, thermostat or water pump
causes.clues: Overheating mostly in traffic, or the heater blowing cold.

causes.name: Head gasket failure
causes.clues: White smoke from the exhaust and coolant loss with no visible leak.

result.title: A brake may be stuck on and holding the car back
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, turn off the engine and let the brakes cool. Don't drive it further. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the parking brake was partly on, release it fully and let the wheels cool. Brakes that got hot enough to smell can be weaker afterward, so have them checked before relying on the car. If the pedal feels soft or sinks, don't drive it.
If there's smoke or flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
If the brake warning light is on or you see fluid near a wheel, don't drive it.
result.why: A brake that won't release fights the engine every time you accelerate, which feels like a loss of power. It also builds up heat fast, which can boil the brake fluid and leave you with weak brakes.

causes.name: Stuck brake caliper
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter, smells burnt, or the car pulls to one side.

causes.name: Parking brake on or sticking
causes.clues: The parking brake light is on, or the drag comes from the rear.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose
causes.clues: One brake stays on after heavy braking.

you: Check that the parking brake is fully released.
Without touching, look for smoke near each wheel.
shop: Brake inspection with the wheels off

result.title: The car may have gone into limp mode to protect itself
result.now: Get off busy roads safely and have the codes read within a day. If you must move the car, keep it to short, low-speed trips.
if: If the check engine light is flashing, the temperature is high, or the transmission won't shift, stop driving and have it towed.
If you can't keep up with traffic, don't drive it on highways. Call roadside assistance instead.
If a red warning light comes on, such as oil pressure or temperature, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: When the engine or transmission computer sees a serious fault, it limits power or locks the transmission in one gear. This protects parts from damage, but it also makes the car slow and unsafe in fast traffic. The stored codes help point a shop toward the cause.

causes.name: Electronic throttle or accelerator pedal sensor fault
causes.clues: A "reduced engine power" message and a pedal that seems to do little.

causes.name: Transmission fault
causes.clues: Stuck in one gear, harsh shifts, or a transmission warning.

causes.name: Turbo, sensor or wiring fault
causes.clues: A turbo engine, or a recent repair near the engine wiring.

you: Note any messages on the dash before turning the car off.
Have the codes read at a shop or auto parts store.
shop: Code scan of engine and transmission modules
Throttle body and pedal sensor test

result.title: The transmission or clutch may be slipping
result.now: Have it checked within a few days. Until then, accelerate gently, avoid highways and heavy loads, and check the transmission fluid if your car has a dipstick.
if: If the car won't move in gear, or you smell burning fluid, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the slipping gets worse quickly, don't wait. It can leave you stuck in traffic.
If a transmission temperature or warning light comes on, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
result.why: When the engine revs climb but the car doesn't speed up, power isn't getting through to the wheels. In an automatic that usually points to low or worn fluid or worn internal parts. In a manual, the clutch is the usual cause.

causes.name: Low or worn transmission fluid
causes.clues: Red fluid under the car, or slipping that's worse when warm.

causes.name: Worn transmission clutches or bands (automatic)
causes.clues: Harsh or delayed shifts, and high mileage.

causes.name: Worn clutch (manual)
causes.clues: Slipping in higher gears, a burning smell, or the clutch engages high in the pedal travel.

you: Check the transmission fluid level and color if your car has a dipstick (follow the owner's manual).
Look for red or brown fluid where you park.

result.title: An engine sensor or fuel problem may be cutting power
result.now: Have the codes read within a few days. Many auto parts stores do this free, which gives the shop a head start.
if: If the light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over and turn off the engine.
If you can't keep up with traffic safely, stay off highways until it's fixed.
If you smell raw fuel, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: A steady check engine light with low power means the engine computer has spotted a fault, often one that affects how much air or fuel the engine gets. The stored code points a shop to the right system, and testing then confirms which part is at fault.

causes.name: Faulty mass airflow (MAF) or oxygen sensor
causes.clues: Hesitation, poor mileage, or a rough idle.

causes.name: Weak fuel pump or clogged fuel filter
causes.clues: Power fades going uphill or at highway speed.

causes.name: Vacuum or intake leak
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or a high or uneven idle.

causes.name: EGR valve problem
