causes.clues: Rough idle and stumbling at low speeds.

you: Have the codes read and write them down.
Check the engine air filter.

result.title: A fuel delivery or ignition problem is possible
result.now: Have it checked within a few days. Drive gently, and keep the tank above a quarter full until then.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and turn off the engine.
If it stalls or cuts out while driving, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If you smell raw fuel, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: Sputtering or jerking when you press the gas means the engine isn't getting a steady supply of fuel or spark when it needs more. Worn spark plugs, weak coils and fuel supply problems are common causes.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs or failing ignition coil
causes.clues: Jerking under load, rough idle, plugs overdue for replacement.

causes.name: Weak fuel pump or clogged fuel filter
causes.clues: Worse uphill, at highway speed, or when the tank is low.

causes.name: Dirty fuel injectors
causes.clues: Hesitation and poor mileage that came on gradually.

causes.name: Dirty mass airflow sensor
causes.clues: Hesitation right after pressing the gas.

you: Check your service records for when the spark plugs were last changed.
Notice whether it's worse when the fuel tank is low.

result.title: A clogged catalytic converter or exhaust could be choking the engine
result.now: Have the exhaust checked within a few days. Avoid long highway drives and steep climbs until then.
if: If you see a red glow under the car or smell something very hot, pull over and turn off the engine away from dry grass.
If the check engine light is flashing, stop driving. A misfire may be damaging the converter.
result.why: The engine has to push its exhaust out. If the catalytic converter is clogged or melted inside, the exhaust backs up and the engine loses power, most noticeably at higher speeds and uphill. A converter usually fails because of another problem, like a misfire or burning oil, so a shop will normally test back-pressure and look for that root cause before replacing it.

causes.name: Clogged or melted catalytic converter
causes.clues: Power fades at higher speeds, rotten egg smell, extra heat under the car.

causes.name: Collapsed or blocked exhaust pipe or muffler
causes.clues: Recent damage underneath, or a rattle.

causes.name: Misfire or oil burning that damaged the converter
causes.clues: A history of check engine lights, misfires or blue smoke.

you: Note whether power is fine at low speed but fades on the highway.
Notice any rotten egg smell after driving.
shop: Check for the root cause (misfire, oil burning)

result.title: A boost leak or turbocharger problem is possible
result.now: Have the turbo and intake hoses checked within a few days. Drive gently and avoid hard acceleration until then.
if: If you hear a loud whine or siren-like noise, or see blue smoke, pull over and turn off the engine. Have it towed.
If the oil level is dropping, don't keep driving it until it's checked.
If the oil pressure light comes on, turn the engine off as soon as it's safe and don't restart it.
result.why: A turbocharger pushes extra air into the engine. If a hose has split or come loose, or the turbo itself is worn, that air escapes with a hiss or whoosh and the engine loses much of its power.

causes.name: Split or loose intake or intercooler hose
causes.clues: A hiss or whoosh under acceleration, and oily residue on a hose.

causes.name: Turbo wastegate or boost control problem
causes.clues: A check engine light for underboost, or power that comes and goes.

causes.name: Worn turbocharger
causes.clues: Whining noise, blue smoke, and rising oil use.

you: With the engine off and cool, look for loose clamps or split hoses between the turbo and the engine.
Check the oil level.

result.title: Wear and overdue maintenance are common causes of slow, gradual power loss
result.now: Check the engine air filter and when the spark plugs were last changed, then book a check when convenient.
if: If a check engine light comes on, have the codes read.
If it suddenly gets worse, sputters, or struggles to keep up with traffic, get it checked within a few days.
If the check engine light flashes or you smell burning, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: Power that slips away over months usually comes from wear rather than a sudden failure. A dirty air filter, worn plugs, dirty injectors or a clogged fuel filter each take a little off, and together they add up.

causes.name: Dirty engine air filter
causes.clues: Long time since the last change, or dusty driving.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs
causes.clues: Plugs overdue per the maintenance schedule, or slightly rough idle.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or fuel injectors
causes.clues: Uneven idle and slightly worse fuel mileage.

causes.name: Restricted exhaust or fuel filter
causes.clues: Power fades more at higher speeds or uphill.

you: Check the engine air filter.
Compare your maintenance records with the schedule in the owner's manual.

result.title: Have the codes read and the car road-tested to find the cause
result.now: Have the codes read, even if no light is on, and book a check. Note when the power loss happens so you can tell the shop.
if: If a warning light comes on, the engine shakes, or you smell burning, pull over and stop.
If the car can't keep up with traffic, don't drive it on highways until it's checked.
result.why: Loss of power can come from the engine, the transmission, the exhaust or the brakes. A scan and a short road test with a technician usually narrow it down quickly.

causes.name: Fuel or ignition problem
causes.clues: Sputtering or hesitation.

causes.name: Transmission slipping
causes.clues: Revs rise without the car speeding up.

causes.name: Restricted exhaust or dragging brake
causes.clues: The car feels held back, especially at higher speeds.

you: Write down when it happens: cold or warm, uphill, at highway speed, or with a low tank.

q_danger.q: Do you notice either of these?
q_danger.help: Exhaust fumes contain carbon monoxide, which you can't see or smell. A fume smell inside the car means it may be getting in too.

opts.a: An exhaust smell inside the car, or headache, dizziness or drowsiness while driving
Something hanging down or scraping the road under the car
Neither of these
I'm not sure
Suddenly and very loud the first time I started the car after it was parked
Suddenly, right after hitting a pothole, curb, speed bump or something in the road
It has been getting louder gradually
I'm not sure

q_where.q: Where does the noise seem to come from, and what does it sound like?
q_where.help: Listen from outside the car while someone else starts it and gently revs it in Park.

opts.a: Near the engine: a ticking or puffing sound, loudest on a cold start
Under the middle of the car: a deep roar or rumble when accelerating
From the back, near the muffler or tailpipe
I'm not sure

result.title: Exhaust fumes may be getting into the cabin
result.now: Pull over, turn the engine off and get everyone out into fresh air. Don't drive it again until the leak is fixed. Have it towed.
if: If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone into fresh air right away and call 911 from outside the car.
If the smell only appears with the windows down at low speed and nobody feels unwell, it still needs to be fixed before the car is driven again.
If anyone feels unwell again once back in the car, even after airing it out, don't use it until the exhaust has been repaired.
result.why: Exhaust contains carbon monoxide, a gas you can't see that can make you sick or cause you to pass out without warning. A loud exhaust means there's a leak, and a fume smell inside means the gas may be reaching you.

causes.name: Exhaust leak under the cabin
causes.clues: The noise is loudest under the middle of the car, and the smell is worse when stopped.

causes.name: Leak near the engine reaching the vents
causes.clues: The smell comes through the vents, especially with the fan on.

causes.name: Rusted pipe with holes in several places
causes.clues: An older car with heavy rust underneath.

shop: Exhaust system inspection on a lift
Body seal and trunk seal check for fume entry

result.title: Part of the exhaust has broken loose
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe and away from dry grass. Don't drive it with the pipe dragging. Call roadside assistance or a tow.
if: If you see smoke or flames under the car, get everyone away and call 911.
A roadside technician may be able to secure the pipe temporarily once it's cool, but it still needs a proper repair soon.
If you smell fuel or see fluid dripping near the damaged pipe, keep everyone away from the car and call for help. Fuel and brake lines run close to the exhaust.
result.why: Exhaust pipes hang from rubber hangers and metal brackets. When one breaks or a rusted pipe snaps, the pipe can drag, catch on the road, damage other parts or come loose in traffic. The hot metal can also set dry grass or debris on fire.

causes.name: Broken rubber hanger or bracket
causes.clues: The pipe hangs low but is still in one piece.

causes.name: Rusted pipe that snapped
causes.clues: An older car, and the noise got very loud at the same time.

causes.name: Impact damage
causes.clues: It started after hitting something on the road.

you: From a safe spot, look under the car to see what's hanging. Don't touch the exhaust until it has cooled.
shop: Exhaust system inspection on a lift
Check for damage to fuel and brake lines nearby

result.title: The catalytic converter may have been stolen
result.now: With the car parked and cool, look under the car, between the engine and the muffler, for a missing section or pipes with clean, freshly cut ends. If it's gone, report it to the police and your insurer, and arrange the repair within the next few days. Until then, use the car as little as possible and never sit in it while it idles.
if: If you smell exhaust inside the car, don't drive it. If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning: get everyone into fresh air and call 911 from outside the car.
If nothing is missing, the noise is likely a broken pipe or gasket. Have the exhaust inspected within a few days.
If a cut pipe end is hanging low or scraping, or you see damaged wires or fluid dripping near the cut, don't drive it. Thieves sometimes nick nearby lines.
result.why: A car that's suddenly very loud the first time you start it after it was parked, with no warning before, is a common sign of catalytic converter theft. Thieves cut it out in minutes. Without it, the car is loud, the check engine light will usually come on, and exhaust exits under the middle of the car.

causes.name: Stolen catalytic converter
causes.clues: Freshly cut pipe ends, and the car was parked overnight or in a public lot.
causes.against: If all the exhaust parts are still there, theft is ruled out.

causes.name: Broken or separated exhaust pipe
causes.clues: A rusted joint or a pipe that's come apart, with no cut marks.

causes.name: Blown exhaust gasket
causes.clues: Loud, but not as loud, and there's no visible damage.

you: With the car parked and cool, look underneath for a missing section or cut pipe ends.
Take photos for the police and insurance report.
shop: Exhaust system inspection on a lift

result.title: The impact may have broken or knocked loose part of the exhaust
result.now: Once the car is cool, look underneath for a bent, cracked or separated pipe. Get it inspected within the next few days, and keep any driving short.
if: If you smell exhaust inside the car, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If something is hanging or scraping, pull over and call for a tow.
If you also see fluid dripping, the impact may have damaged other parts. Have it checked before driving.
If a warning light comes on, the brake pedal feels different, or you smell fuel after the hit, don't drive it until it's been checked. Something besides the exhaust may be damaged.
result.why: Exhaust pipes run low under the car, so they're often the first thing to hit a curb or road debris. A hit can crack a pipe, break a joint or tear a hanger, which lets exhaust escape before the muffler.

causes.name: Cracked or separated pipe joint
causes.clues: A visible gap or a pipe that's out of line.

causes.name: Damaged flex pipe
causes.clues: A woven, braided section of pipe that's torn or crushed.

causes.name: Crushed or punctured muffler
causes.clues: A dent or hole in the muffler, with the noise loudest at the back.

you: With the car cool, look underneath for dents, gaps or hanging parts.
Look for any fluid drips on the ground under the car.
shop: Exhaust system inspection on a lift
Check of nearby fuel and brake lines and the oil pan

result.title: Possibly a leak at the exhaust manifold near the engine
result.now: Book an exhaust inspection when convenient, and mention that the ticking is loudest on a cold start.
if: If you smell exhaust inside the car, especially through the vents, stop driving it and have it checked right away.
If you smell burning plastic or rubber under the hood, have it checked soon. Hot exhaust may be reaching nearby wiring or hoses.
If the check engine light is flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. If the engine runs rough, have it checked within a day or two.
result.why: The exhaust manifold collects gas right where it leaves the engine. A cracked manifold or a blown gasket leaks in quick puffs, which sounds like ticking. It's often loudest when cold because the metal shrinks and the gap is bigger until it warms up.

causes.name: Blown exhaust manifold gasket
causes.clues: Ticking that matches engine speed and quiets down as the engine warms.

causes.name: Cracked exhaust manifold
causes.clues: Common on some trucks and older engines, with sooty marks near the crack.

causes.name: Broken or missing manifold bolt
causes.clues: Black soot at one corner of the manifold.

you: Listen near the engine on a cold start, staying clear of belts and the fan.
Look for black soot marks where the exhaust meets the engine.
shop: Code scan if the check engine light is on

result.title: Possibly a leak in the pipe or a joint under the middle of the car
result.now: Have the exhaust inspected within the next few days. Until then, don't sit in the car with the engine idling for long periods.
if: If you smell exhaust inside the car, stop driving and get fresh air. If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning: get everyone into fresh air and call 911 from outside the car.
If the check engine light comes on, mention it. A leak near an oxygen sensor can affect how the engine runs.
If you see smoke or smell burning from under the car, pull over and turn the engine off. A loose pipe can heat up nearby parts or debris.
result.why: The middle section of the exhaust runs right under where you sit. A leak there makes a deep roar under acceleration and is the most likely place for fumes to reach the cabin, which is why it shouldn't wait.

causes.name: Worn or torn flex pipe
causes.clues: A woven, braided section of pipe near the front that's frayed or cracked. Common on front-wheel-drive cars.

causes.name: Rusted pipe or failed joint gasket
causes.clues: Heavy rust or black soot at a joint.

causes.name: Damaged catalytic converter shell or connection
causes.clues: The noise is near the converter, sometimes with a rattle.

you: With the car cool, look under the middle of the car for rust holes, gaps or black soot marks.
shop: Exhaust system inspection on a lift

result.title: Often a rusted or damaged muffler or tailpipe
result.now: Book an exhaust inspection when convenient. Avoid idling with the trunk or rear hatch open.
if: If you smell exhaust inside the car, especially in the back seat or with the hatch closed, stop driving it and have it checked before using the car again.
If the noise gets much louder suddenly, or something starts rattling or hanging, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: The muffler and tailpipe sit at the back, where water and road salt collect, so they often rust from the inside out. A hole there makes the car louder and is farther from the cabin, but fumes can still get in through worn trunk or hatch seals, especially when you're stopped.

causes.name: Rusted-through muffler
causes.clues: An older car, rust spots or holes, often on the bottom or seams.

causes.name: Rusted tailpipe or joint at the muffler
causes.clues: Soot or a gap where the pipe enters the muffler.

causes.name: Broken baffles inside the muffler
causes.clues: A rattle when you tap the muffler (when it's cold).

you: With the car cool, look at the muffler and tailpipe for rust holes or soot.
With the engine idling and the car in Park, carefully listen from behind for where the noise is loudest.
shop: Exhaust system inspection on a lift

result.title: There's likely an exhaust leak somewhere. Have it inspected
result.now: Book an exhaust inspection, ideally within the next week or two. Keep idling to a minimum until then.
if: If you smell exhaust inside the car, stop driving and get fresh air. If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning: get everyone into fresh air and call 911 from outside the car.
If something starts dragging or the noise gets much louder suddenly, pull over and call for help.
If you see smoke or smell burning from under the car, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: A suddenly loud exhaust usually means gas is escaping somewhere before it should. With the car on a lift, a technician can usually find the spot quickly.

causes.name: Rusted muffler or pipe
causes.clues: An older car, or one driven where roads are salted.

causes.name: Failed gasket or flex pipe
causes.clues: A rumble or puffing under the front or middle of the car.

causes.name: Broken hanger letting a joint separate
causes.clues: Rattling or clunking along with the noise.

you: Record a short video with sound of the car starting and revving in Park.
Look under the car for anything hanging low.
shop: Exhaust system inspection on a lift

q_when.q: When is the smell strongest?

opts.a: For the first minute or so after turning on the A/C or fan, then it fades
All the time, even with the fan off
After rain or a car wash
It smells like something died, or like urine
It smells more sweet, like syrup, than musty
I'm not sure

q_ac_drip.q: After using the A/C on a warm day, does clear water drip under the front of the car?
q_ac_drip.help: A small puddle of clear, plain water under the front passenger side after using the A/C is normal. It's condensation draining from the A/C.

opts.a: Yes, a normal clear drip
No drip, even on hot, humid days
I'm not sure

q_wet.q: Press your hand into the carpet in both front footwells, the back and the trunk. Is any of it damp?
q_wet.help: Lift the floor mats. Water often hides under them or in the padding below the carpet.

opts.a: Yes, the front passenger-side floor is wet
Yes, somewhere else (driver side, back seat area or trunk)
No, it's all dry
I'm not sure

result.title: Mold or mildew may be growing on the A/C evaporator
result.now: Replace the cabin air filter, then get in the habit of turning off the A/C button and running just the fan for the last few minutes of each drive to dry the system out.
if: If the smell is still there after a few weeks, have a shop clean and disinfect the evaporator and air ducts.
If anyone in the car has asthma or allergies that flare up, have it cleaned sooner.
If the smell turns sweet, or the windshield fogs with a greasy film, it may be coolant rather than mold. Get it checked within a few days.
result.why: The A/C evaporator, behind the dashboard, gets cold and wet as it pulls moisture from the air. Mold and bacteria grow on it when the car sits, and the first blast of air carries the smell out. A normal drip suggests the drain is working, so cleaning and drying are the usual first steps.

causes.name: Mold or bacteria on the A/C evaporator
causes.clues: The smell is worst in the first minute after the A/C or fan comes on, especially in humid weather.

causes.name: Dirty or damp cabin air filter
causes.clues: The filter hasn't been changed in a long time or looks dark and clogged.

you: Check the cabin air filter (often behind the glove box) and replace it if it's dirty.
Run the fan with the A/C off for a few minutes before parking.

result.title: The A/C drain may be clogged, letting water build up inside
result.now: Feel the front passenger-side carpet for dampness and have the A/C drain cleared within a few days.
if: If the wet carpet smells sweet or feels slimy, it may be coolant from the heater core rather than A/C water. Get it checked soon, and watch the temperature gauge.
If water is soaking the carpet, dry it out right away to stop mold and protect wiring under the floor.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward hot, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: The A/C makes water as it cools the air, and that water should drain out through a small tube under the car. If the tube is blocked by debris or insects, water pools inside the A/C housing and can overflow onto the passenger-side floor, feeding mold.

causes.name: Clogged A/C drain tube
causes.clues: No drip under the car after using the A/C, and a sloshing sound behind the dash when turning or braking.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: The wet spot smells sweet, the liquid is colored, or the windshield fogs with a greasy film.
causes.against: Plain, clear water with no sweet smell points to the A/C drain.

causes.name: Leaking windshield or cowl drain
causes.clues: The floor gets wet after rain even without using the A/C.

you: Lift the passenger-side mat and press on the carpet.
After running the A/C on a warm day, look for a drip under the front passenger side.
shop: A/C drain tube inspection and clearing
Heater core leak check if the water smells sweet

result.title: Rain water is probably leaking into the car
result.now: Dry out the wet carpet as soon as you can, and have the leak found and sealed within a few days.
if: If water reaches the seats or wiring and electrical items start acting up, have it checked right away.
If the car was driven through deep water or a flood, have it inspected before relying on it.
If the airbag or other warning lights come on, have it checked before relying on the car. Wiring and connectors under the seats and carpet don't like water.
result.why: When water gets past a seal, it soaks into the carpet padding, which stays damp for a long time and grows mold. That smell then spreads through the cabin and the ventilation. Finding the leak matters more than treating the smell.

causes.name: Clogged sunroof drains
causes.clues: Wet headliner, damp front or rear footwells, and the car has a sunroof.

causes.name: Worn door, window or trunk seals
causes.clues: Water in one footwell or the trunk after rain or a car wash.

causes.name: Leaking windshield seal or blocked cowl drains
causes.clues: Water in the front footwells after rain, and leaves or debris at the base of the windshield.

you: Check the spare tire well in the trunk for water.
Clear leaves from the base of the windshield.
Have someone run a hose over the car while you look inside for drips.

result.title: A dirty cabin air filter or debris in the air intake is a common cause, and the easiest to check first
result.now: Replace the cabin air filter, usually behind the glove box, and clear any leaves or debris from the air intake at the base of the windshield.
if: If the smell continues with a new filter, have a shop check the A/C drain and look for water inside the car.
If you find a wet carpet, get the leak found within a few days.
result.why: The cabin air filter catches dust, pollen and leaves before they reach the vents. Once it's clogged and damp, it grows mildew and every breath of air passes through it. Leaves rotting in the air intake can do the same.

causes.name: Old or damp cabin air filter
causes.clues: The filter hasn't been changed in a year or two, or looks dark and full of debris.

causes.name: Leaves or debris in the fresh air intake
causes.clues: The car is parked under trees, and you can see debris at the base of the windshield.

causes.name: Mold on the A/C evaporator
causes.clues: The smell is strongest when the A/C first comes on.

you: Check and replace the cabin air filter. Your owner's manual shows where it is.
Clear leaves from the cowl area at the base of the windshield.
shop: A/C drain and water leak check

result.title: A rodent may have nested in the air intake or ducts
result.now: Check the cabin air filter and the air intake at the base of the windshield for nesting material or droppings, and book a check when convenient.
if: If you find droppings or a dead animal, wear gloves and a mask while cleaning, or have a shop do it.
If warning lights come on or electrical items stop working, have it checked soon. Rodents often chew wiring.
result.why: Mice and other small animals like the sheltered space in the air intake and ducts, especially in cooler months. Their nests, droppings or a dead animal create a strong, sour smell that the fan pushes into the cabin.

causes.name: Nest or droppings in the cabin air filter housing
causes.clues: Shredded material, seeds or droppings on the filter.

causes.name: Dead animal in the ducts or blower
causes.clues: A strong, rotten smell that's worse with the fan on.

causes.name: Chewed wiring under the hood
causes.clues: Warning lights or electrical problems along with the smell.

you: Remove and inspect the cabin air filter.
Look under the hood for nesting material or droppings.
shop: Cleaning and disinfecting the air intake and ducts

result.title: A sweet smell from the vents can mean a coolant leak, not mold
result.now: Open the windows. When the engine is fully cold, check the coolant level. If it's low, top it up with the type in your owner's manual, and have the car checked within a few days. Never open the coolant cap on a hot engine.
if: If the temperature gauge rises, a coolant warning comes on, or you see steam, pull over and turn off the engine. Don't drive it until it's checked.
If the inside of the windshield fogs with a greasy film you can't clear, pull over until you can see.
If the coolant level keeps dropping and you can't see a leak, have it inspected before relying on the car. Coolant can be leaking inside the heater box or the engine.
result.why: Engine coolant smells sweet. If you smell it through the vents, the heater core behind the dashboard may be leaking, or coolant from the engine bay may be getting pulled into the air intake. Losing coolant can lead to overheating.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: A greasy film on the windshield or wet passenger-side carpet.

causes.name: Coolant leak in the engine bay
causes.clues: Colored drips under the front of the car.

you: Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
Feel the passenger-side carpet for dampness.

q_urgent.q: First, are any of these happening?

opts.a: The oil pressure light (an oil can symbol) is on or flickering
Oil is dripping steadily, or there's a fresh puddle bigger than a dinner plate
Smoke or a burning-oil smell from under the hood
None of these
I'm not sure

q_level.q: With the engine off for a few minutes and the car on level ground, where is the oil on the dipstick?
q_level.help: Pull the dipstick out, wipe it clean, push it fully back in, then pull it out again and read it. Some newer cars have no dipstick and show the oil level on the dashboard screen instead.

opts.a: Between the low and full marks
Below the low mark
No oil shows on the dipstick at all
My car has no dipstick / I'm not sure

q_where.q: Where does the oil seem to be coming from?
q_where.help: With the engine off and cool, use a flashlight from above and from the front. Look for the area that's wet and shiny, not just dusty and grimy.

opts.a: Top of the engine, along the edge of the top cover or around the spark plugs
Around the drain plug or oil filter, and the oil was changed recently
Along the bottom of the engine, around the oil pan
Where the engine and transmission meet
Front of the engine, behind the belts and pulleys
I can't tell / I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may not be getting enough oil pressure
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off and leave it off. After a few minutes, check the dipstick. If it's low, adding the oil type listed in your owner's manual is a good first step, but have the car checked before driving it further. A tow or a mobile mechanic is the safest option.
if: If the light stays on after the level is correct, or you hear ticking or knocking, don't run the engine. Have it towed.
If oil is pouring out, don't refill and restart. Have it towed.
If the light goes out after adding oil and the engine sounds normal, still have the leak and the oil pressure checked before relying on the car. The engine may have run low before the light came on.
result.why: The oil pressure light means oil isn't reaching the engine's moving parts with enough pressure to protect them. Running the engine like that, even briefly, can cause major damage. With a known leak, a very low oil level is a common reason, but it isn't the only one.

causes.name: Oil level too low from the leak
causes.clues: The dipstick shows low or no oil.

causes.name: Failing oil pump or blocked oil pickup
causes.clues: The light stays on even with a full oil level, often with ticking or knocking.

causes.name: Faulty oil pressure sensor
causes.clues: The level is full, the engine sounds normal, and the light flickers randomly.
causes.against: Don't assume it's the sensor until a technician has measured the actual pressure.

you: Check the oil level with the engine off and the car on level ground.

result.title: A large oil leak can drain the engine quickly
result.now: Don't start the engine. Have the car towed or ask a mobile mechanic to come to you.
if: If the oil was changed in the last few days, call the shop that did it. A loose drain plug or filter is a common cause, and they should check it.
If oil is dripping onto the exhaust or you see smoke, keep away from the car and call for help.
result.why: Engines hold only a few quarts of oil. A steady drip or a pour can drop the level dangerously low in a short trip, and running without enough oil can destroy an engine quickly.

causes.name: Loose or missing drain plug, or a loose oil filter
causes.clues: The oil was changed recently, and the oil is coming from the bottom center of the engine or the filter.

causes.name: Damaged oil pan
causes.clues: You recently hit debris, a curb or a pothole, or there's a fresh dent or scrape underneath.

causes.name: Failed oil cooler line or filter housing
causes.clues: Oil spraying around the filter area or along a line, often on trucks and some larger engines.

you: Without getting under the car, look from the front for where the oil is coming from.
Take a photo of the puddle to show the shop.
shop: Lift inspection of the drain plug, filter and oil pan
Refill and leak check before the car is driven

result.title: Oil may be dripping onto hot engine or exhaust parts
result.now: Pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and let it cool. If you see smoke or flames, don't open the hood: get everyone away from the car and call 911. Once it's cool, check the oil level and look for wet oil on or above the exhaust. Have it checked before using the car again, since oil on hot parts can catch fire.
if: If you see heavy smoke or any flames, pull over, turn the engine off, get everyone out, move at least 100 feet away and call 911.
If the oil level is low, or the oil pressure light comes on, don't run the engine. Have it towed.

If the smoke stops once cool and you only find a small amount of residue, it still needs to be looked at before the car is used again. A shop will usually clean the area and recheck to find the true source.
result.why: A small oil leak that lands on the exhaust burns off with a sharp smell and wisps of smoke. A leaking valve cover gasket is a common source. It needs fixing because leaks grow, and oil on very hot parts is a fire risk.

causes.name: Leaking valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Smoke rises from the top or side of the engine after driving.

causes.name: Leaking oil filter housing or oil cooler seal
causes.clues: Wet oil around the oil filter area.

causes.name: Oil spilled during a recent top-up or oil change
causes.clues: The smell started right after oil was added, and it fades after a few drives.
causes.against: If the smell lasts more than a few drives, look for a real leak. Let a shop confirm it's only a spill.

you: After the engine cools, look for wet oil on top of the engine and above the exhaust.
Check the oil level.
shop: Engine clean and recheck with leak dye if needed

result.title: The engine is low on oil, so this leak matters
result.now: Before driving, top up to between the marks with the oil type in your owner's manual. If you can't top it up, don't drive it. Get the leak checked within the next few days, and recheck the level before every drive until it's fixed.
if: If the oil pressure light comes on, or the engine starts ticking or knocking, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off right away and have it towed.
If you need to add oil again within a few days, or you see a steady drip or puddle, the leak is significant. Have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Running low on oil makes the engine wear faster and can lead to serious damage. If the level is low and you're seeing drips, the leak is big enough to matter. Some engines also burn oil, which adds to the loss.

causes.name: Oil pan gasket or drain plug leak
causes.clues: Drips under the center of the engine.

causes.name: Valve cover gasket leak
causes.clues: Oil on top of the engine and a burning smell after driving.

causes.name: Engine burning oil
causes.clues: Blue-gray exhaust smoke, or more oil loss than the drips explain.

you: Recheck the oil level a few days after topping up.
Slide cardboard under the engine overnight to see how much drips.
shop: Oil consumption check if no big leak is found

result.title: Often a leaking valve cover gasket
result.now: Make sure the oil fill cap is tight, then book a check when convenient. Keep an eye on the oil level until it's fixed.
if: If you smell burning oil or see smoke after driving, get it fixed within a few days.

If the engine starts misfiring or the check engine light comes on, oil may be getting into the spark plug wells. Get it checked soon. If the check engine light flashes, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you see smoke from under the hood, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: The valve cover sits on top of the engine and seals with a rubber gasket that hardens with heat and age. It's one of the most common oil leaks. It's usually slow, but the oil can run down onto the hot exhaust.

causes.name: Hardened valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Wet oil along the edge of the top cover.

causes.name: Leaking spark plug tube seals
causes.clues: Oil found in the spark plug wells, sometimes with a misfire.

causes.name: Loose or worn oil fill cap
causes.clues: Oil only around the cap.

you: Check that the oil fill cap is on tight and its seal isn't cracked.
With the engine off and cool, look for wet oil along the edge of the top cover.

result.title: The drain plug or oil filter may not be sealing after the oil change
result.now: Check the oil level, then call the shop that did the oil change and ask them to check it within the next day or two.
if: If it's dripping steadily, or the oil is below the low mark, don't drive it. Ask the shop to come to you or have it towed.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off right away.
result.why: Leaks that start right after an oil change usually come from the drain plug, its washer or the filter. These can loosen or seal poorly, and they can lose oil faster than an old gasket. It's often a quick fix once it's found.

causes.name: Loose drain plug or worn drain plug washer
causes.clues: Drips land directly under the drain plug.

causes.name: Loose oil filter, or the old filter's seal left in place
causes.clues: Oil runs down from the filter, sometimes quickly.

causes.name: Oil spilled during the service
causes.clues: The drips slow down and stop after a day or two.

you: Check the oil level.
Without getting under the car, look for fresh, wet oil near the drain plug and filter.

result.title: Possibly a leaking oil pan gasket
result.now: Book a check when convenient, and check the oil level weekly until it's fixed.
if: If the spot grows bigger than your hand overnight, get it checked within a few days.
If you recently hit something on the road, have the pan checked soon for damage.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off right away.
result.why: The oil pan is the reservoir at the bottom of the engine. Its gasket can harden with age, and the pan itself can get dented or rusted. These leaks are usually slow but steady.

causes.name: Hardened oil pan gasket
causes.clues: Oil along the seam where the pan meets the engine.

causes.name: Damaged or rusted oil pan
causes.clues: A dent, scrape or rust on the pan.

causes.name: Leaking drain plug washer
causes.clues: Drips land right under the drain plug.

you: Slide cardboard under the engine overnight to see how fast it drips.
Check the oil level weekly.
shop: Lift inspection of the oil pan and drain plug
Leak dye test if the source isn't clear

result.title: Oil where the engine meets the transmission can mean the rear main seal
result.now: Book a check when convenient and keep an eye on the oil level. A shop needs to see it on a lift to find the exact source.
if: If the fluid is red or pink, it's more likely transmission fluid. Get it checked within a few days.
If it's a manual and the clutch starts slipping or chattering, oil may be reaching the clutch. Get it checked soon.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off right away.
result.why: The rear main seal keeps oil in where the crankshaft comes out the back of the engine. When it leaks, oil drips where the engine and transmission meet. Oil running down from higher up can end up in the same spot, so the source has to be traced. Because a rear main seal is a big job, a shop will usually clean the area and confirm the source before replacing it.

causes.name: Leaking rear main seal
causes.clues: Drips right at the joint between engine and transmission, often on higher-mileage engines.

causes.name: Oil running down from a leak higher up
causes.clues: Oil streaks down the back of the engine from the valve cover area.

causes.name: Transmission front seal
causes.clues: The fluid is red or pink rather than brown or black.

you: Wipe a drop on a white paper towel to check whether it's brown or black, or red.
Check the oil level.
shop: Clean and recheck to trace the source
Check the oil pan gasket's rear corner

result.title: Possibly a front engine seal or timing cover leak
result.now: Book a check when convenient and keep an eye on the oil level.
if: If oil is soaking the drive belt, or the belt squeals or slips, get it checked within a few days. Oil damages belts.
If your engine has a timing belt, ask the shop to check it. Oil can ruin a timing belt, and if it breaks the engine stops.
If the oil pressure light comes on, or the engine suddenly loses power or stalls, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn it off and have it towed.
result.why: Seals at the front of the engine keep oil in where shafts come out to drive the belts. As they age, oil seeps out and can be flung onto the belts and pulleys as they spin.

causes.name: Front crankshaft seal
causes.clues: Oil behind the large bottom pulley.

causes.name: Timing cover gasket
causes.clues: Oil along the edge of the cover at the front of the engine.

causes.name: Camshaft seal
causes.clues: Oil near the top of the timing area.

you: With the engine off, look for oil on the belts and pulleys.
Check the oil level.
shop: Front seal and timing cover inspection

result.title: A slow oil leak that still needs its source found
result.now: Check the oil level every week or two and book a check when convenient. A shop can trace the leak on a lift.
if: If the level drops below the low mark between checks, get it checked within a few days.
If you see smoke or smell burning oil, pull over, turn the engine off and let it cool. Have it checked before driving again.
If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off right away.
result.why: Oil runs downhill and gets blown back by airflow, so the wet spot is often below or behind the real leak. Cleaning the engine and adding a dye lets a shop find the true source.

causes.name: Valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Oil on top of the engine, or a burning smell.

causes.name: Oil pan gasket or drain plug
causes.clues: Drips under the center of the engine.

causes.name: Front or rear crankshaft seal
causes.clues: Oil at the front behind the belts, or where the engine meets the transmission.

you: Slide cardboard under the engine overnight and photograph the spots.
Check the oil level regularly.

q_when.q: Which of these best describes the oil light?
q_when.help: The oil pressure light usually looks like an old-fashioned oil can with a drip. It's normal for it to light up briefly when you first turn the key, then go out once the engine starts.

opts.a: It's red and stays on while I'm driving or idling
It flickers at idle or at stops, and goes out when I press the gas
It flickers on sharp turns, hard braking or steep hills
It came on soon after an oil change
It's yellow or orange, or a message says oil level low or oil change due
I'm not sure

q_noise.q: Is the engine making a new noise, like loud ticking, tapping or knocking?

opts.a: Yes, knocking, loud tapping or grinding
No, it sounds normal
I'm not sure

q_level.q: With the engine off for a few minutes on level ground, what does the oil dipstick show?
q_level.help: Pull the dipstick, wipe it, push it all the way back in, then pull it out again. The oil should sit between the two marks near the tip. Some cars have no dipstick and show the oil level on the dash instead.

opts.a: Below the low mark, or no oil on the stick at all
Between the low and full marks
The oil looks milky or foamy, or smells strongly of fuel
I can't check it / I'm not sure

q_idle_level.q: With the engine off for a few minutes on level ground, what does the oil dipstick show?
q_idle_level.help: Pull the dipstick, wipe it, push it all the way back in, then pull it out again. The oil should sit between the two marks near the tip.

opts.a: Below the low mark, or no oil on the stick at all
Between the low and full marks
The oil looks milky or foamy, or smells strongly of fuel
I can't check it / I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may already be running without enough oil. Shut it off now
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe, turn off the engine, and don't restart it. Have the car towed.
if: If the oil level is very low, adding oil won't undo damage that's already happened. Still have it towed and let a shop check it.
If you see oil spraying or smoke, step away from the car.
result.why: Low oil pressure plus knocking or loud tapping means metal parts inside the engine are rubbing without a protective oil film. Every extra second of running can turn a repairable problem into an engine replacement.

causes.name: Very low oil level from a leak or burning oil
causes.clues: Oil spots where you park, blue smoke, or a long time since the last oil change.

causes.name: Failed oil pump or clogged oil pickup
causes.clues: The oil level is fine but the light and noise came on together.

causes.name: Worn engine bearings
causes.clues: A deep knock that gets faster with engine speed, often on a high-mileage engine.

you: Once the engine is off, check the oil level and look under the car for a fresh puddle.
shop: Oil pressure test with a mechanical gauge

result.title: The oil level may be low. Don't run the engine until oil is added
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off and leave it off until oil is added. With the engine off, add the type of oil your owner's manual lists, a little at a time, until it reaches the full mark. Then have the car checked before driving further, because the oil went somewhere.
if: If the light stays off after adding oil and the engine sounds normal, call a shop and ask whether to bring it in or have it towed or seen by a mobile mechanic. Check the level before every drive until the cause is found.
If the light stays on after adding oil, or you hear ticking or knocking, don't drive it. Have it towed.
result.why: When the oil level drops too low, the pump can suck in air, especially when oil sloshes during turns, braking or hills. That makes the pressure drop and the light come on. Running low on oil wears the engine quickly, and the oil went somewhere: a leak or the engine burning it.

causes.name: Oil leak
causes.clues: Dark brown or black spots where you park, or oil on the underside of the engine.

causes.name: Engine burning oil
causes.clues: Blue or gray exhaust smoke, or oil needing top-ups between changes with no puddles.

causes.name: Overdue oil change
causes.clues: It's been well past the recommended interval.

you: Check the dipstick on level ground with the engine off.
Look for oil spots where you park.
Note how long since the last oil change.

result.title: The oil level looks right, so the pump, a blockage or the sensor is suspect
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic to test the oil pressure.
if: If a mechanic measures normal oil pressure with a gauge, the oil pressure switch or its wiring becomes the likely suspect. Replacing the switch is usually a quick repair once that's confirmed.
If you hear any ticking or knocking, don't start the engine again.
result.why: A full dipstick with a steady red light means either the oil isn't being pumped at enough pressure, or the sensor is giving a false warning. A faulty sensor is common, but there's no safe way to tell the two apart without a pressure gauge, and guessing wrong can ruin the engine.

causes.name: Faulty oil pressure switch or wiring
causes.clues: The engine sounds completely normal, and the switch is leaking oil or its plug looks damaged.
causes.against: Any engine noise makes a real pressure problem more likely.

causes.name: Clogged oil pickup or filter
causes.clues: Oil changes have been skipped, or the oil looks thick and sludgy.

causes.name: Worn or failed oil pump
causes.clues: A high-mileage engine, or pressure that's been low for a while.

you: Check the oil's color and thickness on the dipstick.
Note how long since the last oil change.
shop: Oil pressure test with a mechanical gauge
Oil pressure switch and wiring check

result.title: Coolant or fuel may be getting into the oil
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed to a shop for testing.
if: If the oil looks milky and the coolant level is low, an internal coolant leak such as a head gasket problem is possible. Don't run the engine. A shop will usually pressure-test the cooling system and test for combustion gases before deciding on a repair.
If the oil smells of fuel, also mention any rough running or check engine light to the shop.
result.why: Oil only protects the engine when it's clean. Milky or foamy oil often means coolant is leaking in, and a strong fuel smell means fuel is thinning it out. Either one can drop the oil pressure and wear the engine fast.

causes.name: Coolant leaking into the oil
causes.clues: Milky, light-brown oil, coolant level dropping, or white sweet-smelling exhaust smoke.

causes.name: Fuel thinning the oil
causes.clues: A strong fuel smell on the dipstick, rough running, or lots of short trips.

causes.name: Condensation from short trips in cold weather
causes.clues: A little milky residue only on the oil filler cap.
causes.against: Milky oil on the dipstick itself points to a coolant leak, not condensation.

you: Check the coolant level once the engine is cool.
Look at the underside of the oil filler cap.

result.title: Something may be wrong with the oil change: a leak, low fill or wrong filter
result.now: Pull over, turn off the engine, and look under the car for fresh oil. Check the dipstick. Don't drive it until the cause is found.
if: If oil is dripping from the filter or drain plug, or the level is low, call the shop that did the change. Ask them to send someone or arrange a tow.
If the level is full and there's no leak, still don't drive it. Have the oil pressure tested.
result.why: When the oil light comes on right after an oil change, the cause is often in the work itself: a loose drain plug or filter, a doubled-up filter gasket, too little oil, or the wrong filter. These can drain oil fast or starve the engine.

causes.name: Loose drain plug or oil filter
causes.clues: Fresh oil dripping under the engine.

causes.name: Not enough oil added
causes.clues: The dipstick reads low with no puddle.

causes.name: Wrong or faulty oil filter
causes.clues: The level is fine but the light came on right after the change.

you: Look under the car for fresh oil.
Check the dipstick.

result.title: Oil pressure may be dropping too low at idle
result.now: Avoid driving it until the oil pressure has been tested with a gauge. A mobile mechanic can often test it where the car sits, or have it towed. Check the oil level and when it was last changed so you can tell the shop.
if: If the light stays on while driving, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off.
If you hear new ticking or knocking, stop driving it and have it towed.
If a gauge test shows normal pressure, the switch or wiring may be giving a false warning. Ask the shop what they found before replacing parts.
result.why: Oil pressure is lowest at idle when the engine is hot. If the light flickers there but goes out with a little gas, pressure is right at the warning point. That can come from oil that's too thin or overdue, a worn engine, or a weak sensor.

causes.name: Old or wrong-thickness oil
causes.clues: The oil is overdue, or a different oil grade than the manual lists was used.

causes.name: Worn engine or oil pump
causes.clues: A high-mileage engine, or the flicker has been getting worse.

causes.name: Faulty oil pressure switch
causes.clues: The engine sounds normal and a mechanic's gauge shows good pressure.

you: Check the oil level and when it was last changed.
Check the owner's manual for the right oil grade.
shop: Oil pressure test with a mechanical gauge, hot and at idle
Oil change with the correct grade

result.title: Probably a low oil level warning or an oil change reminder
result.now: Check the oil level on the dipstick, or in the dash menu if your car has no dipstick, and top it up if it's low. If it's a maintenance message, book an oil change.
if: If the light turns red, or the oil can light comes on with a warning to stop, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you keep needing to add oil, have it checked for a leak or oil burning.
If the engine starts ticking or knocking, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn it off and have it checked before driving again.
result.why: Many cars have a yellow or orange low oil level warning and a separate service reminder, which are less urgent than the red oil pressure light. They're telling you to add oil or schedule a change before it becomes a pressure problem.

causes.name: Oil level getting low
causes.clues: A yellow oil light or a "low oil level" message.

causes.name: Oil change due
causes.clues: A wrench symbol or "oil change due" message, and the mileage is near the interval.

causes.name: Oil level sensor fault
causes.clues: The level is correct, but the warning keeps coming back.

you: Check the oil level.
Look up the light or message in the owner's manual.
shop: Oil change and maintenance reminder reset
Oil level sensor check if the warning persists

result.title: Treat a red oil light as serious until you know otherwise
result.now: Pull over where it's safe, turn off the engine, and wait a few minutes. Then check the oil level if you can, or call roadside assistance.
if: If the oil is low, adding the right oil up to the full mark is a good first step, but have the car checked before driving further. The oil went somewhere, and the engine may have run without enough pressure.
If the level is fine, or you can't check it, have the car towed rather than risk the engine.
If the engine is ticking, knocking or grinding, don't restart it.
result.why: A red oil light can mean anything from low oil to a failed pump, and the damage from running without oil pressure happens quickly. Checking the level takes two minutes and is the best first step.

causes.name: Low oil level
causes.clues: Oil spots where you park, or a long time since the last change.

causes.name: Faulty oil pressure sensor
causes.clues: The level is fine and the engine sounds normal.

causes.name: Oil pump or pickup problem
causes.clues: The light came on suddenly with a full dipstick.

you: Check the oil level with the engine off.
Look under the car for leaks.
shop: Oil pressure test with a mechanical gauge

overheats-only-in-traffic.title: Overheats in traffic or at idle

q_how_hot.q: How hot does it get when you're stopped or crawling in traffic?
q_how_hot.help: On most cars the needle sits near the middle once warm. Some cars only have a warning light.

opts.a: Into the red, a red temperature light or message comes on, or there's steam
Above normal, then it drops back once I'm moving
I'm not sure

q_fan_running.q: With the engine warm and idling and the A/C turned on, is the radiator fan spinning?
q_fan_running.help: Look through the grille or open the hood and look behind the radiator. On most cars, turning on the A/C makes the electric fan run. Stay well clear of the blades.

opts.a: No, it isn't spinning at all
It spins slowly, or only one of two fans runs
My fan is driven by the engine belt (common on trucks and older rear-wheel-drive cars)
Yes, it spins normally
I'm not sure

q_coolant.q: With the engine cold, where is the coolant level in the see-through overflow tank?
q_coolant.help: The overflow tank is a plastic bottle near the radiator with MIN and MAX (or COLD and FULL) marks. Only check it when the engine is cold.

opts.a: Below MIN, or empty
Between MIN and MAX
I haven't checked / I'm not sure

q_ac.q: Does the A/C also blow warmer when you're stopped, then get cold again once you're moving?

opts.a: Yes, the A/C gets weak at idle too
No, the A/C stays cold
My A/C doesn't work / I'm not sure

result.title: It's overheating. Stop before it damages the engine
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, turn the engine off and let it cool for at least 30 minutes. Then have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you can't pull over yet, turn the A/C off and the heater on full hot with the fan on high. It pulls some heat away from the engine.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, pull over as soon as it's safe and shut it off right away.
If the coolant is low once it has cooled, topping it up doesn't fix the cause. Have it checked before driving again.
If you see coolant pouring out, or smell a strong sweet smell inside the car, keep the engine off.
result.why: Once the gauge reaches the red, the engine is hotter than it's designed to run. Sitting in traffic gives it no cooling airflow at all, so it will keep climbing. Stopping quickly can be the difference between a fan repair and a damaged engine.

causes.name: Cooling fan not working
causes.clues: It gets hot only when stopped and cools down when moving.

causes.name: Low coolant
causes.clues: Steam, a sweet smell, or an empty overflow tank once cool.

causes.name: Thermostat or water pump problem
causes.clues: It also runs hot at speed, or the heater blows cold.

you: Once cool, check the overflow tank level and look for drips.
Note whether the fan was running when it overheated.
shop: Code scan for fan and temperature codes

result.title: The cooling fan may not be turning on
result.now: Avoid driving it until the fan works, because without the fan it will overheat whenever you're stopped or in slow traffic. With the engine off, check the fan fuse. If the fuse is fine or the fan still won't run, have a mobile mechanic look at it or have it towed.
if: If the gauge reaches the red, a temperature warning comes on, or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off right away.

If a fuse is blown, replacing it may get the fan working, but a fuse that blows again means something is drawing too much current. A shop will usually test the fan motor and wiring before replacing parts.
result.why: When you're stopped there's no air rushing through the radiator, so the fan has to pull air through. A fan that never runs explains overheating that only happens in traffic and clears up once you're moving.

causes.name: Failed fan motor
causes.clues: The fan doesn't run under any condition, or it's stiff or noisy when turned by hand with the engine off.

causes.name: Bad fan relay or blown fuse
causes.clues: The fan stopped working suddenly, or the fan fuse is visibly blown.

causes.name: Faulty temperature sensor, fan control module or wiring
causes.clues: A check engine light, or the fan works sometimes.

you: Check the fan fuse in the under-hood fuse box, using the diagram on the lid or in your owner's manual.
Turn on the A/C with the engine warm and see whether the fan starts.
shop: Fan motor power and ground test
Code scan and fan command test

result.title: The cooling fan may be running, but not hard enough
result.now: Have the fans checked within the next few days, and avoid long idling until then.
if: If the gauge climbs toward the red, a temperature warning comes on, or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the high fan speed never kicks in, the fault is often a relay or resistor rather than the motor.
If you notice a sweet smell or coolant dripping, have it checked before driving again.
result.why: Many cars use two fans or two fan speeds. If one fan or the high speed isn't working, there's enough airflow on a mild day but not in heat, heavy traffic or with the A/C on.

causes.name: One fan motor failed (dual-fan cars)
causes.clues: One fan spins and the other stays still with the A/C on.

causes.name: Fan speed relay or resistor fault
causes.clues: The fan runs, but never at high speed.

causes.name: Worn fan motor
causes.clues: The fan spins slowly or makes noise.

you: With the engine warm and the A/C on, check whether both fans spin.
shop: Fan speed and current draw test

result.title: A worn fan clutch is a common cause
result.now: Get the fan clutch checked within the next few days, and avoid towing and long idling until then.
if: If the gauge reaches the red, a temperature warning comes on, or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the fan wobbles or the blades are cracked, don't drive it. A broken fan can damage the radiator.
result.why: Belt-driven fans use a clutch that locks up when the engine is hot to pull more air. When the clutch wears out, the fan freewheels and moves too little air at idle, even though it looks like it's spinning.

causes.name: Worn fan clutch
causes.clues: With the engine off and cold, the fan spins freely for several turns when you give it a push.
causes.against: A stiff fan with a loud roar when the engine is hot suggests the clutch is working.

causes.name: Missing or damaged fan shroud
causes.clues: Broken plastic around the fan, or a gap between the fan and radiator.

causes.name: Debris blocking the radiator
causes.clues: Leaves, bugs or dirt packed into the front of the radiator.

you: With the engine off and cold, give the fan a push and see how freely it spins.
Look for cracks or missing pieces in the fan shroud.

result.title: Low coolant may be making it run hot
result.now: With the engine fully cold, top up the overflow tank to MAX with the coolant type in your owner's manual. Then have the cooling system checked before relying on the car, since the coolant went somewhere and it has already run hot. A mobile mechanic or a tow avoids overheating it again.
if: If the level drops again quickly, the gauge reaches the red, or you see steam, keep the engine off and have it towed.
If you see white sweet-smelling exhaust smoke or milky oil, don't drive it. That points to an internal leak.
If the heater blows cold while the gauge is high, coolant may not be circulating. Pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: With less coolant, the system has less capacity to carry heat away. That shows up first when airflow is weakest, which is when you're stopped. The coolant had to go somewhere, so a leak still needs finding.

causes.name: External leak (hose, radiator, water pump)
causes.clues: Drips under the front of the car or crusty colored deposits.

causes.name: Worn radiator or tank cap
causes.clues: Coolant residue around the cap.

causes.name: Internal leak, such as a head gasket
causes.clues: White exhaust smoke, milky oil, or no leak anywhere.
causes.against: Usually confirmed with a pressure test and a combustion gas test, not by the symptoms alone.

you: Top up and mark the level, then check it again after a few days.
Put cardboard under the engine overnight to spot drips.
shop: Combustion gas (block) test if no leak is found

result.title: Start by checking the coolant and the fan
result.now: With the engine fully cold, check that the overflow tank is between MIN and MAX. Then warm the engine, turn on the A/C, and see whether the radiator fan spins.
if: If the coolant is low, top it up with the right coolant once the engine is cold, and have it checked before relying on the car.
If the fan doesn't spin, get the fan checked before driving in traffic.
If the gauge reaches the red, a temperature warning comes on, or you see steam at any point, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Overheating only at idle usually comes down to a fan that isn't moving enough air or a cooling system that's low on coolant. Both are quick checks once you know where to look, as long as the engine is cold for the coolant check and you stay clear of the fan.

causes.name: Cooling fan not working
causes.clues: The fan doesn't spin with the engine warm and the A/C on.

causes.name: Low coolant
causes.clues: The tank is below MIN.

causes.name: Blocked radiator airflow
causes.clues: Debris on the front of the radiator.

you: Check the coolant level when cold.
Watch for the fan with the engine warm and the A/C on.

result.title: Not enough air is getting through the radiator
result.now: Look at the front of the radiator and A/C condenser through the grille for leaves, bugs or dirt, and book a cooling system check.
if: If you find debris, gently rinse it with a garden hose at low pressure. Don't use a pressure washer, which can flatten the fins.
If the gauge starts reaching the red, a temperature warning comes on, or you see steam, pull over, turn the engine off, and have it checked before driving again.
result.why: The A/C condenser sits in front of the radiator and shares the same airflow. When both the engine and the A/C struggle only at idle, something is limiting the air the fan can pull through, or the fan isn't pulling as hard as it should.

causes.name: Debris clogging the condenser or radiator fins
causes.clues: Visible leaves, bugs or dirt, or bent and flattened fins.

causes.name: Fan running too slowly
causes.clues: The fan spins, but sounds or looks slower than you'd expect.

causes.name: Missing air guide or fan shroud
causes.clues: Recent front-end damage or repair, or broken plastic around the fan.

you: Look through the grille at the condenser and radiator.
Check that the plastic shroud around the fan is intact.

result.title: The radiator or coolant flow may be weak
result.now: Get the cooling system checked within the next few days, and avoid long idling until then.
if: If it starts running hot at highway speed too, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the heater blows cold while the gauge is high, coolant isn't circulating. Don't drive it.
If the gauge reaches the red or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: If the fan and coolant level are fine, the problem may be inside the system: a radiator that's partly clogged, a thermostat that doesn't open fully, or a water pump that moves less coolant at low engine speed. Idling is when these show up first.

causes.name: Partly clogged radiator
causes.clues: Coolant that hasn't been changed in years, or cold spots on the radiator.

causes.name: Weak water pump
causes.clues: A whine near the belt, or a coolant trail from the pump.

causes.name: Thermostat sticking partly closed
causes.clues: The gauge rises slowly and never quite settles.

you: Note how long it takes to heat up at idle.
shop: Radiator temperature scan with an infrared thermometer
Code scan and live temperature data

result.title: Often a fan or airflow problem. Have it checked
result.now: Book a cooling system check within the next few days, and avoid idling and heavy traffic until then.
if: If the gauge reaches the red or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you can safely see that the fan never spins with the engine hot, tell the shop. It narrows things down fast.
result.why: Running hot only when stopped means the cooling system can't get rid of heat without help from moving air. The fan, airflow through the radiator, or coolant flow is the usual cause.

causes.name: Cooling fan problem
causes.clues: The most common cause of overheating only at idle.

causes.name: Blocked radiator or condenser
causes.clues: Debris visible through the grille.

causes.name: Weak coolant flow
causes.clues: An older water pump or radiator.

you: Check the coolant level when cold.

q_signs.q: Along with the worse mileage, do you notice any of these?
q_signs.help: These signs change how urgent it is, so pick the most serious one that applies.

opts.a: A flashing check engine light, or the engine shaking or misfiring
A smell of raw gasoline, inside or outside the car
A burning smell from a wheel, or the car feels held back, like the brakes are on
The check engine light is on steadily (not flashing)
None of these
I'm not sure

q_pattern.help: For an accurate number, fill the tank, reset the trip meter, drive normally, then divide the miles driven by the gallons it takes to refill. Dash readouts can be off.

opts.a: It started when the weather turned cold, or I'm making more short trips
The tires look low, or the tire pressure light has come on
Something changed: new tires, a roof rack, towing, a heavier load or a different fuel
The temperature gauge reads lower than usual, or the heater is slow to warm up
The engine feels sluggish, hesitates or idles rough
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be misfiring, which wastes fuel and can damage the exhaust
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If the light stops flashing after a restart, don't count on it. The misfire may come back, so have it checked before driving further.
If you see smoke or smell burning from under the car, step away from it. An overheated catalytic converter can get extremely hot.
If you smell raw fuel, keep sparks and flames away and don't restart the engine.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means the engine is misfiring badly. Unburned fuel goes out the exhaust, which is why mileage drops, and it can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter. Stopping early can prevent a much bigger repair.

causes.name: Worn spark plug or failed ignition coil
causes.clues: Shaking at idle or when accelerating, or plugs overdue for replacement.

causes.name: Fuel injector problem
causes.clues: The misfire is in one cylinder, or the exhaust smells of fuel.

causes.name: Vacuum leak or mechanical engine problem
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or misfires in several cylinders at once.

you: Note when the light flashes: at idle, when accelerating or when cruising.
shop: Spark plug and ignition coil check

result.title: A fuel leak may be causing both the smell and the lost mileage
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off and keep flames and sparks away. Look for wet spots or drips under the car, then have it towed.
if: If fuel is dripping or pooling, move away from the car and call for help.

If the smell was only near the gas cap right after filling up and is now completely gone, a loose or damaged cap is possible. Tighten it, but let a shop confirm that's all it is before relying on the car.
result.why: You should never smell raw gasoline strongly around a car. A leaking fuel line, injector seal or tank can waste fuel quickly, which shows up as worse mileage, and it's a fire risk.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line or fitting
causes.clues: A wet spot under the car, and the smell is strongest outside.

causes.name: Leaking injector or fuel rail seal
causes.clues: The smell is strongest under the hood after driving.

causes.name: Leaking fuel tank or filler neck
causes.clues: Wet spots or a smell near the rear of the car.

causes.name: Loose or damaged gas cap
causes.clues: The smell is near the fuel door, and the check engine light may be on.
causes.against: A loose cap alone rarely makes a big difference to mileage.

you: Without starting the engine, look for wet spots or drips under the car.
Check that the gas cap is tight.

result.title: A brake may not be releasing and could be dragging the car
result.now: Pull over when it's safe, make sure the parking brake is fully released, and let the brakes cool. Don't drive it until the brakes have been checked. A brake that keeps dragging can overheat and lose stopping power. A mobile mechanic or a tow is the safest option.
if: If a wheel is smoking or too hot to go near, keep everyone away from it until it cools. If you see flames, call 911.
If the car pulls to one side, the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, or the brake warning light is on, don't drive it.
If the parking brake was partly on and releasing it stops the drag, the brakes may still have been overheated. Have them checked before relying on them.
result.why: A brake caliper or parking brake that doesn't fully release keeps rubbing, which wastes fuel and creates heat. Left alone, it can overheat the brakes, wear them out fast and weaken your stopping power.

causes.name: Sticking brake caliper
causes.clues: One wheel is hotter than the others, has more brake dust, or the car pulls to one side.

causes.name: Parking brake not fully releasing
causes.clues: The brake warning light stays on, or the rear wheels get hot.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose
causes.clues: One wheel keeps dragging for a while after you brake.

you: Check that the parking brake is fully off.
After a drive, hold your hand near (not on) each wheel to feel if one is much hotter than the others.

result.title: A sensor or engine fault may be making the engine use extra fuel
result.now: Have the trouble codes read. Many auto parts stores do it free, and the code points to the system to test. It doesn't by itself prove which part has failed.
if: If the light starts flashing or the engine runs rough, pull over and stop.
If the gas cap was loose, tighten it. The light may go off on its own after several days of driving.
If you smell raw fuel, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and keep sparks and flames away.
result.why: The engine computer uses sensors to decide how much fuel to add. When one reads wrong, the engine can run rich (with too much fuel), which costs mileage, and the computer usually turns on the check engine light. The code tells you where to start.

causes.name: Faulty oxygen sensor
causes.clues: Oxygen sensor codes, or mileage that dropped over weeks.

causes.name: Dirty or faulty airflow sensor
causes.clues: Hesitation, rough idle, or airflow sensor codes.

causes.name: Coolant temperature sensor or thermostat
causes.clues: The temperature gauge reads low, or the heater is slow to warm up.

causes.name: Evaporative system leak, like a loose gas cap
causes.clues: Evap codes.
causes.against: This turns the light on but usually doesn't change mileage much.

you: Get the codes read.
Check that the gas cap is tight.
shop: Code scan and live sensor data

result.title: Cold weather and short trips may be the main reason
result.now: Check your tire pressure, since cold weather lowers it, and combine short errands into one trip where you can.
if: If mileage doesn't recover when the weather warms up, look for another cause.
If the temperature gauge stays lower than usual even after a long drive, the thermostat may be stuck open.
result.why: Engines use more fuel until they warm up, and in cold weather that takes longer. Winter-blend gasoline holds slightly less energy, cold air and low tire pressure add drag, and the heater, defroster and seat heaters add load. On short trips the engine spends most of its time cold.

causes.name: Cold engine and short trips
causes.clues: Lots of short drives, especially on cold mornings.

causes.name: Lower tire pressure in cold weather
causes.clues: The tire pressure light comes on during cold mornings.

causes.name: Winter-blend fuel and more heater and defroster use
causes.clues: The drop started in late fall and is similar every year.

causes.name: Long warm-up idling
causes.clues: You let the car idle for several minutes before driving.

you: Track mileage by hand over a few full tanks.
Check tire pressure at least monthly in cold weather.
shop: Thermostat and coolant temperature check if the gauge reads low

result.title: Low tire pressure may be costing you fuel
result.now: Check all four tires with a gauge when they're cold, and fill them to the pressure on the sticker inside the driver's door.
if: If one tire keeps losing air, have it checked for a puncture or a leaking valve.
If the tire pressure light stays on after filling, have the tires and their sensors checked.
If a tire is very low, bulging or damaged, don't drive on it. Use the spare or call for help.
result.why: Underinflated tires flex more and roll with more resistance, so the engine works harder to keep the car moving. They also wear faster and grip less. It's the easiest mileage problem to fix.

causes.name: Normal air loss over time
causes.clues: All four tires are a little low.

causes.name: Cold weather
causes.clues: The light comes on during cold mornings.

causes.name: Puncture or leaking valve
causes.clues: One tire is much lower than the others.

you: Check pressure with a gauge, not by eye.
Use the pressure on the door sticker, not the maximum printed on the tire.

result.title: A recent change may be the reason
result.now: Think about what changed around the time the mileage dropped, and undo it where you can, like removing an empty roof rack or extra weight.
if: If you switched to fuel with more ethanol, lower mileage is expected. Only use fuels your owner's manual approves.
If the drop came right after new tires, check their pressure. Some tires simply roll with more resistance.
If the drop came right after a repair, mention it to the shop that did the work.
result.why: Fuel economy depends on how hard the engine has to work. Extra weight, towing, roof racks and cargo boxes add load or wind drag, and tires with more grip or a different size can roll harder. Fuel with more ethanol holds less energy per gallon.

causes.name: Roof rack, cargo box, towing or extra weight
causes.clues: The drop appeared right after you added it.

causes.name: New tires
causes.clues: A different type or size, or they're underinflated.

causes.name: Fuel with more ethanol
causes.clues: You switched stations or fuel types.

causes.name: A change in how or where you drive
causes.clues: More fast highway driving, or more stop-and-go traffic.

you: Remove unneeded weight and racks, then track the next tank.
Check tire pressure.
shop: Tire and alignment check if the drop came with new tires

result.title: The thermostat may be stuck open, so the engine never fully warms up
result.now: Watch where the temperature gauge settles on your next longer drive, and book a check when convenient.
if: If the gauge ever climbs toward hot, pull over and turn the engine off. That's a different and more serious problem.
If the heater barely warms the cabin in winter, get it checked sooner, because the defroster may not clear the windshield.
result.why: The thermostat keeps coolant in the engine until it warms up. If it sticks open, the engine runs cooler than it should. The engine computer then adds extra fuel as if the engine were still cold, which lowers mileage.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck open
causes.clues: The gauge sits low on the highway, and the heater is lukewarm.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: A check engine light, or the gauge acting oddly.

causes.name: Low coolant
causes.clues: The coolant reservoir is low, and the heater blows cool air at times.

you: Note where the gauge settles after a 15-minute drive.
Check the coolant level when the engine is cold.

result.title: An engine performance problem may be making it work harder
result.now: Have the engine checked in the next few days, including a code scan even if the check engine light isn't on.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the car struggles badly uphill or the exhaust smells like rotten eggs, a blocked catalytic converter is possible. Get it checked sooner.
If you smell raw fuel, see smoke, or smell burning from under the car, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: An engine that's down on power has to work harder to do the same job, so it uses more fuel. Worn spark plugs, a dirty airflow sensor or a partly blocked exhaust are common reasons, and they usually get worse over time.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs or a weak ignition coil
causes.clues: Plugs overdue for replacement, hesitation, or a rough idle.

causes.name: Dirty airflow sensor
causes.clues: Hesitation, surging or a rough idle.

causes.name: Restricted catalytic converter
causes.clues: Sluggish mostly uphill or at highway speed, a rotten egg smell, or a rattle underneath.

causes.name: Clogged air filter
causes.clues: The filter is visibly dirty.
causes.against: On modern fuel-injected cars a dirty filter mostly hurts acceleration, not mileage.

you: Note when it hesitates: cold, warm, uphill or at idle.
Check your service records for when the spark plugs were last changed.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim data

result.title: Confirm the drop over a tank or two, then have the basics checked
result.now: Check tire pressure, then measure your mileage by hand over the next full tank to confirm the drop.
if: If the drop is large and sudden, or another symptom shows up, have it checked sooner.
If the check engine light comes on, get the codes read.
If you smell raw fuel or burning from a wheel, stop driving and have it checked first.
