result.why: Mileage naturally varies with weather, traffic, fuel and driving style, and dash readouts can be off. A measured drop that sticks around usually comes from tires, brakes, sensors or engine wear, and a shop can check those quickly.

causes.name: Tire pressure or wheel alignment
causes.clues: Tires look low, or uneven tire wear.

causes.name: Changes in driving or weather
causes.clues: More short trips, more traffic, or colder weather.

causes.name: Sensor or engine problem not yet setting a warning light
causes.clues: The engine feels slightly less lively.

causes.name: Slightly dragging brake
causes.clues: One wheel has more brake dust or feels warmer.

you: Measure mileage by hand over a full tank.
Check tire pressure.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim data

q_when.q: When do you hear the popping or backfiring?
q_when.help: A pop from the tailpipe is usually unburned fuel igniting in the exhaust. A pop from under the hood, sometimes with a puff from the air filter area, is a backfire into the intake.

opts.a: Mostly when I let off the gas or coast, a crackle or pop from the tailpipe
When I press the gas or accelerate
At idle or all the time, and the engine feels rough
A pop or cough from under the hood, near the air filter
I'm not sure

q_light.q: Is the check engine light on, and how is the engine running?
q_light.help: The check engine light is the amber engine-shaped symbol on the dash. Flashing is much more serious than steady.

opts.a: The check engine light is flashing
The light is on steady, or the engine shakes, stumbles or feels weak
There's a strong fuel smell or black smoke from the tailpipe
No light and it runs fine, but the exhaust is louder or puffing
I'm not sure

q_decel.q: Which of these fits your car best?

opts.a: It has an aftermarket exhaust or engine tune, or it's a sporty model that crackles on purpose
The exhaust got louder, puffs or ticks, or I smell exhaust
The check engine light is on, or the engine runs rough
I smell raw fuel or see black smoke
None of these, it's a stock car that just started doing it
I'm not sure

result.title: A severe misfire is possible, and it can damage the catalytic converter
result.now: Pull over safely and turn off the engine. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the light stops flashing after a restart, don't count on it. The misfire may still be there and needs to be checked before you drive it again.
If you see smoke or smell burning from under the car, get away from the car and call for help.
If you smell raw fuel, keep sparks and flames away and don't restart it.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means one or more cylinders aren't firing properly. Unburned fuel goes into the exhaust, where it pops and burns inside the catalytic converter. That can overheat and ruin the converter quickly and, in rare cases, start a fire.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: The engine shakes, especially at idle or when accelerating, and the problem came on fairly suddenly.

causes.name: Fuel injector stuck or not spraying
causes.clues: A fuel smell, or the misfire stays on one cylinder after the coil and plug are checked.

causes.name: Mechanical engine problem
causes.clues: A ticking or knocking sound, or a car that has overheated recently.
causes.against: Much less common than an ignition problem.

you: Note whether the engine was shaking and when the light started flashing.
shop: Code scan for misfire codes and the cylinder involved
Spark plug and ignition coil inspection
Compression test if ignition and fuel check out

result.title: Possibly a misfire, often from a worn ignition part
result.now: Have the engine scanned for codes within the next few days. Until then, keep trips short and avoid hard acceleration.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over and turn it off. Don't keep driving it.
If the spark plugs are past their service interval, mention it. They're a common cause and part of normal maintenance.
If you smell raw fuel, see smoke, or smell burning from under the car, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: When a cylinder doesn't fire properly, its unburned fuel can ignite later in the exhaust and make a pop. A rough-running engine or a steady check engine light along with popping often points to a misfire.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs
causes.clues: The plugs haven't been changed in a long time, or the misfire is worse when accelerating.

causes.name: Weak ignition coil or plug wire
causes.clues: The misfire is worse in damp weather or under load, or it's on one cylinder.

causes.name: Vacuum leak or dirty fuel injector
causes.clues: A rough idle, a hissing sound, or the misfire is spread across several cylinders.

you: Check your maintenance records for the last spark plug change.
Many auto parts stores will read the codes for you.

result.title: A backfire into the intake often means the engine is running too lean
result.now: Have it checked within the next few days. Avoid hard acceleration until then, since that's when intake backfires happen most.
if: If you see flames or smoke from under the hood, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off, get everyone out and call 911.
If there's a loud bang and the engine then won't start or runs very badly, don't keep cranking it. The timing belt or chain may have slipped. Have it towed.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and turn off the engine.
result.why: A pop from under the hood means the air-fuel mixture is igniting in the intake instead of the cylinder. That usually happens when there's too much air and not enough fuel, or when the spark is firing at the wrong moment.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: A hissing sound, a rough or high idle, or a cracked hose you can see.

causes.name: Faulty airflow sensor or weak fuel delivery
causes.clues: Hesitation or loss of power when you press the gas, sometimes with a check engine light.

causes.name: Ignition timing problem or slipped timing belt
causes.clues: An older engine, a recent timing belt job, or the backfire came with a sudden drop in power.
causes.against: Less common on modern engines than a lean mixture.

you: With the engine running, listen for hissing around the hoses on top of the engine.
Note whether the check engine light is on.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim data
Airflow sensor and fuel pressure tests

result.title: Possibly an exhaust leak letting air in and causing pops
result.now: Book an exhaust inspection. Mention that it pops when you let off the gas.
if: If you smell exhaust inside the car, stop driving it until it's fixed. If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning: get everyone into fresh air and call 911 from outside the car.
If the check engine light comes on or the engine starts running rough, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: When you let off the gas, a small amount of unburned fuel goes into the exhaust. If a leak lets fresh air in, that fuel can ignite and pop. A leak usually also makes the exhaust louder or adds a ticking or puffing sound.

causes.name: Leaking exhaust gasket or joint
causes.clues: A ticking or puffing sound, loudest on a cold start, that may quiet down as the engine warms.

causes.name: Rusted or cracked exhaust pipe or muffler
causes.clues: The exhaust is louder than it used to be, or there's visible rust or a hole.

causes.name: Engine running slightly rich
causes.clues: Fuel economy has dropped, or there's a fuel smell at the tailpipe.
causes.against: Less likely if the engine runs smoothly and mileage is normal.

you: With the engine cold and off, look under the car for black soot marks or rust holes along the exhaust.
Listen at the back of the car on a cold start for puffing or ticking.
shop: Exhaust system inspection on a lift
Smoke test of the exhaust for leaks
Code scan and fuel trim check

result.title: The engine may be getting too much fuel
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off. Without restarting it, look and smell for fuel around the engine and under the car. Don't drive it until it's been checked. A strong fuel smell can mean a leak or a stuck injector, which is a fire risk. A mobile mechanic or a tow is the safest option.
if: If fuel is dripping or pooling, move away from the car and call for help.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and turn off the engine.
If there's only black smoke and no fuel smell at all, tell the shop. That points more toward a sensor or mixture problem, but it still needs a code scan before more driving.
result.why: Extra fuel that doesn't burn in the engine can ignite in the hot exhaust and pop. It also wastes fuel and can overheat and damage the catalytic converter. If you can smell raw fuel, fuel may also be leaking where it can reach hot parts.

causes.name: Leaking or stuck-open fuel injector
causes.clues: A strong fuel smell, a rough idle, or hard starting when warm.

causes.name: Faulty sensor giving the computer wrong readings
causes.clues: A check engine light, poor fuel economy, or black smoke on acceleration.

causes.name: Misfire leaving fuel unburned
causes.clues: The engine shakes or stumbles along with the popping.

you: Look and smell for fuel around the engine and under the car.
Note any change in fuel economy.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim data
Oxygen and coolant temperature sensor checks
Fuel pressure and injector leak tests

result.title: Crackling on deceleration is normal for some sporty exhausts and tunes
result.now: Check whether your model or its tune is known to crackle when you let off the gas. If it's always done this and nothing else has changed, it may be by design. A shop familiar with your model can confirm it.
if: If the popping is new, getting louder, or comes with a check engine light or rough running, have it checked.
If you smell exhaust inside the car, stop driving it until the exhaust is inspected.
result.why: Some performance cars and aftermarket tunes add a little fuel when you lift off the gas so it burns in the exhaust and crackles. Aftermarket exhausts with less muffling also make normal small pops easier to hear.

causes.name: Factory or aftermarket sport tuning
causes.clues: It has always done it, mainly in a sport mode or after a tune.
causes.against: Less likely if the popping started suddenly on a car that never did it.

causes.name: Less restrictive aftermarket exhaust
causes.clues: It started after an exhaust change.

causes.name: Exhaust leak
causes.clues: A ticking or puffing sound, or a louder exhaust than before.

you: Check whether it only happens in a sport driving mode.
Ask the shop or seller that installed the exhaust or tune whether it's expected.
shop: Code scan to rule out a misfire

result.title: Get the engine scanned for codes to narrow it down
result.now: Have the engine scanned within the next few days, and note when the popping happens so you can tell the shop.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over and turn it off.
If you smell fuel or exhaust inside the car, stop driving it until it's checked.
result.why: Popping can come from a misfire, an exhaust leak or a fuel mixture problem. A code scan and a quick look at the exhaust usually help tell them apart quickly, and catching a misfire early protects the catalytic converter.

causes.name: Misfire
causes.clues: Rough running, shaking, or a check engine light.

causes.name: Exhaust leak
causes.clues: Pops mostly when you let off the gas, with a louder or ticking exhaust.

causes.name: Fuel mixture too rich or too lean
causes.clues: A fuel smell, black smoke, or hesitation when accelerating.

you: Record a short video with sound of the popping. It helps the shop a lot.
shop: Fuel trim and misfire data review

q_symptoms.q: Besides the leak, have you noticed any of these?
q_symptoms.help: These are the signs that change how urgent a power steering leak is.

opts.a: The steering is suddenly heavy or very hard to turn
Smoke or a burning oil smell from under the hood
A whine or groan when I turn the wheel, but steering still feels normal
None of these. I've just seen fluid or a low level
I'm not sure

q_where.q: Where are you seeing the fluid?
q_where.help: The power steering pump is usually at the front of the engine, driven by the belt. The steering rack sits low, between the front wheels.

opts.a: Drips or a puddle under the front of the engine
Wet, oily hoses or grime around the reservoir or pump
Near the front wheels, or on the rubber boots behind them
I'm not sure it's power steering fluid

q_reservoir.q: Does your car have a power steering fluid reservoir, and what's the level?
q_reservoir.help: Many newer cars use electric power steering, which has no fluid at all. If yours has a reservoir, the cap usually shows a steering wheel symbol. Your owner's manual will say which type you have.

opts.a: It has a reservoir and the level is low
It has a reservoir and the level is full
There's no reservoir, or the manual says it has electric steering
I'm not sure
A few drops or a spot about the size of a coin overnight
A puddle the size of a plate, or the level drops noticeably within a few days
It's dripping steadily or spraying, or the reservoir empties after a short drive
I'm not sure

result.title: The system may have lost enough fluid or pressure to stop assisting
result.now: Park it and don't drive it until it's repaired. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If the reservoir is nearly empty, topping it up won't fix the leak, and the steering can go heavy again without warning.
If the belt is broken or missing, other parts it drives, like the alternator or water pump, may also have stopped working.
If the battery light comes on or the temperature gauge climbs, the drive belt may be broken. Keep the engine off.
result.why: Heavy steering means the pump is no longer giving you assist. That makes the car hard to control in a turn or an emergency, and running the pump without enough fluid quickly damages it.

causes.name: Fluid level too low from a leak
causes.clues: A low or empty reservoir, a whine before the steering went heavy, and fluid under the front of the car.

causes.name: Burst high-pressure hose
causes.clues: It happened suddenly, with a fresh wet spray around the engine bay.

causes.name: Broken or slipping drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal or slap before it happened, or the battery light came on too.
causes.against: If the belt is in place and tight, this is less likely.

causes.name: Failed power steering pump
causes.clues: The fluid is full but the pump has been noisy for a while.

you: With the engine off, look at the reservoir level.
Check that the drive belt is still in place.

result.title: Power steering fluid may be dripping onto hot engine or exhaust parts
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off and let it cool. Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you see smoke or flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
If the smoke stops once cool and you find only a little oily residue, the leak still needs fixing before the car is used again.
result.why: Power steering fluid is an oil and will smoke, and can catch fire, if it lands on the exhaust or a hot engine. That's why smoke turns a routine leak into a stop-now problem.

causes.name: Leaking pressure hose near the exhaust
causes.clues: Wet hoses near the front of the engine, with smoke after driving.

causes.name: Leaking pump seal
causes.clues: Fluid around the pump at the front of the engine.

causes.name: Overfilled reservoir pushing fluid out of the cap
causes.clues: It started right after someone topped up the fluid.

causes.name: A different fluid, like engine oil
causes.clues: The fluid is dark brown or black, and the power steering level is full.

shop: Engine bay leak inspection with the engine cool
Pressure test of the power steering system
Check for oil residue on the exhaust

result.title: A whine when turning often means the fluid is low
result.now: With the engine off, check the power steering fluid level and add the type listed in your owner's manual if it's low. Then have the leak found within a few days.
if: If the steering starts to feel heavy, stiff or jerky, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the level is full and it still whines, the pump or belt may be wearing out. Book a check.
If the reservoir was empty or nearly empty, have it checked before driving further. The pump may have been running dry.
If you smell burning oil or see smoke from under the hood, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: When fluid runs low, the pump draws in air, which makes a whine or groan, especially at full lock. If you keep driving that way, the pump wears out quickly.

causes.name: Low fluid from a slow leak
causes.clues: The reservoir is below the mark, and you've seen drips or wet hoses.

causes.name: Worn power steering pump
causes.clues: The fluid is full, but the noise keeps getting louder.

causes.name: Old or foamy fluid
causes.clues: The fluid looks dark, bubbly or milky.

you: Check the reservoir level with the engine off.
Notice whether the noise is loudest when turning the wheel all the way.

result.title: A hose or fitting near the reservoir or pump may be seeping
result.now: Wipe the area clean, check the fluid level, and book a check. Look again in a day or two to see where fresh fluid appears.
if: If the level drops noticeably or you see drips on the ground, get it checked within a few days.
If the hose is near the exhaust and you smell burning, don't drive it until it's fixed.
If the steering whines, feels heavy or the level drops below the minimum mark, have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Rubber hoses and their clamps harden with age and start to seep where they connect. A seep is slow, but it tends to get worse and leaves the system low over time.

causes.name: Aging return or low-pressure hose
causes.clues: Oily grime around a rubber hose and its clamp.

causes.name: Leaking high-pressure hose fitting
causes.clues: Wetness at a metal fitting near the pump or rack.

causes.name: Reservoir cap or seal
causes.clues: Residue only around the top of the reservoir.

you: Wipe the area clean and check it again after a drive.
Keep an eye on the reservoir level.
shop: Leak inspection with the engine running
Dye test if the source isn't obvious

result.title: The steering rack or its seals may be leaking
result.now: Check the fluid level and top it up if needed, then have the steering rack looked at within a few days.
if: If the steering feels heavy, notchy or loose, clunks, or the wheel is off-center when driving straight, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the rubber boots behind the wheels are full of fluid or torn, mention it to the shop. Dirt getting in speeds up wear.
If the level is below the minimum mark again after topping up, don't drive it until it's been checked.
result.why: The steering rack sits between the front wheels and has seals at each end. When they wear, fluid collects in the rubber boots or drips near the wheels. Rack leaks usually get worse and can let the system run low.

causes.name: Worn steering rack seals
causes.clues: Fluid in or on the rubber boots behind the front wheels.

causes.name: Leaking line fitting at the rack
causes.clues: Wetness at the metal lines where they connect to the rack.

causes.name: A different fluid, like engine or transmission oil
causes.clues: The power steering level isn't dropping.

you: Check the reservoir level.
With the car parked, look at the rubber boots behind the front wheels for wetness.

result.title: A slow power steering seep, often from a hose or seal
result.now: Check the fluid level weekly and top it up as needed with the type in your owner's manual. Book a check to find the source.
if: If the spot gets bigger or the level drops faster, get it checked within a few days.
If the steering starts to whine or feel heavy, have it checked before driving further.
If you smell burning oil or see smoke from under the hood, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: A coin-size spot usually means a slow loss of fluid. Low fluid still wears out the pump and can make the steering heavy, and seeps rarely stop on their own.

causes.name: Aging hose or clamp
causes.clues: Oily grime on the hoses at the front of the engine.

causes.name: Pump shaft seal
causes.clues: Wetness right behind the pump pulley.

causes.name: Steering rack seals
causes.clues: Drips farther back, near the front wheels.

you: Put cardboard under the front of the car overnight to see exactly where it drips.
Note the reservoir level so you can tell if it's dropping.
shop: Dye test if the source isn't clear

result.title: An active leak, possibly a hose, the pump or the steering rack
result.now: Avoid driving it until the leak has been found. A leak this size can leave the steering heavy with little warning. With the engine off, top up to the full mark with the type in your owner's manual to protect the pump, and have a mobile mechanic look at it or have it towed.
if: If fluid is dripping onto the exhaust, or you see smoke or smell burning oil, keep everyone away from the car until it cools.
If the steering whines, feels heavier or jerks, don't drive it.
result.why: A plate-size puddle or a level that drops in days means the system will run low soon. Once it's low, the steering gets heavy and the pump can be damaged.

causes.name: Leaking pressure or return hose
causes.clues: Wet hoses, and drips under the front of the engine.

causes.name: Worn pump seal
causes.clues: Fluid around the pump and on the belt.

causes.name: Steering rack seals
causes.clues: Fluid near the front wheels or in the rubber boots.

you: Note how much fluid you add and how fast it goes down.
Put cardboard under the car overnight to mark where it drips.
shop: Leak inspection with the engine running

result.title: A major leak, often a burst hose or a failed seal
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If fluid is getting onto the exhaust or you see smoke, keep everyone away from the car until it cools.
result.why: At this rate the system can run dry within minutes of driving. You'd lose steering assist, the pump would be damaged, and fluid spraying onto hot parts is a fire risk.

causes.name: Burst or cracked high-pressure hose
causes.clues: A sudden heavy leak with fluid sprayed around the engine bay.

causes.name: Failed pump seal
causes.clues: Fluid pouring from behind the pump pulley.

causes.name: Loose or broken line fitting
causes.clues: Recent work on the steering, or fluid at a metal fitting.

shop: Pressure test to confirm which hose, fitting or seal is leaking

result.title: If the power steering level is full, the leak is probably another fluid
result.now: Dab a drop on white paper and note the color, then check your engine oil, coolant, brake and transmission fluid levels.
if: If the brake fluid level is low, don't drive it until it's checked. Brake fluid leaks can cause brake failure.
If the fluid is green, orange or pink and smells sweet, it may be coolant. Watch your temperature gauge, and if it climbs toward hot, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you smell fuel, don't start the engine. Keep sparks and flames away.
result.why: Power steering fluid can look like transmission fluid or light oil. If its reservoir stays full, something else is leaking, and a few quick checks usually show what.

causes.name: Transmission fluid
causes.clues: Red or pink fluid, closer to the middle of the car.

causes.name: Engine oil
causes.clues: Brown or black fluid under the engine.

causes.name: Coolant
causes.clues: Green, orange or pink fluid with a sweet smell.

causes.name: Brake fluid
causes.clues: Clear to yellowish, slick fluid near a wheel or behind the engine.

you: Check every fluid level you can reach.
Look at the color of a drop on white paper.

result.title: Your car likely has electric steering, so the fluid is from something else
result.now: Dab a drop on white paper and note the color, then check your engine oil, coolant, brake and transmission fluid levels.
if: If the brake fluid level is low, don't drive it until it's checked.
If the steering feels heavy and a steering warning light is on, have it checked before driving. Electric steering can fail without any leak.
If the fluid is green, orange or pink and smells sweet, it may be coolant. Watch your temperature gauge.
result.why: Electric power steering uses a motor instead of fluid, so it has no power steering fluid to leak. The fluid you're seeing is coming from another system.

causes.name: Engine oil
causes.clues: Brown or black fluid under the engine.

causes.name: Transmission fluid
causes.clues: Red or pink fluid.

causes.name: Coolant
causes.clues: Green, orange or pink fluid with a sweet smell.

you: Confirm your steering type in the owner's manual.
Check the fluid levels you can reach.

result.title: Start by checking the level to see how fast it's dropping
result.now: With the engine off, check the power steering reservoir level and note where it sits. Put cardboard under the front of the car overnight.
if: If the reservoir is empty or nearly empty, don't drive it until it's been checked.
If the level is low and you see drips by morning, get it checked within a few days.
If the steering whines or feels heavy, have it checked before driving further.
result.why: How fast the fluid drops tells you how urgent the leak is. One night of cardboard under the car shows how much is leaking and where.

causes.name: Hose or clamp seep
causes.clues: Drips under the front of the engine.

causes.name: Pump seal
causes.clues: Wetness right behind the pump pulley.

causes.name: Steering rack seals
causes.clues: Drips near the front wheels.

you: Check the reservoir level with the engine off.
Check the cardboard in the morning.

result.title: Not sure what's leaking? A shop check can identify it
result.now: Put white paper or cardboard under the car overnight and note the color and spot, then book a leak check.
if: If the steering feels heavy, the brake pedal feels soft or the temperature gauge rises, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If the puddle grows quickly, get it checked within a day or two.
result.why: Several fluids look alike, and some cars don't use power steering fluid at all. The color, the location and which level is dropping usually help a technician identify what's leaking quickly.

causes.name: Power steering fluid
causes.clues: Red, pink, amber or clear fluid under the front of the engine.

causes.name: Transmission fluid
causes.clues: Red or pink fluid closer to the middle of the car.

causes.name: Engine oil or coolant
causes.clues: Brown or black oil, or sweet-smelling green, orange or pink coolant.

you: Note the color and location of the drips.
Take a photo of the puddle for the shop.

q_feel.q: How does the steering feel right now?
q_feel.help: Power steering is what makes the wheel easy to turn. Without it, the car still steers, but it feels like turning a heavy truck at low speed.

opts.a: Very heavy or hard to turn, especially at low speed
It jerks, pulls by itself, feels notchy, or sticks in one spot
Sometimes heavy, sometimes normal
Normal. Only the light is on
I'm not sure

q_other_lights.help: The steering motor uses a lot of electricity. If the battery or alternator is struggling, the steering is often one of the first things to lose power.

opts.a: The battery light is on too, or the headlights and dash look dim
It started after a lot of slow, full-lock steering, like parking or a three-point turn
It happened right after a jump start or a battery change
None of these. Only the steering light (maybe with the traction light)
I'm not sure

q_before.q: Did anything happen just before the light came on?

opts.a: The battery was replaced, disconnected, or the car was jump-started
The light came on and then went off again by itself
I hit a curb or pothole, or had suspension or alignment work
Nothing I noticed
I'm not sure

result.title: The charging system may be failing, and the steering may have lost power because of it
result.now: Pull over where it's safe and turn the engine off. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic rather than driving on.
if: If the engine temperature is also climbing, the drive belt may have broken. Don't restart the engine.
If you're in a dangerous spot, turn on your hazard lights and steer firmly to the nearest safe place before stopping.
result.why: When the battery light and the steering light come on together, the car is often running on battery power alone. The steering motor is one of the first systems to cut out as voltage drops, and the engine may stall soon after.

causes.name: Alternator not charging
causes.clues: The battery light is on, the lights look dim, and things like the radio or wipers act strangely.

causes.name: Broken or slipping drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal before it happened, or the temperature gauge rising too.
causes.against: Some cars drive the alternator with a separate belt, so the temperature may stay normal.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery cable
causes.clues: Crusty buildup on the terminals, or a clamp you can move by hand.

you: With the engine off, look for a missing, shredded or loose drive belt.
Check that the battery clamps are tight and clean.
shop: Steering system code scan once voltage is fixed

result.title: The steering motor may have got hot and be protecting itself
result.now: Park, turn the engine off, and let the car sit for 10 to 15 minutes without turning the wheel. Then restart and, while still parked, check whether the steering feels normal. Don't drive it while the steering is heavy.
if: If the steering is back to normal and the light is off, heat protection is a likely explanation. Mention it at your next service, avoid holding the wheel at full lock while stopped, and have it checked if it happens again.
If the light stays on or the steering is still heavy after cooling down, treat it as a steering fault. Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
If the battery light comes on too, or the dash lights look dim, the cause may be electrical rather than heat.
result.why: Many electric steering systems cut back their help when the motor gets hot from a lot of turning while the car is barely moving. Once it cools, the assist normally returns on its own.

causes.name: Heat protection after heavy low-speed steering
causes.clues: Lots of parking moves or turning the wheel all the way while stopped, especially on a hot day.
causes.against: If it happened during normal driving, heat protection is unlikely.

causes.name: Weak battery adding to the load
causes.clues: Slow cranking lately, or a battery older than 4–5 years.

causes.name: Steering motor starting to fail
causes.clues: It keeps happening with only light steering use.

you: Let it cool, then check the steering while parked with the engine running.
Note how often it happens and what you were doing.

result.title: The steering system may need to reset after the battery work
result.now: Make sure the battery clamps are tight. Then, parked with the engine running, turn the wheel slowly all the way left, all the way right, and back to center, and restart the car.
if: If your owner's manual lists a steering reset step, follow that instead. It varies by car.
If the steering feels normal but the light stays on after the reset, the steering angle sensor may need to be calibrated with a scan tool. Ask a shop before relying on the car.
If the steering is heavy, jerks or pulls, don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: Low voltage or a lost connection can make the steering computer store a fault or forget where center is. After a jump start or new battery, some cars need a simple reset or a short drive before the light goes out.

causes.name: Steering angle sensor lost its calibration
causes.clues: The light came on right after the battery was disconnected or replaced.

causes.name: Battery still low after a jump start
causes.clues: The battery went flat recently and hasn't been fully recharged.

causes.name: Loose battery clamp
causes.clues: A clamp that moves when you twist it by hand.

you: Check that the battery clamps are tight.
Try the slow lock-to-lock steering reset and restart.

result.title: The power steering assist may have shut off because of a fault
result.now: Find a safe place to stop, turn the car off for a minute and restart it. If the steering is still heavy, don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you can't comfortably steer at parking speeds, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If the steering returns to normal after a restart, still have the codes read before relying on the car. The fault is stored and may come back without warning.
result.why: When the steering system detects a fault, it switches the motor off so it can't steer the car the wrong way. In most cars the wheel is still mechanically connected to the wheels, but turning takes much more effort, especially when parking.

causes.name: Steering torque or angle sensor fault
causes.clues: The light came on suddenly with no other warning.

causes.name: Failing steering motor or control module
causes.clues: Groaning or clicking from the steering column or under the car, or it's happened before.

causes.name: Wiring or connector problem
causes.clues: The fault comes and goes over bumps or in wet weather.

you: Ask a dealer for your brand whether a steering recall is open on your VIN.
Note whether the traction or stability light came on at the same time.

result.title: The steering is behaving abnormally. Treat this as a safety problem
result.now: Pull over where it's safe and don't drive it. Have the car towed to a shop.
if: If the problem started right after a crash or hitting something hard, tell the shop. A bent steering part can cause this too.
result.why: Steering that tugs by itself, feels notchy or sticks can mean the steering system is giving the wrong amount of help or a part is binding. That can make the car hard to control, so it isn't worth the risk.

causes.name: Faulty steering torque sensor or control module
causes.clues: The wheel pulls or kicks even when the road is flat and straight.

causes.name: Worn or damaged steering rack, column or joint
causes.clues: Clunking, a notchy feel when turning, or a recent hard hit.

causes.name: Known defect covered by a recall
causes.clues: Your car has an open steering recall.

you: Ask a dealer for your brand whether a steering recall is open on your VIN.
shop: Steering rack, column and tie rod inspection

result.title: An on-and-off steering fault, often linked to low voltage or a loose connection
result.now: Check that the battery clamps are tight, then get the battery, charging system and steering codes checked within the next few days.
if: If the steering goes heavy at any point, especially at speed or in a turn, stop driving it until it's checked.
If the battery light also flickers, mention it. The charging system becomes a likely suspect.
result.why: Electric steering needs steady voltage and good connections. A weak battery, a loose cable or a tired motor can make the assist drop out and come back. It usually gets worse over time.

causes.name: Weak battery or charging problem
causes.clues: Slow cranking, dim lights at idle, or a battery older than 4–5 years.

causes.name: Loose or corroded connection
causes.clues: It happens over bumps or after rain.

causes.name: Steering motor or module starting to fail
causes.clues: The battery tests fine but the problem keeps coming back.

you: Check the battery clamps.
Note when it happens: cold starts, bumps, rain, or after long drives.

result.title: The steering system has stored a fault, even though it feels normal for now
result.now: Get the steering codes read within the next few days. Until then, keep both hands on the wheel and be ready for the steering to get heavier.
if: If the steering becomes heavy, jerky or pulls by itself, stop driving it.
If the light came on after a curb hit or alignment work, mention that. The steering angle sensor may need to be recalibrated, and a shop will usually also check for bent steering parts.
result.why: The light means the system found a problem, even if it's still giving you help. Some faults only reduce assist under certain conditions, and the assist can switch off without much warning.

causes.name: Steering angle sensor out of calibration
causes.clues: Recent alignment, suspension work or a hard curb strike. The traction light may be on too.

causes.name: Voltage dip that set a stored fault
causes.clues: An aging battery or a recent hard start.

causes.name: Early sensor or motor fault
causes.clues: No obvious trigger.

you: Ask a dealer for your brand whether a steering recall is open on your VIN.
Note whether the steering wheel is centered when driving straight.

result.title: Have the steering system checked before you rely on it
result.now: In an empty parking lot, turn the wheel slowly at walking speed. If it's much harder than usual, have it towed. If it feels normal, book a check within a few days.
if: If the battery light is on too, stop driving and have it towed.
If the steering pulls, jerks or sticks, don't drive it.
result.why: The steering light can mean anything from a stored glitch to a complete loss of assist. A quick low-speed test tells you which, and a shop scan finds the reason.

causes.name: Steering sensor or motor fault
causes.clues: Only the steering light is on.

causes.name: Low voltage from the battery or alternator
causes.clues: The battery light, dim lights or slow cranking.

you: Do the slow steering test in a safe, empty space.
Look at which other lights are on.

result.title: Heavy steering after battery work. Try a reset, but don't drive it heavy
result.now: Don't drive it while the steering is heavy. Make sure the battery clamps are tight. Then, parked with the engine running, turn the wheel slowly all the way left, all the way right, and back to center, and restart the car. If the steering is still heavy, have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If your owner's manual lists a steering reset step, follow that instead. It varies by car.
If the battery light is on or the dash lights look dim, the battery may still be too low to power the steering. Have the battery and charging system tested.
If the steering is back to normal but the light stays on, the steering angle sensor may need to be calibrated with a scan tool. Ask a shop before relying on the car.
result.why: Low voltage or a lost connection can make the steering computer store a fault or forget where center is. After a jump start or new battery, some cars need a simple reset or a short drive before the light goes out.

causes.name: Steering angle sensor lost its calibration
causes.clues: The light came on right after the battery was disconnected or replaced.

causes.name: Battery still low after a jump start
causes.clues: The battery went flat recently and hasn't been fully recharged.

causes.name: Loose battery clamp
causes.clues: A clamp that moves when you twist it by hand.

you: Check that the battery clamps are tight.
Try the slow lock-to-lock steering reset and restart.

result.title: Steering assist that comes and goes. Get it checked before relying on it
result.now: Avoid driving it until it's checked, because the assist can drop out in the middle of a turn. Check that the battery clamps are tight. A mobile mechanic can test the battery, charging system and steering codes where the car sits, or have it towed.
if: If the steering jerks, pulls by itself or sticks, don't drive it.
If the battery light also flickers, or the lights dim at idle, mention it. The charging system becomes a likely suspect.
result.why: Electric steering needs steady voltage and good connections. A weak battery, a loose cable or a tired motor can make the assist drop out and come back. Sudden heavy steering is hard to react to, and the fault usually gets worse over time.

causes.name: Weak battery or charging problem
causes.clues: Slow cranking, dim lights at idle, or a battery older than 4–5 years.

causes.name: Loose or corroded connection
causes.clues: It happens over bumps or after rain.

causes.name: Steering motor or module starting to fail
causes.clues: The battery tests fine but the problem keeps coming back.

you: Check the battery clamps.
Note when it happens: cold starts, bumps, rain, or after long drives.

q_what_happens.q: What happens when you press Start with your foot on the brake?

opts.a: A "Key not detected" message or a key symbol shows on the dash
The dash lights up, but the engine doesn't crank
Nothing at all: no lights, no message, and the doors may not unlock
Rapid clicking, or the dash lights flicker or dim
The engine cranks or starts but then won't keep running
I'm not sure

q_remote.q: Does the remote lock and unlock the doors from a normal distance?

opts.a: Only when I'm very close, or not at all
Yes, it works normally
I'm not sure

q_spare.q: Have you tried your spare key fob?

opts.a: Yes, and the spare works
Yes, and the spare doesn't work either
I don't have a spare / I'm not sure

q_brake.q: Are you pressing the brake firmly, and is the car fully in Park?
q_brake.help: Most push-button cars won't crank unless the brake is pressed (or the clutch, on a manual) and the shifter is all the way in Park or Neutral.

opts.a: Yes, the brake is pressed firmly and it's in Park
Not sure I pressed hard enough, or it may not be fully in Park
I'm not sure

q_brake_lights.q: Do the brake lights come on when you press the pedal?
q_brake_lights.help: Ask someone to look, or back up close to a wall or garage door and check for the red glow. Some cars also show a "press brake" message that doesn't go away when you press it.

opts.a: No, the brake lights don't come on
Yes, they work
I'm not sure

result.title: The key fob battery may be low
result.now: Hold the key fob right against the Start button (or put it in the backup spot your owner's manual shows) and press Start with your foot on the brake. Then replace the fob battery.
if: If it starts with the fob against the button, a new fob battery often fixes it.
If it still says key not detected after a new battery, try the spare fob. If that fails too, the car's key system needs a check.
result.why: The car looks for a weak radio signal from your fob. As the fob battery fades, the car stops detecting it from your pocket. Push-button cars have a backup spot where the fob can still be read with a dead battery.

causes.name: Weak or dead fob battery
causes.clues: The remote's range has been getting shorter, or a low key battery message has appeared.
causes.against: If the remote works normally from a distance, the fob battery is less likely.

causes.name: Signal interference
causes.clues: The fob is near a phone, charger or other electronics, or you're near radio towers or strong transmitters.

causes.name: Damaged key fob
causes.clues: It was dropped or got wet.

you: Hold the fob against the Start button and try again.
Replace the fob battery (often a coin battery). The size is in your owner's manual or inside the fob.
Move the fob away from phones and chargers.

result.title: Your main key fob may be faulty or have lost its programming
result.now: Use the spare for now. Replace the main fob's battery first, and if it still isn't detected, book a dealer or locksmith visit to check or reprogram it.
if: If the main fob was dropped or got wet, it may need replacing. A dealer or locksmith can test it first.
If you only have one working fob left, get a replacement made soon so you aren't stranded.
result.why: If the spare works, the car's key system is probably working and the problem is more likely in the main fob: a dead battery, internal damage, or a chip that's lost its pairing with the car.

causes.name: Dead fob battery
causes.clues: The remote buttons are weak or dead too.
causes.against: If the remote buttons work well from a distance, the battery is less likely.

causes.name: Physical or water damage
causes.clues: The fob was dropped, crushed or went through the wash.

causes.name: Lost programming
causes.clues: It stopped working suddenly, with no damage.

you: Replace the fob battery.
Check the fob for cracks or water damage.

result.title: The car's key detection system or its power may be the problem
result.now: Move phones and chargers away, hold the fob against the Start button and try again. If it still isn't detected, have a dealer or locksmith come to you, or have the car towed to one.
if: If the dash lights are dim or flicker, the car battery may be too weak to run the key system. A jump start may help.
If it works in a different location, something nearby was interfering with the signal.
If the battery is cracked, leaking, swollen or smells like rotten eggs, don't jump start it. Call for roadside help instead.
result.why: When neither fob is detected but both remotes work, the problem is more likely on the car's side: low car battery voltage, interference, or a faulty antenna or key control module.

causes.name: Weak car battery
causes.clues: Dim or flickering lights, or slow cranking recently.

causes.name: Signal interference
causes.clues: It happens in one place, like a parking garage or near transmitters.

causes.name: Faulty key antenna or control module
causes.clues: It fails everywhere, with both fobs and a good battery.

you: Try the fob-against-the-button backup method.
Try a jump start if the lights are dim.
shop: Code scan of the keyless and immobilizer systems

result.title: The car may not be sensing the brake, Park or an unlocked steering wheel
result.now: Press the brake pedal hard and hold it, move the shifter firmly into Park, then press Start. If the steering wheel is locked, gently turn it left and right while you press Start.
if: If it starts in Neutral but not Park, the gear-position switch may be faulty. Book a check.
If it still won't crank with the brake pressed firmly, check whether your brake lights work.
result.why: As a safety feature, push-button cars won't crank unless they sense the brake pedal and Park (or the clutch on a manual). A light press or a shifter not fully in Park is a common reason nothing happens.

causes.name: Brake not pressed firmly enough
causes.clues: It works some days and not others.

causes.name: Shifter not fully in Park
causes.clues: A gear indicator that doesn't show P clearly.

causes.name: Steering lock engaged
causes.clues: The steering wheel won't turn, or a steering lock message appears.

you: Press the brake firmly before pressing Start.
Try starting in Neutral.
Wiggle the steering wheel while pressing Start.

result.title: A faulty brake light switch may be blocking the start
result.now: Don't drive the car until the brake lights work: drivers behind you get no warning when you brake. Have the brake light circuit checked within the next few days.
if: If only one brake light is out, that's a bulb, not the switch. Look at whether all of them stay dark.
If you need to move the car before it's fixed, a mobile mechanic can often test and repair the brake light circuit where the car sits.
If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, or the red brake warning light is on, don't drive it until the brakes have been checked.
result.why: The car uses the brake light switch to know your foot is on the pedal. If none of the brake lights come on, the switch is a common cause, though a fuse or wiring fault can do the same. A shop will usually check the fuse and wiring before replacing the switch. Either way the car won't let you start it, and drivers behind you get no warning when you brake.

causes.name: Failed brake light switch
causes.clues: No brake lights at all, and a press-brake message that won't clear.

causes.name: Blown brake light fuse
causes.clues: Brake lights and other items on the same fuse stopped working together.

causes.name: Loose switch or wiring at the pedal
causes.clues: It works sometimes depending on how hard you press.

you: Have someone check whether any brake lights come on.
Check the brake light fuse listed in your owner's manual.
shop: Brake light circuit and fuse check

result.title: The starter, a weak battery or the Park switch may be the problem
result.now: Try starting in Neutral with the brake pressed. If that doesn't work, try a jump start. If it still won't crank, have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If it starts in Neutral but not Park, that points toward the gear-position switch or its adjustment.
If it starts with a jump, have the battery and charging system tested soon.
If the battery is cracked, leaking, swollen or smells like rotten eggs, don't jump start it. Call for roadside help instead.
If you smell burning or see smoke after trying to start it, stop trying and step away from the car.
result.why: With the key detected and the brake working, the car is ready to crank, but the starter isn't turning the engine. That points to a battery too weak to crank, a gear-position switch not reporting Park, or a failing starter.

causes.name: Weak battery
causes.clues: Dim lights, a slow crank recently, or a battery more than 4 years old.
causes.against: If the lights stay bright while pressing Start, the battery is less likely.

causes.name: Gear-position (Park/Neutral) switch
causes.clues: It starts in Neutral but not Park.

causes.name: Failing starter
causes.clues: A single click, or starting has been hit-or-miss lately.

you: Try starting in Neutral.
Try a jump start or booster pack.

result.title: The car's main battery is probably dead
result.now: Use the metal key hidden inside your fob to open the driver's door, then jump start the car or use a battery booster.
if: If the battery is cracked, leaking, swollen or smells like rotten eggs, don't jump start it. Call for roadside help instead.
If a jump works, drive at least 30 minutes or have the battery and charging system tested soon.
If nothing happens even with a good jump, a main fuse or cable may have failed. It will need a tow or a mobile mechanic.
On a hybrid or electric car, check your owner's manual for where to connect jumper cables before you start.
If the battery light comes on while driving after a jump, the charging system may not be working. Have it checked before relying on the car.
result.why: With no lights and no response, the car has no power to run the key system or the starter. The usual reason is a drained 12-volt battery, which many push-button cars have even if they're hybrid or electric.

causes.name: Drained or dead 12-volt battery
causes.clues: Lights left on, the car sat for weeks, cold weather, or an older battery.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery cable
causes.clues: Crusty buildup on the terminals, or a loose clamp.

causes.name: Blown main fuse
causes.clues: A jump start changes nothing at all.
causes.against: Much less common than a battery problem.

you: Check the battery terminals for corrosion or loose clamps.
Try a jump start or booster pack.
shop: Parasitic draw test if the battery keeps dying

result.title: The battery may be too weak to crank the engine
result.now: Check that the battery clamps are tight and clean, then try a jump start or a battery booster.
if: If the battery is cracked, leaking, swollen or smells like rotten eggs, don't jump start it. Call for roadside help instead.
If it starts with a jump, have the battery and alternator tested soon.
If it still only clicks with a good jump, the cables or starter are the more likely problem.
result.why: Rapid clicking or flickering lights mean there's enough power to run the dash, but not enough to spin the starter. A weak battery can also cause key-not-detected messages because the key system needs steady voltage.

causes.name: Weak or discharged battery
causes.clues: Dim lights, cold weather, or a battery more than 4 years old.

causes.name: Corroded or loose battery terminal
causes.clues: Visible buildup, or the clicking changes when you wiggle a cable.

causes.name: Alternator not charging
causes.clues: The battery light came on recently while driving.

you: Check the battery terminals.
Try a jump start or a booster pack.
shop: Voltage-drop test on the battery cables

result.title: The key system or fuel delivery may be stopping the engine
result.now: Look for a flashing key or security light, and try the spare fob. If it still won't keep running, have the codes read or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the spare fob works, replace the main fob's battery or have it checked.
If you smell raw fuel, stop trying to start it and keep flames away.
result.why: If the engine cranks or fires and then dies, the button and starter are working. The anti-theft system cutting fuel because it doesn't recognize the key is common, followed by fuel or idle problems.

causes.name: Immobilizer not recognizing the key
causes.clues: A flashing key or security light, or it works with one fob but not the other.

causes.name: Fuel delivery problem
causes.clues: No hum from the rear when the car is switched on, or low fuel.

causes.name: Idle control or sensor problem
causes.clues: A check engine light, or a rough idle before it dies.

you: Try the spare fob.
Watch for a security light.

q_danger.q: Along with the rattle, do you notice any of these?

opts.a: Exhaust smell inside the car, or someone feels dizzy or gets a headache
Something is scraping on the road or hanging down under the car
The check engine light is flashing, or the engine has lost a lot of power
None of these, just the rattle
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When does the rattle happen?

opts.a: At a certain engine speed, even when parked (a tinny, buzzing metal rattle)
Mostly at startup or idle, and it fades or changes as the engine warms
Only over bumps or rough roads
Only when braking, or it stops when I press the brake
I'm not sure

q_tap.q: With the engine OFF and the exhaust completely cool, tap along the exhaust pipe and its thin metal covers with your hand or a rubber mallet. What happens?
q_tap.help: The exhaust runs from the engine to the tailpipe under the car. Heat shields are thin metal covers above or around the pipe and the catalytic converter (a wider section near the front). Wait at least an hour after driving, and only reach in from the side unless the car is safely on ramps or stands.

opts.a: A thin metal cover buzzes or rattles when I tap it
It sounds like loose gravel or rocks inside a wider section of the exhaust
The pipe swings or knocks against the car, or a rubber hanger is broken
Nothing rattles, or I can't safely reach under the car
I'm not sure

result.title: Exhaust may be leaking into the car. Don't drive it
result.now: Get out and get to fresh air. Don't drive the car again until it's repaired. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic inspect it.
if: If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion, get them into fresh air and call 911 or seek medical care.
If the car is parked in a garage, don't run the engine there to listen for the rattle.
result.why: A rattle can come from a broken or loose exhaust part, and the same damage can let exhaust leak out under the car. Exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which has no smell of its own and can cause drowsiness and worse. Any exhaust smell in the cabin is a reason to stop.

causes.name: Cracked or broken exhaust pipe or joint
causes.clues: The exhaust is louder than usual, and the rattle is near the front or middle of the car.

causes.name: Leaking exhaust manifold or gasket
causes.clues: A ticking or puffing from the engine and a smell when idling.

causes.name: Rusted-through muffler or pipe
causes.clues: Visible holes or heavy rust, and a deeper exhaust sound.

shop: Exhaust leak inspection on a lift
Check body seals and floor for holes

result.title: A part has come loose and may be dragging
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe and look from the side of the car. Don't drive on with something dragging. Call roadside assistance or have it towed.
if: If it's a plastic splash shield or panel and you can safely remove or tie it up, that may be enough until it's fixed properly.
If it's the exhaust, don't touch it until it has cooled for at least an hour.
result.why: A part dragging on the road can catch on something, damage other parts, throw sparks or come off and hit other vehicles. The usual culprits are the exhaust after a hanger breaks, or a plastic underbody panel that has torn loose.

causes.name: Broken exhaust hanger or clamp
causes.clues: A metal scraping sound and a louder exhaust.

causes.name: Loose underbody splash shield or panel
causes.clues: A plastic flapping or scraping sound, often after hitting a curb, snow or debris.

causes.name: Loose heat shield
causes.clues: A thin metal sheet hanging down near the exhaust.

you: From the side of the car, look underneath for anything hanging down.

result.title: The catalytic converter may be breaking up or blocked
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic rather than driving on.
if: If you smell burning, see smoke, or notice a strong rotten egg smell, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
If the light stops flashing, still get it checked before driving any distance.
If the engine stalls, won't rev, or the exhaust or floor area gets very hot, keep the engine off. A blocked or overheated converter can damage the engine and is a fire risk near dry grass or leaves.
result.why: A flashing check engine light means a serious misfire, which sends unburned fuel into the catalytic converter and can overheat it. The inside of the converter can then crack apart and rattle, and loose pieces can block the exhaust, which causes a big loss of power.

causes.name: Engine misfire overheating the converter
causes.clues: A flashing check engine light, shaking, or a fuel or rotten egg smell.

causes.name: Broken-up converter blocking the exhaust
causes.clues: Power has dropped steadily, and the engine struggles to rev.

causes.name: Collapsed muffler inside
causes.clues: A rattle further back, with power loss.

you: If you have a code reader, read and save the codes.

result.title: A loose suspension link, exhaust hanger or underbody panel is a common cause
result.now: Book an inspection when convenient. Tell the shop the rattle only happens over bumps and rough roads.
if: If the steering feels loose, wanders, or a front wheel clunks hard over bumps, stop driving and have it inspected before driving further.
If it becomes a heavier clunk, get it checked within a few days.
If something starts scraping on the road, pull over and look.
If you smell exhaust inside the car, get to fresh air and have it checked before driving again.
result.why: A rattle that only shows up on rough roads means something is loose enough to move when the car bounces. Common possibilities are a worn sway bar link, a sagging exhaust that taps the body, or a loose plastic panel.

causes.name: Worn sway bar link
causes.clues: A light knock or rattle near a wheel on small bumps.

causes.name: Exhaust hitting the body or a loose hanger
causes.clues: A metallic bang under the middle or back of the car, sometimes when shifting into gear too.

causes.name: Loose underbody panel or splash shield
causes.clues: A plastic rattle, often after hitting debris or deep snow.

you: With the car cool and parked, push gently on the tailpipe and see if the exhaust knocks against anything.
Look from the side for loose plastic panels.

result.title: A brake part may be loose or worn
result.now: Have the brakes inspected in the next day or two, and keep driving to a minimum until then. Leave extra stopping distance.
if: If you hear grinding, the pedal feels soft or sinks, the car pulls when braking, or the brake warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If you hear a clunk when you first press or release the brake, stop driving and have it inspected. A loose caliper bolt can't be ruled out from here.
If the rattle started right after brake work, call the shop that did the work and have them check it before driving any distance.
result.why: If the rattle changes or stops when you press the brake, the brakes are a likely source. Pads can rattle when the anti-rattle clips are missing or worn, A loose caliper or bracket bolt is less common but more serious, which is why this needs a look soon.

causes.name: Missing or worn anti-rattle clips or pad hardware
causes.clues: A light rattle over bumps that stops when you touch the brake.

causes.name: Loose caliper or bracket bolt
causes.clues: A clunk when you start braking or switch between forward and reverse.

causes.name: Badly worn brake pads
causes.clues: Squealing or grinding when braking.

you: Note whether the rattle stops when you lightly press the brake pedal.

result.title: A loose heat shield is a likely cause
result.now: Look at where the shield is attached. If a bracket has rusted away, the shield can often be secured with a large stainless hose clamp around the pipe. If you're not comfortable doing it, an exhaust shop can usually secure it.
if: If the shield is badly rusted or hanging down, have it repaired or replaced rather than removing it.
If the rattle continues after securing the shield, have the exhaust checked.
If you smell exhaust inside the car, the exhaust gets louder, or anything is hanging down, stop and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Heat shields are thin metal covers that keep exhaust heat away from the floor, fuel lines and dry grass under the car. Their fasteners rust over time, and the loose shield buzzes at certain engine speeds. It's one of the most common rattles under a car.

causes.name: Rusted heat shield fastener or bracket
causes.clues: A tinny buzz at a certain engine speed, even when parked.

causes.name: Loose exhaust clamp
causes.clues: The rattle is at a pipe joint rather than a thin cover.

causes.name: Catalytic converter internal rattle
causes.clues: Tapping the converter itself makes a gravel-like sound.
causes.against: Less likely if the rattle stops when you hold the shield.

you: With the exhaust cool, press on each shield and see whether the rattle stops.
Look for rusted-out fasteners or brackets.
shop: Exhaust and heat shield inspection on a lift

result.title: The inside of the catalytic converter or muffler may be breaking up
result.now: Get the exhaust checked within a few days, and avoid long trips and hard acceleration until then.
if: If the engine loses power, struggles to rev, or the check engine light flashes, stop driving and have it towed.
If the check engine light is on steady, ask the shop to check for a misfire too. Misfires are a common reason converters fail.
If you smell burning or a strong rotten egg smell, or see smoke from under the car, pull over, turn the engine off and have it towed.
result.why: A catalytic converter has a honeycomb core inside. Heat, age, a hard impact or an engine problem can crack it, and the pieces rattle like gravel in a can, often worst at startup. Over time the broken pieces can block the exhaust and choke the engine.

causes.name: Broken catalytic converter core
causes.clues: A gravel or rock rattle when you tap the converter, often worse at startup or idle.

causes.name: Broken baffle inside the muffler
causes.clues: The gravel sound is from the muffler near the back.

causes.name: Loose heat shield on the converter
causes.clues: The rattle stops when you press on the outer cover.

you: Note whether the engine has lost any power.
Check whether the check engine light is on.

result.title: A broken exhaust hanger or mount may be letting the exhaust move
result.now: Book an exhaust repair within the next week or two. Hangers are usually a simple repair, and catching it early protects the rest of the exhaust.
if: If the exhaust starts hanging low or dragging, pull over and have it towed.
If you smell fumes inside the car, get to fresh air and don't drive it until it's checked.
If the exhaust gets louder, get it checked right away.
result.why: Rubber hangers hold the exhaust in place while letting it move a little. When one breaks, the pipe swings and knocks against the car, especially when starting off or going over bumps. The extra movement can also crack pipes and joints.

causes.name: Broken or stretched rubber hanger
causes.clues: The pipe swings freely, or a hanger is torn or missing.

causes.name: Rusted-off hanger bracket
causes.clues: The rubber is fine, but the metal rod or bracket has broken.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mount
causes.clues: The exhaust knocks mostly when shifting into gear or taking off.

you: With the exhaust cool, push the tailpipe side to side and listen for knocking.
Look along the pipe for broken rubber hangers.

result.title: A shop should put it on a lift to find the rattle
result.now: Book an inspection when convenient. Tell the shop when the rattle happens: at a certain engine speed, at startup, over bumps or when braking.
if: If you smell exhaust inside the car, get to fresh air and have it checked before driving again.
If the steering feels loose, the brake pedal feels different, or something is hanging down, stop driving and have it checked first.
If the rattle becomes a clunk, a grind or a scrape, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: Under-car rattles are much easier to find with the car lifted, the engine running, and a technician listening and tapping parts. Many turn out to be minor, like a heat shield, but it's worth ruling out exhaust leaks and loose brake or suspension parts.

causes.name: Loose heat shield
causes.clues: A tinny buzz at certain engine speeds.

causes.name: Exhaust hanger or clamp
causes.clues: A knock when starting off or over bumps.

causes.name: Suspension or brake hardware
causes.clues: The rattle happens over bumps or when braking.

you: Record a short video with sound of the rattle, and note the engine speed or road conditions when it happens.

q_power.q: How much power do you have right now?

opts.a: Almost none: it crawls, can't keep up with traffic, or stalls
Noticeably less, but I can still move with slower traffic
It went back to normal after I turned the car off and on
I'm not sure

q_signs.q: Do you notice any of these as well?
q_signs.help: A DPF is the diesel particulate filter, a soot filter in the exhaust of most modern diesels.

opts.a: The engine temperature gauge is high, or there's steam
The check engine light is flashing, or the engine shakes or stumbles
It's stuck in one gear, shifts oddly, or a transmission light is on
It has a turbo, and I hear a loud whoosh or hiss when accelerating
It's a diesel and a DPF or exhaust filter light is on
None of these. Just the message, maybe with a steady check engine light
I'm not sure

result.title: Power is cut too far to drive safely
result.now: Turn on your hazard lights, get out of traffic and park. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the temperature gauge is high, steam appears or the check engine light is flashing, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off.
If a red oil pressure light comes on, or you hear knocking, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off to avoid engine damage.
If you smell burning or fuel, or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: When a car can barely move, it's a hazard on any road with traffic. The computer usually cuts power this hard only for a fault it treats as serious, and pushing on can damage the engine or transmission.

causes.name: Electronic throttle or accelerator pedal sensor failure
causes.clues: The gas pedal does almost nothing, and the engine idles fine.

causes.name: Engine overheating protection
causes.clues: A high temperature gauge or steam.

causes.name: Severe transmission fault
causes.clues: The engine revs but the car barely moves.

causes.name: Badly clogged exhaust or catalytic converter
causes.clues: Power faded over weeks, with a rotten-egg smell or a red-hot glow under the car.

you: Note any other warning lights and take a photo of the dash for the shop.

result.title: The engine may be overheating and cutting power to protect itself
result.now: Pull over where it's safe and turn the engine off. Don't open the radiator cap while it's hot. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see steam, keep the hood closed until it stops and everything has cooled.
If a red oil pressure light comes on, you hear knocking, or you see smoke, keep the engine off and don't restart it.
If you smell coolant inside the car or see fog on the inside of the windows, keep the windows open and get it checked before driving again.
result.why: Some engines reduce power when they get too hot to slow down the damage. Driving an overheating engine can warp or crack major parts in minutes.

causes.name: Low coolant from a leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, steam, or puddles under the front of the car.

causes.name: Cooling fan or water pump failure
causes.clues: It overheats mostly in traffic (fan) or at any speed (pump).

causes.name: Stuck thermostat
causes.clues: The gauge climbed quickly with no leak.

you: Once fully cool, check the coolant level in the see-through reservoir.
Look for coolant puddles.
shop: Cooling fan and water pump tests

result.title: A severe misfire is possible, and it can damage the engine and exhaust
result.now: Pull over where it's safe and turn the engine off. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you smell something hot or see a glow under the car, move away from it. The catalytic converter may be overheating.
If you smell fuel, see smoke, or the red oil pressure light comes on, keep the engine off and don't restart it.
If the temperature gauge climbs, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and let it cool.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means the engine is misfiring badly enough to send unburned fuel into the exhaust. That can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter, and the car may cut power because of it.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: The shaking is worse when you accelerate.

causes.name: Fuel injector fault
causes.clues: A fuel smell or rough idle.

causes.name: Engine mechanical problem
causes.clues: Ticking or knocking, or low oil.

you: Check the oil level once the engine is off and cool.
shop: Ignition coil and spark plug tests

result.title: The transmission may have a fault that put the car in limp mode
result.now: Get off highways and busy roads when it's safe and have it towed to a shop.
if: If the transmission slips, smells burnt, the car won't move, or you see smoke, stop and have it towed.
If a transmission temperature warning comes on, or the engine temperature gauge climbs, pull over and turn the engine off.
If a restart clears it, still get the codes read within a few days.
result.why: When the transmission computer sees a problem, it often holds the transmission in one gear and limits power. The car can still move slowly, but it isn't built to be driven this way for long.

causes.name: Shift solenoid or speed sensor fault
causes.clues: It went into one gear suddenly.

causes.name: Low or overheated transmission fluid
causes.clues: Slipping, a leak, or towing before it happened.

causes.name: Wiring or low battery voltage
causes.clues: Several warning lights came on at once.

you: Look under the car for red fluid.

result.title: The turbo may be losing boost through a leak or fault
result.now: Drive gently, avoid hard acceleration and highways, and get it checked within the next few days.
if: If you see blue or heavy smoke from the exhaust, or oil around the turbo, stop driving it. A failing turbo can damage the engine.
If you hear a new loud whine or grinding from the turbo, stop driving it.
If the check engine light flashes, the temperature gauge climbs, or you smell burning, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: A whoosh or hiss under acceleration often means pressurized air is escaping before it reaches the engine. The computer sees too little boost and cuts power. A split hose or loose clamp is a common cause, and a shop will usually pressure-test the hoses before looking at the turbo itself.

causes.name: Split or loose boost hose or clamp
causes.clues: The hiss is loudest under acceleration, and you may see an oily hose.

causes.name: Wastegate or boost control fault
causes.clues: Power comes and goes with no hiss.

causes.name: Failing turbocharger
causes.clues: Whining, blue smoke, or oil in the intake hoses.

you: With the engine off and cool, look for loose clamps or split hoses between the turbo and the engine.
shop: Code scan and live boost readings

result.title: The diesel exhaust filter may be clogged with soot
result.now: Have a shop check it within the next few days. They can run a forced cleaning cycle. Avoid more short trips until then.
if: If only the filter light is on and power is normal, your owner's manual may say a steady highway drive will let it clean itself. Follow the manual, not a guess.
If the engine temperature rises, you smell burning, or you see smoke, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the check engine light flashes or power drops further, stop driving and have it checked.
result.why: Diesel soot filters clean themselves by burning off soot during longer drives. Lots of short trips stop that from happening, and once the filter is too full, the engine cuts power to protect itself.

causes.name: Too many short trips
causes.clues: Mostly town driving, few highway runs.

causes.name: Faulty pressure sensor or hose on the filter
causes.clues: The light returns soon after a cleaning.

causes.name: An engine fault making extra soot
causes.clues: Black smoke, or other engine codes.

you: Check your owner's manual for what it says about the filter light.
shop: Code scan and soot level reading

result.title: Often the electronic throttle or gas pedal sensor
result.now: Find a safe place to stop, turn the car off for a minute and restart it. Then have the codes read within the next few days, and avoid highways until it's fixed.
if: If power drops so low you can't keep up with traffic, stop driving and have it towed.
If the engine races, surges, or doesn't slow down when you lift off the pedal, shift to neutral, brake to a stop, turn the engine off and have it towed.
If the check engine light starts flashing or the temperature gauge climbs, pull over and turn the engine off.
If several other warning lights come on too, ask for the battery and charging system to be tested as well.
result.why: On modern cars, the gas pedal is a sensor, and a motor opens the throttle. If the computer gets readings it can't trust from either one, it limits power so the car can't speed up on its own. A dirty throttle, a sensor or a wiring connection are common causes. A shop will usually read the codes and test the sensors and wiring before replacing parts.

causes.name: Dirty or failing electronic throttle body
causes.clues: A rough or uneven idle, or it happens more often in cold or damp weather.

causes.name: Accelerator pedal sensor fault
causes.clues: The pedal feels normal but the engine doesn't respond in step with it.

causes.name: Wiring or connector problem
causes.clues: It comes and goes, especially over bumps.

causes.name: Low battery voltage
causes.clues: A weak battery or other warning lights coming on.

you: Note whether the check engine light is on, and take a photo of the dash.

result.title: A fault that clears with a restart is still a fault
result.now: Get the stored codes read within the next few days, before it happens again in traffic.
if: If it keeps coming back, avoid highways and busy merges until it's fixed.
If it happens with a flashing check engine light, high temperature, a red warning light, or a burning smell, stop driving it.
result.why: Restarting resets the computer, so power comes back, but the code that caused it is often still stored. Problems like this tend to return, often at a bad moment.

causes.name: Electronic throttle or pedal sensor glitch
causes.clues: It happened suddenly, with nothing else wrong.

causes.name: Loose or corroded wiring connector
causes.clues: It happens over bumps or in wet weather.

causes.name: Weak battery or charging problem
causes.clues: Slow cranking, dim lights, or other lights coming on.

you: Note the speed, weather and what you were doing when it happened.
shop: Code scan, including stored and history codes

q_danger.q: Does either of these apply right now?

opts.a: The check engine light is flashing, or the engine is shaking or losing power
The smell is strongest at the battery, or the battery is hot, hissing, swollen or leaking
Neither of these
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When and where do you notice the smell most?

opts.a: From the exhaust, mostly when accelerating hard, climbing hills or right after a drive
Mostly after filling up at one particular gas station, and it fades
Near a wheel or the middle or back of the car, with oily drips underneath
Along with the battery light, or lights that are unusually bright or flickering
I'm not sure

q_cel.q: Is the check engine light on, or has the car changed how it drives?
q_cel.help: A steady (not flashing) check engine light means the car has stored a trouble code. Any auto parts store or shop can read it.

opts.a: The check engine light is on steady
It feels down on power, or rattles from under the car
No light, and it drives normally
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be misfiring and overheating the catalytic converter
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see smoke or a glow under the car, get everyone away from the vehicle and call 911.
If the light stops flashing after a restart, don't trust it. Have the misfire diagnosed before driving any distance.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means the engine is misfiring badly. Unburned fuel goes into the catalytic converter and burns there, making it extremely hot. That causes the sulfur smell and can melt the converter or set fire to things underneath the car.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: Shaking at idle or under load, and the problem started suddenly.

causes.name: Leaking or stuck fuel injector
causes.clues: A strong fuel smell along with the sulfur smell, or black smoke.

causes.name: Overheated or damaged catalytic converter
causes.clues: Heat felt through the floor, or loss of power that gets worse as you drive.

shop: Code scan and misfire counter check
Ignition coil and spark plug test
Exhaust back-pressure test on the catalytic converter

result.title: The battery may be overcharging or failing inside
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn off the engine, open the hood to let it vent if you can do it without leaning over the battery, and step away. Don't touch the battery. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the battery is swollen, cracked or leaking liquid, keep everyone well away. Battery acid burns skin and the gas it gives off can ignite.
If the smell fades and the battery looks normal once cool, still don't drive it until the charging system has been tested.
If you see smoke or flames, get everyone well away from the car and call 911.
