result.why: When a battery gets too much charging voltage or shorts inside, the acid boils and gives off a sulfur smell along with flammable gas. The battery can swell, leak or, rarely, burst. Common causes are a faulty alternator voltage regulator or a battery at the end of its life. A shop will usually test the charging voltage and the battery before replacing either.

causes.name: Alternator overcharging (faulty voltage regulator)
causes.clues: Lights that seem unusually bright, bulbs burning out, or the battery light flickering.

causes.name: Internal short in an old battery
causes.clues: The battery is more than 4–5 years old, or one side feels much hotter.

causes.name: Wrong charger or charger left on
causes.clues: The battery was recently charged with a home charger.

you: From a safe distance, look for swelling, cracks or wet residue on the battery case.

result.title: The charging system may be cooking the battery
result.now: Have the battery and charging system tested within the next few days. Most auto parts stores can test both.
if: If the battery is hot, hissing, swollen or leaking, stop driving, turn the engine off and keep away from it.
If the smell gets strong, you see smoke from under the hood, or you smell burning plastic, pull over, turn the engine off and step away.
If the battery light stays on and the lights start to dim, the alternator may be failing. Get it checked right away before the car dies on the road.
result.why: A sulfur smell alongside a battery warning or odd lighting can mean the alternator isn't regulating voltage correctly. Too much voltage overcharges the battery and makes it give off sulfur gas. Too little and the car can stall.

causes.name: Faulty voltage regulator in the alternator
causes.clues: Unusually bright lights, bulbs failing often, or the battery light on.

causes.name: Failing battery
causes.clues: The battery is old, starts have been slow, or there's crusty buildup on the terminals.

causes.name: Bad charging system wiring or ground
causes.clues: The lights flicker over bumps or the gauges jump around.

you: Note how old the battery is (often on a label on top).
Look for crusty buildup or swelling on the battery.
shop: Charging voltage test with the engine running
Voltage-drop test on charging wires and grounds

result.title: The engine may be running rich or the catalytic converter may be failing
result.now: Get the check engine code read and have the car checked within a few days. Avoid hard acceleration and long trips until then.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes, pull over and turn it off.
If the car keeps losing power or the floor feels hot, stop driving it. A blocked converter can overheat.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the car, pull over, turn the engine off and step away.

If you smell it inside the car, open the windows. If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning: get everyone into fresh air and call 911 from outside the car.
result.why: The catalytic converter normally turns sulfur in the exhaust into odorless gases. When the engine sends it too much fuel, or the converter is worn out, it can't keep up, and you smell sulfur. An engine problem left alone can also damage the converter, so a shop will usually check the fuel mixture and sensors before replacing the converter.

causes.name: Engine running rich (too much fuel)
causes.clues: Worse gas mileage, a fuel smell, or a code for an oxygen sensor or fuel trim.

causes.name: Worn or damaged catalytic converter
causes.clues: A catalyst efficiency code, a rattle from under the car, or power loss at speed.

causes.name: Faulty oxygen sensor
causes.clues: An oxygen sensor code with no other symptoms.

you: Have the trouble code read for free at many auto parts stores.
Note whether gas mileage has dropped recently.
shop: Code scan with fuel trim and oxygen sensor data

result.title: An occasional sulfur smell after hard driving can be the catalytic converter working hard
result.now: Try a different gas station for your next couple of fill-ups, and book a check when convenient if the smell continues.
if: If the smell becomes constant or the check engine light comes on, get it checked within a few days.
If the check engine light flashes or the engine shakes, pull over and turn it off.

If you smell it inside the car, open the windows. If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea or sleepiness, this may be carbon monoxide poisoning: get everyone into fresh air and call 911 from outside the car.
result.why: Fuel naturally contains a little sulfur. Under hard acceleration the catalytic converter can briefly release some as a rotten egg smell, especially on newer cars or with certain fuel. If it's rare and the car runs normally, it's less likely to mean damage, but a code scan is the way to rule out a fuel mixture problem.

causes.name: Normal converter odor under heavy load
causes.clues: Only after hard acceleration, towing or long climbs, and it fades quickly.

causes.name: Fuel with higher sulfur content
causes.clues: It started after filling up at a new station.

causes.name: Engine running slightly rich
causes.clues: Gas mileage has crept down over time.
causes.against: If mileage and performance are unchanged, this is less likely.

you: Switch gas stations or fuel brands for a few tanks.
Keep track of your gas mileage.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim check

result.title: The fuel may be the cause
result.now: Fill up at a different station for the next few tanks and see if the smell goes away.
if: If the smell continues with different fuel, have the car checked when convenient.
If the check engine light comes on or the engine runs rough, get it checked within a few days.
If the check engine light flashes, or you smell it strongly inside the car, pull over and turn the engine off. That's no longer a fuel issue.
result.why: All gasoline has a small amount of sulfur, and some batches have more than others. The catalytic converter can't always clean all of it up, so a tank of higher-sulfur fuel can leave a temporary rotten egg smell.

causes.name: Higher-sulfur fuel batch
causes.clues: The smell started right after a fill-up and fades as you use the tank.

causes.name: Catalytic converter or fuel mixture problem
causes.clues: The smell continues no matter where you fill up.

you: Try a different station for two or three fill-ups.
Note whether the smell comes back with each fill-up at the original station.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim check

result.title: Gear oil may be leaking from the transmission or a differential
result.now: Look under the car for thick, dark drips, and book a check when convenient so the leak can be found and the fluid level topped up.
if: If the drips are steady or you hear new whining, grinding or howling from that area, get it checked within a few days. Running low on gear oil can ruin gears and bearings.
If the leak is near a wheel and there's oil on the brake parts, have it checked before driving. Oil on brakes reduces stopping power.
If you see smoke from under the car or smell burning oil, pull over and turn the engine off. Oil dripping on a hot exhaust can catch fire.
result.why: Gear oil used in manual transmissions, differentials and transfer cases contains sulfur additives with a strong rotten egg smell. A leak that drips onto hot exhaust parts or collects underneath can make the whole car smell.

causes.name: Leaking differential seal or cover
causes.clues: Oily drips near the rear axle on rear-wheel-drive, all-wheel-drive or 4WD vehicles.

causes.name: Leaking manual transmission or transfer case
causes.clues: Drips under the middle of the car.

causes.name: Leaking axle seal
causes.clues: Oil on the inside of a wheel or tire.

you: Put cardboard under the car overnight and note where thick, dark drops land.
Check the inside of each wheel for oily residue.
shop: Differential and transmission fluid level check
Brake inspection if oil is near a wheel

result.title: Often the exhaust or catalytic converter. Have it checked
result.now: Note when the smell happens and whether any warning lights are on, then book a check when convenient.
if: If a warning light comes on, the engine runs rough, or the smell is strong inside the car, get it checked within a few days.
If the check engine light flashes, or you see smoke or a glow under the car, pull over and turn the engine off.
If anyone gets a headache, feels dizzy or drowsy, pull over, get everyone into fresh air and call 911 from outside the car.
If the battery is hot, hissing or swollen, turn the engine off and keep away from it.
result.why: The catalytic converter is a common source of a rotten egg smell, but an overcharged battery or leaking gear oil can smell the same. A shop can usually tell them apart with a code scan, a charging test and a look underneath.

causes.name: Catalytic converter or fuel mixture problem
causes.clues: The smell comes from the exhaust, especially after accelerating.

causes.name: Overcharging or failing battery
causes.clues: The smell is strongest under the hood near the battery.

causes.name: Gear oil leak
causes.clues: Oily drips under the middle or rear of the car.

you: With the engine off and cool, sniff near the battery and near the tailpipe to see where the smell is strongest.
Check for warning lights.

rough-idle-shaking.title: Rough idle or shaking when stopped

q_warning.q: Do you see any of these warning signs on the dash?
q_warning.help: The check engine light is the amber engine-shaped symbol. The oil pressure light looks like a red oil can.

opts.a: The check engine light is flashing
The temperature gauge is high or in the red, or there's steam
The red oil pressure light is on
The check engine light is on steady
No warning lights
I'm not sure
It also stumbles, jerks or feels weak when I accelerate
A hissing sound from the engine, or the idle speed goes up and down
It only shakes at idle and drives fine
I smell raw fuel
I'm not sure

q_no_light.help: Engine mounts are rubber blocks that hold the engine in place and soak up its vibration.

opts.a: Worse in Drive or Reverse at a stop, smoother in Park or Neutral
There's a clunk or jolt when I shift or accelerate
Worse when the A/C is on
Rough only when cold, and smooths out when warm
Rough and uneven all the time, even in Park
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be misfiring badly, which can damage the catalytic converter
result.now: Pull over safely and turn off the engine. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the light stops flashing after a restart, the problem is still there. Get it checked before driving any distance.
If you see smoke or smell burning from under the car, get away from the car and call for help.
If the oil pressure light comes on or you hear knocking, keep the engine off and don't restart it.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means the engine is misfiring badly enough to send unburned fuel into the exhaust. That fuel can overheat the catalytic converter within minutes and ruin it, and the shaking itself means a cylinder isn't doing its share.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: A sudden, rhythmic shake at idle and when accelerating.

causes.name: Fuel injector not working
causes.clues: The misfire stays on one cylinder after the ignition parts check out.

causes.name: Mechanical engine problem
causes.clues: A ticking or knocking noise, or a recent overheat.
causes.against: Much less common than an ignition problem.

you: Note when the flashing started and whether the shaking was sudden.

result.title: The engine may be overheating. Stop before it causes damage
result.now: Pull over safely and turn off the engine. Don't open the radiator cap while it's hot. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see steam or coolant leaking, stay clear of the engine until it cools completely.
If the coolant was low and you top it up, still have the cooling system checked before driving. Running hot again can warp the cylinder head.
If the oil pressure light comes on or you hear knocking, don't restart the engine.
result.why: An engine that runs too hot can start to misfire and shake, and continued driving can damage the head gasket or the engine itself. A rough idle with high temperature is a sign to stop right away.

causes.name: Low coolant from a leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, steam, or a puddle of green, orange or pink fluid.

causes.name: Cooling fan not working
causes.clues: It overheats mostly at idle or in traffic, and cools down on the highway.

causes.name: Head gasket failure
causes.clues: White exhaust smoke with a sweet smell, or coolant keeps disappearing.

you: Once the engine is completely cool, check the coolant level in the see-through reservoir.
Look for puddles under the front of the car.
shop: Combustion gas test for a head gasket leak

result.title: The engine may be low on oil or losing oil pressure
result.now: Turn off the engine as soon as it's safe. Check the oil level once it's parked on level ground. Don't run the engine again until the cause is found.
if: If the oil is very low, adding oil may turn the light off, but have it checked before driving. Find out where the oil went.
If the oil level is full and the light is still on, have it towed. The oil pump or a sensor may have failed.
result.why: Low oil pressure means the engine's moving parts aren't getting enough lubrication. Running it this way can destroy the engine within minutes, and a rough idle with this light can mean damage is already starting.

causes.name: Low oil level
causes.clues: An oil leak, burning oil, or a long time since the last oil change.

causes.name: Failing oil pump or clogged pickup
causes.clues: The oil level is fine but the light stays on, maybe with a ticking or knocking sound.

causes.name: Faulty oil pressure sensor
causes.clues: The light flickers, and the engine sounds normal.
causes.against: Don't assume it's the sensor until pressure is tested.

you: With the engine off and the car level, check the oil dipstick.

result.title: A misfire is a common cause, often from a worn ignition part
result.now: If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Otherwise: Have the engine scanned for codes within the next few days. Until then, keep trips short and avoid hard acceleration.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the oil pressure light comes on, the temperature gauge climbs, or you smell raw fuel, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the engine stalls, especially while moving or at intersections, avoid driving until it's checked. When the engine dies, steering and braking take much more effort.
If the spark plugs are due by your maintenance schedule, mention it. They're a common cause, and a shop will usually confirm which cylinder is misfiring before replacing parts.
result.why: When one cylinder doesn't fire properly, the engine loses its smooth rhythm and shakes, especially at idle and when accelerating. A steady check engine light along with stumbling often points to a misfire, and leaving it can damage the catalytic converter over time.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs
causes.clues: The plugs haven't been changed in a long time, or it's worse when accelerating.

causes.name: Failing ignition coil or plug wire
causes.clues: A misfire on one cylinder, or worse in damp weather.

causes.name: Clogged or failing fuel injector
causes.clues: The misfire stays on one cylinder after the ignition parts are checked.

you: Check your records for the last spark plug change.
Many auto parts stores will read the codes for you.

result.title: A vacuum leak or dirty throttle body is a common cause
result.now: Book a check and ask for a code scan and a vacuum leak test. Mention that it's worst at idle.
if: If the engine stalls, especially while moving or at intersections, avoid driving until it's checked. When the engine dies, steering and braking take much more effort.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the oil pressure light comes on, the temperature gauge climbs, or you smell raw fuel, pull over and turn off the engine.
result.why: At idle, the engine runs on a small, carefully measured amount of air. A cracked hose or leaking gasket lets in extra air the computer doesn't know about, which makes the idle shaky or hunt up and down. A dirty throttle body can cause a similar rough idle.

causes.name: Cracked vacuum hose or leaking intake gasket
causes.clues: A hissing sound with the engine running, or a lean code on a scan.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control fault
causes.clues: A low or uneven idle that may improve slightly when you touch the gas.

causes.name: Faulty PCV valve or hose
causes.clues: A whistle or hiss, or oil residue around the hose.

you: With the engine idling, listen carefully around the top of the engine for hissing.
Look for cracked or disconnected rubber hoses (keep hands clear of belts and fans).
shop: Code scan and fuel trim data

result.title: A fuel leak or a leaking injector is possible
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn off the engine and look for wet spots or dripping fuel under the car and around the engine. If you find any or the smell is strong, have it towed.
if: If you see fuel dripping, keep everyone away from the car and call for help.
If you can't find a leak and the smell is faint, still have it checked before driving. Fuel leaks are a fire risk.
result.why: A rough idle with a raw fuel smell can mean an injector is leaking or stuck open, flooding a cylinder, or that fuel is leaking outside the engine. Either way, fuel near a hot engine is a fire risk.

causes.name: Leaking or stuck-open fuel injector
causes.clues: A misfire on one cylinder, black smoke, or hard starting when warm.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line or fuel rail
causes.clues: A wet spot or drips under the car or on the engine.

causes.name: Engine running very rich
causes.clues: Black smoke and a fuel smell at the tailpipe, with poor fuel economy.

you: Look for wet spots or drips under the car. Don't smoke or use flames nearby.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim data

result.title: Worn engine or transmission mounts are a likely cause
result.now: Book an inspection of the engine and transmission mounts. Mention that it shakes more in Drive than in Park.
if: If you hear loud clunks when shifting or accelerating, or the engine visibly lurches, get it checked within a few days.
If a hard clunk is followed by a fuel or coolant smell, a leak, or a warning light, stop and have it checked before driving further. A badly broken mount can let the engine pull on hoses and wiring.
If the shake is the same in Park and Drive, the engine itself may be running rough instead.
result.why: Mounts are rubber blocks that hold the engine and soak up its normal vibration. When they crack or collapse, you can feel the engine through the car, mostly in gear at a stop where the engine is pulling against the brakes. A badly broken mount can let the engine move enough to strain hoses and wiring.

causes.name: Worn or collapsed engine mount
causes.clues: More shaking in Drive or Reverse than in Park, and a clunk when shifting.

causes.name: Worn transmission mount
causes.clues: A clunk or jolt when accelerating from a stop.

causes.name: Engine idling slightly rough
causes.clues: The shake is there in Park too, or the idle speed wanders.

you: Compare the shake in Park, Neutral and Drive with your foot firmly on the brake.
shop: Watch for engine movement while shifting with the brakes held
Code scan to rule out a misfire

result.title: The idle may be too low to handle the A/C load
result.now: Book a check when convenient and mention that the shake gets worse with the A/C on.
if: If the engine stalls when the A/C kicks on, get it checked within a few days, and avoid driving if it stalls while moving. Steering and braking get much heavier when the engine dies.
If the temperature gauge climbs with the A/C on, turn the A/C off, pull over and turn off the engine.
If it also shakes more in Drive than in Park, worn engine mounts may be adding to it.
result.why: The A/C compressor adds load to the engine. The engine computer should raise the idle slightly to make up for it. If the idle control is dirty or a mount is worn, you feel the engine labor and shake.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control fault
causes.clues: The idle drops noticeably when the A/C turns on.

causes.name: Worn engine mounts
causes.clues: The shake is also worse in Drive than in Park.

causes.name: A/C compressor problem
causes.clues: A grinding or rattling noise when the A/C turns on.

you: At a stop, switch the A/C on and off and watch whether the engine speed dips.
shop: Idle control and throttle body check

result.title: A cold-start rough idle often points to a sensor or carbon buildup
result.now: Book a check when convenient. Note the outside temperature and how long it takes to smooth out.
if: If the check engine light comes on or it starts running rough when warm too, get it checked within a few days.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and turn off the engine.
If it stalls when cold, mention it. That makes it more urgent, and if it stalls while moving, avoid driving until it's checked.
result.why: A cold engine needs extra fuel and a slightly higher idle. If a temperature sensor gives the computer a wrong reading, or carbon has built up on the valves or injectors, the engine can run rough until it warms up.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: The temperature gauge acts oddly, or fuel economy has dropped.

causes.name: Carbon buildup or dirty injectors
causes.clues: A higher-mileage engine, especially a direct-injection one.

causes.name: Small vacuum leak
causes.clues: A hiss that's louder when cold, as rubber and gaskets shrink.

you: Note how long after a cold start the shake goes away.
shop: Code scan and live sensor data

result.title: The engine may be running unevenly at idle. A misfire or air leak is possible
result.now: If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Otherwise: Book a check and ask for a code scan, even with no warning light. Problems at idle often show up as stored data before the light comes on.
if: If the check engine light comes on or the car stumbles when accelerating, get it checked within a few days.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the oil pressure light comes on, the temperature gauge climbs, or you smell raw fuel, pull over and turn off the engine.
result.why: A rough idle that's the same in Park and in gear usually comes from the engine itself rather than the mounts. Early ignition wear, a small vacuum leak or a dirty throttle body are common causes, and they're easiest to fix before they cause a misfire.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs or weak ignition coil
causes.clues: A rhythmic shake or stumble, and plugs that are due for a change.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or an idle speed that hunts up and down.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body
causes.clues: A low idle that improves slightly when you touch the gas.

you: Check your records for the last spark plug change.
Listen for hissing around the top of the engine while it idles.
shop: Code scan, misfire counts and fuel trim data

result.title: Get a code scan to narrow it down
result.now: Book a check and ask for a code scan. Note whether the shake changes in Park versus Drive and with the A/C on or off.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the temperature gauge rises, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the oil pressure light comes on or you smell raw fuel, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the engine stalls, especially while moving or at intersections, avoid driving until it's checked. When the engine dies, steering and braking take much more effort.
result.why: A rough idle can come from the engine running unevenly or from worn mounts letting normal vibration through. A code scan and a quick test in different gears can usually separate these quickly.

causes.name: Misfire from worn ignition parts
causes.clues: A rhythmic shake, or stumbling when accelerating.

causes.name: Vacuum leak or dirty throttle body
causes.clues: A hissing sound or a hunting idle speed.

causes.name: Worn engine mounts
causes.clues: Worse in Drive than in Park, or a clunk when shifting.

you: Record a short video at idle showing the engine speed on the tachometer, with sound.

q_what_happens.q: What happens when you try to start the car?
q_what_happens.help: "Cranking" is the whirring sound of the engine turning over (rrr-rrr-rrr) before it fires up.

opts.a: The engine cranks but never fires up
It starts, then dies after a second or two
Nothing happens, or just a click, and the security light flashes
The light only blinks while the car is parked and locked, and the car starts fine
I'm not sure

q_power.q: When you turn the key to ON (or press Start without your foot on the brake), are the dash lights and headlights bright?
q_power.help: A weak car battery can stop the anti-theft system from reading your key properly, so it's worth ruling out first.

opts.a: No, they're dim, flicker or don't come on
Yes, they're bright and normal
I'm not sure

q_spare.q: Have you tried your spare key or spare key fob?

opts.a: Yes, and the spare works
Yes, and the spare doesn't work either
No, or I don't have a spare
I'm not sure

q_recent.q: Has any of this happened recently?

opts.a: The car battery died, was jump-started, disconnected or replaced
A new key or remote was cut or added
The key has been hard to turn, or a remote starter or alarm was installed
None of these
I'm not sure

result.title: A security light that blinks while the car is parked is usually normal
result.now: If the light goes out a few seconds after you turn the key to ON or press Start, and the car starts and runs, this is usually just the anti-theft system showing it's armed. Your owner's manual will confirm how the light should behave on your car.
if: If the light stays on or flashes fast with the engine running, have the anti-theft system checked when convenient.
If the car later cranks but won't start while the light flashes, start this guide again.
If the engine ever shuts off by itself while you're driving, avoid driving the car until it's checked. Steering and braking take much more effort with the engine off.
result.why: Many cars blink the security light when they're off to show the immobilizer is armed and to discourage thieves. The light is designed to draw very little power. It only points to a problem when it stays on or flashes while you're trying to start or drive.

causes.name: Normal anti-theft indicator
causes.clues: The light blinks slowly with the car off and goes out when you start the engine.
causes.against: If the light stays on with the engine running, it's not just the normal indicator.

causes.name: Early sign of a key or immobilizer problem
causes.clues: Starting has needed a second try now and then.

you: Check the owner's manual section on the security or immobilizer indicator.
Watch whether the light goes out after the engine starts.
shop: Immobilizer code scan if the light stays on while running

result.title: A weak car battery may be confusing the anti-theft system
result.now: Check that the battery clamps are tight and clean, then try a jump start or a battery booster.
if: If the battery is swollen, cracked, leaking, hissing or smells of rotten eggs, don't jump-start it. Keep sparks away and call roadside assistance.
If it starts with a jump, have the battery and charging system tested soon so it doesn't happen again.
If it still won't start with good power and the security light keeps flashing, try your spare key next.
result.why: The immobilizer and the key reader need steady voltage to talk to each other. When the battery is low, the system can fail to read the key and block the start, so the security light flashes even though the key is fine.

causes.name: Weak or discharged car battery
causes.clues: Dim lights, a slow crank recently, cold weather, or a battery older than 4–5 years.
causes.against: If the headlights are bright and steady, the battery is probably not the issue.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery terminal
causes.clues: Crusty white or green buildup, or a clamp you can twist by hand.

causes.name: Key or immobilizer problem
causes.clues: The battery tests good but the light still flashes.

you: Check whether the headlights are bright or dim.
Look at the battery terminals for buildup or loose clamps.
Try a jump start or booster pack.
shop: Immobilizer code scan if it still won't start

result.title: The car may not be reading your key. Try the simple fixes first
result.now: Take other keys and key cards off the ring, then try again. For push-button start, hold the fob right against the Start button, or where your owner's manual shows, while you press Start.
if: If your spare key works, the main key or its fob battery is the likely problem.
If nothing works and you're stuck, call roadside assistance. A dealer or automotive locksmith can read the immobilizer and help with key problems.
If you smell raw fuel after several tries, stop cranking and keep sparks and flames away.
result.why: A flashing security light while the engine won't run usually means the immobilizer is blocking the start because it didn't get a valid signal from the key. Often the cause is simple: a weak fob battery, interference from other keys or cards, or the key not being where the reader expects it.

causes.name: Dead or weak key fob battery
causes.clues: The lock and unlock buttons only work up close, or the dash shows a "key not detected" message.

causes.name: Interference from other keys or cards
causes.clues: Another car's key, a building pass or a toll tag sits on the same ring.

causes.name: Damaged key or immobilizer fault
causes.clues: The key was dropped or got wet, or the spare doesn't work either.

you: Try the spare key.
Remove other keys and cards from the key ring.
Replace the key fob battery (usually a coin battery).

result.title: Your main key is the likely problem, often a weak fob battery
result.now: Use the spare for now and replace the battery in your main key fob.
if: If a fresh fob battery doesn't fix it, the chip inside the key may be damaged. A dealer or automotive locksmith can test it before programming a new key.
If you're down to one working key, get a replacement made soon. Losing your only key costs more and can strand you.
result.why: If the spare starts the car, the car's anti-theft system is probably working, and the fault is most likely in the main key: either the fob battery is too weak, or the small chip that identifies the key has been damaged.

causes.name: Weak key fob battery
causes.clues: The remote's range has been getting shorter, or a "key battery low" message has appeared.

causes.name: Damaged key chip (transponder)
causes.clues: The key was dropped, crushed or went through the wash.
causes.against: If a new fob battery fixes it, the chip is probably fine.

causes.name: Key lost its programming
causes.clues: It stopped working suddenly with no damage.

you: Replace the fob battery and try the main key again.
Check the key for cracks or water damage.

result.title: The anti-theft system may need to relearn your key after a battery problem
result.now: Check that the battery clamps are tight, then look up the security or immobilizer relearn steps in your owner's manual. Some cars need the key left in ON for several minutes until the security light stops flashing.
if: If the relearn steps work, have the battery and charging system tested soon.
If the light keeps flashing after the relearn and a good battery, a dealer or automotive locksmith can check it with a scan tool.
result.why: A dead battery, a jump start or a battery swap can briefly confuse the car's computers. Some models need a short relearn routine before they accept the key again. A loose clamp after battery work can also leave the system with too little voltage to read the key.

causes.name: Immobilizer needs a relearn after power loss
causes.clues: It started right after the battery was disconnected, replaced or jumped.

causes.name: Loose battery clamp or low voltage
causes.clues: Dim dash lights, or a clamp that moves when you twist it.

causes.name: Immobilizer module fault
causes.clues: The relearn steps don't help and both keys fail.

you: Check that both battery clamps are tight.
Follow the relearn steps in your owner's manual, if your car has them.
shop: Key relearn with a scan tool

result.title: The new key probably wasn't programmed to your car
result.now: Start the car with your original key if you have it, and have the new key programmed by a dealer or automotive locksmith.
if: If the original key also stopped working after the new one was added, the programming may have erased the old keys. Bring every key you have to the shop.
If you have no working key, the car will need a tow or a mobile locksmith.
result.why: A key can be cut to fit the lock and still not start the car. The chip inside must be registered with the car's immobilizer, which takes special equipment. Until then, the engine cranks or starts and dies while the security light flashes.

causes.name: New key not programmed
causes.clues: The key was recently cut or bought online.
causes.against: If the new key worked for a while first, programming is less likely the issue.

causes.name: Old keys erased during programming
causes.clues: Your original key stopped working at the same time.

causes.name: Wrong type of key chip
causes.clues: An aftermarket key that turns the lock but never started the car.

you: Try the original key.
Collect every key for the car before going to the shop.

result.title: A worn ignition reader or an add-on alarm may be blocking the start
result.now: Try both keys again while gently wiggling the key in the ignition. If it still won't start, call a mobile mechanic or have it towed to a shop.
if: If an add-on remote starter or alarm was installed recently, have the installer check it first.
If the key won't turn at all, don't force it. A broken key in the ignition makes the repair harder.
If the engine ever shuts off by itself while you're driving, avoid driving the car until it's checked. Steering and braking take much more effort with the engine off.
result.why: The ring around the ignition reads the chip in your key. If the ignition is worn or the reader is loose, it can lose the signal. Add-on remote starters and alarms tap into the same wiring and can block the start if they fail or were installed poorly.

causes.name: Faulty add-on remote starter or alarm
causes.clues: The problem began after it was installed, or its own light or beeps act strangely.

causes.name: Worn ignition or loose key reader ring
causes.clues: The key has been hard to turn, or wiggling it changes things.

causes.name: Worn key
causes.clues: The key's edges are badly worn or bent.

you: Try both keys.
Note whether the problem started after any add-on alarm or remote starter was fitted.
shop: Add-on alarm or remote starter wiring inspection

result.title: The anti-theft system itself may have a fault
result.now: Call a mobile mechanic or automotive locksmith, or have the car towed to a dealer or shop that can read immobilizer codes.
if: If the car starts after sitting for a while, don't count on it. Get it checked before you need it.
If you smell fuel after repeated tries, stop cranking and keep flames away.
If the engine ever shuts off by itself while you're driving, avoid driving the car until it's checked. Steering and braking take much more effort with the engine off.
result.why: When neither key works and the battery is strong, the problem is often in the immobilizer system: the key reader, the wiring, or the module that approves the key. These need a scan tool to diagnose, so repeated cranking won't help.

causes.name: Key reader or antenna fault
causes.clues: Both keys fail the same way, and the problem came on suddenly.

causes.name: Immobilizer or engine computer fault
causes.clues: Other warning lights also appear, or the problem comes and goes.

causes.name: Wiring or connector problem
causes.clues: It's intermittent, or recent work was done under the dash.

you: Note exactly how the security light behaves (fast flash, slow flash or steady). It helps the shop.
Check for open recalls using your VIN.

q_severity.q: How does the pedal feel, and how does the car stop?
q_severity.help: Try it parked with the engine running. A healthy pedal feels firm well before it gets near the floor.

opts.a: It goes to the floor or nearly, or the car barely slows down
The pedal is soft and the red BRAKE warning light is on
It slowly sinks toward the floor when I hold it down at a stop
It feels soft or spongy, but the car still stops normally
It went soft after the brakes got very hot, like on a long downhill or while towing
I'm not sure

q_stops.q: When you brake normally, does the car still stop as quickly as it used to?

opts.a: Yes, it stops fine
No, it takes longer to stop, or I have to push the pedal much further
I'm not sure

q_sink.q: With the engine off, check the brake fluid reservoir. What do you see?
q_sink.help: It's a see-through plastic tank near the back of the engine bay on the driver's side, with MIN and MAX marks. Don't open it, just look at the level from outside.

opts.a: The level is below MIN, or there's wet fluid around a wheel or under the car
The level is fine and there's no sign of a leak
I'm not sure / I can't check

q_when.q: Which of these fits best?
q_when.help: If you can, check the brake fluid reservoir too: a see-through tank near the back of the engine bay with MIN and MAX marks.

opts.a: It started right after brake work (new pads, rotors, calipers or fluid)
The brake fluid is below MIN, or there's wet fluid near a wheel
The brake fluid looks dark brown, or hasn't been changed in years
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: Your brakes may be losing pressure. Don't drive the car
result.now: Don't drive it. Park somewhere safe, set the parking brake, and have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If this happened while driving, the pedal may come back after a few pumps. Don't trust it.
If you see fluid under the car or at a wheel, tell the shop. A burst hose or rusted line is a common cause.
If the red BRAKE light is on, or you smell burning near a wheel, mention it to the shop or tow driver.
result.why: A pedal that goes to the floor usually means the hydraulic system can't build enough pressure, often because fluid is leaking out or a seal in the master cylinder has failed. Most cars split the brakes into two circuits, so you may still have some braking, but not enough to stop safely.

causes.name: Brake fluid leak from a hose, line or caliper
causes.clues: Wet fluid near a wheel or under the car, a low reservoir, or the red brake light.

causes.name: Failed master cylinder
causes.clues: No visible leak, the fluid level is fine, and the pedal sinks under steady pressure.

causes.name: A lot of air in the system
causes.clues: Recent brake work, or the reservoir ran dry.

you: From outside the car, look for wet fluid underneath and on the inside of each wheel.
shop: Pressure check of each brake circuit

result.title: Brake fluid may be leaking or low. Don't drive it yet
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If the level is only near MIN, there are no wet spots and the pedal feels firm, worn brake pads may be what lowered the level. Still have the brakes inspected before driving.
Not seeing a leak doesn't prove the brakes are safe. Fluid can leak inside the master cylinder, or somewhere you can't see from outside.
Don't just top it up and keep using the car. Fluid that leaks once will usually leak again, and the pedal can fail suddenly.
result.why: Brakes work by pushing fluid through lines to each wheel. If fluid is escaping or the level is low, air can get in and the pedal goes soft, and the red brake light often comes on as the level drops. A leak can get worse without warning, so it needs fixing before the car is driven.

causes.name: Leaking brake hose or rusted steel brake line
causes.clues: A wet spot along the line under the car, or an older car from a salted-road area.

causes.name: Leaking caliper or wheel cylinder
causes.clues: Wet, oily fluid on the inside of a tire or wheel.

causes.name: Leaking master cylinder
causes.clues: Fluid at the back of the engine bay, below the reservoir.

causes.name: Worn brake pads
causes.clues: The level dropped slowly over months with no wet spots.
causes.against: Pad wear lowers the level but doesn't make the pedal soft by itself.

you: With the engine off, check the reservoir level.
Look for wet, oily fluid inside each wheel and under the car.

result.title: A worn seal, often in the master cylinder, may be letting fluid slip past
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic check it.
if: If the pedal only sinks a little and then stays firm, it may be less serious, but a technician still needs to rule out a failing master cylinder before the car is driven.
If you find a leak or low fluid, tell the shop.
If the red BRAKE light comes on or the pedal reaches the floor, don't try to move the car. Have it towed.
result.why: When you hold steady pressure and the pedal slowly creeps toward the floor with no outside leak, a common cause is fluid slipping past worn seals inside the master cylinder. A shop will usually test the master cylinder and look for leaks before replacing anything. It tends to get worse and can fail when you need to stop hard.

causes.name: Worn master cylinder seals
causes.clues: No visible leak, and the fluid level stays steady.

causes.name: Slow external leak
causes.clues: The fluid level is slowly dropping, or there are damp spots at a wheel or along a line.

causes.name: Leak inside the ABS unit
causes.clues: The ABS light is on.
causes.against: Much less common than a master cylinder problem.

you: Check the reservoir level and look for damp spots under the car and inside the wheels.

result.title: Your brakes may have overheated (brake fade)
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, set the parking brake and let the brakes cool for at least 30 minutes. Braking may take much more force, or may not work well, until they cool. Don't rely on these brakes again until the pedal is firm and the fluid has been checked.
if: If the pedal is still soft once the brakes have cooled, don't drive it. The fluid may have boiled or there's another fault. Have it towed.
If the pedal is firm again after cooling, call a shop or roadside assistance and describe what happened before going any further. Boiled fluid can fade again sooner the next time.
If you see smoke from a wheel or smell burning, keep everyone back from that wheel until it cools.
On long downhills, shift to a lower gear so the engine helps slow the car, instead of riding the brakes.
result.why: Hard, repeated braking makes brakes very hot. Brake fluid absorbs moisture over the years, which lowers its boiling point, and boiling fluid forms bubbles that make the pedal soft. The pedal often comes back once things cool, but that doesn't prove the system is healthy. A shop will usually test the fluid for moisture and check the pads and rotors before deciding what needs replacing.

causes.name: Boiled brake fluid
causes.clues: The pedal went soft after a long downhill or towing, and the fluid is old.

causes.name: Overheated pads
causes.clues: The pedal stays firm but the car slows less, with a burning smell.

causes.name: Dragging brake adding heat
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter than the others.

you: Note whether the pedal firms up after the brakes cool.
Check the fluid color. Dark brown fluid is old.
shop: Brake fluid boiling point or moisture test

result.title: Air may have been left in the brake lines during the repair
result.now: Call the shop that did the work before driving further. Tell them the pedal feels soft and ask them to check it, either by coming to you or arranging a tow. Braking may take much more force than usual.
if: If the pedal sinks further, goes near the floor, or you have to pump it to stop, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If you see wet fluid at a wheel that was worked on, or the red BRAKE light comes on, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If a caliper or hose was replaced, ask them to check that every connection is tight and dry.
result.why: Any time the brake system is opened, air can get trapped in the lines. Air squeezes where fluid doesn't, so the pedal feels spongy. Bleeding the brakes properly pushes the air out.

causes.name: Air in the brake lines
causes.clues: The pedal was soft right after the work and firms up when pumped.

causes.name: Loose fitting or bleeder screw
causes.clues: Wet fluid at a wheel that was worked on.

causes.name: Caliper pistons not pumped back out
causes.clues: The pedal went low on the first press after new pads, then firmed up after a few pumps.
causes.against: If it stays firm after a few pumps and never goes soft again, this may have been the cause, but mention it to the shop anyway.

you: Look for wet fluid at the wheels that were worked on.
Note whether pumping the pedal makes it firmer.

result.title: Old brake fluid that has absorbed moisture can make the pedal feel soft
result.now: If the pedal sinks, goes near the floor or the red BRAKE light is on, stop driving and have it towed. Otherwise have the brakes inspected and the fluid tested before driving any distance, and avoid heavy braking.
if: If the pedal gets softer, starts to sink, or goes near the floor, stop driving and have it towed.
If the fluid level is below MIN, or the red BRAKE light comes on, don't drive it until it's inspected. Old fluid doesn't explain a low level.
If the fluid hasn't been changed in years, have the whole brake system inspected at the same time.
result.why: Brake fluid slowly absorbs water from the air. That lowers its boiling point, so small vapor bubbles can form when the brakes get hot, which feels soft or spongy. Old fluid is a possibility to test, not a confirmed cause, so a shop will usually check for air, leaks and master cylinder wear as well. Most manufacturers list a fluid change interval in the maintenance schedule.

causes.name: Old fluid holding moisture
causes.clues: Dark fluid, or no record of it ever being changed.

causes.name: Small amount of air in the system
causes.clues: The pedal firms up when pumped.

causes.name: Aging rubber brake hoses swelling
causes.clues: An older car, with the pedal softest under hard braking.

you: Look at the fluid color in the reservoir.
Check your service records for the last brake fluid change.

result.title: Possibly air in the system or a brake part starting to wear. Get it checked first
result.now: Get the brakes inspected before driving further. Braking may take much more force than you expect. If you can't get it checked where it is, have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to look at it.
if: If the pedal sinks, goes near the floor, or the red brake light comes on, don't try to move the car. Have it towed.
If the fluid level is below MIN, or you couldn't check it, treat it as a possible leak. Not seeing a leak doesn't prove the brakes are safe.
If the pedal gets firmer after pumping it twice, tell the shop. That can point to air or a rear brake adjustment problem.
result.why: A pedal that feels soft but still stops the car often means something in the hydraulic system is giving a little: air bubbles, swelling hoses, or rear drum brakes that need adjusting. These tend to get worse, sometimes suddenly, and a slow leak or a wearing master cylinder can feel the same at first.

causes.name: Air in the brake lines
causes.clues: The pedal firms up when pumped.

causes.name: Rear drum brakes out of adjustment
causes.clues: An older car or truck with rear drums, and the parking brake needs many clicks.

causes.name: Aging rubber brake hoses
causes.clues: An older car, with the pedal softest under hard braking.

causes.name: Master cylinder starting to wear
causes.clues: The pedal also creeps down slowly at a stop.

you: Check the brake fluid level and color.
Note whether pumping the pedal makes it firmer.

result.title: A soft pedal needs a brake check before it gets worse
result.now: Get the brakes inspected before driving further. Braking may take much more force than you expect. If you can't get it checked where it is, have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to look at it.
if: If the pedal goes near the floor, sinks at a stop, or the red brake light comes on, don't try to move the car. Have it towed.
If the fluid reservoir is below MIN, don't drive it.
Not seeing a leak doesn't prove the brakes are safe.
result.why: Without knowing how the car is stopping, the safe assumption is that a soft pedal means a problem in the hydraulic system. Many causes can be found in a brake inspection, and catching them early helps prevent a sudden failure.

causes.name: Air or moisture in the brake fluid
causes.clues: The pedal firms up when pumped, or the fluid is old.

causes.name: Small fluid leak
causes.clues: The fluid level is dropping, or there are damp spots at a wheel.

causes.name: Wearing master cylinder
causes.clues: The pedal creeps down at a stop.

you: Check the brake fluid level.
Look for wet spots inside the wheels and under the car.

q_when.q: Which of these fits the squeak best?
q_when.help: Bushings are rubber cushions where suspension parts bolt to the car. A ball joint is a pivot joint that lets the wheel steer and move up and down.

opts.a: It squeaks over bumps and the steering feels loose, wanders, or there's a clunk too
It squeaks over bumps and also when I turn the steering wheel
Mostly in cold weather, and it fades once the car warms up
It sounds like it's inside the car, from the dash, seats or trim
Just a squeak or creak over bumps and speed bumps
I'm not sure

q_push.q: With the car parked, push down hard on each corner a few times. What happens?
q_push.help: Push on the fender right above each wheel and let go. A helper can listen near the wheel while you push.

opts.a: It squeaks when I push on one corner
It keeps bouncing more than once or twice after I let go
No squeak when parked, only when driving over bumps or uneven driveways
I'm not sure

q_steering.q: When you turn the steering wheel, what do you notice?

opts.a: A creak or groan mainly when turning slowly, like when parking
The steering feels loose, the car wanders, or there's a knock
Nothing besides the squeak
I'm not sure

result.title: A worn ball joint or steering joint is possible. Get it checked before driving
result.now: Avoid driving until the front suspension and steering have been inspected. Have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to check it where it's parked. If you weren't sure what you noticed, an inspection is still the safest next step.
if: If the steering suddenly gets much looser, a wheel looks tilted, or the clunking gets louder, don't move the car. Have it towed.
If the shop finds only worn bushings or links, it becomes a lower-priority repair.
result.why: A squeak that comes with loose steering, wandering or clunks can point to a worn joint in the suspension or steering. A ball joint that wears too far can separate, which can let the wheel collapse and cause loss of control. A shop will usually check each joint for play with the wheels off the ground before replacing anything.

causes.name: Worn ball joint
causes.clues: Squeaking or creaking over bumps and in turns, clunks, and uneven tire wear.

causes.name: Worn tie rod end
causes.clues: Loose or vague steering, or the car wanders on the highway.

causes.name: Worn control arm bushing
causes.clues: A clunk when braking or going over bumps, with the steering feeling a bit off.

you: Look at the front tires for uneven wear on the inner or outer edge.
Note whether the noise is louder on one side.
shop: Ball joint and tie rod play check with the wheels off the ground

result.title: Often a worn strut mount or a dry joint in the front suspension
result.now: Book a suspension check when convenient. Tell the shop it squeaks over bumps and when turning.
if: If the steering feels loose, wanders, or you hear clunks from the front, avoid driving until it's inspected. Have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to check it.
If the steering starts to feel notchy or sticky, get it checked within a few days.
If the noise started right after suspension work, call the shop that did the work. A part may not be tightened or seated correctly.
result.why: The top of each front strut sits in a mount with a bearing that turns when you steer. When that bearing or its rubber wears, it can creak over bumps and while turning. A dry ball joint or sway bar bushing can make a similar sound.

causes.name: Worn strut mount or mount bearing
causes.clues: Creaking or groaning when turning at low speed, and over bumps, from the top of the wheel area.

causes.name: Dry or worn sway bar bushing
causes.clues: Squeaks over bumps and while turning, worse in cold weather.

causes.name: Ball joint starting to wear
causes.clues: The squeak comes from low on the wheel, or the tires are wearing unevenly.
causes.against: Less likely if the steering feels tight and normal.

you: With the car stopped, turn the steering wheel lock to lock and listen near the top of each front wheel.
shop: Ball joint and tie rod check
Sway bar bushing and link inspection

result.title: Cold, stiff rubber bushings are a common cause
result.now: Note whether the squeak goes away after the car has been driven for a while. If it does, mention it at your next service so the bushings can be inspected.
if: If the squeak starts happening when warm too, or you hear clunks, book a suspension check.
If the steering feels loose, wanders, or you hear clunks from the front, avoid driving until it's inspected. Have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to check it.
result.why: Rubber bushings get stiff in the cold and can squeak against metal until they warm up and flex more easily. This is common, but a squeak alone can't show whether a bushing or a joint is worn, so it's worth having a technician look at your next service.

causes.name: Dry or hardened sway bar bushings
causes.clues: A squeak over bumps and while turning, worst on cold mornings.

causes.name: Aging control arm bushings
causes.clues: An older car, or bushings with visible cracks.

you: Compare the noise on a cold morning with after a 20-minute drive.
Look behind the front wheels for cracked or split rubber where the bar meets the frame.
shop: Sway bar and control arm bushing inspection

result.title: Often a dry or worn bushing at that corner
result.now: Book a suspension inspection when convenient and tell the shop which corner squeaks.
if: If you also hear clunks, get it checked within a few days.
If the steering feels loose, wanders, or you hear clunks from the front, avoid driving until it's inspected. Have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to check it.
If a tire on that corner shows uneven wear, ask for an alignment check too.
result.why: A squeak you can make by pushing on one corner comes from a part that moves as the suspension compresses. Rubber bushings are a common source, since they dry out, crack and start rubbing with age.

causes.name: Dry or worn control arm or sway bar bushing
causes.clues: A rubbery squeak or creak, worse in cold or dry weather.

causes.name: Worn shock or strut
causes.clues: The car bounces more than usual, or there's oily residue on the shock.

causes.name: Dry ball joint
causes.clues: The squeak comes from low on the wheel, near the bottom of the knuckle.

you: Have a helper push on the corner while you listen closely near the wheel to pinpoint the spot.
Look for cracked or torn rubber around the suspension arms.

result.title: The shocks or struts may be worn
result.now: Book a shock and strut inspection. Worn shocks make the car bounce more and can lengthen stopping distance.
if: If you see oil running down a shock, or the car dips hard when braking or sways a lot in turns, get it checked within a few days.
If one corner sits lower than the others, a spring may be broken. Avoid driving until it's checked, since a broken spring can damage a tire or affect steering.
If the steering feels loose, wanders, or you hear clunks from the front, avoid driving until it's inspected. Have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to check it.
result.why: Shocks and struts keep the car from bouncing after a bump. When they wear out, the car keeps moving up and down, and their mounts and bushings often start to squeak. Worn shocks also make it harder to keep the tires on the road during a sudden stop or swerve.

causes.name: Worn shocks or struts
causes.clues: More than one or two bounces after pushing down, a floaty ride, or nose-diving when braking.

causes.name: Worn shock or strut mounts
causes.clues: Squeaks or clunks from the top of the shock over bumps.

causes.name: Broken or sagging spring
causes.clues: One corner sits lower, or there's a clunk over bumps.

you: Look for oily residue on the shocks behind each wheel.
Park on level ground and check whether one corner sits lower than the others.
shop: Shock and strut inspection for leaks and damping

result.title: A sway bar link or bushing is a common cause
result.now: Book a suspension check when convenient. Mention it squeaks over uneven bumps, like angled driveways.
if: If the squeak turns into a clunk or rattle over bumps, get it checked within a few days. A link may be loose or broken.
If the car leans much more than usual in turns, have it checked soon.
If the steering feels loose, wanders, or you hear clunks from the front, avoid driving until it's inspected. Have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to check it.
result.why: The sway bar connects the left and right sides of the suspension to reduce body lean. Its rubber bushings and small end links work hardest when one wheel moves more than the other, which is why they often squeak over uneven bumps but not when you push straight down.

causes.name: Dry or worn sway bar bushings
causes.clues: A squeak over uneven bumps, worse in cold weather.

causes.name: Worn sway bar end links
causes.clues: A squeak that becomes a clunk or rattle over rough roads.

causes.name: Control arm bushing
causes.clues: A squeak or creak over all bumps, not just uneven ones.

you: Drive slowly over an angled driveway or speed bump and note which side the noise comes from.
shop: Sway bar bushing and end link inspection

result.title: It may be a trim, seat or dash squeak, not the suspension
result.now: Have a passenger listen while you drive over bumps to pinpoint where it comes from. Press on the suspected panel or seat to see if the noise stops.
if: If the noise seems to come from under the car or near a wheel, book a suspension check.
If it's a seat or seat belt part that's loose, have it checked soon. Seats and belts need to stay firmly mounted.
If a wheel looks tilted, the car pulls hard, or the steering suddenly changes, don't drive it.
result.why: Bumps flex the car's body slightly, and plastic panels, seat frames and loose items can squeak against each other. These noises often sound like they come from the suspension but are inside the cabin.

causes.name: Dash or door trim rubbing
causes.clues: The noise stops when you press on a panel, or changes with temperature.

causes.name: Seat frame or seat track
causes.clues: The noise changes when someone sits in or shifts in the seat.

causes.name: Loose items or the trunk area
causes.clues: The noise goes away after emptying the trunk or glovebox.

you: Empty the trunk, door pockets and glovebox, then retest.
Press on panels and seats while driving over bumps (with a passenger doing it, not the driver).
shop: Road test with a technician to locate the noise

result.title: Often a worn suspension bushing, but an inspection is the way to confirm it
result.now: Book a suspension inspection when convenient and describe when the squeak happens.
if: If the steering feels loose, wanders, or you hear clunks from the front, avoid driving until it's inspected. Have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to check it.
If a wheel looks tilted, the car pulls hard, or the steering suddenly changes, don't drive it.
result.why: Squeaks over bumps often come from rubber bushings or joints that have dried out or worn. Many aren't urgent, but a technician can rule out the joints that affect steering.

causes.name: Dry or worn bushings
causes.clues: A rubbery squeak, worse in cold weather.

causes.name: Worn shocks or mounts
causes.clues: A bouncy ride or squeaks from the top of the wheel area.

causes.name: Worn ball joint
causes.clues: Squeaks along with clunks or uneven tire wear.

you: Record a short video with sound while a helper pushes down on each corner.
shop: Suspension and steering inspection on a lift

q_other_signs.q: Along with the squeal, is any of this happening?
q_other_signs.help: The drive belt (often called the serpentine belt) is the long ribbed rubber belt on the front or side of the engine. On many cars it turns the alternator, power steering pump and water pump.

opts.a: The temperature gauge is climbing, or the steering suddenly got heavy
The battery warning light is on, or the lights are dimming
A slapping or flapping sound, or the belt looks frayed or has pieces missing
No, it's just the squeal
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When does the squeal happen?

opts.a: For a few seconds on a cold start, then it goes quiet
When I turn the steering wheel, especially at full lock or while parking
When the A/C or defroster turns on
When I rev the engine or accelerate hard
All the time: a steady squeal, chirp or squeak while the engine runs
Only in wet weather or after driving through puddles
I'm not sure

result.title: The drive belt may have broken or come off
result.now: Pull over safely and turn the engine off. Have the car towed, or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you see steam or the gauge is in the red, don't open the radiator cap. Hot coolant can burn you.
If the belt is still in place but the engine overheated, tell the shop. The water pump or cooling system may also need checking.
If you smell burning rubber or see smoke from under the hood, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: On many engines the same belt drives the water pump and power steering. If it slips badly or comes off, the engine can overheat within minutes and steering gets very heavy. Driving on can cause serious engine damage.

causes.name: Broken or thrown drive belt
causes.clues: The squeal stopped suddenly, then the gauge rose or steering got heavy.

causes.name: Failed tensioner or pulley
causes.clues: A rattle or grinding came before the belt failed.

causes.name: Seized water pump or accessory
causes.clues: A loud squeal that never let up before the belt failed.

you: With the engine off and cooled down, look at whether the belt is still on its pulleys.
shop: Accessory bearing check (water pump, alternator, power steering pump)
Cooling system pressure test if it overheated

result.title: The belt may be slipping on the alternator, so the battery may not be charging
result.now: Get it checked within a day. Keep driving to a minimum, turn off accessories like the heated seats and radio, and watch the temperature gauge.
if: If the temperature gauge rises or the steering gets heavy, pull over and turn the engine off. The belt may have come off.
If the lights keep dimming or the dash flickers, the car could die on the road. Don't drive it; have it towed.
If you smell burning rubber or see smoke from under the hood, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: The alternator recharges the battery, and it's turned by the drive belt. A squeal plus the battery light often means the belt is slipping or the alternator is struggling. If so, the car is running on battery power, which won't last long. A shop will usually test charging output and the belt tension before replacing the alternator.

causes.name: Worn or loose drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal that's been getting worse, and a shiny or cracked belt.

causes.name: Weak belt tensioner
causes.clues: The tensioner arm bounces or shakes while the engine idles.

causes.name: Failing alternator
causes.clues: A whining or grinding from the alternator, or the battery light comes and goes.

you: With the engine off, look for cracks, shiny glazing or fraying on the belt.
Have the battery and alternator tested. Many parts stores do this free.

result.title: The belt may be coming apart, or a pulley may be failing
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off. Have the car towed, or have a mobile mechanic inspect and repair it where it's parked.
if: If a piece of belt is missing, ask the shop to check that it didn't get caught behind a pulley or cover.
If you smell burning rubber or see smoke, keep the engine off and stay clear of the engine bay until it cools.
result.why: A frayed or slapping belt can come off at any moment, taking out charging, power steering and often cooling at once. A loose strand can also wrap around other parts and damage them.

causes.name: Worn-out belt
causes.clues: Cracks across the ribs, missing chunks or loose threads.

causes.name: Misaligned or wobbling pulley
causes.clues: The belt edge is chewed up on one side.

causes.name: Failing tensioner
causes.clues: The tensioner arm jumps around, letting the belt flap.

you: With the engine off, look at the belt from above for missing pieces or fraying.

result.title: The belt may be worn or a bit loose, and slipping until it warms up
result.now: Book a belt and tensioner check when convenient. Mention that it only happens on cold starts.
if: If the squeal lasts longer, gets louder, or the battery light flickers, get it checked soon.
If you see cracks or missing pieces on the belt, have it checked before your next long trip.
If the temperature gauge climbs or the steering suddenly gets heavy, pull over and turn the engine off. The belt may have slipped off, and it often drives the water pump and power steering.
result.why: A cold, stiff belt grips less, and the alternator works hardest right after startup to recharge the battery. If the belt is worn or the tensioner is weak, it slips for a few seconds and squeals. It usually gets worse over time.

causes.name: Worn or glazed drive belt
causes.clues: The belt is several years old, looks shiny on the ribs, or has cracks.

causes.name: Weak automatic tensioner
causes.clues: A new belt still squeals, or the tensioner arm wobbles.

causes.name: Battery that needs a lot of recharging
causes.clues: The car cranks slowly in the morning.

you: With the engine off, look at the belt for cracks, shine or fraying.
Notice whether the squeal is worse on colder or damp mornings.
shop: Water spray test to tell slipping from pulley misalignment

result.title: The power steering may be loading up a slipping belt, or the fluid may be low
result.now: With the engine off, check the power steering fluid level if your car has a reservoir, and book a check when convenient.
if: If the fluid is low, top it up with the type in your owner's manual and look for a leak. Have the leak checked soon, since low fluid means it's going somewhere.
If the steering suddenly gets heavy while driving, slow down, pull over and turn the engine off. Steering takes much more effort without assist.
If the squeal turns into a constant whine or groan, get it checked soon.
If you see fluid dripping onto hot engine or exhaust parts, or smell burning, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off. Leaking fluid on hot parts is a fire risk.
If your car has electric power steering (no fluid reservoir), the noise likely isn't the steering pump. Have the belt and suspension checked.
result.why: A hydraulic power steering pump is usually turned by the drive belt. Turning the wheel, especially all the way to one side, makes the pump work hardest. A worn belt or low fluid can make it squeal at that moment.

causes.name: Worn or loose drive belt
causes.clues: The squeal happens mostly at full lock, and the belt is old.

causes.name: Low power steering fluid
causes.clues: The reservoir is below the mark, or there's reddish or amber fluid under the front of the car.

causes.name: Failing power steering pump
causes.clues: A whine or groan along with the squeal, even with full fluid.

you: Check the power steering fluid level with the engine off.
Avoid holding the wheel all the way to one side for more than a few seconds.
shop: Power steering fluid and leak check

result.title: The belt may be slipping when the A/C compressor kicks on
result.now: Book a belt and A/C check when convenient. Mention that the squeal starts when the A/C or defroster turns on.
if: If the squeal becomes a grinding or rattling noise with the A/C on, stop using the A/C and get it checked soon.
If you smell burning rubber with the A/C on, turn the A/C off. If the smell continues or you see smoke, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the temperature gauge climbs or the steering suddenly gets heavy, pull over and turn the engine off. The belt may have slipped off, and it often drives the water pump and power steering.
result.why: When the A/C compressor engages, it adds a sudden load to the belt. A worn belt or weak tensioner can slip for a moment and squeal. The defroster often runs the A/C too, which is why it can happen in winter.

causes.name: Worn belt or weak tensioner
causes.clues: A short squeal right as the A/C clicks on.

causes.name: A/C compressor clutch or bearing problem
causes.clues: A grinding or constant noise from the compressor with the A/C on.

causes.name: A/C compressor starting to seize
causes.clues: The squeal is long and loud every time, and the A/C isn't cooling well.

you: Turn the A/C on and off while parked and listen for the squeal to start and stop.
With the engine off, look at the belt for wear.
shop: A/C compressor clutch and bearing check

result.title: The belt may be slipping under load
result.now: Book a belt and tensioner check within the next couple of weeks.
if: If the battery light comes on, get it checked right away.
If the temperature gauge climbs or the steering suddenly gets heavy, pull over and turn the engine off. The belt may have slipped off, and it often drives the water pump and power steering.
If you see cracks or missing pieces, have the belt checked before any long trip.
result.why: Revving the engine makes the belt speed up quickly, and accessories resist that change. A belt that's worn, stretched or not held tight enough slips briefly and squeals.

causes.name: Worn or stretched belt
causes.clues: The belt is old, shiny or cracked.

causes.name: Weak tensioner
causes.clues: The tensioner arm jumps when you rev the engine.

causes.name: Oil or coolant on the belt
causes.clues: Wet spots or residue near the belt, or a leak at the front of the engine.

you: With the engine off, look for cracks, shine or oily residue on the belt.

result.title: A pulley, tensioner or accessory bearing may be wearing out
result.now: Get it checked within a few days. Keep trips short until then.
if: If the noise turns into a grinding or rattling, or the battery light or temperature gauge changes, stop driving and have it towed.
If the noise is a regular chirp rather than a squeal, a misaligned pulley is possible. Still get it checked soon.
If you smell burning rubber or see smoke from under the hood, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: A squeal or chirp that never stops usually isn't just a cold belt. A pulley or bearing that's starting to drag, or a pulley that's out of line, makes the belt squeal constantly. If that bearing seizes, the belt can come off.

causes.name: Worn idler or tensioner pulley bearing
causes.clues: A squeal or growl that's steady at idle.

causes.name: Misaligned pulley
causes.clues: A regular chirp, and one edge of the belt is worn.

causes.name: Failing accessory bearing (alternator, water pump, A/C)
causes.clues: The noise is loudest near one part of the engine.

you: With the engine off, look for uneven wear on one edge of the belt.
Look under the car for coolant drips near the front of the engine.
shop: Engine-running stethoscope check of each pulley

result.title: Water on the belt may be making it slip for a moment
result.now: If it clears up within a few minutes once the belt dries, it's often just water on the belt. Keep an ear on it and mention it at your next service.
if: If it squeals for more than a few minutes, or also on dry days, book a belt check.
If the battery light comes on, get it checked soon.
If the temperature gauge climbs or the steering suddenly gets heavy, pull over and turn the engine off. The belt may have slipped off, and it often drives the water pump and power steering.
result.why: Water reduces the grip between the belt and pulleys, so it can slip and squeal briefly after rain or puddles. A belt in good shape usually goes quiet once it dries. A worn belt gets noisier in wet weather first.

causes.name: Water splashed on the belt
causes.clues: Only after puddles or heavy rain, and it stops once dry.

causes.name: Worn belt that slips easily
causes.clues: The belt is old, and the squeal is getting longer each time.

you: Notice how long the squeal lasts.
With the engine off, check the belt for cracks or shine.
shop: Belt and tensioner inspection if it continues

result.title: Often a drive belt that needs a check
result.now: Book a belt and tensioner check when convenient. Note when the squeal happens so you can tell the shop.
if: If the battery light comes on, the temperature gauge climbs, or the steering gets heavy, stop driving and have it checked right away.
If you smell burning rubber or see smoke from under the hood, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Many squeals from under the hood come from the drive belt slipping or a pulley wearing out. An inspection can usually pinpoint which part is making the noise.

causes.name: Worn or loose drive belt
causes.clues: The belt is old or looks shiny or cracked.

causes.name: Weak tensioner or worn pulley
causes.clues: The squeal is steady, or a new belt didn't fix it.

causes.name: Power steering or A/C load
causes.clues: It happens when turning or with the A/C on.

you: Record a short video with sound when it happens. It helps the shop.

q_other_signs.q: Along with the squeal, is any of this happening?
q_other_signs.help: These signs tell us whether this is more than a noise. Pick the most serious one that fits.

opts.a: The pedal feels soft or sinks, the car takes longer to stop, or the red brake light is on
A burning smell, smoke, or one wheel is much hotter than the others after driving
There's also a grinding or metal-scraping sound
The car pulls to one side when I brake
No, it's just the squeal
I'm not sure

q_when.q: When do you hear the squeal?

opts.a: Only on the first few stops in the morning, or after rain or a car wash, then it goes away
Almost every time I brake, and it's been getting more frequent
A steady squeal or chirp while driving, even when I'm not braking
Only when I brake lightly; firm stops are quiet
Mostly when backing up or creeping along at very low speed
It started right after new brakes were put on
I'm not sure

q_pad_age.q: When were the brake pads last replaced?
q_pad_age.help: Check your service records or the last shop invoice. Pads usually last a few years, but city driving and heavy loads wear them faster.

opts.a: Recently, within the last year or so
It's been a while, or not since I've owned the car
I'm not sure

result.title: The brakes may not be stopping the car properly
result.now: Don't drive it. Park it somewhere safe and have it towed, or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you're on the road now, slow down gently, use a lower gear if you can, and pull over somewhere safe.
If the brake fluid reservoir under the hood is low or there's a wet spot near a wheel, mention that to the shop. It points to a leak.
result.why: A squeal by itself is usually a wear warning. A soft or sinking pedal, longer stops or the red brake light usually mean the braking system itself has a problem, such as low fluid, a leak or badly worn parts. That's a safety risk, not just a noise.

causes.name: Brake fluid leak or low fluid
causes.clues: A soft or sinking pedal, the red brake light, or a damp spot near a wheel or on the ground.

causes.name: Pads worn down to metal
causes.clues: The squeal has been there a while, and now stopping takes more effort.

causes.name: Air in the brake lines or a failing master cylinder
causes.clues: A spongy pedal that slowly sinks while you hold it at a stop.
causes.against: Less likely if the pedal feels firm and the only change is noise.

you: With the engine off, look at the brake fluid reservoir level. Don't open it if the engine is hot.
Look for wet spots on the inside of the wheels or under the car.
shop: Brake system inspection, including pad thickness and rotors
Master cylinder and brake line test

result.title: A brake may be sticking and dragging on one wheel
result.now: Pull over safely and let the wheel cool down. Don't touch it. Have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic check it before using it again.
if: If you see smoke or flames, get everyone out and away from the car and call for help.
If the parking brake was left partly on, release it fully and let the brakes cool. Have them checked before relying on them. Overheated brakes can fade, and the fluid may need testing.
result.why: A brake that stays partly applied keeps rubbing, which creates heat, noise and a burning smell. The heat can damage the brake and wheel bearing and make the brakes fade when you need them.

causes.name: Sticking caliper or caliper slide pins
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter or dustier than the others, and the car may pull to that side.

causes.name: Parking brake not fully releasing
causes.clues: The heat is at a rear wheel, or the parking brake lever or button feels odd.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose
causes.clues: The brake releases slowly, and the problem comes and goes.

you: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.
Notice which wheel smells or feels hotter from a distance. Don't touch it.
shop: Wheel temperature comparison after a test drive
Brake hose and parking brake check

result.title: The pads may be worn down to metal
result.now: Get the brakes inspected before driving further. If the pads are down to metal, braking may take more force and can get worse quickly. Have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to check it where it's parked.
if: If the pedal feels soft, the car pulls, or stops take longer, don't try to move the car. Have it towed.

If the noise only happened on the first stops after rain and then went away, it may have been surface rust. Our grinding-brakes guide covers that, but have the pads looked at before relying on the brakes.
result.why: Squealing that turns into grinding often means the pad material is nearly or fully gone and metal is touching the rotor. That reduces braking and can quickly damage the rotor. A shop will measure the pads and rotors to see what's actually needed.

causes.name: Brake pads worn through
causes.clues: The squeal came first, then grinding started. It happens on most stops.
