causes.against: Less likely if the pads were replaced recently.

causes.name: Stone or debris caught in the brake
causes.clues: A sudden scraping sound after driving on gravel.

causes.name: Rusted or damaged rotor
causes.clues: The car sat for a long time, or you feel a pulse in the pedal.

you: Look through the wheel spokes at the brake pads. If you see very little pad left against the rotor, tell the shop.
Notice whether the noise happens on every stop or only some.

result.title: One side may be braking harder than the other
result.now: Get the brakes checked in the next day or two, and keep driving to a minimum until then. Leave extra stopping room and avoid hard stops where you can.
if: If the pull is strong, gets worse, or comes with a burning smell, stop driving and have it towed.
If you see wet fluid near one wheel, or the pedal feels soft, don't drive it. A leaking caliper or hose can cause a pull.
If the pull only happens when you're not braking, it's more likely tire pressure or alignment.
result.why: A squeal plus a pull to one side often means one brake isn't working the same as the other. A sticking caliper or contaminated pads on one side can do this, and it can make the car harder to control in a hard stop.

causes.name: Sticking caliper or slide pins
causes.clues: One wheel gets hotter or dustier than the other.

causes.name: Uneven pad wear or contaminated pads
causes.clues: Oil or brake fluid near one wheel, or one side was serviced and the other wasn't.

causes.name: Tire or alignment problem
causes.clues: The car also drifts when you're not braking, or one tire looks low.
causes.against: Less likely if it only pulls while braking.

you: Check the tire pressures on both sides.
Notice whether it pulls only when braking or all the time.
shop: Pad and rotor wear comparison side to side

result.title: Often a thin layer of surface rust on the rotors
result.now: If the squeal fades within the first few stops, it's often just surface rust. Brake gently for the first few stops and listen for whether it clears.
if: If the squeal stays after the first few miles, or starts happening on every stop, have the brakes checked.
If you hear grinding, not just squealing, have the brakes inspected soon.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the car takes longer to stop, the red brake light comes on, or you smell burning from a wheel, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: Brake rotors are bare iron, so moisture leaves a light film of rust overnight or after rain. The first few stops scrape it off, which can squeal or squeak briefly. This is common and usually clears up quickly.

causes.name: Light surface rust from moisture
causes.clues: Happens after the car sits overnight, after rain or a wash, and goes away quickly.
causes.against: If it lasts all day, something else is going on.

causes.name: Moisture on the pads
causes.clues: Worse in humid or damp weather.

you: Notice whether the squeal is gone after the first few stops.
If the car sits for weeks at a time, drive it more often or have the rotors looked at for heavy rust.
shop: Rotor inspection if the noise doesn't clear

result.title: The brake pad wear indicator may be telling you the pads are low
result.now: Book a brake inspection within the next week. Ask the shop to measure the pads and the rotors so you know what's actually needed.
if: If the squeal turns into grinding, get the brakes inspected before driving further. That can mean metal is touching metal.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the car takes longer to stop, the red brake light comes on, or you smell burning from a wheel, stop driving and have it towed.
If the car pulls to one side when braking, get it checked within a day or two.
result.why: Many brake pads have a small metal tab that scrapes the rotor when the pad gets thin, making a high-pitched squeal on purpose. It's a built-in reminder. Acting now usually means just pads; waiting can mean rotors too.

causes.name: Pad wear indicator touching the rotor
causes.clues: A high-pitched squeal that's become steady, and the pads haven't been changed in a while.
causes.against: Less likely if the pads are nearly new.

causes.name: Worn or glazed pads
causes.clues: The brakes feel a little less grabby than before.

causes.name: Stone or bent dust shield rubbing
causes.clues: A scraping squeal that started suddenly, even when you're not braking.

you: Look through the wheel spokes at the pad thickness on the brake caliper.
Check your records for when the pads were last replaced.
shop: Pad thickness measurement on all wheels

result.title: Often pad vibration, from missing shims, lube or glazed pads
result.now: Book a brake check when convenient. Ask the shop to look at the pad shims, clips and lubrication, not just pad thickness.
if: If the squeal gets louder, becomes constant, or turns into grinding, get it checked soon.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the car takes longer to stop, the red brake light comes on, or you smell burning from a wheel, stop driving and have it towed.
If the pads were just replaced, call the shop that did the work first.
result.why: Brake squeal is often a high-frequency vibration between the pad and rotor. Light braking is where it shows up most. Worn shims, dry contact points, glazed pads or certain pad materials can cause it even when there's plenty of pad left.

causes.name: Missing, worn or dry shims and contact points
causes.clues: Squeals on light stops, quiet on firm ones, and the pads aren't worn.

causes.name: Glazed pads or rotors
causes.clues: Hard braking down hills or a stuck brake in the past. The rotor may look shiny.

causes.name: Pad material
causes.clues: Some harder pads are naturally noisier, especially when cold.

you: Notice whether light or firm braking makes the noise.
Check whether one wheel seems to be the source by listening with a window down at low speed.

result.title: Low-speed squeak is often normal pad noise
result.now: Look through the wheels to make sure the pads aren't thin, and keep an ear on it. If it doesn't change, mention it at your next service.
if: If the noise starts happening at normal speeds or gets louder, book a brake check.
If you also hear grinding, have the brakes inspected soon.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the car takes longer to stop, the red brake light comes on, or you smell burning from a wheel, stop driving and have it towed.
result.why: Many pads squeak a little when you're barely moving, especially when reversing or creeping in traffic. The pads can shift slightly when you change direction, and some pad materials are just noisier at low speed.

causes.name: Normal pad noise at low speed
causes.clues: Only when backing up or creeping, and braking feels normal.

causes.name: Pads shifting when the car changes direction
causes.clues: A single click or squeak right after you switch from Reverse to Drive.

causes.name: Early pad wear
causes.clues: The pads haven't been replaced in a long time.

you: Look at pad thickness through the wheel spokes.
Notice if it only happens in Reverse.
shop: Brake inspection at your next service

result.title: New brakes may need breaking in, or something may need adjusting
result.now: Give the new brakes a few days of normal driving to bed in. If the squeal is still there, call the shop that did the work and have them recheck it.
if: If the pedal feels soft or different, the car pulls, or you hear grinding, don't drive it. Call the shop that did the work and have them check it or arrange a tow.
If you see wet fluid at a wheel, or the red brake light comes on, don't drive it.
If the noise started after old shims or clips were reused, ask the shop to check those.
result.why: New pads need some normal stops to bed into the rotor and can squeak at first. If the noise continues, common reasons are missing shims or lube, pads that don't suit the rotors, or old rotors that weren't replaced or resurfaced.

causes.name: Pads still bedding in
causes.clues: The brakes are only a few days old and the noise is fading.

causes.name: Missing shims, clips or lubricant
causes.clues: The noise is constant and isn't fading.

causes.name: Old rotors not replaced or resurfaced
causes.clues: Only the pads were changed.

you: Check the invoice to see whether rotors and hardware were replaced.
Notice whether the noise is getting better or worse.
shop: Recheck of pad fit, shims and clips

result.title: Have the brakes inspected to find the source
result.now: Book a brake inspection when convenient. Note when the squeal happens so you can tell the shop.
if: If the pedal feels soft, the car takes longer to stop, or you hear grinding, stop driving and have it towed.
If you smell burning from a wheel or the car pulls when braking, stop driving and have it checked.
If it gets louder or more frequent, move the appointment up.
result.why: Brake squeal has several common causes, from harmless moisture to worn pads. When it's hard to say when it happens, a look at the pads and rotors usually narrows it down.

causes.name: Pad wear indicator
causes.clues: The pads haven't been replaced in a while.

causes.name: Pad vibration or glazing
causes.clues: Squeals on some stops but not others.

causes.name: Surface rust
causes.clues: Mostly in the morning or after rain.

you: Record a short video with sound when it happens. It helps the shop.
Look at pad thickness through the wheel spokes.

opts.a: It also stalls while I'm driving, not just after starting
It runs for only 1 to 3 seconds, then shuts off cleanly
It idles rough or sputters for a while, then dies
I'm not sure

q_security.q: Is a key, lock or car-with-a-padlock light flashing on the dash when it dies?
q_security.help: This is the anti-theft (immobilizer) light. It's often near the speedometer or clock. Some cars show a message like "Key not recognized" instead.

opts.a: Yes, a key or security light is flashing or on
No security light
I'm not sure
I smell raw fuel, or see a wet spot under the car
The fuel gauge is low, or it started right after filling up
It keeps running if I hold the gas pedal down a little
The battery was just replaced or disconnected
The check engine light is on
None of these / I'm not sure
It only happens on cold mornings, and it's fine once warm
A hissing sound, or the idle surges up and down
It dies when I shift into gear or turn on the A/C
It keeps running if I hold the gas pedal down a little
I'm not sure

result.title: Stalling while driving is a safety problem. Don't drive it until it's fixed
result.now: Park it and have it towed to a shop, or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If a warning light came on before it stalled, write down which one. It helps the shop.
If it restarts after cooling down, still don't rely on it. Parts that fail when hot often get worse.
If you smell raw fuel, stop trying to start it and keep sparks and flames away.
result.why: When the engine dies on the road, power steering and brake assist go with it, making the car much harder to steer and stop. The same fault that kills it at startup is now happening at speed.

causes.name: Failing fuel pump or fuel pump relay
causes.clues: Sputtering or loss of power before it died.

causes.name: Failing crankshaft position sensor
causes.clues: It cuts out suddenly, often when hot, and restarts once cool.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control fault
causes.clues: It dies mostly when slowing down or stopping.

you: Note when it stalls: at speed, when slowing, or when hot.
Note any warning lights.

result.title: The anti-theft system may be shutting the engine off
result.now: Try your spare key. For push-button start, hold the key fob right against the Start button, or put it where your owner's manual says, while you press Start.
if: If the spare works, try a new battery in your main key or fob, or have the key checked.
If neither key works, a dealer or locksmith with the right equipment may need to check or reprogram the key.
result.why: Many cars let the engine fire for a second or two and then cut fuel if they don't recognize the key. A flashing key or security light right when it dies is a strong clue.

causes.name: Weak key fob battery
causes.clues: The remote's range has been getting shorter.

causes.name: Damaged or unprogrammed key
causes.clues: A new copy, or a key that was dropped or got wet.
causes.against: If the spare key does the same thing, the key itself is less likely.

causes.name: Immobilizer system fault
causes.clues: Neither key works.

you: Try the spare key.
Replace the key fob battery.

result.title: Possible fuel leak. Stop trying to start it
result.now: Don't try to start it again. Keep sparks and flames away and have the car towed.
if: If fuel is dripping or pooling, move people away from the car and call the fire department.
result.why: A raw fuel smell or wet spot often means fuel is getting somewhere it shouldn't. A leak can also drop fuel pressure, which makes the engine die, and fuel near hot parts is a fire risk.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line or fitting
causes.clues: A wet spot under the car along the fuel line route.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector seal or fuel rail
causes.clues: The smell is strongest at the engine.

causes.name: Flooded engine from repeated tries
causes.clues: Lots of short start attempts, and no visible leak.

you: From a distance, look for drips or wet spots under the car.
Don't smoke or use flames nearby.

result.title: It may not be getting enough fuel, or the fuel may be bad
result.now: If the tank is low, add several gallons and try again. If it started right after a fill-up, note where you bought the fuel and book a check.
if: If it still starts and dies with plenty of fuel, the fuel pump or filter may be weak. Have it checked before driving any distance.
If it started after filling up and the car has a diesel engine, make sure diesel, not gasoline, went in. If the wrong fuel went in, don't start it again and have it towed.
If it stalls while driving, including when slowing down or coming to a stop, don't drive it until it's checked. Steering and braking get much heavier when the engine dies.
If you smell raw fuel, stop trying to start it and keep sparks and flames away.
result.why: An engine can start on the fuel already in the lines and then die when the supply can't keep up. A nearly empty tank, a weak pump or water or the wrong fuel in the tank can all do this.

causes.name: Very low fuel
causes.clues: The gauge is near empty, especially on a slope.

causes.name: Weak fuel pump or clogged fuel filter
causes.clues: Hesitation or loss of power when accelerating in recent weeks.

causes.name: Water or the wrong fuel in the tank
causes.clues: It began right after a fill-up.

you: Add fuel.
With the car quiet, turn the key to ON and listen for a 2-second hum from the back.
shop: Fuel sample check for water or contamination

result.title: The engine may not be getting enough air to idle on its own
result.now: Book a check soon. If you need to restart it, a light foot on the gas for a few seconds may help it settle, but don't rely on that if it's dying at stops.
if: If it stalls while driving, including when slowing down or coming to a stop, don't drive it until it's checked. Steering and braking get much heavier when the engine dies.
If the check engine light comes on, have the codes read.
If you smell raw fuel, stop trying to start it and keep sparks and flames away.
result.why: When a little gas pedal keeps it running, the engine may need more air at idle than it's getting. Carbon buildup in the throttle body or a sticking idle control part are common reasons, and a shop will usually check the codes and idle data before cleaning or replacing parts.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body
causes.clues: Higher mileage, and the idle has been low or uneven.

causes.name: Faulty idle air control valve (older cars)
causes.clues: The idle speed is erratic or too low.

causes.name: Mass airflow sensor reading wrong
causes.clues: Poor fuel economy, hesitation, or a check engine light.

you: Note whether it's worse cold or hot.
Check that the air filter isn't clogged.

result.title: The engine computer may need to relearn its idle
result.now: Start the car and let it idle with everything off (A/C, lights, radio) for about 10 minutes. Check your owner's manual for an idle relearn procedure.
if: If it still won't stay running after that, a shop can run the idle relearn with a scan tool.
If the battery terminals were disturbed, make sure both clamps are tight.
If it stalls while driving, including when slowing down or coming to a stop, don't drive it until it's checked. Steering and braking get much heavier when the engine dies.
result.why: On many cars, disconnecting the battery erases the learned idle settings. Until the computer relearns them, the engine may start and then stumble or die.

causes.name: Lost idle settings after battery work
causes.clues: It started happening right after the battery was replaced or disconnected.

causes.name: Loose battery clamp
causes.clues: A clamp you can turn by hand.

you: Check that both battery clamps are tight.
Let it idle with accessories off.
shop: Idle relearn with a scan tool

result.title: A sensor or engine fault is possible. The stored code is the best clue
result.now: Have the trouble codes read. Many parts stores do this free, or book a shop check soon.
if: If the check engine light is flashing, don't drive it. That usually signals a serious misfire that can damage the catalytic converter.
If it stalls while driving, including when slowing down or coming to a stop, don't drive it until it's checked. Steering and braking get much heavier when the engine dies.
If you smell raw fuel, stop trying to start it and keep sparks and flames away.
result.why: The engine computer relies on sensors to set fuel and air at startup. If one reads wrong, the engine can fire up and then die, and the computer often stores a code that points a shop toward what to test.

causes.name: Mass airflow sensor fault
causes.clues: Hesitation or poor fuel economy.

causes.name: Crankshaft or camshaft position sensor
causes.clues: Stalling that's worse when the engine is hot.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: A hissing sound or a lean-condition code.

you: Get the codes read and write them down.
shop: Code scan and live sensor data

result.title: Cold-start stalling often points to idle control or a sensor reading wrong
result.now: Let it idle for 30 seconds before driving off on cold mornings, and book a check when convenient.
if: If it starts stalling when warm too, or the check engine light comes on, get it checked sooner.
If it stalls while driving, including when slowing down or coming to a stop, don't drive it until it's checked. Steering and braking get much heavier when the engine dies.
result.why: A cold engine needs extra fuel and a higher idle. If the coolant temperature sensor gives the computer the wrong reading, or the idle system is dirty, the engine can die until it warms up.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control fault
causes.clues: A low, uneven idle.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: The temperature gauge acts oddly, or fuel economy has dropped.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or a rough idle that smooths out when warm.

you: Note the outside temperature when it happens.
Listen for hissing from the engine bay.
shop: Code scan and live sensor data

result.title: A vacuum leak may be letting in extra air
result.now: Book a check when convenient. Mention the hissing or surging idle so the shop can test for leaks.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing, stop driving it.
If it stalls while driving, including when slowing down or coming to a stop, don't drive it until it's checked. Steering and braking get much heavier when the engine dies.
If a hose has visibly popped off, a shop can often fix it quickly.
result.why: The engine computer measures the air coming in and adds fuel to match. A cracked hose or leaking gasket lets in air it doesn't know about, so the mixture runs too lean to idle and the engine surges or dies.

causes.name: Cracked or disconnected vacuum hose
causes.clues: A hissing sound from the engine bay.

causes.name: Leaking intake gasket or air intake boot
causes.clues: A rough idle, sometimes with a lean code.

causes.name: Faulty PCV valve or hose
causes.clues: A whistle or hiss near the top of the engine.

you: With the engine running and parked, listen for hissing.
Look for hoses that are cracked or off.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim data

result.title: The idle may be too low to handle extra load
result.now: Book an inspection soon. Until it's checked, keep your foot lightly on the gas when you shift into gear.
if: If it stalls while driving, including when slowing down or coming to a stop, don't drive it until it's checked. Steering and braking get much heavier when the engine dies.
If you smell raw fuel, stop trying to start it and keep sparks and flames away.
result.why: Shifting into gear or turning on the A/C adds load to the engine. If the idle control can't raise engine speed to match, the engine stumbles and dies.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body or idle control fault
causes.clues: The idle drops noticeably when the A/C kicks on.

causes.name: Vacuum leak
causes.clues: Hissing, or a rough idle.

causes.name: Torque converter clutch not releasing (automatic)
causes.clues: It stalls when coming to a stop, like stalling a manual car.

you: Notice whether the A/C makes the stall more likely.

result.title: It needs a quick shop diagnosis to pin down
result.now: Have the trouble codes read, then book a check. Until then, avoid relying on the car for important trips.
if: If it stalls while driving, including when slowing down or coming to a stop, don't drive it until it's checked. Steering and braking get much heavier when the engine dies.
If you smell raw fuel, stop trying to start it and keep sparks and flames away.
result.why: Starting and then dying means the battery and starter are doing their job, but fuel, air or the security system isn't keeping the engine running. A few quick tests usually separate these.

causes.name: Idle control or throttle body problem
causes.clues: A low or uneven idle.

causes.name: Fuel delivery problem
causes.clues: Hesitation or sputtering when driving.

causes.name: Security system cutting the engine
causes.clues: A key or lock light on the dash.

you: Record a short video with sound of it starting and dying.
Note any dash lights that come on.

steam-from-under-hood.title: Steam or smoke from under the hood

q_danger.q: Do you see either of these right now?
q_danger.help: The temperature gauge usually has a C (cold) and H (hot) or a thermometer symbol. Some cars only have a red or blue thermometer warning light instead of a gauge.

opts.a: Flames, or dark smoke that keeps getting thicker
The temperature gauge is in the red, or a red temperature warning light is on
Neither of these: the gauge looks normal
I'm not sure

q_smell.help: Stand a few steps back from the front of the car. Don't put your face near the engine.

opts.a: Sweet, a bit like syrup or maple
Burning oil, sharp and heavy
Burning rubber or melting plastic
No real smell, just light white wisps
I'm not sure

q_coolant.q: When you look (from a safe distance), what do you see?
q_coolant.help: Coolant (antifreeze) is usually green, orange, pink, blue or yellow and feels slimy. The overflow tank is the see-through plastic bottle with MIN and MAX marks.

opts.a: Coolant spraying or pouring out, or a big puddle forming fast
Coolant bubbling or boiling out of the overflow tank
A slow drip, or a wet or crusty spot on a hose or the radiator
I can't see where it's coming from / I'm not sure

q_when.q: When did you notice it?

opts.a: After rain, a car wash, or driving through puddles or snow, and it faded within a few minutes
Within a few days after an oil change or other engine work
It's actually from the tailpipe on a cold morning, not the hood
It keeps coming every time I drive, even in dry weather
I'm not sure

result.title: This could be an engine fire starting. Get away from the car
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn off the engine, get everyone out and at least 100 feet away, and call 911. Don't open the hood and don't go back for belongings.
if: If the smoke stops on its own, still don't restart the car. Have it towed and inspected before anyone drives it.
result.why: Flames or thick, darkening smoke mean something is burning, not just steam. Opening the hood lets in a rush of air that can make a fire flare up suddenly, and fuel lines and tires can burn quickly.

causes.name: Fuel leaking onto hot engine or exhaust parts
causes.clues: A strong gasoline smell before or with the smoke.

causes.name: Electrical short or melting wiring
causes.clues: A burning plastic smell, fuses blowing, or lights and gauges acting up beforehand.

causes.name: Oil or other fluid burning on the exhaust
causes.clues: A recent oil leak or engine work, and a heavy burning oil smell.

shop: Fire damage inspection of wiring, fuel lines and hoses

result.title: The engine is overheating. Stop now to avoid serious damage
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe, turn off the engine and let it cool for at least 30 minutes. Don't open the radiator cap. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you're in a dangerous spot and need a moment to reach a safe place, turn the heater to full hot with the fan on high. It pulls some heat away from the engine.
If the coolant tank is empty once the engine is cool, there's a leak or another fault behind it. Topping it up doesn't fix the cause, so still have it checked before relying on the car.
If you think it may be smoke rather than steam, or you see flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
result.why: Steam with the gauge in the red means the engine is running far hotter than it's designed to. Keeping it running can warp the cylinder head or blow the head gasket, turning a simple repair into a major one.

causes.name: Coolant leak (hose, radiator or water pump)
causes.clues: A sweet smell, coolant under the car, or a low overflow tank.

causes.name: Radiator fan not working
causes.clues: It overheated in traffic or at idle but was fine on the highway.
causes.against: If it overheated at highway speed, the fan is a less likely cause.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck closed
causes.clues: The gauge climbed quickly after a normal start, with no visible leak.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: Coolant keeps disappearing with no leak, white smoke from the tailpipe, or bubbles in the coolant tank.

you: Once fully cool, check the coolant level in the overflow tank.
Look under the front of the car for a coolant puddle.
shop: Radiator fan and fan circuit test
Combustion gas (block) test for a head gasket leak

result.title: A coolant hose, the radiator or the water pump may be leaking badly
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn off the engine and stay back while it cools. Don't restart it. Have the car towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If the temperature gauge was already climbing before you stopped, mention it to the shop so they check for heat damage too.
If you think it may be smoke rather than steam, or you see flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
result.why: When coolant is pouring out, the engine will lose most of it within minutes and overheat quickly. Running it even a short distance this way can cause serious engine damage.

causes.name: Burst or split coolant hose
causes.clues: Coolant spraying from a rubber hose near the top or front of the engine.

causes.name: Cracked radiator or radiator seam
causes.clues: Coolant pouring from behind the front grille.

causes.name: Failed water pump
causes.clues: Coolant pouring from the front of the engine, near the drive belt.

you: From a safe distance, note where the coolant is coming from.
shop: Visual inspection of hoses, radiator and water pump

result.title: Coolant boiling over usually means the engine is overheating
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn off the engine and let it cool for at least 30 minutes without opening any caps. Then have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the gauge reads normal, don't trust it. When coolant is low, the sensor can read low even though the engine is very hot.
If you see bubbles in the tank with the engine running and fully warm, tell the shop. That can be a sign of a head gasket leak.
result.why: Coolant boiling out of the overflow tank means it's getting hotter than the system can handle. That happens when coolant is low, flow is blocked, the cap isn't holding pressure, or exhaust gases are leaking into the coolant.

causes.name: Low coolant from a leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, drips under the car, or the tank has been low before.

causes.name: Faulty radiator or tank cap
causes.clues: Coolant seeps from around the cap, but there's no other leak.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck or fan not working
causes.clues: It happened in traffic or soon after a normal start.

causes.name: Head gasket leak
causes.clues: Coolant keeps disappearing, white smoke from the tailpipe, or constant bubbling in the tank.

you: Once fully cool, check the coolant level.
Look for drips under the front of the car.

result.title: Coolant may be leaking onto hot engine parts
result.now: Don't drive until you've checked the coolant level with the engine fully cool. If it's between MIN and MAX, top it up with the type listed in your owner's manual and get the leak checked within a few days. If the tank is empty or well below MIN, have it inspected before driving.
if: If the level drops noticeably between checks, or the temperature gauge rises above its usual spot, stop driving and have it towed.
If the gauge reaches the red, a temperature warning light comes on, or the heater suddenly blows cold, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the steam gets heavier or keeps pouring out, stop and let the engine cool before going any further.
If you also see white smoke from the tailpipe with a sweet smell, get it checked right away. That can mean coolant is leaking inside the engine.
result.why: A sweet smell or steam with a normal temperature gauge often comes from a small amount of coolant dripping or seeping onto hot parts and steaming off. Leaks tend to grow, and running low on coolant will make the engine overheat. When coolant is very low, the gauge can also read normal even though the engine is hot, so the level check matters more than the gauge.

causes.name: Leaking hose or loose hose clamp
causes.clues: A wet or crusty spot where a rubber hose connects.

causes.name: Leaking radiator
causes.clues: Drips or crusty colored residue at the front of the car.

causes.name: Water pump seal leak
causes.clues: Drips or residue near the drive belt at the front of the engine.

causes.name: Heater core leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell inside the car, foggy windows, or a damp passenger-side floor.
causes.against: Steam from under the hood alone points more to the engine bay than the heater core.

you: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold, and note it each day.
Look for colored drips under the front of the car after it's parked overnight.
Watch the temperature gauge on every drive.

result.title: Oil may be dripping onto the hot exhaust
result.now: Pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and let it cool. Oil on a hot exhaust can catch fire. Once it's cool, check the oil level. If the oil is low, you can see a leak, or the smoke comes back when you drive, don't drive it any further: have it checked or towed.
if: If it started right after an oil change, a little spilled oil can smoke for a drive or two. If it continues, ask the shop that did the work to check the oil filter, drain plug and filler cap.
If the oil level is below the minimum mark, or you see oil dripping steadily, don't drive until it's been checked.
If the oil pressure warning light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and turn it off right away.
If the smoke gets thick or you see flames, get out, move away and call 911.
result.why: Oil smoking on the exhaust gives off a heavy, sharp burning smell and bluish-white smoke. Common causes are a leaking gasket or a loose part, but oil on hot parts is a fire risk and the engine can run low on oil.

causes.name: Leaking valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Oily residue along the top edge of the engine.

causes.name: Spill or loose part from a recent oil change
causes.clues: It started right after a service, and the oil filter or filler cap area is wet.

causes.name: Other engine oil leak
causes.clues: Brown or black drops under the car.

you: Check the oil level on the dipstick with the engine off and cool.
Make sure the oil filler cap is on tight.
Look for wet, oily areas on top of and under the engine.
shop: Oil leak inspection (sometimes with UV dye)
Oil filter and drain plug check

result.title: Something may be melting or a belt may be burning. Don't keep running it
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn off the engine and don't restart it. Once it's cool, look for anything stuck to the exhaust. Have the car towed if you can't find a simple cause.
if: If you find a plastic bag or debris melted onto the exhaust and nothing else looks damaged, have a mechanic confirm it's clear before you rely on the car.
If the smell is coming from one wheel instead of the hood, a brake may be dragging. Don't drive on it.
If you see flames or the smoke gets thicker, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
result.why: Burning rubber or plastic smells mean something that shouldn't be getting hot is. A belt slipping on a seized pulley, melting wiring, or debris on the exhaust can each start a fire if you keep going.

causes.name: Drive belt slipping on a seized pulley or A/C compressor
causes.clues: A squeal before the smell, or the smell is strongest at the front of the engine.

causes.name: Electrical short or melting wiring
causes.clues: A sharp plastic smell, blown fuses, or electrical items acting up.

causes.name: Plastic bag or road debris on the exhaust
causes.clues: It started right after driving over something.

you: Once cool, look under the car at the exhaust for melted plastic.
Check that the drive belt is in place and not shredded.

result.title: This could be water steaming off hot engine parts
result.now: Watch it for a few minutes. If the steam fades, has no smell and the temperature gauge stays in its normal spot, water burning off is the likely explanation. Check the coolant level the next time the engine is cold.
if: If it keeps steaming after 10 to 15 minutes of driving in dry weather, check the coolant level once the engine is cool.
If you notice a sweet smell, or the coolant level is below MIN, treat it as a coolant leak and get it checked.
If the gauge climbs toward the red or a temperature warning light comes on, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the smoke turns dark, smells burnt or gets thicker, stop and get away from the car.
result.why: Rain, a car wash or splashing through puddles leaves water on the hot engine and exhaust. It turns to light, odorless white steam that disappears quickly. That's common and usually stops on its own once things dry out.

causes.name: Rain or wash water evaporating
causes.clues: It happened after wet weather or washing, faded quickly, and had no smell.
causes.against: A sweet or burning smell points to something else.

causes.name: Small coolant seep
causes.clues: It keeps happening in dry weather, or the coolant tank drops over time.

you: Watch the temperature gauge.
Check the coolant level when the engine is cold.
shop: Cooling system pressure test if the steam keeps coming back

result.title: White vapor from the tailpipe on a cold morning is usually normal
result.now: Watch whether the vapor fades once the engine is fully warmed up, usually within 10 to 15 minutes of driving.
if: If thick white smoke continues after the engine is warm, especially with a sweet smell, get it checked before relying on the car. Coolant may be leaking inside the engine.
If the coolant level keeps dropping with no leak you can find, ask the shop to test for a head gasket leak.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward the red or a temperature warning light comes on, pull over and turn off the engine.
result.why: Burning fuel makes water vapor. When the engine and exhaust are cold, that vapor condenses into white clouds out of the tailpipe. Once things warm up, it should become hard to see.

causes.name: Normal condensation
causes.clues: Cold or damp weather, thin vapor that fades as the engine warms, no smell.
causes.against: Thick smoke that keeps going after warm-up is not normal.

causes.name: Coolant burning inside the engine (head gasket)
causes.clues: Thick white smoke after warm-up, a sweet smell, and a coolant level that keeps dropping.

you: Note whether the vapor stops once the car is fully warm.
Check the coolant level once a week for a few weeks.

result.title: Treat it as overheating until you know it isn't
result.now: Pull over when it's safe, turn off the engine and wait at least 30 minutes before opening the hood. Don't open the radiator cap.
if: If you see flames or the smoke grows, get everyone away and call 911.
If, once cool, the coolant and oil levels are full, there are no leaks and nothing smells burnt, it may have been water steaming off. Have a mechanic confirm before you rely on the car.
result.why: Without knowing the temperature reading or the smell, it's hard to rule out overheating, and driving an overheating engine can ruin it quickly. Stopping costs a few minutes; guessing wrong can cost the engine.

causes.name: Engine overheating
causes.clues: The gauge climbs, the heater blows cold, or there's a sweet smell.

causes.name: Coolant or oil leaking onto hot parts
causes.clues: A sweet or burning oil smell.

causes.name: Water evaporating
causes.clues: Recent rain or a car wash, and it faded quickly with no smell.

you: Once cool, check the coolant and oil levels.
Look under the car for fresh drips.
shop: Code scan for temperature sensor data

q_how.q: How did the steering become hard to turn?

opts.a: Suddenly, while I was driving or right after starting
Gradually over days or weeks, mostly when parking or at low speed
It's stiff for the first few minutes on cold mornings, then gets easier
It catches, sticks or binds at certain points as I turn
I'm not sure

q_sudden_signs.q: Did anything else happen at the same time?

opts.a: The engine stalled or shut off
A loud squeal or slap from the engine, or the battery light came on
A steering wheel warning light or a 'power steering' message came on
Nothing else I noticed
I'm not sure

q_fluid.q: With the engine off, check the power steering fluid reservoir under the hood. What do you find?
q_fluid.help: The reservoir is usually a small plastic tank with a cap marked with a steering wheel symbol. Many newer cars have electric power steering with no fluid at all; your owner's manual will say.

opts.a: The fluid is low, or there's fluid leaking under the front of the car
The fluid looks full
My car doesn't have a reservoir (electric power steering)
I'm not sure
A whine or groan when I turn the wheel, louder at full lock
The front tires look low or soft
A creak, pop or clunk when I turn, especially over bumps
None of these, it's just heavier than it used to be
I'm not sure

q_warning.q: Is a steering wheel warning light or a power steering message showing on the dash?
q_warning.help: It often looks like a steering wheel with an exclamation mark, and may be yellow or red.

opts.a: Yes
No
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine stopping cut your power steering. The stall is likely the main problem
result.now: Get the car somewhere safe and don't use it until the stalling is diagnosed. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If it restarts and the steering feels normal again, the stall is the more likely cause, but have both checked. The stalling alone makes the car unsafe in traffic.
If it won't restart, follow our car won't start guide while you wait for help.
result.why: Power steering only works while the engine is running (or, on electric systems, while the car is fully on). When the engine dies, steering and brakes both get much heavier. Fixing the stall fixes the steering.

causes.name: Engine stalling from a fuel, sensor or idle problem
causes.clues: Sputtering, rough idle or a check engine light before it died.

causes.name: Charging system failure
causes.clues: The battery light came on or lights dimmed before it stalled.

causes.name: Broken accessory belt
causes.clues: A squeal or slap from the engine, and the temperature gauge rising.

you: Note any warning lights that were on before the stall.
Check whether the belt at the front of the engine is still in place (engine off, keys out).

result.title: The accessory belt may have slipped off or broken
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn off the engine and don't run it again until the belt is checked. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the temperature gauge was rising, the belt may drive the water pump too. Running the engine could overheat it badly.
If the belt is in place but badly glazed or cracked and squealing, it may be slipping. Have it checked before the car is used; a shop will usually check the tensioner and pulleys at the same time.
If you smell burning rubber or see smoke from the front of the engine, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn it off and step away from the car.
result.why: On many cars one belt drives the power steering pump, the alternator and often the water pump. When it breaks, you lose steering assist, the battery stops charging, and the engine can overheat within minutes.

causes.name: Broken or thrown accessory (serpentine) belt
causes.clues: A loud slap or squeal, then heavy steering and a battery light.

causes.name: Failed belt tensioner or seized pulley
causes.clues: A squeal or chirp in the days before, or a pulley that wobbles.

causes.name: Seized power steering pump or other accessory
causes.clues: A grinding noise before the belt failed.

you: With the engine off and keys out, look at the front of the engine for a missing or loose belt.
shop: Accessory spin check for a seized component
Charging system and cooling system check after repair

result.title: The electric power steering system may have shut off its assist
result.now: Once you're safely parked, turn the car off for a minute and restart. If the warning stays on or the steering is still heavy, have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the warning clears after a restart and steering feels normal, don't assume it's fixed. Have the stored fault code read before relying on the car.
If the battery light is also on, low voltage may be shutting the steering off. The charging system needs checking.
If the assist drops out again while you're driving, grip the wheel firmly, slow down gradually and pull over when it's safe.
result.why: Electric power steering uses a motor to help you turn. When it detects a fault or low voltage, it shuts the assist off, and the wheel suddenly takes much more effort. It can come back and fail again without warning.

causes.name: Low battery voltage or charging problem
causes.clues: A battery light, dim lights, or a recent dead battery.

causes.name: Steering sensor or control module fault
causes.clues: The warning comes and goes, and steering feels normal when the light is off.

causes.name: Failed steering assist motor
causes.clues: The warning stays on and the steering stays heavy after restarting.

you: Note exactly which warning lights came on.
Ask a dealer for your brand whether a steering-assist recall is open on your VIN.
shop: Steering assist motor and sensor tests

result.title: Low power steering fluid from a leak is a possible cause
result.now: Don't use the car until the leak has been looked at. Topping up with the fluid type in your owner's manual may bring the assist back for a while, but a leak big enough to drop the assist suddenly can do it again. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see fluid spraying, smell burning fluid or see smoke from under the hood, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn off the engine and step away from the car.
If the pump whines loudly even after topping up, it may already be damaged. Tell the shop.
If the steering ever binds or catches as you turn, keep the car parked.
result.why: The power steering pump needs fluid to create pressure. When the level drops, assist fades, and running the pump low can damage it. Topping up can buy time, but a leak usually comes back, and power steering fluid dripping onto hot engine parts can burn.

causes.name: Leaking power steering hose
causes.clues: Wet, oily hoses near the pump or along the front of the engine.

causes.name: Leaking steering rack seals
causes.clues: Fluid inside the rubber boots at the ends of the steering rack, or drips behind the front wheels.

causes.name: Leaking pump seal
causes.clues: Fluid around the pump at the front of the engine.

you: Check the fluid level with the engine off.
Put cardboard under the front of the car overnight to see where it drips.

result.title: The power steering pump, belt or steering rack may not be providing assist
result.now: Don't use the car until it's diagnosed. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the belt at the front of the engine is missing or loose, the belt is the more likely cause. Tell the shop what you saw.
If the steering also binds or catches, it may be a more serious steering fault. Keep the car parked.
result.why: If the fluid is full but the assist suddenly disappeared, the pump may not be making pressure or the rack may not be using it. Steering usually still works, but it takes much more effort, which is dangerous in an emergency move.

causes.name: Failed power steering pump
causes.clues: A whine or groan in recent weeks, or foamy fluid.

causes.name: Slipping or broken belt
causes.clues: A squeal, or the belt looks loose, glazed or missing.

causes.name: Internal steering rack failure
causes.clues: Steering is heavier in one direction than the other.

you: With the engine off and keys out, look at the belt at the front of the engine.

result.title: Sudden loss of power steering needs checking before you rely on the car
result.now: Keep the car parked and have it towed or call a mobile mechanic to find the cause.
if: If the temperature gauge rose or the battery light came on, a broken belt is a strong possibility. Don't run the engine.
If a restart brings the steering back to normal, still have the fault diagnosed. It may happen again.
result.why: When steering assist drops out suddenly, the cause is usually a failure, not wear, and it can happen again at a bad moment. Without assist, quick steering moves take much more strength.

causes.name: Electric power steering fault or low voltage
causes.clues: A steering or battery warning light.

causes.name: Broken or slipping belt
causes.clues: A squeal, or the battery light came on too.

causes.name: Low fluid or failed pump (hydraulic systems)
causes.clues: Whining when turning, or fluid under the front of the car.

you: Note any warning lights.
Look under the front of the car for fresh fluid.

result.title: A whining pump often means low fluid or a pump that's wearing out
result.now: Check the power steering fluid level with the engine off. If it's low, top it up with the type in your owner's manual and have the system checked within a few days. If the reservoir is empty, have it inspected before driving.
if: If the fluid was low, there may be a leak. Ask the shop to find it before the pump is damaged.
If the steering suddenly gets much heavier, binds, or a steering warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If you see fluid spraying or smell burning fluid, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn off the engine and step away from the car.
result.why: A whine or groan when turning often means the pump is struggling, sometimes because it's drawing in air from low fluid. Left alone, it can wear out the pump and leave you with no assist.

causes.name: Low power steering fluid
causes.clues: Fluid below the minimum mark, or drips under the front of the car.

causes.name: Worn power steering pump
causes.clues: The whine stays even with the fluid full.

causes.name: Slipping belt
causes.clues: A squeal on cold starts or when turning at full lock.

you: Check the fluid level and color. Dark or foamy fluid is a bad sign.
Look under the front of the car for drips.

result.title: Low front tire pressure can make steering feel heavy
result.now: Check the tire pressures when cold and set them to the numbers on the driver's door jamb sticker.
if: If a tire keeps losing air, have it repaired soon.
If steering is still heavy with correct pressures, have the steering system checked.
If the steering suddenly becomes much heavier, binds, or a steering warning light comes on, stop driving and have it checked before going further.
result.why: Underinflated tires put more rubber on the road, which makes the wheel harder to turn, especially when parking. Pressure is quick to check, but it may not be the only cause.

causes.name: Low tire pressure
causes.clues: The tires look soft or the tire pressure light is on.

causes.name: Wider or different tires than original
causes.clues: New tires or wheels were fitted recently.

causes.name: Wheel alignment out of spec
causes.clues: Uneven tire wear, or the car pulls to one side.

you: Check and set all four tire pressures.
shop: Power steering system check if the problem stays

result.title: Worn or dry steering and suspension joints may be making it stiff
result.now: Have the front suspension and steering inspected within the next few days.
if: If you hear a loud clunk and the steering suddenly feels loose or different, stop driving it and have it towed. A failing ball joint can let a wheel collapse.
If the noise only happens on cold mornings and goes away, it may be strut mounts. Still have it checked.
If the steering binds, sticks at certain points or doesn't return to center, keep the car parked until it's inspected.
result.why: Ball joints, tie rod ends and strut mounts let the wheels turn smoothly. When they wear out or lose their grease, they can bind and creak, which makes steering feel stiff and can lead to a part failing. A shop will usually check for play in each joint before deciding which part needs work.

causes.name: Worn or dry ball joints
causes.clues: Creaking when turning or going over bumps, and uneven tire wear.

causes.name: Worn strut mounts or bearings
causes.clues: A pop or clunk when turning the wheel while parked.

causes.name: Worn tie rod ends
causes.clues: Loose or wandering steering on the highway.

you: Turn the wheel slowly while parked with the window down and listen for where the noise comes from.
shop: Ball joint and tie rod play check

result.title: Wear in the power steering system or front end is a possible cause
result.now: Check the tire pressures and power steering fluid (if your car has it), then book a steering inspection.
if: If the steering suddenly becomes much heavier or a steering warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If you start to hear whining or clunking, get it checked within a few days.
If the steering binds, sticks or feels loose, stop driving and have it inspected first.
result.why: Steering that slowly gets heavier often comes from wear rather than a sudden failure: low tire pressure, a tired pump, worn joints or a steering rack losing efficiency. A shop can test each of these to narrow it down.

causes.name: Low tire pressure
causes.clues: Tires look soft, or the tire pressure light comes on.

causes.name: Worn power steering pump or old fluid
causes.clues: Dark fluid, or it's worse when the engine is cold.

causes.name: Worn steering rack or suspension joints
causes.clues: Creaks, uneven tire wear, or a wheel that doesn't return to center easily.

you: Check tire pressures.
Check the power steering fluid level and color if your car has a reservoir.

result.title: Something in the steering is binding. It needs checking before you drive
result.now: Don't use the car until the steering is inspected. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If it only catches slightly right after the car has been parked with the wheels turned, it may be the steering lock or a sticky shaft joint. It still needs checking.
result.why: Steering that sticks at certain points instead of turning smoothly can stop you from steering where you need to go. It usually means a part in the steering column, shaft, rack or front suspension is seizing or damaged.

causes.name: Sticking steering shaft joint
causes.clues: A notchy or catching feel in the steering wheel, often at the same spot.

causes.name: Seizing ball joint or tie rod end
causes.clues: Creaking, and the steering doesn't return to center on its own.

causes.name: Damaged steering rack
causes.clues: A recent curb or pothole hit, or it binds in one direction only.

shop: Ball joint and tie rod inspection

result.title: Old fluid or a tired pump often makes steering stiff when cold
result.now: Check the power steering fluid level and color if your car has a reservoir, and book a check when convenient.
if: If the stiffness lasts longer each day or you hear whining, get it checked within a few days.
If a steering warning light comes on, have it checked before driving further.
If the steering stays heavy after the engine is warm, or it binds or suddenly gets heavier while driving, stop and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Power steering fluid thickens in the cold. Old or low fluid, or a pump that's wearing, may not keep up until things warm up. On electric systems, a weak battery on cold mornings can do the same.

causes.name: Old or low power steering fluid
causes.clues: Dark fluid, or the level is near the minimum mark.

causes.name: Wearing power steering pump
causes.clues: A groan or whine while it's stiff.

causes.name: Weak battery (electric power steering)
causes.clues: Slow cranking on the same cold mornings.

you: Check the power steering fluid level and color.
Note whether the engine cranks slowly on those mornings.
shop: Power steering fluid and pump check
Steering system scan on electric systems

q_when.q: When does the steering wheel shake?

opts.a: It started suddenly, with a thump, or right after hitting something
Only when I brake
At highway speeds (around 50 to 70 mph), and it's smooth at lower speeds
At all speeds, and it gets worse the faster I go
At low speeds, like a slow wobble from side to side
I'm not sure

q_sudden.q: Once you're parked safely, look at the front tires and wheels. What do you see?
q_sudden.help: Look at the sidewall (the side of the tire) and the tread. Check that every lug nut, the large nuts holding the wheel on, is there and not visibly backed out.

opts.a: A bulge, bubble, lump or exposed cords on a tire
Loose or missing lug nuts, or a wheel that was off recently
A dent or bend in the wheel rim, or nothing visible
I'm not sure
It started right after new tires, a rotation or a flat repair
It started after hitting a pothole or curb
The tires are worn unevenly, or the tread feels wavy or scalloped
None of these / I'm not sure

q_all_speeds.q: Do you notice any of these as well?

opts.a: A humming or growling noise that rises with speed
Clunking over bumps, or the steering feels loose
A bulge or lump on a tire, or a rhythmic thump
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: A damaged tire may be causing the shake and could fail
result.now: Don't drive on that tire. Put on the spare or call roadside assistance.
if: If the spare is a small temporary one, follow the speed and distance limits printed on it and replace the damaged tire soon.
If more than one tire looks damaged, have the car towed.
If the steering feels loose, the car pulls hard, or you hear clunking from that corner, have the car towed instead of fitting the spare yourself.
result.why: A bulge or lump means the tire's internal structure is broken, often from a pothole or from belts separating inside. A tire in that state shakes the steering and can blow out without warning.

causes.name: Sidewall bulge from an impact
causes.clues: A bubble on the side of the tire after hitting a pothole or curb.

causes.name: Tread separation
causes.clues: A lump in the tread, or a rhythmic thump that speeds up with the car.

causes.name: Bent wheel as well
causes.clues: A dent in the rim near the damaged part of the tire.

you: Look at the tire from a few angles in good light.
Check the spare's pressure before you rely on it.
shop: Balance after the new tire is fitted

result.title: A loose wheel is dangerous. Don't drive until it's secured
result.now: Don't drive the car. Call roadside assistance or a mobile mechanic to tighten the lug nuts to the correct torque and check the wheel studs.
if: If any wheel studs are broken or the holes in the wheel look worn or oval, the wheel or hub needs repair before the car is moved.
If the wheel was recently taken off at a shop, contact them. Lug nuts should be rechecked after wheel work.
result.why: Loose lug nuts let the wheel shift on the hub, which you feel as a shake or clunk in the steering. If they keep loosening, the wheel can come off while you're driving.

causes.name: Lug nuts not tightened properly after wheel work
causes.clues: A tire change, rotation or brake job in the last few days.

causes.name: Damaged wheel studs
causes.clues: A nut that spins without tightening, or a stud that's bent or missing.

you: Count the lug nuts on each wheel and look for any that are visibly backed out.
shop: Torque the lug nuts to the vehicle's specification
Inspect wheel studs and wheel mounting holes
Check the wheel bearing and hub for damage

result.title: A bent wheel or tire damage from an impact is a likely cause
result.now: If the shake is strong, or you weren't able to check the tires and lug nuts, don't drive on. Call roadside assistance. If it's mild and the tires and lug nuts look normal, keep your speed down and have the wheels and tires inspected within the next few days.
if: If the shake gets worse, you hear a thump, or the car pulls hard to one side, stop driving and have it towed.
If you hear clicking or clunking from one wheel, or a lug nut looks loose, stop and don't drive until the wheel is checked.
If you later spot a bulge, lump or exposed cords on a tire, don't drive on that tire.
If the car also pulls or the steering wheel is now off-center, ask for an alignment check too. The impact may have bent a steering or suspension part.
result.why: Hitting a pothole or curb can bend the edge of a wheel or damage the tire inside where you can't see it. Either one makes the wheel spin unevenly, and you feel it as a shake that grows with speed. Damage you can't see can still get worse, which is why a shop will usually check the wheel on a balancer before deciding what needs replacing.

causes.name: Bent wheel
causes.clues: A visible dent in the rim edge, or a shake that started right after an impact.

causes.name: Internal tire damage
causes.clues: A small bulge or lump, or a thump at low speed.

causes.name: Bent steering or suspension part
causes.clues: The steering wheel is off-center or the car now pulls to one side.

you: Look at the inner and outer edge of each wheel for dents.
Check each tire for bulges.
shop: Wheel runout (bend) check on a balancer

result.title: Uneven brake rotors are a common cause of shaking when braking
result.now: Book a brake inspection and mention that the steering wheel shakes when you brake.
if: If the brake pedal feels soft, sinks toward the floor, or the brake warning light comes on, don't drive the car. Have it inspected first.
If you also hear grinding, or smell burning from a wheel, get the brakes checked before driving much further.
If the car pulls hard to one side when you brake, have it checked before relying on the car. A brake caliper may be sticking.
result.why: When the brake rotors (the metal discs the pads squeeze) wear unevenly, the pads grip a surface that isn't flat. That pulses back through the steering wheel and the brake pedal every time you slow down. A shop will usually measure the rotors before deciding whether to resurface or replace them.

causes.name: Uneven or worn brake rotors
causes.clues: A pulsing brake pedal along with the shake, worse when stopping from higher speeds.

causes.name: Sticking brake caliper
causes.clues: One wheel is hotter than the others after driving, or the car pulls when braking.

causes.name: Worn front suspension parts
causes.clues: Clunking over bumps as well.

you: Notice whether the brake pedal also pulses.
After a drive, carefully hold your hand near (not on) each wheel to feel if one is much hotter.

result.title: A wheel may be out of balance or not seated right after the tire work
result.now: Go back to the shop that did the work and ask them to recheck the balance and the lug nut torque.
if: If you hear clicking or clunking from one wheel, stop and check the lug nuts before driving further.
If the shake is strong or getting worse quickly, don't drive on. Call the shop or roadside assistance.
If rebalancing doesn't help, ask them to check for a defective new tire or a bent wheel.
result.why: A shake that starts right after tire work often means a wheel weight was missed or fell off, or the tire wasn't seated evenly on the wheel. Good shops expect to recheck their work, and it's usually a quick check.

causes.name: Wheel out of balance
causes.clues: A smooth ride at low speed and a shake in one speed range on the highway.

causes.name: Tire not seated evenly, or a defective tire
causes.clues: The shake stays even after rebalancing.

causes.name: Lug nuts tightened unevenly
causes.clues: A shake mainly when braking, or a clicking from one wheel.

you: Look for an empty spot on the wheel where a weight may have fallen off.
Check the tire pressures against the sticker in the driver's door jamb.

result.title: Tire balance is a common cause of a highway-speed shake
result.now: Have the front tires balanced and inspected at a tire shop.
if: If balancing doesn't fix it, ask for a check of the wheels for bends and the tires for internal damage.
If the shake suddenly gets worse or you hear a thump, slow down and have the tires checked right away.
If you see a bulge or lump on a tire, or hear clicking or clunking from a wheel, don't drive on it until it's checked.
result.why: A shake that appears in one speed range, often around 50 to 70 mph, and fades above or below it is a classic sign of a wheel out of balance. Wheel weights fall off and tires wear unevenly over time.

causes.name: Front tire out of balance
causes.clues: The shake is felt mainly in the steering wheel, in one speed range.

causes.name: Rear tire out of balance
causes.clues: The shake is felt more in the seat or floor than the steering wheel.

causes.name: Out-of-round tire or bent wheel
causes.clues: Balancing doesn't fix it, or the shake is there at lower speeds too.

you: Note the speed when the shake starts and stops.
Check tire pressures and look for uneven wear.

result.title: Worn steering or suspension parts may be letting the wheels shimmy
result.now: Have the front suspension and steering inspected within the next few days. Avoid high speeds until then.
if: If the steering suddenly becomes very loose or the car is hard to keep in its lane, stop driving and have it towed.
If you hear a loud clunk and the steering suddenly feels different, pull over and have it towed.
If the tires have uneven wear, ask for an alignment after any repair.
result.why: Tie rods, ball joints and control arm bushings hold the front wheels steady. When they wear, small vibrations can turn into a shimmy you feel in the wheel. Worn shocks can also let the tires bounce, which wears the tread into a wavy pattern that makes the shake worse. A shop will usually check each joint for play before deciding which part to replace.

causes.name: Worn tie rod ends
causes.clues: Extra play in the steering, or wear on the inner or outer edges of the front tires.

causes.name: Worn ball joints or control arm bushings
causes.clues: Clunking over bumps or when turning.

causes.name: Worn shocks or struts with cupped tires
causes.clues: A bouncy ride and a wavy or scalloped feel to the tread.

you: Run your hand across the tread (carefully) to feel for uneven, scalloped wear.
Listen for clunks over speed bumps.
shop: Steering and suspension inspection on a lift
Tie rod and ball joint play check

result.title: A worn wheel bearing may be causing the shake and noise
result.now: Have the wheel bearings checked within the next few days. Keep speeds moderate until then.
if: If the noise turns into grinding, or the wheel feels loose or wobbly, stop driving and have it towed.
If one wheel is much hotter than the others after a drive, or you smell burning from a wheel, don't keep driving. Have it inspected first.
If the noise changes when you gently weave left and right, mention which way makes it louder. It helps the shop find which side.
result.why: A wheel bearing lets the wheel spin smoothly on the hub. When it wears, it usually hums or growls first, and as it gets worse it can let the wheel wobble, which you feel in the steering.

causes.name: Worn front wheel bearing
causes.clues: A hum or growl that rises with speed and changes when turning.

causes.name: Uneven tire wear
causes.clues: Noise that sounds like a bearing but comes from cupped or feathered tread.

causes.name: Worn suspension parts
causes.clues: Clunks over bumps along with the noise.

you: Note whether the noise is louder turning left or right.
shop: Wheel bearing play check on a lift

result.title: A low-speed wobble often comes from a damaged tire or a bent wheel
result.now: Look over each tire for lumps or uneven spots, then have the tires and wheels inspected within the next few days.
if: If you see a bulge, lump or exposed cords, don't drive on that tire. Put on the spare or call roadside assistance.
If the wobble is getting worse quickly, stop driving and have it towed.
If the steering feels loose or you hear clunking from a wheel, don't drive until it's checked.
result.why: Balance problems mostly show up at higher speeds. A slow, side-to-side wobble at low speed more often comes from a tire whose internal belts have shifted or a wheel that's bent, so it doesn't roll true.

causes.name: Shifted or separated belt inside a tire
causes.clues: A lump in the tread, or a wobble you can see if someone watches the tire roll slowly.

causes.name: Bent wheel
causes.clues: A recent hard impact with a pothole or curb.

causes.name: Worn steering parts
causes.clues: Loose-feeling steering or clunks.

you: Check each tire's tread and sidewall for lumps.
Have someone watch each wheel as you roll forward slowly in a parking lot.

result.title: Start with a tire and wheel check, the most common source
result.now: Check the tire pressures and look over each tire, then book a tire balance and front-end inspection.
if: If the shake started suddenly or is getting worse quickly, pull over and inspect the tires before driving further.
If you hear clicking or clunking from a wheel, see a bulge on a tire, or the steering feels loose, don't drive on. Have it checked first.
If it only happens when braking, ask for the brakes to be checked as well. If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, don't drive the car.
result.why: Most steering wheel shakes come from the front tires and wheels. If those check out, the brakes and the steering and suspension parts are the next things a shop will usually test.

causes.name: Tire out of balance
causes.clues: A shake in one speed range on the highway.

causes.name: Bent wheel or damaged tire
causes.clues: A recent pothole or curb hit.

causes.name: Uneven brake rotors
causes.clues: Shaking mainly when braking.

causes.name: Worn steering or suspension parts
causes.clues: Clunks over bumps or loose steering.

you: Note the speed when it shakes and whether braking changes it.
Look over each tire.

q_what.q: What happens when you press the brake and try to shift out of Park?
q_what.help: Have the key in ON or the engine running, and press the brake pedal firmly before you try.

opts.a: The shifter is locked solid, or the button on the shifter won't press in
It feels jammed, and the car is parked on a slope
The shifter moves, but the dash still shows P or the car won't move
It's a push-button or dial shifter, and it won't change gears
The car is dead, or the dash lights are dim
I'm not sure

q_brake_lights.q: Do the brake lights come on when you press the pedal?
q_brake_lights.help: Ask someone to look, or check for a red glow reflected in a window, wall or garage door behind the car.

opts.a: No, they don't come on
Yes, they work
I'm not sure / I can't check

q_electronic.q: Does the car start and run normally, with bright dash lights?

opts.a: No, it won't start, or the lights are dim
Yes, but it still won't leave Park, or there's a shifter warning message
I'm not sure

result.title: The car's weight may be pressing on the Park lock
result.now: Set the parking brake, start the engine, press the brake pedal firmly, and shift out of Park with a firm, steady pull rather than a jerk.
if: If it releases with a clunk, that's common in this situation. Next time, set the parking brake before you shift into Park on a slope.
If it still won't move, check whether the brake lights work. The problem may be electrical instead.
If the car rolls while the shifter shows Park, or the gear display doesn't match the shifter, keep the parking brake set and don't drive it. Have it checked first.
result.why: When you park on a slope and shift into Park before setting the parking brake, the car rolls slightly until its weight rests on a small metal pin in the transmission (the Park pawl). That load can make the shifter very hard to move. This usually isn't a fault, but it puts extra stress on parts if it happens often.

causes.name: Car's weight on the Park pawl
causes.clues: Parked on a slope, and the shifter feels jammed rather than locked.
causes.against: If the car is on flat ground, look at the brake lights and battery instead.

causes.name: Shift lock not releasing
causes.clues: The brake lights don't work, or you don't hear a faint click near the shifter when you press the brake.

causes.name: Binding shift cable
causes.clues: The shifter has felt stiff in every position lately.

you: Set the parking brake before shifting into Park on any slope.
Check whether the brake lights work.
shop: Park pawl inspection if it keeps happening

result.title: A brake light switch or a blown fuse is a likely cause
result.now: Check the fuse for the brake lights or stop lamps (your owner's manual shows which one) and replace it if it's blown.
if: If the fuse is fine, the brake light switch near the top of the brake pedal or its wiring is the next thing to check. A shop will usually test the switch and its signal before replacing it. Avoid driving until the brake lights work.
If a new fuse blows right away, there may be a short in the wiring that a shop needs to find.
If the brake pedal feels soft, sinks, or feels different than usual, or the brake warning light is on, don't drive. Have the brakes inspected first.

If you must move the car before then, use the shift lock release, a small slot or button near the shifter (see your owner's manual). Use it only to move the car out of the way or onto a tow truck, not to drive in traffic without brake lights.
result.why: The car only unlocks the shifter when it gets a signal that the brake is pressed, and on most cars that signal comes from the brake light switch. No brake lights plus a locked shifter most often points to the switch, its fuse or its wiring. It's often a simple repair, but brake lights are essential so drivers behind you know you're stopping.

causes.name: Failed brake light switch
causes.clues: The brake lights stopped working, and on many cars the cruise control won't engage either.

causes.name: Blown stop lamp fuse
causes.clues: All the brake lights went out at once, including the center one.

causes.name: Wiring or connector problem
causes.clues: The brake lights flicker or work some of the time.

you: Check the brake light fuse.
Note whether the cruise control still works.

result.title: The shift lock itself may be sticking or not releasing
result.now: Use the shift lock release: with the parking brake set and your foot on the brake, press into the small slot or button near the shifter (your owner's manual shows where) while you move the shifter out of Park.
if: If the release lets you shift, get the shift lock checked when convenient so you don't get stuck again somewhere inconvenient.
If even the release doesn't free it, the shift cable or the shifter itself may be damaged. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
If the car rolls while the shifter shows Park, or the gear display doesn't match the shifter, set the parking brake and don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: Working brake lights suggest the brake signal is probably reaching the shifter. The problem may be the small electric lock (solenoid) in the shifter that's supposed to release, or something jamming the shifter, like a spilled drink that has gone sticky. The manual release bypasses that lock.

causes.name: Failed shift lock solenoid
causes.clues: You don't hear a faint click from the shifter when you press the brake.

causes.name: Sticky residue or debris in the shifter
causes.clues: A drink was spilled near the console, or it's worse in hot weather.

causes.name: Worn or misadjusted brake switch
causes.clues: It sometimes works if you press the brake harder.

you: With the cabin quiet, listen for a faint click near the shifter when you press the brake.
Try the shift lock release.

result.title: A weak or dead battery may be keeping the shifter locked
result.now: Jump-start the car or use a battery booster, then press the brake firmly and try the shifter again.
if: If it shifts once the car has power, have the battery and charging system tested soon.
If the battery light comes on after the car starts, or the battery goes flat again soon, have the charging system checked before relying on the car.
If you need to move the car without power, your owner's manual explains the shift lock release, or how to put an electronic shifter in Neutral for towing.
result.why: The shift lock, and electronic shifters in particular, need electrical power to release. With a dead or weak battery they can stay locked even when the transmission itself has no fault.

causes.name: Dead or weak battery
causes.clues: Dim dash lights, slow cranking, or the car sat for a while.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery cable
causes.clues: Crusty buildup on the terminals, or a cable you can wiggle.

causes.name: Charging system problem
causes.clues: The battery light came on while driving recently.

you: Check the battery terminals.
Try a jump start or a booster pack.

result.title: The shift cable may have broken or come loose
result.now: Set the parking brake firmly and don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you're not certain which gear the transmission is actually in, block the wheels too before you get out.
If the shifter feels loose or floppy, a broken cable bushing is a common cause. A shop will usually check the bushing and cable before looking further.
result.why: The shifter is connected to the transmission by a cable. When the cable or the small bushing that holds it breaks, the shifter moves but the transmission stays where it was. The car can't be shifted reliably, and you can't trust Park to hold it.

causes.name: Broken shift cable bushing
causes.clues: The shifter feels loose or floppy.

causes.name: Stretched, broken or disconnected shift cable
causes.clues: The shifter moves through the positions with almost no resistance.

causes.name: Fault in the transmission's shift mechanism
causes.clues: The cable checks out fine.
causes.against: Much less common than a cable or bushing problem.

you: Note whether the dash gear display changes when you move the shifter.

result.title: The electronic shifter or one of its sensors may have a fault
result.now: Turn the car off, wait a minute, then restart it with your foot firmly on the brake and try again. If it still won't leave Park, contact a dealer or repair shop.
if: If a transmission or shifter warning stays on, have it towed rather than forcing it. Your owner's manual explains how to put the car in Neutral for towing.
If the car rolls while the display shows Park, set the parking brake, block the wheels and don't drive it.
Ask a dealer for your brand whether a shifter recall is open on your VIN.
result.why: Push-button and dial shifters don't move the transmission directly. They send a signal to a control module, which needs good battery voltage, a brake signal and working sensors. If any of those is missing, the car may keep itself in Park as a safety measure.

causes.name: Low battery voltage
causes.clues: Slow cranking, or other electrical glitches.

causes.name: Brake signal not detected
causes.clues: The brake lights don't work.

causes.name: Shifter, sensor or control module fault
causes.clues: A warning message on the dash.

you: Restart the car with your foot firmly on the brake.
Check that the brake lights work.
Look up recalls by VIN.
shop: Code scan of the transmission and shifter modules

result.title: Start with the common, simple causes
result.now: With the parking brake set, turn the key to ON or start the engine, press the brake firmly and try again. If it won't move, use the shift lock release near the shifter (your owner's manual shows where).
if: If the dash is dim or the car won't start, a weak battery is a likely cause.
If the release works, find out why within a few days, starting with whether the brake lights work. Don't drive in traffic without working brake lights.
If the car rolls while the shifter shows Park, or the gear display doesn't match the shifter, set the parking brake and don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: Many cars stuck in Park have one of a few simple problems: the brake signal isn't reaching the shift lock, the battery is weak, or the car's weight is resting on the Park lock. The shift lock release lets you move the car while you sort out which.

causes.name: Brake light switch or fuse
causes.clues: The brake lights don't work.

causes.name: Weak battery
causes.clues: Dim dash lights or slow cranking.

causes.name: Car parked on a slope
causes.clues: The shifter feels jammed rather than locked.

you: Have someone check the brake lights.
Try the shift lock release.

q_gauge.q: Is the temperature gauge high or rising, is a temperature warning light on, or is there steam from under the hood?
q_gauge.help: The temperature gauge usually sits near the middle once the engine is warm. Some cars only have a warning light that turns red when the engine runs hot.

opts.a: Yes: the gauge is high or climbing, the warning light is on, or there's steam
No, the gauge looks normal
I'm not sure

q_where.q: Where do you notice the sweet smell most?

opts.a: Inside the car, especially with the heater or defroster on
Outside, near the front of the car or under the hood after driving
From the tailpipe, along with white exhaust smoke
I'm not sure
