q_inside.q: Do you notice any of these inside the car?

opts.a: A greasy film that fogs the inside of the windshield
Damp or wet carpet on the front passenger-side floor
The heater blows cold or only lukewarm air
None of these
I'm not sure

q_puddle.q: After the car has been parked for a while, is there a puddle or drips under the front?
q_puddle.help: Slide a piece of light-colored cardboard under the engine overnight. Coolant is usually bright green, orange, pink or yellow and feels slightly slimy.

opts.a: Yes, a brightly colored, slightly slimy drip
Only clear water that drips after using the A/C
No puddle, but I smell it or see a wisp of steam after driving
I'm not sure

q_smoke.q: How much white smoke comes from the tailpipe?
q_smoke.help: A little thin vapor on a cold morning that disappears once the engine warms up is normal condensation. Coolant smoke is thicker, smells sweet and keeps coming.

opts.a: Thick white smoke that keeps coming, even once the engine is warm
Light white smoke with a sweet smell, mostly at startup
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be losing coolant and overheating
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine. Let it cool for at least 30 minutes, then have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the gauge only crept up a little and dropped back once you stopped, check the coolant level once the engine is cold. Still have it towed or checked where it sits rather than driving on.
If you see coolant pouring out or a burst hose, don't add coolant and restart. The engine will overheat again quickly.
If you see smoke from under the hood or flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
result.why: A sweet smell plus a high temperature reading usually means coolant is escaping and the engine can't shed its heat. Driving an overheating engine even a few more miles can warp or crack major parts, turning a hose or radiator repair into a much bigger engine repair.

causes.name: Burst or leaking coolant hose
causes.clues: Steam or spray from one spot under the hood, or a wet, sticky hose.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or water pump
causes.clues: Coolant dripping from the very front of the car or from the front of the engine.

causes.name: Head gasket failure
causes.clues: White, sweet-smelling exhaust smoke, or coolant disappearing with no visible leak.
causes.against: Less likely if you can see coolant spraying from a hose or the radiator.

you: Once the engine is cold, check the level in the coolant overflow tank.
Look for wet, colorful residue on hoses, the radiator and the ground.
shop: Combustion gas (block) test for a head gasket leak

result.title: Coolant may be leaking inside the engine and being burned
result.now: Park the car and don't run the engine. Have it towed to a shop or have a mobile mechanic diagnose it.
if: If the coolant tank is nearly empty, coolant is likely being lost fast. Running the engine risks overheating and serious damage.
If the oil on the dipstick looks milky or like chocolate milk, coolant may be mixing with the oil. Don't start the engine.
result.why: Thick, sweet-smelling white smoke usually means coolant is getting into the cylinders and burning off. A failed head gasket is the most common reason, but a cracked part or a leaking intake gasket can do the same, which is why a shop will usually run a block test and pressure test before deciding on a repair. Coolant in the oil can wreck the engine bearings.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: The engine overheated recently, coolant keeps dropping, or the engine runs rough at startup.

causes.name: Cracked cylinder head or engine block
causes.clues: A history of severe overheating, or freezing weather with weak coolant.
causes.against: Much less common than a head gasket leak.

causes.name: Leaking intake manifold gasket (some engines)
causes.clues: Coolant loss with milky oil but little or no overheating.

you: With the engine cold, check the coolant tank level.
Pull the oil dipstick and look for a milky, tan color.

result.title: A small amount of coolant may be getting into the engine
result.now: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold. If it's between MIN and MAX, top it up with the type in your owner's manual and get it checked within a few days. If the tank is empty or well below MIN, or the oil on the dipstick looks milky, have it inspected before driving.
if: If the smoke gets thicker or keeps coming once the engine is warm, stop driving and have it towed.
If the temperature gauge rises at all, a temperature warning light comes on, or the heater suddenly blows cold, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the check engine light flashes or the engine starts running rough, pull over and turn it off.
If the coolant level stays full for a week and the smoke stops, it may have been normal condensation. Still mention it at your next service.
result.why: Light, sweet-smelling smoke at startup can mean a small internal coolant leak that seeps in while the car sits. These leaks tend to grow, and catching one early can prevent overheating and bigger engine damage.

causes.name: Early head gasket leak
causes.clues: The coolant level slowly drops with no puddles, and the smoke is worst on the first start of the day.

causes.name: Leaking intake manifold gasket (some engines)
causes.clues: Slow coolant loss with no outside leak.

causes.name: Normal condensation
causes.clues: Cold or humid weather, and the vapor is thin and disappears within a few minutes.
causes.against: Condensation doesn't smell sweet and doesn't lower the coolant level.

you: Mark the coolant tank level with tape and check it again after a few days.
Check the oil dipstick for a milky color.
shop: Spark plug inspection for coolant contamination

result.title: The heater core may be leaking coolant into the cabin
result.now: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold. If it's only a little low, top it up and book a repair within a few days. If the tank is empty or well below MIN, have it inspected before driving.
if: If the windshield fogs up so you can't see, pull over. Use the A/C with the defroster to clear it, and don't drive until you can see clearly.
If the temperature gauge starts to climb, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the heater suddenly blows cold or you see steam from the vents or under the hood, pull over and turn off the engine.
If kids or pets ride in the car, keep them away from the wet carpet. Coolant is poisonous.
result.why: The heater core is a small radiator behind the dashboard that heats the cabin with hot coolant. When it leaks, coolant vapor can come out of the vents, leaving a sweet smell and a greasy film on the glass, and liquid can soak the passenger-side carpet. A shop will usually pressure test the system to confirm it's the heater core and not a hose behind the engine.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: Greasy fog on the windshield, a sweet smell that's strongest with the heat on, or wet passenger-side carpet.

causes.name: Leaking heater hose or connection behind the engine
causes.clues: The smell is also strong under the hood near the back of the engine.

causes.name: Clogged A/C drain dripping water into the cabin
causes.clues: The wet carpet is clear water with no sweet smell or slimy feel.
causes.against: A sweet smell or greasy windshield points to coolant, not A/C water.

you: Press a paper towel into the wet carpet and smell it, or check for a colored, slippery residue.
Wipe the inside of the windshield and see if a greasy film comes back with the heat on.
shop: Heater core and heater hose inspection

result.title: The coolant may be very low from a leak. Don't keep driving
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Once it's fully cold, check the coolant tank. Even if a top-up brings the heat back, have the leak found before relying on the car. If the tank is empty, have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the temperature gauge is high, a temperature warning light is on, or you see steam, keep the engine off and let it cool before doing anything else.
If the gauge reads normal, don't rely on it. When coolant is very low, the sensor can read normal even though the engine is hot.
If you see white, sweet-smelling smoke from the exhaust or the oil looks milky, don't restart the engine.
result.why: When the heater blows cold and you smell coolant, the level may have dropped so far that hot coolant isn't reaching the heater. The same low level can leave the engine close to overheating, even before the gauge shows it.

causes.name: External coolant leak (hose, radiator, water pump)
causes.clues: Drips or colored, crusty residue under the hood or on the ground.

causes.name: Heater core leak
causes.clues: A greasy windshield film or wet passenger-side carpet.

causes.name: Internal leak such as a head gasket
causes.clues: No visible leak, and white, sweet-smelling exhaust smoke.

you: Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
Look for colored drips or crusty residue around hoses and the radiator.
shop: Combustion gas (block) test if no outside leak is found

result.title: Coolant appears to be leaking from the engine's cooling system
result.now: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold. If it's between MIN and MAX, top it up, keep an eye on the temperature gauge and have the leak repaired within a few days. If the tank is empty or well below MIN, have it inspected before driving.
if: If the drip is steady or forms a puddle bigger than your hand overnight, have it towed rather than driving it.
If the temperature gauge rises, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the heater suddenly blows cold or you see steam from under the hood, pull over and turn off the engine.
Clean up the puddle. Coolant is poisonous, and its sweet smell attracts pets and children.
result.why: A colorful, slimy drip under the front of the car is usually coolant. Small leaks often show up as a sweet smell when coolant drips onto hot engine parts. Leaks tend to grow, and running low on coolant leads to overheating.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or radiator hose
causes.clues: The drip is near the very front of the car, or a hose looks wet or crusty.

causes.name: Failing water pump
causes.clues: Drips from the front of the engine, near the drive belts, or a crusty trail below the pump.

causes.name: Loose hose clamp or worn coolant tank cap
causes.clues: Small seepage at a hose end, or residue around the cap.

you: Put cardboard under the engine overnight to see where the drip lands.
Look for crusty white, green or orange residue on hoses and the radiator.

result.title: A small coolant seep may be burning off on hot engine parts
result.now: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold and top it up if it's a little low, then book a cooling system check when convenient. If the tank is empty or well below MIN, have it checked before driving.
if: If the coolant level drops noticeably in a week, get it checked within a few days.
If the temperature gauge ever climbs above normal, a temperature warning light comes on, or the heater suddenly blows cold, pull over and turn off the engine.
If you see steam from under the hood or white, sweet-smelling smoke from the exhaust, stop driving and have it checked.
result.why: A tiny leak may not drip to the ground at all. Instead, the coolant lands on the hot engine or exhaust and evaporates, which is why you smell it after driving. Clear water dripping after A/C use is usually normal condensation and isn't the source of the smell.

causes.name: Seeping hose connection or clamp
causes.clues: A damp or crusty spot where a hose connects.

causes.name: Small water pump or radiator seep
causes.clues: Dried, colored residue at the front of the engine or on the radiator.

causes.name: Coolant tank cap or overflow tank seep
causes.clues: Residue around the cap or a crack in the plastic tank.

you: Mark the coolant level with tape and recheck it after a few days of driving.
With the engine cold, look for dried, colored residue around hoses and the tank.
shop: Coolant leak dye test with UV light

result.title: A coolant leak is a likely cause. Check the level first
result.now: With the engine cold, check the coolant tank level. If it's a little low, top it up, watch the temperature gauge and have the leak found within a few days. If the tank is empty or well below MIN, have it inspected before driving.
if: If the temperature gauge rises, a temperature warning light comes on, the heater suddenly blows cold, or you see steam, pull over and turn off the engine.
If you see thick white, sweet-smelling smoke from the exhaust, or the oil on the dipstick looks milky, don't drive. Have it inspected.
If the level is fine and stays steady for a week, the smell may be from something else, such as a spilled drink. Mention it at your next service anyway.
result.why: Engine coolant is the most common source of a sweet smell from a car. It can leak inside the engine, behind the dash or from the hoses and radiator. Checking the level is the quickest way to know whether coolant is actually going missing.

causes.name: External coolant leak
causes.clues: Colored drips under the front of the car.

causes.name: Heater core leak
causes.clues: The smell is strongest inside with the heat on, or the windshield fogs with a greasy film.

causes.name: Something spilled inside the car
causes.clues: The coolant level stays full and the smell never changes with the heater or engine temperature.

you: Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
Look under the car for colored drips after it's been parked.

temperature-gauge-fluctuating.title: Temperature gauge goes up and down

q_pattern.help: Think about the last few times it happened, once the engine was fully warmed up.

opts.a: It climbs into the red, or a temperature warning light or message comes on
It rises above normal, then drops back, but never reaches the red
It rises when I'm stopped in traffic and drops once I'm moving
It drops toward cold while cruising or in cold weather, then rises when I slow down
It jumps suddenly or flicks between hot and cold, sometimes with other gauges acting up
I'm not sure

q_heater.q: When the gauge is higher than normal, what does the heater do?
q_heater.help: Set the heat to full hot with the fan on. You can turn it back off once you know.

opts.a: It blows cold or lukewarm air
It stays hot
I'm not sure

q_coolant.q: With the engine cold, what do you see in the see-through coolant overflow tank?
q_coolant.help: The overflow tank is a plastic bottle near the radiator with MIN and MAX (or COLD and FULL) marks. Only check it when the engine is cold.

opts.a: The level is below MIN, or the tank is empty
It's full, but it bubbles or overflows when the engine is running
It's full and looks normal
I haven't checked / I'm not sure

q_warning.q: Has a temperature warning light or message come on, or have you seen steam from under the hood?

opts.a: Yes
No
I'm not sure

result.title: Treat this as real overheating. Stop and let it cool
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, turn the engine off and let it cool for at least 30 minutes. Then have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you can't pull over right away, turn the A/C off and the heater on full hot with the fan on high to pull some heat away.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, pull over as soon as it's safe and shut it off right away.
If you see smoke from under the hood or flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
result.why: A gauge that reaches the red or a temperature warning should be treated as real overheating, even if it drops back later. Each episode can damage the head gasket or cylinder head, so it's not worth chancing another one.

causes.name: Low coolant from a leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, steam, drips, or an empty overflow tank.

causes.name: Cooling fan, thermostat or water pump fault
causes.clues: Coolant is full but it still overheats.

causes.name: Head gasket failure
causes.clues: Bubbles in the coolant tank or white sweet-smelling exhaust smoke.

you: Once fully cool, check the overflow tank level and look under the car for drips.
shop: Code scan and live temperature data

result.title: The cooling fan may not be keeping up at idle
result.now: Check the coolant level once the engine is cold, then get the radiator fan checked within the next few days. Avoid long idling and stop-and-go traffic until then.
if: If the gauge climbs toward the red, a temperature warning comes on, or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the heater blows cold while the gauge is high, coolant may be low or not circulating. Pull over and let the engine cool.
If the coolant tank is low, top it up when cold. Low coolant makes this worse, and an empty tank means have it checked before driving.
result.why: At speed, moving air cools the radiator. When you're stopped, the fan has to do that job. A gauge that climbs only at a standstill and drops when you move often points to a fan that isn't running or isn't running hard enough. A shop will usually test the fan, relay and fuse before replacing the motor.

causes.name: Fan motor, relay or fuse fault
causes.clues: The fan doesn't spin with the engine warm and the A/C on.

causes.name: Worn fan clutch (belt-driven fans)
causes.clues: Trucks and older rear-wheel-drive cars. The fan spins freely by hand when the engine is off and cold.

causes.name: Debris blocking the radiator
causes.clues: Leaves or dirt visible through the grille.

you: With the engine warm and the A/C on, see whether the fan spins. Keep hands and clothing clear.

result.title: The thermostat may be stuck open
result.now: Book a thermostat check when convenient. This pattern usually isn't urgent, but it's worth fixing before winter.
if: If the check engine light comes on, that's often the computer noticing the engine is warming up too slowly.
If the gauge ever goes above normal instead of below, a temperature warning comes on, or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off, then follow the overheating advice.
If the gauge reading doesn't match the heater (for example the gauge reads cold but the heat is very hot, or the reverse), have the sensor checked too.
result.why: The thermostat holds coolant in the engine until it warms up. If it stays open, cold air rushing through the radiator at speed overcools the engine, so the gauge sags on the highway and rises again when you slow down. This pattern more often shows up as weak heat and worse fuel economy than as overheating. A shop will usually confirm with live temperature data before replacing the thermostat.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck open
causes.clues: Slow warm-up, weak heat in winter, and a gauge that drops at highway speed.

causes.name: Faulty temperature sensor
causes.clues: The gauge reads cold, but the heater is hot.

causes.name: Cooling fan running all the time
causes.clues: The fan runs even on a cold engine.

you: Note how long it takes the gauge to reach normal on a cold day.
Notice whether the heater gets weaker on the highway.
shop: Code scan and live temperature data

result.title: A sensor, wiring or gauge fault is possible, but rule out real overheating first
result.now: With the engine cold, check the coolant level first. Low coolant can also make the needle jump, because air pockets form around the sensor. If the level is fine, book a check of the temperature sensor and gauge wiring, and until then use other signs, like heater output and any warning lights, to judge the engine's temperature.
if: If a temperature warning comes on, you see steam, or the heater suddenly blows cold, treat it as real overheating. Pull over and turn the engine off.
If the coolant level is below MIN or the tank is empty, don't drive it. Have the cooling system checked first.
If other gauges or lights flicker too, the problem may be a loose ground or the instrument cluster.
result.why: Real engine temperature usually changes slowly, because there's a lot of coolant to heat up or cool down. A needle that jumps instantly between hot and cold more often comes from a bad signal from the sensor, its connector or the gauge, but very low coolant can cause the same jumps. A shop will usually compare live sensor data with the gauge before replacing anything.

causes.name: Faulty coolant temperature sensor
causes.clues: Sudden jumps, a check engine light, or hard starting.

causes.name: Loose or corroded connector or ground
causes.clues: It changes over bumps or in wet weather, or other gauges flicker.

causes.name: Instrument cluster fault
causes.clues: Several gauges act up at once.

you: Note whether other gauges move at the same time.
Notice whether the heater stays hot when the needle reads high.
shop: Code scan and compare live sensor data with the gauge

result.title: The thermostat or radiator may not be keeping the temperature steady
result.now: Check the coolant level once the engine is cold, then get the cooling system checked within the next few days. Watch the gauge closely until then.
if: If the gauge ever reaches the red, a temperature warning comes on, or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the heater suddenly blows cold while the gauge is high, pull over and let the engine cool.
If it happens mostly in traffic, the cooling fan is a more likely cause.
result.why: If the heater stays hot, coolant is probably reaching it, though the level is still worth checking. A gauge that drifts above normal and back often means the thermostat is opening late or sticking, or the radiator can't shed heat fast enough.

causes.name: Thermostat sticking or opening late
causes.clues: The gauge rises, then drops suddenly as it opens.

causes.name: Partly clogged radiator
causes.clues: Coolant that hasn't been changed in years, or it gets worse on hills and in hot weather.

causes.name: Cooling fan working only some of the time
causes.clues: It's worse when stopped or with the A/C on.

you: Note when it happens: traffic, hills, highway or hot weather.
Check the coolant level when cold.
shop: Radiator temperature scan with an infrared thermometer
Code scan and live temperature data

result.title: Low coolant may be letting the temperature swing. Don't keep driving
result.now: Keep the engine off until it's fully cold. Topping up to MAX with the coolant listed in your owner's manual may steady the gauge for a while, but with the heater going cold the engine is close to overheating, so have the leak found before relying on the car. If the tank was empty, have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the gauge reaches the red, a temperature warning comes on, or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you see white, sweet-smelling exhaust smoke or the oil looks milky, don't start the engine.
If the level drops again soon after a top-up, the leak is significant. Don't drive it.
result.why: When coolant is low, air pockets can form around the temperature sensor and in the heater. The gauge swings as hot coolant and air pass by, and the heater goes cold. It's an early warning that the engine is close to overheating, and the gauge may not show how hot it really is.

causes.name: External leak
causes.clues: Drips under the car, crusty deposits on hoses, or a sweet smell.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: Foggy windows, a sweet smell inside, or a damp passenger floor.

causes.name: Internal leak (head gasket)
causes.clues: No visible leak, white exhaust smoke or milky oil.

you: Once the engine is cold, mark the level on the tank so the shop can see how fast it drops.
Look under the car and on the passenger floor for wet spots.

result.title: Bubbles in the coolant suggest a head gasket leak
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic test it.
if: If the coolant was just changed, a few bubbles for the first minutes can be trapped air working its way out. Steady bubbling that doesn't stop is the warning sign.
If the oil looks milky, don't start the engine at all.
result.why: Steady bubbles or coolant pushing out of the tank while running usually mean combustion gas is leaking into the cooling system. The gas creates air pockets that make the gauge swing and can quickly lead to serious overheating.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: Steady bubbles, white sweet-smelling exhaust smoke, or coolant loss with no leak.

causes.name: Cracked or warped cylinder head
causes.clues: The engine was badly overheated in the past.

causes.name: Air still trapped after coolant work
causes.clues: It started right after a coolant change, and the bubbling fades over a few drives.

you: With the engine off and cool, check the dipstick and under the oil cap for milky sludge.

result.title: Coolant may not be circulating well: trapped air or a weak water pump
result.now: Don't drive it until the cooling system has been bled and the water pump checked. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If coolant was changed or added recently, trapped air is a likely cause, and a shop can usually bleed it out.
If you hear grinding near the engine belt or see coolant dripping there, mention it. The water pump is worth checking first.
If the gauge reaches the red or you see steam, keep the engine off and let it cool.
result.why: If the coolant is full but the heater goes cold when the gauge rises, coolant may not be flowing through the engine properly. Air trapped after a repair or coolant change is a common cause, and a worn water pump is another. Either can tip into real overheating with little warning.

causes.name: Air trapped in the system
causes.clues: It started after coolant service or a repair, or you hear gurgling behind the dash.

causes.name: Worn water pump
causes.clues: A whine or grinding near the belt, or a crusty trail below the pump.

causes.name: Thermostat sticking
causes.clues: The gauge rises, then drops suddenly.

you: Note whether it started after any coolant work.
Listen for gurgling behind the dash when you start the car.
shop: Combustion gas (block) test to rule out a head gasket

result.title: Check the coolant level first
result.now: With the engine fully cold, check the overflow tank. If it's a little below MIN, top it up to MAX with the coolant type in your owner's manual. If it's empty, don't drive it until the cooling system has been checked.
if: If it was low, there may be a leak. Have it checked soon. It's likely to happen again.
If the coolant is full and the gauge keeps rising above normal, get the cooling system checked within a few days.
If the heater blows cold when the gauge rises, coolant may not be reaching it. Pull over, let the engine cool and have it checked before driving further.
If the gauge reaches the red, a temperature warning comes on, or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Low coolant is one of the most common reasons a gauge swings, especially if the heater also goes cold when the needle rises. Checking the level when cold is safe, quick, and helps decide what to look at next.

causes.name: Low coolant
causes.clues: The most common reason for a swinging gauge and a cold heater.

causes.name: Trapped air
causes.clues: Recent coolant work.

causes.name: Water pump or thermostat problem
causes.clues: The coolant is full but it still happens.

you: Check the overflow tank when cold.
Look under the car for drips.

result.title: Have the cooling system and sensor checked
result.now: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold and book a cooling system check. Note when the gauge moves so you can tell the shop.
if: If the gauge reaches the red, a temperature warning comes on, or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the heater blows cold when the gauge rises, pull over and let the engine cool before going further.
If the coolant is low, top it up and get it checked within a few days. If the tank is empty, have it checked before driving.
result.why: A gauge that moves around can be anything from a sensor fault to an early sign of overheating. Without clearer signs, a quick check of the coolant and a shop scan is the safest way to find out which.

causes.name: Thermostat problem
causes.clues: The gauge drifts slowly up or down.

causes.name: Low coolant or trapped air
causes.clues: The heater goes cold when the gauge rises.

causes.name: Sensor or gauge fault
causes.clues: Sudden jumps with no other signs.

you: Check the coolant level when cold.
Take a photo of the gauge when it moves, and note the driving conditions.
shop: Code scan and live temperature data

q_state.q: What does the tire look like right now?
q_state.help: Use a tire gauge if you have one. The correct pressure is on a sticker inside the driver's door, not the number printed on the tire.

opts.a: It's flat, or so low it looks squashed
There's a bulge, bubble, cut or crack on the side of the tire
It looks normal but needs air every few days or weeks
All my tires drop, mostly when the weather turns cold
I'm not sure

q_inspect.q: Inflate the tire, then look closely at it. What do you find?
q_inspect.help: Spray or brush soapy water over the tread, the valve stem and the edge where the tire meets the wheel. Growing bubbles show where air is escaping.

opts.a: A nail, screw or other object in the tread
Bubbles at the valve stem (where you add air)
Bubbles where the tire meets the wheel, or the wheel is corroded or was hit hard on a pothole or curb
The tire was plugged or patched before
Nothing visible / I'm not sure

result.title: The tire is too low to drive on
result.now: Don't drive on it. Put on the spare or call roadside assistance. If you have a portable inflator, you can try adding air where the car is parked.
if: If it holds air after inflating, it still needs inspecting the same day. A tire that was driven on while flat or very low can be damaged inside where you can't see it, so the spare is the safer choice for getting it there.
If it won't hold air or you see sidewall damage, use the spare and have the tire replaced.
If the tire shakes, thumps or loses air again quickly after inflating, don't drive on it.
result.why: A very low tire flexes too much, builds heat and can come apart. It also makes steering and braking less predictable. Even a short drive on a flat can ruin a tire that could have been repaired.

causes.name: Puncture from a nail or screw
causes.clues: An object in the tread, or a hiss when you add air.

causes.name: Leaking valve stem
causes.clues: Bubbles or a hiss at the valve.

causes.name: Sidewall or rim damage
causes.clues: A recent pothole or curb strike.

you: Look the tire over for nails, cuts and bulges.
Check the spare's pressure before you rely on it.
shop: Remove the tire and inspect it inside and out
Leak test in a water tank
Repair from the inside or replace

result.title: Sidewall damage usually means the tire needs replacing
result.now: Don't drive on this tire. Put on the spare or call roadside assistance, then have the tire replaced.
if: If the spare is a small temporary one, follow the speed and distance limits printed on it.
If the wheel is also bent or cracked, have it checked when the tire is replaced.
result.why: A bulge usually means the cords inside the tire are broken and only the rubber is holding the air. Cuts and cracks in the sidewall generally can't be safely repaired. The tire can burst without warning.

causes.name: Impact damage from a pothole or curb
causes.clues: A bulge appeared after hitting something hard.

causes.name: Cut from road debris
causes.clues: A visible slice or gouge in the side of the tire.

causes.name: Age or long-term underinflation
causes.clues: Fine cracks across the sidewall, or a tire more than several years old.

shop: Wheel inspection for bends or cracks
Check the other tires for similar damage

result.title: Cold weather lowers tire pressure in all tires
result.now: Check all four tires when they're cold (before driving) and fill them to the pressure on the driver's door sticker.
if: If one tire keeps dropping faster than the others, it probably has its own leak. Go back and check it with soapy water.
If the tire pressure light stays on after filling all tires correctly, have the sensors checked.
If any tire looks squashed, or you see a bulge, cut or cords, don't drive on it. Put on the spare or call roadside help.
If you feel a shake, thump or pull while driving, slow down gently, pull over and check the tires.
result.why: Air contracts as it cools, so pressure drops when the temperature falls, by about 1 psi for every 10 degrees Fahrenheit. All the tires drop together, and it often turns on the tire pressure light on the first cold morning. A leak in one tire can hide behind this, so it's worth comparing the tires a week later.

causes.name: Normal pressure drop with colder weather
causes.clues: All tires are low by about the same amount, and the light comes on in the morning.
causes.against: If one tire is much lower than the rest, look for a leak.

causes.name: Tires not checked in a while
causes.clues: Tires lose a little air naturally over weeks and months.

you: Check all tires with a gauge before driving.
Recheck a week later and see if one tire dropped more.
shop: Tire pressure sensor check if the light stays on

result.title: A puncture in the tread is a likely source of the leak
result.now: Leave the object in place and have the tire inspected and repaired within a few days. Check and set the pressure before each drive until then.
if: If the hole is near the edge of the tread or on the sidewall, a shop will usually say it can't be repaired safely and recommend a new tire.
If the tire loses air quickly or goes flat, use the spare instead of driving on it.
If you feel a vibration or thump, or see a bulge, stop and put on the spare.
result.why: Nails and screws often seal themselves partly, so air leaks out slowly instead of all at once. The safe fix is to take the tire off the wheel and repair it from the inside with a patch and plug, so the shop can also check for hidden damage.

causes.name: Nail or screw in the tread
causes.clues: A shiny metal head in the tread, or bubbles around it.

causes.name: Small object that already fell out
causes.clues: A small hole that bubbles with soapy water.

you: Spray soapy water on the object to confirm it's leaking.
Note where it is: center tread, near the edge, or on the side.
shop: Remove the tire and inspect the inside
Patch-and-plug repair from the inside if repairable

result.title: The valve stem appears to be leaking
result.now: Make sure the valve cap is on. If you have a valve core tool, snug the core gently, then test again with soapy water.
if: If it still bubbles, or the rubber stem is cracked, have the valve stem replaced soon.
If your car has tire pressure sensors in the valve, a shop should replace the seal or valve so the sensor isn't damaged.
If the tire is losing air quickly or is low by the time you next drive, put on the spare or have it fixed before driving.
result.why: The small spring valve inside the stem can loosen or get dirt in it, and rubber stems crack with age. Air can then seep out slowly even when the tire itself isn't damaged.

causes.name: Loose or dirty valve core
causes.clues: Bubbles from the center of the valve opening.

causes.name: Cracked or worn rubber valve stem
causes.clues: Cracks when you bend the stem gently, or bubbles at its base.

causes.name: Worn seal on a tire pressure sensor valve
causes.clues: A metal valve stem with bubbles where it meets the wheel.

you: Spray soapy water on the valve opening and the base of the stem.
Make sure a cap is fitted.
shop: Valve core or valve stem replacement

result.title: Air may be leaking where the tire seals against the wheel
result.now: Check and set the pressure before each drive, and book a tire shop visit to have the tire taken off and the wheel edge cleaned and resealed.
if: If you see a crack in the wheel, or bubbles from the wheel itself, use the spare until it's inspected.
If the wheel is bent from a pothole, it may need repair or replacement. A bent wheel can also cause a vibration.
If the leak gets fast enough that the tire goes flat overnight, or you feel a new vibration or thump, use the spare.
result.why: The tire seals against a smooth lip on the wheel. Corrosion, dirt or a bend from an impact can break that seal so air seeps out slowly. It's common on older aluminum wheels and in places where roads are salted. A shop will usually test the wheel in water and check it for bends and cracks before deciding whether it can be resealed.

causes.name: Corrosion on the wheel's sealing edge
causes.clues: Older aluminum wheels, salty winters, and bubbles at several spots around the rim.

causes.name: Bent wheel from an impact
causes.clues: The leak started after a pothole or curb strike, or there's a new vibration.

causes.name: Cracked wheel
causes.clues: Bubbles from a spot on the wheel itself, not where the tire meets it.

you: Spray soapy water all the way around the edge where the tire meets the wheel.
Look at the wheel lip for dents or flat spots.
shop: Dismount, clean and reseal the tire bead

result.title: The earlier repair may be failing
result.now: Have the tire inspected within a few days and ask the shop to check the old repair from the inside.
if: If the old repair is a plug pushed in from the outside only, ask about a proper inside repair or a new tire.
If the repair is near the edge of the tread or the tire was driven on flat, a shop will often recommend replacing it.
If the tire goes low quickly, shakes or thumps, or you see a bulge, use the spare instead of driving on it.
result.why: A plug put in from the outside, without a patch on the inside, can work loose over time. Shops also find that a tire driven while low may have hidden inner damage that makes a new repair unsafe.

causes.name: Outside-only plug working loose
causes.clues: Bubbles at the old plug.

causes.name: Second puncture nearby
causes.clues: Bubbles at a different spot in the tread.

you: Spray soapy water over the old repair.

result.title: A slow leak you can't see is best found by a tire shop
result.now: Check the pressure before each drive and book a tire shop to find the leak. Note how many pounds it loses per day.
if: If it starts going low overnight or faster, get it in sooner and use the spare if needed.
If the tire pressure light flashes for a minute and then stays on, the system itself may have a fault.
If you see a bulge, cut or cords, or feel a vibration or thump, don't drive on the tire. Use the spare.
result.why: Many leaks are tiny: a small object hidden in a tread groove, a pinhole, or corrosion under the wheel edge. A shop can dunk the wheel in water to find exactly where air is escaping.

causes.name: Small puncture hidden in the tread
causes.clues: The leak is steady no matter the weather.

causes.name: Leak at the wheel edge
causes.clues: Older wheels, or a recent pothole.

causes.name: Valve stem leak
causes.clues: A missing cap or an old rubber stem.

you: Check the tire with a gauge each morning and note the readings.
Spray soapy water over the whole tire and the valve.

q_tires.q: Look at all four tires, and think about how the car feels. Which fits best?

opts.a: A tire is flat or looks much lower than the others, or the car is pulling, wobbling, or making a flapping or thumping noise
The tires look okay and the car drives normally
I'm not sure

q_flash.q: When you start the car, what does the light do?
q_flash.help: Watch the light for about a minute and a half after starting. Some cars also show a TPMS or tire pressure message on the screen.

opts.a: It's on steadily right from the start
It flashes for about a minute, then stays on
I'm not sure

q_tire_work.q: Did the light start after any tire work?

opts.a: Yes, after new tires, new wheels, a swap to winter or summer tires, or a tire repair
I'm driving on the spare tire
No, nothing like that
I'm not sure

q_gauge.q: Check all four tires with a tire gauge before driving far. How do they compare with the pressure on the sticker inside the driver's door?
q_gauge.help: Use the pressure on the door sticker (or owner's manual), not the maximum number on the tire's sidewall. Check when the tires are cold: parked for a few hours or driven only a mile or so.

opts.a: One tire is noticeably lower than the others
All of them are a bit low, especially after a cold night
All are at the right pressure, but the light stays on
I don't have a gauge, or I'm not sure

result.title: A tire may be flat or losing air fast
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe and don't drive further on it. Put on the spare if you can do it safely, or call roadside assistance.
if: If your car has no spare but has a tire sealant kit, follow the kit's instructions and then get the tire checked right away.
If the tire is shredded or the wheel is bent, don't try a sealant kit. Use the spare or get a tow.
result.why: A tire that's flat or very low can overheat and come apart, damage the wheel, and make the car pull or sway. The light did its job: the tire needs attention before any more driving.

causes.name: Puncture from a nail, screw or road debris
causes.clues: Air loss over minutes or hours, sometimes with an object visible in the tread.

causes.name: Damaged tire or wheel from a pothole or curb
causes.clues: A bulge in the sidewall, or a dent in the rim edge.

causes.name: Leaking valve stem
causes.clues: Hissing near the valve, or the cap was missing.

you: From a safe spot, look for nails, cuts or bulges.
Check the spare's pressure before you rely on it.
shop: Tire inspection and puncture repair if it's in the tread
Tire replacement if the sidewall is damaged

result.title: One tire is losing air, most likely from a slow leak
result.now: Inflate it to the door-sticker pressure, then have it checked for a leak within a few days. Check its pressure every day until then.
if: If it drops a lot overnight or won't hold air at all, use the spare and don't drive on that tire.
If you see a bulge or a cut in the sidewall, don't drive on it. Use the spare.
If the car starts pulling, wobbling, vibrating or thumping, slow down, pull over somewhere safe and check the tire.
result.why: When one tire is clearly lower than the rest, it's likely losing air on its own, often through a small puncture, the valve stem, or the seal between the tire and the wheel. Small leaks are often repairable if caught early, and a shop will usually water-test the tire to find the spot.

causes.name: Nail or screw in the tread
causes.clues: A metal head visible in the tread, or bubbles when you spray soapy water on it.

causes.name: Leaking valve stem or TPMS sensor seal
causes.clues: Bubbles at the valve when you spray soapy water.

causes.name: Leak where the tire meets the wheel
causes.clues: Corroded or curb-scraped wheel edge, often worse in winter.

you: Look over the tread for nails or screws.
Spray soapy water on the tread, valve and rim edge and look for bubbles.
shop: Tire leak test in a water tank
Puncture repair or valve stem replacement

result.title: Cold weather has likely lowered the pressure in all four tires
result.now: Fill all four tires to the door-sticker pressure. The light usually goes out after a few minutes of driving.
if: If the light comes back within a few days and one tire is lower than the others, that tire probably has a slow leak.
If the light doesn't go out after inflating and driving, your car may need a TPMS reset. See the owner's manual.
If any tire looks much lower than the others, or you see a bulge, cut or cords, don't drive on it. Use the spare or call roadside assistance.
If the car pulls, wobbles or thumps, slow down and pull over somewhere safe.
result.why: Air pressure drops when it gets colder, roughly 1 psi for every 10°F. A cold snap can push all four tires low enough to turn on the light, especially if they were already a little under.

causes.name: Temperature drop
causes.clues: The light came on on a cold morning, and all tires read low by a similar amount.
causes.against: If one tire is much lower than the others, look for a leak.

causes.name: Normal slow air loss over time
causes.clues: The tires haven't been checked in a month or more.

you: Check all four tires when cold and fill them to the door-sticker pressure.
Check them again in a week.
shop: Tire pressure check and TPMS reset if needed

result.title: The system may need a reset, or a sensor is reading wrong
result.now: Look up the TPMS reset in your owner's manual. Some cars have a reset button or a menu option, then need 10 to 20 minutes of driving to relearn.
if: If the light is still on after a reset and a few drives, have the TPMS sensors checked when convenient.
If you checked the pressures while the tires were warm, recheck them cold. Warm tires read higher.
If a tire starts to look low, or the car pulls, wobbles or thumps, pull over and check the tires before driving further.
result.why: Some cars don't measure pressure directly. They compare how fast each wheel spins, and they need a reset after you inflate the tires or rotate them. Cars with a sensor in each wheel can also show a light if one sensor sends a wrong reading.

causes.name: TPMS needs a reset or relearn
causes.clues: The tires were just inflated, rotated or replaced.

causes.name: Spare tire low (on cars that monitor it)
causes.clues: Your owner's manual says the spare is monitored.

causes.name: Faulty TPMS sensor
causes.clues: The reset doesn't help, or one tire's reading on the dash doesn't match your gauge.

you: Recheck all four tires cold, plus the spare if your car monitors it.
Follow the owner's manual reset steps.
shop: TPMS sensor scan for each wheel

result.title: Treat it as a low tire until you've checked the pressures
result.now: First look at all four tires. If none look low, drive gently a short distance to the nearest gas station or tire shop and check all four against the pressure on the driver's door sticker.
if: If a tire looks low, or the car pulls, wobbles or thumps on the way, pull over safely and use the spare or call roadside assistance.
If all four tires are fine, follow the TPMS reset steps in your owner's manual.
result.why: A steady tire pressure light most often means at least one tire is truly low. Low tires wear out faster, hurt braking and handling, and can overheat. The only way to know is to measure.

causes.name: Low tire from a slow leak
causes.clues: One tire looks a bit flatter than the others.

causes.name: Cold weather
causes.clues: The light came on on a cold morning.

causes.name: System needs a reset, or a sensor fault
causes.clues: All tires turn out to be at the right pressure.

you: Check all four tires with a gauge.
Look for nails, cuts or bulges.

result.title: The tire sensors may not be installed, matched or programmed after the tire work
result.now: Go back to the shop that did the tire work and ask them to check and program the TPMS sensors. Check your tire pressures with a gauge in the meantime.
if: If a tire also looks low, inflate it and check it for a leak first. The system can't warn you while it's faulty.
If the car pulls, wobbles or thumps, pull over and check the tires. The light may not warn you while the system is faulty.
result.why: A light that flashes and then stays on usually means the monitoring system can't read one or more sensors. After new wheels or a tire swap, the sensors may be missing, damaged during mounting, or not yet matched to the car. Most tire shops can scan the sensors and program them quickly.

causes.name: Sensors not programmed to the car
causes.clues: New sensors or a seasonal wheel set were just installed.

causes.name: Wheels without sensors
causes.clues: Aftermarket or winter wheels were installed.

causes.name: Sensor damaged during tire mounting
causes.clues: Only one tire was replaced or repaired.

you: Check all four tires with a gauge until the system is fixed.
shop: TPMS sensor scan for each wheel
Sensor replacement if one is damaged

result.title: The spare tire probably doesn't have a pressure sensor, so the system flags a fault
result.now: Get the original tire repaired or replaced and put back on. Check the spare's pressure with a gauge, and follow any speed and distance limits printed on a compact spare.
if: If the light keeps flashing after the original wheel is back on, have the TPMS sensors checked.
If the spare looks low, or the car pulls, wobbles or thumps, pull over and check it. The light can't warn you about the spare's pressure.
result.why: Most spare tires don't have a TPMS sensor. When the car can't find the sensor it expects, it flashes the light and then leaves it on to show the system isn't working.

causes.name: Spare tire without a sensor
causes.clues: The light started flashing once the spare went on.

causes.name: Original wheel sensor out of range in the trunk
causes.clues: The removed wheel is in the car.

you: Check the spare's pressure; compact spares often need much higher pressure than regular tires.
Read the speed and distance limits on the spare's sidewall.
shop: TPMS sensor check after the original wheel is reinstalled

result.title: The tire pressure monitoring system likely has a fault, often a worn sensor battery
result.now: Book a TPMS check when convenient. Until it's fixed, check your tire pressures with a gauge every week or two and before long trips.
if: If any tire looks low or the car feels different, check the pressures right away. The light can't warn you while the system is faulty.
If the car pulls, wobbles or thumps, slow down and pull over somewhere safe.
result.why: A light that flashes at startup and then stays on usually means the system can't read one or more sensors. That doesn't tell you anything about the actual tire pressures, so check them with a gauge. Sensor batteries are sealed inside and wear out with age, so older cars often lose a sensor.

causes.name: Sensor battery worn out
causes.clues: The car or its wheels are several years old, and no tire work was done recently.

causes.name: Damaged sensor
causes.clues: A recent hard pothole or curb hit.

causes.name: TPMS receiver or module fault
causes.clues: All sensors test fine with a scan tool.
causes.against: Less common than a sensor.

you: Check all four tires with a gauge so you know their actual pressures.
shop: TPMS sensor scan for each wheel

q_pattern.help: Depending on the car, it may be called TCS, ESC, ESP, VSC, VSA, DSC or StabiliTrak. They all control wheel spin and skids.

opts.a: It flickers briefly when I accelerate or turn on a wet, icy, snowy or gravel road, then goes out
It includes the word OFF, or it came on after a button was pressed
It stays on steadily
It flashes on dry roads, or the car cuts power or brakes a wheel for no reason
I'm not sure

q_other_lights.q: Are any other warning lights on with it?

opts.a: The ABS light and the red BRAKE light
The ABS light only
The check engine light is flashing, or the engine runs rough
The check engine light is on steadily
No other lights
I'm not sure

q_recent.q: Has any of this happened recently?

opts.a: New tires on only some wheels, a spare tire in use, or a tire that looks low
The battery was disconnected, replaced or jumped, or there was an alignment or steering work
Brake or wheel work, or a hard hit on a pothole or curb
None of these, or I'm not sure

result.title: The system is likely doing its job on a slippery road
result.now: Ease off the gas, steer smoothly, and slow down for the conditions. The light usually goes out once the tires have grip again.
if: If it flickers often on dry roads too, the tires may be worn or a sensor may be reading wrong. Get it checked.
If you're stuck in snow or mud, briefly turning traction control off can help you rock free. Turn it back on once you're moving.

If the light stays on steadily, or the ABS or check engine light comes on with it, the system may have a fault. Get it checked within a few days. If the red BRAKE light comes on, don't drive until the brakes are checked.
result.why: When a wheel starts to spin or the car starts to slide, the system brakes that wheel or cuts engine power for a moment. The light flickers to tell you it's stepping in, which means the road is slippery.

causes.name: Wheel spin on a slippery surface
causes.clues: It happens when pulling away or accelerating on wet, icy or loose roads.

causes.name: Worn tires
causes.clues: It happens often, even in light rain.

you: Check tread depth and tire pressures.

result.title: Traction or stability control has been switched off
result.now: Press the traction control button (often a car with skid marks and the word OFF) once, or turn the car off and restart it. Most systems turn back on at startup.
if: If the OFF light won't go out after a restart, the system may have a fault. Get it checked within a few days.
If the button is stuck or was pressed by something in the console, free it and try again.
If the ABS or red BRAKE light is also on, or the brake pedal feels different, don't drive until the brakes are checked.
result.why: Most cars let you switch traction control off, which is useful when stuck in snow or mud. The OFF light usually just shows it's switched off. It's easy to press the button by accident.

causes.name: Button pressed by accident
causes.clues: The light came on right after something touched the console or dash.

causes.name: Stuck button
causes.clues: The button feels sticky or doesn't spring back.

causes.name: System fault shown as OFF
causes.clues: The light stays on after a restart and the button doesn't change it.

you: Press the button and watch the light.
Restart the car.

result.title: The system may be stepping in when it shouldn't, often from a bad sensor reading
result.now: Get the stability control system scanned within a few days. Until then, allow extra time when pulling into traffic, because the car may cut power without warning.
if: If the car cuts power or brakes hard on its own in traffic, stop driving it and have it towed.
If one tire is lower or a different size than the others, fix that first. It can confuse the system.
If the ABS or red BRAKE light comes on, or the brake pedal feels soft or different, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
result.why: The system compares wheel speeds and steering angle to detect skids. If a sensor sends a wrong reading, or one tire spins at a different speed, the system can think the car is sliding and brake a wheel or cut power on a dry road. A shop will usually watch live sensor data on a test drive before replacing a sensor.

causes.name: Faulty wheel speed sensor
causes.clues: The ABS light comes on at times too.

causes.name: Mismatched or underinflated tire
causes.clues: One new tire, a spare in use, or the tire pressure light is on.

causes.name: Steering angle or yaw sensor reading wrong
causes.clues: It happens mostly in turns, or started after an alignment or battery work.

you: Check all four tire pressures and look for a mismatched tire.
shop: Stability control and ABS code scan
Live wheel speed and steering angle data on a test drive

result.title: Traction, ABS and red brake lights together can point to a brake system problem
result.now: Don't drive it. Check that the parking brake is fully released and look at the brake fluid level, then have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the red BRAKE light goes out once the parking brake is fully released and the pedal feels normal, the ABS and traction lights still need checking within a day or two. If the red light stays on, keep the car parked.
If the brake fluid is low, topping it up doesn't make the car safe to drive, even if you can't see a leak. Have the brakes inspected before driving.
If the brake pedal feels soft, sinks toward the floor, or needs much more force, don't drive the car.
result.why: Traction and stability control rely on the ABS system. When the red brake light joins them, fluid may be low or the system that balances front and rear braking may not be working. The car can skid or spin in a hard stop, and low fluid can also mean a leak or very worn brakes.

causes.name: Low brake fluid
causes.clues: Fluid at or below the MIN mark, or wet spots near a wheel.

causes.name: ABS module or wheel speed sensor fault
causes.clues: Fluid level is normal and the pedal feels normal.

causes.name: Parking brake not fully released
causes.clues: The red light goes out when you release it fully.

you: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.
Check the brake fluid level with the engine off.
shop: ABS and brake system code scan

result.title: A wheel speed sensor fault may have switched off ABS and traction control
result.now: Get the ABS codes read within the next few days. Until then, brake earlier and leave extra room, especially in rain or snow, and pay attention to how the brakes feel.
if: If the red BRAKE light comes on, or the pedal feels soft, sinks or needs more force, stop driving it.
If you hear grinding, smell burning from a wheel, or the car pulls when braking, have it checked before driving further.
If the lights came on right after brake or wheel work, contact the shop that did it. A sensor or connector may have been disturbed, and they can check it.
result.why: Traction control, stability control and ABS all use the same wheel speed sensors. When one stops sending a signal, the car switches these systems off and lights the warnings. Regular braking is designed to keep working without ABS, but the wheels can lock in a hard stop, so allow more distance. A shop will usually check live sensor data and the wiring before replacing a sensor.

causes.name: Failed wheel speed sensor
causes.clues: A common cause, especially on older cars in salty areas.

causes.name: Damaged sensor wiring
causes.clues: Recent brake or suspension work, or a pothole hit.

causes.name: ABS module fault
causes.clues: All sensors test fine.
causes.against: Less common than a sensor.

you: Check the brake fluid level.
Look behind each wheel for a loose connector or dangling wire.

result.title: The engine may be misfiring, and traction control has shut off as a result
result.now: Pull over safely and turn the engine off. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you smell fuel or see smoke, get everyone out and away from the car.
If the temperature gauge is high or the oil pressure light is on, don't restart the engine.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means a misfire bad enough to overheat and damage the catalytic converter. Many cars switch traction control off when the engine has a serious fault, because they can't control engine power reliably.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: Shaking at idle or when accelerating.

causes.name: Fuel injector problem
causes.clues: Rough running with a fuel smell.

causes.name: Serious engine mechanical problem
causes.clues: Knocking, or loss of coolant or oil.

result.title: An engine fault may have switched off traction control
result.now: Have the engine codes read within a few days. Many auto parts stores can read basic codes for you.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine runs rough, pull over and stop driving.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward the red or the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the car goes into a low-power mode, have it checked before relying on it. Low power can make merging and passing dangerous.
result.why: Traction control works partly by reducing engine power. When the engine computer finds a fault, many cars switch traction control off as a precaution. Fixing the engine fault often turns the traction light off too.

causes.name: Engine sensor or emissions fault
causes.clues: The engine runs normally, and the check engine light is steady.

causes.name: Throttle or accelerator pedal sensor fault
causes.clues: Hesitation, or a low-power mode.

causes.name: Shared wiring or voltage problem
causes.clues: Several other lights flicker, or the battery is weak.

you: Get the engine codes read with a code reader.
shop: Engine and stability control code scan

result.title: The steering angle sensor may need to be reset or calibrated
result.now: Check your owner's manual for a reset step, such as turning the wheel fully left and right with the engine running. If that doesn't work, book a calibration.
if: If the light came on after an alignment, ask the alignment shop to calibrate the sensor. It's a normal part of the job on many cars.
If the car brakes a wheel or cuts power on its own, especially in turns, stop driving it and have it checked.
If the ABS or red BRAKE light comes on, or the steering feels different, have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Stability control needs to know where the steering wheel is pointed. After the battery is disconnected or the wheels are aligned, some cars lose that setting and turn the light on until the sensor is reset.

causes.name: Steering angle sensor lost calibration
causes.clues: The light came on right after battery or alignment work.

causes.name: Steering wheel off-center after an alignment
causes.clues: The wheel isn't straight when you drive straight.

causes.name: Faulty steering angle sensor
causes.clues: Calibration doesn't fix it.

you: Try the reset steps in the owner's manual.
Notice whether the steering wheel is straight when driving straight.

result.title: Mismatched or low tires can confuse the system
result.now: Check all four tire pressures and set them to the door-sticker values. If a compact spare is on, get the regular tire back on soon.
if: If the light stays on after the tires are matched and inflated, get a stability control scan.
If only two tires were replaced, ask the tire shop whether the tire sizes and wear levels are close enough for your car, especially if it's all-wheel drive.
If you see a bulge, cut or cords on a tire, or the ABS or red BRAKE light comes on, don't drive until it's checked.
result.why: The system compares how fast each wheel turns. A low tire, a smaller spare, or tires with very different wear spin at a different speed, which can look like wheel slip and turn the light on.

causes.name: Underinflated tire
causes.clues: The tire pressure light is on, or one tire looks low.

causes.name: Compact spare in use
causes.clues: A smaller temporary spare is on the car.

causes.name: Mismatched tire sizes or wear
causes.clues: Only some tires were replaced.

you: Check all tire pressures.
Compare the size printed on each tire's sidewall.
shop: Tire size and tread depth check

result.title: Traction and stability control may have switched off because of a fault
result.now: Get the stability control and ABS codes read within the next few days. Until then, drive more gently, leave extra room, especially on slippery roads, and pay attention to how the brakes feel.
if: If the ABS or red BRAKE light comes on, or the brakes feel different, stop driving it.
If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine runs rough, pull over and turn it off.
If the car brakes a wheel or cuts power on its own, stop driving it and have it checked.
If the check engine light comes on steadily too, mention it. Fixing the engine fault may clear the traction light.
result.why: A steady traction or stability light without the word OFF usually means the system found a fault and turned itself off. The car won't get the system's help if a wheel spins or the car starts to slide. A scan shows which sensor or circuit to test next.

causes.name: Wheel speed sensor fault
causes.clues: A common cause. The ABS light may come on too.

causes.name: Steering angle sensor fault or calibration
causes.clues: Recent battery, steering or alignment work.

causes.name: Engine or throttle fault
causes.clues: The check engine light is on, or the engine feels sluggish.

you: Note any other lights on the dash.
Check the tire pressures.
shop: Stability control, ABS and engine code scan
Wheel speed and steering angle sensor data

q_behavior.help: "Slipping" means the engine revs climb but the car doesn't speed up to match, as if it briefly slipped out of gear.

opts.a: It slips, or it's slow or refuses to go into Drive or Reverse
A transmission warning or temperature light is on, or there's a burning smell
It shifts harder or later than it used to
It drives normally
I'm not sure

q_amount.q: How much fluid is there after the car sits overnight?
q_amount.help: Slide a piece of white cardboard under the car before you park for the night. It shows both the size and the color.

opts.a: A few drops, or a spot about the size of a coin
A spot about the size of your hand
A puddle bigger than a dinner plate, or it's dripping steadily
I'm not sure

q_where.q: Where is the drip coming from?
q_where.help: With the engine off, look from the side and front with a flashlight. The transmission sits behind the engine, usually under the middle or front of the car.

opts.a: Under the middle of the car, from the flat metal pan at the bottom of the transmission
Toward the front, near the radiator or along metal lines running forward
Right where the engine and transmission bolt together
Where a drive axle or the driveshaft comes out of the transmission
I'm not sure

result.title: Low fluid may be making the transmission slip. Stop driving
result.now: Stop driving it. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If a technician finds the fluid very low, topping it up may bring back normal shifting, but the leak still has to be fixed before the car is used.
If it starts slipping on the road, get to a safe spot and stop rather than trying to make it home.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke from under the car, pull over, turn the engine off and move away from the car.
result.why: An automatic transmission uses fluid pressure to engage its internal clutches. When the level gets too low, they can slip, overheat and wear fast. Driving on a slipping transmission can turn a leak repair into a much bigger transmission repair. A shop will usually check the fluid level and condition and scan for codes before deciding what's needed.

causes.name: Low fluid from the leak
causes.clues: Red drips where you park, and slipping that started recently.

causes.name: Worn internal clutches
causes.clues: High mileage, and fluid that's dark and smells burnt.

causes.name: Failing pump or clogged filter
causes.clues: A whine that rises with engine speed, along with the slipping.

you: Note the color and smell of the fluid on the ground. Dark, burnt-smelling fluid can mean it has overheated.

result.title: The transmission may be overheating from low fluid
result.now: Pull over when safe, put it in Park and turn the engine off. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the light goes out after it cools, don't count on it. Have the fluid level and leak checked before using the car.
If you see smoke from under the car or flames, get everyone away from the car and call 911.
result.why: Transmission fluid also carries heat away. When it runs low, the transmission runs hot, which breaks down the fluid and damages internal parts. A burning smell often means fluid is dripping onto the hot exhaust, or the fluid itself is cooking.

causes.name: Low fluid from the leak
causes.clues: Red drips where you park, and the light came on after driving a while.

causes.name: Fluid leaking onto the exhaust
causes.clues: A sharp burning smell, or light smoke from under the car.

causes.name: Blocked or leaking transmission cooler
causes.clues: It overheats when towing, climbing or in hot weather.

you: Note which warning light came on and what you were doing at the time.

result.title: Harsh shifting plus a leak can mean the fluid is getting low
result.now: Book a check within the next few days. Until then, drive gently and avoid towing or heavy loads.
if: If it starts slipping, is slow to go into gear, or a warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke from under the car, pull over, turn the engine off and move away from the car.
If your car has a transmission dipstick, check the level as your owner's manual describes. Only add the exact fluid it lists. The wrong type can cause damage.
result.why: Shift quality depends on having the right amount of healthy fluid. As the level drops, shifts often get firmer or later before slipping starts. Finding and fixing the leak at this stage can help protect the transmission. A shop will usually check the level and scan for codes before recommending other work.

causes.name: Low fluid from the leak
causes.clues: Harsh shifts began around the same time you noticed drips.

causes.name: Old or burnt fluid
causes.clues: The fluid is dark brown and smells burnt.

causes.name: Shift solenoid or control problem
causes.clues: A check engine or transmission warning light, or shifts that are fine one day and harsh the next.

you: Check the fluid level and color if your car has a transmission dipstick.
Note which shifts feel harsh, such as first to second, or into Drive.

result.title: A large transmission leak can run it dry quickly
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or ask a mobile mechanic to come to you.
if: If the transmission was just serviced, call the shop that did it. A loose pan, drain plug or line fitting is a common cause.
If fluid is dripping onto the exhaust, keep away from the car until it cools.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke from under the car, pull over, turn the engine off and move away from the car.
result.why: An automatic transmission holds a limited amount of fluid. A steady leak can drop the level enough to cause slipping and overheating within a short drive, and that damage is far more serious than the leak itself.

causes.name: Failed cooler line or fitting
causes.clues: Fluid toward the front of the car, dripping or spraying steadily.

causes.name: Loose or damaged transmission pan or drain plug
causes.clues: A recent transmission service, or you hit debris on the road.

causes.name: Failed axle or front seal
causes.clues: Fluid running from where an axle enters the transmission, or from between the engine and transmission.

you: Take a photo of the puddle and note where it sits under the car.
shop: Cooler line, pan and seal inspection
Refill and leak check before the car is driven

result.title: A steady transmission leak that needs attention soon
result.now: Book a check within the next few days. Keep trips short, and look under the car before each drive.
if: If it starts slipping, is slow to go into gear, or a transmission warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If the spot gets bigger day to day, have it towed rather than risk running low.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke from under the car, pull over, turn the engine off and move away from the car.
result.why: A hand-sized spot overnight means the transmission is losing a real amount of fluid. It may shift fine now, but once the level drops past a certain point, slipping and overheating can start quickly.

causes.name: Leaking pan gasket
causes.clues: Drips from the flat pan under the middle of the car.

causes.name: Leaking cooler line or fitting
causes.clues: Drips toward the front, near the radiator.

causes.name: Leaking axle or front seal
causes.clues: Drips near where an axle goes in, or where the engine and transmission meet.

you: Check the fluid level if your car has a transmission dipstick.
Note where the spot is under the car.
shop: Leak dye test if the source isn't clear

result.title: Possibly the transmission pan gasket
result.now: Book a check when convenient, and watch whether the spot gets bigger.
if: If it starts slipping, is slow to go into gear, or a transmission warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke from under the car, pull over, turn the engine off and move away from the car.
If the spot grows or shifting changes, get it checked within a few days.
If the transmission was recently serviced, ask that shop to check the pan bolts and drain plug first.
result.why: The pan is the metal tray at the bottom of an automatic transmission, sealed with a gasket. Gaskets harden with heat and age, and bolts can loosen. It's one of the most common transmission leaks and often one of the simpler ones to fix, but a shop will confirm the source before replacing anything.

causes.name: Hardened pan gasket
causes.clues: Fluid along the seam all around the pan.

causes.name: Loose pan bolts or drain plug
causes.clues: A recent fluid service, or drips from one spot on the pan.

causes.name: Dented or cracked pan
causes.clues: Visible damage from road debris or a curb.

you: Slide cardboard under the car overnight to track the size of the spot.

result.title: Possibly a transmission cooler line or fitting
result.now: Book a check within the next few days, and look under the car before each drive.
if: If the drip becomes a steady stream or a spray, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If it starts slipping, is slow to go into gear, or a transmission warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke from under the car, pull over, turn the engine off and move away from the car.
If the steering whines or feels heavier, it may be power steering fluid instead. Mention it to the shop.
result.why: Many automatics send fluid through lines to a cooler at the front of the car, often in or next to the radiator. Those lines and fittings can rust, crack or loosen. They carry fluid under pressure while the engine runs, so a small leak can become a fast one.

causes.name: Rusted or cracked cooler line
causes.clues: Wet, rusty metal lines running from the transmission toward the radiator.

causes.name: Loose fitting or worn rubber section of the line
causes.clues: Wetness right at a connection or hose clamp.

causes.name: Power steering fluid leak
causes.clues: Red fluid near the front, with a whine when turning the wheel.
causes.against: Many newer cars use electric power steering with no fluid.

you: With the engine off, look along the lines from the transmission toward the radiator for wet spots.
shop: Leak check with the engine running

result.title: Possibly the transmission front seal, or an engine oil leak
result.now: Wipe a drop on a white paper towel: red or pink means transmission fluid, brown or black usually means engine oil. Book a check when convenient.
if: If the leak grows or shifting changes, get it checked within a few days.
If it starts slipping, is slow to go into gear, or a transmission warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If it turns out to be engine oil and the level is below the minimum mark, top it up before driving. If the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: The transmission's front seal sits where the engine and transmission bolt together. The engine's rear main seal is right next to it, so both leaks drip from the same place. A shop needs to trace which one it is.

causes.name: Transmission front seal
causes.clues: Red or pink fluid at the joint between engine and transmission.

causes.name: Engine rear main seal
causes.clues: The fluid is brown or black and the engine oil level is dropping.

causes.name: Fluid running back from a leak further forward
causes.clues: Wet streaks leading back from a cooler line or the pan.

you: Check the color of the fluid on a white paper towel.
Check the engine oil level.
shop: Inspection of the area between engine and transmission

result.title: Possibly a worn axle or driveshaft seal
result.now: Book a check when convenient, and watch whether the spot gets bigger.
if: If the leak gets bigger or shifting changes, get it checked within a few days.
If it starts slipping, is slow to go into gear, or a transmission warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If you also hear clicking when turning, ask the shop to check the axle joints too.
result.why: On front-wheel-drive cars the drive axles plug into the sides of the transmission. On rear-wheel-drive cars the driveshaft comes out the back. Each has a seal that wears over time, faster if the axle or joint is worn and wobbles.

causes.name: Worn axle seal
causes.clues: Fluid where an axle enters the side of the transmission.

causes.name: Worn rear output (tail) seal
causes.clues: Fluid at the back of the transmission where the driveshaft connects.

causes.name: Torn CV axle boot
causes.clues: Thick black grease flung around, not runny red fluid.
causes.against: Boot grease is thick and dark, not red and runny.

you: With the engine off, look where each axle enters the transmission for wet, red fluid.
Check the rubber boots on the axles for tears or grease.

result.title: A transmission leak that needs its source found
result.now: Book a check when convenient. Slide white cardboard under the car overnight so you can show the shop the color and location.
if: If shifting changes, it slips, or a warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If the spot gets bigger, get it checked within a few days.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke from under the car, pull over, turn the engine off and move away from the car.
result.why: Fluid spreads and runs along parts before it drips, so the spot on the ground isn't always under the actual leak. A lift inspection, sometimes with a dye, finds the source.

causes.name: Pan gasket
causes.clues: Drips under the middle of the car.

causes.name: Cooler line or fitting
causes.clues: Drips toward the front.

causes.name: Axle or front seal
causes.clues: Drips near an axle or where the engine and transmission meet.

you: Photograph the spots on the cardboard.
Check the fluid level if your car has a transmission dipstick.

q_severity.q: Which of these best describes it right now?

opts.a: The car barely moves or won't move in some gears
There's a burning smell, or red or pink fluid under the car
A transmission warning or temperature light is on
It slips now and then, but the car still drives
I'm not sure

q_trans_type.q: Is your car an automatic or a manual (stick shift with a clutch pedal)?
q_trans_type.help: CVTs (continuously variable transmissions) count as automatics here. They don't have fixed gears, so slipping feels like the revs rising with little extra speed.

opts.a: Automatic or CVT
Manual with a clutch pedal
I'm not sure

q_fluid.q: Have you been able to check the transmission fluid?
q_fluid.help: Many cars have a transmission dipstick, often with a yellow or red handle; others have none and must be checked by a shop. Your owner's manual explains how (usually engine running, warmed up, in Park on level ground). Healthy fluid is usually red or pink and doesn't smell burnt.

opts.a: Yes, it's low
The level is OK, but the fluid is dark brown or smells burnt
The level and color look normal
My car has no dipstick / I'm not sure

q_when.q: When does it slip?

opts.a: Mostly when cold, and it gets better as it warms up
Mostly when hot, after a long drive, towing or stop-and-go traffic
During one particular shift, like from 2nd to 3rd
At steady highway speed, the revs creep up without any gear change
Along with a check engine light
I'm not sure

result.title: The transmission has lost most of its ability to drive the car
result.now: Don't try to force it by revving the engine. Put it in Park, turn it off and have the car towed.
if: If you're stuck in a lane, turn on your hazard lights and call for help from a safe place.
If there's red or pink fluid under the car, a leak may be the cause. Mention it when you call.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
