result.why: When the engine runs but the car barely moves, the transmission isn't holding. Revving it harder makes the slipping parts even hotter and can turn a repair into a full replacement.

causes.name: Very low fluid from a leak
causes.clues: Red or pink fluid under the car, or a recent bump or scrape underneath.

causes.name: Badly worn internal clutches or bands
causes.clues: High mileage and slipping that got worse over weeks.

causes.name: Failed pump or torque converter
causes.clues: A whining or grinding noise that changes with engine speed.

you: From outside the car, look for red or pink fluid underneath.

result.title: The transmission may be leaking fluid or overheating
result.now: Pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and have the car towed.
if: If you see smoke, step away from the car. Fluid dripping on the exhaust can catch fire.
If the leak is only a few drops and there's no burning smell, still have it inspected before driving it. Note the color and size of the drips for the shop.
If there are flames, or the smoke keeps growing, move well away from the car and call 911.
result.why: Transmission fluid cools and lubricates the transmission and gives it the pressure to hold each gear. A leak lowers that pressure and causes slipping, and a burning smell means fluid or parts are overheating. Both cause fast, expensive wear.

causes.name: Leaking pan gasket, cooler line or seal
causes.clues: Red or pink fluid under the middle or front of the car.

causes.name: Overheating from slipping
causes.clues: A sharp burnt smell after driving, with no visible leak.

causes.name: Fluid dripping onto the hot exhaust
causes.clues: Smoke from under the car along with the leak.

you: Note the color of any fluid under the car. Red or pink usually means transmission fluid.

result.title: The transmission may be overheating or has detected a fault
result.now: Pull over when it's safe, put it in Park and let it cool. Then have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the light goes off after cooling, it still needs checking before you rely on it. Slipping and overheating feed each other.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
If the engine temperature gauge is high too, don't restart the engine. Have it towed.
result.why: Transmission fluid breaks down quickly when it gets too hot, which leads to more slipping and more heat. A warning light plus slipping means the transmission is already protecting itself or warning you that damage is possible.

causes.name: Low fluid
causes.clues: A leak, or a level below the mark on the dipstick.

causes.name: Slipping clutches making heat
causes.clues: Slipping that started before the light came on.

causes.name: Blocked or damaged transmission cooler
causes.clues: It mostly happens when towing, in hot weather or in heavy traffic.

you: Once it's cool, check for leaks under the car.

result.title: On a manual, the clutch is the first thing to check
result.now: Have the clutch checked within the next few days. Until then, drive gently and avoid hard acceleration in high gears.
if: If the clutch pedal feels soft, sinks or stays down, don't rely on the car. You may not be able to shift or take it out of gear. Have it checked before driving further.
If you smell burning, pull over and let it cool. Slipping that bad can mean the clutch is close to failing, so have it checked before driving further.
If the car won't move in gear, or you can't get it into gear, have it towed.
result.why: A clutch grips the engine to the transmission. When it wears thin, or gets oil on it, it may not hold full power, so the revs jump without more speed. It's usually most noticeable in higher gears and going uphill.

causes.name: Worn clutch disc
causes.clues: High mileage, and the clutch engages near the top of the pedal travel.

causes.name: Oil or fluid on the clutch
causes.clues: An oil leak where the engine and transmission join.

causes.name: Clutch hydraulic problem
causes.clues: A soft, sinking or sticking clutch pedal, or low clutch fluid.

you: Notice where the clutch starts to grab. Very high on the pedal usually means wear.
Check the clutch fluid reservoir if your car has one.
shop: Inspection for oil leaks at the clutch

result.title: Low transmission fluid may be causing the slip, and a leak is likely
result.now: If your car has a dipstick, top up with the exact fluid type listed in your owner's manual, following its check procedure and not overfilling. Then have the leak found within the next few days. If you're unsure of the fluid type or procedure, let a shop do it.
if: If it still slips after topping up, avoid driving it until it's checked. Each slip adds heat and wear.
If the level drops again quickly, or you see drips, stop using the car until the leak is fixed.
If the car loses drive, you smell burning, see smoke, or a transmission warning light comes on, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and have it towed.
result.why: An automatic transmission uses fluid pressure to hold each gear. When the level is low, pressure drops and the clutches inside slip. Fluid doesn't get used up like fuel, so a low level usually means a leak.

causes.name: Leaking pan gasket or seal
causes.clues: Red or pink drips under the middle of the car.

causes.name: Leaking cooler line
causes.clues: Drips near the front of the car, under the radiator.

causes.name: Wrong level after a recent service
causes.clues: The problem started soon after a fluid change.

you: Check the level again after a few days of driving.
Put cardboard under the car overnight to spot drips.
shop: Correct fluid level check to factory procedure

result.title: Burnt-smelling fluid suggests the transmission has been running hot and may be worn inside
result.now: Have the transmission inspected within the next few days. Keep trips short and gentle until then.
if: If the slipping gets worse, you smell burning, or a warning light comes on, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the shop finds metal particles or a lot of debris in the pan, a bigger repair is more likely than a simple fluid change. Ask them to show you what they found.
result.why: Dark, burnt-smelling fluid has usually been overheated, often by the very slipping you're feeling. Overheated fluid protects poorly, so wear speeds up. A shop can tell from the fluid and pan whether a service may help or whether there's internal damage.

causes.name: Worn clutches inside the transmission
causes.clues: High mileage and slipping that's slowly getting worse.

causes.name: Overdue fluid service
causes.clues: No record of a fluid change, especially with towing or heavy use.

causes.name: Overheating from towing or a cooler problem
causes.clues: Slipping started after towing, mountain driving or hot weather.

you: Find your records of the last transmission fluid service.

result.title: Slipping only when cold can point to early wear or hardened internal seals
result.now: Let the car warm up for a minute or two before driving off, go easy until it's warm, and book a transmission check when convenient.
if: If it starts slipping when warm too, get it checked within a few days.
If the fluid level turns out to be low, top it up with the correct type and look for a leak.
If the car loses drive, you smell burning, see smoke, or a transmission warning light comes on, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and have it towed.
result.why: Cold fluid is thicker, and rubber seals inside the transmission shrink and harden with age. Worn seals can leak pressure when cold, so a gear doesn't fully grip until things warm up and expand. It tends to get worse over time, so it's worth having it looked at before it does.

causes.name: Hardened or worn internal seals
causes.clues: Older or high-mileage car, and the problem fades once warm.

causes.name: Slightly low fluid
causes.clues: A small leak, or a level at the low mark.

causes.name: Old or wrong-type fluid
causes.clues: No recent fluid service, or a recent service with a fluid not listed in the manual.

you: Note the outside temperature and how long it takes to go away.
shop: Line pressure test cold and warm

result.title: Slipping when hot can point to worn parts or fluid that's breaking down
result.now: Have the transmission checked within the next few days. Until then, avoid towing, long highway runs and heavy traffic when you can.
if: If a transmission temperature warning comes on, pull over and let it cool, then have it towed or checked by a mobile mechanic.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and have it towed.
If the car loses drive or the slipping gets suddenly worse, stop driving it and have it towed.
result.why: As fluid heats up it gets thinner, and worn parts that seal fine when cold start leaking pressure. Heat also breaks the fluid down further. Slipping when hot tends to make the transmission run even hotter, so it can get worse quickly.

causes.name: Worn internal clutches or seals
causes.clues: High mileage and slipping that's slowly getting worse.

causes.name: Worn or overheated fluid
causes.clues: Dark fluid, or no record of a fluid change.

causes.name: Transmission cooler blocked or not working
causes.clues: Worse in summer, when towing or in stop-and-go traffic.

you: Note how long you'd been driving and the outside temperature when it slipped.

result.title: Slipping on one shift is often traced to a shift solenoid or the clutch for that gear
result.now: Have the transmission checked within the next few days, and note exactly which shift slips so you can tell the shop.
if: If the check engine or transmission light comes on, have the codes read right away. They often name the solenoid involved.
If the car gets stuck in one gear, avoid highways and fast traffic and have it towed or checked as soon as you can.
If the car loses drive, you smell burning, see smoke, or a transmission warning light comes on, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and have it towed.
result.why: Each gear change is controlled by an electric solenoid that sends fluid to a set of clutches. If one solenoid sticks, or one clutch pack wears, you get slipping on that shift only while the others feel normal. A shop will usually test the solenoid and read live data before deciding whether the problem is electrical or inside the transmission.

causes.name: Sticking or failing shift solenoid
causes.clues: A check engine light, and the slip comes and goes.

causes.name: Worn clutch pack for that gear
causes.clues: The slip is always on the same shift and slowly getting worse.

causes.name: Valve body problem
causes.clues: Harsh or erratic shifts along with the slipping.

you: Write down which shift slips and at what speed.
shop: Road test with live transmission data

result.title: The torque converter's lockup may be slipping
result.now: Have it checked within the next few days. Keep highway trips short until then.
if: If you also feel a shudder like driving over rumble strips at steady speed, mention it. That's a common sign of a lockup problem.
If a check engine light comes on, have the code read. Lockup faults usually set a code.
If the car loses drive, you smell burning, see smoke, or a transmission warning light comes on, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and have it towed.
result.why: At cruising speed, an automatic locks the torque converter so the engine and transmission turn together. If that lockup clutch slips, or isn't being told to lock, the revs creep up a few hundred without any gear change and fuel economy drops.

causes.name: Worn torque converter lockup clutch
causes.clues: Revs creep up at steady speed, sometimes with a shudder.

causes.name: Faulty lockup solenoid
causes.clues: A check engine light, and the problem comes and goes.

causes.name: Worn or wrong fluid
causes.clues: Dark fluid, or a recent fluid change with a different type.

you: Watch the tachometer at a steady highway speed and note if the revs drift up.
shop: Road test watching converter slip data

result.title: An electronic fault may be causing the slipping. Get the codes read
result.now: Have the codes read within the next few days. Many parts stores read engine codes free, but transmission codes may need a shop scan tool.
if: If the car is stuck in one gear or feels very sluggish, it may be in a protective "limp" mode. Avoid highways and fast traffic, and get it checked right away.

A code points a shop toward a circuit or system, not always to a failed part. A shop will usually test the sensor, solenoid and wiring before replacing anything, and the fix may turn out simpler than a rebuild.
If the car loses drive, you smell burning, see smoke, or a transmission warning light comes on, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and have it towed.
result.why: Modern automatics are computer-controlled. A bad speed sensor, solenoid or wiring problem can make the transmission shift wrong or slip, and the computer usually stores a code. Reading it first avoids guessing.

causes.name: Faulty shift or pressure control solenoid
causes.clues: Codes about a solenoid or line pressure.

causes.name: Faulty speed sensor or wiring
causes.clues: The speedometer acts strangely, or shifts happen at odd times.

causes.name: Internal wear the computer detected
causes.clues: Codes about a gear ratio being wrong.

you: Have the codes read and write them down.

result.title: Have the transmission checked before the slipping gets worse
result.now: Book a transmission check within the next few days, and keep trips short and gentle until then.
if: If the car loses drive, you smell burning, see smoke, or a warning light comes on, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and have it towed.
If you can check the fluid and it's low, top it up with the correct type, then still have it checked. Low fluid usually means a leak.
result.why: Slipping almost never fixes itself, and each slip adds heat and wear. Catching it early gives you the best chance that a fluid service, solenoid or seal repair fixes it rather than a rebuild.

causes.name: Low or worn fluid
causes.clues: Drips under the car or no record of a fluid service.

causes.name: Solenoid or sensor fault
causes.clues: A check engine light or erratic shifting.

causes.name: Internal wear
causes.clues: High mileage and slipping that's gradually getting worse.

you: Look for red or pink drips where you park.
Note when it slips: cold or hot, which shift, what speed.

q_driving.q: How is the car driving right now?
q_driving.help: "Slipping" means the engine revs rise but the car doesn't speed up to match, as if it's briefly in neutral.

opts.a: It won't move, barely moves, or the engine revs but the car doesn't go
There's a burning smell, smoke, or red fluid dripping
It's stuck in one gear: slow to pick up speed and won't shift up
It drives normally. Only the light or message is on
I'm not sure

q_which_light.help: Your owner's manual shows each symbol. A thermometer means temperature. A gear shape with an exclamation mark, or a flashing gear letter, usually means a fault.

opts.a: A temperature warning: a thermometer, "Trans Temp", "AT Oil Temp" or "Transmission Hot"
A gear symbol with an exclamation mark, "Service/Check Transmission", or a flashing gear letter or O/D OFF light
I'm not sure

q_temp_when.q: What was happening when the temperature warning came on?

opts.a: Towing, carrying a heavy load, climbing a long hill, or creeping in hot stop-and-go traffic
The engine temperature gauge is high too
Normal driving, with no heavy load
I'm not sure

result.title: The transmission has lost drive. Don't try to force it
result.now: Put the car in Park, set the parking brake and turn the engine off. Have it towed to a shop.
if: If you're in traffic, turn on your hazard lights and let the car roll to the shoulder if you can.
If you find a large puddle of red fluid under the car, tell the tow company and the shop. A leak may be the whole problem.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: When the engine revs but the car won't move, the transmission isn't connecting the engine to the wheels. Running it like this can turn a smaller problem, like low fluid, into a much bigger repair.

causes.name: Very low transmission fluid from a leak
causes.clues: Red or brown fluid under the car, or slipping that got worse over a few days.

causes.name: Internal transmission failure
causes.clues: Slipping, harsh shifts or a burning smell in the days before.

causes.name: Broken shift cable or linkage
causes.clues: The shifter moves freely or feels disconnected, and the gear display doesn't change.
causes.against: If the gear display changes and you feel a clunk going into gear, a linkage problem is less likely.

you: Look under the car for red or brown fluid.
Check whether the gear display changes when you move the shifter.
shop: Transmission fluid level and condition check

result.title: Fluid may be leaking onto hot parts, or the transmission is overheating badly
result.now: Pull over where it's safe, turn the engine off and get out of the car if you see smoke. Have it towed.
if: If there are flames or the smoke keeps growing, move well away and call 911.
If you see smoke or flames, don't open the hood: get everyone away from the car and call 911. Let the fire service deal with it.
If the smell fades once it cools, it still needs a leak inspection before you drive it again.
result.why: Transmission fluid burns and smokes when it hits the exhaust or gets far too hot. Either way, the transmission is losing fluid or being damaged, and leaking fluid near hot parts is a fire risk.

causes.name: Leaking transmission cooler line or seal
causes.clues: Red fluid dripping, or wet spots along the lines that run toward the radiator.

causes.name: Severely overheated, slipping transmission
causes.clues: Slipping or a flaring engine speed before the smell started.

causes.name: Leaking pan gasket or axle seal
causes.clues: Fluid near the bottom of the transmission or at the inner end of a front axle.

shop: Transmission fluid level and condition check

result.title: The transmission may be in backup (limp) mode because of a fault
result.now: Get off busy roads and highways as soon as it's safe and have it towed. Limp mode can let go without warning.
if: If it starts slipping, smells burnt, shows smoke or won't move, stop and have it towed.
If turning the car off and back on makes it shift normally, the fault is still stored and can return without warning. Get it scanned within a few days and avoid highways until then.
If the engine temperature gauge is high or the check engine light is flashing, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: When the transmission computer sees a problem, it often locks the transmission in one gear to protect it. That's why the car feels sluggish and won't shift up. The stored code points the shop to the right area to test.

causes.name: Shift solenoid or speed sensor fault
causes.clues: It went into one gear suddenly, with no slipping first.

causes.name: Low or burnt transmission fluid
causes.clues: Slipping or harsh shifts in recent weeks, or a leak.

causes.name: Wiring, connector or low battery voltage
causes.clues: Other warning lights came on at the same time, or the battery is weak.

you: Look under the car for red fluid.
Note whether other warning lights came on at the same time.

result.title: The transmission fluid may have got too hot from the extra work
result.now: Pull over where it's safe, shift into Park and let the engine idle until the warning goes out, unless your owner's manual says to do something different. Don't continue towing or carrying the heavy load until the transmission has been checked.
if: If the warning doesn't go out after 15–20 minutes, or comes back soon after, have it towed.
If it happens again under the same load, have the fluid and cooling checked. You may be near the limit of what the car is built to tow or carry.
If you smell burning, see smoke, the car slips or the engine temperature gauge is high too, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and have it towed.
result.why: Towing, heavy loads, long climbs and slow traffic in the heat all make the transmission work harder and heat its fluid. Idling in Park lets the fluid circulate and cool. Very hot fluid wears out quickly, so it's worth having it checked afterward.

causes.name: Heavy load or towing beyond what the cooling can handle
causes.clues: It only happens when towing or loaded, especially uphill or on hot days.

causes.name: Low or old transmission fluid
causes.clues: The fluid hasn't been changed in a long time, or there's a leak.

causes.name: Clutch overheating (dual-clutch transmissions)
causes.clues: Creeping in traffic or holding the car on a hill with the gas pedal.

you: Check your owner's manual for the towing limit and the right warning procedure.
Look under the car for leaks once it's parked.
shop: Transmission fluid level and condition check

result.title: The transmission may be running hot without an obvious reason
result.now: Pull over where it's safe, shift into Park and let it idle until the warning goes out. Have the transmission checked before relying on the car, and have it towed if the warning comes back.
if: If the warning comes back on a normal drive, have it towed instead of driving it again.
If the car slips, shifts harshly, smells burnt or you see smoke, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and have it towed.
If the engine temperature gauge is high too, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and don't restart it.
result.why: Normal driving shouldn't overheat a healthy transmission. When it does, common causes are fluid that's low or worn out, the cooler is blocked, or the transmission is slipping inside and making extra heat.

causes.name: Low transmission fluid
causes.clues: Red spots where you park, or slipping when cold.

causes.name: Blocked transmission cooler or damaged cooler lines
causes.clues: Debris in front of the radiator, or a recent front-end bump.

causes.name: Slipping inside the transmission
causes.clues: Engine revs flaring between shifts.

causes.name: Faulty temperature sensor
causes.clues: The warning comes on right after a cold start.
causes.against: If the car shifts and drives perfectly, a sensor fault becomes more likely, but a shop should confirm the real temperature with a scan tool before you rely on that.

you: Look for red fluid where you park.
Check in front of the radiator for leaves, bags or debris.
shop: Transmission fluid level and condition check
Transmission temperature reading with a scan tool

result.title: The engine may be overheating and heating the transmission too
result.now: Pull over where it's safe and turn the engine off. Don't open the radiator cap while it's hot. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see steam or smell sweet coolant, stay away from the hood until it cools.
If the temperature gauge was in the red, don't restart the engine to "get it home". Overheating can damage the engine quickly.
If you smell burning or see smoke rather than steam, step away from the car.
result.why: On many cars, the transmission fluid is cooled by the engine's radiator. When the engine overheats, the transmission does too. The engine problem is the one to deal with first.

causes.name: Engine cooling problem (low coolant, fan, thermostat, water pump)
causes.clues: The engine temperature gauge is high, steam, or a sweet smell.

causes.name: Blocked radiator
causes.clues: Debris in front of the radiator, or towing in very hot weather.

you: Once fully cool, check the coolant level in the see-through reservoir.
Look for coolant puddles under the front of the car.

result.title: The transmission computer has found a fault
result.now: Have the transmission codes read within the next few days. Until then, drive gently and avoid towing or heavy loads.
if: If the car starts slipping, shifting harshly or gets stuck in one gear, avoid highways and get it checked right away rather than waiting.
If the light is flashing and the car won't shift at all, have it towed.
If you smell burning, see smoke or the engine temperature gauge is high, pull over, turn the engine off and have it towed.
result.why: This light means the transmission computer has stored a fault, even if you can't feel a problem yet. Faults caught early are often a sensor, solenoid or low fluid, and a shop will usually test those before suggesting bigger repairs. Driving on them can lead to bigger damage.

causes.name: Speed sensor or shift solenoid fault
causes.clues: Shifts feel slightly late or firm, or the speedometer flickers.

causes.name: Low or worn-out fluid
causes.clues: It's been a long time since the fluid was changed, or there's a leak.

causes.name: Wiring or connector problem
causes.clues: The light comes and goes, especially over bumps or in wet weather.

you: Look for red fluid where you park.
Note when the light comes on and how the shifts feel.
shop: Transmission code scan (needs a tool that reads the transmission computer)

result.title: Treat it as a transmission fault and get it scanned
result.now: Look up the light in your owner's manual. If it's a temperature warning, pull over and let it idle in Park until it goes out. Either way, get the codes read within a few days.
if: If the car slips, won't shift, smells burnt or you see smoke, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the engine temperature gauge is high as well, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and don't restart it.
result.why: Transmission warnings cover overheating and electrical faults, and they're handled differently. Your owner's manual will tell you which one you're seeing, and a scan will show why.

causes.name: Transmission fluid overheating
causes.clues: A thermometer symbol, towing, hills or heavy traffic.

causes.name: Transmission sensor or solenoid fault
causes.clues: A gear symbol or a flashing gear letter.

you: Take a photo of the warning to show the shop.
Look for red fluid under the car.

q_tread_left.q: Look at the most worn part of the tread. What do you see?
q_tread_left.help: Wear bars are small raised bridges in the bottom of the tread grooves. When the tread is level with them, the tire is worn out. A quick check: put a penny in the shallowest groove with Lincoln's head down. If you can see all of his head, the tread is too low.

opts.a: Cords, wires or fabric showing, or a bulge
The tread is level with the wear bars or fails the penny test in some spots
There's still a fair amount of tread, it's just worn unevenly
I'm not sure

q_pattern.q: Where is the tire worn most?
q_pattern.help: Compare the tread depth at the inner edge, the center and the outer edge. Run your hand around the tire too, feeling for dips or ridges.

opts.a: Both outer edges worn more than the center
The center worn more than both edges
Only one edge (the inner or the outer)
Choppy dips or patches around the tire (cupping or scalloping)
One bald flat spot in one place
Each tire wears evenly, but the front pair or the rear pair wears much faster
I'm not sure

q_one_edge.help: Rub your hand gently across the tread, side to side. Feathering feels smooth one way and sharp or ridged the other way, like a saw blade.

opts.a: The tread feels smooth, just worn down more on one edge
The tread feels feathered or ridged, smooth one way and sharp the other
I also hear clunks over bumps, or the steering feels loose or wanders
I'm not sure

result.title: The tire is worn through. Don't drive on it
result.now: Don't drive on this tire. Put on the spare or call roadside assistance, then replace the tire.
if: If the other tire on the same axle is close to this worn, replace both.
If the wear is on one edge, have the alignment and suspension checked when you replace it, or the new tire will wear the same way.
If your spare is a small temporary one, follow the speed and distance limits printed on it.
result.why: Once the cords show, there's almost nothing left between the air inside and the road. The tire can burst or lose air suddenly, especially at highway speed or in heat.

causes.name: Alignment problem left too long
causes.clues: The cords show on one edge while the rest of the tread is still deep.

causes.name: Tire simply worn out
causes.clues: The whole tread is thin.

causes.name: Long-term low pressure
causes.clues: Both edges are worn through.

result.title: The tire is at or near the end of its life
result.now: Plan to replace the tire within a few days. Drive gently, leave extra following distance, and avoid heavy rain or snow if you can.
if: If cords or a bulge appear, stop driving on it and use the spare.
If the low spot is on one edge or in patches, have the alignment and suspension checked so new tires don't wear the same way.
If you feel a new thump or vibration, or the tire pressure light comes on, pull over safely and look at the tire before driving further.
result.why: Tread grooves push water out from under the tire. When the tread gets this low, the tire can skim over water and stopping distances get much longer on wet roads. In many places a tire this worn may also fail inspection.

causes.name: Normal wear plus an underlying problem
causes.clues: One area wore down much faster than the rest.

causes.name: Tires simply due for replacement
causes.clues: The tread is low all the way across.

you: Do the penny test at several spots on each tire.
Note where the wear is worst.

result.title: Edge wear on both sides often points to low tire pressure
result.now: Check the pressure in all four tires when cold and set them to the number on the driver's door sticker. Recheck monthly.
if: If one tire keeps going low, it may have a slow leak. Have it found and fixed.
If you often carry heavy loads, check your owner's manual. Some vehicles call for higher pressure when loaded.
If a tire is very low or flat, or you see a nail, cut or bulge in the sidewall, don't drive on it. Use the spare or call for help.
If the pressures were already correct, have the tires and alignment checked, since something else may be causing the wear.
result.why: When a tire is low, its center sags inward and the edges carry the weight. The edges wear faster, the tire runs hotter and fuel economy drops.

causes.name: Tire pressure regularly too low
causes.clues: Pressures haven't been checked in a while, or the tire pressure light has come on.

causes.name: Slow leak in that tire
causes.clues: Only one tire shows this pattern.

causes.name: Frequent heavy loads
causes.clues: Towing or carrying heavy cargo often.

you: Check all tire pressures with a gauge before driving.
Look for nails or damage on the tire that wore worst.

result.title: Center wear often points to tires that are overinflated
result.now: Set the tires to the pressure on the driver's door sticker, not the maximum pressure printed on the tire.
if: If the pressure is already correct, the tire size may not suit the wheel. Ask a tire shop to check.
If only the drive wheels show this, hard acceleration can add to it.
If you see cords, a bulge or a cut, don't drive on that tire.
result.why: Too much air makes the center of the tread bulge slightly and carry most of the weight. The center wears out first, and the tire grips less because less rubber touches the road.

causes.name: Tires filled to the sidewall maximum
causes.clues: The pressure is well above the door sticker number.

causes.name: Tire and wheel width mismatch
causes.clues: Aftermarket wheels or tires of a different size than original.

you: Check the pressure with the tires cold and compare to the door sticker.
shop: Tire size and wheel fitment check

result.title: One-edge wear often points to the wheel alignment
result.now: Book a wheel alignment and ask the shop to check the suspension parts first. Rotate or replace the worn tires as advised.
if: If the wear is severe or the car pulls, get it done sooner.
If the problem came on after hitting a pothole or curb, ask the shop to check for bent parts, not just adjust the alignment.
If you hear clunks over bumps or the steering feels loose, have the steering and suspension checked before driving at speed.
If you can see cords or a bulge, don't drive on that tire.
result.why: If a wheel leans in or out at the top, more weight rides on one edge of the tread and it wears faster. Alignment can drift from potholes and age, and worn parts can make it change while driving.

causes.name: Camber out of spec (wheel tilted in or out)
causes.clues: Smooth wear on one edge only.

causes.name: Bent suspension part from an impact
causes.clues: The wear started after a pothole or curb strike.

causes.name: Lowered or lifted suspension
causes.clues: The vehicle's ride height has been changed.

you: Note which tires and which edge show the wear.
Notice whether the car pulls to one side on a straight road.

result.title: Feathered wear often points to the toe setting
result.now: Book a wheel alignment, and ask the shop to check the tie rod ends for wear before aligning.
if: If the steering wheel is off-center or the car pulls, mention it. It supports an alignment problem.
If you hear clunks or the steering feels loose or wanders, have the steering checked before driving at speed.
result.why: Toe is whether the wheels point straight ahead or slightly in or out. When they point the wrong way, the tire scrubs sideways as it rolls, leaving ridges across the tread. It can wear a tire out fast.

causes.name: Toe out of adjustment
causes.clues: Feathered tread and an off-center steering wheel.

causes.name: Worn tie rod ends
causes.clues: Loose or wandering steering, or a clunk when turning.

causes.name: Bent steering part from an impact
causes.clues: The wear started after hitting something.

you: Check whether the steering wheel is centered when driving straight.

result.title: Worn steering or suspension parts may be causing the wear
result.now: Don't rely on the car until the steering and suspension have been inspected. A badly worn ball joint or tie rod end can come apart with little warning. Have it towed, or ask a mobile mechanic to check it where it's parked.
if: If the steering feels very loose, the car wanders, or you hear a loud clunk followed by a change in steering, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If parts are replaced, get an alignment afterward.
If the shop finds only minor play, ask them how soon the repair is needed and whether the car is OK to use until then.
result.why: Loose ball joints, tie rods or bushings let the wheel shift while driving, so the alignment keeps changing and the tire wears unevenly. An alignment may not hold with worn parts, so a shop will usually check each joint for play first and align after any repairs.

causes.name: Worn ball joint
causes.clues: A clunk over bumps and inner or outer edge wear on one front tire.

causes.name: Worn tie rod end
causes.clues: Loose or wandering steering and feathered tread.

causes.name: Worn control arm bushings
causes.clues: Clunks when braking or accelerating.

you: Note when you hear clunks: over bumps, turning, or braking.
shop: Steering and suspension inspection with the wheels lifted
Ball joint and tie rod play check

result.title: Cupping often points to worn shocks or struts, or wheel balance
result.now: Book an inspection of the shocks, struts and wheel balance, and ask whether the tires can be rotated or need replacing.
if: If the car bounces more than once after a bump, or nose-dives when braking, get it checked sooner.
If there's a growling noise that changes when you steer, a wheel bearing may also be worn.
If you feel a vibration that's getting worse, or you see cords or a bulge, stop and have the tire looked at before driving further.
result.why: When shocks or struts are worn, or a wheel is out of balance, the tire bounces slightly as it rolls and scuffs the road in spots. That leaves a pattern of dips, and usually a humming noise that gets louder with speed.

causes.name: Worn shocks or struts
causes.clues: Bouncy ride, or more body sway than before.

causes.name: Wheel out of balance
causes.clues: Vibration in the steering wheel at highway speed.

causes.name: Loose wheel bearing or suspension parts
causes.clues: A hum or growl, or a clunk over bumps.

you: Push down hard on each corner of the car and let go. It should settle after about one bounce.

result.title: A single flat spot often comes from a skid or a sticking brake
result.now: Have the tire and the brake on that wheel checked when convenient.
if: If that wheel feels much hotter than the others after driving, or the car pulls when braking, the brake may be dragging. Get it checked within a day or two.
If the flat spot goes deep or you feel a thump at speed, have the tire inspected. It may need replacing.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, or the brake pedal feels different, pull over and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: A tire that slides without rolling scrubs off rubber in one spot. That happens in a hard skid, or when a brake grabs or doesn't release fully. A car that sits for weeks can also get a temporary flat spot that smooths out after driving.

causes.name: Skid from hard braking or a locked wheel
causes.clues: A recent emergency stop, or an older car without ABS.

causes.name: Sticking brake caliper or parking brake
causes.clues: One wheel gets hotter than the others, or a burning smell.

causes.name: Tire out of round or damaged
causes.clues: A thump or vibration that started suddenly.

you: After a drive, hold your hand near (not on) each wheel to feel for one that's much hotter.

result.title: This looks like normal front-versus-rear wear that rotation can help even out
result.now: Have the tires rotated on the schedule in your owner's manual and keep the pressures set to the door sticker.
if: If the faster-wearing pair is close to the wear bars, replace them.
If one axle wears very fast even with rotation, have the alignment checked.
If any tire shows cords, a bulge or a cut, don't drive on it.
result.why: Front tires do most of the steering and, on front-wheel-drive cars, most of the pulling. They naturally wear faster than the rears. Rotating them regularly spreads the wear so all four last longer.

causes.name: Tires not rotated regularly
causes.clues: It's been a long time since the last rotation.

causes.name: Front-wheel or rear-wheel drive wear pattern
causes.clues: The drive wheels wear faster.

you: Check your owner's manual for the rotation schedule.
Check tread depth front and rear.
shop: Alignment check if wear is fast

result.title: A tire shop can read the wear pattern for you
result.now: Check the tire pressures today, then book a tire and alignment inspection.
if: If any tire shows cords or a bulge, don't drive on it.
If the car pulls or the steering feels loose, mention it. It helps narrow down the cause.
If you hear clunks or the steering feels loose or wanders, have the steering checked before driving at speed.
result.why: Uneven wear usually comes from tire pressure, alignment, or worn suspension parts. A technician can measure the tread across each tire and narrow it down quickly.

causes.name: Incorrect tire pressure
causes.clues: Pressures haven't been checked recently.

causes.name: Wheel alignment off
causes.clues: The car pulls or the steering wheel is off-center.

causes.name: Worn suspension or steering parts
causes.clues: Clunks or a bouncy ride.

you: Check tire pressures with a gauge.
Take photos of the tread on each tire for the shop.
shop: Tread depth measurement across each tire

q_start.help: Suddenly means it was fine one day and shaking the next. Gradually means it crept in over weeks or months.

opts.a: Suddenly, after hitting a pothole or curb, or I see a bulge on a tire
Right after new tires, a tire rotation or a flat repair
It comes with a humming or growling noise, or clunks, or the car wanders
It crept in gradually, with no other symptoms
I'm not sure

q_where.q: Where do you feel the vibration most?
q_where.help: The front tires usually shake the steering wheel. The rear tires and the drive parts are felt more in the seat and floor.

opts.a: Mostly in the steering wheel
Mostly in the seat or floor
It's only there, or much worse, when I brake
I'm not sure

q_throttle.q: At the speed where it vibrates, does it change when you ease off the gas and coast?
q_throttle.help: Only test this on a quiet, safe stretch of road. Tire and wheel vibrations stay the same at a given speed whether you're on the gas or not. Vibrations that change with the gas pedal point to the axles, driveshaft or engine mounts.

opts.a: No, it feels the same at that speed either way
It's worse when accelerating and fades when I coast
I'm not sure

result.title: A tire or wheel may be damaged
result.now: Pull over safely and look at the tires. If you see a bulge, bubble, cut or bent wheel, put the spare on or call for roadside help.
if: If the tires look fine, don't assume they are. Internal tire damage isn't always visible, so have them checked by roadside service or a mobile tire service before relying on them.
If a wheel looks bent or a lug nut is missing, don't drive on that wheel at all.
If you hear clicking or clunking from a wheel, or the car wobbles, pull over and don't drive further. A wheel may be loose.
result.why: A sudden vibration after a pothole or curb strike can mean a bent wheel or a tire with internal damage, such as a separated belt. A damaged tire can fail suddenly at speed, so it needs to be checked before you rely on it.

causes.name: Damaged tire, bulge or separated belt
causes.clues: A visible bump or bubble on the sidewall or tread, or a thumping that gets faster with speed.

causes.name: Bent wheel
causes.clues: A hard pothole or curb hit, or a visible dent on the rim edge.

causes.name: Lost balance weight
causes.clues: A clean spot on the rim where a weight used to be.
causes.against: Less likely if the vibration is strong or came with a loud impact.

you: With the car parked safely, look over each tire for bulges, cuts and uneven wear.
Check the rims for dents or cracks.
shop: Tire inspection on and off the wheel
Wheel runout check on a balancer
Alignment check after a hard impact

result.title: Often a balance or wheel-seating issue from the recent tire work
result.now: Look over the wheels for missing or loose-looking lug nuts, avoid highway speeds, and ask the tire shop to recheck the balance and lug nut torque today or as soon as they can. Shops expect these rechecks.
if: If you hear clicking or clunking from a wheel, or feel a wobble, pull over and stop driving. A wheel may be loose.
If rebalancing doesn't fix it, ask for a road-force balance or a check for a bent wheel or a defective tire.
result.why: A new vibration right after tire work often comes from a wheel that needs rebalancing, a weight that came off, or a wheel that isn't seated evenly on the hub. These are usually quick to fix, but loose lug nuts are a safety issue, so it's worth checking promptly.

causes.name: Wheel out of balance
causes.clues: A steady vibration that starts at a certain speed and may ease off at higher speeds.

causes.name: Lug nuts not tightened evenly, or a wheel not seated flat
causes.clues: The vibration started right away, or there's a wobble at low speeds too.

causes.name: Defective or out-of-round new tire
causes.clues: Balancing doesn't help, and the vibration follows the tire if it's moved.

you: Check that no lug nuts look loose or missing.
Note the speed where the vibration starts and stops.
shop: Road-force balance or tire uniformity check

result.title: A worn wheel bearing or suspension part may be causing it
result.now: Avoid driving it, especially at highway speed, until the wheel bearings, steering and suspension are inspected. Have it towed, or ask a mobile mechanic to check it where it's parked.
if: If a wheel feels like it's wobbling, the steering feels loose, or you smell burning from a wheel, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If you noticed the growl change when turning left or right, mention it. That can point a shop toward a wheel bearing.
result.why: A vibration that comes with a hum, growl or clunk suggests a worn part rather than simple balance. A wheel bearing that wears too far can overheat and fail, and worn steering joints can lead to loss of control.

causes.name: Worn wheel bearing
causes.clues: A hum or growl that rises with speed and changes when you turn left or right.

causes.name: Worn tie rod end or ball joint
causes.clues: Loose or wandering steering, clunks over bumps, or uneven tire wear.

causes.name: Unevenly worn or cupped tires
causes.clues: A rhythmic humming and a scalloped feel when you run a hand over the tread.

you: Run your hand over the tread (car parked) and feel for uneven, wavy wear.
shop: Wheel bearing play and noise check
Tire wear inspection and alignment check

result.title: A front wheel out of balance is a common cause
result.now: Book a tire balance and inspection soon. Mention the speed where the steering wheel starts to shake.
if: If the vibration gets stronger quickly, or you notice a bulge, stop driving on that tire.
If balancing doesn't fix it, ask the shop to check for a bent wheel, a tire defect or worn steering parts.
If you hear clicking or clunking from a wheel, or the car wobbles, pull over and don't drive further. A wheel may be loose.
result.why: A steering wheel shake that starts around highway speed and often fades a bit at higher speeds is a common sign of a front wheel out of balance. Small weights on the rim keep each wheel balanced, and they can fall off or the tire can wear unevenly over time.

causes.name: Front wheel out of balance
causes.clues: A shake that starts at a certain speed and may smooth out above it.

causes.name: Unevenly worn tire
causes.clues: Tires that haven't been rotated in a long time, or visible uneven wear.

causes.name: Bent wheel or worn steering part
causes.clues: A past pothole hit, or the shake doesn't go away after balancing.

you: Look for a clean spot on the rim where a balance weight may have fallen off.
Check tire pressures with a gauge.

result.title: A rear wheel out of balance or uneven tire wear is a common cause
result.now: Book a tire balance and inspection. Mention that you feel it in the seat at highway speed.
if: If the vibration gets stronger quickly, or you see a bulge on a tire, stop driving on it.
If balancing doesn't help, ask the shop to check the driveshaft or axles.
If you hear clicking or clunking from a wheel, or the car wobbles, pull over and don't drive further. A wheel may be loose.
result.why: A vibration that stays the same at a given speed, whether you're on the gas or coasting, usually comes from something turning with the wheels. Felt mostly in the seat, it usually points to a rear tire out of balance or with uneven wear.

causes.name: Rear wheel out of balance
causes.clues: A steady shake in the seat that starts at a certain speed.

causes.name: Uneven tire wear or a tire defect
causes.clues: Tires that haven't been rotated recently, or uneven tread you can see or feel.

causes.name: Bent wheel
causes.clues: A past pothole or curb hit.

you: Check tire pressures with a gauge.
Look over the rear tires for uneven wear or bulges.
shop: Driveshaft inspection if balancing doesn't help

result.title: An axle, driveshaft or engine mount may be worn
result.now: Have it inspected within the next few days. Until then, accelerate gently and avoid long highway trips.
if: If you hear clunking when shifting or accelerating, or the vibration gets suddenly worse, stop driving and have it towed.
If you hear clicking when turning sharply, mention it. That can point to a worn CV joint on a front-wheel-drive car.
If you smell burning or the car suddenly loses drive, pull over, turn the engine off and have it towed.
result.why: A vibration that's worse when you accelerate and fades when you coast is tied to the parts that send power to the wheels. These include the axle shafts (CV joints), the driveshaft and its joints, and the engine and transmission mounts. Worn drive parts can fail and leave you stranded.

causes.name: Worn inner CV joint (front-wheel drive)
causes.clues: A shudder when accelerating, sometimes with a torn rubber boot and grease on the inside of the wheel.

causes.name: Worn driveshaft U-joint (rear-wheel or all-wheel drive)
causes.clues: A clunk when shifting into gear, or a vibration felt in the floor.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mount
causes.clues: A clunk when accelerating or shifting, or extra shaking at idle in gear.

you: Look behind the front wheels for a torn rubber boot or grease splatter.

result.title: The brakes are the likely source, and uneven rotors are a common cause
result.now: Have the brakes inspected within the next few days. Allow extra stopping distance and avoid hard braking from high speed until then.
if: If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, the brake warning light comes on, or you hear grinding, stop driving and have it towed.
If there's a burning smell or smoke from a wheel, pull over and let the brakes cool, then have them checked before driving further. A dragging brake can overheat.
If the car pulls hard to one side when braking, have it checked before driving further.
result.why: A vibration that appears only when you brake points to the brakes, not the tires. Uneven brake rotors make the pads grab and release as the wheel turns, which you feel as a pulse or shake, worst when slowing from highway speed. A shop will usually measure the rotors and check the calipers before deciding what to replace.

causes.name: Uneven front rotors
causes.clues: A pulsing pedal and a shaking steering wheel when braking.

causes.name: Sticking caliper
causes.clues: One wheel runs hotter, or there's a burning smell.

causes.name: Uneven rear rotors or drums
causes.clues: The shake is felt in the seat rather than the steering wheel.

you: Note whether the shake is in the pedal, the steering wheel, or the seat.

q_temp.q: Is the temperature gauge higher than normal, or is a temperature or coolant warning light on?
q_temp.help: On most cars the needle normally sits near the middle once the engine is warm. Some cars show a blue or red thermometer light instead of a gauge.

opts.a: Yes, it's high or in the red, or I see steam
No, the gauge is normal and no warning lights
I'm not sure

q_where.q: Where is the water dripping from?

opts.a: Under the middle or front passenger side, roughly below the dashboard
From the tailpipe at the back
Under the very front of the car, near the radiator
Somewhere else, or I'm not sure

q_ac.q: Had you been using the A/C, or the defroster, before it dripped?
q_ac.help: The defroster often runs the A/C compressor automatically to dry the air, even when you haven't pressed the A/C button.

opts.a: Yes, and the water is clear with no smell
Yes, but the liquid is colored, slimy or smells sweet
No, the A/C was off
I'm not sure

q_exhaust.q: What does it look like at the tailpipe?

opts.a: A few drips of clear water, maybe a little white vapor that clears once the engine warms up
Thick white smoke that keeps going after it's warm, or a sweet smell
I'm not sure

q_feel.q: Wipe up a little with a white paper towel. What is it like?
q_feel.help: Coolant is usually green, orange, pink, yellow or blue, feels slightly slimy, and smells sweet. Plain water has no color, smell or slickness.

opts.a: Clear, no smell, feels like plain water
Colored, slightly slimy, or smells sweet
Bright blue and smells like glass cleaner
Oily or slick, and doesn't feel like water
I'm not sure

q_coolant_amount.q: How much coolant does it seem to be losing?
q_coolant_amount.help: With the engine cold, look at the see-through coolant overflow tank. It has MIN and MAX (or LOW and FULL) marks.

opts.a: Just a few drops, and the tank is still between the marks
A steady drip or a puddle, or the tank is below the low mark
It's pouring or spraying, or the tank is empty
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be overheating, and the liquid may be coolant
result.now: Pull over safely, turn off the engine and don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you see steam, stay back and don't open the hood until it stops.
If you're still moving and need a few seconds to reach a safe place to stop, turn the heater on full blast. It pulls some heat away from the engine.
If you see smoke rather than steam, or smell fuel or burning, move away from the car.
result.why: A high temperature reading along with dripping liquid often means coolant is escaping. Driving an overheating engine can warp or crack expensive parts within minutes.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or hose
causes.clues: Colored, sweet-smelling liquid under the front of the car.

causes.name: Failed water pump
causes.clues: Drips from the front of the engine, sometimes with a whine or grinding.

causes.name: Cooling fan not working
causes.clues: It overheats mostly when stopped in traffic.

causes.name: Head gasket failure
causes.clues: White, sweet-smelling exhaust and coolant loss with no obvious drip.

you: Once the engine is fully cold, check the coolant overflow tank level.
shop: Combustion gas (block) test for a head gasket leak

result.title: This sounds like normal A/C condensation
result.now: Clear, odorless water here is usually normal and needs no repair. To be sure, check the coolant tank when the engine is cold over the next week and keep an eye on the temperature gauge.
if: If the passenger floor gets wet inside the car, the A/C drain may be blocked. Get it cleared.
If the A/C stops dripping on a hot, humid day but runs cold, the drain may be clogging. Watch for a damp carpet.
If the coolant level drops, the drip turns colored or sweet-smelling, or the temperature gauge rises, have the cooling system checked.
result.why: The A/C pulls moisture out of the cabin air, and it drains out through a small tube under the car, usually near the front passenger footwell. On hot, humid days it can leave a surprisingly big puddle of plain water.

causes.name: Normal A/C condensation
causes.clues: Clear, odorless water under the front passenger area after running the A/C or defroster.
causes.against: If the liquid is colored, slimy or sweet-smelling, it isn't just condensation.

causes.name: Rain or car wash water running off
causes.clues: It's been raining, or the car was recently washed.

you: Touch and smell a drop. It should feel and smell like plain water.
Check that the coolant tank level stays steady over the next week.
shop: A/C drain tube check if the inside floor gets wet

result.title: Water from the tailpipe is usually normal condensation
result.now: This is usually normal. Keep an eye on your coolant level and the temperature gauge for the next few weeks to be sure.
if: If the white smoke doesn't clear after the engine is fully warm, or it smells sweet, have the cooling system checked soon.
If the coolant level keeps dropping with no visible leak, get it checked within a few days.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal, or you see steam, pull over and turn off the engine.
result.why: Burning fuel makes water vapor. On cold starts and short trips it condenses inside the exhaust and drips out the tailpipe. Once the exhaust heats up, it should dry out.

causes.name: Normal exhaust condensation
causes.clues: Cold weather, short trips, and drips that stop once the car is warm.

causes.name: Coolant getting into the engine
causes.clues: Thick white smoke that stays when warm, a sweet smell, and a dropping coolant level.
causes.against: If the coolant level stays steady, this is less likely.

you: Note whether the drips and vapor stop after 10–15 minutes of driving.
Check the coolant tank level when cold, once a week for a few weeks.
shop: Cooling system pressure test if coolant is dropping

result.title: Coolant may be leaking into the engine and burning
result.now: Stop driving it. Once the engine is cold, check the coolant tank level, then have it towed or have a mobile mechanic check it.
if: If the temperature gauge rises at all, pull over as soon as it's safe and shut the engine off.
If the engine oil on the dipstick looks milky, like chocolate milk, coolant may be mixing with the oil. Don't start it again.
result.why: Thick, sweet-smelling white smoke that doesn't clear often means coolant is getting into the cylinders and burning. That can point to a head gasket or cracked part, which a shop will confirm with tests before any repair, and driving on it can overheat the engine and cause major damage.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: Steady white smoke, coolant loss with no visible leak, and possible overheating.

causes.name: Cracked cylinder head or block
causes.clues: The engine overheated badly at some point.

causes.name: Leaking intake gasket (some engines)
causes.clues: Coolant loss and a rough idle.

you: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold.
Pull the oil dipstick and look for a milky, light-brown color.

result.title: Clear, odorless water is often condensation or rain runoff
result.now: Check the coolant tank level when the engine is cold. If it's between the marks and stays there over the next few days, this water is most often condensation or runoff.
if: If the coolant level drops over the next week, the drip may be watered-down coolant. Have the cooling system checked.
If water also shows up inside the car, check our guide to water leaking inside the car.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal, or you see steam, pull over and turn off the engine.
result.why: Plain water with no color, smell or slickness is usually A/C condensation or rain and wash water dripping off the body. Coolant mixed with a lot of water can look clear, though, so the coolant level is the real test.

causes.name: A/C condensation
causes.clues: It drips under the passenger side after the A/C or defroster has run.

causes.name: Rain or wash water
causes.clues: It rained or the car was washed recently.

causes.name: Diluted coolant
causes.clues: The coolant tank level slowly drops, or the drip is near the radiator.

you: Check the coolant tank level when cold, then again in a few days.
Put cardboard under the car overnight on a dry night.
shop: Cooling system pressure test if the level drops

result.title: It looks like windshield washer fluid
result.now: Check the washer fluid tank and its hoses for cracks or a loose connection. Refill it and see if the level drops.
if: If the washer fluid empties quickly, the tank, pump or a hose may be cracked. Get it fixed so you're not left without washers in bad weather.
If the fluid looks green or orange and smells sweet rather than like glass cleaner, it may be coolant. Check the coolant level.
result.why: Washer fluid is usually bright blue and smells like glass cleaner. Its tank sits near the front of the car, and cracked tanks or loose hoses are common.

causes.name: Cracked washer fluid tank
causes.clues: It drips near a front corner, especially after filling.

causes.name: Loose or split washer hose
causes.clues: It leaks when you use the washers.

causes.name: Leaking washer pump seal
causes.clues: Drips at the bottom of the tank.

you: Fill the washer tank and watch for drips.
Use the washers and look for leaks from the hoses.

result.title: If it's oily, it isn't water. Another fluid is leaking
result.now: Note the color on the paper towel and where it drips, then check your engine oil, brake fluid, transmission and power steering fluid levels. Have the leak identified within a day or two.
if: If the drip is near a wheel, or it's clear to yellowish and slick, it could be brake fluid. Don't drive it until it's been inspected, even if the brake fluid level looks OK.
If the brake fluid level is low or the brake pedal feels soft, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If you can't tell what it is, or it leaves a puddle bigger than a plate overnight, have it inspected before driving much.
If it smells like gasoline, don't start the engine. Keep sparks and flames away and have it towed.
If a warning light comes on or the steering feels heavy, pull over and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Water doesn't feel slick. An oily liquid means engine oil, transmission fluid, power steering fluid or brake fluid. The color and where it drips help narrow it down, and a shop can confirm it.

causes.name: Engine oil
causes.clues: Brown or black, under the engine.

causes.name: Transmission or power steering fluid
causes.clues: Red, pink or amber.

causes.name: Brake fluid
causes.clues: Clear to yellowish and slick, often near a wheel.

you: Check every fluid level you can reach.
Take a photo of the puddle and the paper towel for the shop.

result.title: Check the coolant level to rule out a leak
result.now: When the engine is cold, look at the coolant overflow tank and note where the level sits. Check it again in a few days.
if: If the level drops, have the cooling system checked within a few days.
If the temperature gauge ever climbs above normal, pull over and turn off the engine.
If you see steam or smell something sweet, stop the engine and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Most clear drips turn out to be condensation, but a slow coolant leak can look similar. A dropping coolant level is the simplest way to tell them apart.

causes.name: A/C or exhaust condensation
causes.clues: Clear water, and the coolant level stays steady.

causes.name: Slow coolant leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, colored drips, or a coolant level that keeps dropping.

you: Check the coolant tank level when cold.
Put cardboard under the car overnight and look at the color of any drips.

result.title: This sounds like a small coolant seep, often from a hose, clamp or the radiator
result.now: Check the coolant level when cold every few days, top it up with the type in your owner's manual if needed, and book a check.
if: If the level keeps dropping or the drips get bigger, get it checked within a few days.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn off the engine.
If you see steam, white smoke from the exhaust, or smell coolant inside the car, have it checked before driving further.
result.why: A few drops with a steady level means a slow seep. If the level holds steady it can usually wait for a booked check, but cooling system leaks tend to grow, and running low on coolant leads to overheating.

causes.name: Loose clamp or aging hose
causes.clues: Dried, crusty coolant residue on a hose end.

causes.name: Radiator seep
causes.clues: Residue or dampness on the radiator, at the very front.

causes.name: Water pump starting to leak
causes.clues: Drips or residue near the front of the engine, by the belt.

you: Look for crusty white, green or pink residue on hoses and the radiator.
Track the coolant level when cold.
shop: Dye test if the source isn't clear

result.title: An active coolant leak that needs checking soon
result.now: When the engine is cold, top up the coolant to the full mark with the type in your owner's manual. Limit driving to what's necessary, watch the temperature gauge closely, and get it checked within a few days. If you can't top it up, don't drive it.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal or you see steam, pull over and turn off the engine. Don't restart it.
If the level drops a lot after one short trip, or you see a stream rather than drips, don't drive it. Have it towed.
result.why: A steady drip or a low tank means the engine is losing coolant faster than is safe. Without enough coolant it will overheat, which can cause serious engine damage.

causes.name: Leaking radiator hose
causes.clues: Drips at a hose end, or a soft, swollen hose.

causes.name: Leaking radiator
causes.clues: Drips from the very front, under the radiator.

causes.name: Water pump leak
causes.clues: Drips from the front of the engine, near the belt.

you: Note how much coolant you add and how quickly the level drops.
Put cardboard under the car overnight to mark the drip spot.

result.title: A major coolant leak. The engine could overheat within minutes
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you see steam, stay back and don't open the hood or the coolant cap until it has fully cooled.
If the temperature gauge was in the red before you stopped, tell the shop. They may want to check for overheating damage.
result.why: With coolant pouring out or the tank empty, the engine has nothing to carry heat away. Running it, even briefly, risks warping or cracking engine parts.

causes.name: Burst or split radiator hose
causes.clues: A sudden gush, often with steam.

causes.name: Cracked radiator or overflow tank
causes.clues: Coolant pouring from the front of the car.

causes.name: Failed water pump
causes.clues: Coolant streaming from the front of the engine.

shop: Hose, radiator and water pump inspection

q_type.help: Press a white paper towel into the wet carpet and smell it. Coolant is often green, orange or pink and smells sweet.

opts.a: Plain water, no color or smell
Sweet-smelling or slightly slimy, or there's a greasy fog on the inside of the windshield
It smells musty or moldy, but I'm not sure what it is
I'm not sure
The front passenger footwell
The driver's footwell
Dripping from the headliner, dome light or roof pillars
Rear footwells or under the rear seats
The trunk or cargo area
Several places, or I'm not sure

q_passenger_when.q: When does the passenger floor get wet?
q_passenger_when.help: The A/C drain usually exits under the car near the passenger footwell, so this question helps separate the two most common causes.

opts.a: After running the A/C, even on dry days
After rain or a car wash
Both, or I'm not sure

q_when.q: When does it get wet?

opts.a: Only after rain or a car wash
After running the A/C
After driving through deep water, or the car sat in a flood
I'm not sure

q_sunroof.q: Does your car have a sunroof or moonroof?

opts.a: Yes
No
I'm not sure

result.title: The heater core may be leaking coolant into the cabin
result.now: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold, top it up if needed, and get the car checked within a few days. Keep the windows cracked while you drive.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn off the engine. Don't restart it.
If the windshield fogs so badly you can't see, don't drive it until it's fixed.
If the coolant level is dropping fast, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If steam or hot liquid comes from the vents or under the dash, pull over, turn the engine off and get out.
If the fumes make your eyes sting or give you a headache, open the windows and stop driving.
result.why: The heater core is a small radiator behind the dashboard. When it leaks, hot coolant can soak the passenger carpet and its vapor leaves a greasy, sweet-smelling film on the glass. You're losing coolant, and the vapor isn't something you want to breathe.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: A sweet smell inside, a greasy film on the windshield, and wet passenger carpet.
causes.against: If the liquid is plain water with no smell, this is unlikely.

causes.name: Leaking heater hose connection
causes.clues: Coolant loss and wetness near the firewall, where the hoses go into the dash.

causes.name: Blocked A/C drain
causes.clues: The water is clear and odorless, and it happens after running the A/C.
causes.against: A sweet smell points away from this.

you: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold.
Smell the wet carpet and look for a greasy film on the inside of the windshield.
shop: Check for coolant in the HVAC case

result.title: The A/C drain may be blocked
result.now: Look under the car near the passenger footwell while the A/C runs. If no water drips out, the drain tube may be clogged. Book a check to have it cleared and the carpet dried.
if: If the carpet stays wet for more than a few days, have it dried properly to prevent mold and damage to wiring under the floor.
If the water smells sweet, it may be coolant, not A/C water. Check your coolant level.
result.why: The A/C pulls water out of the air and drains it through a small tube under the car. If leaves, dirt or insects block that tube, the water backs up and spills onto the passenger floor instead.

causes.name: Clogged A/C evaporator drain
causes.clues: No drip under the car when the A/C runs, and a wet passenger floor on dry days.

causes.name: Drain tube kinked or disconnected
causes.clues: It started after work behind the dashboard.

causes.name: Heater core leak
causes.clues: The water smells sweet or the windshield fogs with a film.
causes.against: Plain, odorless water points away from this.

you: Run the A/C for 10 minutes on a warm day and check for a drip under the car.
Feel the carpet after an A/C-only drive with no rain.

result.title: Rainwater may be getting in at the base of the windshield
result.now: Open the hood and clear any leaves or debris from the vented panel below the windshield, then book a check if it still leaks.
if: If water reaches the fuse box or wiring under the dash, or electrical things start acting up, get it checked within a few days.
If the carpet stays wet, have it dried to prevent mold.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the dash or seats, turn the car off and get out. If the airbag light or other warning lights come on, have it checked before relying on the car.
result.why: The area below the windshield, called the cowl, collects rainwater and drains it away. When its drains clog with leaves, water can overflow into the fresh-air intake or past seals and end up on the passenger floor.

causes.name: Clogged cowl drains
causes.clues: Leaves or debris in the panel below the windshield, and it's worse after heavy rain.

causes.name: Windshield seal leak
causes.clues: Water appears high up, near the top of the dash or the pillar.

causes.name: Missing cabin air filter cover or seal
causes.clues: Recent cabin filter replacement.

you: Clear leaves and debris from the cowl area.
Have someone run a garden hose over the windshield base while you watch inside.
shop: Water test of the cowl, windshield and door seals

result.title: A door seal, windshield seal or body drain may be letting rain in
result.now: Dry the carpet and book a water test so a shop can find exactly where it's getting in.
if: If the carpet stays wet or smells musty, have it dried properly to prevent mold.
If electrical things start acting up, get it checked within a few days. Wiring and modules often sit under the carpet.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the dash or seats, turn the car off and get out. If the airbag light or other warning lights come on, have it checked before relying on the car.
result.why: Rubber seals harden and shrink with age, and doors have drain holes at the bottom that can clog. Either one lets rain or car wash water work its way into the footwell.

causes.name: Worn or damaged door seal
causes.clues: Water near the door sill, or light visible around the closed door.

causes.name: Clogged door drain holes
causes.clues: Water sloshing inside the door, or a wet sill after rain.

causes.name: Windshield or cowl leak
causes.clues: Water appears at the top of the footwell, near the dash.

you: Look for torn or flattened rubber seals around the door.
Check that the drain holes at the bottom of the door are clear.

result.title: The sunroof drains may be clogged
result.now: Open the sunroof and slowly pour a cup of water into the channel near a corner. It should drain out under the car within a few seconds. If it pools, that drain is clogged.
if: If the water doesn't drain, have a shop clear the drains. Forcing high-pressure air into them can pop the hoses loose.
If water drips near the dome light or airbag areas, or electrical things act up, get it checked within a few days.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the dash or seats, turn the car off and get out. If the airbag light or other warning lights come on, have it checked before relying on the car.
result.why: Sunroofs aren't watertight. They catch water in a tray and send it out through small hoses in the roof pillars. When those hoses clog or come loose, water overflows into the headliner and runs down the pillars.

causes.name: Clogged sunroof drain tubes
causes.clues: Water pools in the sunroof channel instead of draining.

causes.name: Disconnected or cracked drain tube
causes.clues: Water drains from the channel but still ends up inside, often down a pillar.

causes.name: Worn sunroof seal
causes.clues: It leaks only in heavy rain, around the glass edge.

you: Pour a little water into each corner of the sunroof channel and watch where it goes.
Look for water stains on the headliner near the pillars.
shop: Sunroof drain cleaning and tube inspection

result.title: A windshield, roof or roof-rack seal may be leaking
result.now: Dry the area, then book a water test to find where it's getting in.
if: If water drips near the dome light, airbag covers or other wiring, get it checked within a few days.
If the headliner stays damp or smells musty, have it dried to prevent mold.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the dash or seats, turn the car off and get out. If the airbag light or other warning lights come on, have it checked before relying on the car.
result.why: Without a sunroof, water coming through the roof area usually gets past the windshield seal, a roof-rack mount or an antenna base. These leaks often show up at the headliner or run down a pillar.

causes.name: Windshield seal leak
causes.clues: Water at the top corners of the windshield, especially after a windshield replacement.

causes.name: Roof rack or antenna mount seal
causes.clues: A drip spot directly below the rack or antenna.

causes.name: Rear window or hatch seal
causes.clues: Water near the back of the headliner.

you: Look for water stains on the headliner and note where they start.
Check whether the windshield was replaced recently.

result.title: Water in the rear may be coming past a door seal, drain or body plug
result.now: Lift the floor mats to see how wet it is, dry it out, and book a water test.
if: If the car has a sunroof, check the rear sunroof drains too. They often empty near the rear doors.
If the carpet stays wet, have it dried properly to prevent mold and corrosion.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the dash or seats, turn the car off and get out. If the airbag light or other warning lights come on, have it checked before relying on the car.
result.why: Rear footwells usually get wet from rear door seals, clogged door drains or a missing rubber plug in the floor. On cars with a sunroof, a blocked rear drain can also send water down the back pillars.

causes.name: Rear door seal or clogged door drains
causes.clues: Water near the rear door sills after rain.

causes.name: Missing or loose floor plug
causes.clues: It gets wet after driving through puddles, not just after rain.

causes.name: Rear sunroof drain
causes.clues: Water stains on the rear pillars or headliner.
causes.against: No sunroof rules this out.

you: Check the rear door seals and the drain holes at the bottom of the doors.
Look under the carpet for wet padding.

result.title: A trunk seal, taillight gasket or body plug may be leaking
result.now: Lift the trunk floor and check the spare tire well for water, then look for cracked taillights or a torn trunk seal.
if: If water keeps collecting, book a water test so it doesn't cause rust in the floor.
If there's wiring or a battery in the trunk area, get it checked within a few days.
If you smell burning or see smoke from the trunk area, turn the car off and get out.
result.why: Trunks commonly leak through worn lid seals, taillight gaskets or a rear window seal. Water often collects unseen in the spare tire well and can lead to rust and a musty smell.

causes.name: Taillight gasket
causes.clues: Water trails below the taillights inside the trunk.

causes.name: Trunk lid or hatch seal
causes.clues: Water near the trunk opening after rain.

causes.name: Missing or loose body plug
causes.clues: Water in the spare tire well after driving in wet weather.

you: Check the spare tire well.
Look for cracked taillights and torn seals.

result.title: Water may have gotten into the engine, electrical system or airbags
result.now: Don't start the car. Have it towed to a shop and contact your insurance company.
if: If the car is already running and the water was only at the bottom of the doors, turn it off and have it inspected before relying on it.
If the engine stalled while driving through water, don't try to restart it. That can badly damage the engine.
If you smell burning or see smoke, get out and stay away from the car.
result.why: Deep water can get into the engine's air intake, which can wreck the engine if you start it. It can also soak wiring, computers and airbag parts under the seats and carpet, causing problems that show up weeks later.

causes.name: Water entering through door seals and floor openings
causes.clues: Wet carpet and padding after deep water.

causes.name: Water in the engine air intake
causes.clues: The engine stalled in the water or won't turn over normally.

causes.name: Water in electrical connectors and modules
causes.clues: Warning lights, odd electrical behavior, or a musty smell later on.

you: Note how high the water came on the outside of the car.
Take photos for your insurance company.
shop: Air intake and engine oil check for water
Carpet and padding removal to dry the floor

result.title: A water test will show where it's getting in
result.now: Dry the carpet, then on a dry day run the A/C for 10 minutes and check the floor. If it's still dry, have someone run a garden hose over the car while you watch inside.
if: If it only gets wet with the A/C on, the A/C drain may be blocked.
If it smells sweet or the windshield fogs with a greasy film, check your coolant level. It may be the heater core.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the dash or seats, turn the car off and get out. If the airbag light or other warning lights come on, have it checked before relying on the car.
result.why: Most interior water comes from either the A/C drain or a rain leak. Testing them one at a time, A/C first and then a hose, tells you which one, and a shop can pinpoint it from there.

causes.name: Blocked A/C drain
causes.clues: Wet passenger floor after A/C use, even on dry days.

causes.name: Clogged cowl or body drains
causes.clues: It's worse after heavy rain or a car wash.

causes.name: Worn door or windshield seal
causes.clues: Water near a door sill or the top of the dash.

you: Test with the A/C first, then with a hose.
Feel under the carpet to see where it's wettest.

q_danger.q: Along with the whine, do you notice any of these?

opts.a: The engine revs up but the car doesn't speed up, or it slips or bangs into gear
The temperature gauge is climbing, or the steering suddenly feels heavy
The battery light is on, or the lights dim and flicker
None of these, just the whine
I'm not sure

q_park_test.q: With the car in Park (or Neutral with the parking brake on), gently rev the engine. Do you hear the same whine?
q_park_test.help: Parts driven by the engine's belt, like the alternator and power steering pump, whine whenever the engine revs. The transmission, axles and differential usually only whine when the car is moving.

opts.a: Yes, it whines when I rev in Park
No, it only whines while driving
I'm not sure
