It gets louder when I turn the steering wheel
It sounds electrical, or the headlights pulse along with it
A whistle or siren that rises sharply when I accelerate hard (turbocharged engine)
A steady whine or squeal from the front of the engine, near the belts
I'm not sure

q_driving_whine.q: While driving, which best describes the whine?

opts.a: It changes pitch when the transmission shifts, or it's tied to engine speed in each gear
It rises with road speed and changes when I let off the gas (rear-wheel, 4WD or AWD vehicle)
It's an electric or hybrid car, and it's a smooth, faint whine that's always been there
I'm not sure

result.title: The transmission may be slipping. Driving on can cause major damage
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and check under the car for red or pink fluid. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic rather than driving further.
if: If you find the transmission fluid is low on a car with a dipstick, adding the correct fluid may help, but have it checked before relying on it.
If the car won't move at all, turn on your hazard lights and call roadside assistance.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: A whine together with revs that climb without the car speeding up often means the transmission isn't gripping properly. Low fluid is a common reason. Continuing to drive can overheat and destroy the transmission, and it can lose drive without warning.

causes.name: Low transmission fluid from a leak
causes.clues: Red or pink drips under the middle of the car, or a burnt smell.

causes.name: Worn clutches or bands inside the transmission
causes.clues: Slipping that has been getting worse over weeks, especially in one gear.

causes.name: Torque converter or CVT problem
causes.clues: A whine and shudder when pulling away, or a loud whine that rises with engine speed.

you: Look for red or pink fluid under the car.
Check the transmission fluid level if your car has a dipstick for it, following the owner's manual.
shop: Transmission fluid level and condition check

result.title: A belt or belt-driven pump may be failing
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe and shut the engine off. Once it cools, check whether the belt is still in place, then have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic rather than driving on.
if: If the temperature gauge went into the red, don't restart the engine. Overheating can seriously damage it.
If you see coolant leaking from the front of the engine, the water pump may have failed.
If the steering went heavy, expect it to take much more effort until the car is stopped. Slow down gradually and steer gently.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: On many engines one belt drives the water pump, power steering pump and alternator. A whining bearing that seizes, or a belt that slips or breaks, can make the engine overheat and the steering go heavy within minutes.

causes.name: Failing water pump bearing
causes.clues: A whine from the front of the engine, coolant drips near the pump, and a rising temperature gauge.

causes.name: Slipping or broken drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal before the problem started, then heavy steering and a battery light.

causes.name: Seized idler or tensioner pulley
causes.clues: A loud whine or squeal that got worse quickly, then the belt came off.

you: With the engine off and cool, check that the belt is on its pulleys and not frayed.
Look for coolant drips at the front of the engine.

result.title: The alternator or charging system may be the source
result.now: Have the battery and charging system tested within a few days. Many auto parts stores can run this test. Avoid long trips and night driving until then.
if: If the battery light comes on and stays on, avoid driving any distance. The car may stall once the battery runs down, and steering and braking can then take much more effort. Have it checked as soon as you can, or towed if you're not close.
If you smell burning or the engine bay smells hot, pull over and shut the engine off.
If the temperature gauge rises or the steering suddenly gets heavy, the drive belt may have come off. Pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: The alternator spins fast and makes electricity as you drive. A worn bearing whines, and a failing internal part can make an electrical whine that rises with engine speed. If it stops charging, the car runs on the battery until it goes flat.

causes.name: Worn alternator bearing
causes.clues: A whine from the alternator that rises with engine speed, even in Park.

causes.name: Failing alternator diode or regulator
causes.clues: A whine through the radio speakers, dimming lights, or a battery light.

causes.name: Worn idler or tensioner pulley
causes.clues: The whine is from the belt area but not directly at the alternator. A shop will usually listen with a stethoscope or spin the pulleys by hand before replacing the alternator.

you: Watch for the battery light while driving.
Note whether the lights pulse or dim with engine speed.
shop: Charging system and alternator output test

result.title: Low power steering fluid or a worn pump may be the cause
result.now: With the engine off, check the power steering fluid level against the marks on the reservoir, and top it up with the fluid type in your owner's manual if it's low.
if: If the fluid was low, look for a leak and have it checked within a few days. Fluid doesn't get used up on its own.
If the whine stays after topping up, book a check. If the steering feels heavy or jerky, have it checked before driving further.
If your car has electric power steering with no fluid reservoir, a whine needs a shop to check it.
If fluid is dripping near the exhaust, or you smell burning, pull over and turn the engine off. Power steering fluid can catch fire on hot parts.
result.why: A hydraulic power steering pump works hardest when you turn the wheel, so a whine that rises when steering often points to it. Low fluid makes the pump suck in air and whine, and a worn pump whines even when full.

causes.name: Low power steering fluid
causes.clues: The reservoir is below the mark, or there's oily residue on hoses or under the front of the car.

causes.name: Worn power steering pump
causes.clues: The fluid is full, but the whine is loudest at full lock.

causes.name: Air or old fluid in the system
causes.clues: The fluid looks foamy or dark.

you: Check the power steering fluid level and color.
Look for leaks around the pump, hoses and steering rack.

result.title: Some turbo whistle is normal, but a louder siren needs a check
result.now: Book a check when convenient if the sound is new or louder than it used to be. Make sure the oil is full and changed on schedule, since turbos depend on clean oil.
if: If you see blue or gray smoke from the exhaust, or the oil level drops, get it checked within a few days.
If the engine loses power or a warning light comes on, get it checked soon.
If there's a grinding or scraping sound from the turbo, stop driving and have it towed.
If you see heavy smoke or the oil warning light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Turbochargers spin very fast and naturally make a light whistle when they build boost. A loud siren-like whine that's new can mean worn turbo bearings or a boost leak from a loose or split hose.

causes.name: Normal turbo spool sound
causes.clues: A light whistle you've always heard when accelerating.
causes.against: If it's new or much louder, something else is more likely.

causes.name: Boost leak from a loose clamp or split hose
causes.clues: A whoosh or whistle with less power than usual.

causes.name: Worn turbocharger bearings
causes.clues: A loud siren whine, oil use, or blue smoke.

you: Check the oil level.
Look for loose or split hoses between the turbo and the engine.

result.title: Often a worn pulley bearing or another belt-driven part
result.now: Book a check within the next week or two. With the engine off, look at the belt for cracks or glazing.
if: If the noise gets much louder, turns into a grind, or the battery light comes on, get it checked within a few days.
If the belt breaks, the engine can overheat and the steering can go heavy. Pull over right away if that happens.
If you smell burning rubber or see smoke from the engine bay, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: The front of the engine has several pulleys turned by one or more belts. When a pulley bearing wears, it whines in step with engine speed, in Park or driving. Catching it early can prevent a broken belt. A shop will usually check each pulley with the belt off before deciding which part to replace.

causes.name: Worn idler or tensioner pulley
causes.clues: A steady whine or rumble from the belt area that changes with engine speed.

causes.name: Worn alternator bearing
causes.clues: The whine is loudest at the alternator.

causes.name: Worn water pump bearing
causes.clues: Coolant seepage near the pump.

you: With the engine off, look at the belt for cracks or a shiny, glazed surface.
Record a short video with sound with the hood open.

result.title: The transmission may be the source of the whine
result.now: Have the transmission fluid level and condition checked within a few days. Avoid towing or heavy loads until then.
if: If the transmission starts slipping, shifting harshly or a warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If you see red or pink fluid under the car, mention it. A leak can quickly lead to low fluid.
If you smell burning or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: A whine that changes when the transmission shifts is likely coming from inside it. Low or worn-out fluid is a common cause and is much cheaper to fix early. Worn bearings, a torque converter or a CVT belt can also whine.

causes.name: Low or old transmission fluid
causes.clues: A leak, a burnt smell, or no fluid service on a high-mileage car.

causes.name: Worn torque converter or pump
causes.clues: A whine that's loudest when pulling away and changes with engine speed.

causes.name: CVT wear
causes.clues: On a car with a CVT (no distinct gear shifts), a whine or drone that's getting louder.

you: Look for red or pink fluid under the car.
Check the transmission fluid if your car has a dipstick, following the owner's manual.
shop: Transmission fluid level and condition check

result.title: The differential may be the source, from low fluid or wear
result.now: Have the differential fluid checked within a few days, and avoid towing or heavy loads until then.
if: If the whine becomes a grind or clunk, or you see gear oil leaking near the axle, stop driving and have it towed.
If the fluid is low, topping it up may quiet it. A shop will usually check the fluid for metal before deciding whether parts are worn.
If you feel a new vibration, or smell hot gear oil or burning near the rear axle, pull over and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: The differential sends power to the drive wheels through a set of gears in thick gear oil. Worn gears or bearings, or low oil, make a whine that rises with road speed and changes when you switch between accelerating and coasting.

causes.name: Low or worn-out differential fluid
causes.clues: Oily residue on the differential, or the fluid has never been changed.

causes.name: Worn ring and pinion gears
causes.clues: A whine mostly when accelerating at certain speeds.

causes.name: Worn pinion or carrier bearings
causes.clues: A whine or growl that's worse when coasting or decelerating.

you: Look for oil leaking from the differential housing.
Note whether the whine is worse when accelerating or coasting.
shop: Differential fluid level and condition check
Road test and chassis microphone test

result.title: A faint whine is often normal in electric and hybrid cars
result.now: Notice whether the sound is the same as it has always been. A smooth, faint whine that rises with speed is typical of the electric motor and its gears.
if: If the whine gets louder, changes in tone, or comes with a warning light or vibration, book a check with a shop that works on hybrids or EVs.
If you hear grinding or clunking, get it checked within a few days.
If a red warning light comes on, power drops suddenly, or you smell burning, pull over when it's safe, turn the car off and contact a shop or roadside assistance before driving further.
result.why: Electric motors and their reduction gears spin very fast and make a light whine, which you notice more because there's no engine noise to cover it. Some cars also play an artificial sound at low speed so pedestrians can hear them.

causes.name: Normal electric motor and gear noise
causes.clues: A smooth whine that has always been there and rises with speed.
causes.against: If it's new or getting louder, wear is more likely.

causes.name: Pedestrian warning sound
causes.clues: A hum or whine heard mostly at low speeds, from the front of the car.

causes.name: Worn reduction gear or bearing
causes.clues: The whine is louder than before, or there's a vibration.

you: Compare the sound with a similar car, or record it now so you can tell if it changes later.
shop: Road test by a hybrid or EV technician

result.title: A driveline whine needs a road test to pin down
result.now: Book a road test and inspection within the next week or two. Tell the shop the whine only happens while driving, not when revving in Park.
if: If the transmission starts slipping or shifting oddly, get it checked within a few days.
If you hear grinding or feel a new vibration, get it checked soon.
If you smell burning, see smoke, a warning light comes on or the car loses drive, pull over and have it towed.
result.why: A whine that only happens while moving comes from something that turns with the wheels or carries power to them: the transmission, the differential, or a wheel bearing. A technician can usually tell them apart on a road test.

causes.name: Transmission noise
causes.clues: The whine changes with gear shifts.

causes.name: Differential noise
causes.clues: The whine rises with road speed and changes between accelerating and coasting.

causes.name: Worn wheel bearing
causes.clues: More of a hum or growl that changes when you steer left or right.

you: Look for fluid leaks under the car.
Note the speed and gear when the whine is loudest.

q_steering_feel.q: Is the steering harder to turn than usual, or is a warning light on?
q_steering_feel.help: A steering warning light usually shows a steering wheel symbol, often with an exclamation mark.

opts.a: Yes, it suddenly became very hard to turn
A steering warning light is on
Steering feels normal, or only slightly heavier
I'm not sure

q_type.q: Does your car have a power steering fluid reservoir under the hood?
q_type.help: It's usually a small plastic tank with a cap marked with a steering wheel symbol or "power steering". Many newer cars use electric power steering, which has no fluid at all. Your owner's manual will say which you have.

opts.a: Yes, it has a reservoir
No, it has electric power steering
I'm not sure

q_fluid.q: With the engine off, check the fluid level on the reservoir or its dipstick. What do you find?
q_fluid.help: Many reservoirs have separate HOT and COLD marks. Use the COLD mark if the engine hasn't been run for a while.

opts.a: The level is low or empty
The level is fine, but the fluid looks foamy or bubbly, or very dark and smells burnt
The level is fine and the fluid looks normal
I'm not sure, or I can't check it

q_when.q: When is the whine loudest?

opts.a: Only when I hold the wheel turned all the way to one side
On cold mornings, and it fades as the car warms up
Every time I turn, and it's been getting louder
It's more of a high squeal, especially right after starting
I'm not sure

result.title: The power steering may have lost its assist
result.now: Pull over safely and turn the engine off. With the engine off, look for a broken or missing belt and for fluid leaks, then have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the battery or temperature light also came on, the main engine belt may have broken. Don't restart the engine.
If the fluid reservoir is empty, don't just refill it and carry on. A pump run dry can fail completely, and the leak needs to be found.
If you smell burning or see smoke, step away from the car.
result.why: A whine that turns into suddenly heavy steering usually means the system has stopped helping you steer. Steering then takes a lot of effort, which is risky in an emergency. On many cars the same belt also drives the alternator and water pump.

causes.name: Power steering fluid has leaked out
causes.clues: An empty or very low reservoir, and fluid under the front of the car.
causes.against: Doesn't apply to electric power steering.

causes.name: Broken or slipping drive belt
causes.clues: A loud squeal or slap before it happened, or battery and temperature lights on.

causes.name: Failed power steering pump or electric steering motor
causes.clues: Fluid and belt are fine, but there's no assist.

you: With the engine off, check whether the belt is still in place.
Check the power steering fluid level, if your car has a reservoir.
shop: Code scan for electric steering faults

result.title: The electric power steering has detected a fault
result.now: Once parked safely, turn the car off for a minute and restart it. If the light stays on, have it checked within the next few days and avoid highways and fast traffic until then. The assist can drop out without warning, so be ready for the steering to need more effort.
if: If the steering is heavy, or the steering warning light is red, don't drive it. Have it towed or checked where it's parked.
If the battery light is also on or the car has been slow to start, the battery or charging system may be the root cause. Electric steering needs steady voltage.
result.why: Electric steering uses a motor to help you turn the wheel. When the computer finds a problem, it turns on the warning light and may reduce or switch off the assist. A whine can come from the motor working harder than it should.

causes.name: Low battery voltage or charging problem
causes.clues: The battery light, slow starting, or dim lights.

causes.name: Steering sensor or motor fault
causes.clues: The light stays on after a restart, and assist varies.

causes.name: Hydraulic system low on fluid
causes.clues: Only on cars that have a power steering fluid reservoir.

you: Restart the car and see whether the light goes out.
Note whether the battery light has come on recently.
shop: Code scan for the steering system

result.title: Low power steering fluid, which usually means a leak
result.now: Top up the reservoir to the correct mark using the fluid type listed in your owner's manual or on the cap. Then get the leak found within the next few days.
if: If the whine goes away after topping up, keep checking the level every few days. If it drops again, the leak needs fixing soon.
If the steering gets heavy or the reservoir empties quickly, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If fluid is dripping near the exhaust, or you smell burning, pull over and turn the engine off. Power steering fluid can catch fire on hot parts.
result.why: Power steering fluid works in a closed loop, so a low level means it's leaking somewhere. When the pump runs short of fluid it pulls in air and whines, and running it low for long can wear out the pump.

causes.name: Leaking hose or fitting
causes.clues: Wet, oily spots on the hoses running from the pump.

causes.name: Leaking steering rack
causes.clues: Fluid inside the rubber boots at the ends of the rack, or drips near the front wheels.

causes.name: Leaking pump seal
causes.clues: Wetness on or under the pump at the front of the engine.

you: Top up the fluid and recheck the level after a few days.
Put a piece of cardboard under the front of the car overnight to look for drips.
shop: Steering rack boot and hose inspection

result.title: Air in the system or worn-out fluid may be the cause
result.now: Book a power steering check when convenient. Ask for the system to be inspected and the fluid flushed or bled if needed.
if: If the fluid level starts dropping, look for a leak and get it checked within a few days.
If the steering feels heavy or jerky, have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Foamy fluid usually means air is getting into the system, often through a loose hose clamp or a seal on the pump's supply side. Very dark, burnt-smelling fluid has broken down and doesn't protect the pump well. Both can cause a whine.

causes.name: Air in the system
causes.clues: Foamy or bubbly fluid, often after a repair or with a loose return hose.

causes.name: Old or wrong type of fluid
causes.clues: Dark, burnt-smelling fluid, or fluid recently topped up with a different type.

causes.name: Clogged reservoir screen
causes.clues: The whine continues even with the right amount of fresh fluid.

you: Note when the fluid was last changed or topped up, and with what.
Look for loose clamps on the hoses at the reservoir.

result.title: Electric steering can make a faint whir, but a loud whine needs a check
result.now: Book a check when convenient, and mention whether the noise happens when parked, at low speed, or only at full lock.
if: If a steering warning light comes on or the steering gradually gets heavier, get it checked within a few days.
If the battery light comes on or the car has been slow to start, have the battery and charging system tested. Low voltage can affect electric steering.
If the steering suddenly becomes very hard to turn, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
result.why: Electric power steering uses a motor instead of a fluid pump. A light whir when turning slowly or while parked can be normal. A whine that's loud or getting louder can mean a worn motor, gear or a nearby part like the alternator.

causes.name: Normal electric steering motor sound
causes.clues: A faint whir only when turning while stopped or at walking speed.

causes.name: Worn steering motor or gear
causes.clues: The noise is getting louder over time, or the steering feels notchy.

causes.name: Whining alternator or other belt-driven part
causes.clues: The whine rises with engine speed even when you're not turning.

you: With the car parked, turn the wheel slowly and listen for where the sound comes from.
Rev the engine gently in Park without turning, and note whether the whine still happens.
shop: Code scan for the steering system

result.title: A brief whine at full lock is often normal pressure relief
result.now: Avoid holding the wheel turned all the way to one side for more than a few seconds. Back it off slightly once you reach the stop.
if: If the whine is loud even when you're not at full lock, or the steering gets heavier, check the fluid level and book a check.
If your car has a reservoir, make sure the fluid is at the right level, because low fluid makes this whine louder.
If the steering feels heavy or jerky, or you smell burning fluid, have it checked before driving further.
result.why: When the wheel is turned all the way, a hydraulic system hits its maximum pressure and a relief valve opens, which makes a whine. That's normal for a moment, but holding it there heats the fluid and wears the pump.

causes.name: Normal relief valve noise
causes.clues: The whine happens only at the very end of the wheel's travel.

causes.name: Slightly low fluid
causes.clues: The whine has become louder than it used to be.

causes.name: Early pump wear
causes.clues: The whine is starting to appear in normal turns too.

you: Check the power steering fluid level, if your car has a reservoir.
Notice whether the whine stops as soon as you ease off full lock.

result.title: Thick cold fluid or an aging pump are common causes
result.now: Let the engine idle for a minute on cold mornings before turning the wheel hard, and book a check when convenient.
if: If the whine starts lasting after the car is warm, get it checked within a few days.
If the steering is heavy when cold, check the fluid level and type.
If the steering suddenly becomes very hard to turn, pull over when it's safe and have it towed.
result.why: Power steering fluid gets thicker in the cold, so the pump works harder until it warms up. Old fluid or a pump that's starting to wear makes this worse, and the whine is often an early sign.

causes.name: Old or thickened fluid
causes.clues: The fluid is dark or hasn't been changed in years.

causes.name: Early pump wear
causes.clues: The cold whine is getting louder or lasting longer each winter.

causes.name: Slightly low fluid level
causes.clues: The level sits just below the COLD mark.

you: Check the fluid level with the engine cold.
Note the outside temperature and how long the whine lasts.

result.title: The power steering pump may be wearing out
result.now: Check the fluid level if your car has a reservoir, then get the steering checked within the next few days.
if: If the steering becomes heavy or jerky, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If the fluid is low, top it up and look for a leak. The pump may be fine and simply running short of fluid.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke from the engine bay, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: A whine that gets louder month by month often means the pump's internal parts or bearing are wearing. Pumps often give plenty of warning, but when they fail the steering suddenly gets heavy. A shop will usually check the fluid and pressure-test the pump before replacing it.

causes.name: Worn power steering pump
causes.clues: A steady whine that rises with engine speed and gets louder when you turn.

causes.name: Low fluid from a slow leak
causes.clues: The level drops over time.
causes.against: If the level hasn't changed, a leak is less likely.

causes.name: Worn steering rack
causes.clues: The steering feels uneven, heavier in one direction, or has a slight knock.

you: Check the fluid level and condition.
Record a short video with sound while turning the wheel in a parking lot.
shop: Power steering pump pressure and flow test

result.title: The engine drive belt may be slipping
result.now: Book a belt check when convenient. With the engine off, you can look at the belt for cracks, glazing or fraying.
if: If the battery or temperature light comes on, or the squeal suddenly stops along with heavy steering, pull over and turn the engine off. The belt may have broken.
If the belt looks badly cracked or frayed, have it checked within a few days.
result.why: Turning the wheel puts extra load on the power steering pump, and a worn or loose belt can slip and squeal under that load. The same belt often runs the alternator and water pump, so it's worth having the belt and tensioner checked before it breaks.

causes.name: Worn or glazed drive belt
causes.clues: A shiny or cracked belt, and a squeal that's worse in damp weather.

causes.name: Weak belt tensioner
causes.clues: The tensioner arm bounces or the belt flutters with the engine running.

causes.name: Fluid on the belt
causes.clues: An oily or wet belt from a nearby leak.

you: With the engine off, look at the belt for cracks, shine or fraying.

result.title: The power steering system needs a quick check
result.now: Book a check when convenient. If your car has a power steering reservoir, check the fluid level in the meantime.
if: If the steering gets heavier or a steering warning light comes on, get it checked within a few days.
If the steering suddenly becomes very hard to turn, pull over and have it towed.
result.why: A whine when steering usually comes from the power steering system or the belt that drives it. A technician can check the fluid, pump and belt quickly.

causes.name: Low power steering fluid
causes.clues: The reservoir is below the mark.

causes.name: Worn power steering pump
causes.clues: The whine is getting louder over time.

causes.name: Slipping drive belt
causes.clues: More of a squeal, especially at startup.

you: Check the power steering fluid level, if your car has a reservoir.
Record a short video with sound of the whine.
shop: Power steering fluid and leak inspection

q_smoke.q: Which best describes the white smoke?
q_smoke.help: Water vapor is thin and wispy and disappears within a foot or two of the tailpipe. Smoke from burning coolant is thicker, hangs in the air, and often smells sweet.

opts.a: Thick white smoke, and the temperature gauge is high or a warning light is on
Thin, wispy vapor on a cold start that's gone once the engine warms up
Thick white smoke that keeps going even after the engine is warm
Whitish-gray smoke with a burnt oil smell
It's a diesel, and the smoke is heavy on cold starts
I'm not sure

q_coolant.q: With the engine cold, check the coolant reservoir. Is the coolant level dropping, or does the smoke smell sweet?
q_coolant.help: The coolant reservoir is the see-through plastic tank under the hood with MIN and MAX marks. Only check it when the engine has been off for a few hours.

opts.a: Yes, I keep having to add coolant, or the smoke smells sweet
No, the coolant level stays where it should and there's no sweet smell
I haven't checked yet / I'm not sure

result.title: This sounds like normal water vapor
result.now: Watch the exhaust after the engine has fully warmed up. If the vapor is gone by then, it's usually just condensation. Keep an eye on the coolant level for the next few weeks to be sure.
if: If the white smoke is still there after a 15–20 minute drive, or gets thicker, check the coolant level when the engine is cold.
If you're adding coolant regularly, have the cooling system checked soon even if the smoke looks light.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal or a temperature warning comes on, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the smoke smells sweet, have it checked before driving further. If the check engine light is flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: Burning fuel makes water. On cold or damp days, that water condenses in a cold exhaust and comes out as white vapor until the system heats up. It's most noticeable on short trips and in winter.

causes.name: Normal condensation in the exhaust
causes.clues: Cold or humid weather, thin vapor that fades within a few minutes, and sometimes a few drops of water from the tailpipe.
causes.against: If it stays thick after the engine is warm, condensation is less likely.

causes.name: Small coolant leak into the engine (early stage)
causes.clues: The coolant level is slowly dropping with no visible leak.
causes.against: Less likely if the coolant level stays steady for weeks.

you: Look at the exhaust after a longer drive, once fully warm.
Check the coolant reservoir level with the engine cold, and note it so you can compare in a week.
shop: Cooling system pressure test if coolant is dropping

result.title: The engine may be overheating and burning coolant
result.now: Pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine. Don't drive it any further. Have it towed to a shop.
if: If you see steam or smoke from under the hood, step away from the car and don't open the hood until it has cooled.
If the engine cools down and the gauge looks normal, it still needs to be checked before you drive it. Restarting can make the damage worse.
result.why: Thick white smoke together with a high temperature reading often means coolant is leaking into the engine and the engine is losing its ability to cool itself. Driving an overheating engine can warp or crack major parts very quickly. A shop will usually pressure-test the cooling system and test for combustion gases before deciding on a repair.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: Sweet-smelling smoke, coolant that keeps disappearing, bubbles in the coolant tank.

causes.name: Cracked cylinder head or engine block
causes.clues: Overheating happened before, or the problem came on suddenly after overheating.
causes.against: Less common than a head gasket.

causes.name: Coolant leak causing the overheat
causes.clues: Coolant on the ground or steam from under the hood.

shop: Combustion gas (block) test on the coolant

result.title: Coolant may be leaking into the engine and being burned
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed to a shop and ask for a cooling system pressure test and a combustion gas test.
if: If you're stranded somewhere unsafe, call roadside assistance rather than driving on it.
If the oil on the dipstick looks milky or like chocolate milk, coolant may be mixing with the oil. Don't start the engine again.
If the temperature gauge rose while you were driving, tell the shop. They may want to check for overheating damage.
result.why: Steady white smoke with a sweet smell and a dropping coolant level often means coolant is getting into the cylinders. Each drive loses more coolant, which can lead to overheating, and coolant in the oil can quickly ruin the engine's bearings.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: Sweet smell, coolant loss, bubbles in the coolant tank, or rough running on startup.

causes.name: Cracked cylinder head
causes.clues: The engine has overheated in the past.

causes.name: Leaking intake manifold gasket or EGR cooler
causes.clues: Common on certain engines, and more likely on diesels for the EGR cooler.

you: With the engine off and cold, pull the oil dipstick and check for a milky, light-brown color.
Note how much coolant you've had to add and how often.

result.title: Could be heavy condensation, but worth a check if it continues
result.now: Keep an eye on the coolant level each week and book a check if the smoke doesn't clear up after longer drives.
if: If the coolant level starts dropping or the smoke starts smelling sweet, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the check engine light flashes or the engine runs rough, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: With no coolant loss and no sweet smell, a serious coolant leak is less likely. Lots of short trips in cold or humid weather can keep the exhaust from ever fully drying out, so vapor lasts longer than you'd expect.

causes.name: Heavy condensation from short trips
causes.clues: Mostly short drives, cold or humid weather, water dripping from the tailpipe.

causes.name: Small oil burning (whitish-gray smoke)
causes.clues: A burnt oil smell, or the oil level dropping between changes.

causes.name: Very slow internal coolant leak
causes.clues: The level drops a little over several weeks.
causes.against: Less likely if the level is truly steady.

you: Mark the coolant level and check it weekly with the engine cold.
Check the oil dipstick for a low level or milky color.
shop: Exhaust smoke check on a warm engine

result.title: Check the coolant and oil before driving it again
result.now: Avoid driving it until you've checked. Once the engine is completely cool, check the coolant reservoir and the oil dipstick. If the coolant is low, the oil looks milky, or you can't check, have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to look at it.
if: If the coolant is low or the oil looks milky, don't start it again. Have it towed.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal at any point, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the coolant is full and steady, the oil looks normal and there's no sweet smell, it may be heavy condensation. Still book a check within a few days and watch the temperature gauge.
result.why: Thick white smoke after warm-up is often coolant being burned, and the coolant level is the quickest clue. Until you know, it's safest not to drive it, so a coolant leak doesn't turn into an overheated engine.

causes.name: Coolant leaking into the engine
causes.clues: A sweet smell, dropping coolant, or a temperature gauge that creeps up.

causes.name: Heavy condensation
causes.clues: Cold weather and short trips, with smoke that thins out on longer drives.

causes.name: Oil burning
causes.clues: Grayish smoke with a burnt oil smell.

you: Check the coolant reservoir level with the engine cold.
Check the oil dipstick for a milky color.
Watch the temperature gauge on your next drive.

result.title: Grayish smoke with a burnt oil smell often means oil is being burned
result.now: Check the oil level on the dipstick and top it up if it's low. Have the engine checked within a few days.
if: If the oil warning light comes on or the engine starts knocking, pull over and turn off the engine. Don't restart it.
If the smoke is coming from under the hood rather than the tailpipe, pull over, turn the engine off and step away. Oil on the hot exhaust can catch fire. Have it inspected before driving again.
If the oil level was very low, have it checked before driving further. If the check engine light is flashing, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: Burning oil often looks blue-gray, but in some light it looks whitish. The burnt oil smell is a strong clue. Oil can get into the cylinders past worn seals or rings, or through a turbocharger or a faulty PCV valve.

causes.name: Worn valve stem seals or piston rings
causes.clues: You add oil between changes, and there's a puff of smoke on startup or when accelerating.

causes.name: Faulty PCV valve
causes.clues: Oil in the air intake, or a whistling or rough idle.

causes.name: Leaking turbocharger seals (turbo engines)
causes.clues: Smoke when accelerating hard, and oil in the intake pipes.

you: Check the oil level with the engine off on level ground.
Note whether the smoke shows up on startup, when accelerating, or all the time.

result.title: On a diesel, cold-start white smoke is often unburned fuel
result.now: Wait for the glow plug light to go out before starting, and book a check if the smoke is heavy or lasts more than a few minutes.
if: If the smoke continues once fully warm, or the coolant level drops, have it checked within a few days.
If the engine is hard to start, runs rough, or the check engine light is on, get it checked soon.
If the smoke smells sweet or the temperature gauge rises, pull over and turn off the engine.
result.why: A diesel relies on heat from compression to ignite its fuel. When the engine is cold, some fuel may not burn fully and comes out as white smoke. Weak glow plugs or worn injectors make this worse.

causes.name: Weak or failed glow plugs
causes.clues: Hard starts in cold weather, rough running for the first minute, and smoke that clears as it warms.

causes.name: Worn or leaking fuel injectors
causes.clues: Rough idle, a raw diesel smell, or poor fuel economy.

causes.name: Coolant leaking into the cylinders
causes.clues: Sweet smell, coolant loss, and smoke that continues when warm.
causes.against: Less likely if the coolant level is steady.

you: Note whether the glow plug light stays on longer than usual or flashes.
Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
shop: Glow plug and glow plug relay test
Cooling system pressure test if coolant is dropping

windows-fogging-up.title: Windows fog up and won't clear

q_fog_type.help: Fog on the inside clears when you wipe the inside of the glass. Fog on the outside clears with the wipers.

opts.a: A greasy film on the inside that smears when wiped, often with a sweet, syrup-like smell
Normal fog on the inside that comes back quickly or takes ages to clear
Fog on the inside that won't clear at all, even with the defroster on
Fog on the outside of the glass, usually in hot, humid weather
I'm not sure

q_wipe.q: Wipe a small patch on the inside of the windshield with a clean, dry cloth. What happens?

opts.a: It clears, but fogs up again within a few minutes
It smears and leaves an oily or greasy film
Nothing changes, because the fog is on the outside
I'm not sure

q_coolant.q: Look at the temperature gauge and the coolant reservoir under the hood. Which fits?
q_coolant.help: The coolant reservoir is a see-through plastic tank with MIN and MAX marks. Only check it with the engine cold, and never open a hot radiator cap.

opts.a: The temperature gauge is high or in the red, or a temperature warning is on
The gauge is normal, but the coolant is low or keeps dropping
The gauge is normal and the coolant looks full
I'm not sure

q_ac.q: When you turn on the A/C, does it blow cold air?
q_ac.help: The A/C dries the air as well as cooling it, which is why most cars turn it on automatically in defrost mode.

opts.a: Yes, the A/C works
No, the A/C blows warm or doesn't seem to work
I'm not sure

q_wet.q: Is there any dampness inside the car?

opts.a: Yes: wet carpet, water on the floor, or a damp, musty smell
No, it seems dry inside
I'm not sure

q_airflow.q: With the defroster on and the fan on high, what comes out of the vents at the base of the windshield?

opts.a: No air, or only a weak trickle
Air comes out of the floor or dash vents instead, even on defrost
Plenty of air, but it stays cold even after the engine warms up
Plenty of warm air, but the fog still won't clear
I'm not sure

result.title: Coolant may be leaking into the cabin, and the engine may be overheating
result.now: Pull over, shut the engine off and let it cool. Don't drive it any further. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see steam or smell strong coolant inside the car, get out and open the doors to air it out.
If the floor on the passenger side is wet and sticky, that's a strong sign coolant is getting inside. Tell the shop.
result.why: A greasy film with a sweet smell often means hot coolant is escaping from the heater core behind the dashboard and condensing on the glass. With the temperature gauge high, the engine may have lost enough coolant to overheat, and driving on can cause serious engine damage.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: A sweet smell inside, greasy fog, and a damp passenger-side floor.
causes.against: If the cabin smells normal and the floor is dry, a heater core leak is less likely.

causes.name: Leaking heater hose or hose connection
causes.clues: A sweet smell under the hood as well as inside, or drips near the firewall.

causes.name: Wider cooling system failure
causes.clues: Coolant puddles under the car, or the gauge climbs even with the heater off.

you: Once the engine is fully cold, look at the coolant reservoir level.
Feel the passenger-side carpet for dampness.
shop: Check for overheating damage, such as a head gasket leak

result.title: The heater core may be leaking coolant into the cabin
result.now: Have the cooling system checked within the next few days. Until then, watch the temperature gauge closely, keep trips short, and only drive when you can see clearly.
if: If the temperature gauge rises or a temperature warning comes on, pull over and shut the engine off. Don't keep driving.
If the greasy film keeps building up, clean the glass with a glass cleaner. Wiping alone just smears it.
If steam or hot liquid comes from the vents, pull over, turn the engine off and get out.
If the fumes make your eyes sting or give you a headache, open the windows and stop driving.
If the coolant level is low or dropping fast, don't drive it. Have it towed.
result.why: Fog that leaves a greasy film is often a fine mist of coolant, not plain water. That most often comes from a leaking heater core, which sits behind the dashboard. Breathing coolant fumes isn't healthy, and losing coolant can lead to overheating.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: A sweet smell inside, a damp or sticky passenger-side floor, and coolant that slowly drops.
causes.against: If the coolant level never changes and there's no smell, it's less likely.

causes.name: Leaking heater hose or connection
causes.clues: A sweet smell near the firewall under the hood.

causes.name: Residue from interior cleaners or vinyl off-gassing
causes.clues: A hazy film that builds up slowly with no smell and no coolant loss.
causes.against: This usually doesn't come with a sweet smell or fog that appears when the heater runs.

you: Check the coolant reservoir level with the engine cold, and recheck it after a few days.
Feel the passenger-side carpet for dampness.
Notice whether the smell and fog get worse when the heater is on.
shop: Check the coolant for signs of a head gasket leak

result.title: The A/C may not be drying the air, so the fog can't clear
result.now: Use the defroster on hot with the fan on high and fresh air (recirculation off), and crack a window. Book an A/C check when convenient.
if: If the fog is bad enough that you can't see, wait for the glass to clear before driving.
If it's below freezing, many A/C systems won't run at all. That's normal, and heat plus fresh air is the main way to clear the glass.
result.why: The A/C pulls moisture out of the air before it reaches the glass. Without it, the defroster blows warm but damp air, so fog clears slowly and comes back, especially in rain or with several people in the car.

causes.name: Low refrigerant from a slow leak
causes.clues: The A/C has been getting weaker over time.

causes.name: A/C compressor not turning on
causes.clues: No click from under the hood when you press the A/C button, and no change in engine sound.

causes.name: Blown fuse or relay for the A/C
causes.clues: The A/C stopped working suddenly.

you: Press the A/C button and listen for a click from under the hood.
Check the A/C fuse in the fuse box using the owner's manual diagram.

result.title: Humid air and the climate settings are the usual cause
result.now: Turn on the defroster with the A/C on, set the heat high, switch recirculation off so fresh air comes in, and crack a window for a minute.
if: If it still fogs up quickly with those settings, replace the cabin air filter and look for hidden dampness inside.
If the glass also has a greasy film or the cabin smells sweet, have the cooling system checked.
If you can't see clearly through the windshield, don't drive until it clears.
result.why: Recirculating air keeps the moisture from your breath and wet clothes trapped inside. Fresh air plus the A/C swaps in drier air, and heat helps the glass hold less condensation. A dirty windshield gives fog more to cling to.

causes.name: Recirculation left on
causes.clues: The recirculation light (a car with a curved arrow) is on.

causes.name: Clogged cabin air filter
causes.clues: Weak airflow even on high, or a musty smell.

causes.name: Moisture brought into the car
causes.clues: Wet umbrellas, coats, snowy boots or floor mats.

causes.name: Dirty inside of the windshield
causes.clues: A haze you can see when the sun hits the glass.

you: Make sure recirculation is off in defrost mode.
Replace or inspect the cabin air filter (often behind the glove box).
Clean the inside of the glass with a glass cleaner.
Remove wet items and dry out wet floor mats.

result.title: Water is getting inside the car and keeping the air damp
result.now: Find and dry the wet area, then book a check for the leak when convenient. Use the defroster with the A/C and fresh air in the meantime.
if: If the water feels slick or smells sweet, it may be coolant from the heater core. Have it checked within a few days.
If the carpet stays wet, mold can grow and electrical parts under the carpet can be damaged. Get it fixed sooner.
If you smell burning, or the airbag or other warning lights come on, have it checked before relying on the car.
result.why: A wet carpet keeps adding moisture to the cabin air, so the glass fogs no matter what the settings are. The water usually comes from a blocked drain or a worn seal, not from the climate system itself.

causes.name: Blocked A/C drain
causes.clues: Water on the passenger-side floor, especially after using the A/C.

causes.name: Clogged sunroof or cowl drains
causes.clues: Water appears after rain or a car wash, sometimes dripping near the pillars.

causes.name: Worn door or windshield seal
causes.clues: Wet spots near one door or under the windshield after rain.

you: Press on the carpet in each footwell to find the wet area.
Check that leaves aren't blocking the area at the base of the windshield.
After using the A/C on a warm day, look for a drip under the car near the firewall. That drip is normal; no drip may mean a blocked drain.
shop: A/C drain and sunroof drain clearing

result.title: The fan isn't pushing enough air to the windshield
result.now: Check the blower fuse, and get the fan fixed within the next few days. Only drive when the glass is fully clear.
if: If the fan works only on the highest setting, a failed blower resistor or speed control is a common cause.
If it's cold, rainy or snowy, don't drive until it's fixed. Without airflow the windshield can fog or ice over quickly.
If you smell burning or see smoke from the vents, turn the fan off, pull over and turn the car off.
result.why: The defroster depends on the blower fan to push dry, warm air across the glass. With little or no airflow, there's nothing to clear the fog, which makes this a visibility problem.

causes.name: Failed blower resistor or speed control
causes.clues: The fan works on high but not on lower speeds.

causes.name: Failed blower motor
causes.clues: No fan on any speed, or the fan squeals, rattles or works only after a tap on the dash.

causes.name: Blown fuse or relay
causes.clues: The fan stopped suddenly on all speeds.

causes.name: Badly clogged cabin air filter
causes.clues: You hear the fan running, but very little air comes out.

you: Try every fan speed and note which ones work.
Check the blower fuse using the owner's manual diagram.
Inspect the cabin air filter.
shop: Blower motor power and ground test
Blower resistor or control module test

result.title: A door inside the dash isn't sending air to the windshield
result.now: Have the climate controls checked within the next few days. Only drive when you can see clearly.
if: If you hear clicking or tapping behind the dashboard when you change settings, a mode door motor is a common cause.
If the weather is cold or wet, don't drive until it's fixed, because the windshield may not stay clear.
result.why: Small flaps inside the dashboard direct air to the floor, the dash vents or the windshield. If the flap that controls defrost is stuck, the air goes elsewhere and the glass never gets the airflow it needs.

causes.name: Failed mode door motor (actuator)
causes.clues: Clicking or tapping behind the dash, or settings that don't change where the air comes out.

causes.name: Climate control panel fault
causes.clues: Buttons or knobs that don't respond, or lights on the panel that don't come on.

causes.name: Broken door or linkage
causes.clues: A snapping sound when you change settings, then air stuck in one place.

you: Cycle through each vent setting and note where the air comes out.
Listen for clicking behind the dash when you change settings.

result.title: The heater isn't warming the air, so the glass stays fogged
result.now: Check the coolant level with the engine cold, and have the heating checked within the next few days. Use the A/C with fresh air to help in the meantime.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and shut the engine off. Low coolant can cause overheating.
If the temperature gauge stays low after a long drive, a thermostat stuck open is a common cause.
If you see steam or smell something sweet, pull over, turn the engine off and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Warm air holds more moisture and warms the glass, which is what lets the defroster clear fog. If the air stays cold, the engine may be low on coolant, the thermostat may not be letting it warm up, or the heater's controls may not be working.

causes.name: Low coolant
causes.clues: The reservoir is below MIN, or there's a sweet smell or puddles.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck open
causes.clues: The temperature gauge takes a long time to rise, or stays below normal.

causes.name: Blend door or heater control fault
causes.clues: Clicking behind the dash, or heat on one side only.

you: Check the coolant reservoir level with the engine cold.
Watch where the temperature gauge settles after a 15-minute drive.
shop: Blend door and heater control test

result.title: The glass is colder than the humid air outside
result.now: Use the wipers, and turn the temperature up a little or point less cold air at the windshield.
if: If fog forms on the outside in cold weather, use the defroster on hot to warm the glass.
If your wipers smear instead of clearing, replace the wiper blades.
If you can't see clearly through the windshield, don't drive until it clears.
result.why: On hot, humid days, cold A/C air chills the windshield so much that moisture outside condenses on it. This is common, and a slightly warmer setting on the glass usually stops it.

causes.name: Cold A/C air hitting the windshield
causes.clues: Happens on humid days with the A/C set very cold or aimed at the glass.

causes.name: Worn wiper blades
causes.clues: Streaks or smears left behind after wiping.

you: Raise the temperature slightly and see if the outside fog stops.
Check the wiper blades for cracks or stiff rubber.

result.title: Start with the settings that clear fog fastest
result.now: Turn on the defroster with the heat high, the fan high, the A/C on and recirculation off. Crack a window for a minute and wait until the glass is clear before driving.
if: If it doesn't clear within a few minutes, note whether air is coming out of the windshield vents and whether it's warm. That tells a shop where to look.
If the glass gets a greasy film or the cabin smells sweet, have the cooling system checked soon.
result.why: Most fogging is caused by damp air and settings that recirculate it. These settings bring in drier air, warm the glass and dry the air with the A/C. If they don't work, the problem is usually the A/C, the fan, or water getting inside.

causes.name: Humid air and climate settings
causes.clues: The most common cause, especially in rain or with passengers.

causes.name: A/C not working
causes.clues: The air never feels cold or dry.

causes.name: Fan or vent problem
causes.clues: Little or no air comes out of the windshield vents.

you: Try the settings above and time how long the glass takes to clear.
Check for wet carpets or a musty smell.
